units.title: Frequency Tables for Raw Data
units.summary: What raw data are, how to use tally marks, how to build a frequency table, and how to find the mode and range.

sections.h: From raw data to a table
p: Raw data are data that have just been collected and are in no particular order. They are messy and hard to read. Tabulation means organising them into a frequency distribution table. Tally marks help to count: one stroke for each item, with the fifth stroke crossing the four before it, so groups of five are easy to count. The frequency f is the total count for each value, and Σf (the sum of the frequencies) is the total number of items.

Here are the shoe sizes of 20 students: 7, 8, 9, 7, 8, 10, 6, 8, 9, 7, 8, 8, 7, 6, 8, 9, 7, 8, 10, 8. The smallest size is 6 and the largest is 10. Go through the list and make a tally mark for each value, then count the tallies.

img.alt: A bar chart of shoe sizes 6 to 10 with frequencies 2, 5, 8, 3 and 2, with gaps between the bars
img.cap: Bar chart of the shoe-size data: note the gaps between the bars.

p: The table is much clearer than the raw list. We can see that size 8 is the most common (8 students). This most frequent value is called the mode. Sizes 6 and 10 are the least common (2 students each). The total is 20. The range is the largest value minus the smallest: 10 − 6 = 4.

Frequency table: mark 4 has f = 2; mark 5 has f = 4; mark 6 has f = 5; mark 7 has f = 9; mark 8 has f = 5; mark 9 has f = 4; mark 10 has f = 1. The total is 2 + 4 + 5 + 9 + 5 + 4 + 1 = 30. The modal score is 7, because it has the highest frequency (9).
They are easy to read, show patterns clearly, show the most and least common values, take little space, are ready for graphs and are easy to use to calculate statistics.

units.title: Grouped Data: Class Intervals, Boundaries and Midpoints
units.summary: Why we group data, the class interval, class boundaries, class width and class midpoint, and how to build a grouped frequency table.

p: If we have 100 different heights, a list of every value is too long and hides the pattern. If we group them into ranges, the pattern is clear: for example 150–154 cm: 15 people; 155–159 cm: 25 people; 160–164 cm: 35 people; 165–169: 20 people; 170–174: 5 people.

A class interval is a range of values, such as 10–19, 20–29, 30–39. The class boundaries remove the gaps between classes: subtract 0.5 from the lower limit and add 0.5 to the upper limit. So 10–19 has boundaries 9.5–19.5, 20–29 has 19.5–29.5, and 30–39 has 29.5–39.5. A value such as 19.5 now has a place.

The class width (class size) = upper boundary − lower boundary. For 10–19, the width is 19.5 − 9.5 = 10. The class midpoint (or class mark) = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2. For 10–19 the midpoint is (10 + 19)/2 = 14.5. For 20–29 it is 24.5. For 30–39 it is 34.5.

Group the 30 quiz marks from the last unit into classes 4–5, 6–7, 8–9 and 10–11. Count how many marks fall in each class: 4–5: 2 + 4 = 6; 6–7: 5 + 9 = 14; 8–9: 5 + 4 = 9; 10–11: 1. The total is 6 + 14 + 9 + 1 = 30.

Ages of 30 people at a party, grouped with classes 15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35–39, 40–44 and 45–49: 3, 4, 8, 6, 4, 4 and 1. The total is 30. The modal class is 25–29, because it has the highest frequency (8).
Use classes of equal width. Choose between about 5 and 10 classes. Make sure every value belongs to exactly one class and that the classes cover the smallest and largest values.

units.title: Bar Charts, Line Graphs and Histograms
units.summary: When to use a linear graph, a bar chart and a histogram, and how to draw a histogram with class boundaries.

p: A linear (line) graph joins plotted points by lines. It is used to show trends over time: the temperature during a day, a company's profit over five years, the number of students in each year, or the price of a share.

A bar chart is used for qualitative or discrete data. The bars have gaps between them, they all have the same width, the x-axis lists the categories or values, and the y-axis shows frequency. The bars can be vertical or horizontal. The gaps show that the categories are separate. The bar chart in the previous unit shows the shoe-size data.

A histogram is used for continuous grouped data. The bars touch (there are no gaps) because the data are continuous. The x-axis shows the class boundaries, and the y-axis shows frequency (when the classes have equal widths). The tallest bar shows the modal class.
Bar chart: discrete or qualitative data; gaps; categories or values on the x-axis. Histogram: continuous grouped data; no gaps; class boundaries on the x-axis.

Step 2: set up the axes: the y-axis is frequency from 0 to 20, and the x-axis is height in cm marked with the boundaries. Step 3: draw each bar from the lower boundary to the upper boundary, with a height equal to the frequency. Step 4: label the axes and give the graph a title.

units.title: Pie Charts
units.summary: What a pie chart shows, the formula angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°, and how to draw one, with worked examples.

p: A pie chart is a circle divided into sectors. Each sector shows the share of the whole that belongs to one item. The whole circle (360°) stands for the total frequency (or 100%). It is best for showing market share, percentages, budgets and survey results: parts of a whole.
Angle of a sector = (frequency of the item ÷ total frequency) × 360°. After you work out all the angles, check that they add up to 360°.

In an SS1 class of 80 students, 30 are in Arts, 40 are in Science and 10 are in Commercial. Total = 80. Arts: 30/80 × 360° = 135°. Science: 40/80 × 360° = 180°. Commercial: 10/80 × 360° = 45°. Check: 135 + 180 + 45 = 360°.

img.alt: A pie chart with sectors for Arts (135 degrees), Science (180 degrees) and Commercial (45 degrees)
img.cap: Pie chart of the streams in an SS1 class of 80.

sections.h: How to draw a pie chart
p: Draw a circle with compasses and draw one radius. Use a protractor to measure the first angle from the radius and draw the next radius. Continue with each angle, and the last sector should close the circle. Label each sector with its name (and angle or percentage), colour the sectors differently, and give the chart a title.
If a sector shows 20 people out of 80, its angle is 20/80 × 360° = 90°. If 'Food' takes up 120° of a budget, it is 120/360 = 1/3, or about 33.3% of the budget.

A family spends its monthly income as follows: food ₦30,000, rent ₦20,000, school fees ₦15,000, transport ₦10,000, savings ₦15,000. The total is ₦90,000. The angles are: food 30/90 × 360° = 120°; rent 20/90 × 360° = 80°; school fees 15/90 × 360° = 60°; transport 10/90 × 360° = 40°; savings 15/90 × 360° = 60°. The sum is 120 + 80 + 60 + 40 + 60 = 360°.

units.title: Frequency Polygons
units.summary: What a frequency polygon is, how to find class midpoints, how to ground the polygon, and how to draw one from a table or a histogram.

p: A frequency polygon is a line graph made by joining the midpoints of the tops of the bars of a histogram. It shows the shape of the distribution more clearly and is good for comparing two sets of data on the same graph. On the x-axis we put the class midpoints (marks) and on the y-axis the frequency.
To close the shape into a polygon, add an imaginary class with zero frequency before the first class and after the last class. Join the first and last points to the x-axis. This is called grounding.

Use the heights of 50 students. Class midpoints: 150–154 gives (150 + 154)/2 = 152; 155–159 gives 157; 160–164 gives 162; 165–169 gives 167; 170–174 gives 172. Add grounding points: before the first class, 145–149 with midpoint 147 and f = 0; after the last class, 175–179 with midpoint 177 and f = 0.

img.alt: A frequency polygon joining the points (147, 0), (152, 6), (157, 12), (162, 18), (167, 10), (172, 4) and (177, 0) over a histogram
img.cap: A frequency polygon drawn over the histogram of heights.

p: The polygon starts and ends at the ground (zero). It peaks at 162 cm, which is the midpoint of the modal class 160–164. It shows that most heights are close to the middle and that fewer students are very short or very tall.

Both are made from the same data. The histogram shows amounts with bars (using class boundaries on the x-axis). The polygon shows the trend or shape with a line (using class midpoints on the x-axis). When comparing two data sets, two polygons can be drawn on the same axes, which is hard to do with two histograms.

units.summary: A formula sheet for mensuration, a process sheet for statistics, worked revision questions and examination tips.

p: Circle: circumference 2πr; area πr²; arc (θ/360) × 2πr; sector area (θ/360) × πr²; perimeter of sector = arc + 2r; segment = sector − ½r² sin θ. Sector to cone: radius of sector = slant height l; arc = 2πR; sector area = CSA = πRl; (θ/360) × 2πl = 2πR.

Surface area: cube 6l²; cuboid 2(lw + lh + wh); cylinder CSA 2πrh and TSA 2πr(r + h); cone CSA πRl and TSA πR(R + l) with l² = h² + R²; prism 2 × base + perimeter × length; pyramid base + triangular faces.
Volume: cube l³; cuboid lwh; cylinder πr²h; prism base area × h; pyramid ⅓ × base × h; cone ⅓πr²h; sphere (4/3)πr³; hemisphere (2/3)πr³; frustum = large cone − small cone (use r/R = h_s/H).

Data types: qualitative (categories); quantitative: discrete (counted) and continuous (measured). Sources: primary (you collect) and secondary (collected by others). Graphs: bar chart (discrete or qualitative, gaps), histogram (continuous grouped, no gaps, class boundaries), pie chart (parts of a whole, angle = frequency/total × 360°), frequency polygon (class midpoints, grounded).
A solid cylinder has height 10 cm and radius 7 cm. TSA = 2πr(r + h) = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × 17 = 748 cm². Volume = πr²h = (22/7) × 49 × 10 = 1540 cm³.

sections.h: Worked question 3: a cone from a sector
p: A cone is made by folding a sector with angle 120° and radius 18 cm. (a) Base radius: (120/360) × 2π × 18 = 2πR, so R = (1/3) × 18 = 6 cm. (b) Height: l² = h² + R², so 18² = h² + 6², h² = 324 − 36 = 288 and h = 12√2 ≈ 16.97 cm. (c) Volume = ⅓πR²h = ⅓ × (22/7) × 36 × 16.97 ≈ 640 cm³.

Mensuration: write what is given and what is needed, draw clear diagrams, check whether you need the slant or vertical height, use Pythagoras for heights, remember that a cone is one third of a cylinder with the same base and height, and show all working.

Statistics: decide the data type first, choose the right graph, use boundaries for histograms and midpoints for polygons, check that pie angles add to 360°, label the axes, give titles, and show calculations.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 Christian Religious Studies First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Christian Religious Studies (CRS) helps you to understand the Bible, the teachings of Jesus Christ and how to live a good life. It also trains you to think clearly, to discuss respectfully and to write well. CRS is an examination subject in WAEC and NECO, and its lessons help in character, leadership and relationships.

In First Term you will study the 'I AM' pictures that Jesus used to describe Himself (the Lamb, the Door, the Good Shepherd, the Light, the True Vine, the Living Bread and the Living Water). Then you will study God's love for people, how Christians must love one another, and how a person is made right with God by faith.

Each unit has the Bible texts to read, simple notes, tables and questions. Open your Bible and read the verses given before you read the notes. At the end of each unit there are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you to check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.
Keep a notebook. Write the main verse of each unit, and write one way you can apply the lesson in your school and home.

units.title: Jesus as the Lamb of God
units.summary: John the Baptist's declaration, the Passover lamb, Isaiah's suffering servant and what the title means for sin and for our lives.

p: Read John 1:29-34 and Isaiah 53:7. John the Baptist saw Jesus coming and said, 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' This was a bold statement. It linked Jesus to centuries of Jewish worship and prophecy.
The Passover lamb: Jews sacrificed a lamb at Passover to remember how God spared the Israelites in Egypt. The blood on the doorposts was the sign of safety. Jesus is the final Passover sacrifice.
The Suffering Servant: Isaiah 53:7 describes the coming Messiah as a lamb led to the slaughter, silent and humble. The Saviour would willingly suffer.
Innocence and purity: a sacrificial lamb had to be 'without blemish'. Jesus is sinless, innocent and pure, so He is the perfect sacrifice.
Taking away sin: Old Testament sacrifices covered sin for a time. Jesus takes sin away for good. He took our place and paid the price: this is called substitutionary atonement.
Sin of the world: John says 'the world', so Jesus' work is for all people, not only the Jews.
A surprise: many Jews expected a conquering military Messiah, but John pointed to a gentle Lamb who would save by sacrifice.
Humility: like a lamb, a Christian lives without pride and submits to God's will. Sacrifice: true love sometimes costs us our comfort for the good of others.

units.title: Jesus as the Door
units.summary: The sheepfold picture, what 'I am the door' means: access, protection and abundant life, and why Jesus is the only way.

p: Read John 10:1-10. In Palestine, a sheepfold was often a stone enclosure with one opening and no gate. At night the shepherd slept across the opening. Nothing could go in or out without passing over him. So when Jesus says 'I am the door', He is the barrier between the sheep (believers) and danger.

Access: 'If anyone enters by me, he will be saved.' There is one specific door to salvation. Protection: the door keeps out thieves (false teachers) and wolves (spiritual danger). Abundant life: the sheep go in and out and find pasture, which means freedom and food for the soul.
The thief comes to steal, kill and destroy. Jesus came 'that they may have life, and have it abundantly'.

Why does Christianity teach that Jesus is the only door? Read John 14:6 with John 10:7. Christians believe that Jesus alone made the sacrifice that opens the way to God. We should explain this humbly and respect people who believe differently.
Ask: is my life protected by the Door, or have I let thieves in (bad friends, lies, cheating)? In school, choose to enter by the 'door' of honesty and hard work.

units.title: Jesus as the Good Shepherd
units.summary: The Good Shepherd compared with the hired hand, His sacrifice, His knowledge of the sheep, His other sheep, and the link with Psalm 23.

p: Read John 10:11-18. The Good Shepherd owns the sheep. He acts from love, lays down His life when danger comes, and knows His sheep by name; they know His voice. The hired hand works for wages. He has no personal stake, so when the wolf comes he runs away.

Sacrificial leadership: 'I lay down my life for the sheep.' This points to His death on the cross. Closeness: 'I know my own and my own know me', like the relationship between the Father and the Son. Wide mission: Jesus speaks of 'other sheep not of this fold', meaning the Gentiles, so that there will be 'one flock, one shepherd'.
The shepherd of John 10 matches Psalm 23: 'He leads me' (guidance), 'I will fear no evil' (protection) and 'He restores my soul' (care).

Compare a shepherd leader with a hired-hand leader. A good class captain, prefect or politician serves others, puts the group first and is honest even when it costs. A hired-hand leader only wants the benefits.

units.title: Jesus the Light of the World
units.summary: The meaning of light and darkness, the Feast of Tabernacles, the three functions of Jesus as light, and how Christians reflect His light.

p: Read John 8:12; John 1:1-9; John 9:1-5; Matthew 5:14-16; Psalm 119:105. Light is a form of energy that lets us see objects, colours and shapes. In the Bible, light stands for truth, purity, knowledge, God's presence, righteousness and salvation. Darkness stands for sin, ignorance, evil and separation from God.

sections.h: The setting: the Feast of Tabernacles
p: Jesus spoke these words in the Temple during the Feast of Tabernacles. Huge golden lamps were lit in the Court of Women to remind Israel of the pillar of fire that guided them in the wilderness. Jesus was saying: 'I am the reality that the pillar of fire pointed to.'

Revelation: He shows the truth about God and about life. Without Him people live in spiritual ignorance. Exposure: light shows hidden dirt, and Jesus' life and teaching show sin and call people to repent. Guidance: like a lamp for the feet (Psalm 119:105), He guides believers away from pitfalls.

Jesus is the sun, the source. Christians are like the moon: we have no light of our own and only reflect His. Jesus said, 'You are the light of the world.' We shine by moral integrity (no lying, stealing or examination malpractice), love for all people, bold and respectful witness, and being peacemakers.
John 1:5: 'The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.' Light is stronger than darkness.

units.title: Jesus as the True Vine
units.summary: The vine, vinedresser and branches, pruning and cutting off, what abiding means, the fruit of a Christian life and the command to love.

p: Read John 15:1-17. In the Old Testament, Israel was called God's vine (Isaiah 5, Psalm 80) but often bore bad fruit. Jesus is the 'true' vine: the faithful Israel who gives real life. The vine (Jesus) is the source of life. The vinedresser (God the Father) tends and manages the plant. The branches (believers) receive life from the vine and bear fruit.

God does two things. He cuts off branches that bear no fruit; they are gathered and burned, which pictures judgment. He prunes branches that bear fruit so that they bear more. Pruning removes shoots that drain energy: for a believer, bad habits, distractions and pride. It can be painful, but it is for growth. Pruning is not punishment.
To abide is to stay connected in constant fellowship. We abide through God's word and obedience, prayer, faith and dependence on the Holy Spirit.
Benefits of abiding: answered prayer (John 15:7), fullness of joy and glory to the Father.

Fruit has three sides: character (the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22-23), good works and winning others to Christ. You cannot abide in the vine and fail to love the other branches. Jesus commands, 'Love one another as I have loved you.'

units.title: Jesus as the Living Bread
units.summary: The crowd who followed Jesus for bread, the 'work of God', and the comparison between manna and the true bread from heaven.

p: Read John 6:25-40. After feeding the five thousand, Jesus crossed the sea and the crowd followed Him. He told them they came not because they saw signs of who He was, but because they had eaten bread and were full. They wanted a political provider, not a spiritual Saviour. He urged them: 'Do not labour for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life.'

The people asked what they must do to do God's works. Jesus said the work of God is one thing: 'Believe in him whom he has sent.' Salvation is received through faith in a person, not earned by a list of tasks.

The crowd asked for a sign like the manna Moses gave in the wilderness. Jesus corrected them: it was not Moses but God the Father who gave the bread, and the 'bread of God' is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. He said, 'I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger.'

Bread is a picture: as the body dies without food, the spirit is dead without Christ. Many people still choose 'manna' (money, things) instead of the true bread. Ask yourself what you are really hungry for.

units.title: Jesus as the Living Water
units.summary: The meeting at Jacob's well, social barriers Jesus broke, well water against living water, and the universal invitation.

p: Read John 4:7-15. Jesus rested at Jacob's well in Samaria while the disciples bought food. A Samaritan woman came to draw water and Jesus asked her for a drink. She was surprised, because Jews and Samaritans did not mix. Jesus crossed barriers of race and gender to reach her.

Jesus said if she knew the gift of God and who was speaking, she would ask Him for living water. She took Him literally: He had no bucket and the well was deep. She asked if He was greater than Jacob.

Jesus explained: 'Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' Living water stands for the Holy Spirit, the word of God and complete satisfaction in God.

Jesus uses the most basic needs, bread and water, to teach about the soul. The offer was made to a Samaritan, which shows that salvation is for all nations. In Jesus' day, 'living water' meant flowing spring or river water, fresh and clean, unlike still water in a well. It pictures the active, moving power of the Spirit.
'Broken cisterns' today: fame, money, social media and addictions promise happiness but leave people thirsty again.

units.title: God's Love for Man
units.summary: The meaning of agape, God's love shown in creation and in redemption, an analysis of John 3:16, and how we should respond.

p: Read John 3:16-18; Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:7-10; Genesis 1:26-28. God's love (agape) is deep, unconditional and sacrificial. Human love is often based on attraction or merit ('I love you because...'), but God loves because He is love (1 John 4:8). It is everlasting, and God took the first step: He loved us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8).

Man is the only creature made in God's image. This gives every person dignity, value and purpose. God also gave humans dominion over other creatures, which shows trust. We are loved designs of a Creator, not accidents.

Sin brought separation and condemnation. In His love God sent His only Son to die and shed His blood. Look at the verse: 'God so loved the world' (the scope is universal); 'He gave His only Son' (the sacrifice is the highest price); 'whoever believes in Him should not perish' (the condition is faith, open to all); 'but have eternal life' (the goal is life). Jesus came not to condemn but to save.

Towards God: worship and praise, faith, and obedience ('If you love me, keep my commandments', John 14:15). Towards others: 'If God so loved us, we also ought to love one another' (1 John 4:11), by kindness to strangers, forgiveness and putting others first.
God's love is unconditional, but salvation is received by faith.

units.title: Love for One Another (Brotherly Love)
units.summary: The new commandment, why love is the mark of a disciple, why it matters, and practical ways to show it.

p: Read John 13:34-35; 1 John 4:7-8, 11-12; 1 John 3:17-18. Christian love is not just a feeling. It is selfless, sacrificial care that is shown in action. It is a command from God, so we must act lovingly even when we do not feel like it.

In the Upper Room Jesus said, 'A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you.' The old standard was 'love your neighbour as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18). The new standard is 'as I have loved you', which means sacrificial love. Love is the badge of a disciple, as a uniform identifies a student.

It proves we know God, who is love. It attracts others to Christ when a community loves across tribe and class. It solves conflict through forgiveness and reconciliation. It fulfils the law (Romans 13:10).

Emotional and spiritual: forgiving, praying for others, and encouraging them with words. Material and physical: sharing money, talents and facilities, and showing compassion. If a classmate loses a textbook, share yours or help them to study.

units.title: Justification by Faith
units.summary: What justification means (the courtroom picture), the part of grace and faith, the fruits of justification (peace, access, joy in suffering) and how it differs from sanctification.

p: Read Romans 3:21-24 and 5:1-11. To justify means to declare someone right or innocent. Picture a courtroom: an accused person stands before the judge, who says 'Not guilty' and sets them free. In the same way God declares a sinner innocent and sets them free through the way He has provided.
Man cannot make himself right with God by keeping the law, because everyone has sinned. God stepped in: He sent His Son to redeem us.

God's part is grace, which means unmerited favour: a gift we do not deserve. The price was the blood of Jesus on the cross. Man's part is faith: believing that Jesus died for our sins, with repentance (turning from sin), confession and accepting Jesus as Lord and Saviour. We are justified by faith, not by works or moral perfection.
If you pay a fine yourself you are free. If the judge pays your fine for you, that is grace.

Peace with God: the war between sinner and holy God is over. We are friends, not enemies. Access to grace: the door to God's presence is open. Joy in suffering: suffering is no longer punishment but a tool; it produces endurance, endurance produces character and character produces hope. Assurance: salvation rests on God's promise; Jesus is enough. Freedom from the burden of the law.
Jesus took our guilt and we receive His righteousness. Justification is a one-time declaration of innocence; sanctification is the daily process of growing in goodness.

units.title: New Life in Christ
units.summary: What new life means, baptism as a picture of burial and resurrection, putting off vices and putting on virtues, steps and challenges, and the work of the Holy Spirit.

p: Read 2 Corinthians 5:17; Colossians 3:1-17; Romans 6:3-4; John 3:1-5. New life in Christ is a spiritual change that happens when someone accepts Jesus as personal Lord and Saviour. Character, values and priorities change. It is a 'dying' to sin and a beginning to live in righteousness by the power of the Holy Spirit. 'If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has passed away; behold, the new has come.'

Paul teaches that baptism is a public sign of union with Christ. When a believer goes under the water by immersion it pictures being buried with Christ, and the old self dies. Coming up from the water pictures rising with Christ to a new life. Baptism is a symbol: a person can be baptised and not have a changed heart, so the ritual must go with a real change of heart.

Paul uses the picture of changing clothes: take off the dirty clothes and put on clean ones. Put off vices: anger, rage, malice, slander, filthy language, lying, sexual immorality and evil desires. Put on virtues: compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, forgiveness and love (which binds everything together in unity). Let the peace of Christ rule in your heart and set your mind on things above.

Steps: hear God's word, confess sin, repent and be baptised, and decide to live like Christ and join the body of believers. The new life cannot be lived by willpower alone. The Holy Spirit empowers us to resist sin, guides us into truth (John 14:26) and produces spiritual fruit.

Expect challenges: temptation from peers and the world, ridicule for being different, and struggles with old habits. The rewards are assurance of salvation, peace with God and people, and God's guidance. We become new at once when we are saved, but our minds are renewed every day.

units.title: Sonship: Children and Heirs of God
units.summary: Creation and adoption, the cry 'Abba, Father', Paul's picture of a child heir, unity in Christ, and the duties of a child of God.

p: Read Romans 8:14-17 and Galatians 3:26-4:7. In one sense all people are God's creatures because He made them. But the Bible speaks of a special status, sonship, which is a relationship. Through Adam's disobedience people lost the closeness of being God's children and became estranged. Jesus came and obeyed perfectly so that people can be brought back into God's family.

Paul uses the legal word adoption. In Roman law an adopted son had exactly the same rights as a natural son. God sends the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, and we cry 'Abba! Father!' Abba is an Aramaic word of closeness, like 'Daddy' or 'Papa'. It shows a relationship of love, not fear. The word 'son' here speaks of legal standing and inheritance and applies to women as well as men.

Paul pictures a child who is heir but, while still a minor, is treated like a slave under guardians. Before Christ, people were under strict rules. 'When the fullness of time had come', God sent His Son to redeem those under the law, so we receive adoption. We are no longer slaves but sons, and if sons, then heirs.

In God's family, earthly differences disappear: 'There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ.' Those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs of the promise.

Led by the Spirit: 'All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.' Obedience: as Jesus obeyed the Father, sons obey and do their duties, civic and spiritual. Disobedience hurts fellowship with the Father. Kingdom work: sons share the Gospel and give their 'quota in cash and kind' to support its spread.
Summary: past, slaves to fear and the law; present, adopted children who cry 'Abba, Father'; future, heirs with Christ.

units.title: Faith and Works
units.summary: What faith and works are, the mirror picture, James' three arguments, how Paul and James agree, and practical religion.

p: Read James 1:22-27 and 2:14-26. Faith means trust: not only agreeing with facts but trusting God and accepting that Jesus died and rose for me. Works are faith shown in practical action. Works are the visible proof of invisible faith, as smoke shows that there is fire.

A person who only hears the word is like a man who looks in a mirror, sees his dirty face, walks away and forgets what he looks like. He deceives himself. The doer looks into the perfect law of liberty and acts on it, and is blessed.

Faith without works is dead. 1. The demons: 'Even the demons believe, and shudder.' They accept that God exists, but they do not submit. Believing God exists is not enough. 2. Abraham: he was shown to be right by his obedience when he offered Isaac. His faith was 'completed' by what he did. 3. The body: 'As the body apart from the spirit is dead, so faith apart from works is dead.'

Paul says we are saved by faith (Ephesians 2:8); James says faith without works is dead. They fight different enemies. Paul fights legalism, the idea that we can earn heaven by good deeds, and stresses the root of salvation: faith. James fights laziness, the idea that we can live in sin and still say we believe, and stresses the fruit of salvation: works. We are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone.
Pure religion (James 1:27): to visit orphans and widows in their trouble, which is care for the vulnerable, and to keep oneself unstained by the world, which is moral purity.

units.title: The Fruit of the Spirit
units.summary: The meaning of fruit, love as the root of the nine attributes, works of the flesh against fruit of the Spirit, and how fruit is produced.

p: Read Galatians 5:19-25. Fruit is the natural produce of a plant. It carries seeds and gives food. The fruit of the Spirit means the lasting qualities of a good Christian, the visible sign that God's light is in a believer. Paul says 'fruit' in the singular, so the nine qualities are one cluster, not nine separate items. It is hard to have patience without love or peace without self-control.

Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Love is the root: joy is love rejoicing, peace is love resting, patience is love enduring, kindness is love serving. A person with no love lacks the whole fruit.

Paul contrasts the fruit with the works of the flesh. The flesh produces 'works', which are effort and struggle; the Spirit produces 'fruit', which is natural growth. The works of the flesh include sexual sins (adultery, fornication, uncleanness), religious sins (idolatry, witchcraft) and social sins (hatred, strife, jealousy, anger, selfish ambition, envy, murder, drunkenness). People who live like this will not inherit the kingdom of God.

Fruit cannot be forced; it must grow. First, salvation: confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised Him (Romans 10:9-10). Second, the Holy Spirit living in you, as at Pentecost when tongues of fire rested on the disciples (Acts 2:3-8). Gifts show God's power; fruit shows God's character. A tree is known by its fruit, and a Christian is known by love, patience and self-control, not by how loudly he prays.

units.title: Spiritual Gifts
units.summary: Gifts compared with talents, the nine gifts in three groups, how they are given, and why: the common good and unity in the one body.

p: Read 1 Corinthians 12:1-11; Ephesians 4:11-13; Romans 12:3-8. Spiritual gifts are special abilities that the Holy Spirit gives to believers for service. They are for building up the church and for God's mission, not for personal gain.

Talents are natural or learned skills such as singing, drawing or mathematics. Spiritual gifts are given by the Spirit for spiritual service. Both should be used for God's glory, with humility: 'think with sober judgment' (Romans 12:3).

Revelation gifts (they 'know'): word of wisdom (insight into what to do), word of knowledge (insight into facts and truths of the faith) and discerning of spirits (telling whether a spiritual action is from God, an evil spirit or a human spirit).
Power gifts (they 'do'): faith (bold, mountain-moving trust), gifts of healing and working of miracles.
Utterance gifts (they 'speak'): prophecy (speaking God's message to encourage, strengthen and comfort, which is not only foretelling), speaking in tongues and interpretation of tongues.

They all come from one Spirit. Every believer has at least one gift. The Spirit gives them 'as He wills', so we cannot demand a gift. They are for the common good: the church is like a body where the hand needs the eye, so no one person has every gift and we depend on one another. Using our gifts helps us to resist the world's pattern, to be changed, and to fulfil our calling.
The Corinthian church had many gifts but was immature. Having gifts does not prove maturity; having the fruit of the Spirit does. The aim is a united, mature church where each part does its work.

units.title: Forgiveness: The Story of Philemon and Onesimus
units.summary: What forgiveness means, Paul's letter to Philemon as a model of mediation, three ways forgiveness comes, and what unforgiveness does.

p: Read Matthew 6:14-15 and 18:21-35 and the letter to Philemon. To forgive is to have no further wish to punish someone for an offence: letting go of ill feeling and the desire for revenge. God took the first step in restoring us when we were sinners, and Christians are to restore offenders in the same way. Jesus says that if we do not forgive others, our Father will not forgive us. There is no limit: 'seventy times seven' means a lifestyle of forgiving.

Philemon was a wealthy Christian in Colossae who led a church in his house. Onesimus, his slave, ran away to Rome. Under Roman law a runaway slave could be put to death. In Rome Onesimus met Paul, who was in prison, and became a Christian.

Paul did not use his authority to give orders. He appealed in love. He sent Onesimus back 'no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother'. The name Onesimus means 'useful': once useless to Philemon, he was now useful to both. Paul even offered to pay any debt: 'If he has wronged you or owes you anything, charge that to my account' (verse 18), which is like Jesus taking our debt. Paul's goal was full reconciliation and restored brotherhood.

Repentance: the offender admits wrong and asks for pardon. Unconditional mercy: the offended person, moved by God's love, forgives even without an apology. Mediation: a third person, like Paul, brings the two sides together.

Emotional: hatred and bitterness grow. Social: war, lack of peace and disunity in families and communities. Spiritual: slow growth and hindered prayer. Christians should be peacemakers, obey God by forgiving, and help offenders to find their place again, as Onesimus was restored.

Note: forgiving does not always mean trusting immediately (for example after theft), but it does mean giving up the wish to punish. Some traditions say Onesimus later became a church leader, but this is not certain.

units.title: Humility
units.summary: What humility is, the mind of Christ in Philippians 2, Peter's teaching on humility and anxiety, and expressions of humility in daily life.

p: Humility is a state of mind that holds a modest opinion of oneself. It is the opposite of pride. It means knowing that we depend on God and valuing others above ourselves. It is one of the greatest marks of a Christian and brings understanding, progress, peace and harmony.

Paul wrote to a church in Philippi that was divided; the root causes were selfishness and a lack of humility. He pointed to Jesus. Jesus was 'in the form of God' and equal with God. He did not hold on to this for His own gain. He emptied Himself (the word kenosis), took the form of a servant, was born as a man, and became obedient even to death on a cross.

Because He went to the lowest place, God lifted Him to the highest. 'God has highly exalted him and given him the name that is above every name,' so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. The way up is down.

Peter tells young people to be submissive to their elders, and all to 'clothe yourselves with humility'. 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.' If you humble yourself under God's hand, He will lift you up in due time: promotion comes from God, not self-promotion.

Humility and worry: 'Cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.' Worry can be a form of pride, thinking we must solve everything ourselves. Peter also warns that the devil prowls like a roaring lion; we resist him by being sober, watchful and firm in faith.

Serving without seeking applause. Forgiving readily. Obeying rules and lawful authority. Putting the community's good above personal gain. True humility is not hiding your talents. Jesus knew He was God and chose to serve. Humility is using your strength to serve others, not to dominate them.

units.title: Effective Prayer
units.summary: What prayer is, James's teaching for different seasons, the conditions and hindrances of prayer, types of prayer (ACTS) and Elijah as an example.

p: Read James 1:5-8; 4:2-3; 5:13-18; Matthew 6:5-6. Prayer is close, personal communion with God. It is not just reciting words; it needs concentration and attention. We bring our will in line with God's will and, as Jesus taught, pray to the Father in His name. Effective prayer is prayer that gets results: it comes from someone who does not doubt that God is real, willing and able to answer.

If you lack wisdom, ask God in faith. If you are suffering, pray. If you are cheerful, sing praise. If you are sick, call the elders of the church to pray and anoint with oil. The prayer of faith will save the sick and the Lord will raise him up.

Conditions for success: faith (we must believe that God hears); right motive ('You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions'); righteousness and confession of sin; and humility and privacy, not praying to impress people.
Hindrances: doubt (a doubter is like a wave of the sea driven by the wind); cherished sin and unforgiveness; giving up too soon.

Adoration: praising God for who He is. Thanksgiving: thanking Him for what He has done. Confession: admitting sins and deciding to leave them. Petition: asking for our own needs. Intercession: standing in the gap for others, such as the sick or the nation. Dedication: promising to be God's own and to submit to His will. The memory aid ACTS stands for Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication.

James says 'Elijah was a man with a nature like ours' (James 5:17), with feelings, fears and weaknesses. Yet he prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain for three and a half years; then he prayed again and the heavens gave rain. The power of prayer lies in the God who answers, and in a person who is right with Him.

units.title: Witnessing to Christ: A Holy Life among Others
units.summary: Witnessing as a lifestyle, Peter's call to holiness and good conduct among unbelievers, and Paul's call to wake up and put on Christ.

p: Read 1 Peter 1:13-17; 2:9-25; Romans 13:11-14. Witnessing is not only preaching. It is a life that is open, accountable and holy, a 'silent sermon' that others can see.

Prepare your mind ('gird up the loins of your mind'): be self-controlled and set your hope on the grace to come. Do not go back to your former desires and ignorance. Among non-believers keep your conduct honourable, so that even if they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God.
Peter's four commands: honour everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honour the king. Submit to every human authority for the Lord's sake.

Paul says the time is urgent: 'The night is far gone; the day is at hand.' Christians must wake from spiritual sleep. Throw off the works of darkness (drunkenness, immorality, quarrelling, jealousy) and 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' like armour, making no provision for the flesh. The aim is to be a copy of Christ in society.
In school, witnessing means honesty in tests, respect for teachers and prefects, kindness to classmates and care for the school compound. Your life will speak before your words do.

units.title: Civic Responsibility, Social Vices and Peaceful Living
units.summary: Social vices that damage witness, tolerance and coexistence, why Christians obey government (Romans 13), and the duties of a good citizen.

p: Social vices are bad habits and tendencies in a community that work against peace and progress: drug abuse, bribery, corruption, stealing, armed robbery, sexual immorality, tribalism, nepotism and examination malpractice. A Christian who cheats in exams or takes bribes destroys his witness.

Tolerance means being fair and understanding towards people with different views, cultures, religions or races. Coexistence is living together without rancour. They build the nation and help the economy. Tolerance does not mean accepting sin; it means respecting the person while keeping your own faith.

Paul teaches that authority comes from God, and that rulers are God's servants for our good, to punish wrong and to reward good. So to resist lawful government is to resist what God has set up. In Peter's and Paul's day the ruler was the Roman emperor, who often persecuted Christians, so the call to respect leaders is strong.
But submission has limits: when the government commands something clearly against God's law, as in Daniel 3, believers must obey God first, peacefully and respectfully.

Pay taxes, rates and bills on time. Obey the law and road signs. Use freedom as a servant of God, not as a cover for evil. Keep away from crimes such as drug trafficking and cultism. A Christian lives in two kingdoms, God's kingdom and the state, and should be a model citizen in both.

units.title: Christian Attitudes towards Persecution
units.summary: What persecution is, Peter's picture of gold in the fire, rejoicing and hope, and James on the difference between trials and temptation.

p: Persecution is mistreating, threatening, harming or killing someone because of their religious beliefs. Christians may be hated because they stand against wrongs like fraud, corruption and cultism; their goodness shows up the darkness in others. Because it hurts, people are tempted to give in and tolerate evil.

sections.h: Peter: gold in the fire (1 Peter 1:6-9; 3:13-17; 4:12-19)
p: Faith is like gold, which is purified by fire. Persecution is the fire that burns away impurities such as hypocrisy and self-reliance, leaving a pure faith that gives praise to Jesus.

Do not be surprised at the fiery trial as if something strange were happening. Rejoice, because you share in Christ's sufferings and will share His glory. If you suffer as a murderer or thief, be ashamed; if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed. Suffering for doing wrong is not persecution. Set your hope on the grace to be given when Jesus returns.

'Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life.' James also corrects a mistake: God does not tempt anyone. God tests faith to strengthen it, but temptation comes from our own desire. The chain is: desire, then sin, then death.

It is not easy to live right among friends who do wrong. Prayer gives grace to stand. Persecution is not a sign that God is absent; it is a trial of faith. The Christian answer is joy, endurance and hope. Forms in school: being left out, mocking, and cyberbullying because of faith.

units.title: Impartiality
units.summary: What impartiality means, James's warning about favouring the rich, four reasons against partiality, the Golden Rule, and the harm of nepotism and tribalism.

p: Impartiality is acting without bias. It treats all people as equal brothers and sisters regardless of race, background or influence, and gives right judgment without fear or favour: looking at the facts, not the faces. All people are equal because God made each one in His own image, and He treats all generously.

sections.h: James 2:1-13: the rich man and the poor man
p: Two men come into the church. One wears gold rings and fine clothes; the other is poor and dressed in rags. The usher tells the rich man 'Have a seat here, please' and tells the poor man 'Stand there' or 'Sit at my feet'. James says, 'Have you not made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?'

Four reasons against partiality: God has chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom; the rich often oppress believers and drag them to court; favouritism breaks the 'royal law', 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself'; and God Himself is not partial.
Jesus taught in Matthew 7:12 and Luke 6:31: 'Whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them.' Before you act, ask: 'If I were in his place, how would I want to be treated?'

Nepotism is giving jobs and favours to relatives. Favouritism is treating some people better out of feeling. Tribalism is loyalty to your tribe together with hostility to others. These vices slow development, because wealth and power are shared unfairly. They also divide people, cause distrust and strife, and kill patriotism as people serve their clan, not the nation.
Loving your family is good, but when it twists justice it becomes sin. Choosing people by merit (their ability) is more in line with impartiality than choosing by connection.

units.title: The Resurrection of Jesus Christ
units.summary: What the Resurrection is and why it is the hub of the Christian faith, Matthew's account, and the role of the women.

p: Read Matthew 28:1-8 and Mark 16:1-8. The Resurrection means that Jesus rose from the dead on the third day after His crucifixion. It is the hub, the centre, of the Christian faith: without it the faith is empty (1 Corinthians 15:17). It confirms that Jesus is the Son of God and has power over sin and death. It also fulfils prophecy that God's Holy One would not see corruption (Psalm 16:10), and it shows that life continues beyond the grave.

On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to the tomb. There was a great earthquake as an angel of the Lord came down, rolled back the stone and sat on it. His appearance was like lightning. The guards shook with fear and became like dead men. The angel told the women, 'Do not be afraid. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said.' They were told to go quickly and tell the disciples to meet Jesus in Galilee.

In a world where a woman's word counted for little, the Gospels name women as the first witnesses. They stayed near Jesus when most of the male disciples ran away. They went early to anoint His body, using spices they bought. Their love and courage were rewarded by being first to hear the news. If the disciples were inventing a story, they would not have chosen women as the first witnesses, which supports the truth of the accounts.
Lazarus was brought back to life but died again. This is resuscitation. Jesus rose to eternal life, and He is the first of many who will rise (1 Corinthians 15:20).

units.title: The Second Coming of Jesus Christ
units.summary: What the Second Coming and the Rapture mean, the signs Paul gives (rebellion and the man of lawlessness), and how Christians should prepare and comfort one another.

p: Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 and 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12. The Second Coming (Parousia) means that Jesus Christ will return. The notes teach that He will take faithful Christians to be with Him, which is often called the Rapture, and it is the believer's 'blessed hope'. No one knows the day or hour. He will come suddenly, 'like a thief in the night'.

Paul warns the Thessalonians not to be deceived by rumours that the day has already come. First, a great rebellion or falling away from the faith must happen. The 'man of lawlessness' will be revealed. He will exalt himself above God and use false miracles with Satan's power. God sends a strong delusion on those who refused to love the truth. The Lord Jesus will overthrow him 'with the breath of his mouth' and the brightness of His coming. Christians hold different views about how and when these things happen, but all agree that we must stay faithful.

Live holy lives as children of light. Show love and hospitality (Matthew 25). Share the Gospel to save others. Because the time is unknown, we must always be ready. This should affect even hidden sins: He comes like a thief.

Paul wrote about this to comfort Christians who had lost loved ones. For a believer, death is like sleep, a passing to be with Christ. The dead in Christ will rise first; then those alive will be caught up with them in the clouds to meet the Lord. 'Therefore encourage one another with these words.'

units.title: The Sovereignty of God
units.summary: What sovereignty means, the first account of creation (six days of order), the second account (God close to man), and how the two fit together.

p: Sovereign means holding the highest power without limit. God's sovereignty is His supremacy over all things. He is the supreme commander and controller who made everything. He gave man dominion over the earth (Genesis 1:28), but God's power is above man's. Man is a steward; God is the owner.
God brings order out of chaos ('without form and void'). By His word:

head: Day
What God made
rows: The sky (firmament), dividing waters above and below
Land and sea; plants and trees
Land animals and man in God's image
God rested, blessed the day and made it holy

p: This account looks closely at man and his home. There was no rain yet and no one to farm, so a mist watered the ground. God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, so man became a living being: a close, personal Creator. God planted the Garden of Eden with trees for beauty and food. Four rivers flowed from Eden: Pishon, Gihon, Tigris and Euphrates. God caused a deep sleep to fall on Adam, took one of his ribs, and made woman to be a suitable helper.

The two accounts do not contradict each other. They give two views: the wide view of God's power over the universe (Genesis 1, 'Elohim', God of power) and the close view of God's care for people (Genesis 2, 'Yahweh', God of relationship). God's 'rest' on the seventh day does not mean that He was tired; it means that the work was complete.
Because God is sovereign, we are accountable to Him. He is the owner; we are tenants and stewards of what He has made.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 Economics First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Economics is the study of how people, businesses and governments make choices when resources are limited. Every day you make economic choices: how to spend your pocket money, whether to buy food or a book, how to use your time. Economics helps you to understand these choices and the way your community and country earn and spend money.

In First Term you will learn what economics is, the tools economists use (tables, averages, graphs and charts), how demand and supply work, how goods are produced, how work is shared among workers, how different countries organise their economies, the types of business, the size of the population and the labour market.

Each unit has simple notes, tables, diagrams and worked examples. Read slowly, and copy the tables and graphs into your notebook. At the end of every unit there are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you to check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.
Economics is also an examination subject in WAEC and NECO, so learn the key words in each unit: you will meet them again in the exam.

units.title: The Meaning of Economics
units.summary: Where the word economics comes from and the three famous definitions: Adam Smith's wealth definition, Marshall's welfare definition and Robbins' scarcity definition.

p: The word economics comes from the Greek word oikonomia, which means the management of a family or household. The subject was first studied in ancient Greece by thinkers such as Aristotle (384-322 BC). Between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries, European traders called mercantilists thought of economics as the 'study of wealth'. Adam Smith, the 'Father of Economics', supported this view in the late eighteenth century.
Since then the subject has grown, and economists have given different definitions. They fall into three groups.

Adam Smith (1723-1790) was a Scottish economist. His book An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776) treated economics as the science of wealth: how it is produced, consumed and built up. He said the aim of political economy is to increase the riches and power of a country. Unlike the mercantilists, he did not think wealth meant gold and silver. He defined wealth as goods and services that have value in exchange.
Key points: economics deals with the creation and sharing of wealth, and a market economy is guided by the 'invisible hand' of the price system.

Alfred Marshall wrote Principles of Economics (1890). He moved attention from wealth to human welfare. He said economics is 'a study of men as they live and move and think in the ordinary business of life'. Wealth is only a means to an end: the end is human welfare and well-being.

The most widely accepted definition was given by Lord Robbins in 1932: 'Economics is the science which studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses.'

It rests on three ideas: (1) Wants are unlimited: people always want more, and luxuries become necessities. (2) Resources are scarce: the means to satisfy wants are limited. (3) Resources have alternative uses: they can be used in different ways, so choosing one means giving up another, which is called opportunity cost.
This definition applies to all societies, from a person alone on an island to a rich nation. It also makes economics a positive science, one that deals with facts rather than opinions.

units.title: Nature, Scope and Basic Concepts of Economics
units.summary: Economics as a social science, its branches, why it matters, and the key ideas: wants, scarcity, scale of preference, choice and opportunity cost.

p: Economics is a social science that studies how people make decisions. It is not only about money; it is about choices, such as what job to do, what to buy and what policy to follow. Every decision has a cost and a benefit (a trade-off).

Microeconomics studies individuals and firms: demand, supply and production. Macroeconomics studies the whole economy: national income (GDP), inflation and unemployment. International economics studies trade, exchange rates and world institutions. Development economics studies growth and the reduction of poverty. Environmental economics studies the sustainable use of resources.

It helps society to use scarce resources well. It guides businesses, governments and consumers in decisions. It supports growth, fairer incomes and sustainable development, and it is needed for trade and finance. It also helps each of us to manage our own money.
Wants: desires for goods and services that give satisfaction. They are unlimited, since new wants appear as old ones are met.
Scarcity: resources are limited but wants are unlimited, so people must choose.
Scale of preference: a list of our wants arranged in order of importance. A student's scale might be: 1. school uniform, 2. exercise books, 3. wristwatch, 4. dictionary.
Choice: selecting one option and giving up others because of scarcity.
Opportunity cost: the next best alternative that you give up when you choose. If you have N100 and choose a book instead of a calculator that also costs N100, the calculator is the opportunity cost.

units.title: Basic Tools of Economic Analysis: Statistics, Averages and Tables
units.summary: Why economists use mathematical tools, what statistics is, the measures of central tendency, and how to make and use a good table.

p: Economists use tables, charts, graphs, algebra and equations. These help them to predict and to see what economic theories mean in practice.

Statistics is the science of collecting, analysing and interpreting data. It is used to describe an event or result and so to save time, money and effort. It is also used to draw conclusions: policy makers use statistics to find the pattern hidden in data.

A measure of central tendency is an average figure that sits at the centre of a set of values. The main ones are the arithmetic mean (the sum of the values divided by their number), the median (the middle value when the values are put in order) and the mode (the most frequent value). The geometric and harmonic means are also used. Example: for the marks 2, 4, 4, 6, 9 the mean is 25 ÷ 5 = 5, the median is 4, and the mode is 4.
A table is an orderly list of information in rows and columns that shortens data and makes it easy to understand.
Characteristics of a good table: simple; easy to understand; has a title; states the units; states its purpose; is numbered if there are many; gives its source if known.
Importance of tables: they summarise data, arrange it in order, make comparison easy, bring out the important features, help us understand the data and speed up decisions.

units.title: Graphs and Charts: Demand Graph, Pie, Bar Charts and Pictograms
units.summary: How to draw a graph from a schedule, pie charts with degrees, simple, component and multiple bar charts, pictograms and the importance of charts.

sections.h: Drawing a graph from a schedule
p: A graph shows the relationship between two variables. Take a demand schedule for tins of milk: quantity 10 at price 1, 9 at 2, 8 at 3, 7 at 4, 6 at 5, 5 at 6, 4 at 7, 3 at 8, 2 at 9, 1 at 10. On the horizontal axis we put the quantity and on the vertical axis the price. For each pair we mark the point where the quantity line meets the price line (for example quantity 4 meets price 7). Joining the points gives the curve DD, a demand curve showing the relationship between price and quantity.

img.alt: A graph of price against quantity with a downward-sloping line DD through points from (1, 10) to (10, 1)
img.cap: A demand curve drawn from a schedule: price falls as quantity rises.

p: A pie chart is a circle divided into sectors. The whole circle (360°) stands for the whole data, and each sector shows the share of one item. Angle of a sector = (value ÷ total) × 360°. Percentage = (value ÷ total) × 100.

Example: the populations (in thousands) of three towns: A 70, B 100, C 30. Total = 200. Angle for A = 70/200 × 360° = 126°. B = 100/200 × 360° = 180°. C = 30/200 × 360° = 54°. Check: 126 + 180 + 54 = 360°. In percentages: A 35%, B 50%, C 15%.

img.alt: A pie chart of towns A, B and C with angles 126, 180 and 54 degrees
img.cap: Pie chart of the populations of towns A, B and C.

p: A simple bar chart is used for one category of data. The bars can be vertical or horizontal. Choose a suitable scale. The bars must have the same width and equal spaces between them. Example: the population of three age groups in the town of Kota (0-17, 18-60 and over 60).

img.alt: A simple bar chart of population by age group
img.cap: A simple bar chart.

p: A component (or compound) bar chart is used when the data has more than one part. Each bar is divided into sections that match the size of each part. Example: the population of five towns divided into male and female.

img.alt: A compound bar chart of the population of towns A to E, each bar divided into two parts
img.cap: A component bar chart: each bar is split into parts.

p: A multiple bar chart is like a component bar chart, but the parts are drawn as separate bars placed side by side. Example: the quantities of yam, maize and cassava planted in three towns.

img.alt: A multiple bar chart showing yam, maize and cassava planted in towns A, B and C
img.cap: A multiple bar chart: separate bars for each crop.

sections.h: Pictograms and the value of charts
p: A pictogram uses pictures to show amounts. Example: the chickens eaten in a country from 1998 to 2003 were (in thousands) 30, 60, 20, 50, 40 and 10. If one chicken picture stands for 10,000 chickens, then 1998 has 3 pictures, 1999 has 6, 2000 has 2, 2001 has 5, 2002 has 4 and 2003 has 1.

Charts are important because they are easy to understand even for people with little education, they use pictures and colours to make the message clear, they allow two or more things to be compared in one chart, and they are easy to make.

units.title: Frequency Distributions, Histograms and Frequency Polygons
units.summary: Making a frequency table from raw data, drawing a histogram for ungrouped and grouped data, class boundaries, and the frequency polygon.

p: The frequency of an observation is how many times a value occurs. A frequency table lists the values and their frequencies. For raw data, use tally marks and then count them.

A histogram is a graph of a frequency distribution. It uses bars that touch each other, and the area of each bar is proportional to its frequency. Example: the ages of 30 students in a school press club. The frequencies are: age 10: 2; 11: 6; 12: 4; 13: 4; 14: 3; 15: 1; 16: 1; 17: 1; 18: 4; 19: 1; 20: 2; 21: 1. Total 30.

img.alt: A histogram of the ages 10 to 21 of 30 students
img.cap: Histogram of ungrouped data: ages of 30 students.

p: Group the ages in classes of width 3: 10-12 has 12 students; 13-15 has 8; 16-18 has 6; 19-21 has 4. Next find the class boundaries. Reduce the lower limit by half a unit and raise the upper limit by half a unit: 10-12 becomes 9.5-12.5; 13-15 becomes 12.5-15.5; 16-18 becomes 15.5-18.5; 19-21 becomes 18.5-21.5. This closes the gaps between classes. The class midpoint is the middle value of a class (for 10-12 it is 11).

img.alt: A histogram of grouped ages 10-12, 13-15, 16-18 and 19-21
img.cap: Histogram of grouped data.

p: A frequency polygon is made by joining the midpoints of the tops of the bars of a histogram with straight lines. It shows the shape of the distribution.

img.alt: A frequency polygon drawn over a histogram
img.cap: A frequency polygon joins the midpoints of the tops of the bars.

units.title: Demand: Meaning, Law, Schedule and Curve
units.summary: What demand is, price systems, the law of demand, individual and market demand schedules (with corrected totals), the demand curve and the factors that influence demand.

p: Demand is the quantity of a good or service that a consumer is willing and able to buy at a given price in a given period. Wanting something is not demand unless the person can pay for it.

A price system is the way in which values of goods are set. A fixed price system is controlled by an authority; a free price system (the market) lets demand and supply decide; a mixed system combines both.

The law of demand says that, other things being equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises. Buyers hesitate to spend more on a good for fear of running out of money.
A demand schedule is a table showing the quantity demanded at different prices. An individual demand schedule is for one person. A market demand schedule adds up the demand of all consumers.
Individual schedule: Bola's demand for Fanta: at N100 she buys 10 bottles a week; at N80, 20; at N60, 30; at N40, 40; at N20, 50.
Market schedule for Coca-Cola (bottles per week) with five buyers. The totals are found by adding across each row.

The demand curve is a graph of the demand schedule. Price is on the vertical axis and quantity is on the horizontal axis. It slopes downward from left to right: as the price falls from p0 to p1, the quantity demanded rises from q0 to q1.

img.alt: A downward-sloping demand curve with prices p0 and p1 and quantities q0 and q1
img.cap: A demand curve slopes downward: lower price, greater quantity demanded.

p: Tastes and preferences. Income: higher incomes usually raise demand. Prices of related goods: substitutes (goods that can replace each other, like tea and coffee) and complements (goods used together, like bread and butter). Expectations about future prices, incomes or supplies. Population and its make-up (age, size).

units.title: Supply: Meaning, Law, Schedule and Curve
units.summary: What supply is, the law of supply, individual and market supply schedules (with corrected totals), the supply curve and the factors that influence supply.

p: Supply is the amount of a good or service that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price in a given period.

The law of supply says that, other things being equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, and when the price falls, the quantity supplied falls. Existing producers make more of high-priced goods to earn more profit, and new producers may join the market.

An individual supply schedule shows how much one firm or farmer supplies at different prices. For a farmer supplying bags of beans: at N100 per bag, 50 bags; at N80, 40; at N60, 30; at N40, 20; at N20, 10.
A market supply schedule adds up the supply of all sellers. Example (bags per week):

The supply curve is a graph of the supply schedule with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. It slopes upward from left to right: when the price rises from A to B, the quantity supplied rises.

Natural conditions: good rains raise farm output; drought reduces it.

units.title: The Theory of Production: Types and Factors of Production
units.summary: What production is, direct and indirect production, primary, secondary and tertiary production, and the four factors of production with their rewards.

p: Production is the process of using inputs (land, labour and capital) to create outputs, which are goods and services that satisfy human wants. It includes the activities that create goods and services and get them to final consumers.

Direct production: a person produces goods and services only for his own family to use, not for sale. Family labour is used and the scale is small. Indirect production: goods and services are produced on a large scale for sale or exchange, using machines and skilled labour, and the producer uses the money to satisfy other wants.

Indirect production has three levels. Primary production comes from the 'extractive' industries such as farming, forestry, fishing, mining and oil extraction. Secondary production changes raw materials into semi-finished or finished goods (flour into bread, iron ore into steel) in manufacturing and construction. Tertiary production is the services that put goods into the hands of consumers: trade, banking, insurance, transport, communication and government services such as law, education, health and defence.
Factors of production are the resources combined to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and the entrepreneur.

units.title: Division of Labour and Specialisation
units.summary: What division of labour and specialisation mean, the types of specialisation, their advantages, disadvantages and limitations.

p: Adam Smith used the example of making pins to show that when a job is split into small tasks and each worker does one task, much more is produced. Division of labour means giving different tasks to different people so that productivity and profit rise.
Example: to build a house, a manager needs masons, plumbers, carpenters, electricians, painters and interior designers. Each uses a special skill and together they finish the building.

Specialisation means that a person, firm or country concentrates on one kind of work or product. There are four types. By process: the work is divided into stages, and each worker or firm does only one stage. By product: a producer makes only one commodity. By sex: some jobs are done only by men or only by women because of custom, tradition or law. Geographical: a region produces one commodity because of its climate and resources (for example cocoa in the south-west of Nigeria and groundnut in the north).
Higher output, large-scale production, saving of time, growth of specialisation, standard goods, and less tiredness.

Greater interdependence: a problem in one stage stops everything. Difficulty in changing jobs (poor mobility). Boredom from repeating the same job. Loss of craftsmanship as workers become machine-minders.
The size of the market, the level of technology, the nature of the good (for example seasonal goods), the supply of inputs such as capital and labour, special talents, and government policy.

units.title: Economies of Scale and the Scale of Production
units.summary: Economies and diseconomies of scale (internal and external), advantages and disadvantages of large-scale production, and what limits a firm's growth.

p: Economies of scale are achieved when producing more units costs less per unit. As a firm grows and produces more, its average cost per unit falls. Adam Smith named division of labour and specialisation as two main ways to get this. Diseconomies of scale happen when a firm grows too big and the average cost starts to rise.

Internal economies are cost savings that come from the firm's own growth (for example buying materials in bulk, using machines or splitting management). External economies are savings that all firms in an industry enjoy because the industry has grown or is concentrated in one area, for example a better road network, a skilled labour pool or an industrial estate. Alfred Marshall made this distinction.

Internal diseconomies arise within the firm: poor management, too many workers or technical limits that raise costs. External diseconomies arise outside it: traffic jams, high rents or shortage of workers because many industries crowd into one place.

Internal and external economies; more division of labour; lower cost per unit (one manager can supervise a factory making 1,000 units instead of two managers for two factories of 500); ancillary industries grow up to supply inputs or use by-products, such as around a steel mill.

Danger of over-production and falling prices. Less supervision, so waste and dishonesty. Concentration of wealth in a few hands. Dependence on foreign markets, which can be cut off by war. Individual tastes ignored because goods are uniform.

sections.h: Limits to the growth of a firm
p: The extent of the market, the availability of capital, the nature of the business, falling price of the product and rising management costs.

units.title: Economic Systems: Capitalism, Socialism and the Mixed Economy
units.summary: What an economic system is, and the features, advantages and disadvantages of capitalism, socialism and mixed economies.

p: An economic system is the way a society or government organises and shares its resources, goods and services. It decides how production and consumption are controlled: how things are made, who makes them, how they are shared and who gets access. It is like the set of rules a society follows for money and trade. There are three main types.

In capitalism, individuals own and manage property, and free market forces set prices. Private ownership of the means of production is the main feature; private people decide what to produce, how, and for whom. Examples: the USA, Japan, Australia, Singapore, Switzerland and France (although most governments also play some role).
Features: private ownership, competition, profit motive, accumulation of wealth, free enterprise and individual initiative.
Advantages: customers have choice; efficiency; fast development; hard work is rewarded because people can own property; many forms of production; technology grows; talent is used.
Disadvantages: workers can be exploited; job insecurity and unemployment; unhealthy rivalry; profit at all cost; more crime from the chase for wealth; inequality, since few people control production.

In socialism, the state owns and controls the means of production. Industries are owned by the government, and the aim is the welfare of all citizens. Countries with strong state control have included the former Soviet bloc, Cuba, China (before its reforms) and some African states after independence, such as Tanzania and Mozambique. Most of these have since added market features.
Features: state ownership, welfare focus, no profit motive, full use of resources, prevention of private monopoly and stable prices.
Advantages: fairer sharing of resources, job security, central planning, no private monopoly and no exploitation by private owners.
Disadvantages: little competition; a state monopoly; little creativity; little choice for consumers; laziness because the state provides all.

A mixed economy combines capitalism and socialism. Private property is protected and people have economic freedom, but the government also steps in to meet social aims. Resources are owned jointly by public and private owners. Examples: Britain, Mexico, Peru and, in Africa, Nigeria, Egypt, Kenya and Tanzania.

Features: joint participation and decisions, fair competition, checks and balances, freedom of choice. Advantages: no monopoly, job security, economic development, choice and a mix of the best of both. Disadvantages: corruption and mismanagement, inefficiency, labour exploitation, emphasis on profit at the expense of citizens, and a wide gap between rich and poor.

units.title: The Basic Economic Problems of Society
units.summary: The four fundamental questions every society must answer: what, how and for whom to produce, and how efficiently resources are used.

p: Every society has unlimited wants but limited resources. So every society, whether capitalist, socialist or mixed, faces four basic problems.

Because we cannot produce everything, society must decide which goods and services to produce and in what amounts. Factors: cost of production, consumers' income, market demand, availability of resources and consumer needs.

After deciding what to produce, we must choose the method. Factors: the technique of production (labour-intensive or capital-intensive), technological advancement and the relative cost of the factors of production.

Production is not complete until goods reach the final consumers. Factors: the level of consumers' income, the need to satisfy wants, and the economic system. In capitalist and mixed economies, who gets what depends on prices and incomes. In a socialist economy, the state often uses quotas.

Resources are used efficiently if the output is high compared with the inputs. Efficiency depends on the quality of labour (skilled labour raises output and quality) and the techniques of production (machines save time and reduce waste).

units.title: Firm, Factory, Industry and Business Organisation
units.summary: The meaning of a firm, a plant (factory) and an industry, the two groups of business organisation, and private and public enterprises.

p: A firm is a business that produces and sells goods or services to earn revenue and profit. A 'company' is any trade or business and includes sole proprietorships, partnerships and corporations, while a firm usually means a business run by two or more partners, such as a law firm.
A plant or factory is the place where a firm produces: the building and equipment in one location (cement plant, textile mill, steel mill).
An industry is a group of firms making similar goods or services for the same market, such as the banking industry, wood industry or insurance industry.

A business organisation is an enterprise set up by an individual, a group or the government to make a profit and/or to provide goods and services. There are two groups: private and public enterprises.

Owned and managed by private individuals, such as a sole proprietorship or a partnership. Characteristics: private people provide the capital; ownership belongs to them; the aim is profit; they are accountable to the owners; and the owners bear the risk.

Owned, controlled and managed by the federal, state or local government. They are often called authorities, corporations, boards or commissions. Examples: the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) and the Nigerian Railway Corporation (NRC). Characteristics: government provides capital; government owns; the aim is social service; managers answer to government; government and taxpayers bear the risk; a board of directors manages.

Private enterprise: owned by individuals; capital from individuals; aim is profit; controlled by owners or their directors; set up by registration; losses are borne by owners. Public enterprise: owned by government; capital from government; aim is social service; controlled by a board appointed by government; set up by an Act; losses are borne by taxpayers.

Problems of private enterprises in Nigeria: inadequate capital, insufficient raw materials, poor management, poor power supply (so firms run generators, which raises cost), and lack of specialisation.
