units.title: Companies and Their Types
units.summary: What a company is, limited and unlimited liability, private and public limited companies, quoted and unquoted companies.

p: A company is a voluntary group of people who come together to run a business and share the profits. It is a legal body, separate from its owners, formed to reach a common aim.

Limited liability means that owners can lose only the amount they invested. Their private property is safe if the company fails. Unlimited liability means that the owners are fully responsible for all the debts of the business. Sole proprietors and general partners have unlimited liability. The Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) is the Nigerian law that governs companies.

head: Limited liability
Unlimited liability
rows: Often the same as the owner

p: A private limited company has a small number of shareholders (the old law set a limit of fifty) and may not sell shares to the public. A public limited company (Plc) offers its shares to the general public, and anyone can buy them.

A quoted company has its shares accepted for trading on a stock exchange, which makes it easier to raise capital. Examples in Nigeria: Zenith Bank Plc, Dangote Cement Plc, Cadbury Nigeria Plc and BUA Cement Plc. An unquoted (unlisted) company is not traded on the stock exchange. It may be too small to qualify or have been delisted, and it relies on private investors for capital.

units.title: Population: Size, Growth and Migration
units.summary: What population is, birth rate, death rate and migration, population formulas, and the advantages and disadvantages of youthful and ageing populations.

p: Population is the total number of people living in a country or area at a particular time. Three things decide its size and growth: the birth rate, the death rate and migration.

The birth rate (natality rate) is the number of live births per 1,000 people in a year. Birth rate = (number of births ÷ total population) × 1,000. (The notes show × 100, which gives a percentage; for the 'per thousand' form use × 1,000.) Factors: early marriage, desire for a large family, religion, better medical services, higher living standard, ratio of males to females, family planning and infant mortality.

The death rate is the number of deaths per 1,000 people in a year. Death rate = (number of deaths ÷ total population) × 1,000. A high death rate reduces population; a low one raises it. Factors: poor health services, high cost of living, natural disasters, war, ignorance, poverty and high infant mortality.

Migration is the movement of people from one place to another, either for a while or for good. The place people leave is the source region; the place they go to is the receiving region (destination). Immigration is people coming into a country (an immigrant). Emigration is people leaving it (an emigrant). Immigration raises population; emigration lowers it. Factors: disasters, climate, insecurity, economic opportunities, education and wealth, social amenities, political instability and war.
Net migration = immigration − emigration. Natural growth rate = birth rate − death rate. Population growth rate = birth rate − death rate + net migration.

A youthful (increasing) population has a rising share of young people. Advantages: large labour force, large market, respect and attention from other countries, foreign investment and aid. Disadvantages: pressure on resources, crime, shortage of food, crowded cities, and unemployment.

An ageing (declining) population has a rising share of old people. Advantages: lower government spending on children, less crowding, better living standards, more savings and investment. Disadvantages: smaller labour force, under-population, falling GDP, lower rewards for factors, and higher government spending on the elderly.

units.title: The Labour Market, Labour Force, Efficiency and Mobility of Labour
units.summary: What the labour market and labour force are, what affects the size of the labour force, what makes labour efficient, and how labour moves between places and jobs.

p: Labour is all human effort, skilled or unskilled, used to produce goods and services. A market is any place or means by which buyers and sellers exchange goods and services at prices set by market forces. The labour market is where buyers of labour (employers) and sellers of labour (workers) meet and agree on wages and conditions.

The labour force (working population) is the total number of people of working age who are able and willing to work. It includes those who have jobs and those looking for jobs, usually between 18 and 65 years, though this differs by country. Factors affecting its size: population (more people, more workers); income (higher incomes attract workers); education (a more educated society has a bigger labour force); home ownership (owning a home reduces mobility); and other local factors.

Efficiency of labour is the productive power of a worker: the ability to do more or better work in a given time. It depends on personal qualities; general education and intelligence; standard of living (good food, clothes, housing); level of technology; state of health; and job security.

Mobility is the ability of workers to move from place to place, job to job or industry to industry. Geographical mobility is movement from one location to another; it is affected by transport cost, government policy, language barriers, family and cultural ties and available infrastructure. Occupational mobility is movement from one job to another; it is affected by the cost and length of training, trade union or professional restrictions, differences in wages, political or religious crises and personal preference.

units.title: The Nigerian Economy and the Structure of Industry
units.summary: Nigeria's mixed economy, its size and exports, and the three groups of industry: primary, secondary and tertiary.

p: Nigeria has a mixed economy. Private businesses own most of the economic activity, but the government regulates some sectors and controls others (for example, parts of oil and gas, power and railways). Private businesses try to earn profit, so the economy is capitalist at its core.

Nigeria has over 200 million people, which makes it one of the most populous countries in the world and the largest in Africa. A large population gives a large labour force and a large market for goods.

Nigeria depends heavily on exports and imports. Petroleum is the biggest export, and Nigeria is one of the largest oil exporters in Africa. In recent years, about 90 per cent of Nigeria's export earnings have come from petroleum and gas. Most of its crude oil is bought by countries such as India, Spain, the Netherlands and the United States. Relying on one product is risky, because a fall in oil prices reduces the country's income.
Industries are grouped by what they do with resources.

head: Industry
What it does
Examples
rows: Takes (extracts) natural resources from land, water and under the ground. It is called primary because every other industry depends on it.
Farming, fishing, forestry, mining, quarrying, crude oil drilling
Changes the raw materials from primary industry into finished goods (manufacturing and construction).
Cement, steel, cars, textiles, food processing, refining oil
Provides services. It sells and moves goods and helps people.
Banking, teaching, health care, transport, hairdressing, telecoms services, trading

sections.h: How the three industries work together
p: Think of a loaf of bread. The farmer (primary) grows wheat. The flour mill and bakery (secondary) turn it into bread. The shop owner and the delivery rider (tertiary) bring the bread to you. If any group stops working, the others suffer.

The secondary sector has great power to change an economy because it adds value to raw materials, gives skilled jobs and creates goods for export. The tertiary sector is now the largest sector of the world economy by value, and in Nigeria it is also the biggest part of the economy.
Besides oil, Nigeria exports agricultural products such as cocoa, rubber, sesame seeds, cashew nuts and palm products. Palm oil was Nigeria's most important export before oil was found.

units.title: Agriculture: Meaning, Components and Systems
units.summary: What agriculture is, its four parts (crops, livestock, fishing, forestry), food crops and cash crops, and the four farming systems.

p: Agriculture is the production of crops, animals, fish and forest resources for food and other uses by people. It is the main job of a very large share of people in West Africa.

Crop production: growing crops. Food crops are grown mainly to be eaten at home, such as maize, rice, beans, cocoyam, yam, tomatoes, millet. Cash crops are grown mainly to be sold at home or abroad, such as cocoa, oil palm, rubber, palm kernel, cotton and groundnut. A crop can be both: a farmer may eat some of his maize and sell the rest.
Livestock: rearing domestic animals such as cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, horses and donkeys, and also poultry. Most are reared for meat, milk, eggs, hides and work.
Fishing: catching and breeding fish from rivers, lakes, ponds and the sea. It is a main job in riverine and coastal areas.
Forestry: looking after economic trees and taking products from forests such as timber, plywood, poles, paper pulp and boats.

Plantation farming: large estates of land permanently planted with one commercial crop, such as rubber, oil palm, sugarcane or cotton. The land may belong to government, private people or companies. It needs a lot of capital and many workers.

Peasant (subsistence) farming: farming on small pieces of land, mostly by family labour, with simple tools such as cutlasses, hoes and axes. Much of the produce is eaten by the family and only the surplus is sold. Land is often owned by the family or community.
Co-operative farming: farmers form a society or union to help one another. Together they obtain loans, buy fertiliser and seeds, hire or buy machines and sell their produce at better prices.

Mechanized farming: using machines such as tractors, ploughs and harvesters instead of human labour. It allows large-scale production, but machines are costly and the system is not yet widespread in West Africa.

units.title: Importance and Problems of Agriculture, and How Nigerian Farming Has Changed
units.summary: Why agriculture matters, the problems farmers face and their solutions, and the story of Nigerian agriculture since oil was found.

p: It gives raw materials to industries (cotton for textiles, cocoa for chocolate, rubber for tyres). It gives food. It gives jobs to many people. It creates a market for industrial products such as tools, fertiliser and clothes. It is a source of income for farmers and of foreign exchange for the country. It supplies labour to industries when people move from farms to towns.

Illiteracy and ignorance of modern methods. Lack of medical facilities in rural areas. Use of crude tools such as hoes and cutlasses. Poverty of farmers. Lack of credit (loans). Poor storage, so food rots. Poor roads and transport. Problems of the land tenure system (land is divided among families or owned by a few, so farms are small). Pests and diseases. Natural disasters such as flood and drought.

Give farmers cheap loans. Build better roads and storage. Discourage the movement of young people from rural areas to towns (by providing amenities there). Encourage the use of machines. Control pests and diseases. Provide medical facilities. Educate farmers. Use research to produce improved seeds and animals. Use irrigation so that farming does not depend only on rain.

Before the 1970s, Nigeria exported cocoa, palm oil, groundnut and cotton. When oil prices rose sharply in the 1970s, money from petroleum became the main source of income. Many young people left the villages for the towns, and farm production fell. By the mid-1970s Nigeria had to import food such as rice. Population also grew fast, so the food shortage became worse.

Many farmers are small-scale, using hoes and cutlasses on small plots. Poor storage, poor transport, lack of money and the shortage of land hold farm output down. Yam and cassava are the main food crops in the south. Sorghum, millet, cowpea (beans) and maize are the main food crops in the north. Rice is grown in many areas. Oil palm, cocoa and rubber are the main industrial crops of the south, and groundnut and cotton of the north. Cocoa is still the biggest agricultural export.

Governments have tried to help. The Operation Feed the Nation programme (1976 to 1980) encouraged people to farm any empty plot of land. In the 1980s the government closed the produce marketing boards, which had paid farmers prices fixed by government, so that farmers could be paid better prices and plant more tree crops. Governments also set up plantations of oil palm, rubber and cocoa. Fulani herders are still the main source of beef, and fishing supplies more than half of the fish eaten in the country. Lake Chad, the coastal waters and the rivers are the main sources of fish.

units.title: Mining: Meaning, Components, Minerals and Their Uses
units.summary: What mining is, the three parts of the mining sector, Nigerian minerals and where they are found, and what they are used for.

p: Mining is taking useful minerals and metals out of the earth, including from under the sea. Examples are crude oil, gold, iron ore, diamond, coal, limestone, copper and gravel. Crude oil was first found in commercial quantity at Oloibiri (now in Bayelsa State) in 1956 and became the most important source of government money and foreign exchange. Coal mining began near Enugu in 1915.
The mining sector is all the businesses that look for mineral deposits and take valuable minerals from the earth to sell. It has three components.
1. Exploration and mining (upstream): finding mineral deposits in amounts large enough to be worth mining, and then digging them out.

2. Processing and beneficiation (midstream): changing minerals from their natural form into finished or semi-finished goods. For example, cement companies turn limestone into cement, and a jeweller turns raw gold into rings and watches.
3. Marketing and transportation: wholesalers, retailers, agents and drivers who move the products to the final users.

units.title: Effects of Mining and How to Reduce the Bad Effects
units.summary: The good and bad effects of mining on a country and its people, and the steps that can reduce harm.

p: Revenue: taxes, royalties and licence fees from mining companies give money to government. Raw materials: limestone for cement, granite and gravel for building. Better living standards: money from minerals can pay for roads, schools, hospitals and power. Foreign exchange: exports of oil, coal and tin earn dollars and other foreign money and can improve the balance of payments (the record of a country's payments to other countries and receipts from them in a year). Employment: mining gives jobs in digging, processing, transport and sales.

Deforestation: large areas of forest are cleared for mines. Food chain damage: mining chemicals and heavy metals enter water and soil, poison plants and fish and finally harm people who eat them. Air pollution: heavy machines and burning gas release harmful gases and dust. Erosion: digging deep pits makes land unfit for farming and houses. Noise: loud machines can damage the hearing of workers who have no ear protection. In oil areas such as the Niger Delta, oil spills also destroy farms and fishing waters.

sections.h: Ways to reduce the bad effects
p: Government rules: laws that make companies mine responsibly, protect workers and clean up after mining. Reduce consumption: when we buy the newest phone or clothes we do not need, factories use more minerals. Using things longer reduces demand. Education: teach children and the public about the harm mining can do. Proper waste disposal: companies should treat and recycle waste. Better efficiency: watching the supply chain closely helps to find where waste can be cut, so mining harms the environment less. Replanting trees and restoring mined land also helps.

units.title: Financial Institutions and Their Types
units.summary: What a financial institution is, and the traditional institutions, insurance companies, the central bank, commercial banks, development banks and the stock exchange.

p: Financial institutions are organisations that deal mainly in money. They collect savings and spare money from individuals and firms and lend it to those who need it for spending or investment. They link savers with borrowers.

The esusu (also called ajo or adashi in different areas) is a traditional savings club. Members agree to pay a fixed sum at regular times, and each time one member collects the whole amount, until everyone has received a turn. It is a way of saving and borrowing without a bank.

An insurance company protects a person or business against loss. The customer pays a small amount, called a premium, and the company pays when the loss it has agreed to cover (fire, theft, accident, death) happens. Insurance companies also invest the premiums they collect.

The central bank manages the country's money and banking system. Its functions are to issue notes and coins; to act as the bankers' bank (commercial banks keep accounts with it); to act as banker and adviser to the government; to act as lender of last resort (commercial banks borrow from it when no one else will lend); to control the supply of money and credit; and to look after the foreign reserves.

Commercial banks accept deposits from customers and pay them back on demand. Their functions are to accept deposits (current, savings and fixed deposit accounts); to lend money to individuals, businesses and government; to keep valuables safely; to make payments and transfers for customers (cheques, transfers, cards); and to help government to circulate new money and withdraw old money. Examples: Access Bank, GTBank, Zenith Bank, First Bank, UBA.

Development banks are set up by government to give long-term loans at low interest to special sectors such as agriculture, industry and housing that ordinary banks may not want to lend to. Examples in Nigeria are the Bank of Industry (BOI), the Bank of Agriculture (BOA) and the Federal Mortgage Bank. (Older notes mention NIDB, NBCI and NACB. These were merged into newer banks such as the Bank of Industry.)
The stock exchange is a market that brings together people who want to sell shares and stocks and people who want to buy them. In Nigeria it is now called the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) in Lagos.

units.title: The Money Market, the Capital Market and Other Institutions
units.summary: Short-term and long-term markets for money, primary and secondary markets, and special terms such as bureau de change, debenture and market capitalisation.

p: The money market is where short-term funds (usually one year or less) are lent and borrowed. It helps those with too little money (the deficit sector) to borrow from those with extra money (the surplus sector). The institutions in it are commercial banks, merchant banks, the Central Bank, discount houses and hire purchase companies. Its benefits: the public can invest money for a short time and earn interest, and firms and governments can borrow quickly for short-term projects.

The capital market is the market for long-term funds (more than one year) used for investment. The Nigerian Exchange is its centre. The capital market has two divisions. The primary market sells new securities (new shares and debentures) for the first time. Ways of offering include offer for subscription (inviting the public to buy), rights issue and debentures. The secondary market is the stock exchange, where securities that were already issued are bought and sold between investors. Institutions that work in this market include insurance companies, issuing houses, development banks, investment banks, mortgage banks and the stock exchange.

head: Money market
Capital market
rows: Treasury bills, bank loans, commercial paper

p: Bureau de change: a licensed business that buys and sells foreign money (for example dollars and pounds). They were authorised in 1989 to make foreign exchange easier to get for small users.
Discount house: a special non-bank institution that collects money from the surplus sector and channels it to the deficit sector. It acts between the CBN, banks and other institutions.
Distressed banks: banks with problems such as shortage of cash, poor earnings and loans that are not repaid.
New issues: shares or other securities offered to the public for the first time in the primary market.
Rights issue: new shares offered first to the company's existing shareholders in proportion to the shares they hold, usually at a price below the market price.
Debenture: a loan to a company that earns fixed interest.
Preference share: a share whose holders are paid their fixed dividend before ordinary shareholders.
Market capitalisation: the market value of all a company's shares. It equals the price of one share multiplied by the number of shares. Example: 1 million shares at N50 each gives N50 million.

units.title: Money and Trade by Barter
units.summary: What money is, how barter works, its advantages and problems, and how money began.

p: Money is anything that people in a country generally accept as payment for goods and services and for paying debts. It is a medium of exchange that represents value. Money that the law says must be accepted is called legal tender. In Nigeria the legal tender is the naira (N) in notes and coins issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria.

Barter is the direct exchange of goods or services for other goods or services, without using money. It is the oldest form of trade. Examples: exchanging a science textbook for a history textbook, a farmer giving yams for a fisherman's fish, or a plumber repairing a pipe for a dentist who treats the plumber's teeth.

It is a practical way to trade when people have little cash or when the economy is weak. It uses goods and services that would otherwise be wasted. Natural resources are less likely to be over-used because people trade only what they need. Wealth and power are less likely to be gathered in a few hands. There is no balance of payments or foreign exchange crisis. It reduces waste because people swap what they do not need.

There is no common measure of value, so it is hard to decide how many tomatoes equal one shirt. There is no standard unit of account. There is the double coincidence of wants problem: you must find someone who needs what you have and also has what you need. It is hard to store wealth, especially in perishable goods like yam and fresh tomatoes. It is not possible to make deferred payments (promising to pay later) easily. Large items such as a cow cannot be divided without losing their value.

Money began because of the problems of barter. In the past, different commodities were used as money in different places: cattle, cowries, shells, salt, tobacco and beads. Cowries were used as money in West Africa for centuries. Later, precious metals such as gold and silver were used because they last long, can be divided and are valuable in small amounts.

Paper money began with goldsmiths in London who gave receipts for gold deposited with them. People found it easier to trade with the receipts than with the gold, so the receipts became banknotes and the goldsmiths became bankers. Today, most countries use paper money and coins that are not backed by gold. They work because people trust the government that issued them.

units.title: Functions and Qualities of Money
units.summary: The five functions of money, and the qualities that make good money, including acceptability, portability, durability, divisibility and stability.

p: 1. Medium of exchange: money is accepted in return for goods and services. This removes the problem of double coincidence of wants. This is its most important function.
2. Store of value: money can be kept and used later. To be a good store of value, it must keep its worth over time. If it lost value quickly, nobody would accept it as payment.

3. Unit of account (measure of value): money gives a common unit for pricing everything. We say a pen costs N200 and a book costs N1,000, so we can compare them, record business accounts, and compare wages for different jobs.
4. Standard for deferred (later) payment: money lets people buy now and pay later, borrow and lend, and make contracts that are paid in the future, such as loans and mortgages.
Some books list 'measure of value' and 'unit of account' separately, but they are the same idea.

General acceptability: everybody is willing to take it, and the law makes it legal tender. Portability: it is easy to carry and move. Durability: it lasts for a long time without wearing out. Ice and fruits are poor money because they melt or spoil. Divisibility: it can be split into small units to buy small things. A cow cannot be divided without losing its value, but N1,000 can be divided into smaller notes and coins. Homogeneity: all units of the same value look and feel the same and are of equal quality. Cognizability: it is easy to recognise and tell its value, and difficult to forge. Stability: its value does not change much from time to time. This is the most important quality, because if the value keeps changing, money cannot work as a measure of value or a store of value. Relative scarcity: it must not be too plentiful, or it will lose its value.

units.title: Types of Money, Money Compared with Barter, and Why People Hold Money
units.summary: Commodity, representative, fiat, token and deposit money, similarities and differences between money and barter, and the three motives for holding money.

p: Commodity money: a useful item with value of its own that is used as money, such as gold, cattle, beads and salt.
Representative money: a paper certificate that stands for a commodity kept in a vault. For example, a certificate that can be exchanged for a fixed amount of gold.

Fiat money: money that the government says is legal tender but that is not backed by gold or another commodity. Its value comes from the order of the government and people's trust. Nigerian naira notes are fiat money.
Bank notes and coins (currency): money issued by the central bank, in denominations such as N100, N200, N500 and N1,000. (The old N5, N10, N20 and N50 notes are now coins or are no longer used.)
Token money: coins or notes whose face value is greater than the value of the metal or paper they are made from.
Deposit (bank) money: money in the bank accounts of customers. It can be moved by transfer, cheque or card. A cheque is only an order to the bank to pay; the cheque is not itself money.
Similarities: the price of goods in both is decided by demand and supply; money and other goods both have markets; the value of both can go up or down; both are used in exchange; people demand both.

Differences: money does not need a double coincidence of wants but barter does. Money gives a common measure of value but barter does not. Money is easy to move but many goods are not. Money is generally acceptable but goods are not. Money can be divided into small units but many goods cannot. Money can last long and store value but many goods spoil.

Economists give three motives (reasons) for holding money in cash form. The transactions motive: to pay for daily needs such as food, transport and school fees. The precautionary motive: to be ready for emergencies such as illness, accidents or death. The speculative motive: to keep cash because you expect prices of goods or shares to fall (so you can buy cheaply later) or to wait for a good chance to invest.

People also hold money because it is a good store of value and is generally acceptable. (The source notes list these two as additional points, but strictly they are reasons why money is useful rather than motives for holding it.)

units.title: Channels of Distribution: The Wholesaler and the Retailer
units.summary: The path goods take from producer to consumer, and the functions of wholesalers and retailers.

sections.h: What is a channel of distribution?
p: A channel of distribution is the path a product takes from the producer to the consumer. It includes the people and firms in between (agents, wholesalers and retailers) and the services of transport, storage and finance. Good distribution makes sure that the right product gets to the right place, at the right time, in the right amount and at a price people can pay.

img.alt: Four routes from producer to consumer: direct; producer to retailer to consumer; the long chain through wholesaler and retailer; and the route through an agent
img.cap: Channels of distribution. The longer the chain, the more middlemen there are.

p: A wholesaler buys goods in large quantities from producers and sells them in smaller quantities to retailers.

Functions to the manufacturer: finds a market and advertises products; gives information about the market (what sells and what does not); finances the producer by buying and paying quickly; stores goods so that the producer does not need big warehouses; bears risks such as falling prices, damage and spoilage; gives advice on the kind and quantity of goods to produce.

Functions to the retailer: allows the retailer to stock many kinds of goods; breaks bulk (sells in small amounts because manufacturers sell only in large amounts); gives credit; may deliver goods and so saves the retailer the cost of a van; introduces new products; helps to promote the retailer's sales.
The retailer is the last link in the chain. Retailers buy from wholesalers and sell to the final consumer.

Functions: they keep a variety of goods near where consumers live. They sometimes sell on credit. They advise customers on the best brand and how to use it. Retail trade needs little capital, so it gives work to many people. They tell producers what customers want, so production is not wasted, and tell customers about new products. They give after-sales service such as delivery and servicing of TVs, cars and radios. They open for long hours, even on holidays, and are close to homes.

units.title: Government, Co-operative Societies and Distribution
units.summary: How government agencies and co-operative societies help distribution and keep prices fair.

p: Government trading agencies (for example, state-owned stores and marketing boards) join in distributive trade to protect consumers. They reduce the number of middlemen in the chain. They reduce the exploitation of consumers by middlemen. They help to stabilise prices. They ensure a regular supply of goods. They prevent hoarding (keeping goods hidden to sell later at higher prices).

A co-operative society is a group of people with the same goal who pool their resources. It is run democratically: each member has one vote regardless of how much they have put in. Profits are shared according to how much each member has purchased (or sold) through the society.
Types: consumers' co-operative societies (which may be wholesale or retail associations) and farmers' (producers') co-operative societies.

They give credit to members. They stop hoarding by middlemen. They bring products closer to members. They help stabilise prices by selling at lower prices to members. They sell goods in small amounts to members.

units.title: Business Finance: Equity and Debt
units.summary: How a business raises money by selling ownership (ordinary and preference shares, retained profit) or by borrowing (loans, overdrafts, trade credit, bonds).

p: Finance is the lifeblood of a business. Firms need money to buy equipment and stock, pay workers and expand. The money can come from the owners (equity) or from lenders (debt). Each method has costs and benefits, so a business chooses according to cost, control, repayment terms and its stage of growth.
In equity financing, a company raises money by selling a share of ownership. Buyers become shareholders and share in profits.

Ordinary shares (common stock): holders have voting rights, for example in electing directors. The dividend is not fixed; it is paid only if the company declares a profit. If the company closes down, ordinary shareholders are paid last, so the risk is high. Advantages to the company: no repayment duty, and attracts long-term investors. Disadvantages: control is shared with more people (dilution), and dividends are not an expense that reduces tax.

Preference shareholders usually get a fixed dividend, paid before ordinary shareholders, but normally have no voting rights. If the company closes, they are paid before ordinary shareholders but after lenders. Advantages: steady income to investors and lower risk than ordinary shares. Disadvantages: the fixed dividend is a cost to the company whenever profit is available, and preference holders do not gain much when the company grows.

Retained earnings (ploughed-back profit) are profits kept in the business rather than shared as dividends. Advantages: no interest and no repayment, and owners keep full control. Disadvantages: limited by how much profit the company makes, and shareholders may be unhappy if they expected dividends.
In debt financing, a business borrows money and repays it with interest. Lenders do not become owners.

Short-term loans: an overdraft lets a business withdraw more than it has in its account up to an agreed limit, and interest is charged only on the amount used. Trade credit means a supplier lets the business take goods now and pay in about 30 to 90 days. Advantages: flexible and easy to get; trade credit usually needs no security. Disadvantages: overdrafts have high interest, and late payment can spoil relations with suppliers.

Long-term loans: term loans are repaid over several years; mortgages are loans secured on property. Advantages: a fixed repayment plan helps planning, and the interest is normally an allowable business expense. Disadvantages: strict repayment, and a defaulter can lose the asset pledged as security; a good credit record is needed.

Bonds (debentures): long-term loans from investors, paid with regular interest and with the principal returned at a fixed date. Advantages: usually lower interest than bank loans, and they can be traded. Disadvantages: the company must pay even in bad times, and it needs a good credit rating.

units.title: Business Finance: Hybrid and Alternative Sources
units.summary: Convertible debentures, leasing, venture capital, angel investors and crowdfunding, with how to choose a source.

p: A hybrid instrument has features of both equity and debt. A convertible debenture is a loan that can later be changed into shares in the company. Advantages: lower interest because of the conversion option, and the company does not give up ownership immediately. Disadvantage: ownership is shared later if the debenture holders convert.

In leasing, a business uses an asset (such as a vehicle or machine) and pays regular rent to the owner (the lessor), who keeps ownership. Advantages: no big cost at the start, and access to modern equipment without long-term commitment. Disadvantages: total payments may be more than the purchase price, and the business gets no ownership benefits.

Venture capital firms invest money in young businesses with high growth potential in return for part-ownership (equity). Angel investors are wealthy individuals who invest their own money in early-stage businesses. Advantages: they bring advice, skills and business contacts, and the money need not be repaid if the business fails. Disadvantages: the founders lose some control, and the investors expect large returns.

Crowdfunding means raising small amounts of money from many people, usually through websites. Advantages: no need for banks, and public interest shows whether the idea has a market. Disadvantages: strong competition for attention, and ideas shown publicly can be copied.

The best source depends on cost, control, repayment terms and the stage of the business. Equity avoids debt but shares ownership. Debt keeps control but must be repaid. Hybrid and alternative sources can suit businesses with special needs. Other sources in Nigeria include cooperative loans, the Bank of Industry, microfinance banks, esusu contributions and government grants.

units.title: The Production Possibility Curve and Opportunity Cost
units.summary: How a country's choices between two goods are shown on the PPC, why it slopes downward and curves outward, and the link with opportunity cost.

p: The production possibility curve (PPC), also called the production possibility boundary, is a graph that shows all the combinations of two goods that a country can produce when it uses all its resources fully and efficiently with the technology it has.
The main idea: resources are limited. To make more of one good, the country must make less of the other. So the PPC slopes downward from left to right.

sections.h: Example: consumer goods and capital goods
p: Consumer goods (such as food and clothes) satisfy wants directly. Capital goods (such as machines) are used to make other goods. A country has the following choices.

If the country puts all its resources into capital goods, it can make 140 units of capital goods and no consumer goods. If it puts everything into consumer goods, it can make 140 units of consumer goods and no capital goods.

head: Combination
Consumer goods
Capital goods

img.alt: A curve bowed outward from 140 capital goods at the top left to 140 consumer goods at the bottom right, with points inside and outside the curve marked
img.cap: The PPC for consumer goods and capital goods. Points on the curve are efficient; inside the curve is wasteful; outside is not possible now.

p: On the curve: resources are fully used. Inside the curve (point X): some resources are idle or wasted, for example because of unemployment, so the economy could produce more. Outside the curve (point Y): production is not possible with the present resources and technology. The curve can move outwards if the country gets more resources or better technology (economic growth).

Opportunity cost is the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made. On the PPC, the opportunity cost of getting more of one good is the amount of the other good given up. In the table above, going from D to E means 20 more consumer goods, which costs 20 capital goods. Going from F to G costs 50 capital goods for the same 20 consumer goods. The cost rises because resources are not equally good at making both goods; this is why the curve bends outward.

units.title: Total, Average and Marginal Productivity
units.summary: How to work out total, average and marginal product, with a worked table, graphs and the link between them.

p: Total product (or total output) is the whole quantity produced by all the units of the factors employed. TP = AP × number of workers.
Example: 60 men work on a farm and each produces an average of 30 tonnes of rice. TP = 30 × 60 = 1,800 tonnes.
Average product is the output per unit of the variable factor (such as labour). AP = TP ÷ number of workers.
Example: 4,000 tonnes of maize are harvested by 80 men in a day. AP = 4,000 ÷ 80 = 50 tonnes per person.

Marginal product is the extra output obtained when one more unit of the variable factor is used. MP = change in TP ÷ change in number of workers. MP can be negative when adding a worker lowers the total output (for example because the field is too crowded).
Example: if the farm adds one man to the 80 men and the harvest becomes 4,080 tonnes, MP = (4,080 − 4,000) ÷ (81 − 80) = 80 tonnes.
Here is a table for a small farm where land is fixed and the number of workers is changed.

img.alt: Two graphs: total product rising to a peak at 6 workers and then falling; average and marginal product curves with marginal product crossing average product at its highest point and going negative at 7 workers
img.cap: Total product (top) and average and marginal product (bottom), from the table.

p: At first, TP, AP and MP all rise because workers can share tasks and use the land better. MP rises to a highest point (here at 4 workers) and then falls. This is the law of diminishing returns: when more of a variable factor is added to a fixed factor, the extra output eventually starts to fall. TP rises fastest while MP is rising and reaches its highest point when MP is zero or just before it becomes negative. After that, TP falls and MP is negative. MP cuts the AP curve at the highest point of AP (the table shows AP highest at 4 workers, where MP is 16; after that MP is lower than AP so AP falls).

units.title: Cost Concepts: Fixed, Variable, Total, Average and Marginal Cost
units.summary: The meaning of cost in economics, fixed and variable costs, and how to calculate total, average and marginal cost.

p: In economics, cost is the money spent in producing goods and services. Knowing the cost helps a firm to set prices, plan production and make profit. A firm that does not know its costs cannot know whether it is making a profit or a loss.

Fixed costs do not change when the level of output changes. They must be paid even if output is zero. They are also called overhead costs. Examples: rent for the factory, salaries of permanent staff, insurance and depreciation of machinery.
Fixed costs are fixed only in the short run. In the long run, a firm can change them (for example, by moving to a cheaper building).

Variable costs change with output. They rise when more is produced and fall when less is produced. If nothing is produced, variable cost is zero. Examples: raw materials such as flour for a bakery, wages of temporary workers, fuel and electricity for machines and packaging.
Total cost is the sum of fixed and variable cost at a given output.
Formula: TC = FC + VC.
Example: fixed cost is ₦50,000 and variable cost is ₦30,000 at 100 units. TC = 50,000 + 30,000 = ₦80,000.
Average cost is the cost per unit. Formula: AC = TC ÷ Q (Q means the number of units produced).
Example: TC = ₦80,000 for 100 units. AC = 80,000 ÷ 100 = ₦800 per unit.
Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one more unit. Formula: MC = change in TC ÷ change in Q.
A bakery has fixed cost ₦10,000 and its variable cost rises as it bakes more loaves. Check each figure yourself.

units.title: Opportunity, Explicit, Implicit and Sunk Costs, and Cost Curves
units.summary: Other kinds of cost, why opportunity cost matters, the shape of the average and marginal cost curves, and how cost ideas are used.

p: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made. Examples: a student who studies instead of working part-time gives up the earnings; a farmer who plants maize instead of yam gives up the profit from yam. Opportunity cost helps people and firms to choose well and explains trade-offs when resources are limited.

Explicit costs are direct payments of money, such as wages, rent and the cost of materials. Implicit costs are the value of things owned by the business owner that are used but not paid for, such as income given up. For example, a shop owner who works in his own shop without taking a salary has an implicit cost equal to the salary he could have earned elsewhere.

Sunk costs are money already spent that cannot be recovered. They should not affect future decisions. Example: a company spends ₦1 million on research for a product that fails. The money is gone, so the company should decide on new investment by looking only at future costs and benefits.

Average cost usually falls at first, reaches a lowest point and then rises. So the AC curve is U-shaped. The marginal cost curve is also U-shaped but cuts through the AC curve at AC's lowest point. This lowest point of AC is the most efficient level of output (lowest cost per unit). When MC is below AC, AC is falling; when MC is above AC, AC is rising.

img.alt: U-shaped average cost curve AC and marginal cost curve MC, with MC cutting AC at the lowest point of AC
img.cap: The MC curve cuts the AC curve at its lowest point.

p: Pricing: many firms use cost-plus pricing, that is, adding a profit margin to the average cost. A firm that knows its marginal cost can price more competitively. A profit-making firm produces the output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue (MC = MR); this is explained in the next unit.
Government policy: subsidies reduce production costs (for example, support for fertiliser), while taxes (for example, VAT) raise costs.
Personal finance: opportunity cost helps you to choose between going to university and starting work at once.

units.title: Revenue Concepts: Total, Average and Marginal Revenue
units.summary: What revenue is, how to calculate TR, AR and MR, and how they behave in perfect competition and imperfect competition.

p: Revenue is the income a firm earns from selling goods and services. It is used with cost to find profit: profit = total revenue − total cost.
Total revenue (TR) is the total income from sales. TR = price (P) × quantity sold (Q). Example: 100 pens at ₦50 each give TR = 100 × 50 = ₦5,000.
Average revenue (AR) is revenue per unit sold. AR = TR ÷ Q. Since TR = P × Q, AR is always equal to the price. The AR curve is the same as the demand curve.
Marginal revenue (MR) is the extra revenue from selling one more unit. MR = change in TR ÷ change in Q. Example: selling 10 more units raises TR from ₦1,000 to ₦1,200, so MR = 200 ÷ 10 = ₦20.

In perfect competition, the firm is a price taker: it sells as much as it wants at the market price, so the price stays fixed whatever the quantity. Thus AR = MR = price, and TR increases in a straight line.
A firm with some control over price must lower the price to sell more. So price falls as Q rises, and AR is greater than MR. TR rises at first, reaches a peak, and then falls.

img.alt: Two graphs: in perfect competition AR and MR are one horizontal line; in imperfect competition AR slopes downward and MR slopes down more steeply below it
img.cap: AR and MR curves in perfect competition (left) and imperfect competition (right).

p: Profit maximisation: a firm earns the greatest profit at the output where MR = MC. Pricing: revenue curves help firms to choose the best price in different markets. Planning: studying revenue trends helps in production planning.

units.title: Economic Systems: Capitalism, Socialism and the Mixed Economy (Revision)
units.summary: A fuller treatment of the features, advantages and disadvantages of the three economic systems and the countries that use them.

p: An economic system is the organised way in which the means of production in a country are owned, managed and used to satisfy human wants. This unit revises First Term and gives more detail. The three types are capitalism, socialism and the mixed economy.

Private individuals own and control most of the means of production, and government control is small. Examples: the USA, Japan, Germany, France, Italy and Australia (though all of them also have some government role).

Features: private ownership of property; production and consumption guided by the price system (market forces); competition between firms; the aim of production is profit; freedom to choose any job or business; individual satisfaction; accumulation of wealth; freedom of choice for consumers; labour is treated as something bought and sold.

Advantages: freedom of enterprise; profit encourages hard work and efficiency; fast economic growth; competition; a wide choice of goods; a higher standard of living; specialisation and large-scale production; self-reliance; and technological progress.

Disadvantages: monopoly can arise; wealth is unequal; consumers and workers can be exploited; job insecurity and unemployment; unhealthy rivalry; a few people become rich while many stay poor; and profit is chased at all costs.

The state owns and controls the means of production and distribution. Historical and present examples include the former Soviet Union, Cuba and North Korea. (The notes list Poland, Romania, Mozambique, Ethiopia, Angola and Burkina Faso. These countries followed socialist policies in the past but have since moved towards market economies, so they are no longer good examples.)

Features: joint (collective) decision-making on what, how and for whom to produce; state ownership; welfare as the main aim; not all goods are produced for sale; income is shared more equally; and full use of resources and full employment.
Advantages: fairer sharing of income and resources; no exploitation by private owners; central planning; no private monopoly; economic security and guaranteed jobs.

Disadvantages: little or no choice for consumers; laziness because the state provides; less personal initiative; the state becomes a monopoly; difficulty in knowing what people want; risk of dictatorship; and no competition.
Both private individuals and the state own and control the means of production. Examples: Nigeria, Britain, Egypt, Kenya, Tanzania and Mexico.

Features: freedom of choice for consumers, workers and owners; economic freedom; joint decisions by the private and public sectors; fair competition; and the government controls or provides essential services.
Advantages: fairer incomes, job security, the good points of both systems, development, freedom of choice and encouragement of private initiative.
Disadvantages: a wide gap between rich and poor, profit may matter more than people, inefficiency in state-owned firms, corruption and mismanagement, and labour exploitation.

units.title: The Labour Market and the Labour Force
units.summary: The meaning of labour, market and labour market, who is in the labour force and who is outside it, and what affects its size.

p: Labour is the physical or mental effort that people put into producing goods and services. It includes planning, organising and supervising work. Workers are not all the same: they differ in skill, experience, health and motivation, so two workers given the same tools may produce different amounts per hour.

A market is any arrangement by which buyers and sellers come into contact to exchange goods and services, directly or through agents. In the modern economy a market is not only a place; it may be a whole region, or even the internet. Economists define a market as the whole area in which buyers and sellers are in such free contact that the price of the same good tends to become equal quickly.

The labour market is the market in which labour services are bought and sold. Workers compete for jobs, and employers compete for workers. The demand for labour and the supply of labour are determined by the amount of work to be done, the number of workers available and able to do it, and the level of wages workers accept.

The labour force (or workforce) is the number of people in the population who are employed plus those who are unemployed but looking for work. Normally the age range is 18 to 65 years (some countries use 15 to 64).

To belong to the labour force a person must be of working age, be able and willing to work, and be in a job or looking for one. (Some notes say 'able-bodied', but a person with a disability who works or looks for work is also in the labour force.)

sections.h: Persons not in the labour force
p: These make up the 'inactive population': young children, school pupils and students, pensioners, the elderly, and full-time home-makers who are neither working nor looking for work. Some of them may be of working age.

sections.h: Factors affecting the size of the labour force
p: Age: an ageing population has fewer workers because more people retire. Sex: some jobs attract mainly men or mainly women, and attitudes towards women's work affect participation. Occupation: when jobs are available in a field, people join it and the labour force grows. Education: more years of schooling delay entry into work but increase skilled workers. Migration: if more workers leave a country than enter it, the labour force falls.

units.title: Efficiency and Mobility of Labour
units.summary: What makes labour efficient, the two types of labour mobility, the factors that affect each and the obstacles to mobility.

p: Efficiency of labour is the ability of a worker to increase output without increasing the inputs, or to complete a task in the given time without wasting resources. In other words, it is the productive capacity of a worker: how much and how good the output is in a given time.

Climate: working in extreme heat or cold is harder than in a mild climate. Geographical differences: a person brought up in the plains finds it hard to work at high altitude. Mental ability and moral qualities: training helps a worker learn new skills, and discipline, punctuality and self-respect improve the work. Working conditions: a clean, safe workplace and good relations between employer and employees raise efficiency. Promotion: regular promotion motivates workers. Education and training: an educated and trained worker understands the job better. Personal qualities: intelligence, fitness, being responsible and being a team player. Health, good food and housing, and the tools and technology available also matter.

Mobility of labour is the ease with which workers can move between places or between jobs. It matters because labour is a major factor of production, and the economy does best when workers can move to where they are needed.
Geographical mobility is movement from one place to another to find work or better jobs, for example, a worker moving from Kano to Lagos, or from Nigeria to the United States.
Occupational mobility is a worker's ability to change the type of job, for example, a mechanic who trains to become an airline pilot.

Economic: unemployment and low wages push people away; jobs and high wages attract them. Social: family ties, friends and communities of the same culture. Political: political stability and protection of rights; people avoid unsafe regions. Physical: climate, geography and risk of disasters. Technological: telecommunication and the internet let some people work remotely and so reduce the need to move.
The availability of training and retraining, differences in wages (wage differentials), job security, future prospects and fringe benefits (such as housing and medical allowance).

Differences in climate, religion, customs, language and tastes. Illiteracy and ignorance of opportunities. Debt. Attachment to property and place. Poverty. Poor transport and communication. Lack of employment opportunities. The cost and length of training, and professional or union rules.

units.title: Utility: Types, Total, Marginal and Average Utility
units.summary: What utility means, time, form and place utility, and how to calculate total, marginal and average utility from a schedule.

p: Utility is the satisfaction a person gets from consuming a good or service at a particular time. A good has utility if it can satisfy a want. Utility is relative: what satisfies one person may not satisfy another, and a thing can be useful at one time and useless at another (a warm blanket in the harmattan and not at noon in March).
Time utility: a good satisfies a want at a particular time. Storing goods until they are needed creates time utility (for example, storing yam until the lean season).
Form utility: changing a good from one form to another so that it can satisfy wants. Flour does not satisfy hunger until it becomes bread, cake or chin-chin.
Place utility: moving goods from where they are less useful to where they are in demand. Cocoa produced in West Africa is moved to Europe for chocolate. Yam is moved from the farm to the market.

Total utility is the total satisfaction obtained from consuming a given amount of a good. It increases as more is consumed, but not at an equal rate, and at a point called the saturation point, no more satisfaction is gained. TU = AU × Q.
Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit. MU = change in TU ÷ change in Q. It is the difference between two consecutive total utilities.
Average utility is satisfaction per unit consumed. AU = TU ÷ Q.
Utility is measured in imaginary units called 'utils'. Check the figures.

TU rises as long as MU is positive. When MU falls to zero, TU is at its maximum. When MU is negative, TU falls. The sum of all the marginal utilities equals the total utility (for example, 10 + 6 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 25 at the fifth unit).

units.title: Diminishing Marginal Utility, Consumer Equilibrium and Consumer Surplus
units.summary: The law of diminishing marginal utility, the concept of origin, how a consumer gets the most satisfaction, the link to the demand curve, and consumer surplus.

sections.h: The law of diminishing marginal utility
p: The law states that as a consumer consumes more and more units of a good, the extra satisfaction (marginal utility) from each additional unit gets smaller. Total utility increases up to a point and then starts to fall if the consumer carries on.
Example: a very thirsty child drinks water. The first cup gives great satisfaction, the second a bit less, the third even less, and after a few cups more water gives no pleasure at all.

img.alt: Two graphs: total utility rising and levelling off at 31; marginal utility falling from 10 to zero at the seventh unit
img.cap: Total utility (left) rises while marginal utility (right) falls.

p: The concept of origin is the smallest quantity of a good that must be consumed before it gives any real satisfaction. A single drop of water gives a thirsty student no useful satisfaction; a certain minimum quantity is needed before satisfaction starts.

A consumer gets the greatest satisfaction when the marginal utility of the money spent on each good is equal. If the consumer buys only one good: MU = price (when MU is measured in money terms). If the consumer buys many goods: MUa ÷ Pa = MUb ÷ Pb = MUc ÷ Pc and so on. That means that the last naira spent on each good gives the same extra satisfaction.
Example: MU of good A is 12 and its price is ₦4, so MU per naira = 3. MU of good B is 6 and its price is ₦2, so MU per naira = 3. They are equal, so the consumer is in equilibrium.

sections.h: From utility to the demand curve
p: Because marginal utility falls as more is consumed, the consumer will pay less for each extra unit. Therefore the amount a consumer will buy rises only if the price falls. This explains why the demand curve slopes downward, and the demand curve looks like the marginal utility curve.

Consumer surplus is the difference between what a consumer is willing (expects) to pay for a good and what he actually pays. Example: a student plans to pay ₦2,000 for sandals but they cost ₦1,500. His consumer surplus is 2,000 − 1,500 = ₦500.

units.title: Indifference Curves
units.summary: What an indifference curve shows, its shape, why higher curves mean more satisfaction and why two curves cannot cross.

p: An indifference curve shows all the combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same level of satisfaction. The consumer is 'indifferent', which means he has no preference, between any two points on the same curve. If he receives combination X instead of combination Y, he feels neither better nor worse.

Example: a student gets the same satisfaction from 8 bottles of drink and 2 packets of biscuits as from 4 bottles of drink and 4 packets of biscuits, and from 2 bottles of drink and 8 packets of biscuits. All three points lie on the same indifference curve.

img.alt: Two curves bowed toward the origin, IC1 and IC2, with IC2 farther from the origin, and three points on IC1
img.cap: Two indifference curves. IC2 gives more satisfaction than IC1.

p: 1. An indifference curve slopes downward from left to right: if the consumer takes more of one good he must give up some of the other to stay equally satisfied.
2. It is bowed (convex) towards the origin, because of diminishing marginal utility: the more of one good the consumer has, the less of the other he wants to give up for it.
3. Higher indifference curves mean higher satisfaction (more of both goods).
4. Two indifference curves cannot cross each other, because two different curves stand for two different levels of satisfaction, which could not be equal at the point of crossing.
A set of curves for the same consumer is called an indifference map.

units.title: Price Determination: Equilibrium Price and Quantity
units.summary: How demand and supply together fix the price in a free market, equilibrium point, price and quantity, and how to find them from a schedule or from equations.

p: In a free market, price is decided by the interaction of demand and supply. This is called the price system or price mechanism. The price system decides how much of each good is produced, exchanged and shared. Behind every price are three things: the cost of making the good (which sets the lowest price a seller will accept), the demand of consumers (which sets the highest price buyers will pay) and competition between sellers.

The equilibrium point is the point where the demand curve cuts the supply curve. The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. The equilibrium quantity is the quantity bought and sold at that price. At the equilibrium price there is no shortage and no surplus, so there is no pressure for the price to change.

img.alt: Demand curve D sloping down and supply curve S sloping up, crossing at the equilibrium point at price 15 and quantity 60, with areas of excess supply above and excess demand below
img.cap: Equilibrium price and quantity at the point where D and S cross.

p: Yam: the table shows the quantity demanded (Qd) and the quantity supplied (Qs) at five prices. (In the source notes the headings Qs and Qd are written the wrong way round. The numbers only make sense if the first column is demand, because demand must fall as the price rises.)

If the price is higher than the equilibrium price (for example, ₦25), sellers want to sell more than buyers want to buy. There is excess supply (a surplus), so sellers lower the price. If the price is lower than the equilibrium price, buyers want more than sellers will supply. There is excess demand (a shortage), so the price rises. In both cases the price moves back to the equilibrium.
Demand and supply can be written as equations. To find the equilibrium, set Qd = Qs, solve for the price, and then put that price into either equation.

Worked example: Qd = 35 − ½p and Qs = 20 + ¼p. Set 35 − ½p = 20 + ¼p. Move terms: 35 − 20 = ¼p + ½p, so 15 = ¾p, so p = 20. Then Qd = 35 − 10 = 25. Check with Qs = 20 + 5 = 25. Equilibrium price is 20 and equilibrium quantity is 25.

Practice A: Qd = 40 − 4p and Qs = 12p − 24. (a) Find the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) If p = 6, find the excess supply. Solution: 40 − 4p = 12p − 24, so 64 = 16p, p = 4, Q = 40 − 16 = 24. At p = 6: Qd = 40 − 24 = 16 and Qs = 72 − 24 = 48, so excess supply is 48 − 16 = 32.

units.title: Changes in Equilibrium Price and the Laws of Demand and Supply
units.summary: What happens to price and quantity when demand or supply rises or falls, summarised in four rules and five laws.

p: The equilibrium price changes when demand changes, supply changes, or both. There are four basic cases. In each case we change one curve and keep the other the same.
Increase in demand (the D curve shifts to the right): there is excess demand at the old price, so price rises and the quantity bought and sold also rises.
Decrease in demand (D shifts left): excess supply at the old price, so price falls and quantity falls.
Increase in supply (S shifts right): excess supply at the old price, so price falls but quantity rises.
Decrease in supply (S shifts left): excess demand at the old price, so price rises and quantity falls.

img.alt: Four small graphs showing a rise in demand, a fall in demand, a rise in supply and a fall in supply, each with the old and new equilibrium
img.cap: The four shifts. The dotted curve is the old curve, and the solid curve is the new one.

p: Rise in demand: more people want rice before a festival, so the price of rice goes up. Fall in supply: floods destroy yam farms, so there are fewer yams and the price goes up. Rise in supply: a big tomato harvest, so tomato prices fall.

sections.h: The laws of demand and supply
p: 1. Law of demand: the lower the price, the higher the quantity demanded, and the higher the price, the lower the quantity demanded.
2. Law of supply: the higher the price, the higher the quantity supplied, and the lower the price, the lower the quantity supplied.
3. The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied is the equilibrium price.

4. An increase in demand raises both the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity, and a decrease in demand lowers both. (The source notes say 'quantity demanded' here, but it should be a change in demand.)
5. An increase in supply lowers the equilibrium price and raises the equilibrium quantity, and a decrease in supply raises the price and lowers the quantity.

units.title: Types of Demand and Types of Supply
units.summary: Derived, joint, competitive and composite demand, and joint, competitive and composite supply, each with examples.

p: Derived demand: demand for one thing that comes from the demand for another. Demand for road construction creates demand for labour, cement and gravel. Flour and sugar are demanded because people demand bread.

Joint (complementary) demand: demand for two goods that are used together. Examples: bread and butter, tea and milk, car and petrol. When the demand for one rises, the demand for the other also rises.
Competitive demand: demand for goods that are close substitutes. Examples: one brand of detergent and another, butter and margarine. If the price of one goes up, people buy more of the other.
Composite demand: demand for a good that has more than one use. Example: sugar is used in homes for drinks and in industry for biscuits and sweets. If industry buys more, less is left for homes.

Joint (complementary) supply: two or more goods are produced from the same source, so more of one means more of the other. Example: petrol and kerosene both come from crude oil; cattle give meat and hides.

Competitive supply: goods that serve the same purpose are supplied by different producers, or one producer must choose between them. Examples: fish and meat; one toothpaste brand and another. If a farmer uses land for maize, he cannot use the same land for yam.

Composite supply: a good that can be used for more than one purpose. The supply to one use reduces the supply available for the other. Example: sugarcane that can be used to make sugar or ethanol, or land that can be used for farms or buildings. (The source notes give crude oil, petrol and kerosene as the example of composite supply, but that is really joint supply, because both come out of the crude oil together.)

units.title: Market Structures: Perfect and Imperfect Markets
units.summary: What a market is, how markets are classified, and the features of a perfect market and of imperfect markets: monopolistic competition, oligopoly, duopoly, monopsony and oligopsony.

p: A market is any arrangement that brings buyers and sellers together to trade. Markets can be grouped by the type of goods (labour market, consumer goods market, capital market, money market), by how goods move, or by how prices are set (perfect and imperfect markets). Market structure means the features of a market, such as the number of buyers and sellers and the type of product.
A perfect market is one in which the price is decided only by demand and supply, with no interference. It exists only if these conditions hold.
1. Homogeneous goods: all units are identical, with no brand names.
2. A very large number of buyers and sellers, none of whom can change the price on his own.
3. Perfect knowledge: buyers and sellers know all prices.
4. Free entry and exit of firms.
5. No cost of moving goods (assumed).
6. All firms have identical costs.
A perfect market does not exist in real life. It is a model. Farm produce markets come closest.

An imperfect market is one where the sellers or buyers can influence the price. Its features: goods are not identical (trademarks and branding); few buyers or sellers; information is not freely available; sellers can charge different prices to different people; firms cannot freely enter or leave; and transport costs exist.

Monopolistic competition: many sellers selling similar but not identical goods (restaurants, hair salons, soap brands). Oligopoly: a few large sellers; their actions affect each other (telecoms firms MTN, Airtel, Glo; cement producers). Duopoly: only two sellers. Monopsony: only one buyer (for example, one factory buying the whole of a local crop). Oligopsony: only a few buyers and many sellers. Monopoly: only one seller (see the next unit).

units.title: Monopoly
units.summary: What a monopoly is, how it arises, its advantages and disadvantages, and how it can be controlled.

p: A monopoly is a market with only one producer or seller of a good or service that has no close substitute. The monopolist is a price maker: he can choose the price (or the quantity) because there are no competitors, although he cannot decide both at once, because buyers decide how much to buy at that price.

Act of the government: a law gives one organisation the sole right to supply a good or service (for example, a public corporation). Patents and copyright: a patent gives an inventor the sole right to use his invention for a number of years. Natural causes: resources are unevenly spread, so some areas have resources that others lack (crude oil in the Niger Delta). Merging of firms: joining to eliminate competitors. Protection of public interest: government gives a firm special rights to supply essential services such as electricity. High technology: a firm with very advanced methods may produce so cheaply that competitors cannot survive.

Less over-production because the monopolist estimates demand carefully. No wasteful duplication of resources. Possible efficiency and full use of resources. Because he produces on a large scale, cost and price per unit may be lower. Profits may be used for research and invention.

Consumers may be exploited by high prices. The monopolist may restrict output (or hoard) to keep prices high. Lack of competition may reduce efficiency and creativity. Consumers have no choice. A big monopoly may pressurise the government to make laws in its favour.

Government can set laws against unfair practices and fix maximum prices for monopolies. Government can allow other firms to enter (for example, by ending state monopolies, a process called privatisation or liberalisation). It can reduce import duties (tariffs) so that foreign goods compete with the monopolist. It can discourage mergers that create monopolies. It can encourage the production of substitutes. (The notes suggest stopping patents, but patents last only for a limited time and reward inventors, so abolishing them could reduce new inventions.)

units.title: Price and Output Under Perfect Competition, Monopoly and Oligopoly
units.summary: How firms in different markets choose output and price, with graphs of short-run and long-run profit.

p: Every firm earns the greatest profit at the output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue (MC = MR), with MC cutting MR from below. If it makes one more unit when MC is below MR, profit rises. If it makes one more unit when MC is above MR, profit falls.

The firm is a price taker, because there are many buyers and sellers. The price is set by demand and supply in the whole market. The firm's demand curve is a horizontal line at that price (AR = MR = P).
Short run: if the price is above the average cost at the profit-maximising output, the firm makes supernormal (abnormal) profit. This is the rectangle between price and AC.

Long run: supernormal profit attracts new firms. Supply rises and the price falls until it equals the lowest point of the AC curve. Then each firm earns only normal profit (just enough to keep it in business). Long-run equilibrium: MC = MR = AC = AR = P.

img.alt: Two graphs of a perfectly competitive firm: on the left price above average cost gives a profit rectangle; on the right price equals the lowest average cost so only normal profit
img.cap: A perfectly competitive firm: short run (left) and long run (right).

p: The monopolist controls the price or quantity. His demand curve is the downward-sloping AR curve and the MR curve lies below it. He makes maximum profit at MC = MR and charges the price shown on the AR curve at that output. If demand is inelastic (customers keep buying), he can charge a higher price; if demand is elastic, he must keep the price lower. Because new firms cannot enter, he can keep earning supernormal profit in both the short run and the long run.

img.alt: Monopoly graph with downward AR and MR curves, U-shaped MC and AC, the profit-maximising output at MC equals MR and the profit rectangle between price and average cost
img.cap: A monopolist maximises profit where MC = MR; the shaded rectangle is supernormal profit.

p: In an oligopoly, a few firms dominate. The price and output decisions of one affect the others. They may agree together (collude) to fix prices and share the market, in which case they act like a monopoly and earn high profit. Without such agreement, they avoid price wars because a price cut by one will be copied by the others. They compete instead by advertising, branding, packaging, quality and after-sales service. (The source notes claim that oligopolists with differentiated products can change prices without fear of rivals' reactions. This is not correct: firms in an oligopoly always watch their rivals.)

units.title: Industries in Nigeria
units.summary: The four groups of Nigerian industry (primary, secondary, tertiary and emerging) and the main industrial zones and what each makes.

p: An industry is a group of businesses that produce similar goods or services. Industries are important to an economy because they create jobs, add value to raw materials and earn money from sales and exports.

Primary: farming (cocoa, cassava, palm oil, rubber), mining and forestry. Secondary: manufacturing (textiles, cement, food processing, assembly of vehicles) and construction, which builds roads, bridges and houses. Tertiary: services such as banking, education, health care, telecommunications, transport and tourism. Emerging sectors: new areas where technology and new business ideas are growing quickly, such as information technology (software and start-ups), financial technology and renewable energy (solar and wind).

Northern zone: Kano is the oldest industrial centre in the north, known for textiles, leather (tanneries) and food processing. Kaduna and Zaria have textile mills and vehicle assembly. The Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, is mainly administrative but has growing services and information technology. Other states of the north-central zone such as Niger, Kogi, Kwara, Plateau, Benue and Nasarawa have agricultural processing and solid minerals industries.

South-South (Niger Delta) zone: Edo and Delta have oil and gas, and Delta has oil refining. Port Harcourt in Rivers State is a major oil and gas centre with a refinery and petrochemical works. The Bonny liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal is nearby.

Western zone: Lagos is the biggest economic centre, with manufacturing, finance, technology and media. Ikeja is known for electrical goods. Apapa and Tin Can have the biggest seaports. Ogun State, around Ota and Agbara, is a major industrial area for pharmaceuticals and consumer goods. The Dangote refinery and petrochemical plant is at Lekki, Lagos.
South-East zone: Aba is known for leather goods and clothing made by small firms, and Onitsha and Nnewi for trade and spare parts.

units.title: Problems of Manufacturing Industries in Nigeria and Their Solutions
units.summary: The main problems that slow down Nigerian industries and practical ways to solve them.

p: 1. Infrastructure: unreliable power supply and poor roads, rail and ports. Firms must run generators, which raises costs.
2. Policy changes: sudden changes in government policy, taxes and regulations make planning hard.
3. Insecurity: security problems in some regions disrupt production, transport and investment.
4. Access to finance: small and medium enterprises (SMEs) find it hard to get loans at reasonable interest rates.
5. Global economic conditions: world prices, exchange rates and trade rules affect firms that import materials or export goods.
6. Shortage of skilled labour: a lack of trained technicians and managers reduces productivity and new ideas.
7. Dependence on oil: heavy reliance on oil income makes the whole economy weak when oil prices fall, and gives industry less attention.
8. Other problems: competition from cheap imports, smuggling, multiple taxes, and a weak market for some local goods.
1. Infrastructure: invest in power (including solar), roads, rail and ports, with government and private partnership.
2. Policy: keep policies stable and clear, and let industry associations discuss policy with government.
3. Finance: banks and development banks should design special loans for manufacturers; government should support schemes that help SMEs; seek foreign investment.
4. Skills: link schools, technical colleges and universities with industry; offer apprenticeships and on-the-job training.
5. Exports: improve product quality, meet international standards, use trade agreements such as the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to find markets.
6. Local sourcing: use more local raw materials, support local suppliers and build a reliable supply chain.
7. Security: improve security so that factories and transport can operate safely.
8. Diversify the economy so that industry, agriculture and services produce more of the national income.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 Chemistry First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Chemistry is the study of matter: what things are made of, how they behave and how they change. The soap you wash with, the food you cook, the medicines you take, the petrol in a car and even your own body work because of chemistry. In SS1 you will build the foundation on which all later chemistry rests.

In First Term you will learn what chemistry is and how it began, the apparatus used in the laboratory, the states of matter, how mixtures are separated, the structure of the atom, the periodic table, the laws of chemical combination, acids, bases and salts, and finally how to write symbols, formulae and balanced equations.

Each unit has simple notes, tables, diagrams and worked examples. Read slowly, copy the diagrams and tables into your notebook, and try every worked example yourself before you look at the answer. At the end of each unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you to check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

Chemistry uses special words. Learn the key words listed at the top of each unit, and always write chemical symbols and formulae correctly (capital letter first, small letter second, small numbers below the line).
