units.title: What Chemistry Is and the History of Chemistry
units.summary: The definition of chemistry, why it is called the central science, and the four periods of its history from the earliest humans to today.

p: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure, properties and changes of matter.

Composition means the kinds of elements or compounds a substance is made of. Structure means how the atoms or molecules are arranged. Properties are physical (colour, boiling point, density) or chemical (reactivity, flammability). Changes are physical (melting, dissolving) or chemical (rusting, burning, fermentation).

img.alt: A diagram with Chemistry at the centre linked to physics, engineering, geology, and to composition, structure, properties and changes, with the four periods of its history below
img.cap: Chemistry is the central science. It links the other sciences and studies composition, structure, properties and changes of matter.

p: Chemistry is called the central science because it connects physics, biology, geology, medicine, engineering and many other subjects. A doctor needs it to understand drugs, a farmer needs it for fertilisers and a builder needs it for cement.

Early humans learned to use fire, cook food, make pottery and use natural dyes. The Egyptians made glass, processed papyrus, preserved bodies (mummification) and extracted gold and copper. The Chinese made gunpowder from saltpetre, charcoal and sulphur. All this was done by observation and trial and error, not by scientific theory.

Alchemy began in Egypt and Arabia and later spread to Europe. Alchemists tried to turn cheap metals such as lead into gold (transmutation) and to find an 'elixir of life' that would give a person long life. They failed, but they discovered useful laboratory methods: distillation, filtration, crystallisation, and the use of apparatus such as the alembic. Jabir ibn Hayyan (known in Europe as Geber) is called the father of chemistry in the Arab world.

sections.h: 3. The age of modern chemistry (1600s to 1800s)
p: Robert Boyle (1627 to 1691) stressed the use of experiments and gave Boyle's law for gases. Antoine Lavoisier (1743 to 1794), the 'father of modern chemistry', gave the law of conservation of mass, showed what burning really is and named oxygen and hydrogen. John Dalton proposed the atomic theory in 1803: matter is made of tiny particles called atoms.

Dmitri Mendeleev made the periodic table in 1869 and later chemists refined it. The electron, proton and neutron were discovered and the structure of the atom became clear. Chemistry now includes organic chemistry, biochemistry, materials science and nuclear chemistry, and affects medicine, farming, electronics, cosmetics and the environment.

units.title: Branches and Importance of Chemistry
units.summary: The major and applied branches of chemistry and why chemistry matters in daily life, industry, medicine and the environment.

p: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds (except carbonates and simple oxides such as carbon dioxide). Examples: fuels, plastics, drugs, soap.
Inorganic chemistry studies compounds that are not based on carbon chains, such as salts, metals and minerals.
Physical chemistry studies how matter behaves at the level of atoms and molecules and how reactions happen, using ideas from physics.
Analytical chemistry identifies what substances are present (qualitative analysis) and how much of each (quantitative analysis).
Biochemistry studies the chemical processes in living things, such as enzymes, DNA and metabolism.

Environmental chemistry studies chemicals in the environment and how to control pollution. Industrial chemistry applies chemistry to manufacturing. Pharmaceutical chemistry designs and makes drugs. Nuclear chemistry studies radioactive substances and nuclear reactions. Forensic chemistry helps to solve crimes by testing evidence.

What it studies

p: Daily life: making soaps, detergents and cosmetics; cooking (baking, boiling, frying); keeping food fresh with preservatives.

Industry: oil and gas industries make fuels, plastics and synthetic fibres; fertilisers and pesticides improve crop yield; cement, glass, paint, textile and paper industries all depend on chemical processes.
Medicine and health: drugs, vaccines and antiseptics; blood tests and scans.
Environment: purifying water, treating waste, controlling pollution, studying climate change and developing clean energy such as solar cells.
Science and technology: new materials such as nanomaterials and superconductors; rocket fuels and life-support systems in space.

units.title: Chemical Industries
units.summary: What chemical industries are, raw materials and products, natural and synthetic raw materials, heavy and fine chemicals, the main divisions, and their advantages and disadvantages.

p: A chemical industry is an industry that uses chemical processes at one stage or another to make other chemicals or finished goods. A raw material is the starting material for production. A product is what the industry makes; it may be the final good or it may become the raw material of another industry (for example, sulphuric acid made by one factory is a raw material for fertiliser factories).

img.alt: A drawing of a chemical plant with towers and storage tanks, raw materials such as limestone entering and products such as plastic bottles, drugs and chemicals leaving
img.cap: A chemical industry changes raw materials into useful products.

p: Natural raw materials come directly from nature with little or no change: air, water, coal, limestone, petroleum (crude oil), iron ore and sulphur deposits.

Synthetic raw materials are made by people from other materials and are then used to make still other goods: plastic granules, synthetic fibres, nylon thread, soda ash. (The source notes list palm kernel oil as synthetic, but it is a natural raw material from the palm fruit.)
Heavy chemicals are made in very large amounts and do not need to be very pure. Examples: sulphuric acid (tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid), sodium hydroxide, sodium carbonate, cement and fertilisers.

Fine chemicals are made in small amounts and must be very pure and are more costly. Examples: laboratory (analytical) reagents, dyes, pharmaceutical ingredients, food additives and perfumes. Ordinary table salt is made in bulk, but a very pure analytical grade of sodium chloride would be a fine chemical.

sections.h: Divisions of chemical industries by product
p: Glass: sand, sodium carbonate, limestone and colourants. Ceramics: clay and other minerals to make pots, tiles and bricks. Pharmaceutical: organic, inorganic and synthetic chemicals for drugs. Metallurgical: extracting and refining metals from ores. Fertiliser: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium compounds. Paints: pigments, resins and solvents. Others include soap and detergent, plastics, petrochemicals, cement and cosmetics.
Importance: they supply raw materials to other industries, give jobs and income, make goods we need, and serve as centres for research and training.
Disadvantages: they can pollute air, water and land; they may cause people to leave the villages for towns (rural-urban drift); and they are costly to set up because they need much capital.

units.title: Laboratory Apparatus and Safety
units.summary: Common laboratory apparatus grouped by what they do, how to use them, and the rules that keep you safe.

p: Beaker: a flat-bottomed cylinder with a pouring lip. Used for holding, mixing and heating liquids and for rough measurement. Conical flask (Erlenmeyer flask): cone-shaped body with a narrow neck, used for mixing solutions, for titration and for heating without spilling. Test tube: a small glass tube for small samples. Flat-bottomed flask and round-bottomed flask: for heating and for reactions, the round-bottomed type being used with a support and for distillation. Reagent bottle: for storing chemicals. Measuring cylinder: a tall graduated cylinder to measure volumes of liquids.

img.alt: Labelled drawings of common laboratory apparatus: beaker, conical flask, test tube, round-bottomed flask, measuring cylinder, burette on a stand, pipette and Bunsen burner
img.cap: Common laboratory apparatus.

p: Bunsen burner: a gas burner with adjustable air holes, for heating. Spirit lamp: burns ethanol for gentle heating where there is no gas. Tripod stand: a three-legged stand to hold apparatus over a flame. Wire gauze: a metal mesh (often with a ceramic centre) placed on the tripod to spread the heat. Crucible: a small ceramic pot (with a lid) for heating solids to very high temperature. Evaporating dish: a shallow porcelain dish used to evaporate a liquid and leave the solid residue.

Pipette: a narrow tube that delivers a fixed volume (for example 25.0 cm³) exactly. Burette: a long graduated tube with a tap at the bottom, used in titration. Volumetric flask: flask with a long neck and a mark, for making solutions of exact concentration. Stopwatch: for measuring time. Thermometer: for measuring temperature, and it contains mercury or coloured alcohol. Balance: for measuring mass.

Separating funnel: a pear-shaped funnel with a tap, to separate immiscible liquids such as oil and water. Filter funnel: a cone used with filter paper for filtration. Distillation flask: round-bottomed flask with a side arm. Condenser (Liebig condenser): a glass tube with a water jacket that cools vapour to liquid. Desiccator: an airtight container with a drying agent to keep substances dry.

Retort stand with clamp: holds apparatus in place. Tongs: for lifting hot crucibles and dishes. Test-tube holder: holds a test tube during heating. Fume cupboard: a ventilated enclosure for experiments that give off harmful gases. Goggles and lab coat: protect eyes and clothes.

Always wear goggles and a lab coat. Never heat a closed container. Handle acids and alkalis with care and wash off any spill with plenty of water. Read the label on a reagent bottle before using it. Never taste chemicals, and never smell them directly: waft the vapour gently to your nose with your hand. Point the mouth of a heated test tube away from yourself and others. Tie back long hair and do not eat or drink in the laboratory. Tell the teacher at once about any accident.

units.title: Matter and the States of Matter
units.summary: What matter is, the properties of solids, liquids and gases, and how the particles are arranged in each.

p: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. A table is matter, and so is air, even though we cannot see it. All matter is made of tiny particles (atoms and molecules) that are always moving.

Solid: the particles are packed closely in a fixed, regular arrangement and can only vibrate about their positions. A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume and cannot easily be squashed. Examples: wood, metal, stone, ice.

Liquid: the particles are close together but not in a fixed pattern, so they can slide past one another and the liquid flows. It has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container, and it can hardly be compressed. Examples: water, oil, alcohol, mercury.

Gas: the particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions. A gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume; it fills its container, and it can be compressed easily. Examples: air, oxygen, carbon dioxide, nitrogen.
Besides these three, scientists know two more states, plasma and Bose-Einstein condensate, but at school we study the main three.

img.alt: Three boxes showing particles tightly packed in a solid, close but random in a liquid and far apart in a gas
img.cap: How the particles are arranged in a solid, a liquid and a gas.

p: Some people think that gases have no mass. They do: air in a tyre makes the tyre heavier. Some people think melting and dissolving are the same. Melting is a change of state caused by heat; dissolving is mixing a solid with a liquid (a solvent) to form a solution.

units.title: Changes of State and the Kinetic Theory
units.summary: Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporation, condensation, sublimation and deposition, the energy changes involved, and the kinetic theory of matter.

p: A change of state happens when matter changes from one state to another by heating or cooling. It is a physical change: no new substance forms, and the chemical composition stays the same.
Melting: solid to liquid by heating. Ice melts to water. Heat is absorbed to loosen the particles from their fixed positions.
Freezing: liquid to solid by cooling. Water freezes to ice. Heat is given out as the particles slow down and take fixed positions.

Vaporisation: liquid to gas. It has two forms. Boiling is rapid, happens throughout the liquid and only at the boiling point (water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure). Evaporation is slow, happens only at the surface and at any temperature (wet clothes dry).
Condensation: gas to liquid by cooling. Water vapour forms droplets on a cold glass.
Sublimation: solid straight to gas without becoming a liquid. Examples: iodine, dry ice (solid carbon dioxide), naphthalene (mothballs).
Deposition: gas straight to solid. Frost is formed when water vapour changes directly to ice.

img.alt: A diagram with solid, liquid and gas in a triangle and arrows labelled melting, freezing, vaporisation, condensation, sublimation and deposition
img.cap: Changes of state. Heating (red arrows) takes in energy; cooling (blue arrows) gives it out.

p: Study the table.

head: Boiling

rows: Happens at a fixed temperature (boiling point)

p: All matter is made of tiny particles. The particles are always moving. The higher the temperature, the faster they move. The state of matter depends on how far apart the particles are and how freely they move. This explains why gases fill containers (particles move away from each other), why a drop of ink spreads in water (diffusion) and why warming a solid makes it melt (particles vibrate more strongly until they break free).

Melting: ice cubes in a glass in the sun. Boiling: cooking water. Evaporation: sweat drying from the skin. Condensation: a mirror fogging after a hot bath. Sublimation: mothballs becoming smaller in a wardrobe. Deposition: frost on a very cold morning.

units.title: Separation Techniques (1): Filtration, Distillation, Sublimation and Chromatography
units.summary: Why mixtures are separated and how filtration, simple and fractional distillation, sublimation and chromatography work.

p: A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically joined, so they can be separated by physical methods. The method we choose depends on the type of mixture (solid and solid, solid and liquid, liquid and liquid), on the properties of the parts (particle size, density, solubility, boiling point, magnetism) and on how pure we need the result to be.

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid using a porous barrier, filter paper. The principle is particle size: the tiny liquid particles pass through the pores, while the larger solid particles are trapped. The solid left on the paper is the residue and the liquid that passes through is the filtrate. Example: separating sand from water, or removing dirt from drinking water.

img.alt: A funnel lined with filter paper held over a beaker, with a muddy mixture being poured in, the residue on the paper and clear filtrate in the beaker
img.cap: Filtration. The residue stays on the paper and the filtrate passes through.

p: Distillation separates a liquid from a solution by using differences in boiling points. The solution is heated; the liquid with the lower boiling point boils off first as vapour, passes through a condenser and turns back to liquid (the distillate). Example: getting pure water from sea water or salt solution. The salt stays behind in the flask. Cold water enters the bottom of the condenser and leaves at the top so that the jacket stays full.
In the diagram, boiling stones (or chips) are put in the flask so that the liquid boils smoothly, and the thermometer bulb is placed at the side arm to read the boiling point of the vapour.

img.alt: Distillation apparatus: a round-bottomed flask of sea water heated on a Bunsen burner, a thermometer at the neck, a Liebig condenser with water in and water out, and a beaker collecting pure water
img.cap: Simple distillation of sea water.

p: Fractional distillation separates a mixture of liquids whose boiling points are close, such as ethanol (78 °C) and water (100 °C). A fractionating column packed with glass beads is fitted above the flask. As vapour rises through the column it condenses and re-evaporates many times, and the lower-boiling liquid reaches the top first. Examples: separating ethanol from water, separating the parts of crude oil (petrol, kerosene, diesel) in a refinery, and separating gases of liquid air such as nitrogen and oxygen.

img.alt: Fractional distillation apparatus with a fractionating column packed with glass beads on top of a round-bottomed flask, a condenser and a beaker of distillate
img.cap: Fractional distillation. The column is packed with glass beads.

p: Sublimation separates a mixture in which one solid sublimes (changes directly to gas when heated) and the other does not. Example: a mixture of ammonium chloride and salt. When heated, the ammonium chloride changes to vapour and then turns back to solid on the cool upturned funnel, leaving the salt behind. Iodine can be separated from sand in the same way.

img.alt: A china dish of ammonium chloride and salt heated on a tripod with an inverted funnel over it plugged with cotton wool, with solid ammonium chloride on the funnel walls
img.cap: Separating ammonium chloride from salt by sublimation.

p: Chromatography separates the parts of a mixture by how fast they travel through a medium (such as paper). The parts dissolve in the solvent to different extents and cling to the paper to different extents, so they move at different speeds. Example: the pigments in ink or in a green leaf can be separated on paper. It is also used to test the purity of food colours and to check for drugs.

img.alt: Three strips showing a mixture starting as one spot at the bottom, separating over time, and finishing as separated coloured spots
img.cap: In chromatography the parts of a mixture move to different heights.

units.title: Separation Techniques (2): Centrifuging, Decanting, Evaporation, Magnet, Winnowing, Sieving and Sedimentation
units.summary: Seven more separation methods, each with its principle and an everyday or industrial example, and a table to choose the right one.

p: A centrifuge spins a mixture at high speed. The force pushes the denser particles to the bottom or outer edge faster than the lighter ones. Example: a laboratory separates blood cells from plasma; a dairy separates cream from milk.

img.alt: A laboratory centrifuge with its lid open and a hand placing a sample tube in the rotor
img.cap: A laboratory centrifuge.

p: Decantation means carefully pouring off the liquid from a solid that has settled at the bottom, or pouring off one liquid from another that does not mix with it. It depends on a difference in density. A glass rod is used to guide the liquid so that none splashes. Example: pouring the water off settled sand.

img.alt: A beaker of liquid and sediment being poured down a glass rod into a clean beaker, leaving the sediment behind
img.cap: Decanting a liquid from a sediment, using a glass rod.

p: Evaporation removes a liquid by heating (or leaving in the sun) until only the dissolved solid is left. The solvent evaporates because it has a lower boiling point, and the solid stays behind. Example: getting salt from sea water in salt pans, or from salt solution in an evaporating dish.

img.alt: An evaporating basin on a gauze and tripod being heated, with solvent vapour rising from the solution
img.cap: Evaporation of a solution in an evaporating basin.

p: A magnet attracts magnetic materials such as iron, nickel and cobalt and leaves non-magnetic materials behind. Example: separating iron filings from sand, or removing iron objects from scrap metals in a recycling plant.

img.alt: Three steps: a mixture of sand and iron filings, a magnet held above it, and the iron filings lifted away from the sand
img.cap: Separating iron filings from sand with a magnet.

p: Winnowing separates lighter particles (husks, chaff) from heavier grain using the wind or a current of air. Light husks are blown away while the heavy grains fall almost straight down. Example: separating rice or beans from husks after threshing. In Nigeria this is common in many farming communities.

img.alt: A farmer standing on a stool pouring grain from a tray so that the wind blows away the husk and the heavier grain falls into a heap
img.cap: Winnowing grain in the wind.

p: Sieving separates particles of different sizes using a sieve (a mesh): small particles pass through and larger ones stay on top. Example: separating flour from bran, sand from gravel, or garri from lumps.

img.alt: A mixture of particles of different sizes falling through two sieves, a larger mesh and a smaller mesh, and separating into layers
img.cap: Sieving separates particles by size.

p: Sedimentation lets the heavier insoluble particles in a liquid settle to the bottom under gravity. It depends on a difference in density between the solid and the liquid. Example: letting muddy water stand until the mud settles; water works use large tanks for the first stage of cleaning. The clear liquid on top is then poured off (decanted) or filtered.
Use this table.

units.title: The Atom: Models and Subatomic Particles
units.summary: What an atom is, how ideas about the atom changed from Dalton to the modern model, and the proton, neutron and electron.

p: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction and still keep the chemical properties of that element. Atoms are very small; the radius of an atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ metres, and about ten million atoms would fit in a line across one millimetre.

sections.h: How the idea of the atom developed
p: 1. Dalton (1803): atoms are tiny, solid, indivisible spheres. All atoms of one element are alike, and atoms of different elements differ. Atoms join in simple ratios to form compounds. Limitation: he did not know of subatomic particles or isotopes.

2. Thomson (1897): discovered the electron. His 'plum pudding' model pictured the atom as a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded in it like raisins. Limitation: it could not explain how the positive and negative charges were arranged.

3. Rutherford (1911): fired particles at thin gold foil. Most went straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space; a few bounced back, so the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny dense centre, the nucleus. Electrons move around it. Limitation: it could not explain why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus.

4. Bohr (1913): electrons move in fixed circular paths called energy levels or shells (K, L, M, N). An electron gains or loses energy only when it jumps between shells. Limitation: it works well for hydrogen but not for bigger atoms.

5. Modern (quantum mechanical) model: Schrödinger, Heisenberg and others showed that electrons are found in regions called orbitals, where they are most likely to be, rather than in fixed paths. The atom has a dense nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons in shells and subshells around it.

img.alt: A diagram of an atom with a nucleus of red protons and green neutrons, electrons shown as blue balls on orbits, and a key
img.cap: A model of the atom: protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons around it.

p: Look at the picture. The nucleus is at the centre and the electron shells K, L, M and N are drawn around it. The shell closest to the nucleus has the lowest energy.

img.alt: Bohr's model of an atom with a positively charged nucleus and four circular shells labelled K, L, M and N
img.cap: Bohr's model: electrons move in shells K, L, M and N.

p: The atom is made of three main particles. Atomic mass unit (a.m.u.) is a very small unit of mass; the proton and neutron each have a mass of about 1 a.m.u. (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).

The number of protons decides which element an atom is. Neutrons add mass and help to keep the nucleus stable. Electrons are involved in chemical bonding and reactions. In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the charges cancel.

units.title: Atomic Number, Mass Number, Isotopes and Electron Arrangement
units.summary: How to find protons, neutrons and electrons, what isotopes are, and how to write the electron arrangement of the first 20 elements.

p: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus. It identifies the element. Mass number (A) is the number of protons plus neutrons. The number of neutrons is N = A − Z. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
Example: carbon-12 has Z = 6 and A = 12. So protons = 6, neutrons = 12 − 6 = 6 and electrons = 6.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same atomic number) with different mass numbers because they have different numbers of neutrons. Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon. They have the same chemical properties (same electrons) but slightly different physical properties (such as mass and density).

Uses of isotopes: in medicine (radioactive iodine for the thyroid, cobalt-60 in cancer treatment), in agriculture (tracing how plants take up fertiliser), and in industry (finding leaks in pipes, thickness gauges) and carbon-14 dating of old objects.

Electrons are placed in shells around the nucleus. Each shell can hold at most 2n² electrons, where n is the number of the shell: K shell (n = 1) holds 2, L shell (n = 2) holds 8, M shell (n = 3) holds 18 and N shell (n = 4) holds 32.

For the first 20 elements, the electrons fill the shells in order and there is a special rule: the third shell is treated as full when it has 8 electrons, and then the next electrons go into the fourth shell. That is why potassium is 2, 8, 8, 1 and not 2, 8, 9.

Writing the arrangement: sodium (Z = 11) is 2, 8, 1. Oxygen (Z = 8) is 2, 6. Magnesium (Z = 12) is 2, 8, 2. Chlorine (Z = 17) is 2, 8, 7. Nitrogen (Z = 7) is 2, 5. Sulphur (Z = 16) is 2, 8, 6. Potassium (Z = 19) is 2, 8, 8, 1.
Learn this table. The last number is the number of outer (valence) electrons, which decides the group of the element.

units.title: The Periodic Table: History and Structure
units.summary: How the periodic table was developed by Döbereiner, Newlands, Mendeleev and Moseley, and how the modern table is arranged in periods, groups and blocks.

p: The periodic table arranges all the known elements in rows and columns in order of increasing atomic number, so that elements with similar properties are placed in the same vertical column. It helps chemists to classify the elements and to predict the properties of an element and its compounds.

Döbereiner (1829): the law of triads. Elements with similar properties come in threes (triads), and the atomic mass of the middle one is about the average of the other two. Example: lithium, sodium, potassium.
Newlands (1864): the law of octaves. When elements are placed in order of atomic mass, every eighth element resembles the first, like the notes in music. It failed for the heavier elements.

Mendeleev (1869): he arranged the elements in order of atomic mass but put those with similar properties in the same group. He left gaps for undiscovered elements and correctly predicted their properties. For example, he predicted germanium before it was found. His table had some defects: a few elements had to be placed out of order of mass (for example, tellurium and iodine).
Moseley (1913): using X-rays, he showed that atomic number, not atomic mass, is the right basis for the order. This solved the problems in Mendeleev's table and gave the modern periodic table.

The modern table has 7 horizontal rows called periods and 18 vertical columns called groups, with the elements in order of atomic number. It is divided into blocks according to the electron arrangement: the s-block (Groups 1 and 2), the p-block (Groups 13 to 18), the d-block (transition metals, Groups 3 to 12) and the f-block (lanthanides and actinides, usually shown separately at the bottom). A staircase line separates metals (to the left) from non-metals (to the right); elements along the line are called metalloids, such as silicon.

units.title: Groups, Periods and Periodic Trends
units.summary: The main groups and what they have in common, what changes across a period and down a group, and the trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy, electronegativity and metallic character.

p: A group is a vertical column. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer (valence) electrons, so they have similar chemical properties.
Group 1: alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr). Very reactive soft metals; they form +1 ions and react violently with water to give hydrogen and an alkaline hydroxide. They are stored under oil.
Group 2: alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra). Reactive but less than Group 1; they form +2 ions and react with acids to give hydrogen.
Groups 3 to 12: transition metals. They have several oxidation states, form coloured compounds and are often used as catalysts (iron, nickel, platinum).
Group 17: halogens (F, Cl, Br, I, At). Very reactive non-metals; they exist as two-atom molecules (F₂, Cl₂), form -1 ions and are strong oxidising agents.
Group 18: noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn). Almost unreactive because their outer shells are full. Used in lighting (neon signs) and welding (argon).

A period is a horizontal row. There are 7 periods. The atomic number increases from left to right. All elements in one period have the same number of electron shells but a different number of outer electrons. For example, the elements from sodium to argon (Period 3) all have three shells.
Periodicity means the repeating pattern of properties across the periods. The trends come from changes in the nuclear charge and the electron arrangement.

p: Why is fluorine more electronegative than chlorine? Both are in Group 17. Fluorine has only two shells, so its outer electrons are very close to the nucleus, and it attracts shared electrons strongly. Chlorine has three shells, so its attraction is weaker.

Why does Group 1 get more reactive down the group? The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and is held less strongly, so it is lost more easily. That is why potassium is more reactive than sodium.

One exception: chlorine actually has a slightly higher electron affinity than fluorine, because fluorine's small size makes electrons crowd together. The general trend is still that electron affinity decreases down the group.

units.title: Chemical Combination and the Laws of Chemical Combination
units.summary: The difference between a mixture and a compound, and the laws of conservation of mass, definite proportions, multiple proportions, reciprocal proportions and combining volumes.

p: In chemical combination, two or more substances (elements or compounds) join to form a new substance with new properties. The substances that react are the reactants; the new substances formed are the products. In a physical combination (a mixture, such as sand and salt), the parts keep their own properties and can be separated by physical methods.

Example: a mixture of iron filings and sulphur can be separated with a magnet (physical). If it is heated, iron(II) sulphide (FeS) forms, which is not magnetic and has new properties (chemical). The laws below were discovered by experiment and are the foundation of modern chemistry.
Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. The atoms are only rearranged.

Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 4 g of hydrogen and 32 g of oxygen make 36 g of water. When mercury(II) oxide is heated in a closed vessel to give mercury and oxygen, the total mass before and after is the same. This law is the basis for balancing equations and calculations.
A compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed proportion by mass, no matter how it was made or where it came from.
Example: water from a river, from rain or made in a laboratory always has hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1 : 8 by mass (2 × 1 = 2 for H, 16 for O, so 2 : 16 = 1 : 8).
When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio.
Example: carbon monoxide CO has 12 g of C to 16 g of O. Carbon dioxide CO₂ has 12 g of C to 32 g of O. The masses of oxygen that combine with 12 g of carbon are in the ratio 16 : 32 = 1 : 2.
If two elements each combine with a fixed mass of a third element, then when they combine with each other, they do so in the same ratio or in a simple multiple of it.

Example: 1 g of hydrogen combines with 8 g of oxygen (water) and with 35.5 g of chlorine (hydrogen chloride). So oxygen and chlorine should combine in the ratio 8 : 35.5, or 16 : 71. In dichlorine oxide, Cl₂O, 71 g of chlorine combine with 16 g of oxygen, which agrees.
When gases react, the volumes of the gases that react and of the gaseous products are in simple whole-number ratios, if all are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

Example: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g). Volumes are in the ratio 2 : 1 : 2. This led to Avogadro's idea that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules, and to the molar volume of a gas, 22.4 dm³ at standard temperature and pressure (STP).

img.alt: Blocks showing 2 volumes of hydrogen plus 1 volume of oxygen making 2 volumes of steam, and 1 volume of hydrogen plus 1 volume of chlorine making 2 volumes of hydrogen chloride
img.cap: Combining volumes of gases are in simple whole-number ratios.

p: They gave strong evidence for Dalton's atomic theory. They led to the mole concept and to calculations of masses and volumes. They allow chemists to find the formulae of compounds. They are still used in industry where reactions need exact proportions, as in making fertilisers, drugs and metals.

units.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
units.summary: Definitions of acids, bases, alkalis and salts, everyday examples, and the properties of each.

p: An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (H⁺) as the only positive ions when dissolved in water. (Brønsted and Lowry: an acid is a proton donor. Lewis: an acid is an electron-pair acceptor.) Examples: hydrochloric acid HCl, sulphuric acid H₂SO₄, nitric acid HNO₃ and ethanoic (acetic) acid CH₃COOH.

A base is a substance that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water only. (Arrhenius: a base gives hydroxide ions OH⁻ in water. Brønsted and Lowry: a base is a proton acceptor. Lewis: an electron-pair donor.) Examples: NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂, CuO and ammonia NH₃.

An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to give OH⁻ ions. All alkalis are bases but not all bases are alkalis. NaOH, KOH and ammonia solution are alkalis; copper(II) oxide and iron(III) hydroxide are bases that do not dissolve.

A salt is a compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is wholly or partly replaced by a metal ion or the ammonium ion. If all the hydrogen is replaced we get a normal salt (NaCl, K₂SO₄, NH₄NO₃). If only part is replaced, we get an acid salt (NaHSO₄). Basic salts contain some OH⁻, for example Pb(OH)Cl.

Acids: vinegar (ethanoic acid), lemon and orange juice (citric acid), fizzy drinks (carbonic acid), car battery liquid (sulphuric acid). Bases: soap and detergent (alkaline), toothpaste (mildly alkaline), limewater Ca(OH)₂, baking soda NaHCO₃, milk of magnesia. Salts: table salt NaCl, fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate and potassium chloride, washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O and Epsom salt MgSO₄·7H₂O.

They taste sour. They turn blue litmus red. They have pH less than 7. Strong acids are corrosive. They react with metals to give hydrogen: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. They react with bases to give a salt and water (neutralisation). They react with carbonates and hydrogen carbonates to give carbon dioxide: 2HCl + Na₂CO₃ → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.

They taste bitter and feel soapy. They turn red litmus blue. They have pH greater than 7. Strong alkalis such as NaOH and KOH burn the skin. They react with acids to form salt and water. They give off ammonia when heated with ammonium salts: NaOH + NH₄Cl → NaCl + H₂O + NH₃. Some bases do not dissolve in water. (Never taste chemicals in the laboratory; the 'taste' properties are only for common foods and household items.)

Many are crystalline solids. Some dissolve (NaCl, KNO₃) and some do not (BaSO₄, PbSO₄). Neutral salts (NaCl) do not change litmus. Acid salts (NaHSO₄) turn blue litmus red. Basic salts turn red litmus blue. They conduct electricity when molten or in solution because they contain ions.

units.title: The pH Scale, Indicators and Neutralisation
units.summary: How the pH scale measures acidity, the colours of common indicators, how neutralisation works and how it is used.

p: The pH scale tells how acidic or alkaline a solution is. It is a logarithmic scale that runs from 0 to 14 for most solutions. A pH below 7 is acidic, a pH of exactly 7 is neutral (pure water) and a pH above 7 is alkaline. Each step on the scale is a ten-fold change in the hydrogen ion concentration, so a solution of pH 3 is ten times as acidic as pH 4.
A solution with pH 4.5 is acidic because it is less than 7.

img.alt: A coloured bar from pH 0 (red) to pH 14 (purple) with examples such as battery acid, lemon juice, vinegar, pure water, blood, baking soda, soap and bleach marked at their pH values
img.cap: The pH scale with common examples.

p: An indicator is a substance that shows by its colour whether a solution is acidic or alkaline.

head: Indicator
In acid
In alkali
rows: Blue, violet (pH 8 to 14); green at pH 7

p: Agriculture: soil pH decides how well crops grow. Acid soil is treated with lime (calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide). Medicine and the body: stomach acid has pH 1.5 to 2.5, and too much of it is relieved with an antacid. Blood has a pH of about 7.35 to 7.45, and even a small change is dangerous. Environment: acid rain and polluted rivers can be tested and treated by checking their pH.
Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base (or alkali) to form a salt and water.
Acid + base → salt + water.
Examples: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. HNO₃ + NH₄OH → NH₄NO₃ + H₂O.
Neutralisation gives out heat (it is exothermic) and the pH of the mixture moves towards 7. It is the reaction used in a titration to find the concentration of a solution.

Medicine: antacids (such as milk of magnesia) neutralise too much stomach acid. Agriculture: lime reduces soil acidity. Industry and environment: acidic waste from factories is neutralised before it is released into rivers. Daily life: toothpaste neutralises acids in the mouth that attack teeth. For insect stings, traditional advice is to use baking soda for bee stings and vinegar for wasp stings, but the venoms are mixtures of proteins, so it is best to wash the area, remove any sting and apply a cold pack, and seek medical help if the person feels unwell.

units.title: Chemical Symbols and Formulae
units.summary: How elements are represented by symbols, the types of formula, and how to write the formula of a compound using valency.

p: A chemical symbol is a short, universal way to write an element, using one or two letters from the English or Latin name. Chemists in all countries use the same symbols, so we can communicate clearly and save space (write O instead of oxygen and Na instead of sodium).

Rules: the first letter is a capital and the second, if any, is small (Mg, Al, Cl). No two elements have the same symbol. Some symbols come from Latin names. Where several elements begin with the same letter, a second letter is added: C for carbon, Cl for chlorine, Ca for calcium.

A chemical formula shows the composition of a compound using symbols and numbers. The small number written below an element is a subscript and shows how many atoms of that element there are (omitted when it is 1). A formula tells the kinds of atoms, their ratio, and lets us calculate the molar mass and the amounts in a reaction.

Types: empirical formula (simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; CH₂O for glucose); molecular formula (actual number of atoms in a molecule; C₆H₁₂O₆ for glucose); structural formula (shows how the atoms are joined; H–O–H for water); condensed formula (CH₃CH₂OH for ethanol).
Valency is the combining power of an atom (the number of electrons it gains, loses or shares).

Steps: 1. Write the symbols. 2. Write their valencies. 3. Swap (cross over) the valencies so that each becomes the subscript of the other element. 4. Leave out subscripts of 1. 5. Simplify to the smallest whole numbers.

Examples: sodium chloride, Na (1) and Cl (1) give NaCl. Calcium chloride, Ca (2) and Cl (1) give CaCl₂. Aluminium oxide, Al (3) and O (2) give Al₂O₃. Magnesium oxide, Mg (2) and O (2) give Mg₂O₂, which simplifies to MgO.

When a group of atoms (a radical) needs a subscript, put the group in brackets. Ammonium sulphate: NH₄ (1) and SO₄ (2) give (NH₄)₂SO₄. Aluminium hydroxide: Al (3) and OH (1) give Al(OH)₃. Calcium nitrate: Ca (2) and NO₃ (1) give Ca(NO₃)₂.

units.title: Chemical Equations and Balancing
units.summary: Word, skeleton and balanced equations, the steps for balancing, worked examples, and the five main types of reaction.

p: A chemical equation is a short way of showing a chemical reaction using symbols and formulae. It shows the reactants (on the left), the products (on the right) and, when balanced, the amounts in which they react. An equation is important because it describes the change concisely, shows the quantities of substances, and proves that no atoms are lost (conservation of mass).
Word equation: hydrogen + oxygen → water. Skeleton (unbalanced) equation: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. Balanced equation: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

img.alt: Three stages of an equation: word equation, skeleton equation with unequal atoms, and balanced equation 2H2 + O2 giving 2H2O with four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side
img.cap: Balancing 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: the same number of each kind of atom on both sides.

p: 1. Write the correct formula for every reactant and product. 2. Write the skeleton equation. 3. Count the atoms of each element on both sides. 4. Put whole-number coefficients (numbers in front of formulae) to make the numbers equal. 5. Never change the small subscript numbers inside a formula, because that would change the substance. For example, changing H₂O to H₂O₂ would make hydrogen peroxide. 6. Check again and reduce the coefficients to the smallest whole numbers.
Tips: balance the metals first, then the non-metals, then hydrogen, and oxygen last. If you get an odd number on one side, multiply everything by 2.
1. Burning methane: CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Left: C 1, H 4, O 2. Right: C 1, H 2, O 3. Put 2 before H₂O to make H = 4, and 2 before O₂ to make O = 4: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
2. Sodium and water: Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂. Balanced: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.
3. Making ammonia: N₂ + H₂ → NH₃. Balanced: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.
4. Burning ethane: C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Balanced: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. (Check: C 4, H 12, O 14 on each side.)

units.title: Qualitative Analysis: Finding Out What Is Present
units.summary: What analysis means, how qualitative analysis identifies substances using observation, flame tests, chemical tests and precipitation, and why it comes first.

p: Chemistry is an experimental science. It depends on observation and measurement. Analysis is a set of methods used to find out what a substance is (identify it) and how much of it is present. This is the work of analytical chemistry, which has two parts: qualitative analysis and quantitative analysis. They work together: first we find out what is there (qualitative), and then we find out how much (quantitative).

Qualitative analysis identifies the elements, ions or compounds present in a sample. It answers the question 'What is in the sample?' It gives no numbers. It is usually the first step, and depends on observation of changes such as colour, a precipitate, bubbles (effervescence) or a smell.
1. Observing physical properties: colour (copper compounds are usually blue or green), state, smell (ammonia has a sharp smell), and solubility in water.

2. Chemical tests: acid test: carbonates fizz with dilute acid, giving off carbon dioxide. Alkali test: warming an ammonium salt with an alkali gives off ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus blue.
3. Flame tests: a clean wire dipped into a sample is held in a non-luminous flame. Some metal ions give a characteristic colour.

4. Precipitation reactions: certain ions form insoluble solids with certain reagents. Chloride ions with silver nitrate give a white precipitate of silver chloride. Sulphate ions with barium chloride give a white precipitate of barium sulphate.

5. Confirmatory tests: used after the first results to be sure. For example, to tell a carbonate from a sulphite, add dilute acid and test the gas. Both carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide turn limewater milky, but only sulphur dioxide turns acidified potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless.

units.title: Quantitative Analysis and Basic Laboratory Concepts
units.summary: How quantitative analysis measures amounts using volumetric and gravimetric methods and instruments, why analysis matters, and the main laboratory terms.

p: Quantitative analysis finds out how much of a substance is present: the amount, concentration or percentage. It is numerical, needs measurement and calculation, and is essential for quality control, correct drug doses and industrial recipes.

1. Volumetric analysis: measuring volumes of solutions that react together, usually by titration (acid-base, redox or precipitation). Example: finding the concentration of hydrochloric acid by titrating it against a standard solution of sodium hydroxide, using phenolphthalein or methyl orange to show the end point.

2. Gravimetric analysis: finding the amount of a substance by precipitating it, drying it and weighing it. Example: finding the purity of a sodium chloride sample by precipitating all the chloride as silver chloride and weighing it.

3. Instrumental methods: modern machines that are fast and very accurate. Spectrophotometry measures how much light a solution absorbs. Chromatography separates mixtures. Mass spectrometry gives masses and structures of molecules. Atomic absorption spectroscopy measures metals.

units.title: The Mole, Avogadro's Number and Molar Mass
units.summary: Why chemists count in moles, what Avogadro's number is, how to find molar mass, and the formulas that link moles, mass, particles and gas volume.

p: Atoms and molecules are far too small to count one by one. We need a counting unit, like a 'dozen' for 12 things. In chemistry the counting unit is the mole (symbol mol).
A mole is the amount of a substance that contains as many particles (atoms, molecules, ions or other units) as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.
The number of particles in one mole is called Avogadro's number (or constant), symbol Nₐ (N subscript A). Its value is 6.022 × 10²³ per mole.
1 mole of hydrogen atoms has 6.022 × 10²³ atoms. 1 mole of water has 6.022 × 10²³ molecules. 1 mole of sodium chloride has 6.022 × 10²³ formula units (NaCl pairs of ions).
What counts as a 'particle' depends on the substance: atoms for elements like Na and Fe; molecules for O₂, H₂, Cl₂, H₂O, CO₂ and NH₃; formula units for ionic compounds like NaCl and KNO₃.
Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole (g/mol). It is numerically equal to the relative atomic mass (Ar) or the relative formula mass (Mr).

Examples: Ar of carbon = 12, so the molar mass of C is 12 g/mol. Mr of water, H₂O = (2 × 1) + 16 = 18, so its molar mass is 18 g/mol. Mr of NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5, so its molar mass is 58.5 g/mol. Mr of Na₂CO₃ = (2 × 23) + 12 + (3 × 16) = 106.
Always give molar mass the unit g/mol.

units.title: Mole Calculations and Stoichiometry
units.summary: Worked examples with mass, particles and gas volume, then the step-by-step method for mass-mass, mass-volume and limiting-reactant questions.

p: Example 1. How many moles are in 18 g of water? Mr = 18. n = 18 ÷ 18 = 1 mol.
Example 2. How many molecules are in 54 g of water? n = 54 ÷ 18 = 3 mol. Molecules = 3 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.807 × 10²⁴.

Example 3. How many atoms are in 4 g of hydrogen gas, H₂? Molar mass of H₂ = 2. n = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 mol of molecules = 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules. Each molecule has 2 atoms, so atoms = 2.408 × 10²⁴.
Example 4. Volume of 0.25 mol of oxygen at STP: V = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 dm³.

Stoichiometry is calculating the quantities (masses, volumes, particles) of reactants and products in a reaction from the balanced equation. The key idea is the mole ratio: the coefficients in a balanced equation tell the ratio of moles. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O the ratio is 2 mol H₂ : 1 mol O₂ : 2 mol H₂O.

Steps: 1. Write the balanced equation. 2. Write down the mole ratio from the coefficients. 3. Change the given quantity to moles. 4. Use the ratio to find moles of the unknown. 5. Change those moles to the quantity asked for (mass, volume, particles).

Example 5 (mass to mass). How many grams of water form when 8 g of hydrogen burns completely? 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Moles of H₂ = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 mol. The ratio H₂ : H₂O is 1 : 1, so 4 mol of H₂O form. Mass = 4 × 18 = 72 g.

Example 6 (mass to volume). What volume of CO₂ at STP forms when 50 g of CaCO₃ decomposes? CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Mr of CaCO₃ = 100. n = 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5 mol. The ratio is 1 : 1, so 0.5 mol of CO₂ form. Volume = 0.5 × 22.4 = 11.2 dm³.

Example 7 (limiting reactant). 10 g of H₂ reacts with 80 g of O₂. Moles of H₂ = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 mol. Moles of O₂ = 80 ÷ 32 = 2.5 mol. The equation needs 2 mol H₂ for each 1 mol O₂, so 5 mol H₂ needs exactly 2.5 mol O₂. Both are used up fully, so there is no limiting reactant. Moles of water = 5 mol. Mass = 5 × 18 = 90 g.

The limiting reactant is the one that is used up first and decides how much product forms. If, say, we had 10 g of H₂ but only 40 g of O₂ (1.25 mol), the oxygen would limit: it needs 2.5 mol of H₂ and gives 2.5 mol of H₂O (45 g).

Writing molar mass without the unit g/mol. Mixing up an atom (O) with a molecule (O₂). Forgetting that Avogadro's number applies to ions and formula units too. Using 22.4 dm³ for something that is not a gas or not at STP (at room temperature the molar volume is about 24 dm³).

Industry: working out how much raw material is needed for fertiliser, soap and cement. Medicine: preparing exact doses. Environment: estimating carbon dioxide from burning fuels. Laboratory: titration and gravimetric analysis.

units.title: Percentage Composition by Mass
units.summary: How to calculate the percentage by mass of each element in a compound, with worked examples and a picture of ethanol.

p: The percentage composition of a compound is the percentage by mass of each element in it. It tells us how much of each element is in the compound compared to the whole mass. It is useful in analysis and in industry, for example to compare fertilisers.
Percentage of an element = (total mass of that element in the formula ÷ molar mass of the compound) × 100.
The molar mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula. The top line is the number of atoms of the element multiplied by its Ar.

p: Nitrogen in NH₃: Mr = 17; %N = 14 ÷ 17 × 100 = 82.4%. Hydrogen and oxygen in water: Mr = 18; %H = 2 ÷ 18 × 100 = 11.1% and %O = 16 ÷ 18 × 100 = 88.9%. Nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃: Mr = 80; %N = 28 ÷ 80 × 100 = 35%. This is why ammonium nitrate is a rich nitrogen fertiliser.
Uses: pharmaceutical firms check the content of active ingredients; farmers compare fertilisers by their percentage of nitrogen; the food industry works out nutrition.
Forgetting to multiply the Ar by the number of atoms. Using wrong atomic masses. Not checking that all the percentages add up to 100.

units.title: Empirical and Molecular Formulae
units.summary: How to find the empirical formula from percentages, how to get the molecular formula from the molar mass, with several worked examples.

p: The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in the compound. It does not always show the real number of atoms in a molecule.

sections.h: Steps to find the empirical formula
p: 1. Assume 100 g of the compound, so each percentage becomes a mass in grams. 2. Divide each mass by the Ar of the element to get moles. 3. Divide all the mole values by the smallest one. 4. If the ratios are not whole numbers, multiply all by a small number (2, 3 and so on) until they are. 5. Write the formula.

A compound contains 40% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O. Masses in 100 g: C 40, H 6.7, O 53.3. Moles: C = 40 ÷ 12 = 3.33; H = 6.7 ÷ 1 = 6.7; O = 53.3 ÷ 16 = 3.33. Divide by 3.33: C = 1, H = 2, O = 1. The empirical formula is CH₂O.
A substance contains 27.3% C and 72.7% O. Moles: C = 27.3 ÷ 12 = 2.28; O = 72.7 ÷ 16 = 4.54. Divide by 2.28: C = 1, O = 2. The empirical formula is CO₂.

The molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule. It is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula: molecular formula = (empirical formula)ₙ, where n = molar mass of the compound ÷ molar mass of the empirical formula.
Example: the empirical formula is CH₂O and the molar mass is 180 g/mol. Mass of CH₂O = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30. n = 180 ÷ 30 = 6. Molecular formula = (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆, which is glucose.
A compound contains 36% C, 12% H and 52% O (approximate). Moles: C = 3.0; H = 12; O = 3.25. Divide by 3.0: 1 : 4 : 1.08, which is about CH₄O (methanol).
The empirical formula is CH and the molar mass is 78 g/mol. Mass of CH = 13. n = 78 ÷ 13 = 6. The molecular formula is C₆H₆ (benzene).

A hydrocarbon has 85.7% C and 14.3% H and a molar mass of 56. Moles: C = 85.7 ÷ 12 = 7.14; H = 14.3 ÷ 1 = 14.3. Divide by 7.14: C = 1, H = 2. The empirical formula is CH₂ (mass 14). n = 56 ÷ 14 = 4. The molecular formula is C₄H₈.
A compound has 54.5% C, 9.1% H and 36.4% O. Moles: C = 4.54, H = 9.1, O = 2.275. Divide by 2.275: C = 2, H = 4, O = 1. The empirical formula is C₂H₄O.

Uses: checking the purity and the composition of drugs, foods and fertilisers; finding unknown substances in forensic work. Common mistakes: forgetting to change the percentages to grams, stopping at a fraction such as 1.5 instead of multiplying by 2, and mixing up the empirical and molecular formulae.

units.title: Gas Laws (1): Boyle's Law and Charles' Law
units.summary: The properties of a gas, Boyle's law (pressure and volume), Charles' law (volume and temperature) with graphs, explanations and worked examples.

p: Gases have no fixed shape or volume. Their particles are far apart and move constantly at random. Four things describe a gas. Pressure (P): the force of the particles on the walls of the container per unit area, P = force ÷ area, in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m². Volume (V): the space the gas fills, in litres (L), cm³ or m³. Temperature (T): measured in kelvin (K). To change from degrees Celsius: T(K) = T(°C) + 273. Amount (n): the number of moles of gas.
At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure. So P × V = a constant, and for a change from state 1 to state 2: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
Explanation: when a gas is squeezed into a smaller volume, the particles hit the walls more often, so the pressure goes up. If the volume doubles, the pressure halves.
Graphs: a graph of P against V is a curve called a hyperbola. A graph of P against 1/V is a straight line through the origin.
Worked example 1: a gas has volume 4.0 L at 200 kPa. Find its volume at 400 kPa (same temperature). 200 × 4.0 = 400 × V₂, so V₂ = 800 ÷ 400 = 2.0 L.

img.alt: Two graphs: Boyle's law curve of pressure against volume falling steeply, and Charles' law straight line of volume against temperature in kelvin through the origin
img.cap: Boyle's law (left) and Charles' law (right).

p: At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute (kelvin) temperature. V ÷ T = a constant, and for two states V₁ ÷ T₁ = V₂ ÷ T₂. The temperature must be in kelvin.
The graph of V against T (in K) is a straight line through the origin. If the line is extended back, it reaches zero volume at −273 °C (0 K), called absolute zero.
Explanation: a hotter gas has faster particles that hit the walls harder, so the volume must increase to keep the pressure the same.
Worked example 2: a gas has 300 cm³ at 27 °C (300 K). Find its volume at 127 °C (400 K) at constant pressure. 300 ÷ 300 = V₂ ÷ 400, so V₂ = 400 cm³.

2.5 L at 100 kPa is changed to 250 kPa at constant temperature: V₂ = 2.5 × 100 ÷ 250 = 1.0 L. A balloon has 1.2 L at 20 °C (293 K). At 80 °C (353 K) at constant pressure: V₂ = 1.2 × 353 ÷ 293 = 1.45 L. A gas has pressure 150 kPa at 300 K in a fixed volume. At 400 K, P₂ = 150 × 400 ÷ 300 = 200 kPa (this is Gay-Lussac's pressure law).

The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, where the volume of an ideal gas would be zero. Celsius temperatures can be zero or negative, and we cannot divide or multiply volumes by zero or negative temperatures, so gas calculations must use kelvin.

units.title: Gas Laws (2): The Ideal Gas Equation and Applications
units.summary: The general gas equation PV = nRT, the ideal gas model, a worked pressure calculation, a comparison of the laws and their uses.

p: Boyle's law and Charles' law can be combined, and with the amount of gas included, we get the ideal gas equation: PV = nRT.
P = pressure in pascals (Pa); V = volume in cubic metres (m³; 1 L = 0.001 m³); n = number of moles; R = the gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol K); T = temperature in kelvin.
For comparing two states of the same amount of gas: P₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂V₂ ÷ T₂.
Example 1: find the pressure of 0.5 mol of gas in a 10 L container at 300 K. V = 10 L = 0.010 m³. P = nRT ÷ V = (0.5 × 8.314 × 300) ÷ 0.010 = 124,710 Pa, about 125 kPa.
Example 2: find the pressure of 2 mol of gas in 5 L at 350 K. V = 0.005 m³. P = (2 × 8.314 × 350) ÷ 0.005 = 1.16 × 10⁶ Pa.
Example 3: a cylinder holds nitrogen at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K, volume 0.05 m³. n = PV ÷ RT = (2.0 × 10⁵ × 0.05) ÷ (8.314 × 300) = 10,000 ÷ 2494 = 4.0 mol. Mass = 4.0 × 28 = 112 g.

An ideal gas is a model with these ideas: the molecules are in constant, random motion; collisions are perfectly elastic (no energy lost); the volume of the molecules is tiny compared with the container; there are no forces between molecules; and the average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature. Real gases behave almost ideally at low pressure and high temperature.

units.title: Bohr's Model, Energy Levels and Shells
units.summary: How Bohr improved the atomic model, his postulates, the energy levels (shells) and how many electrons each can hold.

p: Dalton (1803) pictured atoms as solid, indivisible spheres, but could not explain their inside. Thomson (1897) found the electron and proposed the 'plum pudding' model. Rutherford (1911) showed from his gold-foil experiment that an atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with electrons around it, but his model could not explain why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus or why atoms give out light of only certain colours. Bohr (1913) improved on this by saying that electrons can have only certain fixed amounts of energy.
1. Electrons move around the nucleus in fixed paths (orbits or shells) and do not lose energy while in them. These are called stationary states.
2. Each shell has a fixed energy. The shells nearest the nucleus have the lowest energy; shells farther out have more.

3. An electron can jump between shells. If it absorbs energy it jumps to a higher shell (an excited state). When it falls back it gives out the energy as light (a photon). This explains why each element gives its own line spectrum.
4. The energy absorbed or given out is ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = hν, where h is Planck's constant (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s) and ν is the frequency of the light.
The shells are named K (n = 1), L (n = 2), M (n = 3), N (n = 4), and then O, P, Q. A shell with number n can hold at most 2n² electrons: K holds 2, L holds 8, M holds 18, N holds 32.
In the first twenty elements, electrons fill the shells in order, but the M shell is treated as full when it holds 8, so the next electrons go into the N shell (for example, calcium is 2, 8, 8, 2).

units.title: Electronic Configuration and Subshells
units.summary: Subshells s, p, d and f, the rules for filling them (Aufbau, Pauli, Hund), examples, and why configuration explains valency and the periodic table.

p: Each shell is divided into subshells called s, p, d and f. An s subshell holds up to 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14. The K shell has only 1s. The L shell has 2s and 2p. The M shell has 3s, 3p and 3d.

Aufbau principle: electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first. Pauli exclusion principle: an orbital holds at most two electrons, and they spin in opposite directions. Hund's rule: electrons go into orbitals of equal energy one at a time before they pair up.
Order of filling: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p. Notice that 4s fills before 3d.
Study the table. Write the full configuration as subshells and as shell numbers.

Valency: sodium (2, 8, 1) has one outer electron, so its valency is 1; oxygen (2, 6) needs two more, so its valency is 2. Chemical properties: elements with the same outer configuration are in the same group. The period number equals the number of occupied shells, and the group number is linked to the number of outer electrons. Stability of noble gases: neon (2, 8) and argon (2, 8, 8) have full outer shells and are very unreactive. Group 1 metals have one loosely held outer electron, so they react readily; noble gases have full shells, so they hardly react.

units.title: Ionic Bonding
units.summary: Why atoms bond, the octet rule, how ionic bonds form by transfer of electrons, examples, and the properties of ionic compounds.

p: Except for the noble gases, atoms are not stable on their own because their outer shells are not full. To become stable they join with other atoms. This is chemical bonding. The octet rule says that atoms gain, lose or share electrons until they have eight electrons in the outer shell, like a noble gas. Hydrogen and helium need only two (the duplet rule).

An ionic bond forms when one atom, usually a metal, gives one or more electrons to another atom, usually a non-metal. The atom that loses electrons becomes a positive ion (cation). The atom that gains them becomes a negative ion (anion). The strong force of attraction between the opposite charges is the ionic bond.

Conditions: a large difference in electronegativity (roughly more than 1.7); usually a metal from Group 1, 2 or 3 and a non-metal from Group 15, 16 or 17 (old numbering: groups 5, 6, 7); the metal has a low ionisation energy and the non-metal a high electron affinity.

Sodium chloride, NaCl: sodium (2, 8, 1) loses one electron to become Na⁺ (2, 8). Chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains one electron to become Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8). Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻. The ions attract each other and pack in a giant lattice.
Magnesium oxide, MgO: Mg (2, 8, 2) loses 2 electrons to form Mg²⁺; O (2, 6) gains 2 to form O²⁻.
Calcium fluoride, CaF₂: Ca (2, 8, 8, 2) loses 2 electrons to form Ca²⁺; each F (2, 7) gains 1 electron to form F⁻, so two F⁻ are needed.

img.alt: Three panels: sodium giving an electron to chlorine to make Na+ and Cl-; two hydrogen atoms sharing a pair of electrons; and a water molecule with oxygen sharing electrons with two hydrogens
img.cap: Ionic bonding (left) and covalent bonding (middle and right).

p: They are crystalline solids at room temperature. They have high melting and boiling points because the lattice is strong. Most dissolve in water (a polar solvent) but not in petrol or benzene. They do not conduct electricity as solids (the ions cannot move) but do when molten or dissolved (the ions are free). They are hard but brittle: if the layers of the lattice slip, like charges meet and repel and the crystal cracks.

units.title: Covalent Bonding and Comparison with Ionic Bonding
units.summary: How atoms share electrons, single, double, triple and coordinate bonds, examples and properties, and a table comparing ionic and covalent compounds.

p: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons so that each gets a full outer shell. It happens mainly between non-metals, when the difference in electronegativity is small (less than about 1.7).
Single bond: one shared pair. Hydrogen, H–H. Each hydrogen gives one electron.
Double bond: two shared pairs. Oxygen, O=O. Each oxygen shares two electrons.
Triple bond: three shared pairs. Nitrogen, N≡N.

Coordinate (dative) bond: both electrons of the shared pair come from one atom. Example: the ammonium ion NH₄⁺ is made when the nitrogen of ammonia (NH₃) gives its lone pair to a hydrogen ion (H⁺). Once formed, a coordinate bond is just like any other covalent bond.

Water, H₂O: oxygen (2, 6) shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms. Methane, CH₄: carbon (2, 4) shares one pair with each of four hydrogens. Carbon dioxide, CO₂: carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen, so there are two double bonds (O=C=O).

They are usually gases (O₂, CO₂), liquids (water) or soft solids (sulphur, iodine). Melting and boiling points are low because the forces between molecules are weak (the bonds inside each molecule are strong). Exceptions are giant covalent structures such as diamond and silicon dioxide, which have very high melting points. Many do not dissolve in water but dissolve in organic solvents, though some small polar molecules such as sugar and ethanol do dissolve in water. They do not conduct electricity because there are no free ions or electrons (graphite is an exception because it has free (delocalised) electrons). Covalent bonds are directional, joining particular atoms.

p: Both are made only of carbon. In diamond, each carbon is bonded to four others in a rigid 3-D network, so it is very hard and does not conduct. In graphite, each carbon is bonded to three others in flat layers, with one electron per atom free to move. The layers slide easily (so graphite is soft and used in pencils) and the free electrons let it conduct electricity.

It explains why matter is stable and why salt dissolves in water but oil does not, why water is a liquid and why metals conduct. It guides the design of ceramics, plastics and semiconductors, and is the basis of proteins, carbohydrates and DNA.

units.title: Oxidation and Reduction
units.summary: Three ways to define oxidation and reduction (oxygen and hydrogen, electrons, oxidation number) with simple examples, and why they always occur together.

p: In many reactions electrons move from one substance to another. These are oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions. They are important in breathing and photosynthesis, extracting metals, batteries, rusting and water treatment.
Oxidation is the addition of oxygen or the removal of hydrogen. Reduction is the removal of oxygen or the addition of hydrogen.
Example 1: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Magnesium is oxidised (it gains oxygen). (The source notes wrote the product as MgO₂, which is wrong; magnesium oxide is MgO.)
Example 2: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Copper(II) oxide is reduced (loses oxygen); hydrogen is oxidised (gains oxygen).
Oxidation is loss of electrons. Reduction is gain of electrons. Remember OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
Examples: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ (sodium is oxidised). Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (chlorine is reduced).

Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is a decrease in oxidation number. Examples: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻: iron goes from +2 to +3, so it is oxidised. Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻: chlorine goes from 0 to −1, so it is reduced.

Simple rules for oxidation numbers: an uncombined element is 0; a simple ion has its charge (Na⁺ is +1); oxygen is usually −2; hydrogen is usually +1; the numbers in a compound add up to 0, and in an ion to the charge.

In a redox reaction, oxidation and reduction happen at the same time. The substance that is oxidised is the reducing agent (it gives electrons). The substance that is reduced is the oxidising agent (it takes electrons).

Example: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Zinc loses electrons: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation; zinc is the reducing agent). Copper ions gain them: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction; Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent). In the picture, a blue copper sulphate solution slowly becomes colourless as a brown layer of copper forms on the zinc.

units.title: Redox Agents, Examples and Balancing
units.summary: Common oxidising and reducing agents, types of redox reaction, two ways to balance a redox equation, uses and common mistakes.

p: An oxidising agent (oxidant) accepts electrons and is itself reduced. Examples: oxygen, chlorine, potassium manganate(VII), potassium dichromate(VI) and nitric acid. A reducing agent (reductant) gives electrons and is itself oxidised. Examples: hydrogen, carbon monoxide, sodium, zinc and iron.

Combination: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O. Displacement: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (carbon goes from −4 to +4, oxidised; oxygen goes from 0 to −2, reduced). Corrosion (rusting): 4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃, which changes to hydrated iron(III) oxide, rust.

sections.h: Balancing by the oxidation number method
p: 1. Give oxidation numbers to every element. 2. Find which change up (oxidation) and which change down (reduction). 3. Make the total electrons lost equal the total electrons gained. 4. Balance the rest of the atoms and charges.

Example: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. Each Na goes from 0 to +1 (loses 1 electron, 2 Na lose 2 electrons). Cl₂ goes from 0 to −1 for each of 2 atoms (gains 2 electrons). The electrons balance, so the equation is balanced.

1. Write the oxidation and reduction half-equations separately. 2. Balance atoms other than H and O. 3. Balance O by adding H₂O. 4. Balance H by adding H⁺ (in acid). 5. Balance charge by adding electrons. 6. Multiply so the electrons are equal, add the two half-equations and cancel the electrons.

Example in acid: Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ → Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺. Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Multiply the iron half-equation by 5 and add: 5Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.
More practice answers: 3H₂S + 2HNO₃ → 3S + 2NO + 4H₂O. MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O. 3Cu + 2NO₃⁻ + 8H⁺ → 3Cu²⁺ + 2NO + 4H₂O. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3SO₂ + 2H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3SO₄²⁻ + H₂O.

Living things: respiration oxidises glucose to carbon dioxide and water and releases energy; photosynthesis reduces carbon dioxide to glucose. Industry: iron is made by reducing iron(III) oxide with carbon monoxide; electroplating and electrolysis; making bleaches. Environment: chlorine kills germs in water. Everyday life: rusting is an unwanted redox reaction; batteries (dry cells, lead-acid, lithium-ion) use redox reactions to make electricity.

Thinking oxidation always means adding oxygen. It may be loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation number. Forgetting that oxidation and reduction always occur together. Mixing up the agents: the oxidising agent is the substance that is reduced, and the reducing agent is the substance that is oxidised.

units.title: Water: Importance and Properties
units.summary: Why water matters to living things, industry and the home, its physical properties and its chemical reactions with metals, non-metals and electricity.

p: Water is the most plentiful compound on Earth and is called the universal solvent because it dissolves so many things. It occurs as ice, liquid water and water vapour.

Biological: carries nutrients and waste in plants and animals; sweating and evaporation cool the body; it is needed for photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Industrial: raw material for hydrogen, oxygen and acids; a coolant in power plants and engines; used for cleaning and dissolving. Domestic: drinking, cooking, washing and sanitation.

Pure water is colourless, odourless and tasteless. It boils at 100 °C and freezes at 0 °C at 1 atmosphere. Its density is greatest, 1 g/cm³, at 4 °C. Water expands when it freezes, so ice is less dense and floats; fish survive under ice in cold lakes. It has a high specific heat capacity: it takes in or gives out much heat for a small change in temperature, which makes the climate near the sea milder. It has a high surface tension because of hydrogen bonding, so small insects can walk on it. Pure water hardly conducts electricity, but natural water does because of dissolved ions.

With metals: active metals (sodium, potassium, calcium) react with cold water to give a hydroxide and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Less reactive metals such as magnesium and zinc react with steam: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂.
With non-metals: chlorine dissolves in water to give hydrochloric acid and chloric(I) acid (HOCl): Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl.
Hydrolysis: some salts react with water; ammonium chloride solution is slightly acidic.
Electrolysis: when electricity is passed through acidified water, it decomposes: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Twice as much hydrogen as oxygen is collected, by volume.

Water with dissolved calcium and magnesium salts does not lather easily with soap and is called hard water. Boiling can remove temporary hardness (due to hydrogencarbonates). Rainwater and distilled water are soft.

units.title: Solutions and Solubility
units.summary: Solute, solvent and solution, the types of solutions, their properties, what solubility is and the factors that affect it.

p: A solution is a uniform (homogeneous) mixture of two or more substances. The substance that dissolves is the solute (usually the smaller amount). The substance that does the dissolving is the solvent (usually the larger amount). Examples: salt (solute) in water (solvent); sugar in water.
By state: solid solutions (brass is copper and zinc; bronze is copper and tin), liquid solutions (vinegar, sugar solution) and gaseous solutions (air).

By how much solute is dissolved: an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at that temperature. A saturated solution holds the most solute it can at that temperature; extra solute stays undissolved. A supersaturated solution holds more solute than normal. It is made by dissolving a lot of solute in a hot solution and cooling it carefully without disturbing it, and is unstable: a small crystal or a tap causes crystals to appear.
By electrical conduction: electrolytic solutions conduct (salt solution, hydrochloric acid) and non-electrolytic solutions do not (sugar in water, ethanol in water).

img.alt: Three beakers showing an unsaturated solution with all solute dissolved, a saturated solution with undissolved solid at the bottom, and a supersaturated solution with crystals forming around a seed crystal
img.cap: Unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions.

p: They are uniform throughout. The particles are the size of molecules or ions, so cannot be seen. They are clear (transparent) and do not scatter a beam of light. The solute cannot be removed by filtration, but can be recovered by evaporation or distillation. They may be dilute (little solute) or concentrated (much solute).

Solubility is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature to make a saturated solution. It is measured in g per 100 g of solvent (at a stated temperature). Example: the solubility of sodium chloride is about 36 g per 100 g of water at 25 °C. (In more advanced work, solubility is also given in mol/dm³, the SI-based unit.)

1. Nature of solute and solvent: 'like dissolves like'. Polar and ionic solutes (salt, sugar) dissolve in polar solvents (water). Non-polar solutes (iodine, fats, oil) dissolve in non-polar solvents (tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, or kerosene). This is why sugar dissolves in water but not in kerosene.
2. Temperature: for most solids, solubility rises as the temperature rises (potassium nitrate). For gases, solubility falls when temperature rises: a warm soft drink loses its fizz.
3. Pressure: has little effect on solids and liquids, but the solubility of a gas rises with pressure (Henry's law). Soft drinks are bottled under CO₂ pressure and fizz when opened.

4. Particle size: small particles dissolve faster because of the larger surface area. 5. Stirring makes a solute dissolve faster, but does not change how much can dissolve in total. 6. Impurities may change solubility.
