units.title: Solubility Curves and Crystallisation
units.summary: How to read a solubility curve, solubility calculations, how to measure solubility, and how to grow crystals of pure substances.

p: Aim: find the solubility of potassium nitrate (KNO₃) in water at 40 °C. Apparatus: beaker, thermometer, balance, stirrer, heat source, evaporating dish.
Method: weigh 100 g of water into a beaker and warm it to 40 °C. Add KNO₃ little by little, stirring, until no more dissolves (the solution is saturated). Record the mass of solute added.

Solubility = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solvent) × 100. If 50 g dissolve in 100 g of water at 40 °C, solubility = (50 ÷ 100) × 100 = 50 g per 100 g of water. (Our standard value for KNO₃ at 40 °C is 64 g per 100 g of water; the 50 g was only an example.)

A solubility curve is a graph of solubility (g per 100 g of water, vertical axis) against temperature (°C, horizontal axis). For most salts, such as KNO₃, the curve slopes upward, because the solubility rises with temperature. For gases, it slopes downward. A point on the curve is a saturated solution. A point below the curve is unsaturated. A point above the curve means more solute than can dissolve (it would appear as undissolved solid, or as a supersaturated solution if cooled carefully).
Uses: read the solubility at any temperature; find the temperature at which a solution becomes saturated; calculate how much solute crystallises when a solution cools; compare solutes.

img.alt: A rising solubility curve of potassium nitrate from 13 g per 100 g of water at 0 degrees to 150 g at 80 degrees, with marked points at 20 degrees (32 g) and 40 degrees (64 g) and the regions unsaturated below and supersaturated above
img.cap: Solubility curve of potassium nitrate (values rounded for teaching).

p: Example 1: a saturated solution at 40 °C holds 64 g of KNO₃ per 100 g of water. At 20 °C the solubility is 32 g. If the solution is cooled to 20 °C, the mass that crystallises = 64 − 32 = 32 g (for each 100 g of water).
Example 2: at 80 °C, 150 g of KNO₃ dissolves in 100 g of water. At 30 °C the solubility is 45 g. Mass that crystallises = 150 − 45 = 105 g.
Example 3: the solubility of NaCl at 25 °C is 36 g per 100 g of water. How much NaCl is needed for a saturated solution in 250 g of water? Mass = 36 ÷ 100 × 250 = 90 g.
Example 4: 90 g of KNO₃ is dissolved in 100 g of water at 60 °C, where the solubility is 110 g per 100 g. Since 90 < 110, the solution is unsaturated (it can take 20 g more).

Example 5: the solubility of KCl is 45 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C and 30 g at 20 °C. How much KCl crystallises when 100 g of saturated solution at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C? A saturated solution at 60 °C has 45 g KCl in 145 g of solution, so 100 g of solution holds 100 × 45 ÷ 145 = 31.0 g KCl and 69.0 g of water. At 20 °C, 69.0 g of water can hold 69.0 × 30 ÷ 100 = 20.7 g. So the mass crystallising = 31.0 − 20.7 = 10.3 g.
Crystallisation is the formation of pure solid crystals from a solution by cooling it or by evaporating some of the solvent. It is used to purify solids.

Making crystals of copper(II) sulphate in the laboratory: 1. Dissolve excess copper(II) sulphate in hot water to make a saturated solution. 2. Filter it to remove undissolved solid and impurities. 3. Let it cool slowly; crystals form because the solubility falls. 4. Filter off the crystals, wash them with a little cold water, and dry them between sheets of filter paper. Slow cooling gives large, well-shaped crystals.
Industrial uses: refining sugar, purifying salt, making alum, drugs and fertilisers.

Drug design (how much of a drug dissolves in the blood), food and drink making, oxygen dissolved in water that fish need to breathe (warm water holds less oxygen), the manufacture of fertilisers, soaps and carbonated drinks, and purification of chemicals.

units.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
units.summary: What organic chemistry is, how it began with Wöhler, which carbon compounds are not organic, and why organic chemistry matters.

p: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies carbon compounds, especially those with carbon-hydrogen bonds (hydrocarbons) and the compounds made from them (their derivatives).

Long ago, people believed that the compounds made by living things (such as sugar and urea) could be made only by living things, through a 'vital force'. In 1828 the German chemist Friedrich Wöhler heated ammonium cyanate, a mineral (inorganic) salt, and obtained urea, which is found in urine. This showed that organic compounds can be made in the laboratory, and it is regarded as the beginning of modern organic chemistry.

Today organic chemistry covers nearly all carbon compounds, whether they come from living things or are made by people. A few simple carbon compounds such as carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, carbonates, hydrogencarbonates and carbides are usually studied in inorganic chemistry.

Everyday life: food (carbohydrates, proteins, fats), medicines (antibiotics, painkillers, vitamins), clothes (cotton, wool, nylon, polyester) and fuels (petrol, diesel, kerosene, cooking gas) are all organic.
Industry: petrochemical, pharmaceutical, plastics, paints, rubber and cosmetics industries are built on organic chemistry.
Agriculture: many fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides contain organic compounds.
Nature: DNA, RNA, enzymes and hormones are organic molecules that control heredity and the working of the body.

Other reasons to study it: to understand the chemistry of life; to make new materials such as drugs and plastics; to support industries; and to find solutions to problems of energy, health and the environment.

units.title: Characteristics of Organic Compounds
units.summary: Why carbon forms so many compounds, and the main properties of organic compounds compared with inorganic compounds.

sections.h: Why there are so many organic compounds
p: There are millions of known organic compounds, far more than inorganic ones. The reasons are: catenation, the power of carbon atoms to join to one another in long chains, branched chains and rings; tetravalency, because carbon has four outer electrons and forms four bonds; multiple bonding, since carbon forms single, double and triple bonds; and isomerism, meaning the same atoms can be arranged in different ways.
Examples: methane CH₄ is the simplest hydrocarbon; hexane C₆H₁₄ has a chain of six carbons; benzene C₆H₆ is a ring.
1. They contain carbon, usually bonded to hydrogen. Carbon has atomic number 6, electron arrangement 2, 4, so it forms four covalent bonds, for example in methane.
2. Covalent bonding: atoms are joined by shared pairs of electrons. So organic compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points and are less soluble in water than ionic salts.

3. Combustibility: most burn in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water, and give out heat: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Compounds with a lot of carbon burn with a smoky, sooty flame because of incomplete combustion.

4. Solubility: they are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as ethanol, benzene and chloroform (like dissolves like). Exceptions: small polar molecules such as ethanol and sugar do dissolve in water.
5. Many decompose or char when heated strongly; sugar chars to carbon and steam.
6. Organic reactions are often slow and need heat, pressure or a catalyst (for example, nickel for hydrogenation of ethene to ethane).
7. Isomerism is common. C₄H₁₀ has two isomers: butane and 2-methylpropane.

8. Many have low melting and boiling points because the forces between the molecules (van der Waals forces) are weak. Large molecules such as glucose and urea decompose or melt at higher temperatures.
9. Many have characteristic smells: esters smell fruity, amines smell of fish, and some aldehydes and ketones have sharp smells.

units.title: Hydrocarbons and Alkanes
units.summary: What hydrocarbons are, the homologous series, and the structure, physical and chemical properties and uses of alkanes.

p: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds made of only carbon and hydrogen. There are three families: alkanes (saturated; only single bonds), alkenes (unsaturated; at least one double bond C=C) and alkynes (unsaturated; at least one triple bond C≡C). 'Saturated' means that the carbon atoms hold as many hydrogen atoms as possible.

A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same general formula, a difference of one –CH₂– group between neighbouring members, similar chemical properties, and a steady change in physical properties (such as boiling point).

General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Bonding: only single bonds. The first four members are methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈ and butane C₄H₁₀. The names end in -ane. The prefixes meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex- show 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 carbon atoms.
From butane upward, alkanes show structural isomerism: butane (CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃) and 2-methylpropane (CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₃).

img.alt: Structural drawings of methane, ethane, ethene and ethyne showing all atoms and bonds, with single, double and triple bonds
img.cap: Methane and ethane (alkanes), ethene (alkene) and ethyne (alkyne).

p: C₁ to C₄ are gases, C₅ to about C₁₇ are liquids, and larger alkanes are waxy solids. Melting and boiling points rise with the size of the molecule because the forces between molecules get stronger. Alkanes are non-polar, so they do not dissolve in water but dissolve in organic solvents.
Alkanes are fairly unreactive because the C–C and C–H bonds are strong.

Combustion: complete: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Incomplete (not enough oxygen) gives carbon monoxide or soot (carbon): 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O. Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas, so never burn charcoal or run a generator in a closed room.
Substitution: in sunlight (ultraviolet light) a halogen replaces hydrogen atoms one at a time: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. Further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄.

Methane is natural gas (fuel for power stations and homes); propane and butane make cooking gas (LPG); petrol, kerosene and diesel are mixtures of alkanes; the waxes and lubricating oils are heavier alkanes.

units.title: Alkenes and Alkynes
units.summary: The structure, formulae, properties and reactions of alkenes and alkynes, how they differ from alkanes, and their uses.

p: General formula: CₙH₂ₙ. They have at least one double bond (C=C) made of one sigma (σ) bond and one pi (π) bond. The pi bond is weaker, so alkenes are more reactive than alkanes. Names end in -ene.

Examples: ethene C₂H₄ (H₂C=CH₂), propene C₃H₆ (CH₃–CH=CH₂), but-1-ene C₄H₈ (CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₃), but-2-ene C₄H₈ (CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃). Isomerism: but-1-ene and but-2-ene differ in the position of the double bond (structural isomers); but-2-ene also has cis and trans forms (next units).
Physical properties: similar to alkanes: the smaller ones are gases, the middle ones liquids, and non-polar, so insoluble in water.
1. Combustion: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O (more smoky than alkanes because of the higher percentage of carbon).

2. Addition reactions (the main reaction): the double bond opens and atoms add on. Hydrogenation: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ (nickel catalyst, heat). Halogenation: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ (this is the test for unsaturation: orange-brown bromine water turns colourless). Hydrohalogenation: C₂H₄ + HCl → C₂H₅Cl. Hydration: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH (phosphoric or sulphuric acid catalyst; this makes ethanol).
3. Polymerisation: many ethene molecules join to form polyethene (polythene), used for bags and bottles: n C₂H₄ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)ₙ.
General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. They have at least one triple bond (C≡C) made of one σ bond and two π bonds. Names end in -yne.
Examples: ethyne (acetylene) C₂H₂ (H–C≡C–H), propyne C₃H₄ (CH≡C–CH₃), butyne C₄H₆ with two isomers: but-1-yne (CH≡C–CH₂–CH₃) and but-2-yne (CH₃–C≡C–CH₃).

Properties: ethyne is a colourless gas with a faint smell and is very flammable. Combustion: 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O. It burns with a very hot flame when mixed with pure oxygen (the oxy-acetylene flame, about 3000 °C), used for welding and cutting metals. Plain air gives a smoky, cooler flame.
Addition reactions: C₂H₂ + 2H₂ → C₂H₆ (nickel); C₂H₂ + 2Br₂ → C₂H₂Br₄.

units.title: Isomerism: Structural Isomers
units.summary: What isomerism is, why it explains the huge number of organic compounds, and the types of structural isomerism: chain, position, functional group and metamerism.

p: Isomerism is the existence of two or more compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms. Such compounds are called isomers. They usually have different physical properties and sometimes different chemical properties. Isomerism is one reason why there are so many organic compounds.

Example: C₄H₁₀ has two isomers: n-butane (CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃) and 2-methylpropane (CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₃). They have the same formula but different structures and different boiling points (butane boils at about 0 °C; 2-methylpropane at about −12 °C).

img.alt: Two drawings: a straight chain of four carbon atoms labelled butane and a chain of three carbons with a branch labelled 2-methylpropane
img.cap: The two isomers of C₄H₁₀.

p: There are two main kinds: structural isomerism (the atoms are joined in a different order) and stereoisomerism (the atoms are joined in the same order but arranged differently in space). In SS1 we study structural isomerism and one kind of stereoisomerism, geometrical isomerism.

1. Chain (skeletal) isomerism: the carbon skeleton is different (straight or branched). Example: butane and 2-methylpropane. Another: C₅H₁₂ has three chain isomers: pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

2. Position isomerism: the same functional group or substituent is on a different carbon atom. Example: butan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH) and butan-2-ol (CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃), both C₄H₁₀O. Similarly but-1-ene and but-2-ene, and but-1-yne and but-2-yne.

3. Functional group isomerism: the compounds belong to different families. Example: ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH, an alcohol) and methoxymethane or dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃), both C₂H₆O. Ethanol is a liquid that dissolves in water; dimethyl ether is a gas.
4. Metamerism: the groups on the two sides of an ether linkage (–O–) differ. Example: diethyl ether (CH₃CH₂–O–CH₂CH₃) and methyl propyl ether (CH₃–O–CH₂CH₂CH₃), both C₄H₁₀O.
(Tautomerism, an advanced type in which two forms change easily into each other, such as keto and enol forms, is met in later years.)

Write all the structural isomers of C₄H₁₀O. Alcohols: butan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH; butan-2-ol CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃; 2-methylpropan-1-ol (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH; 2-methylpropan-2-ol (CH₃)₃COH. Ethers: diethyl ether CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃; methyl propyl ether CH₃OCH₂CH₂CH₃; and methyl isopropyl ether CH₃OCH(CH₃)₂. So there are 7 isomers. (The source notes list only 6 and miss methyl isopropyl ether.)

It explains the huge variety of organic compounds, and why compounds with the same formula behave differently. It matters in drug design, where one isomer of a drug may cure and another may be harmful, and in plastics and fuels (branched alkanes burn more smoothly in engines than straight-chain ones).

units.title: Geometrical (Cis-Trans) Isomerism
units.summary: Why the double bond causes cis and trans forms, with but-2-ene and 1,2-dichloroethene, their properties, and a correction to the notes' diagrams.

p: Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism is a kind of stereoisomerism. The atoms are joined in the same order, but they sit differently in space because rotation around a C=C double bond is not possible. Each of the two carbon atoms of the double bond must carry two different groups for it to occur. It is found in alkenes and in ring compounds. It cannot occur in alkanes, because the groups on a single bond can rotate freely.
Cis means 'on the same side' and trans means 'on opposite sides'.
But-2-ene (C₄H₈): in cis-but-2-ene both CH₃ groups are on the same side of the double bond (and both hydrogens on the other side). In trans-but-2-ene the CH₃ groups are on opposite sides.
1,2-dichloroethene (C₂H₂Cl₂): in the cis form the two chlorine atoms are on the same side; in the trans form, they are on opposite sides.

img.alt: Drawings of cis-but-2-ene with both methyl groups above the double bond and trans-but-2-ene with the methyl groups on opposite sides, and the same for 1,2-dichloroethene
img.cap: Cis (same side) and trans (opposite sides) isomers.

p: In the source notes, the drawing labelled 'cis' has the CH₃ groups at opposite corners (one top, one bottom), which is really the trans form, and the drawing labelled 'trans' has both CH₃ groups on the same side, which is the cis form. They were swapped. Always check that cis has both like groups on the same side of the double bond.
Cis isomers are usually more polar, so they often have higher boiling points. Trans isomers usually pack better in crystals and so have higher melting points. Their reactions can also differ.

Isomerism explains the diversity of organic compounds. It is important in drugs, where different isomers can have very different effects; in polymers (natural rubber has cis units); and in explaining why molecules with the same formula behave in different ways.

units.title: Petroleum and Petrochemicals
units.summary: What petroleum is, how it formed, what it contains, why it matters to Nigeria and the world, and the main petrochemicals and their products.

p: Petroleum (crude oil) is a thick, dark brown or black flammable liquid found underground in porous rocks trapped beneath rock layers that oil cannot pass through. It is a mixture of hydrocarbons with small amounts of sulphur, nitrogen and oxygen compounds and traces of metals such as vanadium and nickel.

Origin: it is a fossil fuel. It was formed from the remains of tiny sea plants and animals that were buried under mud and sediments, perhaps 50 to 500 million years ago. Heat and pressure over millions of years slowly changed them into crude oil and natural gas. The gas often lies above the oil. Oil was first found in Nigeria in 1956 at Oloibiri in the Niger Delta.

Alkanes (paraffins), about 30 to 60%: straight and branched chains such as methane and ethane. Cycloalkanes (naphthenes), about 30 to 40%: ring hydrocarbons such as cyclohexane. Aromatic hydrocarbons, about 3 to 15%: benzene ring compounds such as benzene and toluene. Impurities: hydrogen sulphide and other sulphur, nitrogen and oxygen compounds, and trace metals.

Energy: petrol, diesel and kerosene power vehicles, ships, planes, generators and homes. Raw material: for plastics, synthetic fibres, fertilisers, paints, detergents and drugs. Lubricants: oils that reduce friction in machines. Economy: petroleum is Nigeria's largest export and source of government revenue. Road building and roofing: bitumen (asphalt). Electricity: fuel oil and natural gas drive power stations.
Petrochemicals are chemicals made from petroleum or natural gas, the building blocks of many modern materials.

p: Petroleum products (petrol, diesel, kerosene, lubricants, bitumen) are the fractions obtained mainly by separating and treating crude oil. Petrochemicals are chemicals made from petroleum or gas by further chemical reactions, and used to make plastics, fibres and other materials.

units.title: Refining of Petroleum and the Petroleum Industry
units.summary: Fractional distillation of crude oil, cracking and other processes, the fractions and their uses, the environmental problems and Nigeria's petroleum industry.

sections.h: Stage A: separation by fractional distillation
p: Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with different boiling points. It is heated to about 350 to 400 °C so that most of it turns to vapour and is fed into a tall fractionating tower. The tower is hottest at the bottom and cooler at the top. The vapours rise and each condenses at the height where the temperature matches its boiling point. Small molecules with low boiling points rise to the top; large molecules with high boiling points stay near the bottom. Each part is called a fraction.

img.alt: A tall fractionating tower with crude oil entering at the bottom and fractions leaving at levels: refinery gas at the top, then petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, fuel oil and bitumen at the bottom, with temperature increasing downward
img.cap: Fractional distillation of crude oil.

p: The boiling ranges below are approximate; books give slightly different values.

These change fractions that are in low demand into more useful products. Cracking: breaking large molecules into smaller, more useful ones such as petrol and alkenes. Thermal cracking uses high temperature and pressure; catalytic cracking uses a catalyst such as zeolite. Reforming: rearranging molecules into branched and aromatic ones, which raises the octane number (quality) of petrol. Polymerisation: joining small alkene molecules into large molecules. Alkylation: joining small molecules to make high-octane fuel.
Desulphurisation removes sulphur compounds so that less sulphur dioxide is produced. Fractions are blended to make fuels that meet the right standards.

Air pollution: burning fuels gives carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas), carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide. Oil spills: damage rivers, farms and fisheries, as in parts of the Niger Delta. Resource depletion: petroleum is non-renewable. Fire and explosion: fuels are very flammable. Industrial accidents: leaks of toxic gas.

Control: develop renewable energy such as solar and wind; maintain pipelines to prevent leaks; run refineries efficiently to reduce emissions; strong environmental laws and safety training; clean up spills.

Refineries: Port Harcourt, Warri and Kaduna (the older state refineries) and the large Dangote refinery at Lekki, Lagos. Products: petrol, diesel, aviation fuel, lubricants and asphalt. Importance: oil and gas provide most of Nigeria's foreign exchange earnings and government revenue. Reducing dependence on oil by developing agriculture, manufacturing and services makes the economy safer.

Fossil fuels compared: petroleum is liquid, rich in energy, easy to move by pipeline and tanker; natural gas (mainly methane) is the cleanest fossil fuel; coal is solid, harder to move, and gives the most ash and soot.

units.title: Chemical Reactions: Combination and Decomposition
units.summary: What a chemical reaction is, its signs, and the combination and decomposition types with equations and uses.

p: A chemical reaction is a process in which substances (reactants) change into new substances (products) with different composition and properties. In it, bonds in the reactants are broken and new bonds are formed. Example: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l).

Signs of a chemical reaction: a gas is given off; a colour change; heat or light is given out or taken in; a precipitate (solid) forms. Other features: there is always an energy change; mass is conserved (the law of conservation of mass); many reactions cannot easily be reversed.
Everyday examples: cooking food, burning fuel, rusting of iron, photosynthesis.
Reactions can be grouped as combination, decomposition and displacement (and others, such as neutralisation and redox, which you have met). This unit covers the first two.
Two or more simple substances join to form one product: A + B → AB.

Examples: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s) (magnesium burns with a bright white flame, leaving white ash). C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g). N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) (Haber process). CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) (making slaked lime, used in cement and to treat acid soil).
Features: usually exothermic (give out heat) and only one product. Uses: burning fuels for energy, making ammonia for fertiliser, cement.

Note: the source notes give photosynthesis as an example of combination. Photosynthesis (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂) is not a simple one-product combination and is endothermic, as it takes in energy from sunlight, so we do not treat it as a typical combination reaction. Also, not every combination reaction is exothermic (N₂ + O₂ → 2NO takes in heat).
One compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances: AB → A + B. Usually energy must be supplied (endothermic).
Thermal decomposition (by heat): CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); 2KClO₃(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O₂(g) (with MnO₂ as a catalyst; used to prepare oxygen in the laboratory).
Electrolytic decomposition (by electricity): 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) (by electrolysis).
Photolytic decomposition (by light): 2AgCl(s) → 2Ag(s) + Cl₂(g). This is why silver salts are kept in dark bottles and why photographic film is kept away from light.
Uses: preparing gases in the laboratory, making lime from limestone, electrolysis, photography. Decomposition of food by microbes leads to spoilage.

units.title: Displacement Reactions and the Reactivity Series
units.summary: How a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one, with metals and halogens, the reactivity series, and uses such as galvanising.

p: In a displacement reaction a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound: A + BC → AC + B.

Examples: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s): zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper (the blue solution fades and brown copper forms). Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s): iron displaces copper (an iron nail in copper sulphate becomes coated with copper). Cl₂(g) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq): chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine (the solution turns orange).
The reverse reactions do not happen: copper does not displace zinc from zinc sulphate, because copper is less reactive than zinc.
The reactivity series lists metals from the most reactive to the least reactive. A metal higher in the list can displace one lower in the list from its compound.

img.alt: A vertical list of metals from potassium at the top, most reactive, through sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, hydrogen, copper, silver to gold at the bottom, least reactive
img.cap: The reactivity series of metals.

p: Extraction of metals: carbon displaces (reduces) iron from its oxide, Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, because carbon is more reactive than iron in a furnace. Galvanising: iron is coated with zinc; even if scratched the zinc, being more reactive, reacts first, so the iron does not rust. Recovering metals: copper can be recovered from solution by adding scrap iron. Water purification: halogen displacement and the reactions of chlorine.
Predicting: will Fe react with CuSO₄? Yes (iron is above copper). Will Cu react with ZnSO₄? No. Will Mg react with HCl? Yes (magnesium is above hydrogen), giving hydrogen and magnesium chloride.

units.title: Energy Changes: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
units.summary: How reactions give out or take in energy, enthalpy change ΔH, activation energy and energy profile diagrams.

p: Every chemical reaction involves a change of energy. Energy may appear as heat, light, sound or electricity. Energy can be given out to the surroundings or taken in from them. Knowing this helps us to predict whether a reaction will go, to explain temperature changes and to use chemical energy in industry, in living things and in the home.
An exothermic reaction gives out heat (or other energy) to the surroundings, so the surroundings get hotter. Example: burning methane, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat.
An endothermic reaction takes in heat from the surroundings, so the surroundings get colder. Example: thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (heat is taken in).
1. Conservation of energy: energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. In a reaction, energy passes between the reacting substances and their surroundings.
2. Enthalpy change (ΔH): the heat change of a reaction at constant pressure. ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions (energy released) and positive for endothermic reactions (energy absorbed).

3. Activation energy (Eₐ): even exothermic reactions need a minimum energy to start, to break the first bonds in the reactants. A match must be struck before it burns, even though burning is exothermic.

Energy changes come from bond breaking and bond making: breaking bonds takes in energy; making bonds gives out energy. If more energy is given out in making bonds than is taken in to break bonds, the reaction is exothermic.

In an exothermic reaction the reactants are higher in energy than the products. The energy difference is released, and ΔH is negative. In an endothermic reaction, the products are higher in energy than the reactants, the difference is absorbed, and ΔH is positive. In both cases, there is an energy 'hill', the activation energy, between the reactants and the products.

img.alt: Two energy profile diagrams: exothermic with reactants high and products lower and ΔH negative, and endothermic with reactants low and products higher and ΔH positive, each showing an activation energy hill

units.title: Examples, Uses and Comparison of Energy Changes
units.summary: Characteristics and examples of exothermic and endothermic changes, simple experiments, real-life uses and a comparison table.

p: Heat is given out and the surroundings become warmer. ΔH is negative. The products are more stable (lower in energy) than the reactants. Examples: combustion of fuels (methane, propane, petrol); respiration, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy; neutralisation, HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O + heat; freezing of water, which gives out heat as ice forms; adding quicklime to water; dissolving sodium hydroxide in water.

Heat is taken in and the surroundings become colder. ΔH is positive. The products are higher in energy than the reactants. They often need a continuous supply of energy. Examples: photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + sunlight → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂; thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate; dissolving ammonium chloride in water; electrolysis of water, 2H₂O + energy → 2H₂ + O₂; melting ice (a change of state that takes in heat).

units.title: Rates of Reaction and the Factors That Affect Them
units.summary: What the rate of reaction is, how to measure it, and how concentration, temperature, pressure, surface area, the nature of the reactants and light change it.

sections.h: What is the rate of a reaction?
p: The rate of reaction is how fast reactants are changed into products. It tells us how much reactant is used or how much product is formed in a given time. Rate = change in concentration of a reactant (or product) ÷ time taken. Units: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ for concentration, cm³ s⁻¹ for the volume of gas given off, or g s⁻¹ for a change in mass.

Gas given off: collect the gas in a gas syringe or an upturned measuring cylinder (for example, magnesium with hydrochloric acid). Loss of mass: put the flask on a balance and watch the mass fall as gas escapes (marble chips with acid). Colour change: watch the colour fade or appear. Cloudiness: time how long it takes for a cross under the flask to disappear as a precipitate forms (sodium thiosulphate with hydrochloric acid gives sulphur).

1. Nature of the reactants: ionic reactions in solution, such as HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, are very fast because the ions are already free. Reactions that must break strong covalent bonds, such as methane with chlorine, are slow unless there is light or heat.

2. Concentration: a higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more collisions each second, so a faster reaction. 2 mol/dm³ HCl reacts with magnesium faster than 0.5 mol/dm³ HCl. On a graph of volume of gas against time, the curve is steeper.

3. Temperature: a higher temperature gives the particles more energy, so they move faster, collide more often, and more of the collisions have enough energy to react. As a rough rule, the rate about doubles for every 10 °C rise. Food spoils faster in warm weather and lasts longer in a refrigerator.
4. Pressure (for gases): raising the pressure squeezes gas particles closer together, so there are more collisions. The Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, uses high pressure.

5. Surface area: a reaction takes place at the surface of a solid. Powder has a larger surface than lumps, so it reacts faster. Powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with acid than marble chips; sawdust burns faster than a log; flour dust can explode.

6. Light: some reactions are speeded up or started by light (photochemical reactions), for example photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, and the decomposition of silver halides in photography, 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂.
7. A catalyst (see the next unit).

units.title: Collision Theory, Catalysts and Industrial Uses
units.summary: Why particles must collide effectively, how catalysts lower the activation energy, the types of catalysis, and how rate ideas are used in industry.

p: For a reaction to happen, particles must collide; the collision must be effective, meaning they hit with the right orientation and with enough energy; and the minimum energy needed is the activation energy (Eₐ). Most collisions are not effective. Anything that increases the number of effective collisions per second raises the rate.

A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up or permanently changed. It works by providing a different path with a lower activation energy, so more particles have enough energy to react. A catalyst does not change the products or the total energy released.

Examples: manganese(IV) oxide, MnO₂, catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into oxygen and water (2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂). Iron catalyses the Haber process. Nickel catalyses the hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make margarine. Enzymes are the catalysts of living things.

img.alt: An energy profile with a high hill for the uncatalysed reaction and a lower hill for the catalysed reaction, between the same reactants and products
img.cap: A catalyst lowers the activation energy.

p: Homogeneous catalysis: the catalyst is in the same state as the reactants (for example, nitrogen monoxide gas catalysing the oxidation of sulphur dioxide gas in an older process). Heterogeneous catalysis: the catalyst is in a different state (solid iron in the gaseous Haber process). Autocatalysis: one of the products speeds up the reaction (in the hydrolysis of an ester, the acid produced acts as catalyst).

Concentration: magnesium with hydrochloric acid of different concentrations; measure the hydrogen given off. Temperature: sodium thiosulphate with hydrochloric acid at different temperatures; time the disappearance of a cross. Catalyst: hydrogen peroxide with and without manganese(IV) oxide; collect the oxygen. Surface area: calcium carbonate powder and marble chips with acid.

Haber process (ammonia): iron catalyst, about 200 atmospheres pressure and 450 °C: a high enough temperature for a good rate, without losing too much ammonia. Contact process (sulphuric acid): vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, about 450 °C. Hydrogenation of oils: nickel catalyst to make margarine. Polymerisation: catalysts control the rate and the yield of plastics. In all industries the aim is to make products quickly and cheaply and with little waste.

units.title: Reversible Reactions and Chemical Equilibrium
units.summary: Irreversible and reversible reactions, what dynamic equilibrium is, and what happens to the concentrations over time.

p: An irreversible reaction goes in one direction only, from reactants to products, and the products cannot easily change back. Examples: burning methane, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O; neutralisation, HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

A reversible reaction can go in both directions under the same conditions. It is shown by a double arrow ⇌. Examples: the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g); heating calcium carbonate in a closed vessel, CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), where the products can recombine; heating blue hydrated copper(II) sulphate gives white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate and water, and adding water changes it back to blue (a test for water).

In a reversible reaction carried out in a closed system, the forward and backward reactions both happen until a state called dynamic equilibrium is reached. At equilibrium: the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction; the concentrations of the reactants and products stay constant (they are not necessarily equal); and the system is dynamic: the reactions still go on, but there is no overall change.
In the Haber process, at first the formation of NH₃ is fast. As NH₃ builds up, it decomposes back to N₂ and H₂ faster, until the two rates are equal.

img.alt: A graph of concentration against time: the concentrations of nitrogen and hydrogen fall and the concentration of ammonia rises until all three become constant at equilibrium
img.cap: Concentrations change until equilibrium is reached, then stay constant.

p: The same equilibrium mixture is reached whether we start with N₂ and H₂ or start with NH₃, provided the conditions are the same. This is shown by the two graphs in many textbooks: starting with reactants, the reactants fall and the product rises; starting with the product, the product falls and the reactants rise; in both cases the concentrations level off.

units.title: Le Chatelier's Principle and the Equilibrium Constant
units.summary: How changes in concentration, pressure, temperature and catalyst affect an equilibrium, the equilibrium constant Kc with a calculation, and the Haber and Contact processes.

p: If a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the system shifts in the direction that opposes the change and tries to restore balance.

Adding more reactant shifts the equilibrium towards the products. Adding more product shifts it towards the reactants. In N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, adding more H₂ moves the equilibrium to the right (more NH₃); adding NH₃ moves it to the left. Removing NH₃ as it is formed moves it to the right, which is what is done in industry.

Raising the pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules; lowering the pressure favours the side with more gas molecules. In N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ there are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right. High pressure moves the equilibrium to the right (more NH₃).

For a reaction that is exothermic in the forward direction, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium backward (towards the reactants) and lowering the temperature shifts it forward. For an endothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature shifts it forward. The Haber reaction is exothermic: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat, so a high temperature gives less ammonia.
A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally. It lets the system reach equilibrium sooner but does not change the position of equilibrium or the amount of product at equilibrium.

For the reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, at a fixed temperature: Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ ÷ ([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ), where the square brackets mean concentration in mol/dm³. A large Kc means that products are favoured at equilibrium; a small Kc means reactants are favoured. Kc changes only with temperature.

Example: for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, Kc = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³). At equilibrium, [NH₃] = 0.2, [N₂] = 0.1 and [H₂] = 0.3 mol/dm³. Kc = 0.2² ÷ (0.1 × 0.3³) = 0.04 ÷ (0.1 × 0.027) = 0.04 ÷ 0.0027 = 14.8 (units mol⁻² dm⁶).

Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic): high pressure (about 200 atmospheres) favours the forward reaction; a moderate temperature (about 450 °C) is a compromise, because a lower temperature gives more ammonia but too slowly; iron with promoters is the catalyst; ammonia is liquefied and removed, and unreacted gas is recycled.

Contact process, 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (exothermic, ΔH about −197 kJ per mole of O₂): a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst; a temperature of about 450 °C as a compromise. High pressure would favour SO₃ (3 moles to 2), but the yield is already high at about 1 to 2 atmospheres, so very high pressure is not worth the cost. (The source notes say 'high pressure and low temperature'. That favours the forward reaction in theory, but in practice, moderate conditions are chosen.)
In the body, oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood follow equilibrium ideas, and Le Chatelier's principle helps to explain gas exchange in the lungs.

For CO + 2H₂ ⇌ CH₃OH (forward exothermic; 3 moles of gas to 1): raising the pressure gives more methanol; lowering the temperature gives more methanol; adding a catalyst does not change the yield, it only reaches equilibrium faster.

units.title: Metals and Non-Metals: Properties
units.summary: Where metals and non-metals are found in the periodic table, their physical and chemical properties, metalloids and a comparison table.

p: Elements are grouped as metals and non-metals according to their properties. Metals are on the left and in the centre of the periodic table; non-metals are on the right. A staircase line separates them. They form the materials of industry, farming, building, medicine and technology.
Metals readily lose electrons to form positive ions (cations) and have metallic bonding.

Physical properties: malleable (can be hammered into sheets, like aluminium foil); ductile (can be drawn into wires, like copper); good conductors of heat and electricity because of free (delocalised) electrons; most have high melting and boiling points (mercury is a liquid at room temperature, and Group 1 metals melt at low temperatures); high density; shiny when polished (metallic lustre); sonorous (ring when struck); strong; can form alloys (brass, bronze, steel).

Chemical properties: they lose electrons easily (electropositive); they form basic oxides, 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O (some oxides are amphoteric, such as aluminium oxide); they react with water to differing degrees (sodium violently, calcium more slowly, gold not at all); most react with dilute acids to give a salt and hydrogen (except copper, mercury, silver, gold and platinum); they form chlorides, 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl; they form ionic compounds.
Non-metals tend to gain or share electrons, forming negative ions or covalent compounds.

Physical properties: poor conductors of heat and electricity (graphite is an exception); low melting and boiling points; many are gases or brittle solids; not malleable or ductile; usually low density; dull, with no metallic lustre; brittle; they exist in all three states (oxygen is a gas, bromine a liquid, sulphur a solid); some have allotropes (carbon as diamond and graphite, oxygen as O₂ and O₃).

Chemical properties: they gain or share electrons (electronegative); their oxides are acidic, for example CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃; they form covalent compounds with hydrogen (HCl, CH₄); with metals they form ionic compounds (NaCl); across a period, non-metal reactivity generally increases.

Metalloids have properties between those of metals and non-metals. Examples: boron, silicon, arsenic, antimony and tellurium. Many are semiconductors, so silicon is used in electronics and computer chips.
Study the table.

units.title: Extraction and Uses of Metals and Non-Metals
units.summary: How metals are got from their ores (electrolysis, reduction with carbon, roasting), the uses of metals and non-metals, and the role of recycling.

p: Most metals are found in the ground as ores, rocks that contain a metal compound in enough amounts to be worth mining. The method of extraction depends on how reactive the metal is.

1. Electrolysis: very reactive metals such as aluminium, sodium and potassium. Aluminium is obtained from bauxite. The bauxite is first purified to give aluminium oxide (alumina). The alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite (to lower the melting point to about 950 °C) and electrolysed using carbon electrodes. Molten aluminium collects at the cathode and oxygen is released at the anode, which slowly burns away the carbon anodes. This needs a great deal of electricity.

2. Reduction with carbon (or carbon monoxide): metals of medium reactivity such as iron and zinc. Iron is extracted from haematite (iron(III) oxide) in a blast furnace: carbon burns to make carbon monoxide, which reduces the iron oxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Limestone is added to remove impurities as slag.

3. Roasting and smelting: for sulphide ores, the ore is first roasted in air to give the oxide, which is then reduced. 4. Unreactive metals like gold may occur uncombined in nature (native metals) and need only to be separated from rock.

Iron (as steel): construction, tools and machines. Copper: electrical wiring and plumbing. Aluminium: aircraft, packaging, cooking pots. Gold and silver: jewellery and electronics. Zinc: galvanising and dry-cell batteries. Lead: car batteries and shielding against radiation. Titanium: aircraft and medical implants.

Oxygen: breathing, welding, steel making. Nitrogen: fertilisers, refrigeration (liquid nitrogen), explosives. Sulphur: making sulphuric acid and vulcanising rubber. Chlorine: disinfecting water, making PVC. Carbon: fuel, steel making, graphite in pencils and lubricants, diamond in jewellery and cutting tools. Phosphorus: matches, fertilisers, detergents.

Metals and non-metals are vital for transport, medicine, communication, power and building. Recycling metals such as aluminium and iron saves energy and ore and reduces pollution; recycling aluminium uses only a small fraction of the energy needed to extract new aluminium. Waste plastics and toxic gases from non-metals must be disposed of properly to protect the environment.

units.title: Sets (1): Meaning, Notation, Types, Subsets and Power Sets
units.summary: What a set is, how to write sets, the types of set, the universal set, subsets and the power set, with worked examples.

p: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, called elements or members. 'Well-defined' means we can say for certain whether something belongs to the set or not. 'Distinct' means no repetition.

Well-defined: A = {the months of the year}. Not well-defined: B = {beautiful flowers}, because 'beautiful' is a matter of opinion. Sets are everywhere: the students in a class, the natural numbers, the letters of the alphabet.
Roster (listing) method: write the elements inside curly brackets. A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}.

Set-builder notation: describe the property. A = {x : x is an even number, 0 < x ≤ 10}. Read: 'A is the set of all x such that x is an even number from 1 to 10'. (The vertical bar | is often used instead of the colon.)

head: Symbol
Meaning
Example
rows: is a subset of (may be equal)

p: Null (empty) set ∅: has no elements, such as the set of humans who can fly unaided. Singleton set: has exactly one element. Finite set: the elements can be counted to an end, such as {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Infinite set: the elements never end, such as {1, 2, 3, ...}. Equal sets: exactly the same elements, {1, 2, 3} = {3, 1, 2} (order does not matter). Equivalent sets: the same number of elements, such as {a, b, c} and {1, 2, 3}.
The universal set U is the set of all objects being discussed. It depends on the problem. If U = {1, 2, ..., 10} and A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}, then A is a subset of U.

If every element of A is also in B, then A is a subset of B, written A ⊆ B. A proper subset is a subset that is not equal to the whole set. Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set. Example: A = {1, 2}, B = {1, 2, 3, 4}, so A ⊂ B. (The source notes call ∅ an 'improper' subset. In fact, the only improper subset of A is A itself; ∅ is a proper subset of any non-empty set.)
The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. If A has n elements, it has 2ⁿ subsets, so n(P(A)) = 2ⁿ, and it has 2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets.
Example: A = {a, b}. Subsets: ∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}. So P(A) = {∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}} and n(P(A)) = 4.
Example 1. V = {a, e, i, o, u}. (a) Set-builder: V = {x : x is a vowel in the English alphabet}. (b) Finite. (c) n(V) = 5. (d) a ∈ V is true. (e) b ∉ V.
Example 2. C = {red, green}. Subsets: ∅, {red}, {green}, {red, green}; n(P(C)) = 4.
Example 3. A set X has 63 proper subsets. How many elements? 2ⁿ − 1 = 63, so 2ⁿ = 64 and n = 6.
Example 4. List the elements of P = {x : x is prime and 10 < x < 25}. P = {11, 13, 17, 19, 23}.

units.title: Sets (2): Set Operations and Two-Set Venn Diagrams
units.summary: Union, intersection, complement and difference of sets, the inclusion-exclusion rule, and how to solve two-set problems with a Venn diagram.

p: Study the table. Suppose U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4, 5}.

p: A Venn diagram (invented by John Venn about 1880) shows sets as pictures. The rectangle is the universal set U. Circles are subsets. Where circles overlap we have the intersection. To make a Venn diagram of two sets A and B, draw two overlapping circles inside a rectangle. There are four regions: A only, A ∩ B, B only and outside both circles.
For two sets: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). We subtract the intersection because it was counted twice.
Also: n(A only) = n(A) − n(A ∩ B), and n(outside) = n(U) − n(A ∪ B).
In a class of 35 students, 20 offer Physics (P), 17 offer History (H) and 5 offer neither. Find (a) how many offer both, (b) how many offer History only.

n(P ∪ H) = 35 − 5 = 30. Using n(P ∪ H) = n(P) + n(H) − n(P ∩ H): 30 = 20 + 17 − n(P ∩ H), so n(P ∩ H) = 7. (a) Both = 7. (b) History only = 17 − 7 = 10. Physics only = 20 − 7 = 13. Check: 13 + 7 + 10 + 5 = 35.

If n(A \ B) = 15, n(B \ A) = 10 and n(A ∩ B) = 5, then n(A ∪ B) = 15 + 10 + 5 = 30. If 15 play football and 12 play basketball, and 5 play both, and every student plays at least one, the class has 15 + 12 − 5 = 22 students.

units.title: Sets (3): Three-Set Problems and De Morgan's Laws
units.summary: The inclusion-exclusion rule for three sets, filling a three-circle Venn diagram from the middle outward, and De Morgan's laws.

p: A three-set Venn diagram has eight regions: A ∩ B ∩ C in the centre; three regions where exactly two sets overlap; three regions of 'only' one set; and the region outside all the circles.

img.alt: A three-circle Venn diagram of sets F, C and P with all eight region values filled in: F only 20, C only 12, P only 20, F and C only 8, F and P only 5, C and P only 3, all three 7, none 25
img.cap: The three-set Venn diagram for the worked example.

p: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C).
Of 100 people, 40 belong to club F, 30 to club C and 35 to club P. The overlaps: n(F ∩ C) = 15, n(F ∩ P) = 12, n(C ∩ P) = 10 and n(F ∩ C ∩ P) = 7.

Always start from the middle. Region F ∩ C ∩ P = 7. F ∩ C only = 15 − 7 = 8. F ∩ P only = 12 − 7 = 5. C ∩ P only = 10 − 7 = 3. F only = 40 − (8 + 5 + 7) = 20. C only = 30 − (8 + 3 + 7) = 12. P only = 35 − (5 + 3 + 7) = 20. Total inside the circles = 20 + 12 + 20 + 8 + 5 + 3 + 7 = 75. So 100 − 75 = 25 are in none.

For any sets A and B: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. In words: 'the complement of the union is the intersection of the complements', and 'the complement of the intersection is the union of the complements'.

Check with U = {a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h}, X = {a, b, d, e} and Y = {b, e, f, g}. X ∪ Y = {a, b, d, e, f, g}, so (X ∪ Y)′ = {c, h}. X′ = {c, f, g, h} and Y′ = {a, c, d, h}, so X′ ∩ Y′ = {c, h}. They agree. Also X′ ∩ Y = {f, g}.

A survey of 60 fans: 28 watch football, 22 basketball, 25 cricket; 10 watch football and basketball, 8 watch football and cricket, 7 watch basketball and cricket; 3 watch all three. Centre = 3. F ∩ B only = 7; F ∩ C only = 5; B ∩ C only = 4. F only = 28 − (7 + 5 + 3) = 13. B only = 22 − (7 + 4 + 3) = 8. C only = 25 − (5 + 4 + 3) = 13. Exactly two sports: 7 + 5 + 4 = 16. Inside the circles: 13 + 8 + 13 + 7 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 53, so 60 − 53 = 7 watch none.

units.title: Indices
units.summary: The meaning of an index (power) and the laws of indices, zero, negative and fractional indices, worked examples and indicial equations.

p: Indices (powers) show repeated multiplication. a⁵ = a × a × a × a × a. Here a is the base and 5 is the index (exponent), the number of times the base is multiplied by itself. Example: 2⁵ = 32.
For any positive base a and any numbers m and n:
Example 1. Simplify (16/81)^(−3/4). A negative index inverts the fraction: (81/16)^(3/4). Now the fourth root of 81 is 3 and of 16 is 2, so we get (3/2)³ = 27/8.
Example 2. Evaluate 8^(2/3) × 2⁻². 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 4. 2⁻² = 1/4. The product is 1.
An indicial equation has the unknown in the index. Method: write both sides with the same base, then equate the indices.
Example 4. Solve 3^(x) = 81. 81 = 3⁴ so x = 4. Example 5. Solve (1/4)^x = 32. Write both as powers of 2: (2⁻²)^x = 2⁵, so −2x = 5 and x = −5/2.

Example 6 (quadratic form). Solve 4^x − 6(2^x) + 8 = 0. Let y = 2^x. Then 4^x = (2²)^x = (2^x)² = y². So y² − 6y + 8 = 0, which factorises as (y − 2)(y − 4) = 0, so y = 2 or y = 4. Then 2^x = 2 gives x = 1, and 2^x = 4 gives x = 2. Answer: x = 1 or x = 2.
Example 7. Solve 5^(2k) + 2(5^k) − 3 = 0. Let y = 5^k: y² + 2y − 3 = 0, (y + 3)(y − 1) = 0. y = −3 is impossible (5^k is always positive). So 5^k = 1 and k = 0.

The graph of y = 2^x rises faster and faster as x increases (exponential growth). The graph of y = (1/2)^x falls towards zero (exponential decay). Both pass through (0, 1) because any number to the power 0 is 1.

units.title: Logarithms
units.summary: The meaning of a logarithm, the laws of logarithms, change of base, and solving logarithmic equations.

p: Logarithms do the opposite of indices. If aˣ = N, then log_a N = x, read 'the logarithm of N to base a equals x'. It tells us the power to which the base must be raised to give N.

Examples: 10³ = 1000, so log₁₀ 1000 = 3. 2⁵ = 32, so log₂ 32 = 5. Because log₁₀ 100 = 2, we say 'the log of 100 to base 10 is 2'. Indices and logarithms are two ways of writing the same fact: aˣ = N ⇔ log_a N = x.
Study the table. M and N must be positive.
log_a b = log_c b ÷ log_c a (usually c = 10 or e). A useful corollary: log_a b = 1 ÷ log_b a.
Example. Given log₃ 2 = 0.631, find log₂ 9. log₂ 9 = log₃ 9 ÷ log₃ 2 = 2 ÷ 0.631 = 3.17.
Example 1. Evaluate log₂ 8 + log₃ 9 − log₅ 1. = 3 + 2 − 0 = 5.
Example 2. Express ½ log 25 − 2 log 3 + log 18 as a single logarithm. ½ log 25 = log 5. 2 log 3 = log 9. So log 5 − log 9 + log 18 = log (5 × 18 ÷ 9) = log 10 = 1 (to base 10).
Example 3. Given log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010, find log₁₀ 32. 32 = 2⁵, so log 32 = 5 × 0.3010 = 1.505.

Example 4 (equation). Solve log₂ x + log₂ (x − 7) = 3. Combine: log₂ [x(x − 7)] = 3, so x(x − 7) = 2³ = 8. Then x² − 7x − 8 = 0, (x − 8)(x + 1) = 0. x = 8 or x = −1. We reject −1 because log of a negative number does not exist. Answer: x = 8.
Example 5. Solve log₃ p − log₃ (p − 6) = 2. log₃ [p/(p − 6)] = 2, so p/(p − 6) = 9, p = 9p − 54, 8p = 54, p = 6.75.
Example 6. Solve log₄(x + 1) + log₄(x − 1) = log₄ 8. (x + 1)(x − 1) = 8, x² = 9, x = 3 (reject −3).

units.title: Surds
units.summary: What surds are, the rules for simplifying, adding and multiplying them, and how to rationalise a denominator.

p: A surd is an irrational root that cannot be simplified to remove the root sign, such as √2, √3, √5 and ∛5. √4 = 2 and √9 = 3 are not surds, because they are rational numbers. A simple surd is one term, like √7. A compound surd joins a surd to another term, like 2 + √3 or 5 − 2√2.
Study the table.
To rationalise means to remove the surd from the denominator.
Monomial denominator: multiply top and bottom by the surd. 6/√3 = (6 × √3)/(√3 × √3) = 6√3/3 = 2√3.
Binomial denominator: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate. The conjugate of a + √b is a − √b (change the sign in the middle). This uses (a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b, which has no surd.
Example 2. Rationalise 1/(2 + √3). Multiply by (2 − √3): (2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = 2 − √3.

units.title: Linear Inequalities in One Variable
units.summary: Inequality symbols, solving linear inequalities, the golden rule for negative numbers, and showing answers on a number line.

p: An inequality shows that one side is bigger or smaller than the other. Symbols: > (greater than), < (less than), ≥ (greater than or equal to), ≤ (less than or equal to). A linear inequality has a variable only to the first power, such as 2x + 5 > 9 or 3x − 4 ≤ 8.
Solve a linear inequality like an equation, but when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign.
Why: 6 > 4 is true. Multiply by −2: −12 and −8. −12 > −8 is false; the true statement is −12 < −8.
Open circle ○ for < or > (the end point is not included). Closed circle ● for ≤ or ≥ (the end point is included). An arrow shows the direction of all the solutions.
x > 2: open circle at 2, arrow to the right. x ≤ −3: closed circle at −3, arrow to the left. 2 ≤ x < 6: closed circle at 2, open circle at 6, a line between.
Example 1. Solve 5 − 2x ≥ 11. −2x ≥ 6. Divide by −2 and reverse the sign: x ≤ −3. Closed circle at −3, arrow left.
Example 2. Solve 3x − 5 < 4x + 2. −5 − 2 < 4x − 3x, so −7 < x, or x > −7. Open circle at −7, arrow right.
Example 3 (double inequality). Solve −1 ≤ 2x − 5 < 7. Add 5: 4 ≤ 2x < 12. Divide by 2: 2 ≤ x < 6.
Example 4. Solve and represent x/2 − 5 > −8. x/2 > −3, so x > −6.
Example 5. Solve 7 − 4x ≤ 1. −4x ≤ −6, so x ≥ 3/2.
Example 6. Solve −5 ≤ 3x + 1 ≤ 10. −6 ≤ 3x ≤ 9, so −2 ≤ x ≤ 3.
Example 8. Find the range of x for 3x − 2 > 7 and x − 1 < 5. First: x > 3. Second: x < 6. So 3 < x < 6.

units.title: Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
units.summary: How to graph an inequality such as ax + by > c, using a dashed or solid boundary line and a test point, with several worked examples.

p: An inequality in two variables has the form ax + by > c or ax + by ≤ c. Its solution is a region of the coordinate plane, not a single point: every point in the region makes the inequality true.
1. Change the inequality to an equation to get the boundary line.
2. Draw the boundary: a dashed line for < or > (points on the line are not solutions) and a solid line for ≤ or ≥ (points on the line are solutions).

3. Test a point not on the line, usually the origin (0, 0). Put it in the original inequality. If it is true, shade the side containing the point. If false, shade the other side. (If the line passes through the origin, test another point such as (1, 0).)

Example 1. Graph 2x − y < 3. Boundary: 2x − y = 3, which is y = 2x − 3 (gradient 2, y-intercept −3). Points (0, −3) and (2, 1). Draw it dashed. Test (0, 0): 2(0) − 0 < 3 gives 0 < 3, true. Shade the side containing the origin, which is the region above the line.
Example 2. Graph y > −x + 1. Boundary: y = −x + 1 (gradient −1, intercept 1), dashed. Test (0, 0): 0 > 0 + 1 gives 0 > 1, false. Shade the side not containing the origin, the region above the line.
Example 3. Graph x ≥ 3. The boundary is the vertical line x = 3, solid. The region is to the right of the line.
Example 4. Graph 3x + 2y ≤ 6. Boundary 3x + 2y = 6, solid, through (2, 0) and (0, 3). Test (0, 0): 0 ≤ 6, true. Shade the side with the origin (below the line).

Example 5. Show the region x > 0, y > 0, x + y < 5. This is a triangle in the first quadrant with corners (0, 0), (5, 0) and (0, 5). All three boundaries are dashed, because all the signs are strict. Shade the inside of the triangle.
Example 6. Graph y < 4 and x ≥ −1. The region is below the dashed horizontal line y = 4 and to the right of (and on) the solid vertical line x = −1.

units.title: Binary Operations
units.summary: What a binary operation is, its properties (closure, commutative, associative, distributive), identity and inverse elements, and operation tables.

p: A binary operation is a rule that combines two elements to give one element. 'Binary' means two inputs. Familiar examples are a + b, a − b and a × b. We can also invent our own using symbols such as *, ⊙ or Δ.
If * is a binary operation on a set S, then a * b must belong to S for all a and b in S. Example: if a * b = a + b + 2ab, then 3 * 5 = 3 + 5 + 2(3)(5) = 8 + 30 = 38.

Closure: a * b is in S for every a, b in S (for example, the integers are closed under addition). Commutative: a * b = b * a. Associative: (a * b) * c = a * (b * c). Distributive: a * (b + c) = (a * b) + (a * c), for example multiplication over addition.
An element e is the identity if a * e = e * a = a for every a. For addition, e = 0. For multiplication, e = 1.
The inverse of a, written a⁻¹, satisfies a * a⁻¹ = a⁻¹ * a = e. For addition, the inverse of a is −a. For multiplication, the inverse of a is 1/a (a ≠ 0).
For a small finite set we can write an operation table. Let S = {1, 2, 3, 4} and a Δ b = (a × b) mod 5, meaning the remainder after dividing a × b by 5.

Closed: every entry belongs to S. Commutative: the table is symmetrical about the main diagonal. Identity: the row and column for 1 repeat the headings, so e = 1. Inverses: look for the identity in each row: 1 → 1, 2 ↔ 3 (because 2 Δ 3 = 1), 4 → 4 (4 Δ 4 = 1).

Example 1. For a * b = a + b + ab: (a) it is commutative because a + b + ab = b + a + ba. (b) Identity: a * e = a gives a + e + ae = a, so e(1 + a) = 0, hence e = 0. (c) Inverse of 5: 5 * x = 0 gives 5 + x + 5x = 0, 6x = −5, x = −5/6.
Example 2. For a * b = a + b − 3, find the identity: a + e − 3 = a gives e = 3. The inverse of 10: 10 + x − 3 = 3 gives x = −4.
Example 3. With p Δ q = p + q + 1: identity: p + e + 1 = p, so e = −1. Inverse of 7: 7 + x + 1 = −1, so x = −9.
Example 4. a * b = 2a − b. Then 3 * 5 = 6 − 5 = 1 and 5 * 3 = 10 − 3 = 7. They are different, so * is not commutative.
Example 5. Using the Δ table: (2 Δ 4) Δ 3 = 3 Δ 3 = 4. The inverse of 4 is 4.

units.title: Functions: Definition and Types of Mapping
units.summary: What a function is, domain, co-domain and range, one-to-one, many-to-one, onto and into mappings, and the classes of function.

p: A function is a rule that gives each input exactly one output. Think of a machine: you put in x, the machine follows the rule, and out comes y = f(x). For the rule ×2 + 3: input 2 gives 7, input 5 gives 13, and input 8 gives 19.

A function f from a set A to a set B assigns to each element x of A exactly one element y of B. We write f : A → B and y = f(x). A is the domain (the set of inputs). B is the co-domain. The range is the set of outputs actually obtained; it is a subset of B.
Example: domain A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, rule f(x) = x + 2, co-domain B = {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}. The range is {3, 4, 5, 6}.
One-to-one (injective): different inputs always give different outputs. Example: f(x) = x + 1. Its graph passes the horizontal line test (no horizontal line meets it twice).
Many-to-one: two or more inputs give the same output. Example: f(x) = x²: f(−2) = f(2) = 4. It fails the horizontal line test, so it is not one-to-one.
Onto (surjective): every element of the co-domain is an output, so range = co-domain. Example: f(x) = x − 1 with domain {2, 3, 4} and co-domain {1, 2, 3}.
Into: the range is a proper subset of the co-domain, so some co-domain elements are not used. Example: f(x) = 2x with domain {1, 2, 3} and co-domain {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}: the range is {2, 4, 6}.

units.title: Composite and Inverse Functions
units.summary: How to find a composite function f(g(x)) and an inverse function, with worked examples and checks.

p: A composite function (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) means 'do g first, then f'. Method: take f(x) and replace every x by the expression for g(x).

Example 1. f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x² − 3. (a) f(g(x)) = 2(x² − 3) + 1 = 2x² − 5. (b) g(f(x)) = (2x + 1)² − 3 = 4x² + 4x − 2. (c) f(f(2)) = f(5) = 11. Notice that f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are usually different.
Example 2. f(x) = x² and g(x) = x + 1. Then f(g(x)) = (x + 1)². Example 3. f(x) = 2x − 3 and g(x) = 1/x. f(g(x)) = 2/x − 3; g(f(x)) = 1/(2x − 3); g(f(2)) = g(1) = 1.
The inverse f⁻¹ reverses f: if f(a) = b then f⁻¹(b) = a. Only a one-to-one function has an inverse. To find it: 1. Write y = f(x). 2. Swap x and y. 3. Solve for y. 4. Write y as f⁻¹(x).
Example 4. f(x) = 2x + 3. y = 2x + 3. Swap: x = 2y + 3. Solve: y = (x − 3)/2. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

Example 5. Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x − 1)/(x + 5). Step 1: y = (3x − 1)/(x + 5). Step 2: x = (3y − 1)/(y + 5). Step 3: multiply by (y + 5): x(y + 5) = 3y − 1, so xy + 5x = 3y − 1, xy − 3y = −5x − 1, y(x − 3) = −5x − 1, y = (−5x − 1)/(x − 3) = (5x + 1)/(3 − x). So f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 1)/(3 − x).
A function and its inverse undo each other: f(f⁻¹(x)) = x and f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. For f(x) = 3x − 1: f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)/3. Then (f ∘ f⁻¹)(5) = f(2) = 5, as expected.

Example 7. f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = 3x − 1: find x such that f(g(x)) = g(f(x)). f(g(x)) = 2(3x − 1) + 1 = 6x − 1. g(f(x)) = 3(2x + 1) − 1 = 6x + 2. These are never equal (6x − 1 ≠ 6x + 2), so there is no solution.

units.title: Arithmetic Progression
units.summary: What a sequence and a series are, and the formulas for the nth term and the sum of an arithmetic progression (A.P.), with worked examples.

p: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers that follow a rule, such as 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ... Each number is a term. The first term is a and the nth term is Tₙ (or Uₙ). When the terms are added we get a series: 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + ... Patterns of numbers occur in house numbers, seats in a hall and regular savings.

An A.P. is a sequence in which each term differs from the one before by a fixed number called the common difference d. Examples: 2, 4, 6, 8, ... (d = 2); 100, 90, 80, 70, ... (d = −10). General form: a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, ...
nth term: Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
Sum of n terms: Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = (n/2)(a + l), where l is the last term.
For 3, 7, 11, 15, ...: a = 3, d = 4. The terms are 3, 3 + 4 = 7, 3 + 8 = 11, 3 + 12 = 15. The common difference d = T₂ − T₁.
Example 1. Find the 15th term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ... a = 5, d = 3. T₁₅ = 5 + 14 × 3 = 47.
Example 3. The 1st term of an A.P. is 7 and the 5th is 19. Find d. 7 + 4d = 19, so d = 3.
Example 4. Find the 20th term of 4, 9, 14, ... d = 5; T₂₀ = 4 + 19 × 5 = 99.
Example 5. The 5th and 10th terms are 18 and 33. Find a and d, and S₁₅. a + 4d = 18 and a + 9d = 33. Subtract: 5d = 15, d = 3, a = 6. S₁₅ = (15/2)[12 + 14 × 3] = 7.5 × 54 = 405.
Example 6. Find the sum of all 3-digit numbers divisible by 9. The first is 108 and the last is 999. n: 108 + (n − 1) × 9 = 999 gives n = 100. S = (100/2)(108 + 999) = 50 × 1107 = 55,350.
Example 7. Write the first 5 terms with a = 4, d = 5: 4, 9, 14, 19, 24.
A.P. models salary increments, equal savings every month, seat numbers in a stadium (each row has a fixed number more seats) and simple interest.

units.title: Geometric and Harmonic Progressions
units.summary: The geometric progression (G.P.) with its nth term, finite sum and sum to infinity, and the harmonic progression, with worked examples and a comparison.

p: A G.P. is a sequence in which each term after the first is found by multiplying the one before by a fixed number called the common ratio r. Examples: 2, 4, 8, 16, ... (r = 2); 81, 27, 9, 3, ... (r = 1/3). General form: a, ar, ar², ar³, ...
nth term: Tₙ = a rⁿ⁻¹. Sum of n terms: Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) for r ≠ 1 (or a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)). Sum to infinity, when |r| < 1: S∞ = a/(1 − r).
Example 1. 5th term of 3, 6, 12, 24, ... a = 3, r = 2: T₅ = 3 × 2⁴ = 48.
Example 2. Sum of the first 5 terms of 2, 6, 18, 54, ... a = 2, r = 3: S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 2 × 242/2 = 242.
Example 4. 10th term when a = 2 and r = 3: T₁₀ = 2 × 3⁹ = 39,366.
Example 5. Sum of the first 6 terms with a = 5 and r = 2: S₆ = 5(2⁶ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 5 × 63 = 315.

Example 7. The 3rd and 7th terms of a G.P. are 16 and 256. (a) ar² = 16 and ar⁶ = 256. Divide: r⁴ = 16, so r = 2 (taking the positive value; r = −2 also works). (b) a = 16/4 = 4. (c) T₁₀ = 4 × 2⁹ = 2,048.

A harmonic progression is a sequence whose reciprocals form an A.P. Example: 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, ... is an H.P. because 1, 2, 3, 4, ... is an A.P. The nth term of an H.P. is 1/[a + (n − 1)d], where a and d belong to the corresponding A.P.
Example 9. The first 5 terms of the H.P. whose A.P. is 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 are 1/2, 1/4, 1/6, 1/8, 1/10.
Example 10. If 1/a, 1/b, 1/c are in A.P., then 2/b = 1/a + 1/c = (a + c)/(ac), so b = 2ac/(a + c).
Study the table.

units.title: Trigonometric Ratios of 30°, 45° and 60°
units.summary: Deriving the exact sine, cosine and tangent of 30°, 45° and 60° from an isosceles right triangle and an equilateral triangle, with a summary table.

p: In a right-angled triangle: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent (remember SOH CAH TOA). The angles 30°, 45° and 60° are special because their ratios can be written exactly with surds, without a calculator. They appear in geometry, physics, navigation and engineering.

Take a right triangle with two equal sides of 1 unit. Both acute angles are 45°. By Pythagoras, the hypotenuse h = √(1² + 1²) = √2. So sin 45° = 1/√2 = √2/2, cos 45° = 1/√2 = √2/2 and tan 45° = 1/1 = 1.

Take an equilateral triangle of side 2 units (all angles 60°). Draw the vertical line from the top to the middle of the base. It cuts the triangle into two right triangles with angles 30°, 60° and 90°. The base splits into 1 and 1. The height h satisfies 2² = 1² + h², so h = √3. From the right triangle: sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3; sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3 = √3/3.

units.title: Reciprocal Ratios, Identities and Worked Examples

p: Each ratio has a reciprocal: csc θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ and cot θ = 1/tan θ. Examples: csc 30° = 1/(1/2) = 2; sec 60° = 1/(1/2) = 2; cot 45° = 1.
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ. Also 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ. And sin(90° − θ) = cos θ.

units.title: Logical Reasoning (1): Propositions and Connectives
units.summary: What a proposition is, and the five logical connectives: negation, conjunction, disjunction, conditional and biconditional, with their truth tables.

p: Logical reasoning helps us to judge arguments, test truth and reach valid conclusions. It is used in mathematics, computer programming and clear thinking. A proposition (statement) is a declarative sentence that is either true (T) or false (F), but not both.

'Lagos is the capital of Nigeria' is a proposition (false). '2 + 2 = 4' is a proposition (true). 'What is your name?' is a question, not a proposition. 'Go and shut the door' is a command, not a proposition. 'x + 1 = 5' is an open sentence; its truth depends on x, so it is not yet a proposition.
Connectives join simple statements into compound statements.
Reverses the truth value. p: 'It is sunny'. ~p: 'It is not sunny'.
True only when both p and q are true.
This is the inclusive 'or': true if p or q or both are true. It is false only when both are false.

False only when p is true and q is false. Think of a promise: 'If I get an A (p), I will buy you ice cream (q).' The promise is broken only if I get an A and do not buy the ice cream. If I do not get an A, I have not broken my promise whatever I do.

sections.h: Biconditional (p ↔ q): 'p if and only if q'
p: True when p and q have the same truth value.

Let p = 'It is cold' and q = 'It is raining'. (a) It is cold and it is raining: p ∧ q. (b) It is not cold or it is raining: ~p ∨ q. (c) If it is raining then it is not cold: q → ~p. (d) It is neither cold nor raining: ~p ∧ ~q.

units.title: Logical Reasoning (2): Truth Tables, Tautology and Contradiction
units.summary: How to build the truth table of a compound statement and classify it as a tautology, a contradiction or a contingency, with worked examples.

p: A tautology is always true whatever the truth values of its parts, for example p ∨ ~p. A contradiction is always false, for example p ∧ ~p. A contingency is sometimes true and sometimes false, for example p → q.

sections.h: How to build a truth table
p: List all the combinations of T and F for the simple statements (2 statements give 4 rows; 3 give 8 rows). Add a column for each part of the compound statement, working from the inside out. Read the last column to classify the statement.
Example 1. Truth table for (p → q) ∧ ~q.
The last column is not constant, so (p → q) ∧ ~q is a contingency.
Example 2. Is (p ∧ q) → p a tautology?
The last column is always T, so (p ∧ q) → p is a tautology.
Example 3. p ∧ ~p: for p = T it is F and for p = F it is F, always false: a contradiction.
Example 4. Show that p → q is equivalent to ~p ∨ q.
The two columns ~p ∨ q and p → q are the same, so the statements are logically equivalent. This is a handy way to rewrite 'if ... then' statements.
Example 5. Find the truth value of (p ∧ ~q) → (r ∨ q) when p = T, q = F, r = T. p ∧ ~q = T ∧ T = T. r ∨ q = T ∨ F = T. T → T = T.
Example 6. (~p ∨ q) → p. Rows: (T,T): (F∨T) = T → T = T. (T,F): (F∨F) = F → T = T. (F,T): (T∨T) = T → F = F. (F,F): (T∨F) = T → F = F. The column is T, T, F, F, so it is a contingency.
Example 7. (p ∧ q) ∧ ~(p ∨ q): when p ∧ q is true, p ∨ q is true so ~(p ∨ q) is false; and when p ∧ q is false the whole conjunction is false. Always false: a contradiction.
Example 8. (p → q) ∨ (q → p) is a tautology: if p → q is false (p true, q false), then q → p is true.

units.title: The Abacus and Number Systems (Decimal and Binary)
units.summary: The abacus as an early calculating device, the decimal and binary systems, converting between them and adding binary numbers.

p: Before computers, people used devices to help with arithmetic. An abacus is a simple manual calculating tool: a frame with rods or wires, with beads that slide, and a divider bar. Each rod stands for a place value (units, tens, hundreds). In a common form, each bead in the upper deck stands for 5 and each in the lower deck stands for 1. So 1 upper bead and 3 lower beads show 5 + 3 = 8.

The abacus stores numbers temporarily as bead positions and is used to teach counting. It inspired mechanical calculators, and the idea of a bead being 'on' or 'off' is like a bit in a computer's memory.
The decimal system uses ten digits, 0 to 9, and each place is a power of 10: 345 = 3 × 10² + 4 × 10¹ + 5 × 10⁰ = 300 + 40 + 5.
The binary system uses only 0 and 1 (OFF and ON in a computer), and each place is a power of 2. 1101₂ = 1 × 2³ + 1 × 2² + 0 × 2¹ + 1 × 2⁰ = 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13 in base ten.
Multiply each digit by its power of 2 and add. Example: 10110₂ = 1 × 16 + 0 × 8 + 1 × 4 + 1 × 2 + 0 × 1 = 22. Also 1001₂ = 8 + 1 = 9, and 11101₂ = 16 + 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 29.
Divide by 2 repeatedly, writing down the remainders, until the quotient is 0. Read the remainders from the bottom up.

Example: 1011₂ + 110₂. Align: 1011 + 0110. From the right: 1 + 0 = 1; 1 + 1 = 0 carry 1; 0 + 1 + 1 = 0 carry 1; 1 + 0 + 1 = 0 carry 1; bring down the carry: 1. The answer is 10001₂. Check: 11 + 6 = 17 = 16 + 1 = 10001₂. ✓

units.title: Coordinate Geometry (1): Midpoint, Distance and Gradient
units.summary: The midpoint of a line segment, the gradient (slope) of a line and the distance between two points, with the conditions for parallel and perpendicular lines.

p: Coordinate (analytical) geometry links algebra and geometry. Points, lines and shapes are described by numbers and equations on the Cartesian plane.
The midpoint of the segment joining A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) is M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2), the average of the x-values and the average of the y-values.

The gradient m measures steepness: m = rise ÷ run = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). If m > 0 the line rises from left to right. If m < 0 it falls. If m = 0 it is horizontal. For a vertical line the gradient is undefined.
From Pythagoras' theorem, the distance between A and B is d = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].

img.alt: A coordinate grid with points P(-2, 5) and Q(4, 1), the line joining them, the right triangle with legs 6 and 4, and the midpoint M(1, 3)
img.cap: Midpoint, gradient and distance for P(−2, 5) and Q(4, 1).

p: Two lines are parallel if their gradients are equal: m₁ = m₂. Two lines are perpendicular if the product of their gradients is −1: m₁ × m₂ = −1, so m₂ = −1/m₁.
Example 2. Distance between A(1, −2) and B(4, 2): √(3² + 4²) = 5.
Example 3. Midpoint of P(−3, 0) and Q(5, −6): (1, −3).
Example 4. Gradient of the line through (1, 7) and (3, 1): (1 − 7)/(3 − 1) = −3.
Example 5. Are y = 2x + 1 and 4x − 2y + 5 = 0 parallel? The second is y = 2x + 5/2, gradient 2. Both gradients are 2, so they are parallel.
Example 6. L₁ passes through (2, 5) and (4, 9): m₁ = 4/2 = 2. L₂ passes through (0, 1) and (−4, 3): m₂ = 2/(−4) = −1/2. m₁ × m₂ = −1, so L₁ ⊥ L₂.
Example 7. Find k if the line through (k, 4) and (1, 2) is parallel to y = 5x − 1. (2 − 4)/(1 − k) = 5, so −2 = 5 − 5k, 5k = 7, k = 1.4.

units.title: Coordinate Geometry (2): Equation of a Straight Line
units.summary: The three forms of the equation of a line, finding a line from a point and a gradient, parallel and perpendicular lines through a point, and the perpendicular bisector.

p: Gradient-intercept form: y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept. Example: y = 2x + 3 cuts the y-axis at (0, 3) and has gradient 2.
Point-gradient form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), used when we know the gradient and one point (x₁, y₁).
General form: Ax + By + C = 0. Example: 2x − y − 7 = 0 is the same as y = 2x − 7.
Through two points: find m, then use point-gradient form with either point. Parallel to a given line: use the same gradient. Perpendicular to a given line: use gradient −1/m.

Example 1. Line through (3, −1) perpendicular to 2y + x = 5. Write 2y + x = 5 as y = −x/2 + 5/2, so m₁ = −1/2. The perpendicular gradient is m₂ = 2. y − (−1) = 2(x − 3), so y + 1 = 2x − 6, y = 2x − 7, or 2x − y − 7 = 0.
Example 2. Gradient and intercept of 3x − y = 6. y = 3x − 6: gradient 3, y-intercept −6.
Example 3. Line parallel to y = 3x − 1 through (2, 0): m = 3, y − 0 = 3(x − 2), y = 3x − 6.
Example 4. Perpendicular bisector of A(−1, 4) and B(3, 2). Midpoint M = (1, 3). Gradient of AB = (2 − 4)/(3 + 1) = −1/2. Perpendicular gradient = 2. Through M: y − 3 = 2(x − 1), so y = 2x + 1.
Example 5. Line AB with A(2, −2) and B(4, 8): m = 5, y − 8 = 5(x − 4), y = 5x − 12. A line perpendicular to AB has gradient −1/5.

Example 6. Line perpendicular to x + 3y = 7 through the midpoint of A(2, −2) and B(4, 8). The midpoint is (3, 3). x + 3y = 7 gives y = −x/3 + 7/3, so m = −1/3. Perpendicular gradient 3: y − 3 = 3(x − 3), y = 3x − 6.

units.title: Coordinate Geometry (3): Linear Form and Area of a Polygon
units.summary: How to turn y = axⁿ and y = abˣ into straight-line form using logarithms, and how to find the area of a triangle or quadrilateral from its vertices.

p: In experiments, some non-linear relations can be turned into straight lines using logarithms. The constants can then be read from the graph.

Case 1: y = axⁿ. Take logs: log y = log a + n log x. This matches Y = mX + C with Y = log y, X = log x, m = n, C = log a. So a graph of log y against log x is a straight line with gradient n and intercept log a.
Case 2: y = abˣ. Take logs: log y = log a + x log b. So log y against x gives a straight line with gradient log b and intercept log a.

The variables are related by y = kxⁿ. The table: x = 1, 4, 9 and y = 5, 10, 15. Plot log y (vertical) against log x (horizontal). At x = 1, log x = 0 and log y = log 5, so the intercept is log k = log 5 and k = 5. Between x = 1 and x = 4: 10/5 = 2 = 4ⁿ, so n = 1/2. Check with x = 9: 5 × 9^(1/2) = 15 ✓. So y = 5√x.

sections.h: Area of a triangle (the shoelace method)
p: For A(x₁, y₁), B(x₂, y₂), C(x₃, y₃): Area = ½ |(x₁y₂ + x₂y₃ + x₃y₁) − (y₁x₂ + y₂x₃ + y₃x₁)|. Go around the vertices in order (clockwise or anticlockwise), repeating the first at the end.
Example. A(1, 1), B(4, 5), C(6, 2). First sum: 1×5 + 4×2 + 6×1 = 19. Second sum: 1×4 + 5×6 + 2×1 = 36. Area = ½ |19 − 36| = 8.5 square units.

Split it into two triangles and add their areas, or use the shoelace method with all four vertices in order. Example: P(1, 2), Q(3, 5), R(6, 6), S(4, 1). First sum: 1×5 + 3×6 + 6×1 + 4×2 = 5 + 18 + 6 + 8 = 37. Second sum: 2×3 + 5×6 + 6×4 + 1×1 = 6 + 30 + 24 + 1 = 61. Area = ½ |37 − 61| = 12 square units.
