units.title: Vectors (1): Scalars, Notation and Operations
units.summary: The difference between scalars and vectors, the ways of writing a vector, and adding, subtracting and scaling vectors with components.

p: A scalar has magnitude (size) only. A vector has magnitude and direction. Scalars: distance (5 km), time (30 s), mass (10 kg), speed (60 km/h). Vectors: displacement (5 km north), force (10 N east), velocity (80 km/h west). A vector is drawn as a line with an arrowhead: the length shows the magnitude and the arrow shows the direction.
Geometric form: AB (an arrow over the letters) is the vector from A to B. We also write a single bold or underlined letter, such as a.
Column form: the vector from the origin to the point (x, y) is written as a column with x on top and y below.
Unit vector form: a = xi + yj, where i = (1, 0) is the unit vector along the x-axis and j = (0, 1) is the unit vector along the y-axis. So 3i − 4j is the same as the column (3, −4).
The zero vector 0 = (0, 0) has no size and no direction. The negative vector −a has the same magnitude as a but the opposite direction. If a = (x, y) then −a = (−x, −y).

Add or subtract the components: (a, b) + (c, d) = (a + c, b + d) and (a, b) − (c, d) = (a − c, b − d). Graphically, the triangle law: place p and q head to tail; the resultant p + q goes from the start of p to the end of q.
For a scalar k and a = (x, y): ka = (kx, ky). If k > 1 the vector stretches. If 0 < k < 1 it shrinks. If k < 0 the direction reverses.
Example 3. Given p = 2i + 3j and q = 4i − 5j, find r such that 2p + r = 3q. r = 3q − 2p = (12, −15) − (4, 6) = (8, −21) = 8i − 21j.

units.title: Vectors (2): Magnitude, Direction and Unit Vectors
units.summary: How to find the magnitude and direction angle of a vector (with quadrant care) and how to find a unit vector.

p: For a = (x, y), the magnitude (length) is |a| = √(x² + y²). It is just Pythagoras' theorem.
The direction angle θ (measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis) is found from tan α = |y/x|, where α is the acute reference angle. Then use the signs of x and y to choose the quadrant.
Quadrant I (+, +): θ = α. Quadrant II (−, +): θ = 180° − α. Quadrant III (−, −): θ = 180° + α. Quadrant IV (+, −): θ = 360° − α.
A unit vector has magnitude 1. The unit vector in the direction of a is â = a ÷ |a|. Example: a = 3i + 4j has |a| = 5, so â = (3/5)i + (4/5)j. Check: √(9/25 + 16/25) = 1.

Example 1. Find the magnitude and direction of v = (−5, 12). |v| = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13. tan α = 12/5 = 2.4, so α = 67.38°. x < 0 and y > 0, so the vector is in the second quadrant: θ = 180° − 67.38° = 112.62°.
Example 2. The unit vector in the direction of w = i − 2j. |w| = √(1 + 4) = √5. ŵ = (1/√5)i − (2/√5)j = (√5/5)i − (2√5/5)j.
Example 3. Magnitude of p = 5i + 12j: √(25 + 144) = 13.
Example 4. Unit vector of v = (3, 0): |v| = 3, so v̂ = (1, 0) = i.
Example 5. Magnitude and direction of a = (−1, −1). |a| = √2. α = 45°, third quadrant, θ = 180° + 45° = 225°.
Example 6. Unit vector of b = 4i − 3j: |b| = 5, b̂ = (4/5)i − (3/5)j.
Example 7. If v = (k, 8) and |v| = 10, find k. k² + 64 = 100, so k² = 36 and k = 6 or −6.
Example 8. The unit vector of p = (−3, 4): |p| = 5, p̂ = (−3/5, 4/5).

units.title: Vectors (3): Laws of Addition, Position Vectors and Resolution
units.summary: The triangle and parallelogram laws, position vectors and the vector between two points, and resolving a vector into components.

p: If two vectors are shown by two sides of a triangle taken in order, their resultant is the third side, taken in the opposite order. AB + BC = AC.
If two vectors a and b start from the same point, their resultant is the diagonal of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are a and b. The other diagonal is a − b or b − a, depending on direction.

img.alt: Two diagrams: the triangle law with vectors a and b placed head to tail and resultant a + b closing the triangle, and the parallelogram law with a and b from one point and the diagonal a + b
img.cap: The triangle law (left) and the parallelogram law (right).

p: The position vector of a point P(x, y) is OP = xi + yj, the vector from the origin. The vector from A to B is AB = OB − OA = (x₂ − x₁)i + (y₂ − y₁)j: 'head minus tail'. The position vector of the midpoint M of AB is OM = ½(OA + OB).

A vector v of magnitude |v| making an angle θ with the positive x-axis has components vₓ = |v| cos θ and vᵧ = |v| sin θ. So v = (|v| cos θ)i + (|v| sin θ)j. This is the basis of the analysis of forces and velocities in physics and engineering.

img.alt: A vector V at angle theta from the x-axis with a horizontal component V cos theta and a vertical component V sin theta forming a right triangle
img.cap: Resolving a vector into horizontal and vertical components.

p: Example 1. a = 2i + 5j and b = 6i − j are the position vectors of A and B. (a) AB = b − a = 4i − 6j. (b) The midpoint M: OM = ½(a + b) = ½(8i + 4j) = 4i + 2j.
Example 3. A force of 20 N acts at 30°. Fₓ = 20 cos 30° = 10√3 and Fᵧ = 20 sin 30° = 10, so F = 10√3 i + 10 j.
Example 4. A force has components 10 N east and 10√3 N north. |F| = √(100 + 300) = 20 N and tan θ = 10√3/10 = √3, so θ = 60°: 20 N at 60° north of east.
Example 6. In the parallelogram OABC with OA = a and OC = c: OB = a + c, and AC = c − a.

units.title: Vectors (4): The Scalar (Dot) Product
units.summary: How to multiply two vectors to get a number, the two forms of the dot product, and how to find the angle between vectors and test for perpendicular vectors.

p: The scalar (dot) product of two vectors is a number, not a vector. Component form: if a = a₁i + a₂j and b = b₁i + b₂j, then a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂. Geometric form: a · b = |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors.

Angle between vectors: equating the two forms gives cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Perpendicular test: if θ = 90°, cos θ = 0, so a · b = 0. If a · b = 0 (and neither vector is zero), the vectors are perpendicular.
Example 1. For a = 5i − 2j and b = 3i + 6j: a · b = 15 − 12 = 3.
Example 2. p = 3i + kj and q = 2i − 6j. For p ⊥ q: p · q = 6 − 6k = 0, so k = 1.
Example 3. Angle between a = 2i + j and b = 3i − j. a · b = 6 − 1 = 5. |a| = √5 and |b| = √10. cos θ = 5/(√5 × √10) = 5/√50 = 1/√2, so θ = 45°.
Example 4. u = (1, 1) and v = (1, −4). u · v = 1 − 4 = −3. |u| = √2 and |v| = √17. cos θ = −3/√34 = −0.5145, so θ = 121° (to the nearest degree).
Example 5. a = ti − 2j and b = (t + 3)i + 4j. For a ⊥ b: t(t + 3) − 8 = 0, so t² + 3t − 8 = 0 and t = (−3 ± √41)/2.
Example 6. If |a| = 4, |b| = 5 and the angle is 60°, a · b = 4 × 5 × cos 60° = 10.
Example 7. u = 2i − 8j and v = 4i + j: u · v = 8 − 8 = 0, so u ⊥ v.
Example 8. Given p = (−3, 4) and q = (5, k), find k if p ⊥ q: −15 + 4k = 0, so k = 15/4.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 Further Mathematics Third Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Third Term has two parts. First is Statistics: finding the typical value of a set of data (measures of location), how spread out the data are (measures of dispersion), and how to compare spread fairly (coefficient of variation). Then comes Operations Research, the 'science of better decisions': linear programming, transportation problems and the assignment problem.

There are many calculations. Set them out in tables, use a calculator carefully, and check by estimating. At the end of each unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

units.title: Mean, Median and Mode of Ungrouped Data
units.summary: The three measures of central tendency for a simple list of numbers, with worked examples and a comparison.

p: Statistics is the branch of mathematics that collects, organises, analyses and interprets data. Measures of location (central tendency) find the centre or typical value where the data cluster. They are the mean, median and mode (and the quartiles, deciles and percentiles in the next unit). Ungrouped data is a simple list of numbers, for example 5, 8, 5, 7, 10.
The mean (arithmetic average) is x̄ = Σx ÷ n, the sum of the values divided by how many there are. Example: 2, 5, 5, 8: x̄ = 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
The mode is the value that occurs most often. Data 2, 5, 5, 8 has mode 5. A data set may have one mode (unimodal), two modes (bimodal) or no mode (no value repeats).

The median is the middle value when the data are arranged in order. Odd number of items: take the middle one. 2, 5, 5, 8, 10 has median 5 (the 3rd value). Even number of items: average the two middle values. 2, 5, 5, 8 has median (5 + 5) ÷ 2 = 5.

Data: 2, 3, 3, 6, 18. Mean = 32 ÷ 5 = 6.4. Median = 3. Mode = 3. The large value 18 pulls the mean up, but not the median. So for data with extreme values, the median is often a better 'typical' value than the mean.
Example 1. For 10, 8, 15, 8, 12: sum = 53, mean = 10.6. Sorted: 8, 8, 10, 12, 15, so median = 10 and mode = 8.
Example 2. Median of 20, 25, 21, 30, 22, 27. Sorted: 20, 21, 22, 25, 27, 30. Middle two: 22 and 25. Median = 23.5.

units.title: Mean, Median and Mode of Grouped Data
units.summary: How to find the mean, median and modal value of a frequency distribution using class midpoints, class boundaries and cumulative frequency, with a full worked example.

p: Grouped data are arranged in class intervals with frequencies. We use the class midpoint x to stand for each class.
Mean: x̄ = Σfx ÷ Σf, where f is the frequency, x is the class midpoint and Σf = N.

Median: Median = L₁ + [(N/2 − cfb) ÷ f_m] × C, where L₁ is the lower class boundary of the median class (the class containing the N/2-th item), cfb is the cumulative frequency before that class, f_m is its frequency and C is the class size.

Mode: Mode = L₁ + [Δ₁ ÷ (Δ₁ + Δ₂)] × C, where L₁ is the lower boundary of the modal class (the class with the highest frequency), Δ₁ = f_modal − f_before, Δ₂ = f_modal − f_after and C is the class size.
(b) Median: N/2 = 40, which falls in the class 40–49 (cumulative frequency goes from 21 to 41). L₁ = 39.5, cfb = 21, f_m = 20, C = 10. Median = 39.5 + [(40 − 21)/20] × 10 = 39.5 + 9.5 = 49.0.

units.title: Quartiles, Deciles and Percentiles
units.summary: Quantiles that divide data into equal parts, the position formulas, and worked calculations for grouped data.

p: Quantiles divide ordered data into equal parts. Quartiles divide it into 4 parts: Q₁ (25%), Q₂ (50%, the median) and Q₃ (75%). Deciles divide it into 10 parts: D₁ (10%), D₇ (70%). Percentiles divide it into 100 parts: P₄₀ (40%), P₈₀ (80%). Note that Q₂ = D₅ = P₅₀ = the median.
Using the same method as the median: Quantile = L₁ + [(position − cfb) ÷ f] × C, where the position is: Q₁: N/4; Q₂: N/2; Q₃: 3N/4; D₇: 7N/10; P₄₀: 40N/100 = 2N/5.
Use the table from Unit 3 (N = 80).
(a) Q₁: position 20. This is in the class 30–39 (cumulative frequency 11 before, 21 at the end). L₁ = 29.5, cfb = 11, f = 10. Q₁ = 29.5 + [(20 − 11)/10] × 10 = 38.5.

sections.h: Why use the median or quartiles?
p: For skewed data (a long tail on one side), the mean is pulled towards the tail, so the median is often a better typical value. The quartiles show how the middle half of the data is spread.

units.title: Range and Interquartile Range
units.summary: Measures of spread: why the centre alone is not enough, the range and its weakness, the interquartile range and the semi-interquartile range.

p: Two sets of data can have the same mean but very different spread. A = 10, 10, 10, 10, 10 and B = 1, 5, 10, 15, 19 both have mean 10, but A has no spread and B has a wide spread. Measures of dispersion tell us how spread out the data are.

Range = highest value − lowest value (ungrouped). For grouped data: Range = upper boundary of the highest class − lower boundary of the lowest class. Weakness: one extreme value (an outlier) distorts it. In 10, 11, 12, 13, 100 the range is 90, though most values are close together.

The IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data. IQR = Q₃ − Q₁. It ignores the lowest and highest quarters, so it is not distorted by outliers. The semi-interquartile range (quartile deviation) is (Q₃ − Q₁) ÷ 2. A larger IQR means the middle half of the data is more spread out.
Example 1. For the 80 marks: Range = 79.5 − 9.5 = 70. Q₁ = 38.5, Q₃ = 57.1, so IQR = 57.1 − 38.5 = 18.6.
Example 2. If Q₁ = 20 and Q₃ = 50, the semi-interquartile range is (50 − 20)/2 = 15.
Example 4. For the 30 puzzle times: range = 24.5 − (−0.5) = 25 minutes; Q₁ = 9.0 and Q₃ = 17.71 (Unit 4), so IQR = 8.71.

units.title: Mean Deviation, Variance and Standard Deviation
units.summary: How to measure the average distance of data from the mean (mean deviation) and the root-mean-square distance (standard deviation), with full worked tables.

p: The mean deviation is the average distance of the data from the mean. Ungrouped: M.D. = Σ|x − x̄| ÷ n. Grouped: M.D. = Σf|x − x̄| ÷ Σf. We use absolute values (distances) because otherwise the positive and negative deviations cancel out to zero. A small M.D. means the data are close to the mean.

Variance σ² = Σf(x − x̄)² ÷ Σf. A shorter form is σ² = Σfx² ÷ Σf − (x̄)². The standard deviation is the square root of the variance: σ = √(variance). Squaring gives more weight to large deviations. A small σ means the data are tightly clustered; a large σ means a wide spread. The variance is never negative, because it is a sum of squares.
Interpretation: the average student's mark is about 11.8 marks from the mean, and the standard deviation of 14.75 shows moderate spread.
Why use Σf|x − x̄| and not Σf(x − x̄)? Because the plain deviations add up to zero. What is the relationship between variance and standard deviation? Standard deviation = √variance.

units.title: Coefficient of Variation
units.summary: How to compare the consistency of data sets with different means or units using the coefficient of variation, with examples.

p: The standard deviation tells us the spread, but we cannot fairly compare two data sets by their standard deviations if the means are different. Example: Mathematics has mean 80 and SD 2; English has mean 50 and SD 4. Is Mathematics more consistent just because 2 < 4? We need a relative measure of spread. (The CV is a measure of dispersion, not of location, although the source notes list it under 'measures of location'.)

The coefficient of variation (CV) expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean: CV = (σ ÷ x̄) × 100%. It has no units, so it can compare data measured in different units, such as kilograms and metres. A lower CV means more consistent data.
As a rough guide: below about 10%: very consistent; 10% to 30%: moderate; above 30%: high variability and low reliability. A CV of 0% means every value is the same.
Example 1. For the 80 marks, x̄ = 47.25 and σ = 14.75. CV = (14.75 ÷ 47.25) × 100 = 31.22%. The marks are fairly widely spread.
Example 2. Mathematics: CV = (2/80) × 100 = 2.5%. English: CV = (4/50) × 100 = 8%. Mathematics has the lower CV, so it is more consistent.
Example 3. Mean = 20 and variance = 16. σ = 4, CV = (4/20) × 100 = 20%.
Example 4. Engine A has mean speed 200 km/h and SD 10, so CV = 5%. Engine B has mean 80 km/h and SD 6, so CV = 7.5%. Engine A is more reliable even though its SD is larger.
Example 5. Company A: mean salary N50,000, SD N10,000, CV = 20%. Company B: mean N120,000, SD N18,000, CV = 15%. Company B has the more consistent pay.
Example 6. Brand X: mean life 120 h, SD 18 h, CV = 15%. Brand Y: mean 100 h, SD 16 h, CV = 16%. Brand X is slightly more reliable.
Example 7. CV = 20% and mean = 50: σ = 0.20 × 50 = 10.

units.title: History and Nature of Operations Research
units.summary: What operations research is, where it began, where it is used, and the three main models: linear programming, transportation and assignment.

p: Operations Research (OR) is the scientific approach to decision-making that seeks the best (optimal) course of action when resources are limited. It is sometimes called the 'science of better'. It helps to answer questions like: How can we maximise profit or minimise cost? What is the shortest route? How should we share limited resources most efficiently?
The method: real-life problem → build a mathematical model → analyse and solve it → choose the best decision → carry it out.

OR began in World War II (1939 to 1945). The military needed scientific answers to operational problems: how to find enemy submarines, how to place radar and anti-aircraft defences, and how to arrange convoys to reduce ship losses. Teams of scientists, mathematicians and engineers studied the data and proposed the best strategies. After the war, the same methods were adopted by business, industry and government.
Study the table.
A model is a simplified mathematical picture of a real situation, used to test decisions before applying them.

Linear programming (LP): finds the best value of an objective function (such as profit) subject to linear constraints. Example: a bakery makes bread and cakes with profit N5 per loaf and N8 per cake, using x loaves and y cakes. The objective is P = 5x + 8y and a constraint might be 2x + 3y ≤ 60.
Transportation model: finds the cheapest way to send goods from several sources (factories) to several destinations (depots), such as a cement company with 3 factories and 5 depots.
Assignment model: a special transportation problem that gives each worker exactly one job (or each machine one task) so that the total time or cost is least.

A company makes chairs (x) and tables (y), with profit N5 per chair and N8 per table. Objective function: P = 5x + 8y. If each chair takes 2 hours, each table takes 3 hours, and 60 hours of labour are available, the constraint is 2x + 3y ≤ 60. Also x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.

units.title: Linear Programming: Formulation and Graphical Solution
units.summary: How to write an LP problem, draw the constraints, find the feasible region and its corner points, and choose the best point, with two worked examples.

p: Objective function: the expression to maximise or minimise. Constraints: limits on the resources, written as linear inequalities. Feasible region: the set of all points that satisfy every constraint. Optimal point: the corner point (vertex) of the feasible region that gives the best value of the objective function.

1. Define the decision variables (x, y). 2. Write the objective function. 3. Write the constraints. 4. Add the non-negativity conditions x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. 5. Graph each constraint line (turn the inequality into an equation, find two points). 6. Shade to find the feasible region. 7. Find the corner points (read them from the graph or solve the equations of the lines that meet there). 8. Put each corner point into the objective function and choose the best.
A company makes tables (x) and chairs (y). Profit: N25 per table and N15 per chair. Wood: 4x + 3y ≤ 120. Labour: 2x + 3y ≤ 72. Maximise P = 25x + 15y.

Wood line: 4x + 3y = 120 passes through (0, 40) and (30, 0). Labour line: 2x + 3y = 72 passes through (0, 24) and (36, 0). The lines meet where 4x + 3y = 120 and 2x + 3y = 72. Subtract: 2x = 48, x = 24. Then 48 + 3y = 72 gives y = 8. So the intersection is (24, 8).

The corner points of the feasible region are (0, 0), (30, 0), (24, 8) and (0, 24). Profit at each: (0, 0): 0. (30, 0): 25 × 30 = N750. (24, 8): 600 + 120 = N720. (0, 24): 15 × 24 = N360. The maximum profit is N750, at (30, 0): make 30 tables and no chairs.

Profit is N400 per hectare of maize and N500 per hectare of beans. Formulate: maximise P = 400x + 500y subject to x + y ≤ 100; 2000x + 3000y ≤ 240000 (that is 2x + 3y ≤ 240); x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

units.title: The Transportation Model
units.summary: How to set up a transportation table and find a starting solution using the North-West Corner method and the Least Cost method, with cost comparison.

p: The transportation model finds the cheapest way to move goods from several sources (factories) to several destinations (warehouses or markets), when we know the cost per unit on each route, the supply at each source and the demand at each destination. If total supply equals total demand, the problem is balanced.
Costs per unit (N) from factories F₁, F₂, F₃ to warehouses W₁, W₂, W₃. Total supply = 100 + 150 + 120 = 370 = total demand 80 + 110 + 180, so it is balanced.

Start at the top-left (north-west) cell. Give it as many units as possible (the smaller of the supply and the demand). Cross out the row or column that is satisfied, then move right (if demand is met) or down (if supply is used up). Repeat.

F₁ to W₁: 80 units at N5 = N400. F₁ has 20 left: F₁ to W₂: 20 at N7 = N140. W₂ still needs 90: F₂ to W₂: 90 at N4 = N360. F₂ has 60 left: F₂ to W₃: 60 at N9 = N540. F₃ to W₃: 120 at N5 = N600. Total cost = 400 + 140 + 360 + 540 + 600 = N2,040.
Find the cell with the smallest cost. Give it as many units as possible. Cross out the satisfied row or column. Repeat with the smallest remaining cost.

The smallest cost is 4 (F₂ to W₂): 110 units = N440, and W₂ is full. The next smallest is 5 (F₁ to W₁ and F₃ to W₃, a tie): F₁ to W₁: 80 = N400; F₃ to W₃: 120 = N600. Remaining: F₁ has 20 and F₂ has 40, both for W₃ (which needs 60 more): F₁ to W₃: 20 at N8 = N160; F₂ to W₃: 40 at N9 = N360. Total cost = 440 + 400 + 600 + 160 + 360 = N1,960.

LCM (N1,960) is cheaper than NWC (N2,040) because it looks at the costs, while NWC ignores them. Both methods give a starting (basic feasible) solution. The LCM is usually closer to the best, but in general neither is guaranteed to be the cheapest possible; more advanced methods can improve a starting solution.

Practice. Two sources S₁ (supply 50) and S₂ (supply 60), two destinations D₁ (demand 40) and D₂ (demand 70). Costs: S₁ to D₁ 10, S₁ to D₂ 12, S₂ to D₁ 9, S₂ to D₂ 7. NWC: S₁→D₁ 40 (400), S₁→D₂ 10 (120), S₂→D₂ 60 (420) = N940. LCM: cheapest is 7 (S₂→D₂): 60 units (420); D₂ needs 10 more; the next cheapest is 9 (S₂→D₁) but S₂ is empty, so next is 10 (S₁→D₁): 40 (400); then S₁→D₂ 10 (120): total N940. Here both methods give the same cost.

units.title: The Assignment Model and the Hungarian Method
units.summary: What the assignment model is and how to solve it with the Hungarian algorithm: row and column reduction, covering zeros, improving the matrix and making the assignment.

p: The assignment model gives n workers n jobs, one each, so that the total cost (or time) is as small as possible (or the total efficiency as large as possible). It is a special case of the transportation model in which the number of sources equals the number of destinations and each supply and demand is 1. It is used for workers to jobs, machines to tasks, teachers to classes and vehicles to routes.

Step 1: row reduction. In each row subtract the smallest number from every number in that row. Step 2: column reduction. In each column subtract the smallest number in that column from every number. Step 3: cover all the zeros with the fewest straight lines (horizontal or vertical). If the number of lines equals n, the solution is optimal. Step 4: if the number of lines is less than n, find the smallest uncovered number; subtract it from all uncovered numbers and add it to numbers covered by two lines. Step 5: repeat steps 3 and 4. Step 6: make the assignment: pick a row or column with a single zero, assign it, cross out other zeros in its row and column, continue. Work out the total cost from the original table.

Costs ($): A: J1 25, J2 20, J3 23; B: 15, 18, 17; C: 19, 22, 21. Row reduction: A (min 20): 5, 0, 3. B (min 15): 0, 3, 2. C (min 19): 0, 3, 2. Column reduction: J1 minimum 0, J2 minimum 0, J3 minimum 2: subtract 2 from column J3: A: 5, 0, 1; B: 0, 3, 0; C: 0, 3, 0.

Cover the zeros: row B, row C and column J2 give 3 lines, which equals n = 3. The solution is optimal. A has only one zero, so A → J2. Then B and C share J1 and J3: either B→J1, C→J3 or B→J3, C→J1. Costs: 20 + 15 + 21 = 56 or 20 + 17 + 19 = 56. The minimum total cost is $56 (two equally good assignments).

Costs: A: T1 10, T2 15, T3 9; B: 9, 18, 5; C: 6, 14, 3. Row reduction (minima 9, 5, 3): A: 1, 6, 0; B: 4, 13, 0; C: 3, 11, 0. Column reduction (minima 1, 6, 0): A: 0, 0, 0; B: 3, 7, 0; C: 2, 5, 0. Cover the zeros: row A and column T3 cover all zeros with only 2 lines, which is less than n = 3. The smallest uncovered number is 2. Subtract 2 from the uncovered numbers and add 2 to the number covered twice (A, T3): A: 0, 0, 2; B: 1, 5, 0; C: 0, 3, 0. Now it takes 3 lines (for example columns T1, T2 and T3), so it is optimal. Assign: A → T2 (the only zero in column T2), then B → T3 and C → T1. Cost = 15 + 5 + 6 = 26. This is the minimum.
Costs: X: P 8, Q 6, R 10; Y: 10, 12, 11; Z: 7, 8, 9. Checking all 6 possible assignments gives totals 25, 24, 29, 27, 28 and 29. The minimum is 24: X → Q (6), Y → R (11), Z → P (7).

Why do the column reduction after the row reduction? Because some columns may still have no zero, and every worker and job needs at least one zero to work with. What if lines < n? Perform step 4 and test again.

units.summary: What SS1 Biology First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Biology is the study of living things. It helps you to understand your own body, the plants and animals around you, the food we eat, diseases and how to avoid them, and how to look after the environment. It is a very important subject for medicine, farming, nursing, pharmacy and many other careers, and it is an examination subject in WAEC, NECO and JAMB.

In First Term you will learn how to recognise living things, how they are classified into groups, the structure and work of the cell, how substances move into and out of cells, nutrition, respiration, growth and how living things respond to their surroundings.

Read each unit slowly. Study the diagrams and, where you are asked, draw and label them in your notebook, because drawing is a main skill in Biology. At the end of every unit there are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you to check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

units.title: Characteristics of Living Things
units.summary: What living things are and the ten characteristics that distinguish them from non-living things.

p: Everything in nature is either living or non-living. A living thing (organism) has life and shows certain characteristics that non-living things do not have. A stone does not feed, grow or reproduce; a goat does.

img.alt: A wheel diagram of the seven life processes: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition, shown by the letters MRS GREN
img.cap: Seven life processes, remembered as MRS GREN (movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition).

p: 1. Movement: animals move from place to place, usually to find food. Plants move parts of their bodies in response to stimuli, for example shoots bending towards light.

2. Respiration: living things need energy for their activities. They get it by respiration, the release of energy from food. In aerobic respiration, food (glucose) is oxidised in the presence of oxygen to give energy, with carbon dioxide and water as by-products.
3. Nutrition: feeding. All organisms need food. Green plants make their own food (autotrophs). Animals depend on plants, directly or indirectly (heterotrophs).
4. Irritability (sensitivity): the ability to detect and respond to changes (stimuli) inside and outside the body, such as light, heat, water, sound and chemicals.
5. Growth: an irreversible increase in size, length and mass. It lets organisms repair and replace damaged or old tissues. The food eaten supplies what is needed for growth.
6. Excretion: removal of the toxic waste products of metabolism, such as carbon dioxide and urea, and of other unwanted substances.
7. Reproduction: producing offspring to continue the species. It can be sexual (two parents) or asexual (one parent).
8. Life span: each organism lives for a limited time and passes through birth, growth, maturity, decline and death.
9. Competition: living things compete for food, water, light, mates and space.
10. Adaptation: organisms have features that help them to survive in their environment, and they can adjust to change.
A crystal can grow by adding layers on its outside but it does not feed, respire or reproduce, so it is not living. Viruses are a special case; you will study them in Unit 5.

units.title: Plants and Animals Compared, and the Organisation of Life
units.summary: The main differences between plants and animals and the levels of organisation from cells to organ systems.

p: Most living things can be grouped as plants or animals. Study the table.

p: Life on Earth is organised in levels of increasing complexity. Cells are the basic structural and functional units of life, for example muscle cells and nerve cells. Tissues are groups of similar cells doing a particular job, for example muscle tissue contracts and nervous tissue carries signals. Organs are made of different tissues working together, for example the heart (cardiac muscle, blood vessels and connective tissue) pumps blood. Organ systems are groups of organs doing a complex job, for example the digestive system (stomach, liver, intestines). Above these come the whole organism, populations, communities and ecosystems, which you will study in Second Term.

units.title: Classification, Taxonomy and the Kingdoms
units.summary: Why we classify living things, Linnaeus and the seven taxonomic ranks, the binomial system of naming, and the five kingdoms.

p: Classification is grouping things according to their shared characteristics. In Biology it brings order to the huge variety of life. It makes living things easier to study, helps scientists talk about organisms clearly, and shows how organisms are related to one another (their evolutionary relationships).

Taxonomy is the science of classifying, naming and grouping organisms (from the Greek words for 'arrangement' and 'law'). The system used today is based on the work of the Swedish scientist Carolus Linnaeus. He arranged living things in seven major groups (ranks), from the largest to the smallest: Kingdom, Phylum (for animals) or Division (for plants), Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species. The basic unit of classification is the species: a group of organisms that can breed together and produce fertile offspring.

Linnaeus also introduced a way of naming organisms with two names. The first is the generic name (the genus) and begins with a capital letter. The second is the specific name (the species) and begins with a small letter. Scientific names are written in italics or underlined when written by hand. Examples: man, Homo sapiens; lion, Panthera leo; maize, Zea mays. (The source notes wrote 'panthera leo' and 'zea Mays', which break these rules.)

Linnaeus first divided living things into two kingdoms, plants and animals. But many one-celled organisms did not fit well. Biologists later divided living things into five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia (this five-kingdom system was proposed by R. H. Whittaker in 1969). Viruses do not fit into any of the five and are treated separately.

img.cap: The five kingdoms of living things.

units.title: Viruses, and the Kingdoms Monera, Protista and Fungi
units.summary: Why viruses are special, and the features of the kingdoms Monera, Protista and Fungi with examples.

p: A virus is so small that it can be seen only with an electron microscope. It has either DNA or RNA inside a protein coat. It has no cell structure, cannot make its own proteins, and does not respire, feed or excrete. It cannot reproduce by cell division (binary fission); it reproduces only inside a living host cell.

Viruses are like living things because they reproduce inside a host cell and pass their characteristics to the next generation. They are like non-living things because outside a host they can form crystals and do not respire, excrete or respond to stimuli. So they are treated separately from the five kingdoms. Examples of diseases: the common cold, influenza, polio, measles, HIV and COVID-19.

These are the simplest living things: bacteria and blue-green bacteria (cyanobacteria, like Anabaena). They are microscopic and single-celled. They are prokaryotes: they have no true nucleus (no nuclear membrane), and the DNA lies in the cytoplasm. Their cell wall does not contain cellulose; it is made of peptidoglycan (a mixture of sugars and amino acids). (The source says 'protein and fatty materials'.) They have no organelles with membranes except ribosomes. They reproduce asexually by binary fission.

Protists are mostly single-celled eukaryotes: their cells have a definite nucleus. Most live in water. They move by cilia, flagella or pseudopodia. Some are free-living and a few are parasites. There are two groups: Protozoa, which are animal-like (Amoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium, Trypanosoma), and Protophyta, which are plant-like (diatoms, Chlorella, Chlamydomonas). Euglena has both plant-like and animal-like features.

Fungi are non-green organisms without chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise. They have rigid cell walls made of chitin and other polysaccharides. They have no true roots, stems or leaves. Most are non-motile. They reproduce by spores (asexual) and also sexually. Most are saprophytes (feeding on dead matter); some are parasites. A few are single-celled (yeast) but most are many-celled (Rhizopus, Mucor, mushrooms). They store food as glycogen.

units.title: Kingdom Plantae
units.summary: The main groups of plants: thallophytes, bryophytes and tracheophytes, and how seed plants divide into gymnosperms and angiosperms, monocots and dicots.

p: Plants are multicellular, non-motile organisms. Their cells have cellulose cell walls and chloroplasts containing chlorophyll, which lets them make food by photosynthesis. The kingdom is divided into three main groups: Thallophyta, Bryophyta and Tracheophyta.

img.alt: A flow chart of the plant kingdom: thallophytes, bryophytes and tracheophytes; tracheophytes divide into pteridophytes and spermatophytes; spermatophytes divide into gymnosperms and angiosperms; angiosperms divide into monocots and dicots
img.cap: Classification of the plant kingdom.

p: Example: algae. No true roots, stem or leaves. Chlorophyll is present.
Examples: mosses and liverworts. No true roots, stem or leaves; they have thread-like rhizoids that anchor them.

The tracheophytes have vascular tissue (xylem and phloem). They include two groups. Pteridophytes (ferns) have true roots, stems and leaves but reproduce by spores. Spermatophytes make pollen and seeds. They divide into gymnosperms (have cones and naked seeds, usually needle-like leaves, no flowers; for example pine) and angiosperms (flowering plants whose seeds develop inside fruits).

Angiosperms are divided into two classes. Monocots have one seed leaf (cotyledon), parallel-veined narrow leaves; there are no true trees except palms (examples: maize, grasses, palms). Dicots have two seed leaves, net-veined broad leaves; they include herbs, shrubs and trees (examples: beans, hibiscus, mango).

units.title: Kingdom Animalia (1): Invertebrates
units.summary: The main phyla of animals without backbones: Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda and Echinodermata, with their features and examples.

p: The animal kingdom divides into invertebrates (no backbone) and vertebrates (with a backbone). Here are the main invertebrate phyla.

img.alt: A chart of animal classification: vertebrates (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) and invertebrates (Porifera, Cnidaria, Annelida, Mollusca, Platyhelminthes, Echinodermata, Arthropoda with Crustacea, Arachnida, Insects and Myriapoda)
img.cap: Classification of animals.

p: Protozoa (single-celled; now usually classified with the protists): Amoeba, Plasmodium, Trypanosoma. Mostly microscopic. Some are free-living and some are parasites.

Porifera (sponges): many-celled, fixed in one place (sessile), mostly aquatic. One body cavity with many pores; two layers of cells; skeleton of calcium carbonate or silica spicules; no nervous system; reproduce asexually by budding.

Cnidaria / Coelenterata (Hydra, sea anemone, jellyfish): simple many-celled aquatic animals with two cell layers and no organs; stinging cells (nematoblasts); asexual reproduction by budding and sexual by gametes.

Platyhelminthes (flatworms): liver fluke, tapeworm, planaria. Flat, thin bodies, bilaterally symmetrical, three body layers, mostly hermaphrodites, free-living or parasitic; one opening to the gut (the mouth).

Nematoda (roundworms): Ascaris, hookworm, guinea worm, filaria worm, Onchocerca. Long, slender, cylindrical bodies with pointed ends; three layers; mouth and anus; covered with a cuticle; separate sexes; free-living or parasitic. (The source lists tapeworm here, but tapeworms are flatworms.)
Annelida (segmented worms): earthworm, leech (Hirudo), Lumbricus. Long, cylindrical, segmented bodies; three layers; mouth and anus; nervous, excretory, reproductive and circulatory systems.
Mollusca: snail, slug (also oyster and octopus). Soft unsegmented body usually covered by a calcareous shell; head, muscular foot and a visceral hump; eyes and tentacles on the head.
Echinodermata: starfish, sea urchin. Aquatic; radially symmetrical; spiny skin with a calcareous skeleton; tube feet for movement; separate sexes.

The biggest phylum. Arthropods have jointed legs, a hard exoskeleton of chitin and segmented bodies. There are four classes (the source notes wrongly list 'Annelida' as a fifth; Annelida is a separate phylum).

Class Insecta (cockroach, housefly, butterfly, grasshopper): a pair of antennae, a pair of compound eyes, body in head, thorax and abdomen, three pairs of legs on the thorax, breathing by tracheae, often winged, and they usually go through metamorphosis.

img.alt: A labelled grasshopper showing the head, thorax and abdomen, antenna, foreleg, midleg, hind leg, femur, tibia and forewing
img.cap: A grasshopper, a typical insect.

p: Class Myriapoda (centipede and millipede): head and a long trunk of many segments; each segment of a centipede (class Chilopoda) has one pair of legs and the animal is a carnivore; each segment of a millipede (class Diplopoda) has two pairs of legs and it eats plants; breathing by tracheae.

Class Arachnida (spiders, scorpions, ticks): two body regions, the prosoma (cephalothorax) and the opisthosoma (abdomen); four pairs of walking legs; chelicerae and pedipalps; usually simple eyes; breathing by book lungs.

Class Crustacea (crab, prawn, shrimp, water flea, barnacle): two body regions, the cephalothorax and the abdomen; two pairs of antennae; usually five pairs of walking legs; compound eyes; gills for breathing; mostly aquatic.

units.title: Kingdom Animalia (2): Vertebrates
units.summary: The five classes of vertebrates (fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals) with their features and examples.

p: Vertebrates have a backbone (vertebral column) and are divided into five classes: Pisces (fishes), Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves (birds) and Mammalia. (The source notes misspell 'Aves' as 'Eves'.)

Gills for breathing, which stay in the adult. Paired pectoral and pelvic fins. Lateral line for sensing movement. Skin with scales (cycloid scales in bony fishes such as tilapia, placoid scales in cartilaginous fishes such as dogfish). External fertilisation.

img.alt: A labelled fish showing dorsal fin, caudal fin, pectoral fin, pelvic fin, anal fin, mouth and gill flap
img.cap: A bony fish, with its fins labelled.

p: Pentadactyl limbs (five digits). Soft, moist skin without scales. Gills at the tadpole stage and lungs in the adult (also breathing through the skin). Eardrum on the surface, no external ear. External fertilisation in water. Examples: toad, frog, newt and salamander. (The source says 'strew', a mistake for 'newt'; shrews are mammals.)

img.alt: A frog and a toad with labels: bulging eye, tympanic membrane, trunk, forelimb, hind limb and webbed feet
img.cap: A frog and a toad.

p: Pentadactyl limbs. Dry skin covered with scales. Breathe with lungs. Eggs with a leathery shell and plenty of yolk, laid on land; no larval stage. Internal fertilisation. Examples: lizard, snake, crocodile, tortoise.

img.alt: A lizard with labels: head, nostril, bulging eye, ear drum, trunk, fore-limb, hind limb, tail, cloaca and clawed digits
img.cap: A lizard (an agama).

p: Pentadactyl limb, with the forelimb changed into a wing. Warm-blooded. Feathers on the body and scales on the legs and feet. A beak and no teeth. Lungs for breathing. Hard-shelled eggs with much yolk. No larval stage. Internal fertilisation. Examples: pigeon, domestic fowl.

img.alt: A bird with labels: crown, head, nape, back, rump, tail, wing, breast, belly, thigh, leg, upper beak and lower beak
img.cap: External features of a bird.

p: Pentadactyl limbs. Warm-blooded. Hair on the skin, and sweat glands. Mammary glands that produce milk for the young. A four-chambered heart. Internal fertilisation. Most are viviparous (the young develop inside the mother); a few, such as the platypus, lay eggs. Examples: man, goat, dog, bat, whale.

units.title: The Cell: Forms of Cells and the Plant and Animal Cell
units.summary: What a cell is, the forms in which cells exist, and the structure of typical plant and animal cells.

p: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living things, the smallest unit of life that can carry out life processes. Cells differ in structure, function and size, but all have a cell membrane, genetic material (DNA or RNA) and the ability to carry out metabolism and reproduce.
1. Single (unicellular) cells: the whole organism is one cell. Examples: bacteria, Amoeba, Euglena, yeast.
2. Colonies: groups of cells living together, each able to live independently. Examples: Volvox, some algae and bacteria.
3. Filaments: cells joined end to end in a chain or thread. Examples: Spirogyra (a green alga), some cyanobacteria.
4. Part of a many-celled organism: cells organised into tissues, organs and systems, as in a plant or an animal.

A plant cell has a rigid cell wall of cellulose outside the cell membrane, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole, a nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes and the Golgi apparatus.

img.alt: A labelled plant cell showing the cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, nucleolus, vacuole, chloroplast, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and amyloplast
img.cap: A plant cell.

p: An animal cell has a cell membrane but no cell wall, no chloroplasts and usually small vacuoles. It has a nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body, lysosomes and centrioles.

img.alt: A labelled animal cell showing the plasma membrane, nucleus, chromatin, nuclear pores, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, centriole, mitochondrion, Golgi body, lysosome and vacuole

units.title: Cell Organelles and Their Functions
units.summary: The functions of the cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body, lysosomes, vacuoles and other organelles, and a plant-animal comparison table.

p: Cell membrane: controls what enters and leaves the cell; a protective barrier. Nucleus: contains the DNA and controls the cell's activities. Cytoplasm: a jelly-like fluid in which organelles are suspended and many reactions take place. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER): rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins; smooth ER makes lipids and helps remove poisons. Golgi apparatus: changes, packages and transports proteins and lipids. Mitochondria: the 'powerhouses', where cellular respiration releases energy. Ribosomes: make proteins using the instructions from DNA. Lysosomes: contain enzymes for digestion and for removing waste. Vacuole: stores nutrients and wastes; in plants it is large and keeps the cell firm (turgid). Chloroplast (plants): carries out photosynthesis. Cell wall (plants): gives shape and support. Cytoskeleton: gives support and helps movement. Centrioles (animal cells): help in cell division.

units.title: Diffusion
units.summary: What diffusion is, how it happens, the factors that affect its speed and why it is important to living things.

p: Diffusion is the spontaneous movement of particles (atoms, ions or molecules) from a region where they are in high concentration to a region where they are in low concentration. They move down a concentration gradient until they are evenly spread (equilibrium). The particles move by random motion, and no energy from the cell is needed. Diffusion happens in gases, liquids and, very slowly, solids. Examples: the scent of flowers spreading through a room; a drop of ink spreading in water; oxygen entering the blood in the lungs.

img.alt: Two panels: osmosis, with water crossing a semipermeable membrane from pure water to a solution; and diffusion, with red particles spreading from high concentration to low concentration
img.cap: Diffusion (right) and osmosis (left).

sections.h: Factors affecting the rate of diffusion
p: Temperature: higher temperature makes particles move faster, so diffusion is faster. Concentration gradient: a steeper gradient gives faster diffusion. Size of the particles: small particles diffuse faster than large ones. The medium: diffusion is fastest in gases, slower in liquids and slowest in solids. Surface area: a larger surface (such as the many folds of the gut) lets more diffuse. Distance: shorter distances give faster diffusion.

sections.h: Importance of diffusion to living things
p: 1. Gas exchange: oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse in and out of the body in the lungs, leaves and gills.
2. Respiration and photosynthesis: gases move in and out of cells to supply these processes.
3. Uptake of nutrients: digested food diffuses across the gut wall into the blood, and wastes diffuse out of cells.
4. Mixing for chemical reactions: diffusion brings reactants together in the cell.
5. In plants, water vapour diffuses out of the leaves through the stomata (transpiration).

units.title: Osmosis and Active Transport
units.summary: Osmosis, tonicity (hypertonic, hypotonic and isotonic solutions), plasmolysis, turgidity, haemolysis, the importance of osmosis, and active transport.

p: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a region of lower solute concentration (a dilute solution, which has more free water) to a region of higher solute concentration (a concentrated solution, which has less free water) through a semi-permeable (selectively permeable) membrane. The membrane lets water through but not all dissolved substances. It happens only when a membrane separates a weak solution from a strong one. (It is easy to be confused by the wording: the 'concentration' referred to is the concentration of the dissolved substance.)

Hypertonic: the surrounding fluid is more concentrated than the cell contents. Water leaves the cell by exosmosis and the cell shrinks. Hypotonic: the surrounding fluid is less concentrated than the cell contents. Water enters the cell by endosmosis and the cell swells. Isotonic: the same concentration inside and out; there is no net movement of water.

Plant cell: in a hypotonic solution, it takes in water and becomes turgid (swollen and firm), which gives support. In a hypertonic solution, it loses water and becomes flaccid (limp); with severe loss, the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall, which is called plasmolysis. Plasmolysis can be reversed (deplasmolysis) if the cell is placed in a hypotonic solution. Animal cell: a red blood cell in a hypotonic solution takes in water and may burst (haemolysis); in a hypertonic solution, it shrinks.

img.alt: A plant cell and a red blood cell shown in hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic solutions: shrunken or plasmolysed, normal, and swollen (turgid or bursting)
img.cap: Plant and animal cells in hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic solutions.

p: 1. It absorbs water from the soil into the root hairs. 2. It moves water from cell to cell in plants. 3. It controls opening and closing of the stomata (guard cells). 4. It makes plant cells turgid, which supports non-woody parts. 5. It moves water between cells in animals. 6. It reabsorbs water from the kidney tubules into the blood. 7. It can cause haemolysis of red blood cells if they are in pure water.

Osmoregulation is the control of the amount of water and dissolved substances in an organism, so that its internal environment stays balanced. It uses osmosis and active transport. For example, the kidney controls the water content of the blood.

Active transport is the movement of substances against a concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) using energy (ATP) from respiration. It needs carrier proteins in the cell membrane. Examples: root hairs absorbing mineral salts from soil that are in lower concentration than inside the cell; absorption of glucose from the gut.

units.title: Nutrition: Nutrients and Modes of Nutrition
units.summary: Macro and micro nutrients, the two modes of nutrition (autotrophic and heterotrophic), and the types of heterotrophic feeding.

p: Nutrition is the way an organism gets and uses food. Macronutrients are needed in large amounts: carbohydrates, proteins and fats. They supply energy and materials for growth. Micronutrients are needed in small amounts: vitamins and minerals. They help the body to work properly. (Water and fibre are also needed.)

There are two main modes. Autotrophic nutrition: the organism makes its own food from simple inorganic substances, by photosynthesis (using light) or by chemosynthesis (using energy from chemical reactions). Examples: green plants, algae and some bacteria. Heterotrophic nutrition: the organism cannot make its own food and depends on other organisms. Examples: animals, fungi and many bacteria.
Holozoic nutrition: the organism takes in solid or liquid food, digests it inside the body and absorbs it. Most animals feed this way, including man.
Parasitic nutrition: a parasite lives on or inside a host and takes food from it, harming the host. Examples: tapeworm in the human gut; fleas and ticks on a dog; Plasmodium in the blood.

Saprophytic nutrition: feeding on dead and decaying organic matter. Saprophytes (decomposers) such as mushrooms and bread mould, and many bacteria, release enzymes that digest the dead matter outside the body, then absorb the nutrients.

Symbiosis: a close, long-lasting relationship between two species. In mutualism both gain (bees get nectar and flowers are pollinated). In commensalism one gains and the other is not affected (barnacles on a whale). In parasitism one gains at the other's expense.

units.title: Photosynthesis and Heterotrophic Nutrition
units.summary: The process of photosynthesis, its requirements, its products and its importance, and chemosynthesis.

p: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to change carbon dioxide and water into glucose (a sugar) and oxygen. It happens in the chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll.
Equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (in the presence of light and chlorophyll).

img.alt: A leaf in sunlight taking in carbon dioxide and water and giving out oxygen, with the equation for photosynthesis
img.cap: Photosynthesis in a leaf.

p: 1. Light absorption: chlorophyll absorbs light energy. 2. Splitting of water: water molecules are split, releasing oxygen and giving hydrogen (electrons and protons). 3. Carbon fixation: carbon dioxide from the air is built into organic molecules, first into a three-carbon compound, in the Calvin cycle. 4. Making glucose: through a series of reactions, glucose and other organic compounds are made. Glucose is changed to starch for storage.
Light: usually sunlight. Chlorophyll: absorbs the light. Carbon dioxide: enters the leaf through the stomata. Water: absorbed by the roots from the soil. A suitable temperature.

It produces oxygen for breathing. It stores solar energy as chemical energy in glucose. It makes the food that supports all food chains. It removes carbon dioxide from the air and so takes part in the carbon cycle.

Chemosynthesis is the making of carbohydrates using the energy from chemical reactions instead of sunlight. It occurs in places without sunlight, such as deep-sea hydrothermal vents and caves, and in nitrifying bacteria in the soil (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter).

Photosynthesis compared with chemosynthesis: photosynthesis uses light, needs chlorophyll and releases oxygen; chemosynthesis uses chemical energy (for example from oxidising ammonia or hydrogen sulphide), does not need light and is carried out only by some bacteria.

sections.h: Heterotrophic feeding in Amoeba and Paramecium
p: Amoeba flows around food (a smaller organism) with its pseudopodia and engulfs it in a food vacuole (phagocytosis). Enzymes digest the food and the digested food diffuses into the cytoplasm; undigested remains are expelled. Paramecium sweeps food into its oral groove with its cilia; the food is enclosed in food vacuoles that move around the cell while digestion takes place, and waste leaves through the anal pore.

units.title: Cellular Respiration
units.summary: What cellular respiration is, aerobic and anaerobic respiration with correct equations, fermentation, oxygen debt and muscle fatigue.

p: Cellular (internal or tissue) respiration is the breakdown of glucose in cells to release energy. It occurs in all living cells. The energy is stored in a molecule called ATP, which the cell uses for its work. Much of it happens in the mitochondria. (External respiration, or breathing, is the exchange of gases between the organism and its surroundings.)
With oxygen. It releases the largest amount of energy from one glucose molecule. Carbon dioxide and water are the by-products.
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (about 30 to 38 ATP; the source notes give 38 as the traditional figure, but the net yield is nearer 30 to 32 in modern textbooks).
Without oxygen. It releases much less energy (only 2 ATP per glucose). It occurs in yeast and some bacteria, in parasites in the gut, and in the muscles of animals when oxygen is short.
In plants and yeast (alcoholic fermentation): C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy (2 ATP). The ethanol and carbon dioxide are made from pyruvic acid. This is used in brewing and to make bread rise.

In animal muscle (lactic acid fermentation): C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ (lactic acid) + energy (2 ATP). No carbon dioxide is released. (The source notes wrongly include carbon dioxide in this equation.) Lactic acid builds up and causes muscle fatigue and cramps.

During hard exercise, muscles use oxygen faster than the blood can supply it, so they respire anaerobically and lactic acid collects. After the exercise, the extra oxygen needed to break down the lactic acid is the oxygen debt. This is why we keep breathing hard after running.

units.title: The Stages of Respiration: Glycolysis and the Krebs Cycle
units.summary: How glucose is broken down step by step: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix and the electron transport chain, with the ATP yields.

p: Aerobic respiration has three main stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm; the Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle) in the matrix of the mitochondrion; and the electron transport chain on the inner membrane (cristae) of the mitochondrion.

Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen. The 6-carbon glucose is first phosphorylated (a phosphate is added, using ATP) by the enzyme hexokinase. After about ten enzyme-controlled steps, one glucose molecule is split into two molecules of the 3-carbon pyruvic acid (pyruvate). Two ATP are used and four are made, so the net gain is 2 ATP. This direct making of ATP is called substrate-level phosphorylation. Hydrogen is also passed to a carrier (NAD⁺ becomes NADH).

img.alt: The glycolysis pathway from glucose through glucose-6-phosphate, fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to pyruvate, with the enzymes and ATP steps
img.cap: The steps of glycolysis (for reference; you need to know the main ideas, not every enzyme).

sections.h: Stage 2: the link reaction and the Krebs cycle
p: If oxygen is present, pyruvic acid enters the mitochondrion. Each pyruvate loses one carbon as carbon dioxide and becomes a 2-carbon acetyl group, which is carried by coenzyme A as acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetic acid to form citric acid, which begins the Krebs cycle, in the matrix of the mitochondrion. In the cycle, the carbon is completely oxidised to carbon dioxide, and much hydrogen is passed to the carriers NAD⁺ and FAD.

img.alt: The Krebs cycle as a circle: oxaloacetate to citric acid, isocitric acid, alpha-ketoglutaric acid, succinyl CoA, succinate, fumarate and malate, with CO2, NADH, FADH2 and GTP released
img.cap: The Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle).

p: The hydrogen carried by NADH and FADH₂ gives up its electrons to a chain of carriers on the inner mitochondrial membrane. The energy released makes most of the ATP (oxidative phosphorylation). The electrons finally join with oxygen and hydrogen to form water. This is why oxygen is needed.

Total ATP: the traditional figure is 38 ATP per glucose (2 from glycolysis, 2 from the Krebs cycle and 34 from the electron transport chain). The notes say the Krebs cycle itself gives 36 ATP; in fact most of the ATP comes from the electron transport chain that depends on the Krebs cycle. Modern figures are about 30 to 32.
The Krebs cycle is important because it connects the breakdown of carbohydrates, fats and proteins: all can be fed into it.

units.title: Growth and Mitosis
units.summary: What growth is, cell enlargement and differentiation, the stages of mitosis and its importance.

p: Growth is the irreversible increase in size, dry mass and complexity of an organism, due to cell division (mitosis) and cell enlargement. It is measured by changes in height, weight (mass) or volume. It cannot be reversed.

Cell division (mitosis): the number of cells increases. Cell enlargement: after division the new cells take in water and nutrients and grow larger by making more protoplasm. Example: a seedling grows into a tall plant. Cell differentiation: cells become specialised in structure and function. Unspecialised stem cells develop into tissues and organs such as nerve cells and muscle cells. Example: a zygote divides and differentiates into the many tissues of a baby.
Mitosis is the division of one cell into two genetically identical daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent. It is used for growth and repair.

img.alt: Five stages of mitosis drawn as cells: interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase with cytokinesis, with two chromosomes shown
img.cap: The stages of mitosis (shown with two chromosomes).

p: Interphase (the 'resting' stage): the cell prepares to divide; the DNA is copied and the organelles double.
Prophase: the chromatin shortens and coils into visible chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids; the nuclear membrane starts to disappear; spindle fibres form.
Metaphase: the chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell, and spindle fibres attach to their centromeres.
Anaphase: the sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles.
Telophase: the chromatids reach the poles, nuclear membranes form around the two sets, and the chromosomes uncoil. Cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm, gives two daughter cells.

1. Growth of many-celled organisms. 2. Repair of damaged tissues, such as wound healing. 3. Asexual reproduction, such as budding in yeast. 4. It keeps the chromosome number constant from cell to cell.

units.title: Meiosis
units.summary: How meiosis halves the chromosome number to make gametes, the stages of meiosis I and II, and why it makes variation; a comparison with mitosis.

p: Meiosis is the cell division that makes gametes (sperm and egg cells, or spores in some plants). One diploid cell (with two sets of chromosomes) divides twice to give four haploid cells (with one set each). It is also called reduction division because the chromosome number is halved.
Prophase I: homologous chromosomes (one from each parent) pair up (synapsis) to form tetrads. They exchange pieces at points called chiasmata (crossing over), which makes new combinations of genes.

img.alt: Prophase I of meiosis with spindle fibre, nonsister chromatids, centromere, chiasma, sister chromatids and tetrad labelled
img.cap: Prophase I: homologous chromosomes pair and cross over.

p: Metaphase I: the homologous pairs line up on the equator.

img.alt: Metaphase I of meiosis with homologous pairs aligned along the centre of the cell
img.cap: Metaphase I.

p: Anaphase I: whole homologous chromosomes (not chromatids) are pulled to opposite poles.

img.alt: Anaphase I of meiosis with homologous chromosomes moving to opposite poles
img.cap: Anaphase I.

p: Telophase I: two haploid cells form.

img.alt: Telophase I of meiosis with the cytoplasm dividing and two nuclei forming
img.cap: Telophase I.

p: Prophase II: after a short interval with no DNA copying, the chromosomes (still made of two chromatids) prepare to divide again. Metaphase II: they line up singly on the equator. Anaphase II: the sister chromatids are pulled apart. Telophase II and cytokinesis: four haploid daughter cells are formed, each with a single set of chromosomes.

img.alt: The daughter cells of meiosis I dividing in meiosis II to give four haploid cells, each with a single chromosome
img.cap: Meiosis II gives four haploid cells.

p: It keeps the chromosome number the same from generation to generation, because gametes have half the number and fertilisation restores it. It makes genetic variation through crossing over and the random way chromosomes line up and separate in meiosis I. (The source says that separating sister chromatids in meiosis II causes the variation. In fact crossing over and independent assortment in meiosis I do.) It is essential for sexual reproduction.

units.title: Irritability and Movement
units.summary: Stimulus and response, taxis, nastic and tropic movements in plants, and cyclosis and movement in cells.

p: Irritability is the ability of an organism to respond to stimuli. A stimulus is any change in the external or internal environment that causes a change in the activity of the whole organism or a part of it. The change in activity is the response. There are three main types of response: tactic, nastic and tropic movements.

A movement of a whole organism from one place to another in a direction decided by an external stimulus such as light, temperature, water or a chemical. Examples: Euglena or Chlamydomonas swimming away from strong light (negative phototaxis); sperms of a moss swimming towards a chemical given off by the egg (positive chemotaxis).

A movement of part of a plant in response to a stimulus where the direction does not depend on the direction of the stimulus. Examples: the leaflets of the mimosa (sensitive plant) fold when touched; some flowers close when light intensity is low.

A growth movement of part of a plant in a direction decided by the direction of the stimulus. It happens in the growing regions of the root and shoot tips and is controlled by plant hormones called auxins. Tropisms are named by the stimulus.

Phototropism (light): shoots grow towards light (positive); roots grow away from light (negative). Geotropism (gravity): roots grow towards gravity (positive); shoots grow away from it (negative). Thigmotropism (touch): tendrils of climbers twine around a support (positive). Hydrotropism: roots grow towards water.

p: Organisms move from place to place to look for food, water and mates, and to escape enemies or bad weather. Inside cells, cyclosis (cytoplasmic streaming) is the circular flow of the cytoplasm. It carries substances from one part of the cell to another. It occurs in amoeboid movement in Amoeba and in the movement of chloroplasts in some plant cells so that their broad faces are turned to the light.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents

p: In Second Term you look at how bodies are supported (skeletons and supporting tissues), what animals need to eat and why, and then you move out into the environment to study ecology: how living things depend on each other and on their surroundings. You also learn how energy flows through ecosystems, how biology links to farming, and about the micro-organisms around us.

Read each unit, study the diagrams, and draw them in your notebook. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

units.title: The Skeleton: Skeletal Materials, Cartilage and Bone
units.summary: What a skeleton is, the three skeletal materials (chitin, cartilage and bone), the types of cartilage and the differences between bone and cartilage.

p: Tissues are groups of similar cells that carry out a particular function. The skeleton is the framework of the body. It supports the body, gives it shape and protects the soft tissues and organs. In humans it forms the central core of the body, covered by muscles, blood vessels and skin.
There are three forms of skeletal material: chitin, cartilage and bone.

Chitin is a tough, light, flexible, non-living material found in arthropods. It forms a hard covering (exoskeleton) of plates around the body. It can be strengthened by 'tanned' proteins and, in crabs and other aquatic crustaceans, by calcium carbonate.

Cartilage is a tissue in the skeleton of vertebrates. It has a firm matrix with fibres, made by living cells called chondroblasts. The cells later get trapped in spaces (lacunae) in the matrix and are then called chondrocytes. It is tough and flexible and acts as a shock absorber between bones. It is found in mammals and, as the main skeleton, in cartilaginous fishes such as sharks.

Types of cartilage: hyaline cartilage, the commonest, is found on the surfaces of movable joints, in the trachea and bronchi, and in the nose. White fibrous cartilage is tougher and is found in the discs between the vertebrae. Yellow elastic cartilage is found in the external ear (pinna) and the epiglottis (the flap that covers the windpipe when swallowing).

Bone is the main part of the skeleton of vertebrates. It contains living cells (osteocytes), protein fibres (collagen) and minerals (calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate), which make up about two-thirds of the mass. So bone is strong and rigid. It has a rich blood supply.

The skeleton of a young embryo is mostly cartilage. As the embryo grows, bone cells replace cartilage cells, and minerals are added so that the cartilage hardens into bone. This process is called ossification.

units.title: Types and Functions of the Skeleton
units.summary: Hydrostatic skeleton, exoskeleton and endoskeleton, moulting, joints, ligaments and tendons, and the functions of a skeleton.

p: 1. Hydrostatic skeleton: found in soft-bodied animals such as the earthworm and the sea anemone. The body is filled with fluid that is under pressure, and the muscular body wall squeezes against it. The pressure supports the body and, with the muscles, allows movement.

2. Exoskeleton: an outer skeleton found in arthropods. It is made by the cells covering the body and its main material is chitin (non-living). It supports the body against gravity, protects it and lets it move. Animals with an exoskeleton periodically shed it in a process called moulting or ecdysis. They grow rapidly while the new skeleton is still soft and stretchy.

3. Endoskeleton: an internal skeleton found in all vertebrates, made mainly of bones (and cartilage). The bones grow steadily as the animal grows, so there is no moulting. The bones are joined at movable joints by tough, flexible bands called ligaments, so the skeleton can bend. Muscles are attached to the bones by tendons, which gives posture and movement.

It supports the body and is its framework. It protects delicate organs: the skull protects the brain, the ribs protect the heart and lungs. Limbs and muscles allow locomotion. The ribs are involved in breathing. Bone marrow makes blood cells. It also stores minerals such as calcium.

units.title: The Axial Skeleton: Skull and Vertebral Column
units.summary: The axial and appendicular skeleton, the skull, and the vertebral column with the types and structure of vertebrae.

p: The skeleton of a vertebrate (fish, frog, lizard, bird, man) is made of bones and cartilage and has two parts. The axial skeleton consists of the skull, the vertebral column, the ribs and the sternum. The appendicular skeleton is made of the limb girdles (pectoral and pelvic) and the limbs.

img.alt: A human skeleton shown twice, with the axial skeleton (skull, ribs, sternum, vertebral column) highlighted on the left and the appendicular skeleton (limbs and girdles) highlighted on the right
img.cap: The axial skeleton (left) and the appendicular skeleton (right).

p: The skull is made of flat bones joined by fixed (suture) joints. It has three parts: the cranium (brain box), the facial skeleton and the jaws (the upper jaw is the maxilla and the lower jaw is the mandible). Functions: protects the brain; protects the organs of smell, the eyes and the ears; gives the head its shape; bears the teeth.

The vertebral column (backbone) protects the spinal cord. It is made of vertebrae, in five groups, each built on a similar pattern, held together by strong ligaments and separated by cartilage pads (intervertebral discs).

Neural canal: the hole through which the spinal cord passes. Neural spine: projects upward and backward; muscles attach to it. Transverse processes: for attachment of muscles and ligaments. Centrum: the solid body of bone below the neural canal. Zygapophyses: surfaces that join one vertebra to the next (pre-zygapophyses face up and inward; post-zygapophyses face down and outward).

Cervical: the first is the atlas, which has a large neural canal, broad flat transverse processes, a short neural spine and a canal for blood vessels, but no centrum. It allows nodding of the head. The second is the axis, which has a broad flat centrum, a large neural spine and an odontoid process that fits into the atlas and forms a pivot joint, allowing the head to turn.
Thoracic: long prominent neural spine, short transverse processes, large cylindrical centrum, and surfaces for attaching the ribs. They help in breathing.

Lumbar: large flat transverse processes, broad neural spine, thick centrum, well-developed zygapophyses and extra projections. They carry body weight and give attachment to the muscles of the abdomen.
Sacral: fused into one bony mass, the sacrum, which joins the pelvic girdle and gives strength.
Caudal: fused (in man) into the coccyx; no neural spine or canal; they support the tail.

units.title: The Appendicular Skeleton and the Ribs
units.summary: The pectoral and pelvic girdles, the bones of the fore and hind limbs, and the ribs and rib cage.

p: Around the shoulder. Two halves held by muscles. Each half has three bones: the scapula (shoulder blade), the clavicle (collar bone) and the coracoid (fused with the scapula in man). The scapula is flat and triangular with a hollow, the glenoid cavity, which receives the head of the humerus to form the shoulder joint. The clavicle is a small rod joining the sternum to the scapula. Functions: gives attachment to muscles and supports the forelimbs.

Around the hip. Two halves, joined to each other in front and to the sacrum behind. Each half has three bones: the ilium, ischium and pubis. Together they make a hollow, the acetabulum, which receives the head of the femur to form the hip joint.
Most vertebrate limbs follow the same plan: one long bone, then two long bones, then small bones, ending in five digits (pentadactyl).

Forelimb: the humerus (upper arm bone) joins the radius and ulna (forearm; the ulna is longer) at the elbow. Then the carpals (wrist), the metacarpals (palm) and the phalanges (finger bones). Each finger has three phalanges, but the thumb has two.

Hind limb: the femur (thigh bone, the longest and largest bone in the body) joins the tibia (the larger shin bone) and the fibula at the knee, with the patella (knee cap) in front. Then the tarsals (ankle), the metatarsals and the phalanges (toes).

p: The ribs are curved bones joining the thoracic vertebrae to the sternum. In man there are 12 pairs. They form a cage that protects the heart and lungs and help in breathing. Each rib has a head, a neck and a shaft. The first seven pairs join the sternum directly by costal cartilage and are the true ribs. The next five pairs are false ribs: pairs 8 to 10 share a joint to the sternum through the cartilage of the rib above, and pairs 11 and 12 are floating ribs with no connection in front.

units.title: Supporting Tissues in Plants
units.summary: Why plants need support and the supporting tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem.

p: Plants need supporting tissues to give them a definite shape, strength and rigidity, and to resist forces such as wind and water. The supporting tissues are parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem.

img.alt: A diagram of a potted plant with water and minerals moving up the xylem and food moving in the phloem, and enlarged tubes of xylem (stiffened with lignin) and phloem (with perforated end walls)
img.cap: Xylem and phloem.

p: Living cells with thin cellulose walls and many air spaces between them. The most common and abundant plant tissue. Functions: gives firmness and turgidity to non-woody stems (such as hibiscus and herbs); stores food and water; makes food in the leaf (mesophyll).
Living cells which are elongated and thickened at the corners with extra cellulose. Functions: strength and support in young growing parts; gives flexibility.

Thick-walled cells containing cellulose and lignin, mostly dead when mature and rich in fibres. Functions: gives strength, rigidity and hardness, and supports the plant. (It makes the plant strong rather than flexible.)

Found in the vascular tissue of roots, stems and leaves. The tubes are dead, with no end walls, and are stiffened with lignin. Functions: carries water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; gives support, strength and shape to the plant (wood is mainly xylem).

Also in the vascular bundles of roots, stems and leaves. It has sieve tubes with perforated end walls and companion cells. Functions: carries manufactured food (sugars) from the leaves, where it is made, to other parts for use or storage; helps to give support.

units.title: Animal Nutrition: Feeding Habits, Carbohydrates, Proteins and Fats
units.summary: Carnivores, herbivores and omnivores, the seven classes of food, and the sources, uses and digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.

p: Animals cannot make their own food. They depend directly or indirectly on plants, so they are heterotrophs. By food type they are carnivores (feed on flesh, such as lion), herbivores (feed on plants, such as goat) and omnivores (feed on plants and animals, such as man).

img.alt: A plate divided into carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, vitamins and minerals, with water and roughage shown beside it
img.cap: The seven classes of food: carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, mineral salts, vitamins, water and roughage.

p: Seven classes: carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, mineral salts, vitamins, water and roughage.

Sources: bread, yam, rice, cassava, sugar. They contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Types: monosaccharides (simple sugars) such as glucose, fructose and galactose; disaccharides (double sugars) such as maltose, sucrose and lactose; polysaccharides (complex sugars) such as starch, glycogen and cellulose. Digestion: starch is broken down by amylase (ptyalin in saliva) to maltose, and maltase changes maltose to glucose. Extra carbohydrate is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles and changed back to glucose when needed. (The source notes call disaccharides 'reducing sugars', but sucrose is not a reducing sugar.)
Uses: energy; heat to keep the body warm; mucus for lubrication; in insects the polysaccharide chitin forms the exoskeleton.

Sources: egg, meat, fish, beans. Proteins are made of amino acids and contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sometimes sulphur and phosphorus. Digestion: pepsin (in the stomach), trypsin (pancreas) and others break proteins into amino acids. Uses: growth in the young; repair of worn tissue; making enzymes and hormones; reproduction; body building.

Fats are solid and oils are liquid at room temperature. They contain carbon, hydrogen and a little oxygen. Sources: palm oil, groundnut, soya beans, butter. Lipase digests them to fatty acids and glycerol. Uses: give more energy than carbohydrates (about twice as much per gram); supply essential fatty acids; insulate the body and keep it warm; carry fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K); protect organs.

units.title: Mineral Salts and Vitamins
units.summary: The functions of mineral salts and the sources, functions and deficiency diseases of the vitamins.

p: Mineral salts are needed in small amounts, except sodium chloride. The minerals include calcium, magnesium, potassium, phosphorus, sulphur, chlorine, iron, iodine, fluorine, manganese, copper, cobalt and sodium. Their functions: regulate body processes (metabolism); make bones and teeth (calcium, phosphorus); help to make blood (iron); control chemical reactions and nerve action; help to make enzymes and pigments.

Examples: calcium: strong bones and teeth; lack causes rickets and weak bones. Iron: haemoglobin in red blood cells; lack causes anaemia. Iodine: thyroid hormone; lack causes goitre. Sodium: nerve and muscle action and water balance. Chlorine: part of stomach acid. Magnesium: bones and enzymes (and chlorophyll in plants).

Vitamins are organic substances needed in small amounts for normal growth and health. Lack of a vitamin causes a deficiency disease. There are two groups: water-soluble vitamins (B complex and C) and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K).
