units.title: Water, Roughage, Balanced Diet and Digestive Enzymes
units.summary: The importance of water and roughage, what a balanced diet is, malnutrition (kwashiorkor), and enzymes and their properties and classes.

p: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. It makes up about 75% of the human body and comes from drinks and food. Its importance: needed for metabolic reactions; helps digestion; keeps body temperature steady (sweating); transports nutrients and wastes; maintains osmotic balance in tissues; removes wastes in urine and sweat.
Roughage (fibre) is the indigestible part of plant food (cellulose) in vegetables, fruit and whole grains. It adds bulk, helps food to move along the gut and prevents constipation.

A balanced diet contains all the food substances in the right proportions. As a rough guide, about 60% carbohydrate, 15% protein, 15% fats and oils and 10% vitamins, minerals and roughage, plus plenty of water. Functions: keeps us healthy, helps resist disease, provides the energy for all life activities, and prevents malnutrition and deficiency diseases. Kwashiorkor is caused by a diet lacking protein. Signs in a child: slow growth, loss of weight, swollen legs and a swollen belly (oedema), thin arms and legs. (The source notes say 'cracked or split stomach'; the typical sign is a swollen belly.) Marasmus is caused by lack of food in general.

Enzymes are protein catalysts made by living cells that speed up chemical reactions. Digestive enzymes break complex food into simple, soluble, diffusible forms. Properties of enzymes: they are proteins; they are soluble; each acts on one kind of substance (specific); they work best at body temperature (about 35 to 40 °C) and are destroyed by high heat; each works best at a certain pH; they are not used up; they can be slowed by inhibitors such as mercury and cyanide; many need co-enzymes or co-factors (often vitamins or minerals).

Proteases act on proteins (pepsin, rennin, trypsin, erepsin). Carbohydrases act on carbohydrates: amylases act on starch (ptyalin or salivary amylase, pancreatic amylase), and maltase, sucrase and lactase act on the sugars maltose, sucrose and lactose. (The source notes list lactase, maltase and sucrase as amylases.) Lipases act on fats and oils.

units.title: Ecology: Meaning, Branches and Basic Concepts
units.summary: What ecology is, autecology and synecology, and the basic ecological terms: environment, biosphere, habitat, niche, population, community, ecosystem and biome.

p: Ecology is the study of plants, animals and micro-organisms in relation to their environment. In practice, ecological study involves: studying the distribution of living things; finding out how living things depend on one another and on their non-living environment for survival; and measuring the factors that affect the environment.

Autecology is the study of one species (or one individual) and its environment, for example the study of a student and his school surroundings. Synecology is the study of groups of organisms or different species living together in an area, for example the fish, crabs and seaweeds in a pond.
Environment: all the external and internal factors, living and non-living, that affect an organism or group of organisms: the habitat with its light, food, water and air, the predators, and diseases.

Biosphere (ecosphere): the zone of the earth where living things carry out their activities. It has three parts. The lithosphere is the solid part (rocks and minerals), about 30% of the earth's surface, and the basis of human settlement. The hydrosphere is the water part (oceans, lakes, rivers, ponds, ice and water vapour), about 70% of the surface. The atmosphere is the gaseous part: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, about 0.04% carbon dioxide (the source notes give 0.03%) and small amounts of other gases.
Habitat: the place where an organism is naturally found. There are three kinds: aquatic (in water: seas, lagoons, streams), terrestrial (on land: forest, savanna, desert) and arboreal (on trees).
Ecological niche: the role of an organism in its habitat: where it lives and its whole way of life (feeding, breeding, behaviour).
Population: all the organisms of one species living together in a habitat, such as the cockroaches in a biology laboratory.
Community: all the populations of living things living together in a habitat, such as decomposers, insects and birds on a decaying log.

Ecosystem: the basic working unit of nature, made of all the living things in an area and their interaction with the non-living parts. It may be natural (a forest) or artificial (a farm or an aquarium).
Biome: a large natural land ecosystem, such as the tropical rain forest or savanna, shaped by climate.

units.title: Components of an Ecosystem
units.summary: The abiotic and biotic components of an ecosystem, and the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers.

p: The biosphere consists of many ecosystems. Every ecosystem has two kinds of component: abiotic (non-living) and biotic (living).

img.alt: A pond ecosystem diagram with abiotic factors (sun, water, soil) and biotic factors: producers (water plants), consumers (fish) and decomposers (bacteria and fungi) linked by arrows showing energy flow and nutrient cycling
img.cap: The parts of an ecosystem.

p: These are the non-living parts of the environment: organic substances (carbohydrates, proteins and lipids), inorganic substances (carbon dioxide, water, minerals), climatic factors (light, temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind) and edaphic (soil) factors (soil type, texture, pH, slope).
These are the living things. They include the producers, the consumers and the decomposers.
Producers are autotrophs that make food from simple inorganic substances, such as green plants, algae and chemosynthetic bacteria.

Consumers are heterotrophs that feed on producers or on one another. Primary consumers eat plants, secondary consumers eat primary consumers, and tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers. They include animals, protozoa and some bacteria.
Decomposers (saprophytes) break down dead plants and animals and release nutrients into the soil. Plants use these nutrients to make food. Examples are fungi and some bacteria.

Living things affect each other in many ways: by feeding (including parasitism), by shading from sunlight, by pollination and seed dispersal, and by competition. Some of these effects are helpful and others are harmful.

units.title: Population Studies: Size, Density and Methods
units.summary: Population size, density and dominance, and the methods used to study populations: census, mark and recapture, quadrat and transect sampling and remote sensing.

p: Population size: the total number of individuals of a species in an area at a given time. Population density: the number of individuals per unit area or volume = population size ÷ area. Example: 500 mango trees on 50 hectares is 10 trees per hectare. Dominance: the degree to which one species has a large effect on the community, often because of its numbers or size (for example, grasses in a savanna).
Census: counting every individual. Accurate but not practical for large, moving or hidden populations.

Mark and recapture: a sample of animals is captured, marked and released. Later another sample is captured, and the proportion of marked animals in it is used to estimate the whole population. Formula: population = (number first marked × total number in second capture) ÷ number of marked animals recaptured. Example: 40 fish are marked; in a second catch of 50 fish, 10 are marked. Population = (40 × 50) ÷ 10 = 200. Useful for mobile animals.

Quadrat sampling: a frame of known size (quadrat) is placed at random several times in the habitat and the organisms inside are counted. Useful for plants and slow or fixed animals. The mean count per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area) estimates the population. It assumes the quadrats represent the whole area.

Transect sampling: a line or belt is laid through the habitat and the organisms touching or near it are recorded. Useful for seeing how distribution changes along a gradient, such as from the water's edge up a bank.
Remote sensing: use of satellite or aerial images to estimate populations or vegetation cover over large areas.

units.title: Factors Affecting Population, Ecological Instruments and Soil
units.summary: Birth rate, death rate, migration and other factors that change populations, the instruments used to measure ecological factors, and how soil type affects water-holding capacity.

p: Birth rate: the number of births per unit of population in a given time. Death rate: the number of deaths per unit of population in a given time. A high death rate reduces the population. Migration: immigration (movement into an area) increases the population; emigration (movement out) decreases it. Resource availability: food, water, shelter and space. Shortage leads to competition. Environmental conditions: climate, weather and habitat. Disease and parasitism: reduce numbers through illness and death. Natural disasters: floods, fires, earthquakes. Human activities: hunting, fishing, habitat destruction by deforestation, urbanisation and pollution. Climate change: alters the suitability of habitats.

p: The source notes say that a hydrometer measures light intensity in water. In fact a hydrometer measures the density of a liquid. Light in water is measured with a light meter or Secchi disc.

Texture: the mix of sand, silt and clay. Clay soils have tiny particles and hold more water than sandy soils (but may become waterlogged). Porosity: well-structured soil with good pore space holds and drains water well. Organic matter (humus): acts like a sponge and holds water for plants. Depth: deeper soil stores more water. Compaction: compacted soil has little pore space and water runs off. Slope: water runs off steep ground and stays on flat or gently sloping land.

units.title: The Functioning Ecosystem, Trophic Levels and the Roles of Organisms
units.summary: What keeps an ecosystem working (biodiversity, energy flow, nutrient cycling, abiotic factors and the water cycle), the roles of autotrophs, heterotrophs and decomposers, and trophic levels.

p: A working ecosystem has several parts that keep it balanced: biodiversity (many species, each with a role, making the system stable); energy flow (producers capture sunlight and the energy passes through consumers and decomposers); nutrient cycling (carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus are recycled as decomposers return nutrients to the soil); abiotic factors (climate, soil and water shape which organisms live there); and the water cycle (precipitation, evaporation and transpiration keep water available).

Autotrophs (producers) make their own food, usually by photosynthesis, and form the base of the ecosystem. Heterotrophs (consumers) cannot make food and depend on others: primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores that eat herbivores) and tertiary consumers (carnivores that eat other carnivores). Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organisms and wastes with enzymes, releasing nutrients for reuse.

A trophic level is a feeding position in a food chain or web. Level 1: producers (green plants, algae). Level 2: primary consumers (herbivores). Level 3: secondary consumers (carnivores). Level 4: tertiary consumers (top carnivores). Decomposers act on the dead remains of every level and return nutrients to the environment.

units.title: Food Chains, Food Webs and Ecological Pyramids
units.summary: Food chains and webs with Nigerian examples, and the pyramids of energy, numbers and biomass, including the 10 per cent rule.

p: A food chain is a straight line showing the flow of energy from one organism to the next: each arrow means 'is eaten by'. Example: grass → grasshopper → lizard → snake → hawk. Another: maize → rat → snake → eagle.

A food web is a network of interlinked food chains. It is more realistic because most animals eat more than one kind of food and are eaten by more than one kind of predator. A food web is also more stable: if one food source disappears, consumers can switch to another.

img.alt: A food web of a savanna: grass and maize eaten by grasshopper, rat and goat; grasshopper eaten by lizard and toad; rat eaten by snake; lizard, toad and snake eaten by hawk; bacteria and fungi decompose dead remains
img.cap: A food web in a savanna.

p: Pyramid of energy: shows the energy at each trophic level. It is always a true pyramid, because only about 10% of the energy passes to the next level (the 10% rule); the rest is lost as heat in respiration, in wastes and in uneaten parts. For example, if producers hold 10,000 kJ, primary consumers get about 1,000 kJ and secondary consumers about 100 kJ.

Pyramid of numbers: shows the number of organisms at each level. It is often a pyramid, but can be inverted or irregular: one big tree may support thousands of insects (a narrow base and wide second level).
Pyramid of biomass: shows the total dry mass of organisms at each level. It usually narrows upward because of energy loss.

img.alt: A pyramid showing energy decreasing up the trophic levels, 100% at the producers to 10% at primary consumers, 1% at secondary consumers and so on, with energy lost as heat and decomposers on the side
img.cap: A pyramid of energy: about 10 per cent passes to each next level.

units.title: Energy Transformation in Nature and the Laws of Thermodynamics
units.summary: How energy changes form in nature, why energy is lost in food chains, and the first and second laws of thermodynamics applied to ecology.

p: Energy changes form in nature. Sunlight becomes chemical energy in glucose by photosynthesis. That energy passes along food chains as organisms eat each other. Some energy is released as heat in respiration. The water cycle and weather also involve energy changes. Understanding these changes helps to explain the balance in ecosystems.

Energy is lost as it moves through trophic levels: as heat during respiration and other metabolism, in wastes (faeces and urine) and in parts that are not eaten or digested. Each level receives only a part of the energy of the level below. This is why food chains are short and why there are fewer organisms at higher levels.

Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only change from one form to another (the law of conservation of energy). Applications in ecology: energy flow (sunlight → chemical energy in plants → herbivores → carnivores → decomposers; the total energy remains constant); metabolism (energy from food is used for growth, movement and reproduction or lost as heat); energy budgets (ecologists add up the energy that enters and leaves a system).

Energy changes are never 100% efficient: some energy always becomes less useful, usually heat, so disorder (entropy) of an isolated system tends to increase. Heat flows from hot to cold, never the other way by itself. Applications: energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient, so energy is lost as heat; decomposition breaks complex molecules into simple ones; heat flows between warm and cool regions, affecting climate and where organisms live. Living things keep themselves ordered only by constantly taking in energy (from the sun or from food), so the second law does not mean that life breaks the law. (The source notes say that ecosystems evolve towards higher entropy and complexity. That is not correct; ecosystems keep their order because they receive a continuous supply of energy from the sun.)

img.alt: A diagram: the sun gives light to a plant (first law: energy is transformed to chemical energy), the plant to a herbivore to a carnivore, and at each step heat is lost (second law)
img.cap: The two laws in a food chain.

units.title: Relevance of Biology to Agriculture: Classification of Plants
units.summary: Botanical and agricultural classification of plants, and classification by life cycle and size, with Nigerian examples.

p: Plants are grouped into divisions, classes, orders, families, genera and species according to their structure and evolution. The three broad groups are Thallophytes, Bryophytes and Tracheophytes. The tracheophytes divide into pteridophytes and spermatophytes, the spermatophytes into gymnosperms and angiosperms, and the angiosperms into dicots and monocots. Thallophytes and bryophytes are non-vascular; tracheophytes are vascular plants. Pteridophytes do not flower; spermatophytes bear seeds; angiosperms are the true flowering plants.
Farmers group plants by the product, the useful part and the economic importance.

Crops and weeds: crops are wanted on the farm; weeds are unwanted plants. Food crops are grown mainly for people to eat (maize, yam); cash crops are grown mainly to sell (cocoa, coffee, rubber). Root crops store starch in underground roots or stems (yam, cassava, sweet potato). Cereals are grasses (monocots) with edible grains rich in carbohydrates (maize, millet, guinea corn, rice, wheat). Fruit crops are rich in vitamins, minerals and sugar (orange, mango, avocado pear, cashew). Vegetable crops are herbaceous plants whose leaves or other parts are eaten and are rich in vitamins and minerals (spinach, lettuce, carrot, cabbage, okro, tomato, onion, pepper). Legumes belong to the bean family and have protein-rich seeds (cowpea, groundnut, soya bean). Spices flavour food (ginger, pepper, thyme). Latex plants give a milky fluid (rubber). Fibre plants give fibre for rope, textiles and bags (cotton, hemp). Beverage and drug plants (tea, coffee, cocoa, kola nut, the quinine tree). Oil plants (oil palm, shea nut, groundnut, coconut, castor, melon).

img.alt: A table-like diagram of crop groups with examples: cereals (maize, rice), roots (yam, cassava), legumes (beans, groundnut), fruits (orange, mango), vegetables (spinach, tomato), oil plants (oil palm), fibre (cotton), latex (rubber), beverage (cocoa)
img.cap: Agricultural classification of crops, with examples.

p: Annuals complete the life cycle in one season or one year (maize, melon, cowpea, tomato). Biennials complete it in two years (carrot, cabbage, onion). The source notes list banana, plantain and pineapple as biennials, but they are usually treated as perennials. Perennials live for more than two years and crop in many seasons (orange, mango, oil palm, cocoa). Yam is a perennial tuber but is usually grown as an annual crop.

Herbs are small plants with soft, non-woody stems (spinach, waterleaf). Shrubs are medium-sized, woody, and branch near the ground (hibiscus). Trees are tall with a single woody trunk that branches at the top (iroko, mahogany, cashew, oil palm).

units.title: Effects of Agricultural Activities on the Ecosystem
units.summary: The good and bad effects of bush burning, overgrazing, tillage, deforestation, fertiliser use and pesticides on the ecosystem, and how to farm sustainably.

p: Setting fire to bush to clear land. Effects: destroys organic matter (humus) in the soil; pollutes the air with smoke; kills many soil micro-organisms; exposes the soil to erosion and leaching; reduces the soil's water-holding capacity; kills or drives away animals, sometimes leading to extinction; the ash makes the soil slightly alkaline and briefly adds some nutrients.

Putting more animals on pasture than it can support (exceeding the carrying capacity). Effects: removes plant cover; exposes soil to erosion; destroys soil structure; compacts the soil through trampling; reduces the vegetation's ability to grow back. (Dung can add some nutrients and grazing can reduce weeds, but the overall effect is harmful.)

Digging or breaking up the soil before planting. Good effects: loosens the soil, helps air to enter, buries weeds and crop residues. Bad effects: exposes and kills soil organisms; changes the structure and texture of the soil; intensive tillage can lead to loss of fertility, erosion and leaching.

The continuous removal of trees (by burning or felling) without replanting. Effects: less water soaks into the soil; may reduce rainfall locally; harms soil organisms; nutrients are lost by leaching and erosion; wildlife lose their homes; the humus in the soil falls.

Adding chemicals to the soil to improve fertility. Good effects: supplies nutrients; increases yields; encourages plant growth, which covers the soil and reduces erosion. Bad effects: over-use can acidify the soil; can reduce humus and harm soil structure; washes into rivers and causes pollution (eutrophication).

Pesticides kill pests; herbicides kill weeds. Effects: pollute the environment; kill useful organisms (bees, earthworms) as well as pests; leave harmful residues; wash into rivers and kill aquatic life. Safer ways: crop rotation, mixed cropping, biological control, planting trees, mulching and using organic manure.

units.title: Micro-organisms Around Us: Groups and Bacteria
units.summary: What micro-organisms are, their discovery by Leeuwenhoek, and the groups: bacteria (shapes and diseases), viruses, protists, fungi and algae.

p: Micro-organisms (microbes or germs) are living things too small to be seen with the naked eye; we need a microscope. They live almost everywhere: in water, air, soil, on objects and in and on living things. They are carried by air currents, and are most abundant where there is food, moisture and a suitable temperature. The Dutchman Anton van Leeuwenhoek (1632 to 1723) was the first to see them, using a simple microscope, in rain water collected from pools.
Micro-organisms include viruses, bacteria and protists, and also cyanobacteria, some fungi and algae.

Bacteria are tiny single-celled organisms (or simple groups of similar cells) that multiply by binary fission. Most are 0.2 to 2 µm across. A bacterial cell has a cell wall and cytoplasm but no true nucleus, so bacteria are prokaryotes. Some have thread-like flagella for movement. Shapes: cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod-shaped), spirilla (spiral rods), spirochaetes (flexible, tightly coiled) and vibrios (comma-shaped).

img.alt: Diagrams of bacterial shapes: cocci (coccus, diplococci, staphylococci, streptococci, sarcina, tetrad), bacilli (bacillus, diplobacilli, palisades, streptobacilli), vibrio, comma, club rod, helical, corkscrew, filamentous and spirochete
img.cap: Shapes of bacteria.

sections.h: Examples of bacteria and the diseases they cause
p: Streptococci (in chains): sore throat. Staphylococci (in bunches): boils. Diplococci (in pairs), such as pneumococcus: pneumonia. Bacilli: typhoid fever (Salmonella typhi). Spirochaetes: syphilis (Treponema pallidum). Vibrios: cholera (Vibrio cholerae).

Viruses are tiny (about 0.02 to 0.3 µm) and can be seen only with an electron microscope. They show life only inside living cells. A virus has DNA or RNA inside a protein coat. Outside living things they behave like complex chemicals.
Mostly single-celled organisms that need a microscope to be seen. They are common in fresh water and damp soil. Examples: Euglena, Paramecium, Trypanosoma, Plasmodium.
Diverse in form. The blue-green mould on oranges and cheese and the white or grey growth on bread are fungi. They feed saprophytically. Examples: Mucor, Rhizopus, Penicillium and Aspergillus.

Most are single-celled and tiny, with chlorophyll. They live in water, moist soil, bark and stones. Floating microscopic algae are phytoplankton, the main food of many aquatic animals. Examples: Chlamydomonas and Protococcus.

units.title: Culturing, Identification and Carriers of Micro-organisms
units.summary: How micro-organisms are cultured, identified, found in different places and carried, and the vectors of some diseases.

p: To study microbes we grow them in the laboratory. The material on or in which they grow is the culture medium; some media are made from extracts of plant or animal tissues. A culture is the population of organisms grown in a medium. A pure (axenic) culture has only one species; a mixed culture has two or more. Agar, a dried polysaccharide from red algae, is used to make the medium solid; microbes cannot digest it. Petri dishes and media are sterilised first by heat in an autoclave, pressure cooker or oven.
Microbes are identified by using a microscope and different stains, by the shape and colour of the colonies they form, by their food needs and by their oxygen needs.

sections.h: Microbes in the air, water and soil
p: If a dish of nutrient agar is left open to the air, colonies of bacteria and fungi grow, showing microbes in the air. Water microbes include protists, algae, fungi and bacteria. Soil microbes include Rhizobium (fixes nitrogen), Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter (nitrifying bacteria). Sewage microbes include Entamoeba histolytica and Escherichia coli.

Many microbes live in and on our bodies without harm. Pathogens cause disease when our resistance is low or when antibiotics upset the normal microbes. Unpreserved food is spoiled by microbes. Pathogens enter the body in four main ways: in the air, in food and water, by contact (direct or indirect), and by insect bites or cuts.

A carrier is anything that carries microbes from place to place. Non-living carriers: air, water, food. Living carriers: houseflies, mosquitoes, rats, cats and others. A vector is an animal that carries a pathogen from one host to another. Mechanical transmission: the animal carries the pathogens on its body. Biological transmission: the pathogen lives and develops in the vector, which becomes infected by feeding on the blood of an infected person.

p: In Third Term you finish the study of micro-organisms: how they grow, how they help and harm us, the diseases they cause and how we control them. You then explore the habitats where living things are found: the sea, estuaries, fresh water, marshes, forests, grasslands and deserts, and how plants and animals are adapted to each. The term ends with reproduction in single-celled organisms and some invertebrates.

Read each unit, study the diagrams, and draw them in your notebook. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

units.title: Growth of Micro-organisms and Their Beneficial and Harmful Effects
units.summary: How bacteria multiply, the four phases of bacterial growth, the methods used to measure growth, and the many ways micro-organisms help and harm us.

p: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission: one cell divides into two, the two become four, then eight, and so on. This is asexual reproduction. The time a cell needs to divide into two is called the generation time. It is different for different organisms and depends on the supply of nutrients, the temperature, the gases available (for example oxygen) and the pH.
If bacteria are put in a fresh nutrient medium and counted over time, the number of living cells follows a pattern with four phases.
1. Lag phase: the cells are getting used to the new medium and make enzymes. They grow in size but do not yet divide much, so numbers stay about the same.
2. Logarithmic (exponential) phase: the cells divide steadily at a constant rate. The number doubles every generation time and the curve rises steeply.
3. Stationary phase: food runs low and wastes build up, so new cells formed are balanced by cells that die. The number stays constant.
4. Decline (death) phase: more cells die than are formed because food is used up and poisonous wastes have collected. The number falls.

img.alt: A graph of number of living cells against time with four phases: a flat lag phase, a steep rise in the log phase, a level stationary phase and a falling decline phase
img.cap: The growth curve of bacteria.

p: Turbidity method: as bacteria multiply, a clear liquid culture becomes cloudy (turbid). The cloudiness is measured with an instrument and tells us how many cells are present.

Serial dilution method: a sample is diluted step by step (for example 1 in 10 each time), a little of each dilution is spread on nutrient agar, and the colonies that grow are counted. The count is then multiplied by the dilution factor.
Squared transparent paper (cellophane) method: a squared transparent sheet is placed over the culture or colonies and the cells or colonies in a number of squares are counted to estimate the total.

Bacteria in the gut of herbivores help to digest cellulose. In humans, bacteria in the intestine make vitamin K and some B vitamins (including B12). Bacteria and fungi are used to make antibiotics such as penicillin. They are used to make amino acids and vinegar. Bacteria turn milk into yoghurt, cheese and other products with different tastes and flavours. They break down sewage into harmless inorganic substances. Microbial cultures make enzymes for industry. Yeast is a leavening agent that makes bread dough rise. Some algae fertilise the soil. Some micro-organisms are grown to make single-cell protein (SCP) as food. Decomposers recycle nutrients in the soil, and nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium help crops.
They cause decay and spoilage of food. They damage materials such as wood, paper, textiles, rubber and some metals. They cause many diseases in humans, animals and plants (see the next unit).

units.title: Control of Harmful Micro-organisms and Vectors
units.summary: Ways of controlling harmful micro-organisms (heat, cold, drugs, salting, drying and sanitation) and how to control mosquitoes and houseflies.

p: Harmful microbes can be controlled by removing them, stopping their growth or killing them with physical agents or chemicals. Common methods:

1. High and low temperature: boiling or heating food, pasteurisation of milk (heating to a controlled temperature to kill harmful microbes without spoiling the quality), sterilisation of medical instruments, and freezing food, which slows the microbes down to a minimum.
2. Covering food to stop vectors and airborne microbes from reaching it.
3. Antibiotics such as penicillin, ampicillin, amoxicillin and tetracycline are drugs that kill or stop the growth of many bacteria. They do not work on viruses.
4. Antiseptics such as Dettol, chlorine water, medicated soap and hydrogen peroxide kill microbes or stop them multiplying and are gentle enough to be used on skin.

5. Disinfectants are stronger than antiseptics and are used on floors, toilets and surfaces in hospitals, warehouses and public buildings. Examples are Izal and Lysol. Both antiseptics and disinfectants should be diluted as the label directs.
6. High salinity (salting): salt applied to meat and fish draws water out of the microbes by osmosis, so their cells shrink (plasmolysis) and die.
7. Dehydration (drying): microbes need water. Dried fish and meat do not support their growth.
8. Sanitation: keeping the body and the environment clean.
9. Isolation of infected persons, for example patients with tuberculosis or cholera, to stop the disease spreading.
10. A balanced diet every day helps the body to resist disease.
A bacteriostat stops the growth of bacteria; a bactericide kills bacteria. In the same way a fungistat stops fungi from growing and a fungicide kills them. A germicide kills germs in general.

sections.h: Vectors and how to control them
p: A vector is an animal that carries disease-causing organisms (pathogens) from one person to another.

Control of mosquitoes: drain swamps and stagnant water; clear bushes around houses; sleep under a mosquito net; spray rooms and swamps with insecticide; spray oil on water that cannot be drained (it blocks the breathing tubes of larvae and pupae); use insect repellent on the skin; take preventive drugs where advised; bury or cover broken pots and cans so they do not collect water.
Control of houseflies: spray with insecticide; destroy breeding places such as heaps of rubbish and dung; use poison baits; close or cover pit toilets; cover food; keep the environment clean.

units.title: Maintaining Good Health and the Roles of Health Organisations
units.summary: Refuse and sewage disposal, protecting water and food, and the work of the Ministry of Health, WHO, UNICEF, the Red Cross and UNESCO.

p: Refuse is the solid waste from homes and industries. Reckless dumping gives bad smells and gives breeding places to insects and rodents that spread diseases. Good ways to dispose of refuse: provide dustbins in good places; burn it in incinerators; dump it in an isolated area far from houses; bury it in a sanitary landfill. Recycling also reduces waste.

Sewage is waste water from kitchens, laundries, bathrooms and toilets, together with urine and faeces. It can be disposed of in pit latrines (deep pits for faeces and urine), in septic tanks (water flushes the waste into a large tank dug in the ground) or by a community treatment plant, where sewage from many homes is collected and treated before it is let into rivers or the sea.

Unclean water spreads cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea. Water can be protected and made safe by adding alum (which makes dirt settle), boiling before drinking, filtering after it cools, adding chlorine to kill germs, and storing it in clean covered containers.

Keep food in a refrigerator or deep freezer; cook food properly; inspect food sold to the public; wash hands before and after eating; preserve food by canning; keep the place where food is prepared clean; keep food away from flies and dust.

In Nigeria, health services are run through the Federal and State Ministries of Health and the University Teaching Hospitals. Countries also work together through international organisations to control disease and to give aid in the form of drugs, equipment and money.

Helps governments to strengthen health services; trains health workers; promotes co-operation among scientific bodies; helps to improve nutrition, sanitation, housing and working conditions; promotes mother and child health; publishes medical information; supplies drugs and vaccines in emergencies.

Gives emergency help to children in disease or famine areas; improves the feeding of undernourished children; cares for disabled children; immunises children against measles, whooping cough, polio and others; supplies clothing and other needs.
A humanitarian organisation. In war it cares for the wounded, gives emergency aid, helps to exchange prisoners, moves refugees and looks after the welfare of prisoners of war.

units.title: Habitat: Meaning, Types and the Marine Habitat
units.summary: What a habitat is, the three main types, the three kinds of aquatic habitat, and the characteristics of the marine (sea) habitat.

p: A habitat is the place where an organism (plant, micro-organism or animal) is naturally found. For example, the habitat of a tadpole is the bottom of a freshwater pond or stream.
There are three main types. Aquatic habitat: in or around water. Terrestrial habitat: on or in the land. Arboreal habitat: on trees.

There are three kinds of aquatic habitat. Marine (salt water) habitat: oceans and seas. Brackish (estuarine) water habitat, where fresh water and salt water mix: deltas, lagoons and bays. Fresh water habitat, with little or no salt: lakes, rivers, streams and ponds.
1. It is the largest habitat in the biosphere, covering about 70% of the earth's surface.
2. It is the most stable habitat. Temperature, pH and density do not change suddenly.
3. It contains many dissolved ions, including sodium (Na⁺), potassium (K⁺), magnesium (Mg²⁺), calcium (Ca²⁺), chloride (Cl⁻), iodide (I⁻), nitrate (NO₃⁻) and phosphate (PO₄³⁻).
4. Sea water is slightly alkaline. Its pH is about 8.0 near the surface. (The source notes say 8.0 to 9.0; the usual value is about 8.1.)
5. Salinity, the amount of dissolved salt, is high: about 35 parts per thousand.
6. Its density is higher than that of fresh water (about 1.028 compared with 1.0), so many organisms float easily.
7. The temperature of the sea changes more slowly than that of land, and it falls with depth.
8. Oxygen is highest at the surface where air dissolves in the water, and it decreases with depth.
9. Waves are movements of the surface water caused by wind. They mix the water and can wear away the shore.
10. Tides are the rise and fall of the sea surface at least twice a day, caused by the gravitational pull of the moon and the sun on the earth's water.

units.title: Zones of the Sea and Adaptations to Marine Life
units.summary: The horizontal and vertical zones of the sea, the organisms found in each, how plants and animals are adapted to marine life, and marine food chains.

p: The marine habitat consists of the shore and the open sea. From the shore outwards the zones are:
1. Splash (supratidal) zone: the area above the high-tide mark that is only wetted by splashes when waves break. It is exposed and often dry.
2. Intertidal zone: the shore between the high-tide and low-tide marks. It is covered by water at high tide and exposed at low tide. Temperature, salinity and moisture change greatly.
3. Subtidal (neritic) zone: always under water, over the continental shelf to about 200 m deep. There is plenty of sunlight and nutrients, so it holds the richest life in the sea.
4. Oceanic (open sea) zone: the deep water beyond the continental shelf.

On the sea floor, the benthic zone is the bottom. In the deep ocean (the abyssal zone, about 4000 to 6000 m) and in deep trenches (the hadal zone, below about 6000 m) there is no light and no photosynthesis. Producers are absent, so food is made mainly by chemosynthesis near vents and the animals depend on food that sinks from above.
Euphotic zone: the top layer, in direct sunlight (about 0 to 200 m). Producers, consumers and decomposers all live here and photosynthesis takes place.
Disphotic zone: the middle layer with dim light (about 200 to 1000 m). There is too little light for photosynthesis, so only consumers and decomposers live here.
Aphotic zone: the deep, cold, dark water and sea floor with no light and few living things.

img.alt: A cross-section of the sea from the shore with splash, intertidal and subtidal zones, then the oceanic zone, with euphotic, disphotic and aphotic layers by depth
img.cap: The zones of the marine habitat.

p: The source notes join several names in a confusing way (for example 'intertidal or neritic' and 'subtidal or littoral'). In standard biology the intertidal (littoral) zone is the shore between the tide marks, and the neritic zone is the shallow sea over the continental shelf. Learn the zones in the order shown in the diagram.

Splash zone: periwinkles, ghost crabs, seaweeds. Intertidal zone: starfish, sea anemones, sponges, sea urchins, annelid worms, molluscs and barnacles. Subtidal zone: snails, crabs, lobsters and crayfish. Neritic water: plankton (tiny floating organisms such as diatoms, algae, protozoa and small crustaceans) and nekton (strong swimmers such as fish, prawns and whales). Oceanic water: sharks, croaker, mackerel, bonga fish and many more. Benthic zone: only a few scavengers and saprophytes.
Barnacles have a protective shell that stops drying out (desiccation) and holds water, and they attach firmly to rocks. They feed with their cirri (feathery limbs).

Fishes: cartilaginous fish such as sharks keep urea in their blood so that their body fluids are as salty as the sea; bony fish such as tilapia have salt-secreting cells in the gills to keep their salt balance (osmoregulation). Fins give movement and balance; gills are for breathing.
Starfish have tube feet for holding on to rocks and moving.

Whales have fins for stability, a thick layer of fat (blubber) for insulation and food storage, and blowholes for breathing air. (The source notes say whales have 'an organ in front of the nostril' for sensing pressure.)

Shrimps have strong claws for holding food. Periwinkles have a foot for attaching to rocks and a shell. (The notes say periwinkles have lungs; marine periwinkles breathe with gills.) Crabs burrow into mud to hide from predators and strong waves.

Seaweeds have a holdfast for attaching to rocks, a slimy (mucilaginous) coating that prevents drying, and air bladders or divided fronds for floating. Algae such as Sargassum have chlorophyll for photosynthesis and small size or large surface area for floating. Plankton such as diatoms are tiny and have air spaces or oil droplets to keep them afloat.
Diatom → crab → tilapia. Diatom → zooplankton → tilapia → shark.

units.title: The Estuarine (Brackish Water) Habitat
units.summary: What an estuary is, its characteristics, its plants and animals and how they are adapted, and food chains in estuaries.

p: An estuary is a body of water formed at the coast where fresh water flowing towards the sea mixes with sea water coming inland. It is a brackish water habitat. Examples are deltas, lagoons and bays, such as the Lagos Lagoon and the Niger Delta.
1. The salinity changes with the tides and with the season (it falls in the rainy season and rises in the dry season).
2. The density of the water is less than that of sea water.
3. The water is turbid (muddy) because it is often disturbed, so light penetration, photosynthesis and respiration by organisms are reduced.
4. The water is shallow.
5. There are fewer kinds of species than in the sea.
6. It has a high level of nutrients carried down by rivers.
7. Oxygen in the mud is low, so anaerobic activities are common.
Plants found in estuaries include plankton (diatoms), algae, red mangrove and white mangrove.
Plankton such as diatoms have air spaces in their cells for buoyancy. Algae have chlorophyll for photosynthesis and a small size or large surface area for floating.

Red mangrove has stilt roots that support the plant in soft mud and stop the tide from washing it away. Its roots have air spaces that carry air to the root tissues. Its seeds germinate while still on the parent plant (this is called vivipary), so the young seedlings drop into the mud and are not carried away by the water.
White mangrove has pneumatophores (breathing roots) that stick up out of the mud for gaseous exchange.

Mosquito larvae and pupae have breathing tubes (siphons or 'trumpets') that reach up to the surface. Crustaceans and water snails burrow into the mud to hide from predators, strong waves and tides. Worms have a tough, waterproof covering against changes in salinity. Mudskippers have strong fins for crawling on mud and swimming in water, and can breathe air through their skin. Fishes have fins for swimming and a swim bladder for buoyancy.
Detritus (dead organic matter) → worms → snails → birds. Diatoms → shrimps → fishes. Diatoms → small fish → sharks → man.

units.title: The Fresh Water Habitat
units.summary: Lotic and lentic fresh waters, their characteristics, the plants and animals and their adaptations, and fresh water food chains.

sections.h: What is a fresh water habitat?
p: A fresh water habitat is a body of water that comes mainly from inland sources and contains very little or no salt. There are two types, based on movement.
Lotic fresh waters are running waters that flow in one direction: rivers, streams and springs.
Lentic fresh waters are still (stagnant) waters that do not flow: lakes, ponds, puddles, swamps and dams.
1. It contains little or no salt (salinity about 0.5 parts per thousand; the source notes say 5 parts per thousand, or 0.5%, which is too high).
2. It is small compared with the sea.
3. It is rich in oxygen, especially near the surface and where water is moving.
4. It is often shallow, so sunlight reaches the bottom.
5. The temperature changes with the seasons and with depth.
6. There are seasonal changes: the water level falls or the pond dries up in the dry season and rises in the rainy season.
7. Currents affect the distribution of organisms, salts and gases, especially in rivers and streams.

Water lily has air spaces (air bladders) in its stalks and leaves, and broad, flat, light leaves that keep it afloat. Spirogyra has a slimy (mucilaginous) covering that protects it. Water lettuce has hairs on its leaves that trap air to keep it afloat. Elodea (a water weed) has long, flexible stems and leaves that sway with the water current.

Protozoa such as Amoeba and Paramecium have a contractile vacuole that pumps out the water that enters by osmosis (osmoregulation). Ducks have webbed feet for swimming and a flat (serrated) beak for sieving food from water. Hydra has a sticky base (or adhesive disc) and tentacles with stinging cells for attaching and catching food. Pond skaters have long legs that spread their weight so they can skate on the surface. Fishes have gills for breathing, fins for swimming and swim bladders for buoyancy.
Diatoms → fish fry → tilapia. Spirogyra → tadpole → carp → kingfish. Algae → mosquito larva → small fish.

units.title: Terrestrial Habitats: Marsh and Forest
units.summary: The four terrestrial habitats, the formation, characteristics and organisms of a marsh, and the rain forest: characteristics, plants, animals and food chains.

p: Terrestrial organisms live on and under the ground. There are four main terrestrial habitats: marsh, forest, grassland (savanna) and arid land (desert).

A marsh is low-lying land that is flooded in the rainy season and is usually waterlogged because of poor drainage. Grasses and shrubs are the main vegetation. When trees grow in it, it is called a swamp. A marsh is a transition between aquatic and terrestrial habitats.

Formation: marshes develop when water overflows river banks onto low coastal land or flood plains, helped by heavy rain. They also form when ponds and lakes slowly fill up with soil and plant remains, so the process is gradual. Marshes may be fresh water marshes or salt water marshes.
Characteristics: it is low land; it is wet, flooded and waterlogged; it may have pools of standing water; relative humidity is high; the water contains much decaying matter and often smells foul.

Organisms: plants include algae, grasses, water lettuce, water lilies, red and white mangrove and raffia palms. Animals include mangrove crabs, hermit crabs, mudskippers, fishes, frogs, snakes, crocodiles and some mammals.

Adaptations: organisms must tolerate the salt in soil or water in salt marshes, and the low oxygen in the soil or water. Plants of fresh water marshes have adaptations like those of fresh water plants. Saprophytic bacteria must live without oxygen (anaerobically).
Food chains: flowering plants → insects → frogs → crocodiles. Humus → earthworms → frogs → snakes.

A forest is a community of plants in which trees are the dominant plants. The kinds of forest depend mainly on temperature, rainfall, soil and human activities such as farming, logging, bush burning, road building and house building. The main type in southern Nigeria is the tropical rain forest.

Characteristics of a rain forest: it is rich in climbers and epiphytes; the inside is humid and damp with little light; the trees are tall and form layers (stratification) with a thick canopy; the trees are mesophytes with broad leaves; the trees have buttress roots to support their great weight and height; the barks are thin.

Forest plants include African walnut, mahogany, teak, obeche, iroko, oil palm, ferns, mosses and liverworts, orchids (epiphytes), fungi and mistletoe. Adaptations: strong tap roots and buttress roots; tall, unbranched trunks that reach for light; broad leaves to catch the little light that gets through; epiphytes have aerial roots that absorb moisture from the air while growing on the branches of trees; mistletoe is a partial parasite whose roots penetrate the stem of its host to take water and food from it.

Most forest animals are arboreal: bats, monkeys, squirrels, birds, snakes, tree frogs and chameleons. Some live in the soil (earthworms, beetles) and some in the leaf litter (millipedes, ants, snails). Adaptations: monkeys have long limbs and prehensile tails for climbing and jumping; bats have wings for flight; green snakes have colours that match leaves (camouflage); the chameleon has a prehensile tail, grasping digits and camouflage; apes live in groups for safety and have keen sight; earthworms and snails have moist skin or shells that reduce water loss; birds have strong wings.
Green plants → grasshopper → toad → hawk. Green plants → monkey → leopard. (The source notes give 'lion' as the predator of monkeys. Leopards, not lions, live in the forest.)

units.title: Grassland (Savanna)
units.summary: The meaning and characteristics of grassland, the types of savanna in Nigeria, and the plants and animals of the savanna with their adaptations and food chains.

p: Grassland (savanna) is a plant community in which grasses are the dominant plants, though trees and shrubs may be present.
1. The temperature is high and the sunshine is strong.
2. The relative humidity is low and rainfall is moderate to low (about 60 to 150 cm a year, in one season).
3. There is plenty of grass with a few short trees spread out here and there.
4. Bush fires are common, and the trees are fire-resistant.
5. Many plants are deciduous: they shed their leaves in the dry season.
6. Plants have underground stems and deep roots to find water.
7. Trees have small or modified leaves to cut down water loss.
There are four major types, from south to north: Southern Guinea savanna, Northern Guinea savanna, Sudan savanna and Sahel savanna. The Guinea savanna is the largest vegetation zone in Nigeria.

Plants include acacia, elephant grass, guinea grass, spear grass, palms and baobab trees. Adaptations: thick, corky bark that resists fire; grasses with underground stems that survive fire and drought; leaves with a waxy surface (thick cuticle) that cut down water loss; small or curled leaves that reduce transpiration; leaves that fall in the dry season (deciduous); the baobab has thick, spongy trunk that stores water.

Animals include antelopes, elephants, giraffes, zebras, goats, cattle, grasshoppers, lizards, birds, lions, leopards, rats, snakes and grasscutters. (The source notes also list tigers and kangaroos; tigers live in Asia and kangaroos in Australia, not in the Nigerian savanna.) Adaptations: termites build mounds that keep their nests cool; rats and other small animals burrow to escape the heat and fires; zebras and giraffes have patterned coats that make them hard to see in tall grass; lions and leopards have powerful claws and teeth for hunting; elephants, zebras and antelopes move in herds for safety in numbers; many grazers are fast runners with long legs.

units.title: Arid Land (Desert)
units.summary: The meaning and types of desert, its characteristics, and how its plants and animals are adapted, with food chains.

p: Arid lands (deserts) have very low rainfall (less than about 25 cm a year) and a high rate of evaporation. They are the driest habitats. There are hot deserts, such as the Sahara in North Africa and the Kalahari in southern Africa, and cold deserts, such as parts of Asia and North America.
1. Water is very scarce.
2. The temperature is very high by day and very low at night.
3. The vegetation is very thin and scattered.
4. The soil is sandy or rocky and has little humus.
5. Strong winds blow often and the sunshine is very strong.
6. The plants are drought-resistant (xerophytes).

Desert plants include thorny bushes, cacti, dwarf acacia, date palm, wiry grasses, baobab and euphorbia. Adaptations: small or thin leaves, or leaves reduced to spines, which cut down transpiration; fleshy (succulent) stems that store water, as in cactus; deep roots that reach underground water, as in acacia; a thick waxy cuticle and sunken pores (stomata); narrow, slender leaves in wiry grasses; many seeds that stay dormant in the soil until it rains.

Animals include camels, rodents, lizards, snakes, desert tortoises, grasshoppers, wasps, ants and scorpions. Adaptations: most produce very dry droppings and concentrated urine to save water; rats and other small animals stay in burrows by day and come out at night; reptiles have dry scaly skin that reduces water loss; the camel can go many days without drinking, stores fat in its hump, and can tolerate a rise in body temperature; broad padded feet stop it sinking in sand; locusts and insects have waterproof cuticles. (The source notes list zebras as desert animals; zebras live in savanna.)
Plants → desert rat → snake. Plants → ants → scorpion → snake.

units.title: Reproduction: Meaning and Types of Asexual Reproduction
units.summary: What reproduction is, asexual and sexual reproduction, and the types of asexual reproduction: binary fission, budding, spore formation, fragmentation, vegetative propagation, parthenogenesis and schizogony.

p: Reproduction is the process by which living organisms produce new individuals (offspring) of their own kind. It keeps a species from dying out.

Asexual reproduction: one parent produces offspring without gametes (sex cells) and without the joining of nuclei. The offspring are clones: they are genetically identical to the parent. It is common in single-celled organisms, in flowering plants and in organisms that can reproduce both ways depending on conditions such as food and environment.
Sexual reproduction: offspring are produced by the joining (fusion) of two different sex cells, usually from two different parents. The offspring differ from their parents and from each other.

Binary fission: the parent divides by mitosis into two (or more) parts, each able to live alone. It occurs in bacteria and in protists such as Amoeba and Paramecium. Division into many parts is called multiple fission.
Budding: the offspring grows as an outgrowth (bud) of the parent and later breaks off to live on its own. It occurs in Hydra, yeast and corals. Some sponges form internal buds.
Spore formation: spores are tiny, light cells produced in large numbers and spread by wind. They are produced by fungi (Mucor, Rhizopus), mosses, ferns, algae, some protists and some bacteria.
Fragmentation: a part of the organism breaks off and grows into a new one. It occurs in Spirogyra, some algae, planarians and sponges.
Vegetative propagation: in higher plants a new plant grows from part of the old plant other than the seed, such as a stem, root or leaf (for example, yam tubers, cassava stems, sweet potato).
Parthenogenesis: an embryo develops from an unfertilised egg cell. It occurs in aphids, honey bees, ants, wasps, and some fish, amphibians and reptiles. (The source notes spell it 'patogenesis'.)

Schizogony: a form of multiple fission in which a parasite divides many times inside its host. The malaria parasite Plasmodium multiplies in this way in the liver and red blood cells, giving merozoites.

units.title: Reproduction in Amoeba, Paramecium and Spirogyra
units.summary: Binary and multiple fission in amoeba, fission and conjugation in paramecium, and fragmentation and conjugation in spirogyra.

p: Amoeba reproduces asexually by binary fission and, in bad conditions, by multiple fission (sporulation).
Binary fission: when an amoeba has grown to full size it stops moving. The nucleus divides first by mitosis, then the cytoplasm divides, giving two daughter amoebae.

Multiple fission: in bad conditions the amoeba becomes round and makes a hard cover (a cyst) around itself. Inside the cyst, the nucleus divides many times. When conditions improve the cyst bursts, and each nucleus, with a bit of cytoplasm, becomes a small new amoeba.

img.alt: Four stages of binary fission in an amoeba: parent cell, nucleus dividing, cytoplasm dividing, two daughter cells
img.cap: Binary fission in amoeba.

p: Paramecium reproduces asexually by binary fission and sexually by conjugation.

Binary fission: in good conditions the micronucleus divides by mitosis, the macronucleus (the 'meganucleus' in the source notes) lengthens and splits, and the cell constricts across the middle into two new paramecia.

Conjugation: two paramecia of different strains come together and join at their oral grooves. In each one the micronucleus divides twice by meiosis to give four nuclei, and three of them break down. The remaining nucleus divides once more into a migratory nucleus and a stationary nucleus. The migratory nuclei are exchanged through the joined cells. Each migratory nucleus then fuses with the stationary nucleus of its partner to form a new (zygote) nucleus. The two paramecia separate. In each, the new nucleus divides three times to give eight nuclei; four become macronuclei and four become micronuclei. The cell then divides to give four young paramecia, each with one macronucleus and one micronucleus. Conjugation exchanges genetic material, so it adds variety.
Spirogyra is a green alga that forms long, thread-like filaments. It reproduces asexually by fragmentation and sexually by conjugation.
Fragmentation: when a filament has grown long, parts break away and each grows into a new filament.

Conjugation: (1) two filaments lie side by side and cells grow tubes towards each other, forming conjugation tubes; (2) the contents of cells in one filament act as the male gamete and the cells of the other filament as the female; (3) the male gamete passes through the tube and fuses with the female gamete to form a zygote; (4) the zygote forms a thick, resistant wall and is called a zygospore; (5) after a resting period, in good conditions, the wall bursts and a new filament grows.

img.cap: Conjugation in spirogyra: tubes form, the male gamete passes across, and zygospores are formed.

units.title: Reproduction in the Earthworm and the Cockroach
units.summary: How earthworms copulate and produce cocoons, and how cockroaches mate, lay egg cases and develop by incomplete metamorphosis.

p: Earthworms are hermaphrodites: each worm has both male and female sex organs and makes both male and female gametes. Reproduction is sexual. Each worm gives sperm to the other (cross-fertilisation).

Copulation: two worms come together at night outside their burrows and lie with their ventral (under) surfaces touching, facing opposite ways. The reproductive organs are near the front of the body. The segments carrying the male openings (about segments 9 to 15 in the notes) of one worm lie against the clitellum (the thick, smooth band, about segments 32 to 37 in the notes) of the other. The worms are held together by their bristles (chaetae) and by mucus. Sperm pass from one worm to the other and are stored.

After copulation the worms separate. The clitellum makes a ring of mucus (a cocoon) which slides forward over the body, picking up eggs and then the stored sperm so that fertilisation takes place inside the cocoon. The cocoon slips off the head and closes at both ends. The embryos develop inside the cocoon, and young worms hatch out. Only one or a few worms hatch from each cocoon.

Cockroaches reproduce sexually and fertilisation is internal. The male and female mate and the male puts sperm into the female's genital opening. The sperms are stored in a sperm pouch until the eggs are released from the two ovaries; they are fertilised as they come out.

The eggs (about 10 to 16) are laid in a hard, horny egg case called an ootheca, which the female carries at the end of her abdomen for some time and then drops in a safe, dark place. After 30 to 100 days the eggs hatch into nymphs. Nymphs are small, wingless and whitish, and look like small adults.

The nymphs feed and grow and turn brown. They moult (shed their skin) about 13 times. At each moult they get bigger, and wings first show as wing pads and then grow into full wings in the adult (the imago). It takes about 11 to 20 months from egg to adult. The change from egg to adult has no pupa stage, so this is incomplete metamorphosis (gradual change).

units.title: Reproduction in the Housefly and the Snail
units.summary: The life cycle of the housefly (complete metamorphosis) and reproduction in land snails, including torsion.

p: The adult male and female mate and, within two to three days, the female lays fertilised eggs, by day, in moist, dirty places such as rubbish and dung. A female lays 2 to 7 batches of about 100 to 150 eggs. The housefly has complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult.
Egg: the eggs hatch into larvae in about 8 to 24 hours.

Larva (maggot): a white, legless, segmented body with a pointed head that bears a pair of hooks for tearing food and pulling the maggot along. Spiny pads on the underside help it to move, and it breathes through two pairs of spiracles. It feeds, grows and moults several times over about 5 to 14 days, then crawls to a dry place.

Pupa: the maggot shortens and its skin hardens and turns brown, forming a case called the puparium. The pupa does not feed or move. Inside, the body is rebuilt into the adult form. This takes about 3 to 10 days.
Adult (imago): the adult breaks out of the puparium by blowing up a bladder-like sac on its head (the ptilinum). It crawls to the surface of the rubbish and flies away when its wings have dried.

img.alt: Life cycles of the housefly (egg, larva, pupa, adult) and the cockroach (egg case, nymph, adult)
img.cap: Complete metamorphosis in the housefly, compared with the incomplete metamorphosis of the cockroach (Unit 15).

p: Houseflies feed on rubbish and faeces and then land on our food. They carry the microbes of cholera, typhoid, dysentery and polio on their legs and bodies, and in their droppings and vomit. This is why we cover food and keep refuse and toilets clean.

Land snails are hermaphrodites, and fertilisation is internal. Two snails mate and exchange sperm packets (spermatophores). Sperm are passed into the partner's body, are stored and travel to the place where fertilisation takes place. (The source notes name several parts of the sperm duct such as the epiphallus and the bursa duct.) The fertilised eggs are laid in a hole in damp soil.

During the development of a snail, the visceral mass (the soft body part holding the organs) twists through 180°. This brings the anus and the mantle cavity forward to a place above the head. This twisting is called torsion.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 Financial Accounting First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Every business, from a roadside provision store to a big company, must know how much money it has, how much it owes, and whether it is making a profit. Financial Accounting is the subject that teaches you how to record, sort and report this information so that owners, banks, the tax office and workers can all trust it.

In First Term you learn what book-keeping and accounting are, the rules of behaviour (ethics) every accountant follows, the double entry system that is the heart of accounting, how to write ledger accounts and journals, the basic ideas (concepts) behind all accounts, and how to keep an analytical cash book.

Read each unit slowly. Accounting is learned by doing: copy every worked example in your notebook and then try the practice work yourself. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

units.title: Book-keeping and Accounting: Meanings and Differences
units.summary: What book-keeping is, what accounting is, examples of each, and four or more differences between them.

p: Book-keeping is the process of recording financial transactions in a systematic and time-order (chronological) way in the books of account. A transaction is any exchange that has a money value, such as buying goods, selling goods or paying rent.
Features of book-keeping: it deals with recording only; the work is routine and repeated; it is clerical in nature; it does not need special professional skills; it is concerned with HOW to record.
Examples of book-keeping activities: recording sales in the sales book; recording purchases in the purchases book; posting entries to the ledger; keeping the cash book; filing vouchers and invoices.

Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording and communicating financial information so that the people who use it can make informed judgments and decisions. It includes book-keeping and goes further: it summarises, analyses and interprets the records.
Features of accounting: it includes book-keeping plus analysis and interpretation; it needs professional judgment; it is concerned with WHY and WHAT DOES IT MEAN.
Examples of accounting activities: preparing financial statements; analysing profitability; calculating ratios; giving financial advice; auditing accounts (checking that accounts are true and fair).

units.title: Importance of Accounting
units.summary: Ten reasons why accounting matters to owners, managers, banks, the government and the law.

p: A business owner may say, 'I do not need accounting; I know how much money I have.' That thinking is wrong, because money in the pocket does not show what is owed, what is owned, or whether the business earned a profit. Accounting is important for these reasons.
1. Keeping systematic records: all transactions are recorded properly, past records are easy to find and information is not lost.
2. Measuring profit or loss: it shows whether the business is making a profit and whether it is worth continuing.
3. Showing the financial position: it shows what the business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and what the owner has put in (capital), which shows the net worth.
4. Helping decision making: it gives information for planning and for choosing between alternatives, such as whether to buy a van or hire one.
5. Comparison: this year can be compared with earlier years and with other businesses, so trends can be seen.
6. Meeting legal requirements: companies must keep accounts by law, the tax authorities need them, and regulators require them.
7. Control: it helps to detect errors and fraud, prevents theft of money and goods, and makes people accountable.
8. Evidence in court: properly kept records can be used as evidence in disputes and legal cases.
9. Valuing the business: records help to decide the worth of a business for sale, or when a partner joins or leaves.
10. Getting loans: banks ask for financial statements to see whether a business can repay.

Users include the owner, managers, workers, banks and other lenders, suppliers (who may sell on credit), customers, the Federal Inland Revenue Service and state tax bodies, and investors. Each wants different information from the same accounts.

units.title: Ethics of Accounting: Professional Conduct
units.summary: What accounting ethics are, why they matter, and the five principles of professional conduct with examples.

p: Accounting ethics are the moral principles and standards that guide the behaviour of accountants and make sure that financial reports are honest. In Nigeria, professional accountants belong to bodies such as the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria (ICAN) and the Association of National Accountants of Nigeria (ANAN), which set the rules.

Why ethics matter: they keep public trust; they protect the good name of the profession; they protect the interests of everyone who uses the accounts; they make financial information accurate; and they prevent fraud and the changing of figures to deceive people.
Professional conduct means the standard of behaviour expected from accounting professionals. The main principles are these.
1. Integrity: being honest and straightforward, not falsifying records, and admitting mistakes. Example: not increasing profit figures just to please the owner.
2. Objectivity: being fair and unbiased, not favouring any party, and letting facts guide decisions. Example: an auditor who does not favour a friend's company.
3. Professional competence: keeping knowledge and skills up to date and doing work properly. Example: attending training on new tax laws.
4. Professional behaviour: obeying laws and rules and avoiding actions that bring the profession into disrepute. Example: refusing to take part in tax evasion.
5. Due care: working carefully and diligently, meeting deadlines and checking one's work. Example: reviewing financial statements thoroughly before signing.

Professional bodies usually list five fundamental principles: integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care (written together as one), confidentiality, and professional behaviour. Your notes treat confidentiality separately (next unit) and split competence and due care into two. Both ways of grouping teach the same ideas.

units.title: Confidentiality, Transparency, Integrity and Ethical Dilemmas
units.summary: Keeping client information private, being open in reporting, having strong moral principles, and solving common ethical problems.

p: Confidentiality means keeping client information private and not telling it to anyone without proper authority.
Do not disclose: the client's financial information, business secrets, personal details or trade information.

When disclosure is allowed: when the law requires it (for example a court order); when the client gives permission; to professional regulatory bodies; and when it is needed to protect the public interest.

Good examples: not discussing a client's profits with friends; not giving a client list to competitors; keeping salary information private. Bad examples: telling others about a company's money problems; using client information for personal gain.
Breaking confidentiality can lead to loss of licence, legal action, damage to reputation, loss of clients, and fines.

Transparency means being open, honest and clear in all financial reporting. It needs full disclosure (reporting all important information and explaining the accounting policies used), clarity (clear, understandable presentation that does not mislead) and accuracy (correct figures that show the true position).

Examples of transparency: disclosing all liabilities, not just some; explaining unusual transactions; reporting losses honestly. Examples of the opposite: hiding bad debts; creating false invoices; leaving out large expenses.
Benefits: it builds trust, helps better investment decisions, prevents fraud, improves the reputation of the company and supports good governance.

Integrity means being honest and having strong moral principles in all professional dealings. Its parts are: honesty (telling the truth); ethical behaviour (doing what is right, not just what is legal); consistency (keeping the same standard for everyone); and moral courage (standing up for what is right and speaking out against wrong).

Threats to integrity: pressure from management, personal gain, fear of losing a job or client, lack of knowledge and a weak ethical culture. How to protect integrity: know the professional standards; ask for guidance when unsure; write down your decisions; report unethical behaviour; and put the public interest first.

units.title: Double Entry: Meaning and Types of Accounts
units.summary: The double entry system, why every debit has a credit, and the three types of account: personal, real and nominal.

p: The double entry system is a method of recording transactions in which every transaction affects at least two accounts: one account is debited and another is credited, with equal amounts. The rule is: for every debit there must be a corresponding credit.

The method was described in 1494 by the Italian monk Luca Pacioli, who is often called the 'Father of Accounting'. (He wrote down the method that merchants in Venice were already using; he did not invent it.)
Example: goods bought for cash, ₦5,000. Purchases account is debited ₦5,000 (goods come in) and Cash account is credited ₦5,000 (cash goes out).

Benefits: a complete record of transactions; errors can be found (if debits do not equal credits); it shows cause and effect; it allows a trial balance to be prepared; and it gives a check on accuracy.
Personal accounts are accounts of persons: individuals, firms and companies. Examples: John's account, ABC Limited account, creditors and debtors. Rule: debit the receiver, credit the giver.
Real accounts are accounts of assets and property. Examples: land, building, furniture, machinery, stock (goods in hand). Rule: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.

Nominal accounts are accounts of expenses, losses, incomes and gains. Expenses and losses include salaries, rent, electricity and bad debts. Incomes and gains include sales, commission received, interest received and discount received. Rule: debit all expenses and losses; credit all incomes and gains.

units.title: Golden Rules, Debit and Credit, and Simple Entries
units.summary: The golden rules of accounting, which side increases each type of account, the accounting equation and five worked entries.

p: Study the table.

A memory aid: for personal accounts, debit the receiver and credit the giver. For real accounts, debit what comes in and credit what goes out. For nominal accounts, debit expenses and losses and credit incomes and gains.

Debit (Dr) is the left side of an account. It increases assets, expenses and losses, and it decreases liabilities, capital and income. Credit (Cr) is the right side. It increases liabilities, capital and income, and it decreases assets, expenses and losses.
The accounting equation is: Assets = Capital + Liabilities. It must always balance. The diagram shows the effect of debit and credit on each part.

p: Example 1: Started business with cash ₦50,000. Cash (an asset) comes in, so debit Cash ₦50,000. The owner has put in capital, so credit Capital ₦50,000.
Example 2: Bought goods for cash ₦10,000. Purchases are an expense, so debit Purchases ₦10,000. Cash goes out, so credit Cash ₦10,000.
Example 3: Sold goods for cash ₦15,000. Cash comes in, so debit Cash ₦15,000. Sales are income, so credit Sales ₦15,000.
Example 4: Bought furniture from ABC Ltd on credit ₦20,000. Furniture comes in, so debit Furniture ₦20,000. ABC Ltd is the giver, so credit ABC Ltd ₦20,000.
Example 5: Paid salary ₦5,000 in cash. Salary is an expense, so debit Salary ₦5,000. Cash goes out, so credit Cash ₦5,000.

units.title: Ledger Accounts in T Format
units.summary: What a ledger is, the T-account layout, and the five steps for recording transactions in the ledger.

p: The ledger is the book that contains all the accounts of a business. Each account has its own page (or its own T). Entries are first written in the books of original entry (journals and the cash book) and are then posted (copied) into the ledger accounts.

A T-account looks like the letter T. The name of the account is written at the top. The left side is the debit (Dr) side and the right side is the credit (Cr) side. Each side has columns for the date, the details (the name of the other account involved) and the amount in naira (₦).

img.alt: A cash account drawn in T format with debit side on the left and credit side on the right, showing entries, balance c/d, totals and balance b/d

units.title: Balancing Accounts: A Worked Example
units.summary: How to balance a ledger account (c/d and b/d), which accounts have debit and credit balances, and a complete worked exercise.

p: 1. Add up both sides (debit and credit) separately. 2. Find the difference. 3. Write the difference on the side with the smaller total as 'Balance c/d' (carried down). 4. Now both sides add up to the same total; write the total on both sides at the same level. 5. Draw a double line under the totals to show that the account is closed. 6. Bring the balance down on the opposite side as 'Balance b/d' (brought down) to start the next period.

Rules: assets and expenses normally have debit balances. Liabilities, capital and income normally have credit balances. If the debit side is bigger, the balance is a debit balance; if the credit side is bigger, it is a credit balance.

Record these transactions in ledger accounts and balance them. 1 Mar: started business with ₦200,000 cash. 5 Mar: bought goods for cash ₦80,000. 8 Mar: sold goods for cash ₦100,000. 12 Mar: paid rent ₦10,000. 15 Mar: bought equipment from Ade on credit ₦50,000. 18 Mar: received a bank loan ₦150,000. 22 Mar: paid Ade ₦30,000. 25 Mar: paid electricity ₦5,000. 28 Mar: sold goods for cash ₦75,000. 31 Mar: paid salaries ₦20,000.

Cash account: the debits are capital ₦200,000, sales ₦100,000, loan ₦150,000 and sales ₦75,000, which add up to ₦525,000. The credits are purchases ₦80,000, rent ₦10,000, Ade ₦30,000, electricity ₦5,000 and salaries ₦20,000, which add up to ₦145,000. The difference is ₦380,000, the closing balance.
Ade's account: the equipment of ₦50,000 was bought on credit, so Ade is credited ₦50,000. The ₦30,000 payment is a debit. The balance still owed is ₦20,000, a credit balance (we owe Ade).

Balances of the other accounts: Capital ₦200,000 credit; Purchases ₦80,000 debit; Sales ₦175,000 credit; Rent ₦10,000 debit; Equipment ₦50,000 debit; Bank loan ₦150,000 credit; Electricity ₦5,000 debit; Salaries ₦20,000 debit; Ade ₦20,000 credit.

Add the debit balances: cash 380,000 + purchases 80,000 + rent 10,000 + equipment 50,000 + electricity 5,000 + salaries 20,000 = ₦545,000. Add the credit balances: capital 200,000 + sales 175,000 + loan 150,000 + Ade 20,000 = ₦545,000. They agree, which shows that the double entry is correct. A list like this is called a trial balance, which you will meet in Second Term.

units.title: Accounting Concepts: Meaning and the Going Concern Concept
units.summary: What accounting concepts are, why we need them, and the going concern concept with its effect on assets, expenses and liabilities.

p: Accounting concepts are the basic assumptions, rules and principles that guide how financial information is recorded and presented. They are also called accounting assumptions or accounting principles.
Purpose: to make accounting uniform; to make accounts comparable; to make financial statements reliable; to guide accountants when they must decide; and to give a framework for accounting practice.
The going concern concept assumes that the business will continue to operate for the foreseeable future and has no plan to close down or to cut down its activities greatly.

Effect on assets: assets are recorded at cost, not at selling price; depreciation is worked out over the useful life of the asset; there is no need to value assets as if the business were being sold. Example: a machine bought for ₦100,000 is recorded at ₦100,000, not at what it could be sold for today.

Effect on revenue and expenses: they are matched over accounting periods and the long-term view is taken; prepayments and accruals are recognised. Example: rent paid for three years in advance is spread over the three years.

Effect on liabilities: long-term liabilities are treated as long term, and the business does not have to pay all its debts at once. Example: a ten-year loan is not shown as a current (short-term) liability.

sections.h: When going concern does NOT apply
p: The concept does not apply when the business is bankrupt, is closing down, is being liquidated (wound up) or is in severe financial difficulty. Then assets are valued at their break-up value, which is what they can be sold for.

ABC Company bought equipment for ₦500,000 with a life of 5 years. If going concern applies, the equipment is recorded at ₦500,000, depreciation is ₦100,000 a year (₦500,000 ÷ 5) and the balance sheet shows a falling value year by year. If the company is closing down and the equipment can be sold for only ₦200,000, the equipment is valued at ₦200,000 and an immediate loss of ₦300,000 is shown.
