units.title: Accrual and Materiality Concepts
units.summary: Matching revenue and expenses to the right period, prepayments and accruals, cash basis compared with accrual basis, and the materiality concept.

p: The accrual concept says that revenue and expenses must be recognised when they are earned or incurred, not when cash is received or paid. It is also called the matching concept: expenses are matched with the revenue they help to earn in the same period.
Revenue is recognised when goods are delivered or services are done, not necessarily when payment is received. Example: goods sold in December and paid for in January are recorded as a December sale.
An expense is recognised when it is incurred, in the period in which the benefit is received. Example: electricity used in December but paid for in January is a December expense.
A prepayment is a payment made in advance. It is treated as an asset until the period it covers. Example: ₦12,000 rent paid in January for one year gives ₦1,000 of expense each month.
An accrual is an expense that has been incurred but is not yet paid. It is shown as a liability. Example: December salaries paid in January belong to December's accounts.

On the cash basis, we record only when cash changes hands. On the accrual basis, we record when the amount is earned or incurred. The accrual basis gives a truer profit, an accurate financial position, comparable periods and better decisions.
Worked example, December 2023. Sales ₦300,000 (₦200,000 cash and ₦100,000 on credit). Expenses ₦150,000 (₦100,000 paid and ₦50,000 still owing).

The materiality concept says that only items big enough to affect decisions need to be shown separately. Small, unimportant items can be grouped together or treated simply. Do not waste time on trivial things; focus on what matters.

Whether an item is material depends on its size (compared with profit or total assets), its nature, and the business. A guide: an item is usually material if leaving it out or showing it wrongly would change a user's decision, or if it is more than about 5 to 10 per cent of profit. Some items are material whatever the size, such as fraud.

Material items: a ₦1,000,000 expense in a small business; any fraud; a large bad debt; a major lawsuit; a change in accounting policy. Immaterial items: a ₦500 expense in a large company; small office supplies; minor repairs; a tiny petty cash shortage.

Examples: a ₦1,000 stapler is recorded as an expense, not as an asset, because it is not worth depreciating over five years. A ₦2,000,000 delivery van is an asset and is depreciated. A company with an annual profit of ₦10,000,000 has stationery of ₦5,000 (0.05% of profit, immaterial) and a bad debt of ₦800,000 (8% of profit, material and should be shown separately).

units.title: Consistency and Dual Aspect Concepts
units.summary: Using the same methods year after year, when methods may change, and the dual aspect concept with the accounting equation.

p: Once an accounting method has been chosen, it should be used in the same way from one period to the next unless there is a good reason to change. Purpose: to make accounts comparable over time; to stop people from manipulating profits; to keep the accounts reliable; and to allow trends to be studied.

Areas that need consistency: the depreciation method (if vans are depreciated by the straight-line method, keep doing so); stock valuation (if you use FIFO, first in first out, keep using it); and other policies such as how revenue is recognised, the percentage for bad debts and what is treated as an asset.

Acceptable reasons to change: a change in accounting standards; a new method that gives a fairer picture; a change in the nature of the business; or a legal requirement. When a method is changed, the change must be disclosed, the effect stated, the reason given and earlier figures may need to be adjusted.

A machine costs ₦500,000. In Year 1, straight-line depreciation at 10% gives ₦50,000. If the owner switches in Year 2 to reducing balance at 20%, the charge is 20% of ₦450,000 (cost less Year 1 depreciation), which is ₦90,000. Profit in Year 2 falls only because of the new method, so the two years cannot be fairly compared. The right approach is to keep the same method unless there is a justified reason to change. (Your notes show ₦50,000 and ₦80,000; the working above is the correct arithmetic for the reducing balance method.)

The dual aspect concept says that every transaction has two aspects, a debit and a credit, and these are always equal. It is the foundation of the double entry system. The basic equation is Assets = Capital + Liabilities, and it must always balance. In other words, what the business owns equals what the business owes (to the owner and to others).
Transaction 1: started business with ₦100,000 cash. Cash (asset) increases by ₦100,000 (debit) and capital increases by ₦100,000 (credit). Assets ₦100,000 = Capital ₦100,000.
Transaction 2: bought goods for ₦30,000 cash. Purchases (an expense) ₦30,000 is debited and cash falls by ₦30,000 (credit). Assets ₦70,000 = Capital ₦100,000 less the expense ₦30,000.

Transaction 3: bought furniture ₦50,000 on credit. Furniture (asset) rises by ₦50,000 (debit) and the creditor (liability) rises by ₦50,000 (credit). Assets ₦70,000 + ₦50,000 = ₦120,000, which equals capital ₦100,000 + liability ₦50,000 less the expense ₦30,000 = ₦120,000.
Benefits: it lets us check accuracy by a trial balance; it gives a complete record; it shows where funds come from and how they are used; and it is the basis of the financial statements.

units.title: The Prudence Concept and Applying All the Concepts
units.summary: Being careful about profits and losses, how prudence affects stock, debtors and assets, a summary table of the six concepts and a worked example applying them.

p: The prudence concept says that when in doubt, choose the option that is less likely to overstate assets or income. Its motto is: 'Anticipate no profits, but provide for all possible losses.'

Revenue: do not count it until it is reasonably certain; do not record a profit on goods not yet sold, even if you expect a high price. Expenses: record them as soon as possible and provide for likely losses; it is better to overstate expenses than to understate them. Assets: do not overvalue them; write down if the value falls, and do not write up if the value rises. Liabilities: do not understate them; provide for probable liabilities.
An asset that cost ₦100,000 but is now worth ₦80,000 is written down to ₦80,000. If it is now worth ₦120,000, it stays at ₦100,000.

Stock valuation: stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV, the selling price less selling costs). Stock cost ₦50,000 and worth ₦45,000: record ₦45,000. Stock cost ₦50,000 and worth ₦60,000: record ₦50,000. (Your notes say 'market value'; the accounting standard uses net realisable value.)
Provision for doubtful debts: debtors ₦100,000, and 5% may not pay, so provide ₦5,000. This reduces profit now instead of later.
Depreciation: charge depreciation even on an asset that is not being used.
Contingent liabilities: possible losses, such as a lawsuit not yet decided, should be disclosed or provided for.

Do not be too prudent. Do not deliberately understate profit. Aim for a fair presentation. Prudence means provide for an expected loss of ₦10,000. Optimism (wrong) would record an expected profit of ₦10,000 before it is earned.

units.title: The General Journal: Meaning, Format and Uses
units.summary: What the general journal is, its columns, how to write an entry and nine situations in which it is used.

p: The general journal is a book of original (prime) entry used to record transactions that cannot be recorded in the other specialised books. It is also called the journal proper or just the journal. A journal is a record, in order of date, of business transactions showing the accounts to be debited and credited, the amounts and an explanation (the narration).
The journal has five columns.

head: Column
What is written
rows: The date of the transaction (day, month, year)
The account to debit (written first, at the left), the account to credit (written below, indented), and the narration in brackets
The ledger page number, filled in when the entry is posted
The amount to debit, on the same line as the debit account
The amount to credit, on the same line as the credit account

p: The debit account is written first, at the left. The credit account is written below it and moved in. The narration, which starts with 'Being' and explains the transaction, is written in brackets. Total debits must equal total credits.

1. Opening entries: recording assets, liabilities and capital when a business begins or when books are opened. 2. Closing entries: transferring revenue and expense accounts to the profit and loss account at the end of the period. 3. Purchase of assets on credit: for example machinery bought from a supplier on credit. 4. Sale of assets on credit: for example selling old furniture on credit. 5. Correction of errors. 6. Adjustments: bad debts, provision for depreciation, accruals and prepayments. 7. Transfer entries: moving an amount from one account to another, such as goods taken for personal use. 8. Writing off bad debts. 9. Any other entry that does not belong in a specialised book.

Purchases of goods for resale on credit go into the purchases journal (and credit sales into the sales journal). Only purchases or sales of assets such as machinery and furniture, which are not goods for resale, go through the general journal.

units.title: The Analytical Cash Book: Meaning and Format
units.summary: What an analytical cash book is, why it is called analytical, its format, columns and features.

p: An analytical cash book is a cash book with extra columns that split receipts and payments according to their nature or purpose. It is also called a columnar or multi-column cash book. It is 'analytical' because it analyses (breaks down) each amount into its type.
Purpose: to analyse cash and bank transactions; to show different types of receipts and payments separately; to give more detailed information; and to help in budget control.
Analysis can be by source of income (sales, rent, commission), by type of expense (purchases, wages, rent), by department or project, or by customer or supplier.
Receipts side (debit, left): Date, Details, Folio, Total, Sales, Debtors, Other income. Payments side (credit, right): Date, Details, Folio, Total, Purchases, Wages, Rent, Sundry.

The number and names of analysis columns depend on the needs of the business. Common receipts columns are sales, debtors, capital and other income. Common payments columns are purchases, salaries, rent and creditors.
1. The total column shows the whole amount received or paid. It is the sum of the analysis columns for each entry and is the one used for balancing.
2. The analysis columns break the total down by category.
3. The sundry (or other) column is for odd items that do not fit the other columns, such as small or rare transactions.
4. The balance is worked out from the total column only, never from the analysis columns.
Every entry goes in the total column. The same amount goes in only ONE analysis column. For each entry, the total equals the amount in the analysis column. Only the total column is balanced.

units.title: Preparing and Posting the Analytical Cash Book
units.summary: A complete worked example for January 2024, verifying the balance, the advantages, and how to post the analysis columns to the ledger.

p: 1. Decide which analysis columns are needed. 2. Write the date and details. 3. Enter the total amount in the total column. 4. Enter the same amount in the right analysis column. 5. At the end of the period, total all columns and balance using the total column only.

Jan 1: cash balance ₦50,000. Jan 2: cash sales ₦20,000. Jan 5: received from debtor John ₦15,000. Jan 8: paid for purchases ₦25,000. Jan 10: paid wages ₦8,000. Jan 12: cash sales ₦18,000. Jan 15: paid rent ₦10,000. Jan 18: received commission ₦5,000. Jan 20: paid creditor Ade ₦12,000. Jan 25: paid electricity ₦3,000. Jan 28: cash sales ₦22,000. Jan 30: paid salaries ₦15,000.
Receipts side (debit):
The wages column holds both wages and salaries because they are the same kind of expense (staff pay). The balance c/d is the difference between the two totals.

Receipts side total ₦130,000 (the opening balance ₦50,000 plus receipts ₦80,000). Payments made ₦73,000 (25,000 + 8,000 + 10,000 + 12,000 + 3,000 + 15,000). Closing balance = 130,000 less 73,000 = ₦57,000. The analysis columns of each side also agree: receipts 60,000 + 15,000 + 5,000 = ₦80,000; payments 25,000 + 23,000 + 10,000 + 12,000 + 3,000 = ₦73,000.

It gives detailed information; it saves time because analysis is done while recording; it helps decisions by showing spending patterns; it makes posting easier because only the column totals are posted; it gives better control over spending; and it is quick to find and total any category.

The cash account itself is the cash book, so the total column needs no separate posting. From the receipts analysis columns, post a CREDIT to each account: Sales account ₦60,000; Debtors (or John's account) ₦15,000; Commission account ₦5,000. From the payments analysis columns, post a DEBIT to each account: Purchases ₦25,000; Wages ₦23,000; Rent ₦10,000; Creditors (or Ade's account) ₦12,000. Items in the sundry column are posted one by one (here Electricity ₦3,000).
Remember that the debtor and creditor columns are posted to the individual accounts of each person, in the personal ledgers.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 Financial Accounting Second Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: In First Term you learned to record transactions. In Second Term you learn to check the records and then to turn them into the financial statements that tell the owner whether the business made a profit.

You will compare the cash book with the bank statement (bank reconciliation), classify accounts, prepare a trial balance, find and correct errors with a suspense account, and prepare the trading account and the profit and loss account, including the adjustments that make them accurate.

Accounting is learned by doing. Copy each worked example in your notebook, cover the answer, and try again. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

Some figures in the original lesson plan did not add up (for example some trial balances did not balance). In these notes the figures have been corrected, and each correction is explained so that you can see how it was found.

units.title: Bank Reconciliation: Meaning, Need and the Cash Book and Bank Statement
units.summary: What a bank reconciliation statement is, why it is prepared, and why debit in the cash book is credit on the bank statement.

p: A bank reconciliation statement is a statement prepared to reconcile (make agree) the balance in the bank column of the cash book with the balance on the bank statement on a particular date. It shows the reasons for any difference.

Key points: it shows the reasons for differences; it is not part of the double entry system; it is prepared regularly (monthly or quarterly); it helps to find errors and omissions; and it makes sure the records are accurate.

The cash book (bank column) is kept by the business. It records every payment into and out of the bank and shows the balance from the business's point of view. The bank statement is prepared by the bank. It lists all the transactions in the customer's account and shows the balance from the bank's point of view.

The two balances are often different, even when nobody has made a mistake, because the two sets of books record items at different times and the bank records some items that the business does not know about yet.

sections.h: Why do we prepare a bank reconciliation?
p: 1. To detect errors: in the cash book, in the bank statement, wrong postings or wrong amounts. 2. To find omissions: bank charges, interest, standing orders or direct credits not yet recorded. 3. To check accuracy: it is an independent check on the cash book and the statement. 4. For internal control: it helps to prevent fraud and unauthorised withdrawals. 5. To give management the true bank balance for cash flow planning. 6. It is an audit requirement and part of year-end procedures.

What is a debit in the cash book is a credit on the bank statement, and what is a credit in the cash book is a debit on the bank statement. The reason is that the two parties see the same money in opposite ways.
For the business, money paid into the bank increases an asset, so it is a debit in the cash book. Money withdrawn decreases the asset, so it is a credit.

For the bank, money paid in by the customer increases what the bank owes the customer. This is a liability of the bank, so the bank credits the customer's account. Money withdrawn reduces that liability, so the bank debits the customer's account.

Example: ₦10,000 is paid into the bank. The cash book shows Dr Bank ₦10,000. The bank statement shows Cr ₦10,000. Then ₦5,000 is withdrawn. The cash book shows Cr Bank ₦5,000. The bank statement shows Dr ₦5,000.

units.activity: The bank statement shows a credit balance of ₦78,000. What does this mean for the business? (The bank owes the business ₦78,000: the business has ₦78,000 in the bank, which would be a debit balance in its cash book.)

units.title: Causes of Differences Between the Cash Book and the Bank Statement
units.summary: Items in the cash book but not on the statement (timing differences) and items on the statement but not in the cash book, with the effect and treatment of each.

p: Differences fall into two groups. Group 1: items in the cash book but not yet on the bank statement (timing differences). Group 2: items on the bank statement but not yet in the cash book (unrecorded items).

sections.h: Group 1: in the cash book but not on the statement
p: Unpresented (outstanding) cheques are cheques the business has issued and recorded, but the receiver has not yet taken them to the bank. Example: a ₦50,000 cheque to a supplier on 28 January; the supplier has not banked it by 31 January. The cash book shows the payment but the bank statement does not. The cash book balance is lower than the bank balance.

Uncredited lodgements are cash or cheques the business has paid in and recorded, but the bank has not yet recorded (for example, paid in late in the day). Example: ₦30,000 paid in at 4 pm on 31 January and processed on 1 February. The cash book balance is higher than the bank balance.
These need NO change to the cash book. They are dealt with in the reconciliation statement and will correct themselves in the next period.

sections.h: Group 2: on the statement but not in the cash book
p: These are items that the bank has recorded but the business has not. The cash book must be UPDATED for each of them.

units.title: A Worked Example: Finding the Differences
units.summary: Comparing a cash book with a bank statement step by step, updating the cash book and proving the reconciliation.

p: Step 1: compare the opening balances. If they differ, find out why. Step 2: tick off each item that appears in both the cash book and the bank statement. Step 3: list the items left over. Items left in the cash book only are timing differences. Items left on the statement only must be added to the cash book. Step 4: classify each leftover item. Step 5: update the cash book for the items on the statement only. Step 6: prepare the reconciliation statement for the timing differences.
Cash book (bank column):
Bank statement for January 2024:
Cash book balance ₦88,000. Bank statement balance ₦76,000. Difference ₦12,000.
In the cash book but not on the statement: the cash deposited on 28 January, ₦20,000 (an uncredited lodgement), and cheque 003 to XYZ on 22 January, ₦12,000 (an unpresented cheque).
On the statement but not in the cash book: the standing order of ₦5,000, bank charges ₦1,000 and interest ₦2,000. These need a cash book update.
Start with ₦88,000. Less the standing order ₦5,000 and bank charges ₦1,000 (they reduce the balance). Add the interest ₦2,000. The updated balance is 88,000 − 5,000 − 1,000 + 2,000 = ₦84,000.
Study the table. It starts with the updated cash book balance.
The result is ₦76,000, the same as the bank statement. The reconciliation agrees, so we know the cash book is now correct.

units.title: Updating the Cash Book and Preparing the Reconciliation Statement
units.summary: The two steps of bank reconciliation, the format of the updated cash book and the two methods of the reconciliation statement.

p: Step 1: update the cash book. Record every item on the bank statement that is not yet in the cash book, and find the new (updated) balance. Step 2: prepare the bank reconciliation statement. Start with the updated cash book balance or with the bank statement balance, adjust for the timing differences, and arrive at the other balance.

Two methods: Method 1 starts with the updated cash book balance and arrives at the bank statement balance. Method 2 starts with the bank statement balance and arrives at the updated cash book balance. Both are correct. Use the one the question asks for.

Items that increase the balance go on the debit side. Items that decrease the balance go on the credit side. Then total the sides and bring down the new balance. A simple way is to write: old balance, then plus items that increase it, then minus items that decrease it.

sections.h: Method 1: from the cash book balance to the bank statement balance
p: Add unpresented cheques and deduct uncredited lodgements.

sections.h: Method 2: from the bank statement balance to the cash book balance
p: Add uncredited lodgements and deduct unpresented cheques.

Unpresented cheques REDUCE the bank balance (the bank has not yet paid them). So add them to the cash book balance to reach the bank balance, or deduct them from the bank balance to reach the cash book balance.

Uncredited lodgements INCREASE the bank balance when they are finally credited. So deduct them from the cash book balance to reach the bank balance, or add them to the bank balance to reach the cash book balance.
Always use the UPDATED cash book balance.

units.title: Overdrafts, Errors, Examination Tips and Practice
units.summary: Reconciling when there is an overdraft, handling errors in the cash book and on the bank statement, common mistakes, and two practice questions with answers.

p: An overdraft means the account has gone below zero: the business owes the bank. In the cash book, this is a credit balance. Show an overdraft in brackets.

Example: overdraft per cash book (₦25,000). Add unpresented cheques ₦10,000: (₦15,000). Less uncredited lodgements ₦5,000: overdraft per bank statement (₦20,000). With an overdraft, adding a cheque makes the overdraft smaller, because the bank has not yet paid it.

Error in the cash book: a payment of ₦5,000 was recorded as ₦500. The cash book balance is too HIGH (overstated) by ₦4,500, because too little was deducted. (Your lesson notes say 'understated'; an under-recorded payment makes the balance too high.) Update the cash book by crediting the bank with a further ₦4,500.
Error by the bank: a deposit of ₦10,000 was shown by the bank as ₦1,000. The bank balance is too low by ₦9,000. Ask the bank to correct it and, in the reconciliation, add ₦9,000 to the bank balance.
Transposition error: ₦7,300 written as ₦7,030. The difference is ₦270. A transposition difference is always divisible by 9 (270 ÷ 9 = 30), which is a clue when you look for such errors.

Common mistakes to avoid: forgetting to update the cash book first; using the old cash book balance; adding when you should deduct (or the reverse); including updated items again in the reconciliation; using the wrong sign for an overdraft; and not showing workings.
Good practice: update the cash book first; label the 'updated balance'; show all workings; use a proper format; list all cheque numbers; check that the two balances agree.

The cash book (bank column) shows a debit balance of ₦85,000 on 31 March 2024. The bank statement shows a credit balance of ₦63,000 (see the correction below). Unpresented cheques: No. 450, ₦12,000 and No. 451, ₦8,500. Uncredited lodgement ₦15,000. Not yet in the cash book: bank charges ₦1,500; standing order for rent ₦10,000; interest received ₦2,000; a customer's cheque of ₦18,000 dishonoured.
Updated cash book: 85,000 − 1,500 − 10,000 + 2,000 − 18,000 = ₦57,500. Reconciliation: 57,500 + 20,500 (unpresented cheques) − 15,000 (uncredited lodgement) = ₦63,000.

Correction: your lesson notes give the bank statement balance as ₦78,500, which does not agree with the figures (their own working could not make it agree). With the figures as listed, the bank statement balance must be ₦63,000. The reconciliation then proves.

Prepare the updated cash book and reconciliation: cash book balance ₦120,000 (Dr); bank statement ₦114,000; unpresented cheques ₦15,000 and ₦8,000; uncredited deposit ₦20,000; bank charges ₦2,500; standing order for insurance ₦5,000; interest credited ₦1,500; direct debit for electricity ₦3,000.

Answer: updated cash book ₦111,000 (120,000 − 2,500 − 5,000 + 1,500 − 3,000). Add unpresented cheques ₦23,000 = ₦134,000. Less uncredited deposit ₦20,000 = ₦114,000, the bank statement balance. (Your notes give ₦105,000 for the statement, which does not reconcile; the correct figure from the data is ₦114,000.)

units.title: Classification of Accounts: Personal and Real Accounts
units.summary: A closer look at personal accounts (natural, artificial and representative) and real accounts (tangible and intangible), with worked entries.

p: Accounts are grouped into three classes: personal, real and nominal. In First Term you learned the golden rules. This week you study each class in more detail.
Personal accounts relate to persons, firms, companies and organisations. They have three sub-groups.
Natural persons are human beings: John, Mary, Ade Ogunlana, customers and the proprietor.
Artificial (legal) persons are organisations: ABC Limited, XYZ Company, the Government, a school or a club.

Representative personal accounts stand for a group of persons: debtors (all customers), creditors (all suppliers), outstanding salaries (the employees), prepaid expenses and also capital and drawings (the owner).
Golden rule: debit the receiver, credit the giver.
Real accounts relate to the assets and property of the business. They appear in the balance sheet and their balances are carried forward to the next period.
Tangible real accounts are assets you can touch: land, building, machinery, furniture, motor vehicles, stock and cash.
Intangible real accounts are assets with no physical form that still have value: goodwill, patents, trademarks, copyright and franchises.
Golden rule: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.

units.title: Nominal Accounts, Modern Classification and Practice
units.summary: Nominal accounts (expenses, losses, incomes and gains), the five-category classification, worked entries and practice exercises with answers.

p: Nominal accounts relate to expenses, losses, incomes and gains. They have no physical form, relate only to the current period, are closed at the end of the period (transferred to the trading account or the profit and loss account) and start again from nil in the next period.

Expenses and losses (money spent or value lost): salaries, rent, electricity, telephone, stationery, insurance, depreciation, bad debts, discount allowed, interest paid, loss on sale of an asset, carriage outwards.
Incomes and gains (money earned or value gained): sales, commission received, rent received, interest received, discount received, profit on sale of an asset, dividend received.
Note: your lesson notes list carriage inwards among the incomes. That is an error: carriage inwards is an EXPENSE (the cost of bringing goods in).
Golden rule: debit all expenses and losses; credit all incomes and gains.

Paid salaries ₦50,000: Dr Salaries (expense), Cr Cash. Received commission ₦10,000: Dr Cash, Cr Commission received (income). Sold goods to John ₦30,000 on credit: John is a personal account, so Dr John ₦30,000; sales are income, so Cr Sales ₦30,000. Goods worth ₦20,000 destroyed by fire: Dr Loss by fire (nominal) ₦20,000; Cr Purchases (goods) ₦20,000.
Study the table.

Many textbooks use five categories. Assets (debit increases, credit decreases): cash, stock, debtors, machinery. Liabilities (credit increases, debit decreases): creditors, loans, bank overdraft. Capital or equity (credit increases, debit decreases). Expenses (debit increases, credit decreases): salaries, rent, depreciation. Income or revenue (credit increases, debit decreases): sales, commission, interest received.
These five fit the accounting equation, Assets = Capital + Liabilities. A debit increases assets and expenses and decreases liabilities, capital and income. A credit does the opposite.
Salary: nominal. Building: real. Creditors: personal. Sales: nominal. Motor van: real. John's account: personal. Rent: nominal. Furniture: real. Capital: personal. Interest received: nominal.
Study the table.

units.title: Trial Balance: Meaning, Purpose and Format
units.summary: What a trial balance is, why it is prepared, its formats and which accounts go on the debit side and which on the credit side.

p: A trial balance is a list of all the ledger account balances, debit and credit, at a particular date, prepared to check the arithmetical accuracy of the books. If the double entry is correct, the total of the debit balances equals the total of the credit balances.

Key points: it is prepared at the end of an accounting period; it lists the balances of all the accounts; total debits must equal total credits; it is not part of the double entry; it is not a financial statement; it helps to find certain errors.
In the definition: statement (a list, not an account); all ledger balances (every account); a particular date (for example 31 December 2024); arithmetical accuracy (whether debits equal credits).

1. To check the arithmetical accuracy of the books (total debits equal total credits). 2. To give the basis for the final accounts (the trading account, the profit and loss account and the balance sheet), because all the figures are taken from it. 3. To help find errors: if it does not agree, something is wrong. 4. To summarise the ledger in one place. 5. To compare with other periods and spot unusual balances.

Format 1 is the two-column format: account name, debit ₦ and credit ₦. Format 2 is the four-column format: it adds a ledger folio column and a column for the account name. Format 3 (the totals method) shows the total debits and total credits of each account instead of the balance. It is rarely used. The two-column format is the one used in most examinations.

Assets (cash, bank, stock, debtors, land, buildings, furniture, vehicles, machinery, prepaid expenses): debit. Liabilities (creditors, loans, bank overdraft, outstanding expenses): credit. Capital: credit. Drawings: debit. Expenses (purchases, returns inwards, carriage inwards, salaries, rent, rates, insurance, electricity, telephone, stationery, discount allowed, bad debts, depreciation, interest paid, carriage outwards): debit. Income (sales, returns outwards, discount received, commission received, rent received, interest received, profit on sale of assets): credit.

Returns inwards (goods customers send back) is a deduction from sales, so it has a debit balance. Returns outwards (goods we send back to suppliers) is a deduction from purchases, so it has a credit balance.

units.summary: Balancing ledger accounts, listing the balances, a worked example from ledger accounts, a full trial balance and the limits of a trial balance.

p: 1. Balance all the ledger accounts. 2. Decide whether each balance is debit or credit. 3. List the balances in the trial balance. 4. Total both columns. 5. Check that the totals are equal.

Transactions in January: 1 Jan the owner started with cash ₦100,000; 5 Jan bought goods for cash ₦30,000; 10 Jan cash sales ₦50,000; 12 Jan bought goods on credit ₦20,000; 15 Jan paid rent ₦10,000; 20 Jan paid wages ₦5,000; 20 Jan sold goods on credit ₦30,000; 25 Jan received ₦10,000 from debtors; 28 Jan paid creditors ₦15,000.

The other balances: Capital ₦100,000 credit; Purchases ₦50,000 debit (30,000 cash and 20,000 credit); Sales ₦80,000 credit (50,000 cash and 30,000 credit); Debtors ₦20,000 debit (30,000 less 10,000); Creditors ₦5,000 credit (20,000 less 15,000); Rent ₦10,000 debit; Wages ₦5,000 debit.

Your lesson notes balanced the cash account at ₦105,000 because the receipt from debtors and the payment to creditors were left out. With those two items included, the cash balance is ₦100,000 and the trial balance agrees at ₦185,000.

sections.h: A full trial balance: Ojo Enterprises at 31 December 2024
p: Study the table. The capital in your notes is given as ₦150,000, but the other balances add to a debit total of ₦441,000 and a credit total of only ₦436,000. A ₦5,000 shortage on the credit side means the capital must be ₦155,000.

sections.h: What a trial balance cannot show
p: A trial balance that agrees does NOT prove that the books are free from errors. Some errors do not change the totals: a transaction left out completely, an entry in the wrong account of the same type (commission), an entry in the wrong class of account (principle), errors that cancel each other (compensating), and an entry reversed. These are covered in the next units.

units.title: Errors That Affect the Trial Balance
units.summary: Errors of partial omission, casting, posting on the wrong side and posting the wrong amount, which make the trial balance disagree.

p: Errors can be grouped into two kinds. One-sided errors make the trial balance disagree. Two-sided errors keep double entry equal, so the trial balance still agrees even though accounts are wrong. This unit deals with the first kind.

One side of a transaction is recorded and the other is left out. Examples: sales ₦10,000 debited to the customer but not credited to the sales account; a purchase of ₦5,000 credited to the supplier but not debited to purchases. Effect: the trial balance does not agree. Correction: complete the missing entry (the other side goes through the suspense account).

A mistake in adding up an account or a book. For example, the total of the sales day book or the cash book is wrong. If the total is too big it is overcast; if too small it is undercast. Effect: the trial balance does not agree. Correction: adjust the account that has the wrong total.

sections.h: 3. Error of posting on the wrong side
p: An entry is made on the debit side when it should be on the credit side, or the reverse. Examples: a purchase of ₦3,000 credited to the purchases account instead of debited; a payment from a debtor of ₦5,000 debited instead of credited to the debtor. Effect: the trial balance is out by TWICE the amount of the error. Correction: cancel the wrong entry and make the correct one, which means adjusting by double the amount.

sections.h: 4. Error of posting the wrong amount
p: The correct account is used but a different amount is posted to one side. Example: a ₦7,000 purchase is debited to purchases but only ₦700 is credited to the supplier. Effect: the trial balance does not agree (here by ₦6,300). Correction: adjust the account that has the wrong amount.

units.title: Errors That Do Not Affect the Trial Balance
units.summary: Errors of complete omission, commission, principle, compensating errors, errors of original entry and reversal of entries.

sections.h: Why the trial balance still agrees
p: With these errors, the debit and the credit are still equal, so the trial balance agrees. But the accounts are wrong and the final accounts will be wrong too. A balanced trial balance does not mean error-free books.
1. Error of complete omission: a transaction is not recorded at all (no debit and no credit). Example: a sale of ₦20,000 with no entry. Correction: record the whole transaction.

2. Error of commission: an entry is made in the wrong account of the SAME class, on the correct side, with the correct amount. Examples: a payment to Ade debited to John's account (both personal); rent ₦3,000 debited to the rates account (both expenses). Correction: transfer from the wrong account to the right one.

3. Error of principle: an entry breaks an accounting principle by using the wrong CLASS of account. Examples: machinery of ₦100,000 debited to purchases (an asset treated as an expense); repairs of ₦5,000 debited to the machinery account (an expense treated as an asset). Correction: transfer to the correct class of account.

4. Compensating errors: two or more errors that cancel each other out. Example: sales overcast by ₦1,000 (extra credit) and purchases overcast by ₦1,000 (extra debit). Correction: correct each error separately.

5. Error of original entry: the wrong amount is recorded in the book of original entry and then posted correctly from there. Example: an invoice for ₦7,000 is recorded as ₦700 in the day book. Both the debit and the credit are ₦700. Correction: adjust both accounts by the difference.

6. Reversal of entries: the right accounts are used but the debit and credit are the wrong way round. Example: rent ₦5,000 paid, but Dr Cash and Cr Rent were written. Correction: debit Rent and credit Cash with double the amount (₦10,000), which cancels the wrong entry and makes the right one.

units.title: Suspense Account and Correcting Errors by Journal Entries
units.summary: What a suspense account is, how it is opened and cleared, correction entries for each error, and a worked example that clears to nil.

p: A suspense account is a temporary account used when the trial balance does not agree and the cause cannot be found quickly. It lets the accountant make the trial balance agree and carry on until the errors are found.
How it is opened: if the debits are bigger than the credits, CREDIT the suspense account with the difference. If the credits are bigger than the debits, DEBIT the suspense account.

Clearing it: as each error is found, a correcting journal entry is made. Each entry that affects the trial balance has one side in the suspense account. When all the errors have been found, the suspense account balance is nil. If it is not nil, some errors are still undiscovered.
1. Find out what was wrongly done. 2. Find out what should have been done. 3. Cancel the wrong entry and make the right one, or use a single entry that does both. 4. Write a short narration.
Commission: a payment of ₦5,000 to Ade was debited to John. Dr Ade ₦5,000, Cr John ₦5,000. No suspense entry.
Principle: machinery of ₦100,000 was debited to purchases. Dr Machinery ₦100,000, Cr Purchases ₦100,000. No suspense entry.
Partial omission: sales of ₦10,000 were debited to the customer but not credited to sales. Dr Suspense ₦10,000, Cr Sales ₦10,000.
Overcast: the sales day book is overcast by ₦2,000. Dr Sales ₦2,000, Cr Suspense ₦2,000.

Wrong side: ₦8,000 received from a debtor was wrongly DEBITED to the debtor instead of credited. Dr Suspense ₦16,000, Cr Debtor ₦16,000 (twice the amount). (Your notes show the opposite wrong side; a receipt from a debtor must be credited to the debtor.)
Original entry: an invoice for ₦7,500 was recorded as ₦750. Dr Customer ₦6,750, Cr Sales ₦6,750. No suspense entry.
Compensating errors: sales overcast ₦3,000 and purchases overcast ₦3,000. Dr Sales ₦3,000, Cr Suspense ₦3,000; Dr Suspense ₦3,000, Cr Purchases ₦3,000. The suspense effect is nil.

The trial balance disagreed and a suspense account was opened. These errors were found: (1) the sales day book was overcast by ₦3,000; (2) furniture of ₦50,000 was debited to purchases; (3) a payment of ₦12,000 to creditor Ojo was debited to creditor Ade; (4) returns inwards of ₦2,400 were posted to the credit side of the returns inwards account; (5) discount received of ₦3,000 was posted to the debit side of the discount received account; (6) a sale of ₦25,000 was left out completely.

Corrections: (1) Dr Sales 3,000, Cr Suspense 3,000. (2) Dr Furniture 50,000, Cr Purchases 50,000. (3) Dr Ojo 12,000, Cr Ade 12,000. (4) Dr Returns inwards 4,800, Cr Suspense 4,800. (5) Dr Suspense 6,000, Cr Discount received 6,000. (6) Dr Debtors 25,000, Cr Sales 25,000.
Which errors touched the suspense account: (1), (4) and (5) only.

The effect of these errors on the trial balance was credits too high by 3,000 and 4,800, and debits too high by 6,000. The net result is that credits exceed debits by ₦1,800, so the suspense account is opened with a DEBIT of ₦1,800. (Your notes show a ₦15,400 difference, which is not consistent with these errors, and their suspense account did not balance. The figure that makes the suspense account clear to nil is ₦1,800.)
The suspense account debits (1,800 + 6,000) equal the credits (3,000 + 4,800), so the balance is nil: all the errors have been found.

Errors found: (1) the purchases day book was undercast by ₦2,000; (2) the sale of old furniture for ₦15,000 was credited to sales; (3) a cash payment of ₦3,500 to Bisi was debited to Tunde; (4) discount allowed of ₦1,500 was posted to the credit side; (5) bank charges of ₦4,000 were left out completely.

Answers: (1) Dr Purchases 2,000, Cr Suspense 2,000. (2) Dr Sales 15,000, Cr Furniture 15,000. (3) Dr Bisi 3,500, Cr Tunde 3,500. (4) Dr Discount allowed 3,000, Cr Suspense 3,000. (5) Dr Bank charges 4,000, Cr Bank 4,000.

Only errors (1) and (4) affected the trial balance. Together they made the credits exceed the debits by ₦5,000, so the suspense account starts with a debit of ₦5,000, and the two credits of ₦2,000 and ₦3,000 clear it. (Your notes say debits exceeded credits by ₦8,500, which does not match the errors.)

units.title: The Trading Account: Meaning, Format and Items
units.summary: What the trading account is, why it is prepared, its format and the items on its debit and credit sides.

p: The trading account is an account prepared to find the gross profit or gross loss from buying and selling goods. It is the first part of the final accounts. It shows trading activities only, for a given period such as a year, and it is the first part of the profit and loss account.

Gross profit is the excess of sales over the cost of the goods sold. Gross loss is the excess of the cost of goods sold over sales. Cost of goods sold (COGS) is the cost of the goods actually sold in the period: opening stock + purchases + direct expenses − closing stock.

1. To find the gross profit or loss from trading. 2. To judge the trading performance by comparing it with earlier periods and with the plan, and by checking the prices charged. 3. To provide the starting figure for the profit and loss account. 4. For analysis: gross profit margin and stock turnover. 5. For comparison with other businesses and the industry.
Study the table. If the cost of goods sold is greater than net sales, the result is a gross loss.

p: Opening stock: the stock at the start of the period, which is last year's closing stock. Purchases: goods bought for resale, for cash and on credit. Returns outwards: goods returned to suppliers; deduct from purchases (also called purchases returns). Carriage inwards: the cost of bringing the goods in (also freight inwards); it is part of the cost of the goods. Direct expenses: expenses directly connected with getting the goods ready for sale, such as factory wages, factory rent, power, import and customs duties.

Sales: goods sold, for cash and on credit. Returns inwards: goods returned by customers; deduct from sales (also called sales returns). Closing stock: the unsold stock at the end of the period; it is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value and is deducted from the cost of goods because it has not been sold. It can be shown as a deduction on the debit side or as an addition on the credit side. The gross profit is the same either way. Gross profit is the balancing figure, carried to the profit and loss account.

units.title: Cost of Goods Sold, Gross Profit and Special Items
units.summary: The four-step calculation of cost of goods sold and gross profit, two worked examples and how to treat carriage, wages, returns and discounts.

p: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + net purchases + direct expenses − closing stock. Net purchases = purchases − returns outwards + carriage inwards.

Step 1: net purchases. Step 2: cost of goods available = opening stock + net purchases + direct expenses. Step 3: cost of goods sold = cost of goods available − closing stock. Step 4: gross profit = net sales − cost of goods sold, where net sales = sales − returns inwards.

sections.h: What was left out, and why
p: Carriage outwards ₦4,200 is a selling expense, so it goes to the profit and loss account. Office wages ₦28,000 are an administrative expense, so they go to the profit and loss account. Factory wages ₦35,000 are a direct expense, so they go in the trading account. Import duty ₦9,500 is part of the cost of the goods, so it goes in the trading account.

Carriage inwards (on purchases): the cost of bringing goods in; it is part of the cost of goods and goes in the trading account. Carriage outwards (on sales): the cost of delivering goods to customers; it is a selling expense and goes in the profit and loss account.
Wages: factory wages are direct labour and go in the trading account; office wages are administrative and go in the profit and loss account.
Returns: returns inwards are deducted from sales; returns outwards are deducted from purchases.

Trade discount: a reduction in the list price, already deducted before recording, so it is not recorded in the books. Cash discount: given for early payment and recorded in the books; it goes to the profit and loss account, not the trading account.
Drawings in goods: when the owner takes goods for personal use, purchases are reduced (Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases) before the trading account is prepared.

units.title: The Profit and Loss Account: Meaning, Format and Items
units.summary: What the profit and loss account is, gross profit compared with net profit, its purposes, format and how expenses are classified.

p: The profit and loss account is an account prepared to find the net profit or net loss of a business by comparing all income with all expenses. It is the second part of the final accounts, after the trading account. The link is: trading account → gross profit → profit and loss account → net profit.
Net profit is what remains after deducting all expenses from total income. Net loss arises when expenses are more than income.

Gross profit comes from trading only (sales less cost of goods sold) and is shown in the trading account. Net profit is the overall profit after ALL expenses: gross profit + other income − all expenses. It is shown in the profit and loss account.

1. To find the net profit or loss. 2. To show how the gross profit was used and what the other income and expenses were. 3. To provide a basis for tax. 4. To judge performance and control of expenses by comparing periods. 5. To help decisions on expansion, costs, pricing and investment. 6. To inform owners, lenders and management.
Study the table. If total expenses exceed total income, the result is a net loss.

p: Debit side (expenses). Administrative expenses: office salaries, rent, rates, insurance, stationery, telephone, postage, printing, legal fees, audit fees, general expenses. Selling and distribution expenses: advertising, sales commission, carriage outwards, delivery expenses, packaging, marketing, sales promotion. Financial expenses: interest paid, bank charges, loan and overdraft interest. Other expenses: bad debts, discount allowed, depreciation, loss on sale of an asset, donations, fines.

Credit side (income). Gross profit, then other income: commission received, discount received, rent received, interest received, dividend received, profit on sale of an asset, bad debts recovered. Net profit is the balancing figure and is transferred to the capital account.
By nature: direct expenses (factory wages, import duty, carriage inwards) go in the trading account. Indirect expenses (office salaries, rent, electricity) go in the profit and loss account.
By function: administrative, selling, distribution and financial expenses.
By behaviour: fixed expenses do not change with sales (rent, salaries, insurance). Variable expenses change with sales (sales commission, carriage outwards).

Discount allowed is given to customers, reduces income and is debited. Discount received comes from suppliers, increases income and is credited. Carriage inwards is in the trading account. Carriage outwards is in the profit and loss account.

units.title: Adjustments: Closing Stock, Prepayments and Accruals
units.summary: Why adjustments are made, how closing stock, prepaid expenses and accrued expenses are treated, and a formula for the expense of the year.

p: Adjustments are changes made at the end of the period so that the profit is accurate and the financial position is true. They apply the accrual concept: income and expenses are recorded in the period to which they belong, not when cash is paid or received. Common adjustments are closing stock, prepayments, accruals, depreciation, provision for bad debts, bad debts written off, accrued interest and goods taken for own use.

Closing stock is the value of the goods not sold at the end of the period. It is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV). Cost is the purchase price plus costs of bringing the stock to its present state. NRV is the selling price less the costs of making the sale. Example: stock cost ₦50,000, NRV ₦45,000: value at ₦45,000. Stock cost ₦50,000, NRV ₦60,000: value at ₦50,000.

If the closing stock is already in the trial balance, it is shown only in the balance sheet as an asset. If the closing stock is given as an adjustment (not in the trial balance), it appears in TWO places: in the trading account (deducted from the cost of goods) and in the balance sheet (current assets).
Journal: Dr Stock account ₦40,000, Cr Trading account ₦40,000 (being closing stock recorded).

A prepaid expense has been paid in the current period for a benefit in a future period. Examples: rent paid for next year, an insurance premium for the next period, subscriptions and rates paid in advance. Treatment: deduct the prepayment from the amount paid to find the expense, and show the prepayment as a current asset.
Example: rent paid ₦120,000, of which ₦20,000 is for next year. Profit and loss account: rent ₦100,000. Balance sheet: prepaid rent ₦20,000 (current asset).

Detailed example: insurance of ₦36,000 was paid on 1 April 2024 for one year; the year ends on 31 December. The monthly premium is 36,000 ÷ 12 = ₦3,000. The 2024 expense is 9 months = ₦27,000. The prepayment for 2025 is 3 months = ₦9,000. Journal: Dr Profit and loss ₦27,000; Dr Prepaid insurance ₦9,000; Cr Insurance ₦36,000.

An accrued expense has been incurred in the period but not yet paid. Examples: salaries earned but unpaid, rent due but unpaid, electricity used but not billed, interest owing. Treatment: add the outstanding amount to the amount paid to find the expense, and show it as a current liability.
Example: salaries paid ₦480,000, outstanding ₦40,000. Profit and loss account: salaries ₦520,000. Balance sheet: outstanding salaries ₦40,000 (current liability).

Detailed example: rent is ₦10,000 a month and was paid up to November; December is unpaid. Paid 11 months: ₦110,000; outstanding ₦10,000; expense ₦120,000. Journal: Dr Profit and loss ₦120,000; Cr Bank ₦110,000; Cr Outstanding rent ₦10,000.
The general rule is: expense for the year = cash paid in the year + opening prepayment − closing prepayment − opening accrual + closing accrual.

Example: rent paid during the year ₦144,000; rent prepaid at the start of the year ₦12,000 (it was paid last year but belongs to this year); rent outstanding at the end ₦15,000; no prepayment at the end. Expense = 144,000 + 12,000 + 15,000 = ₦171,000. The profit and loss account is charged ₦171,000; the balance sheet shows outstanding rent of ₦15,000 as a liability.

units.title: Adjustments: Depreciation, Provision for Bad Debts and Bad Debts
units.summary: Why and how assets are depreciated (straight-line and reducing balance), the provision for depreciation, provisions for doubtful debts (new, increased and decreased), and bad debts written off or recovered.

p: Depreciation is the systematic spreading of the cost of a fixed asset over its useful life. We provide for it because assets lose value over time, to match the cost with the income they help to earn, to show the true value of assets, and to follow the accrual and prudence concepts.
Causes: wear and tear, obsolescence (becoming out of date), the passage of time and depletion (for natural resources like a mine).

Straight-line method: the same amount every year. Annual depreciation = (cost − scrap value) ÷ useful life, or cost × rate. Example: cost ₦100,000, scrap value ₦10,000, life 10 years. Depreciation = (100,000 − 10,000) ÷ 10 = ₦9,000 a year.

Reducing balance method: a fixed percentage of the book value (cost less depreciation so far). It gives more depreciation in the early years. Example: cost ₦100,000, rate 20%. Year 1: 20% of 100,000 = ₦20,000. Year 2: 20% of 80,000 = ₦16,000. Year 3: 20% of 64,000 = ₦12,800.

Method A: reduce the asset directly. Method B (better): keep the asset at cost and build up a provision for depreciation account, so that the balance sheet shows cost, total depreciation to date and net book value. Example: machinery at cost ₦100,000; less provision for depreciation ₦20,000; net book value ₦80,000.

Journal each year: Dr Depreciation account (expense) ₦20,000; Cr Provision for depreciation ₦20,000. The depreciation account is then transferred to the profit and loss account. In Year 2 the provision account carries ₦20,000 from Year 1 plus ₦20,000 for the year, giving ₦40,000.

A provision is an amount set aside out of profit for debts that may not be paid. It follows the prudence concept. A specific provision is for named debtors likely to default. A general provision is a percentage of all debtors, based on experience.
New provision: debtors ₦100,000, provision 5% = ₦5,000. Profit and loss account: provision ₦5,000. Balance sheet: debtors ₦100,000 less provision ₦5,000 = net debtors ₦95,000.
Increase: old provision ₦5,000; debtors ₦120,000; new provision at 5% = ₦6,000. Only the increase of ₦1,000 is charged to the profit and loss account (Dr Profit and loss, Cr Provision).
Decrease: old provision ₦5,000; debtors ₦80,000; new provision at 5% = ₦4,000. The decrease of ₦1,000 is added to profit (Dr Provision, Cr Profit and loss).

A bad debt is a debt that is definitely lost and must be written off. A provision is an estimate of a loss that may happen. To write off a bad debt: Dr Bad debts, Cr the debtor. It is an expense in the profit and loss account, and debtors are reduced in the balance sheet.
If a debt written off is later recovered: Dr Bank, Cr Bad debts recovered (income).

units.title: The Balance Sheet: Meaning, Purpose and the Accounting Equation
units.summary: What a balance sheet is, why it is prepared, the accounting equation and how transactions affect it.

p: A balance sheet is a financial statement that shows the financial position of a business at a particular date by listing its assets, liabilities and capital. It is also called the statement of financial position or the position statement.

Key points: it shows what the business owns (assets); it shows what the business owes (liabilities); it shows the owner's interest (capital); it is prepared at a point in time, so the heading is 'as at 31 December 2024' and NOT 'for the year ended' (that is for the profit and loss account); it is the last of the financial statements; and it is not part of the double entry.

1. To show the financial position: the assets, the debts and the net worth. 2. To show the ability to pay debts (solvency and liquidity). 3. To help decisions on investment, lending and expansion. 4. To judge performance by looking at the growth of assets and capital and the level of debt. 5. To meet legal requirements: the Companies Act and tax rules. 6. To provide a basis for analysis and for comparing years and businesses. 7. To inform the owners, banks, investors, creditors and the government.

Assets = Capital + Liabilities. Rearranged, Capital = Assets − Liabilities. The equation must always balance. Assets are the resources the business owns. Capital is the owner's investment. Liabilities are amounts owed to outsiders. The business uses the owner's capital and borrowed money to buy its assets.
Example 2: capital ₦400,000, liabilities ₦150,000. Assets = ₦550,000.
Owner introduces more capital ₦50,000: cash (an asset) rises by ₦50,000 and capital rises by ₦50,000. The equation still balances.
Bought goods on credit ₦30,000: stock (an asset) rises by ₦30,000 and creditors (a liability) rise by ₦30,000.
Paid a creditor ₦20,000: cash falls by ₦20,000 and creditors fall by ₦20,000.

units.title: Classification of Items, Order of Arrangement and Working Capital
units.summary: Fixed assets and current assets, current and long-term liabilities, capital, the order of arrangement, balance sheet compared with trial balance and working capital.

p: Fixed (non-current) assets are used in the business for more than a year and are not meant for resale. Examples: land, buildings, machinery, motor vehicles, furniture and fittings, equipment, computers, goodwill, patents and trademarks. They are shown at cost less accumulated depreciation, which is the net book value. (Land is not usually depreciated.)
Current assets are short-term assets that change all the time and can be turned into cash within a year: stock, debtors, prepayments, bank, cash, short-term investments and bills receivable.
Current liabilities are due within one year: creditors, bank overdraft, outstanding (accrued) expenses, short-term loans, bills payable and tax owing.
Long-term (non-current) liabilities are due after more than one year: long-term loans, mortgages, debentures and bonds.
Closing capital = opening capital + additional capital + net profit − drawings (− net loss). It belongs to the owner.

Fixed assets are listed by permanence: the most permanent first (land, buildings, plant and machinery, motor vehicles, furniture and fittings, equipment). Current assets are listed by liquidity (how easily they turn into cash): least liquid first, so stock, debtors, prepayments, bank and then cash. The reason is that stock is sold on credit to give debtors, who pay and so give cash. Current liabilities are listed by urgency, such as overdraft, creditors, outstanding expenses and short-term loans. Some businesses use the reverse order. Both are acceptable if you are consistent.

p: Working capital (net current assets) = current assets − current liabilities. It measures the ability to pay short-term debts and run day-to-day business.

Example: stock ₦50,000, debtors ₦80,000, bank ₦30,000, cash ₦10,000 give current assets of ₦170,000. Creditors ₦60,000 and outstanding expenses ₦10,000 give current liabilities of ₦70,000. Working capital = 170,000 − 70,000 = ₦100,000. A positive amount means the business can pay its short-term debts and still have funds to operate. Negative working capital (current liabilities greater than current assets) suggests liquidity problems.

units.title: Preparing a Balance Sheet: Steps and Formats
units.summary: The six steps for preparing a balance sheet and the horizontal and vertical formats.

p: Step 1: identify the items: separate assets from liabilities and find the capital items and any adjustments. Step 2: classify them: fixed assets, current assets, current liabilities, long-term liabilities and capital. Step 3: calculate the capital: opening capital + additional capital + net profit − drawings − net loss. Step 4: arrange the items in order: fixed assets by permanence, current assets by liquidity, liabilities by urgency. Step 5: calculate the totals, the working capital and the net assets, and check that the equation balances. Step 6: present the statement neatly with a heading, 'as at' date, clear labels and ruled lines.
The left side shows capital and liabilities (the sources of funds). The right side shows the assets (the uses of funds). Both sides must total the same amount.

Depreciation: cost less provision for depreciation = net book value. Provision for bad debts: debtors less provision = net debtors. units.title: Sales Ledger Control Account: Meaning and Structure
units.summary: What control accounts are, why they are used, and the items on the debit and credit sides of the sales ledger control account.

p: A control account is a summary account that shows the total of a group of individual accounts in one account. It is also called a total account. There are two kinds: the sales ledger control account (the total debtors account) and the purchases ledger control account (the total creditors account).

The sales ledger control account shows the total of all the individual debtors' accounts in the sales ledger. It is also called the total debtors account, the debtors control account or the receivables control account.

1. Quick information: the total owed by all customers is available at once, without adding hundreds of accounts. 2. To detect errors: the control account balance is compared with the total of the individual balances; if they differ, there is an error. 3. Division of work: one person keeps the control account and another keeps the individual accounts, which reduces the risk of fraud. 4. To save time when extracting a trial balance: only the control account balance is needed. 5. As an internal check on the ledger clerks. 6. To locate errors quickly, because they are limited to one section. 7. To give management summary figures.

sections.h: Structure of the sales ledger control account

p: Opening balance: the total owed by customers at the start of the period. Credit sales: only sales on credit, from the sales day book; cash sales are NOT included because they do not create debtors. Dishonoured cheques: a cheque from a customer that was banked but returned unpaid; the customer still owes the money. Interest charged: a penalty for late payment, which increases the debt.

Cash or bank received: the money received from customers, from the cash book. Returns inwards: goods the customers sent back, from the returns inwards day book. Discount allowed: cash discount given for prompt payment. Bad debts written off: debts confirmed as irrecoverable, from the journal. Contra: when the same person is both a debtor and a creditor, the smaller amount is set off. Example: a customer owes us ₦10,000 and we owe him ₦4,000; the contra is ₦4,000.
Memory aid: ask 'does this increase what customers owe us?' If yes, it is a debit. If it reduces what they owe, it is a credit.

units.title: Preparing a Sales Ledger Control Account and Reconciling It
units.summary: Worked examples of the sales ledger control account, how to reconcile it with the individual debtors' balances, and causes of differences.

p: Debtors at 1 January ₦80,000; credit sales ₦150,000; cash received from debtors ₦120,000; returns inwards ₦8,000; discount allowed ₦5,000; bad debts written off ₦3,000.

Opening ₦80,000 + credit sales ₦150,000 = ₦230,000. Less cash 120,000, returns 8,000, discount 5,000 and bad debts 3,000 = ₦136,000. Closing balance = ₦94,000. The customers owe ₦94,000 at the end of January.

Debtors at 1 June ₦120,000; credit sales ₦280,000; cash sales ₦150,000; cash received from debtors ₦240,000; cheques received from debtors ₦60,000; returns inwards ₦15,000; discount allowed ₦12,000; bad debts ₦8,000; dishonoured cheque ₦5,000; interest charged ₦2,000; contra with creditors ₦4,000.

The cash sales of ₦150,000 are NOT included because they do not make debtors. Cash and cheques received are both money from debtors and can be shown as one figure of ₦300,000. The dishonoured cheque and the interest go on the debit side because they increase the debt. The contra goes on the credit side because it reduces the debt. The closing balance of ₦68,000 is the total owed by all customers.
Step 1: take the control account balance. Step 2: list and add up the individual debtors' balances from the sales ledger. Step 3: compare them. Step 4: if they differ, find and correct the error.
Example: control account ₦94,000. Individual balances: A 30,000; B 25,000; C 20,000; D 19,000 = ₦94,000. They agree.

Example with an error: control ₦94,000 and individual total ₦97,000, a difference of ₦3,000. The cause: a bad debt of ₦3,000 was written off in the control account but not in the individual debtor's account. Write it off there too and the total becomes ₦94,000.

An error in adding the sales day book; a credit sale posted to the wrong debtor (this affects the individual accounts only); an item in the control account but not in the individual account, or the other way round; different amounts in the two; returns not posted to the individual account; discount recorded in one place only; bad debts written off in one place only; a contra recorded in one place only; a dishonoured cheque reinstated in one place only; and a double posting.

Debtors at 1 March ₦150,000; credit sales ₦320,000; cash sales ₦180,000; cash received from debtors ₦280,000; returns inwards ₦18,000; discount allowed ₦15,000; bad debts ₦10,000; dishonoured cheque ₦8,000; interest ₦3,000; contra ₦6,000. The individual debtors total ₦152,000.

Debit side: 150,000 + 320,000 + 8,000 + 3,000 = ₦481,000. Credit side: 280,000 + 18,000 + 15,000 + 10,000 + 6,000 = ₦329,000. Closing balance ₦152,000, which equals the individual total. The reconciliation shows no difference.

units.title: Purchases Ledger Control Account
units.summary: The purchases ledger (total creditors) control account: its structure, items and worked examples.

p: The purchases ledger control account shows the total of all the individual creditors' accounts in the purchases ledger. It is also called the total creditors account, the creditors control account, the payables control account or the bought ledger control account. It helps management, helps to find errors and acts as an internal check, just as the sales ledger control account does.

The sales ledger control account shows what customers owe us (an asset). The purchases ledger control account shows what we owe suppliers (a liability). They follow the same ideas but with opposite sides.
Creditors are liabilities, so the account has a credit balance. Credit side: things that INCREASE what we owe. Debit side: things that DECREASE it.

Credit side (increases creditors)

p: Credit purchases are only purchases on credit, from the purchases day book; cash purchases are not included because they do not create creditors. A dishonoured cheque issued by us puts the debt back, so we still owe the supplier. Interest charged by suppliers (for late payment) also increases the debt. Cash paid, returns outwards, discount received and the contra reduce the debt.

Cash purchases of ₦90,000 are left out. Cash and cheques paid reduce creditors and are shown as one figure. The dishonoured cheque and the interest are credits because they increase what we owe. The contra is a debit because it reduces what we owe. The ₦71,000 is the total owed to all suppliers at 31 May.

units.title: Contra Entries, Comparison and Reconciliation of Control Accounts
units.summary: How a contra entry is made, a comparison of the sales and purchases control accounts, reconciling the creditors, and practice with answers.

p: A contra is made when the same person is both a debtor and a creditor. Example: Tunde Limited owes us ₦15,000 (a debtor) and we owe Tunde Limited ₦10,000 (a creditor). We agree to set off ₦10,000.
Journal: Dr Purchases ledger control account ₦10,000; Cr Sales ledger control account ₦10,000 (being a contra entry for set-off).

Effect: in the sales ledger control account, ₦10,000 appears on the credit side (debtors fall from ₦15,000 to ₦5,000). In the purchases ledger control account, ₦10,000 appears on the debit side (creditors fall from ₦10,000 to nil). The same amount appears in both control accounts, on opposite sides. After the contra, Tunde owes us ₦5,000 net and we owe him nothing.

units.title: Depreciation: Meaning, Causes and Reasons
units.summary: What depreciation is, which assets depreciate, seven causes and seven reasons for providing for it, and the main methods.

p: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the cost of a fixed asset over its useful life. It is also the fall in value of a fixed asset because of use, the passage of time or obsolescence.

Key points: it applies to fixed assets only, not to current assets; it is a non-cash expense (no money is paid out); it is an estimate; it reduces the value of the asset in the balance sheet; it is charged as an expense in the profit and loss account; and it matches cost with income (the accrual concept).

Assets that depreciate: buildings, machinery, motor vehicles, furniture, equipment, computers and tools. Assets that normally do not: land (it usually keeps or gains value), stock (it is treated differently), investments and antiques.

1. Wear and tear: normal use damages the asset (an engine wears out; furniture is scratched). 2. Obsolescence: new technology makes an asset out of date even though it still works (an old computer replaced by a faster one). 3. Passage of time: assets lose value with age even if not used (rubber perishes, paint fades). 4. Depletion: the quantity of a natural resource falls as it is extracted (a mine, an oil well, a quarry). 5. Effluxion of time: rights that last for a fixed period expire (a 10-year lease, a patent, a licence). 6. Inadequacy: the asset becomes too small for a growing business. 7. Accidents and damage: a vehicle crash, fire damage.

1. To apply the accrual concept: a machine that costs ₦100,000 and lasts 10 years is charged ₦10,000 a year, not ₦100,000 in year one. 2. To show the true profit: without depreciation the profit is overstated (₦50,000 instead of a truer ₦40,000). 3. To show a realistic asset value in the balance sheet. 4. To provide for replacement: keeping back profit each year helps the business to have funds to buy a new asset (note that depreciation itself does not create cash; the profit must actually be saved). 5. To follow the law and accounting standards. 6. To calculate the correct capital. 7. For tax: capital allowances reduce taxable profit.

The main methods are the straight-line method (equal instalment) and the reducing balance method (diminishing balance). Others are the revaluation method (used for small tools and livestock), the depletion method (mines and quarries), the machine hour or units of production method (based on use), the sum of years' digits method and the annuity method. In SS1 you study the first two.

units.title: The Straight-Line Method of Depreciation
units.summary: The formula, advantages and disadvantages of the straight-line method, three worked examples including part-year purchase, and how to record depreciation using a provision account.

p: In the straight-line method an equal amount of depreciation is charged each year over the life of the asset. It is also called the fixed instalment or equal instalment method.

Annual depreciation = (cost − scrap value) ÷ useful life. Or annual depreciation = cost × rate %. Cost is the purchase price. Scrap (residual or salvage) value is the amount the asset is expected to fetch at the end of its life. Useful life is the estimated number of years of use.

Advantages: simple and easy; the same charge each year; suits assets with steady use; easy to predict. Disadvantages: it ignores the pattern of use; it assumes equal benefit each year; it may not match actual wear; and repair costs usually rise with age, so the total cost is not even. It suits buildings, furniture, leases, patents and copyrights.

sections.h: Example 1: using cost, scrap value and life
p: Machine cost ₦100,000; scrap value ₦10,000; life 10 years. Annual depreciation = (100,000 − 10,000) ÷ 10 = ₦9,000 a year.

A vehicle costs ₦500,000 and is depreciated at 20% a year (straight line). Annual depreciation = 500,000 × 20% = ₦100,000. After 5 years the total depreciation is ₦500,000, so the net book value is nil.

Furniture is bought on 1 April 2024 for ₦60,000 and is depreciated at 10% a year. Accounts close on 31 December. Full-year depreciation is 60,000 × 10% = ₦6,000. It was held for 9 months. Depreciation for 2024 = 6,000 × 9/12 = ₦4,500. Formula: cost × rate × (months held ÷ 12).

Keep the asset at cost. Each year: Dr Depreciation account (expense) ₦9,000; Cr Provision for depreciation account ₦9,000. The depreciation account is closed to the profit and loss account. The provision account collects the amounts year by year: ₦9,000 at the end of year 1, ₦18,000 at the end of year 2. The balance sheet shows the machinery at cost ₦100,000, less provision ₦9,000 (year 1) or ₦18,000 (year 2), giving net book value ₦91,000 or ₦82,000.
Advantages of the provision method: it shows the original cost, the total depreciation to date and the net book value.

units.title: The Reducing Balance Method of Depreciation
units.summary: How depreciation is calculated on the reducing book value, the pattern it follows, worked examples including part-year purchase, and how it appears in the accounts.

p: In the reducing balance method (also called diminishing balance or written-down value method), depreciation is calculated each year on the net book value (cost less accumulated depreciation), not on the cost. Year 1: cost × rate. Year 2: (cost − year 1 depreciation) × rate. Each year: opening net book value × rate.

Features: the charge falls each year; it is highest in the early years; it never reaches zero, since a percentage of what remains always leaves something behind (₦100 × 20% = ₦20 leaves ₦80; ₦80 × 20% = ₦16 leaves ₦64; and so on).
A motor vehicle costs ₦500,000 and is depreciated at 25% a year on the reducing balance.
Machinery bought on 1 January 2021 for ₦200,000. Depreciation is 30% a year on the reducing balance. Find the charge for each year and show the machinery in the balance sheet at 31 December 2024.

The machinery account stays at the cost of ₦200,000 every year. The provision for depreciation account is credited each year with the year's charge and the balance builds up: ₦60,000, ₦102,000, ₦131,400, ₦151,980. Each year the journal is Dr Depreciation, Cr Provision for depreciation. Balance sheet at 31 December 2024: machinery at cost ₦200,000, less provision for depreciation ₦151,980, net book value ₦48,020.

An asset is bought on 1 July 2024 for ₦120,000 and depreciated at 20% on the reducing balance. The year ends on 31 December. Full year = 120,000 × 20% = ₦24,000. For 6 months = 24,000 × 6/12 = ₦12,000. Net book value at 31 December 2024 = ₦108,000.
In 2025 the year is a full year: opening NBV ₦108,000 × 20% = ₦21,600, so closing NBV is ₦86,400. After the first part year, each following year is a full year on the reducing balance.
Equipment bought on 1 January 2022 for ₦80,000 at 25% reducing balance: 2022 ₦20,000 (NBV ₦60,000); 2023 ₦15,000 (NBV ₦45,000); 2024 ₦11,250 (NBV ₦33,750).

sections.h: Advantages and disadvantages of reducing balance
p: Advantages: the pattern is realistic (an asset loses most value early); costs are matched with income (a new asset has a high depreciation charge and low repairs, an old asset has a low charge and high repairs, so the total yearly cost is more even); it gives tax advantages by deferring tax; it writes off the asset faster, which suits assets that quickly become out of date; and it is cautious (prudent).

Disadvantages: the calculation is more involved; the asset never reaches zero and may not match the true scrap value; profit is higher in later years, which makes comparisons harder; and the right rate is hard to find.

Use the straight-line method for buildings, furniture, leases, patents and copyrights, and for assets with steady use and a known life (for example, a ₦10 million building over 50 years is ₦200,000 a year). Use reducing balance for motor vehicles, computers, phones and other technology, and for machinery with fast obsolescence or heavy use in the early years.
Think about the pattern of use, the rate of obsolescence, repair costs (rising with age favours reducing balance), what management prefers and the type of asset.

units.title: Manufacturing Account: Meaning, Purpose and Classification of Costs
units.summary: What a manufacturing account is, who prepares it, why it is prepared, and prime cost, factory overheads and factory cost.

p: A manufacturing account is an account prepared by a business that makes goods, to find the cost of producing the finished goods in the period. It is also called the production account, factory account or cost of production account. It is prepared by manufacturers, not traders. It comes before the trading account and is part of the final accounts.

A trading concern buys finished goods and sells them without changing them (a shop or supermarket). It has a trading account only. A manufacturing concern turns raw materials into finished goods (a bread factory, a textile mill). It needs a manufacturing account and a trading account.
Flow: raw materials → manufacturing account → cost of production → trading account → profit and loss account → balance sheet.

1. To find the cost of production (the factory cost). 2. To compare the cost of making goods with the cost of buying them (make-or-buy decisions). 3. For cost control: to watch production costs and find waste. 4. To give the figure used in the trading account (the cost of production takes the place of purchases). 5. To judge factory efficiency over time. 6. To help set selling prices and profit margins. 7. To give management a detailed breakdown of costs.

Prime cost (direct costs) is the cost directly connected with making the goods: raw materials used + direct labour (factory wages) + direct expenses (such as royalties for using a patent). Prime cost = raw materials used + direct labour + direct expenses.

Factory overheads (indirect costs) cannot be traced directly to a product: factory rent, power, lighting, insurance, depreciation of factory machinery, the factory supervisor's salary, factory repairs, lubricants and cleaning. Office, selling and administrative costs are NOT included.
Factory cost (cost of production) = prime cost + factory overheads, adjusted for work in progress.
