p: Opening stock of raw materials: raw materials in hand at the start. Purchases of raw materials. Carriage inwards on raw materials: the cost of bringing them in. Closing stock: raw materials still unused at the end. Raw materials consumed = opening stock + purchases (+ carriage inwards) − closing stock.

Direct labour: wages of production workers. Direct expenses: royalties, special tools, hire of special equipment for a job. Factory overheads: factory rent, power, insurance, depreciation of factory machinery and equipment, supervisor's salary, repairs, lighting, heating, cleaning, security, lubricants, small tools and consumable stores.
Work in progress (WIP): goods that are begun but not finished. Opening WIP is added; closing WIP is deducted.

p: The cost of production of ₦729,000 takes the place of purchases in the trading account. Sales ₦1,200,000. Opening stock of finished goods ₦50,000 + cost of production ₦729,000 = ₦779,000. Less closing stock of finished goods ₦60,000 = cost of goods sold ₦719,000. Gross profit = 1,200,000 − 719,000 = ₦481,000.
The manufacturing account produces a COST. The trading account uses that cost and compares it with sales to find the gross profit.

Raw materials stock and work in progress appear in the manufacturing account. Finished goods stock appears in the trading account. In the balance sheet, all three are current assets and are listed under stock.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 Literature in English First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Literature is the art of words. In this subject you read stories, poems and plays, you learn how writers create their effects, and you learn to explain what you think and to support it with evidence from the text.

In First Term you learn what literature is and why it matters, how to appreciate a text (theme, plot, setting, style, tone and mood), the main figures of speech, and the three genres: prose, poetry and drama. Then you study your first set text, Shakespeare's tragedy Antony and Cleopatra.

Read each unit slowly. When a unit gives an example, try to think of your own. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit. Essay assignments from the school scheme of work are given in the 'Try it yourself' box of the unit, so you can practise writing.

units.title: What Is Literature? Its Functions
units.summary: The meaning of literature, its key characteristics, oral and written literature, and six functions: to entertain, to teach, to mirror society, to criticise society, to preserve culture and to develop feelings.

p: In its widest meaning, literature is all the writing of a particular culture, language or time. In the narrower sense used in this subject, Literature (with a capital L) is imaginative or creative writing that has artistic value and speaks to people everywhere. It explores the human condition, ideas, feelings and experiences through language that is carefully crafted and meant to do more than just give information. A shopping list or a simple news report is writing, but it is not usually called literature.

Imaginative: it comes from the imagination (fiction, poetry, drama). Artistic: language is used skilfully and beautifully, with figures of speech, rhythm and shape. Universal: its themes (love, death, conflict, justice) matter to people in all cultures and times. Open to interpretation: different readers can find different meanings in the same text.
Literature can be oral (passed on by word of mouth: folktales, myths, legends, proverbs, songs) or written (recorded in text).
1. To entertain: literature gives pleasure and escape. The Romans called this the 'sweet' (dulce) side of literature.
2. To educate and inform: literature teaches about the world, cultures, history and human behaviour, and gives moral lessons. This is the 'useful' (utile) side.
3. To mirror society (reflective function): it shows the values, beliefs, problems, vices and virtues of the society in which it was written.
4. To criticise society (corrective function): authors use stories, poems and plays to expose injustice and corruption, as in satire, and to urge change.
5. To preserve culture: literature is an archive of a people's language, myths, customs and history, handed from one generation to the next.
6. Emotional and psychological development: by living through characters' feelings, we understand our own and other people's, and we grow in empathy.

units.title: Why We Study Literature
units.summary: The benefits of studying literature: critical thinking, better language, empathy, a wider worldview and an understanding of history and culture.

sections.h: A part of a rounded education
p: Studying literature does much more than prepare you for an examination. It builds skills and attitudes that you will use for the rest of your life.

1. Critical thinking: a literary text is complex and sometimes ambiguous. To understand it you must read the words carefully, look for patterns, form an opinion (an interpretation) and support it with evidence from the text.
2. Better language and communication: wide reading adds to your vocabulary, shows you how good writers build sentences and shows the power of well-chosen words. Your own speaking and writing improve.
3. Empathy: literature lets you 'step into the shoes' of people from other backgrounds, places and times. This 'vicarious experience' helps you to understand human nature.
4. A broader worldview: it takes you beyond your own limited experience to new ideas, beliefs and ways of seeing the world.
5. Understanding history and culture: a novel or a play can show what a war or a social system felt like for the people who lived through it, which a history textbook cannot do in the same way.
Reading closely, analysing, interpreting, comparing texts, arguing a point with evidence, writing clearly and respecting other people's views are all skills practised in Literature-in-English.

units.title: Literary Appreciation: Theme, Plot and Setting
units.summary: What literary appreciation is, and three of its elements: theme, plot (with the five parts of a plot) and setting.

p: Literary appreciation is the process of analysing, understanding and judging a work of literature to find out how and why it creates its effects. It is more than just liking a book. It involves analysis (breaking the text into parts such as plot, character and setting), interpretation (deciding what it means and what the writer wants to say) and evaluation (judging its artistic quality and impact).

The theme is the central idea or message of a text: a truth about life or human nature that the writer explores. A theme is not a single word such as 'love'. It is a statement about that word, such as 'Love can destroy as well as heal' or 'True love needs sacrifice'. A text can have one major theme and several minor ones.

The plot is the series of connected events that make up the story: the 'what happens'. A typical plot has five parts (called Freytag's pyramid). Exposition: the beginning, which introduces the characters, setting and first conflict. Rising action: complications and obstacles that build tension. Climax: the highest point of tension, the turning point where the conflict comes to a head. Falling action: events after the climax, as tension drops and the results unfold. Resolution (denouement): the end, when the conflict is settled and a new normal is set up.

img.alt: A pyramid-shaped line showing exposition, rising action, climax at the peak, falling action and resolution
img.cap: The five parts of a plot.

p: Setting is the time and place in which the story happens. Physical setting is the location (a city, a jungle, a room). Temporal setting is the time (the 19th century, wartime, one day). Social or cultural setting covers the customs, values and rules of the society in the story. Setting is important because it can affect the plot, influence how characters behave and create the mood.

units.title: Literary Appreciation: Style, Tone and Mood
units.summary: Style (diction, syntax, devices), tone as the writer's attitude and mood as the feeling created in the reader.

p: Style is the writer's own way of using language: how a writer writes, not what the writer writes about. It includes diction (the choice of words: formal or informal, simple or complex, concrete or abstract), syntax (how words are arranged into sentences: long flowing sentences or short choppy ones) and the use of literary devices such as metaphors, similes and imagery.

Tone is the writer's or narrator's attitude to the subject or the audience. It is shown through diction, events and the way characters are described. Examples of tone: serious, humorous, cynical, sarcastic, optimistic, critical, nostalgic, formal.

Mood is the general feeling or atmosphere that the text creates in the reader. Setting is a main tool for creating mood: 'a dark and stormy night' gives a gloomy, tense mood. Examples of mood: suspenseful, joyful, mysterious, terrifying, peaceful, melancholic.

units.title: Figures of Speech I: Simile, Metaphor, Irony, Personification, Oxymoron
units.summary: The meaning of figures of speech and five of them with definitions, functions and examples, including the three types of irony.

p: Figures of speech (also called literary or rhetorical devices) are words or expressions used in a non-literal, imaginative way to create a special effect, to stress a point or to make language vivid and memorable. They let writers 'paint pictures with words' and say more than the dictionary meanings (denotation) of the words.

A simile makes a direct comparison between two different things using 'like' or 'as'. Examples: 'He is as brave as a lion.' 'The memory faded like a dream.' It makes a description vivid by linking something unfamiliar to something familiar.

A metaphor says that one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as'. Examples: 'He is a lion in the fight.' 'All the world's a stage' (Shakespeare). 'She has a heart of stone.' A metaphor is a stronger comparison, because it makes the reader see the likeness more deeply.

Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what actually is. There are three main types. Verbal irony (like sarcasm): a speaker says the opposite of what they mean, for example saying 'Lovely weather we're having' in a hurricane. Situational irony: the result of a situation is the opposite of what was expected, for example a fire station burning down. Dramatic irony: the audience or reader knows something important that a character does not. In Romeo and Juliet, the audience knows that Juliet has only taken a sleeping drug, but Romeo believes she is dead. This creates suspense.

Personification gives human qualities, feelings or actions to objects, animals or ideas. Examples: 'The wind whispered through the trees.' 'Justice is blind.' 'The sun smiled down on us.' It makes abstract ideas easier to picture.

An oxymoron puts two opposite or contradictory words side by side to create a new, complex meaning. Examples: 'jumbo shrimp', 'living dead', 'deafening silence', 'a bittersweet memory'. It is used for dramatic effect or to show mixed feelings.

The lesson plan says that in Romeo and Juliet the audience knows Romeo is only sleeping, but Juliet thinks he is dead. It is the other way round: Juliet takes the drug and appears dead, and Romeo, who does not know the plan, believes she is dead and kills himself.

units.title: Figures of Speech II: Euphemism, Alliteration, Hyperbole, Allusion, Assonance, Paradox, Repetition
units.summary: Seven more figures of speech with definitions, functions, examples and the differences between alliteration and assonance and between oxymoron and paradox.

p: A euphemism replaces a harsh or blunt expression with a mild, indirect one. Examples: 'He passed away' (instead of 'He died'); 'She is between jobs' (instead of 'unemployed'); 'The company is downsizing' (instead of 'sacking workers'). It softens a harsh truth or is used to be polite, and sometimes to mislead.

Alliteration is the repetition of the same initial consonant sound in a series of words. Examples: 'She sells seashells by the seashore.' 'The wicked witch of the West.' 'Pride and Prejudice.' It creates rhythm and makes a phrase easy to remember.
Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration for emphasis or humour, not meant literally. Examples: 'I'm so hungry I could eat a horse.' 'I've told you a million times.' 'This bag weighs a ton.'

An allusion is an indirect reference to a well-known person, place, event or work (from the Bible, mythology, history or Shakespeare). It adds meaning by linking the text to a wider culture and depends on the reader's shared knowledge. Examples: 'He was a real Samaritan about it' (the Good Samaritan); 'She had a Mona Lisa smile'; 'He has an Achilles' heel' (a weak point, from Greek myth).

Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds inside words in a line. Examples: 'The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain' (the long 'ay' sound); 'Try to light the fire.' It creates internal rhyme and music. Alliteration is about the first consonant sounds; assonance is about vowel sounds inside words.

A paradox is a statement that seems to contradict itself or to be absurd but, when you think about it, holds a deeper truth. Examples: 'You must be cruel to be kind.' 'War is peace' (George Orwell's 1984). 'This is the beginning of the end.' An oxymoron is two words ('living dead'); a paradox is a whole statement or idea ('The child is father of the man').

Repetition is the deliberate repeating of a word, phrase or sentence for effect: emphasis, rhythm, suspense or to stress a theme. Examples: 'Rage, rage against the dying of the light' (Dylan Thomas). In Martin Luther King Jr's speech the repeated 'I have a dream' at the start of clauses is a kind of repetition called anaphora.

units.title: The Three Genres: Prose, Poetry and Drama
units.summary: The definitions, structural features and sub-genres of prose, poetry and drama.

p: A genre is a category of literature whose works share similar form, style or subject matter. There are three main genres: prose, poetry and drama.

img.alt: Three coloured boxes for prose, poetry and drama listing their language, units, forms and examples
img.cap: The three genres at a glance.

p: Prose is language in its ordinary form, without a fixed metre or rhythm pattern. It is the language of everyday speech, textbooks, novels and newspapers. It is built of sentences and paragraphs.

Structural features: the sentence (the basic unit of thought); the paragraph (related sentences developing one idea); the chapter (a main division of a long work); and the narrative voice or point of view (first person 'I', third person 'he', 'she', 'they').

Sub-genres. Fiction (imaginative): the novel (long, e.g. Things Fall Apart), the novella (shorter than a novel and longer than a short story) and the short story (a brief narrative about one incident or character). Non-fiction (factual): biography (a life story written by someone else), autobiography (written by the person) and the essay.
Poetry uses the sound and rhythm of language (metre and rhyme) to bring out meaning and feeling. It is language at its most compressed, intense and artistic. It is made of lines and stanzas.

Structural features: the line; the stanza (a group of lines, like a paragraph in prose); rhyme (repeated sounds, usually at the ends of lines); rhyme scheme (the pattern of rhymes, such as ABAB); rhythm or metre (the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables); enjambment (a line running on into the next without a pause).
Sub-genres: lyric poetry (personal feelings: sonnet, ode), narrative poetry (tells a story: epic, ballad) and dramatic poetry (spoken in the voice of a character: dramatic monologue).
Drama (a play) is written to be performed on a stage by actors. A story is told mostly through dialogue and action.

Structural features: dialogue (talk between characters); monologue (a long speech by one character); soliloquy (a character alone on stage speaks inner thoughts aloud); stage directions (the playwright's instructions on movement, setting and tone, often in italics or brackets); act (a major division of a play); scene (a part of an act, usually one place and time); characters (the 'dramatis personae').

Sub-genres: tragedy (a serious play with an unhappy ending, often the fall of the hero), comedy (light-hearted, usually with a happy ending), tragicomedy (a mixture of both) and melodrama (sensational, with exaggerated feelings).

units.title: Shakespeare and the Background of Antony and Cleopatra
units.summary: Who William Shakespeare was, the source and historical setting of Antony and Cleopatra, the Triumvirate, and the contrast between Rome and Egypt.

p: William Shakespeare (1564 to 1616) is widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language. He was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, England, and worked in London as an actor, playwright and part-owner of an acting company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men (later the King's Men). He wrote in the Elizabethan era (named after Queen Elizabeth I) and the Jacobean era (after King James I). He wrote about 38 plays, 154 sonnets and other poems. His plays are grouped as tragedies (Hamlet, Macbeth), comedies (A Midsummer Night's Dream) and histories (Henry V).

Antony and Cleopatra is a tragedy and also a Roman play, because it is based on real history. Shakespeare's main source was Plutarch's Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (in Sir Thomas North's English translation), which told the story of Mark Antony.

The play is set after the murder of Julius Caesar in 44 BC. The Roman world is shared by three rulers, called the Triumvirate (a council of three): Mark Antony; Octavius Caesar (Julius Caesar's great-nephew and heir); and Marcus Lepidus (a weaker, older general).

The action moves between two contrasting worlds. Rome (the West) stands for duty, order, reason, law, self-control and military discipline. It is the world of Octavius. Egypt (the East) stands for passion, pleasure, emotion, excess and luxury. It is the world of Cleopatra. The central conflict is Antony's struggle between his Roman duty and his Egyptian passion.

img.alt: Two boxes, Rome and Egypt, listing what each stands for, with Mark Antony in the middle pulled both ways
img.cap: Antony is torn between Rome and Egypt.

p: Your lesson plan calls Octavius Julius Caesar's grand-nephew. He was Caesar's great-nephew (the grandson of Caesar's sister), whom Caesar adopted as his son and heir. In the play, Octavius is a cold and efficient politician who will become Rome's first emperor, Augustus.

units.title: Antony and Cleopatra: Plot of Acts I and II
units.summary: The key scenes of the first two acts: Antony in Egypt, the news from Rome, his return, the marriage to Octavia, the soothsayer, Cleopatra's rage and the feast on Pompey's ship.

p: Scene 1 (Alexandria, Egypt): we meet Mark Antony, completely in love with Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt. Roman soldiers complain that their great general has become a fool in love ('dotage'). Messengers arrive from Rome, but Antony will not see them. He declares: 'Let Rome in Tiber melt.'

Scene 2 (Egypt): the news is that Antony's wife Fulvia has fought against Octavius Caesar and has died, and that the rebel Sextus Pompey is growing strong at sea and threatening Rome. Antony feels a 'Roman thought' and decides to break free from Cleopatra and return to Rome.

Scene 4 (Rome): Octavius and Lepidus talk. Octavius criticises Antony's wasteful life in Egypt and contrasts it with his former self as a hard, disciplined soldier. We see Octavius as cold, careful and dutiful.
Scene 5 (Egypt): Cleopatra, missing Antony, sends messengers to him every day. We see that she is vain and dramatic and can be manipulative, but also truly passionate.

Scene 2 (Rome): the Triumvirs meet. Octavius and Antony quarrel. To heal the quarrel and make a political bond, Agrippa (Octavius's adviser) and others suggest that Antony marry Octavius's sister, Octavia. Antony agrees. Octavia is the opposite of Cleopatra: virtuous, quiet and devoted to Roman duty.

Scene 3 (Rome): a soothsayer (fortune-teller) warns Antony that his 'guardian angel' (his luck) is weaker than Octavius's when they are near each other, and tells him to stay away from Octavius. Antony knows it is true and decides to return to Egypt.
Scene 5 (Egypt): a messenger tells Cleopatra that Antony has married Octavia. She flies into a rage and beats the messenger. This shows her passion and her royal temper.

Scene 7 (Pompey's ship): the Triumvirs make peace with Sextus Pompey and celebrate with a drunken feast on his ship. Pompey's follower suggests killing the three rulers. Pompey refuses, saying that it would be dishonourable (though he wishes it had been done without telling him). The Romans, especially Antony, behave as 'Egyptians' in their indulgence, and Lepidus is shown as weak and silly.

units.title: Antony and Cleopatra: Plot of Acts III to V
units.summary: The breach with Octavius, the Battle of Actium, Enobarbus's desertion and death, Antony's suicide and Cleopatra's death.

p: Antony, Octavia and Lepidus go their separate ways. Antony returns to Cleopatra. In a public ceremony in Alexandria, he shares the eastern lands of the Roman empire among Cleopatra and her children, including Caesarion, her son by Julius Caesar. This insults Octavius and betrays Rome.
Octavius uses this as propaganda. He has jailed Lepidus on false charges and now declares war, painting Antony as Cleopatra's bewitched puppet. Octavia returns to Rome, heartbroken.

The Battle of Actium (Act III) is the turning point. It is a sea battle. Against the advice of his best soldier, Enobarbus, Antony chooses to fight at sea (where Octavius is stronger) because Cleopatra wants it. In the battle, Cleopatra's ships suddenly flee. Antony turns his own ship and follows her, leaving his men and the fight. Ashamed, he has lost all honour. Enobarbus, seeing his master's lost judgement, deserts and joins Octavius.

Antony challenges Octavius to single combat, but Octavius mocks him and refuses to fight a tired old man. Enobarbus, now with Octavius, is overcome with guilt when Antony sends his treasure after him and kindly forgives him. Enobarbus dies of a broken heart.

Antony wins a small victory on land, which briefly lifts his spirits. But in the final sea battle, the Egyptian fleet surrenders to Octavius. Believing Cleopatra has betrayed him, Antony is furious. Cleopatra, afraid, locks herself in her monument (tomb) and sends a false message that she has killed herself.

Hearing this, Antony's rage becomes grief. He asks his servant Eros to kill him, but Eros kills himself instead. Antony falls on his own sword but does not die at once. He is carried to Cleopatra's monument and lifted up to her. He dies in her arms, telling her to trust Proculeius, one of Octavius's men (which is not wise advice).

Octavius arrives in Egypt. He wants Cleopatra alive, to parade her through Rome in his triumph, which would be the greatest shame for her. Cleopatra pretends to bargain but secretly plans her death. A 'clown' (a countryman) brings her a basket of figs hiding asps (poisonous snakes).

Dressed in her royal robes, Cleopatra puts an asp to her breast and another to her arm, and dies, imagining a reunion with Antony. Her women, Iras and Charmian, also die. Octavius enters and finds her dead. He is annoyed to be outwitted, but respects her noble end. He orders that she and Antony be buried together. The play ends with Octavius as ruler of the Roman world, but the love of Antony and Cleopatra has won the audience.

units.title: Antony and Cleopatra: Themes and Characters
units.summary: The five main themes and the characters of Antony, Cleopatra, Octavius, Enobarbus and Octavia.

p: 1. Love against duty (passion against reason): the central theme. Antony is torn between his passion for Cleopatra (Egypt) and his duty as a Roman soldier and Triumvir (Octavius's world).
2. The clash of cultures (East against West): Rome values order, duty and self-control; Egypt values emotion, pleasure and excess. The two value systems fight each other to the death.
3. Honour and betrayal: characters ask what honour means: Roman duty, or loyalty to a person? Antony betrays Octavia, Enobarbus betrays Antony, and Octavius betrays Lepidus.
4. Power and politics: the play is a political drama. A love story sets off a huge civil war to decide who will rule the Roman world.
5. Change and decline: Antony falls from 'the triple pillar of the world' to a 'strumpet's fool'. The old world of heroes gives way to the cold, efficient world of Octavius.

Mark Antony: the tragic hero. He is passionate, charming and a brilliant soldier, but also impulsive, self-indulgent and lacking the self-control of his rival. His 'dotage' on Cleopatra brings his downfall.

Cleopatra: the heroine, 'a woman of infinite variety'. She is vain, dramatic, manipulative and sometimes cruel (she beats the messenger), but she is also clever, politically shrewd and powerful. At the end she shows a nobility that lets her die on her own terms rather than be shamed.

Octavius Caesar: the antagonist (or, from a Roman view, the hero). He is cold, calculating, unemotional and ruthlessly efficient. He stands for the 'new Rome', acts only for political gain, wins the world but cannot understand the passion of Antony and Cleopatra.

Enobarbus: Antony's loyal soldier. He acts as the play's commentator or chorus, is witty and cynical, and sees the truth clearly (for example in his famous description of Cleopatra on her barge). His desertion and his death from guilt show the tragic depth of loyalty and betrayal.
Octavia: Antony's Roman wife, a symbol of Roman duty and virtue. She is used as a pawn in politics. Her quiet dignity contrasts with Cleopatra's passion.

units.title: Antony and Cleopatra: Language, Imagery, Techniques and Relevance
units.summary: Blank verse, hyperbole, the difference between Roman and Egyptian speech, patterns of imagery (cosmos, water, animals), dramatic techniques and why the play is still relevant.

p: The language of Antony and Cleopatra is among Shakespeare's richest and most poetic. Blank verse: like most of his plays, it is written mainly in blank verse, which is unrhymed iambic pentameter. An iamb is one unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one (da-DUM). Pentameter means five such feet in a line. For example: 'Let Rome in Tiber melt, and the wide arch / Of the ranged empire fall!' This rhythm is close to natural English speech, but sounds formal and powerful.

Hyperbole: the language is grand and exaggerated, matching the huge passions. Antony says, 'Kingdoms are clay.' Enobarbus says of Cleopatra that 'Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale her infinite variety', making her a goddess who beats time.

Rome and Egypt speak differently. In Rome (Octavius), speech is plainer, direct, logical and businesslike. In Egypt (Antony and Cleopatra), speech is poetic, exaggerated and full of rich images: the language of passion.
Imagery is descriptive language that appeals to the senses. Shakespeare uses patterns of imagery to support his themes.

The world and the heavens: characters see themselves in cosmic terms. Antony is 'the triple pillar of the world'. Octavius holds the world in his hands. Cleopatra compares Antony to the sun and moon. This shows that the love story will decide the fate of the world.

Water and sea: the sea is central. It is the source of Rome's power (its navy) and the River Nile is the source of Egypt's wealth. The Nile stands for fertility, mystery and excess. The sea battle at Actium is where Antony's world sinks.

Animals: Cleopatra is called the 'serpent of old Nile'. This is double-sided: it means dangerous and tempting (like the serpent in Eden), but also wise, ancient and able to renew herself (like a snake shedding its skin). She dies by an asp's bite. The horse stands for Roman manhood and war; Antony's decline is shown by loss of control of it.

Contrast: the whole play is built on contrasts: Rome and Egypt; Octavius (cold) and Antony (hot); Cleopatra (passionate) and Octavia (virtuous); public life (battle plans, politics) and private life (lovers' quarrels). They show that private passion has public results.
Foreshadowing: hints of what will come. The soothsayer's warning that Antony will always lose to Octavius foreshadows his defeat. Enobarbus's witty speeches often hint at coming doom.
Dramatic irony: the audience knows more than the characters. As Antony dies believing Cleopatra is dead, the audience knows that she is alive, which makes his suicide even sadder.

The play is 2,000 years old in its setting, but its themes are timeless. The pull between what we want (passion, love) and what we should do (duty, work) is felt by everyone. Octavius wins by controlling the story as well as by force, painting Antony as a wasted man: a lesson for an age of media and 'fake news'. The play also asks whether Antony and Cleopatra's love is great or selfish and destructive, which links to modern celebrity culture. The clash of values (East and West, traditional and modern) is still a source of conflict in a globalised world.

The lesson plan contains several broken lines of joking text under 'Hyperbole', where a quotation from Antony was meant to appear. The line used here, 'Kingdoms are clay: our dungy earth alike / Feeds beast as man', is from Antony in Act I, Scene 1.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 Literature in English Second Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: In Second Term you study drama. First you learn what makes African drama special: its roots in oral tradition, music, dance and audience participation. Then you study two African plays, Once Upon an Elephant (Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan) and The Marriage of Anansewa (Efua Sutherland), and two non-African plays, An Inspector Calls (J. B. Priestley) and A Man for All Seasons (Robert Bolt).

Read each unit, then if you can, read the play itself. The notes are a guide, not a replacement for the text. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

The summaries here were checked against published study guides and reviews. In some places the original lesson plan gave a plot or names that do not match the published text (especially for Once Upon an Elephant and The Marriage of Anansewa). Those places are corrected and marked, so that you will not lose marks in examinations.

units.title: Features of African Drama
units.summary: Six features of traditional African drama: communal and functional, total theatre, audience participation, masks and costumes, ritual roots and didacticism.

p: African drama is not simply drama written by Africans. It is a form with its own recognisable features, which set it apart from European theatre.

1. Communal and functional: traditional African drama has a purpose in the community, such as to teach, to settle disputes, to perform religious rites or to mark historical events. It is a shared experience that includes and reflects the whole community, not 'art for art's sake'.
2. Total theatre: African drama does not separate the arts. Dialogue is joined with music, song, dance, mime and spectacle. A play is an event and a celebration, not only spoken words.

3. Audience participation: the 'fourth wall' (the invisible wall between actors and audience) hardly exists. The audience joins in songs (call and response), comments to the actors, or even moves into the playing area.

4. Masks and costumes: masks are not just decoration. They are strong symbols that stand for gods, ancestors, spirits or types of character, and they let the actor become a supernatural or symbolic force.

5. Ritual and ceremonial roots: much African drama grew out of religious rituals, festivals (such as the Mmanwu masquerade of the Igbo) and ceremonies. This gives it a serious, spiritual and community feeling.
6. Didacticism: African drama almost always teaches. It aims to pass on moral lessons, social values and the history of the people. The story is the vehicle for a message.

units.title: Oral Tradition and Cultural Elements in African Plays
units.summary: How African plays draw on the storyteller, myths and folktales, proverbs and riddles, symbolism and the mixing of languages.

p: African drama grew out of oral tradition, the stories, songs and sayings passed on by mouth. The playwright is, in a way, the modern-day griot or storyteller (a griot is a West African traditional storyteller, singer and keeper of history).

The storyteller or narrator: many African plays, such as Efua Sutherland's The Marriage of Anansewa, use a storyteller who speaks directly to the audience, guides the plot and comments, as a village storyteller would.

Myths, legends and folktales: plots are often taken from the stock of oral stories, such as the Ananse (spider) tales or the tortoise tales, or from legends, and are adapted to comment on modern problems.

Proverbs and riddles: the dialogue is rich in proverbs, idioms and riddles. Chinua Achebe wrote that 'proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten'. Proverbs show wisdom and say much in few words.
Symbolism: African plays are often not realistic. A stool can stand for kingship, a pot of water for life or purity, and an animal (the tortoise, the elephant) for a human quality or kind of person.

Language: many playwrights switch between local languages and English, French or Portuguese (code-switching). They also shape a new 'African English' with local rhythms, sentence patterns and images, as Wole Soyinka and J. P. Clark do.

units.title: Once Upon an Elephant: the Playwright, the Text and the Setting
units.summary: Who Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan is, the folktale roots of Once Upon an Elephant and what the play is an allegory of.

p: Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan is a Nigerian playwright, academic and critic who works in drama and theatre at the University of Lagos. Her plays use traditional Yoruba forms to speak about modern Nigerian and African life.

Once Upon an Elephant is a modern Nigerian play. Its title begins like a folktale ('once upon a ...'), and it borrows the idea of a proud elephant from Yoruba oral tradition. In Yoruba folk stories the elephant is large and haughty, and in the end is brought low by his own pride. The play was inspired by Adeboye Babalola's poem 'Salute to the Elephant'.

The play is an allegory: a story in which the characters and events stand for something larger. The king who takes the name Ajanaku (which means 'elephant') stands for any tyrannical ruler who abuses power. Critics read the play as a comment on dictatorship and on rulers who will not leave office ('sit-tightism') in post-colonial Africa.

The play is set in an unnamed Yoruba village (a small kingdom) in traditional times. The main places are the palace of the king and the village around it, where the kingmakers, the priest and the ordinary people meet. The unnamed village is a symbol: it can stand for any community that suffers under a bad ruler.

The lesson plan describes a play set in a fictional animal kingdom called 'Animalu', with a drought, a king elephant who hoards water and a tortoise who tricks him. That is not the published play. The real Once Upon an Elephant has human characters (a prince, a kingmaker and priest, a banished former queen and others), as described in the next units, and its elephant is the nickname of a ruler, 'Ajanaku'. If you studied the animal version, please use the corrected notes for your examinations.

units.title: Once Upon an Elephant: Plot
units.summary: The story of Olaniyonu, who becomes the tyrant Ajanaku, the kingmaker Serubawon, the banished Iya'agba, and how the tyrant is brought down.

p: Olaniyonu (Ajanaku): a proud, power-hungry prince, presented as the illegitimate son of the ailing King Akinjobi (the play later reveals his true father). Serubawon: the chief priest and kingmaker (a medicine man), who plans to crown Olaniyonu and control him. Akinjobi: the ailing king. Ogundele and Odejimi: the other kingmakers, who oppose Serubawon's choice. Iya'agba: the king's banished former wife, thought of as a 'madwoman', who is witty and defiant and tells the truth about the corruption in the palace. Desola: Serubawon's daughter. Odekunle: a man who stands against Ajanaku's men. Adebisi: the woman whose affair with Serubawon produced Olaniyonu.

1. Serubawon is sure that King Akinjobi is doomed, and he schemes to put Olaniyonu on the throne, though the other kingmakers resist. The crowning rites are carried out while the old king is still alive.

2. Olaniyonu is crowned and takes the name Ajanaku, 'the elephant'. His rule becomes one of terror and abuse. Iya'agba, mocked as mad, uses her sharp words to expose the greed and hypocrisy of the palace.
3. Ajanaku grows more and more hungry for power and wants to become immortal. On Serubawon's advice he takes part in a wicked rite, the Ijedodo, which harms six young women.
4. Desola, Serubawon's own daughter, is the sixth. Serubawon realises that he has helped to create a monster.

5. Iya'agba breaks the process and saves Desola. The truth comes out: Ajanaku is the illegitimate son of Serubawon himself, and Serubawon is also the cause of Akinjobi's illness. The community rallies behind Iya'agba.
6. Ajanaku is destroyed and Serubawon is exposed and disgraced. (Published summaries differ on the exact manner of their ends, so check the text in your edition.)

The ruler whose pride and greed know no limits falls at last, and those who helped him (Serubawon) fall too. This is poetic justice: people get what they deserve. Like the elephant in the Yoruba tale, Ajanaku is brought down by his own pride.

units.title: Once Upon an Elephant: Themes, Characters and Style
units.summary: The main themes (tyranny, abuse of power, betrayal, poetic justice, women's strength), the chief characters and the folktale style of the play.

p: Tyranny and abuse of power: the central theme. Ajanaku rules by fear and uses his power to satisfy himself. He is a type of the dictator who cannot let go.
Greed and ambition: the lust for power and for long life (immortality) destroys both Ajanaku and Serubawon.
Betrayal and infidelity: Serubawon's affair with Adebisi produced Olaniyonu; his betrayal of the old king and of the village leads to disaster.
Poetic justice: people receive the fate their deeds deserve.
Hypocrisy and complicity: the people around the tyrant, including the priest who made him, share the guilt.
The strength of women: Iya'agba, who is treated as mad, is the one who sees clearly, speaks bravely and finally stops the evil.
Ajanaku (Olaniyonu): proud, cruel, greedy, power-mad and cowardly under his boasting. He stands for tyrants who misuse office.
Serubawon: clever, scheming and ambitious; he creates the monster he later fears. He is both a kingmaker and a victim of his own plan.
Iya'agba: brave, witty and defiant; a truth-teller. Her 'madness' is a mask which lets her speak freely.
Ogundele and Odejimi: the opposing kingmakers who represent the voice of law and custom.
Desola: an innocent young woman, a victim of the evil that her own father helped to start.

The play uses the form and feeling of a folktale: a simple, strong story with a clear moral, symbolic names (Ajanaku, the elephant), proverbs and the Yoruba setting. Names carry meaning, which is a feature of Yoruba culture. The play also uses rites and ceremony and moves between humour and horror, and its ending is meant to satisfy the audience's sense of justice.

units.title: The Marriage of Anansewa: the Playwright and Anansegoro
units.summary: Who Efua Sutherland was, what Anansegoro is, and the background of The Marriage of Anansewa.

p: Efua Sutherland (1924 to 1996) was a pioneering Ghanaian playwright, director and cultural worker, often called the mother of modern Ghanaian theatre. She founded the Ghana Drama Studio in Accra, which became a centre for a new kind of theatre: modern, but clearly African. Her aim was to join the forms of traditional Ghanaian oral performance with the structure of written drama.

The Marriage of Anansewa is her best-known play. She called its form Anansegoro, which means 'Ananse-play'. Ananse the spider is the best-known trickster in Akan (Ghanaian) folklore. Anansegoro takes the elements of traditional Ananse storytelling (Anansesem) onto a modern stage:

1. A storyteller who controls the story-telling event and speaks to the audience. 2. Ananse himself, clever, greedy, lovable and often in trouble. 3. Songs and dances called mboguo, which comment on the action, express feelings and let the audience join in. 4. A clear moral lesson.
The play also looks at tradition against modernity: old customs, such as marriage customs, meet modern money-making.

units.title: The Marriage of Anansewa: Plot
units.summary: Ananse's scheme to win gifts from four chiefs, the crisis when all four announce a visit, the fake death of Anansewa and the happy ending.

p: Ananse is a poor but ambitious widower with one daughter, Anansewa, a secretarial student about to finish her course. He wants two things: a loving husband for her, and a better life for himself. He travels the country showing photographs of Anansewa to four rich chiefs and starts a 'photograph engagement' with each, at first without Anansewa knowing. When she learns, she objects at first, but she is later persuaded to join the plan.

The four chiefs are: the Chief of Sapaase, Togbe Klu IV (the Chief of Akate), the Chief of the Mines, and Chief-Who-Is-Chief, whom Ananse prefers. Each sends money in expectation of the wedding, which will be settled when one of them places the head-drink (the traditional marriage gift) on the table. Ananse becomes rich. His house, his clothes and his standing change, and he makes lavish gifts at church.
Ananse receives telegrams from all four chiefs. Each says he is coming within a week or two to perform the head-drink ceremony. Ananse is trapped: he cannot marry his daughter to four men.

Ananse has a new idea. Anansewa will pretend to have died. He sends his mother Aya and his aunt Ekuwa away to their home town, Nanka. Christie, a stylish woman who is fond of Ananse, helps him. The chiefs' messengers come one by one with sympathy and funeral gifts. Chief-Who-Is-Chief's messengers come last. They bring heavy gifts and a message that he will take full responsibility for the funeral, even though the marriage was not yet complete. This shows that he is the most devoted suitor.

Ananse then 'revives' Anansewa, saying she heard Chief-Who-Is-Chief calling her back from death, and the preparations begin for a grand wedding. Ananse has got both of his wishes: a worthy husband for his daughter and wealth for himself. The audience laughs at his tricks but also learns from the story.

The lesson plan names the suitors 'Togbe Delume', 'Chief Sapa' and 'Chief Daga' and says that Ananse writes letters on a typewriter. The published play gives the chiefs as listed above, and Ananse uses photographs, gifts and telegrams. Its resolution also comes from the messengers' funeral gifts rather than from speeches by the chiefs themselves.

units.title: The Marriage of Anansewa: Themes, Style, Characters and Values
units.summary: Greed and cunning, tradition against modernity, appearance against reality and the role of women; the style of the play; its characters; its cultural values and morals.

p: Greed and cunning: a classic Ananse theme. The play shows greed (Ananse's scheme) but also admires wit and cleverness.

Tradition against modernity: modern money-making seems to turn old customs, such as marriage and funerals, into business. Ananse uses a traditional heritage (the spider trickster) and modern means (photographs, telegrams).
Appearance against reality: little is what it seems. Anansewa is not dead; Ananse's wealth is built on a trick; and the chiefs show their real characters when they hear of her death.
The role of women: Anansewa is not just a pawn. She is educated and takes part in the plan, and her 'death' becomes a way of finding the right husband.

Anansegoro: the play blends storytelling, drama, music and dance. The storyteller controls the event and talks to the audience. The mboguo (interludes by the Players) comment on the action, summarise it and express feeling while drawing the audience in. The language is rich in Akan proverbs and humour.
Ananse: the trickster: greedy, scheming, selfish but charming, imaginative and a loving father. We admire his cleverness even as we judge his greed.
Anansewa: modern and educated, but also dutiful. She starts as the object of her father's plan and becomes someone who shapes the outcome.
Chief-Who-Is-Chief: the most devoted suitor, who shows true respect and generosity, and so wins Anansewa.
The storyteller and the Players: the voice of the community; they guide the audience's reaction and make sure the moral is clear.
Aya, Ekuwa and Christie: Ananse's mother, his aunt, and his friend Christie, who help carry the family scheme along.

The play celebrates Ghanaian culture (storytelling, music) and also criticises the way it can be abused. Lessons: greed leads to trouble; true respect and generosity matter more than money; and tradition must be able to change with the times, though its core values (respect, love, community) should be protected.

units.title: An Inspector Calls: the Playwright, Context and Setting
units.summary: Who J. B. Priestley was, why the play is set in 1912 but was written in 1945, and why the single dining-room setting matters.

p: John Boynton (J. B.) Priestley (1894 to 1984) was a well-known English novelist, playwright and broadcaster. He was a socialist who worried about social inequality and injustice. He believed that the wealthy business class was selfish and that society could improve only if people took collective responsibility for each other. This belief is the foundation of An Inspector Calls.

When the play is set: 1912. This was Edwardian England, shortly before the First World War, a time of strict class division and false confidence. The wealthy factory-owning class (the Birlings) lived in comfort, while the working class (like Eva Smith) had no rights and no safety net. Mr Birling boasts that the Titanic is 'unsinkable', which the audience knows to be tragically wrong.

When it was written: 1945, at the end of the Second World War. Priestley and his audience had lived through two world wars and the Great Depression. They knew that the selfish attitudes of 1912 had helped to lead to disaster. In 1945 Britain was planning a fairer society (the Welfare State).

The purpose: Priestley sets the play in the past to warn the present. He is saying: 'Look at the arrogance of these people. This is what caused our troubles. We must never go back to this. We must be responsible for one another.'

The whole play happens in the dining room of the Birling family's house in the industrial town of Brumley. The room is comfortable and 'prosperous' but 'not cosy'. The single setting is symbolic: the Birlings are trapped in a pressure cooker with the Inspector, and their bubble of wealth is about to burst. Because the action takes place in one room and in real time, the audience feels the same tension and cannot escape, just as the family cannot.

units.title: An Inspector Calls: Plot
units.summary: The three acts: the Birling celebration, the Inspector's chain of events, the confessions of Eric and the final telephone call.

p: The Birling family (Arthur, his wife Sybil, daughter Sheila and son Eric) celebrate Sheila's engagement to Gerald Croft, son of a rival business owner. Mr Birling makes a pleased speech about capitalism, saying that 'a man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own'. Just then the doorbell rings. Inspector Goole arrives, a mysterious and commanding man, to investigate the suicide of a young working-class woman, Eva Smith.

He explains that a 'chain of events' led to her death, and questions the family one by one. Mr Birling sacked Eva from his factory two years earlier because she led a strike for a small rise (from 22 shillings and sixpence to 25 shillings a week). He feels no regret. Eva then found work in a dress shop, Milward's, but Sheila, in a fit of jealousy and bad temper, had her dismissed because she thought the girl had smiled at her. Unlike her father, Sheila is horrified and feels remorse at once.

Sheila suspects that Gerald also knew the girl, and the Inspector proves it. Last summer Gerald met a girl called Daisy Renton (Eva's other name), rescued her from a rude local councillor and set her up in rooms as his mistress. He dropped her when it suited him. Gerald is ashamed but tries to excuse himself.

Mrs Birling, head of a women's charity, refused help to a pregnant young woman who called herself 'Mrs Birling', because she was offended by the girl's 'impertinence'. She told the girl to look for the father of the child and blamed him entirely. She insists that he should be 'made an example of'. The Inspector says, 'Then wait', as Eric Birling walks back into the room. The act ends on this cliffhanger.

img.alt: Five boxes in a row showing how Arthur Birling, Sheila, Gerald, Eric and Sybil Birling each harmed Eva Smith, with an arrow to her death
img.cap: The chain of events.

p: Eric confesses that he is the father. He met Eva ('Daisy') in a bar, got drunk and forced his way into her room. When she became pregnant he panicked and stole money from his father's office to support her. Eva refused to keep the stolen money, which shows that she had better morals than he did.

The Inspector then gives his last speech: 'There are millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths still left with us... We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other.' He warns that men who do not learn this will be taught 'in fire and blood and anguish'. He leaves.

Afterwards Gerald phones and finds that there is no Inspector Goole on the local police force, and Mr Birling learns that no girl has died today. The older Birlings and Gerald are delighted and think that it was all a hoax. They mock Eric and Sheila. But Sheila and Eric say it does not matter: 'We all did what we did.' They have changed.

The final twist: the phone rings. Mr Birling answers. A girl has just died on her way to the Infirmary after swallowing disinfectant, and an inspector is on his way to ask questions. The family stare in shock, and the play ends.

units.title: An Inspector Calls: Themes, Style and Characters
units.summary: Collective responsibility, class hypocrisy, the old and the young, and judgement; the well-made play, dramatic irony and the single setting; and the characters.

p: Social and collective responsibility: the main message, shown in the Inspector's last speech ('We are members of one body'). Priestley argues against the capitalist view of 'every man for himself' and demands that we care for the Eva Smiths of the world.

Class hypocrisy and inequality: the play shows the rotten core under the respectable surface of the Edwardian upper class. The Birlings use the poor (Mr Birling), abuse them (Eric and Gerald) and refuse them charity (Mrs Birling), while believing themselves to be good and moral.

The older against the younger generation: the older Birlings are set in their selfish ways and learn nothing. The younger ones (Sheila and Eric) can feel remorse, change and accept responsibility. They are the hope for the future.
Judgement and time: the Inspector gives a warning, and the family fails it. The telephone call at the end suggests that the real consequences are still to come.
The 'well-made play': a tight three-act structure in which tension grows, secrets are revealed one at a time, and there is a striking climax and a twist ending.
Dramatic irony: the audience knows that Mr Birling is wrong about the Titanic and about the likelihood of war, so his whole philosophy looks foolish from the start.
The single setting: one room makes the play tense and claustrophobic. The Birlings cannot escape the Inspector or their own guilt.

Inspector Goole: the driving force. Mysterious, all-knowing, commanding and single-minded. His name sounds like 'ghoul', which suggests a ghost or an angel: the voice of Priestley's social conscience, sent to judge the family.
Arthur Birling: pompous, selfish and arrogant; he stands for the faults of capitalism.
Sybil Birling: colder and crueller than her husband, a snob obsessed with class and reputation, who feels no remorse.
Sheila Birling: the most changed. She starts as a naive, giggling girl and becomes a strong, perceptive and moral young woman, the play's new conscience.
Eric Birling: weak and nervous, spoilt by his parents' example, but able to feel guilt and to want to change.
Gerald Croft: the 'in-betweener', polished and upper-class, who at last sides with the older generation, putting business and reputation before morality.

The play is a parable. Eva Smith stands for the whole working class, and the Birlings for the ruling class. Priestley's message is a command: if we do not learn to look after each other and share, we shall repeat the cycle of 'fire and blood and anguish' (wars and revolutions).

units.title: A Man for All Seasons: the Playwright, History and the Central Conflict
units.summary: Who Robert Bolt was, the history behind the play (Henry VIII's divorce and the Act of Supremacy) and Sir Thomas More's dilemma.

p: Robert Bolt (1924 to 1995) was an English playwright and screenwriter, famous for the films Lawrence of Arabia and Doctor Zhivago. Like Priestley, he held strong political views and was once arrested for protesting against nuclear weapons. But where Priestley wrote about collective responsibility, Bolt was interested in the individual conscience and the conflict between a person's private self and the demands of the state.
The play is based on a real conflict in 16th-century England.
The King's 'Great Matter': King Henry VIII was married to Catherine of Aragon, who had given him a daughter (Mary) but no male heir. Henry wanted a divorce so that he could marry Anne Boleyn.
The religious conflict: England was a Catholic country and the Pope in Rome was head of the Church. The Pope, under pressure from Spain (Catherine's homeland), would not grant the divorce.
The break with Rome: Henry broke with the Catholic Church, made himself 'Supreme Head of the Church of England' and granted himself the divorce.
The Oath of Supremacy: to force his subjects to accept this, Henry made them swear an oath (under the Act of Supremacy) recognising his new title. Refusing the oath was treason, punishable by death.
Sir Thomas More was one of the most respected men in England: a brilliant lawyer, a devout Catholic, Lord Chancellor (the highest office after the King), and a personal friend of Henry VIII.

More is trapped. As an Englishman he wants to obey his King. As a Catholic he cannot accept that the King is head of the Church; his conscience forbids it. As a lawyer, he knows that if he simply stays silent the law cannot convict him of treason, because treason needs an act or a spoken word and not a thought.
So the play is about More's attempt to use silence as a shield to save his life without betraying his conscience. His enemies, such as Thomas Cromwell, must bend the law and use lies to trap him.

units.title: A Man for All Seasons: Plot, Themes and Characters
units.summary: The main events of the play, the themes of integrity, conscience, power and the law, and the characters of More, Rich, Cromwell and the Common Man.

p: Richard Rich, an ambitious young man, asks Sir Thomas More for a post at court. More advises him to be a teacher, and refuses to help him get power. Cardinal Wolsey dies and More becomes Lord Chancellor. King Henry visits More at his house and asks for his support for the divorce. More cannot give it, because of his conscience. Rich, meanwhile, turns to Thomas Cromwell, the King's ruthless minister, and starts to rise by betraying More.

More resigns as Chancellor rather than approve the King's plans. Cromwell searches for a way to make him speak. The Act of Supremacy is passed and More refuses the oath. He is sent to the Tower of London. His wife Alice and daughter Margaret beg him to give way, but More will not. At his trial, More says nothing against the King. Rich gives false evidence (perjury) that More denied the King's title. In return, he is made Attorney-General for Wales. More is found guilty. Once he is condemned, he finally speaks openly, saying that the law has been twisted. He is executed in 1535.

Integrity and conscience: the title means that More's 'self' is so firm that he is the same man in every 'season', in good times and in bad. He will not sell his soul. His opposite is Richard Rich, a man for no season, who is bought with power and commits perjury to condemn More.
More's famous line to Rich asks what a man gains by losing his soul for the whole world, 'but for Wales, Richard?'
Power: the state against the individual. The play asks whether a person may refuse the state if the state does wrong.
The law, morality and silence: More loves the law and uses it as a shield. He thinks that silence keeps him safe. His tragedy is that his enemies break the law (with a lying witness) to destroy him.

Sir Thomas More: intelligent, witty, loving, a firm man of conscience. Richard Rich: ambitious, weak and corrupt. Thomas Cromwell: ruthless, practical and willing to bend the law. King Henry VIII: charming but selfish and powerful. Alice and Margaret: More's loving family, who beg him to save himself. The Common Man: a character who plays many small parts (More's steward, a boatman, the jailer, a juror and the executioner). He stands for the average person who is practical, not heroic, and 'goes along' with those in power to survive, the opposite of More's heroic integrity.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 Literature in English Third Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: In Third Term you study prose and poetry. You begin with the elements of prose fiction (plot, setting, characterisation, theme and point of view). Then you study two novels: So the Path Does Not Die by Pede Hollist (African prose) and To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee (non-African prose). After that you study six poems: four African (Gabriel Okara, Niyi Osundare, Wole Soyinka, Syl Cheney-Coker) and two non-African (Maya Angelou and Lord Byron).

If you can, read the novels and the poems themselves; the notes are a guide, not a replacement. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

The notes were checked against published study guides. Where the original lesson plan gave names or details that do not match the published works (for example for So the Path Does Not Die and for Soyinka's 'Night'), the notes say so and use the corrected material.

units.title: Features and Elements of Prose: Plot, Setting and Characterisation
units.summary: What prose is, and three elements of prose fiction: plot, setting and characterisation.

p: Prose is one of the three main genres, with poetry and drama. It is written or spoken language in its ordinary form, without regular metre or rhyme. Form: it is written in sentences grouped into paragraphs (and, in a long work such as a novel, chapters). Language: ordinary, natural and following normal speech and grammar, unlike the compressed, rhythmic language of poetry. Purpose: to narrate (tell a story), describe, inform or argue. Varieties: fiction (imaginative: novels, short stories) and non-fiction (factual: biography, essays, textbooks).

Plot is the series of connected events of a story and how they are arranged to create an effect. It has five parts: exposition (the beginning: characters, setting and first conflict), rising action (complications that build suspense), climax (the highest point of tension, the turning point), falling action (events after the climax, as tension eases) and resolution or denouement (the end, when the conflict is settled and a new normal is set up).

Setting is the time and place of the story: the backdrop of the action. Physical setting: the location (a city, a village, a room). Temporal setting: the time (the 1930s, wartime, a single day). Social or cultural setting: the customs, values and rules of the society in the story (for example, a racist town in the 1930s). Setting is not just a backdrop: it can create mood, influence how characters behave and even be a source of conflict.

Characterisation is how a writer creates and develops the people in a story. The protagonist is the main character, around whom the story revolves. The antagonist is the character or force that opposes the protagonist.

Direct characterisation: the writer tells us what a character is like ('Sade was a kind and generous woman'). Indirect characterisation: the writer shows us through the character's actions, speech and thoughts, and through the way other characters react.
Types of character: a round (dynamic) character is complex and changes and grows through the story. A flat (static) character is simple, one-sided and does not change.

units.title: Theme and Point of View
units.summary: What a theme is (and is not), and the three main points of view: first person, third person limited and third person omniscient.

p: Theme is the central idea, message or deeper meaning of a story: a truth about life or human nature that the writer explores. A theme is not a single word such as 'love'. It is a statement or idea about that word, such as 'Love needs great sacrifice' or 'Love can be a destructive force'. A story can have one major theme and several minor themes.
Point of view is the viewpoint or 'lens' through which the story is told.
First-person point of view: the narrator is a character in the story and uses 'I' ('I walked down the street'). The reader knows only what this one character knows, thinks and sees.
Third-person limited: the narrator stands outside the story and uses 'he', 'she' or 'they', but knows the thoughts and feelings of only one character.

Third-person omniscient (all-knowing): the narrator stands outside the story and knows everything. This 'god-like' narrator can tell what all the characters think and feel and can be in several places at once.

p: The point of view decides what the reader learns and how far the reader trusts the narrator. To Kill a Mockingbird is told in the first person by an adult looking back at her childhood. That combines a child's fresh, honest observation with an adult's understanding.

units.title: So the Path Does Not Die: the Author, Settings and Story
units.summary: Who Pede Hollist is, the novel's settings (Sierra Leone and the United States) and an outline of the story of Fina's journey.

p: Pede Hollist is a Sierra Leonean-American author and academic. He was born in Sierra Leone and later moved to the United States, where he became a professor of English. This diaspora background is the key to his novel: he is interested in the lives of Africans in the West and in their complicated relationship with the 'home' they left. So the Path Does Not Die is his first novel.

The novel moves between two worlds. Sierra Leone (Freetown and the villages of the protagonist's childhood) stands for tradition, community, family obligation and roots. It is the 'path' of the title. The United States (the Washington area) stands for modern life, individual freedom, Western education and a new life, where Fina builds her adult life. The tension between the two worlds drives the novel.

The heroine is Finaba (Fina) Marah. Her story begins on the night that her circumcision, a traditional rite of passage for girls, is stopped, and she escapes from it. The novel then follows her from childhood in Sierra Leone through her teenage years in Freetown to her adult life in the United States. She searches for a place to belong.

In America she builds a life, and she has friendships and a relationship with Cammy, a Trinidadian urologist who becomes her fiancé. The two disagree about circumcision, and secrets from Fina's past put their relationship in danger. Her friend Aman and Aman's Nigerian fiancé Bayo, her foster sister Edna and Edna's husband Kizzy, and a war-traumatised teenager, Mawaf, each have their own stories alongside hers.
At the end Fina goes back to Sierra Leone, where she works for children who have been hurt by the country's civil war.

The lesson plan describes a heroine called 'Adefinah M'bayo' living in Tampa, Florida, with a boyfriend called Chris, and a Sierra Leonean doctor named Bola in a village called Rotifunk. These details do not match the published novel. The heroine is Finaba (Fina) Marah, and the supporting characters are those listed above. Please use these corrected details.

units.title: So the Path Does Not Die: Themes, Characters and Style
units.summary: Belonging and identity, tradition against modernity, the exile's experience, women and custom, and war and trauma, with the characters and the symbol of the path.

p: Belonging and identity: the central theme. Fina belongs to two worlds. In America she is the African, and in Sierra Leone she may be seen as the one who left. The novel asks what 'home' is: the place where you were born, or the place where you build your life. Fina must make an identity that respects both her roots (the 'path') and the route her life takes.

Tradition against modernity: Fina is a modern, educated, independent woman in a society whose customs make demands on a woman. The novel shows her trying to decide which customs to keep and which to resist, especially customs about women's bodies and roles.
The experience of leaving and returning (the diaspora): the novel looks at what it means to live abroad and go back, to see your country with new eyes, with its beauty and its problems.
Women, friendship and support: Fina's friends and her foster sister help her to survive and to understand herself.
War and its trauma: the effects of Sierra Leone's civil war on people, especially children, and the importance of healing.

Fina (Finaba Marah): the protagonist, a round and dynamic character. She starts out as a young person running from something and gradually grows into someone who can face her past and use it to help others.
Cammy: her fiancé, whose different background and views create conflict.
Aman and Bayo, Edna and Kizzy: friends and family who show different ways of living between cultures.
Mawaf: a teenager hurt by war; through him the novel shows the cost of conflict and Fina's calling.
The path: the main symbol. It stands for heritage, connection to family and identity. Keeping it clear so that it does not 'die' means staying in touch with one's roots.
The story uses realistic detail of life in Sierra Leone and in America, the thoughts and feelings of its heroine, and sayings and proverbs of the culture to give a sense of place.

units.title: To Kill a Mockingbird: the Author, Context and Opening Chapters
units.summary: Who Harper Lee was, the Jim Crow South and the Scottsboro case, and the story of chapters 1 to 5.

p: Harper Lee (1926 to 2016) was an American novelist. She was born and grew up in Monroeville, Alabama, a small Southern town that gave her the setting for the novel. The book is partly autobiographical: Lee's father, Amasa Coleman Lee, was a lawyer and member of the Alabama legislature, like Atticus Finch in the novel. She grew up in the Jim Crow South, a time and place of strict, legal racial segregation and deep prejudice. The novel was written in the 1950s and published in 1960, at the start of the American Civil Rights Movement.

The Scottsboro Boys: in the 1930s, nine young Black men in Alabama were falsely accused of raping two white women, and were convicted by all-white juries despite strong evidence of their innocence. This real case is a clear parallel to the fictional trial of Tom Robinson.

Chapter 1: the story is told by Jean Louise 'Scout' Finch, now an adult, remembering her childhood in the 'tired old town' of Maycomb, Alabama. She introduces her family: her father Atticus (a respected lawyer), her older brother Jem and their cook Calpurnia. A boy called Charles Baker 'Dill' Harris comes to spend the summer and becomes fascinated with the 'haunted' house of their neighbour, Arthur 'Boo' Radley, a mysterious recluse.
Chapters 1 to 3: the children dare each other to touch the Radley house, act out stories about Boo and try to make him come out. Boo stands for mystery, superstition and the town's prejudice.

Chapters 2 and 3: Scout starts school and it goes badly. Her new teacher, Miss Caroline, does not understand Maycomb and punishes Scout for already being able to read (Atticus taught her). Scout is also in trouble for explaining why Walter Cunningham will not accept a quarter (the Cunninghams are poor but proud and will not take charity). Scout meets the Ewells, such as Burris Ewell, a poor family who are dirty and disrespectful and live 'like animals'.
Chapter 4: the children find small gifts (gum, old coins) in the knothole of an oak tree on the Radley property. It is the first sign that Boo is not a 'phantom' but a real person who may be kind.

units.title: To Kill a Mockingbird: Setting, Tone and the Whole Story
units.summary: Maycomb in the Great Depression, the novel's nostalgic yet innocent tone, and an outline of the whole story from the trial of Tom Robinson to Boo Radley's rescue.

p: Maycomb, Alabama, 1933 to 1935. Time: the Great Depression, which explains the widespread poverty of families like the Cunninghams and the slow pace of the town. Place: a small, fictional Southern town, 'a tired old town'. Social atmosphere: the town is rigid, gossipy and ruled by Jim Crow laws (racial segregation). It is deeply racist and prejudiced. The 'disease' of Maycomb is its prejudice, which Atticus must face.

The tone comes from a double perspective: an adult Scout looks back at her childhood self. The tone is nostalgic and amusing, because the adult remembers her childhood with humour and affection. It is also innocent and observant, because the child's clear, simple eye sees the adult world logically, which makes the town's racism look absurd. The tone is light and funny in the early chapters, and becomes darker and more serious when the trial begins.

Over three summers the children are fascinated by Boo Radley. Atticus agrees to defend Tom Robinson, a Black man accused of raping a white woman, Mayella Ewell. Many in town turn against Atticus, and Scout fights children who insult him. At the trial, Atticus shows that Tom could not have done the crime (Tom's left arm was crippled) and that Mayella and her father Bob Ewell are lying. Even so, the all-white jury finds Tom guilty. Tom is later shot dead while trying to escape from prison.

Bob Ewell, shamed by the trial, takes revenge. On Halloween night he attacks Jem and Scout as they walk home. Boo Radley rescues them and Bob Ewell is killed in the struggle. The sheriff, Heck Tate, decides to say that Ewell fell on his own knife, to protect Boo from public attention. Atticus agrees. Scout stands on the Radley porch and sees the world from Boo's side, and understands Atticus's advice to 'climb into someone's skin and walk around in it'.

units.title: To Kill a Mockingbird: Themes, Characters and Style
units.summary: Racism and injustice, innocence and the mockingbird symbol, moral courage and other prejudices; the characters; and the child narrator and Southern Gothic style.

p: Racism and social injustice: the central theme. Maycomb is deeply racist. The trial of Tom Robinson shows an innocent Black man convicted because the jury will not take his word against that of a white woman.

Innocence and its loss: the title is the central metaphor. Atticus tells the children it is 'a sin to kill a mockingbird' because mockingbirds only 'sing their hearts out for us'. The 'mockingbirds' in the novel are Tom Robinson and Boo Radley, innocent and harmless men who are damaged by society's evil. The trial forces Jem and Scout to lose their childhood innocence as they see the unfairness of the adult world.

Courage, moral and physical: courage is not 'a man with a gun in his hand'. True courage is moral courage. Atticus defends Tom knowing that he will lose and that his family will suffer. Mrs Dubose, an old racist woman, shows courage by fighting her morphine addiction to 'die free'.

Prejudice beyond race: class prejudice (the town looks down on the poor Cunninghams and the Ewells), social prejudice (the town imprisons Boo Radley in rumour because he is different) and gender prejudice (Scout is told to 'stop being a girl' and act 'like a lady').

Scout (Jean Louise Finch): the narrator and protagonist, a tomboy, intelligent, outspoken and quick-tempered. The novel is a bildungsroman (a coming-of-age story) about her growth from innocence to understanding.
Atticus Finch: the moral centre of the novel. A respected lawyer, widower and patient father, he stands for integrity, justice, quiet courage and empathy.
Jem Finch: Scout's older brother, idealistic and protective. The unfair verdict hits him hardest and pushes him into adolescence.
Boo Radley (Arthur): a 'mockingbird', a recluse hurt by a cruel father. He is a symbol of hidden kindness who leaves gifts for the children and saves their lives.
Tom Robinson: an innocent Black man accused of rape, the other 'mockingbird' and a symbol of racial injustice.
Bob Ewell: the antagonist, a poor, hateful, racist man who represents the evil side of Maycomb.

First-person narrator, past tense: the adult Scout tells the story, which allows Lee to mix the child's fresh observations with an adult's reflection. This double view is the novel's greatest strength and is why the child narrator is so effective in criticising racism.
Southern Gothic: a style that looks at the dark, 'haunted' side of the South. Boo Radley, the 'mad' dog, the town's dark secrets and its decaying social order are all Gothic elements.

units.title: African Poetry: 'Once Upon a Time' by Gabriel Okara
units.summary: The poet, the speaker, the meaning, themes, tone and devices of Okara's poem about a father who has learnt to be false and wants to be genuine again.

p: Gabriel Okara (1921 to 2019) was a Nigerian poet and novelist from the Ijaw people of the Niger Delta. His poems often set traditional African values against the cold, false ways of modern society.

A father is speaking to his young son. He remembers a time ('once upon a time', as in a children's story) when people laughed with their hearts and their eyes. Now, in a modern, Westernised and hypocritical world, people laugh only with their teeth, shake hands without feeling, and their cold eyes search behind your shadow. The father himself has also learnt to be false. He has learnt to wear many faces 'like dresses' (a home face, an office face, a street face, a host face), to say 'Goodbye' when he means 'good riddance', and to say 'glad to meet you' when he is not glad. He begs his son to teach him to 'unlearn' these false habits and to learn again how to laugh as he used to, because his laugh in the mirror shows only teeth, 'like a snake's bare fangs'.

Loss of innocence and cultural nostalgia: the 'once upon a time' stands for a time of genuine, warm African life. Hypocrisy: the false smiles and handshakes of modern society. Cultural conflict (Africa and the West): the poem mourns the loss of warm traditional values to cold modern manners. The innocence of children: the child, still genuine, is the teacher.

Tone: nostalgic, sad, regretful and bitter. Repetition: 'once upon a time', 'laugh', 'good-bye', which stress the loss. Simile: the laugh that is 'like a snake's bare fangs' shows that the new laughter is dangerous and false. Metaphor: wearing many faces 'like dresses' (a simile in form, but the idea of 'faces' as masks is a metaphor) shows personalities that can be put on and taken off. Irony: the father, an adult who should teach, begs to be taught by his son. The poem is written in free verse, close to speech, which suits its sincere feeling.

units.title: African Poetry: 'Not My Business' by Niyi Osundare
units.summary: The poet, the poem's three episodes and final stanza, its themes of apathy and oppression, the refrain and its simple style.

p: Niyi Osundare is a Nigerian poet, born in Ikere-Ekiti. His poetry is known for strong social and political concerns, a love of common people and simple, musical language.

The poem is a political poem about apathy (not caring) and its price. It is set in a country ruled by force, and critics link it to the military rule of the 1990s in Nigeria. The speaker sees an unnamed, powerful 'they' take his neighbours away one by one. Akanni is picked up at night and bundled off. Then Danladi is taken. Then Chinwe suffers too. After each event the speaker does nothing and comforts himself with the refrain 'Not my business'. In the last stanza, 'they' come for the speaker, and now there is no one left to speak for him.

Political oppression: the poem criticises brutal rule. Apathy and complicity: the central theme. It attacks the 'every man for himself' attitude. The price of silence: silence in the face of injustice is not safe. It only delays one's own turn.

Tone: casual, detached and even sarcastic in the early stanzas, then panicked and fearful in the last. Refrain: 'Not my business' is repeated to show the speaker's deliberate, foolish carelessness. Names: Akanni (Yoruba), Danladi (Hausa) and Chinwe (Igbo) are from three of Nigeria's major groups, so the suffering cuts across all ethnic lines. Simple diction: the plain, story-like language reads like a news report, which makes the events seem chillingly normal. Structure: short stanzas with a repeating pattern, and a final stanza that breaks the pattern.

The lesson plan gives specific 'crimes' for the three victims (being 'too bold', stretching a mat 'too wide' and having 'ideas'). Those reasons are not part of the poem's message: what matters is that each is taken away by 'they' and the speaker does nothing. When you answer questions, speak of what the poem makes clear: arbitrary seizure by the powerful, the repeated refrain and the speaker's own turn at the end. Check the text of the poem in your anthology for the exact wording.
