units.title: African Poetry: 'Night' by Wole Soyinka
units.summary: The poet, the meaning of Soyinka's 'Night' as a poem of fear and mortality, its imagery, tone, structure and devices.

p: Wole Soyinka (born 1934) is a Nigerian playwright, poet and essayist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986, the first African to do so. He is known for rich, dense language and for his strong views on freedom and injustice.

Night is normally a time of rest, but in this poem the speaker fears it. He wonders what kind of rest he can expect. The poem is spoken by a poet-figure who feels that he is as vulnerable as anyone who has been harmed in the dark. Night here is more than the time of day. It stands for human mortality, danger, the unknown and the end of life. In Yoruba tradition night is a dangerous time when wicked deeds are done, and life can be divided into morning, afternoon and night (old age). Critics link the poem to the violence, the war and the imprisonment of Soyinka's own time in Nigeria and to the loss of friends.

The poem uses images of fading and fear: a clam retreating into its shell, the light of the sea going out, a dimming crescent (moon), shadows falling through leaves and silent 'night thieves'. Night is personified, spoken of as a presence with power. The combination of images builds a mood of fear, loss and resignation.

Tone: anxious, mournful and resigned, with a trace of thoughtful acceptance. Structure: five stanzas, each building on the last, with enjambment (a thought running on across a stanza break) between stanzas two and three and three and four. The last stanza turns towards a faint hope but still ends with regret. Devices: personification of night, simile and metaphor, paradox, oxymoron (such as 'night children') and unusual word use that gives ordinary words deeper meaning.

The lesson plan describes images such as 'gourds of darkness' and 'metal leaves', and a speaker who is a worshipper at an altar. These do not match published readings of the poem. Use the imagery above, and always check the lines of the poem in your anthology.

units.title: African Poetry: 'The Breasts of the Sea' by Syl Cheney-Coker
units.summary: The poet, the sea as a mothering and murdering force, the poem's allusions to wars, slavery and science, its tone and its devices.

p: Syl Cheney-Coker, born in Freetown in 1945, is a Sierra Leonean poet and novelist. His poems often deal with the history and politics of Africa and with exile. The poem is also known as 'The Breast of the Sea' and appears in his collection Stone Child and Other Poems.

The poem looks at the 20th century as a century of wars, slavery and colonialism, political failure and damage to the environment, and at what these did to Africa and to Europe. Its central symbol is the sea. The sea is a mother, whose 'breasts' feed and comfort. But it is also a place that holds the dead and the dumped waste of many conflicts and of unrestrained science. It keeps a record of history. The poem opens with a sense of loss, at the middle of the action, and moves through references to Noah's flood, the Middle Passage (the slave route), Darwin's theory of evolution and the sinking of the Titanic. Later stanzas turn to Sierra Leone, to the civil conflicts of Africa and to exile.

The shared violence between Africa and Europe (wars, slavery, empire); political failure and civil conflict (Sierra Leone and Nigeria); the sea as a source of both life and death; the link between knowledge and power and the harm of unrestrained science; and the survivors who are left with lasting wounds.

Images: the sea as a mother with 'breasts'; 'new islands' (conflicts that keep appearing); pollution and toxins; a broken (fractured) claw; blight (a plant disease) for the century's sickness; and images of bodily injury, such as a broken back or torn clothing, with a 'balm' that promises healing but may not heal.

Tone: reflective and serious. Mood: pessimistic, doubting that history's damage can be repaired. Devices: metaphor and personification of the sea; allusion to Noah, the Middle Passage, the Titanic and Darwin; and a shift in the meaning of the word 'children', from nations that were harmed to the poor who survive.

The lesson plan reads the poem as a personal 'homecoming' with the speaker's 'blood' mixing with the 'salt' of the sea. Published analyses focus instead on the sea as a witness and dumping ground of 20th-century violence and on the century's wounds. Use the reading above and check your anthology's text.

units.title: Non-African Poetry: 'Still I Rise' by Maya Angelou
units.summary: The poet, the speaker and her oppressors, the poem's themes of resilience and self-worth, its tone and its devices.

p: Maya Angelou (1928 to 2014) was an American poet, memoirist and civil rights activist. 'Still I Rise' is one of her best-known poems and has become an anthem of pride and resistance.

The speaker talks straight to those who try to put her down (racists, sexists and all who try to break her). She asks whether her confidence ('sassiness') and pride upset them. She says that however they 'write her down in history' with bitter, twisted lies, tread her in the dirt or try to kill her with hatefulness, she will always rise. She compares her certainty to the moon, the sun and the tides, and she compares her value to wealth ('oil wells', 'gold mines'). She calls herself 'a black ocean, leaping and wide' and, at the end, 'the dream and the hope of the slave'.

Resilience and defiance: the main theme, the refusal to be beaten. Overcoming oppression: the poem is about overcoming racial (Black) and gender (female) oppression. Self-worth and pride: a bold statement of pride and joy.

Tone: defiant, proud, triumphant, cheeky, angry at times and finally joyful. Refrain: 'Still I rise' ties the poem together like an anthem. Simile: 'like dust, I'll rise'; shoulders 'like teardrops'. Rhetorical questions: 'Does my sassiness upset you?' and 'Did you want to see me broken?' challenge the oppressor directly. Metaphor: she is a 'black ocean' and has 'gold mines' and 'oil wells' (symbols of great natural wealth). The poem uses short stanzas with a strong beat and plain, direct speech.

units.title: Non-African Poetry: 'She Walks in Beauty' by Lord Byron
units.summary: The poet, the poem's praise of a woman whose outer beauty comes from inner goodness, its themes, tone, rhyme scheme and devices.

p: George Gordon, Lord Byron (1788 to 1824) was an English poet of the Romantic movement, which valued feeling, nature and the individual. He wrote 'She Walks in Beauty' in 1814, after seeing a beautiful woman in black mourning dress at a party.

The speaker is amazed by a woman's beauty. He compares it to a clear, starry night. Her beauty is a perfect balance ('dark and bright') of light and shade, seen in her face and hair. The poem's main idea is that her outer beauty comes from her inner goodness. Her thoughts are 'serenely sweet', and her mind is at peace with the world, and her heart is innocent.

Beauty, outer and inner: true beauty is a harmony of the physical and the spiritual. Harmony and perfection: the poem delights in balance, in light and dark, and in calm. Innocence: the woman's innocent heart is the source of her beauty.

Tone: admiring, thoughtful, romantic and peaceful. Simile: the first line compares her to the night. Alliteration: 'cloudless climes and starry skies'. Personification: the woman's thoughts 'express' themselves on her face. Contrast: dark and bright, shade and light. Structure: three stanzas of six lines each, with a strict ABABAB rhyme scheme and iambic tetrameter (four iambs, or eight syllables, in a line: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM). This regular, musical rhythm matches the 'harmony' that the poem describes.

units.title: Grammar: Nominalisation of Adjectives and Verbs
units.summary: How verbs and adjectives are turned into nouns by adding suffixes or by conversion, and why this makes writing formal.

p: Nominalisation is turning another part of speech, mostly a verb or an adjective, into a noun or noun phrase. It moves your writing from simple actions and qualities to ideas and things. It is a mark of formal, academic and professional writing.
Without nominalisation: 'The manager decided quickly. This was efficient.' With nominalisation: 'The manager's quick decision showed efficiency.'
This is the commonest way. Notice that the spelling often changes.

p: The word keeps the same form but works as a noun. 'His daily run keeps him fit.' 'There was a big fight after the match.' 'I need a good rest.' 'She has a great love for music.'
'The company invested heavily in research, which caused it to innovate rapidly' becomes 'The company's heavy investment in research led to rapid innovation.'
'The patient was anxious, and this was evident to the doctor' becomes 'The patient's anxiety was evident to the doctor.'
'If we collaborate effectively, we will succeed' becomes 'Effective collaboration will lead to success.'

units.title: Oral English: Voiced and Voiceless Consonants
units.summary: What voicing means, how to test for it, and the pairs of consonants that differ only in voicing.

p: Consonant sounds differ in whether the vocal cords vibrate. In a voiceless sound the vocal cords are apart and do not vibrate; only air passes. In a voiced sound the vocal cords are close and vibrate, giving a buzzing feeling in the throat.
Test: put your fingers on your throat. Say 'ssssss' (like a snake): nothing. Say 'zzzzzz' (like a bee): you feel a buzz. So /s/ is voiceless and /z/ is voiced.
Many consonants form pairs with exactly the same mouth position; only voicing differs.
Your lesson note gives 'chin / jin' as a pair. 'Jin' is not a normal word, so use 'chin / gin' or 'cheap / jeep'. The words 'thin' and 'thy' in the original table are also fine as /θ/ and /ð/.

units.title: Summary Writing: Features and Rules
units.summary: What a summary is, the features of a good summary, a list of do's and don'ts and a worked example.

p: A summary is a short, objective and fluent statement of the main ideas of a text, written in your own words. It shows that you understand the passage by taking away examples, extra details and repetition and keeping only the central message. It is not a comment on the text or a criticism of it.

Brevity: much shorter than the original. Clarity: easy to understand and correct in grammar. Objectivity: only the author's ideas, not yours. Completeness: all the main points that answer the question. Paraphrasing: mostly in your own words.

units.title: Oral English: Consonant Clusters
units.summary: What consonant clusters are, two-, three- and four-consonant clusters at the start and end of words, and the error of epenthesis.

p: A consonant cluster is a group of two or more consonant sounds together in one syllable with no vowel sound between them. Saying them well makes your English clear and natural. A common mistake is epenthesis, adding a vowel (usually the schwa /ə/) inside a cluster. Correct: film /fɪlm/. Wrong: 'fi-lim'. Another example: 'school' pronounced 'sukool'.

Initial (at the start): /s/ plus consonant (stay, sky, slow, swim, snow); /l/ blends (blow, clean, fly, glass, play); /r/ blends (bring, cry, dry, free, grow, pray, tree). Final (at the end): -st (last, past, test), -nd (hand, send, find), -sk (task, desk, ask), -mp (jump, lamp, camp), -ft (left, gift, soft), -ld (gold, hold, child).

Initial clusters nearly always begin with /s/: /spr/ (spring, spray, sprout), /str/ (street, strong, strike), /skr/ (script, scream, scrub), /spl/ (splash, split, spleen). Final clusters often come from adding -s or -ed: -nts (tents, wants), -mps (jumps, lamps), -sks (tasks, desks), -pts (scripts, adapts), -lps (helps, gulps).

These are usually at the end of words. Say each consonant cleanly and quickly without inserting a vowel: twelfths /twɛlfθs/, fifths, strengths /strɛŋθs/, lengths, texts /tɛksts/, next /nɛkst/, glimpsed /ɡlɪmpst/, prompts /prɒmpts/, attempts.

units.title: Writing: the Expository Essay
units.summary: The purpose and structure of an expository essay: introduction with hook and thesis, three body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion; with a worked outline.

p: An expository essay explains, describes or informs. Its aim is a balanced, factual explanation. Unlike an argumentative essay, it does not try to persuade the reader to share an opinion. It 'exposes' information clearly and logically. The tone is objective.
Think of a house: the introduction is the foundation, the body paragraphs are the walls and the conclusion is the roof.

Introduction (one paragraph): a hook (a striking fact, a question or a statement to catch interest); background (short context or definitions); the thesis statement (one clear sentence stating the main point).

Body (usually three paragraphs): each paragraph develops one main point that supports the thesis. It begins with a topic sentence and continues with supporting details (facts, statistics, examples, explanations), with an optional concluding sentence. Use transitions such as furthermore, moreover, in addition, consequently and for instance.
Conclusion (one paragraph): restate the thesis in new words; summarise the main points; end with a final thought or recommendation. Do not bring in new ideas.

Topic: 'The three major causes of road accidents in Nigeria'. Thesis: 'The high rate of road accidents in Nigeria is chiefly caused by human error, poor vehicle maintenance and inadequate road infrastructure.'

Body 1: human error (speeding, dangerous overtaking, driving under the influence, using the phone). Body 2: poor condition of vehicles (bald tyres, faulty brakes, broken lights, weak inspection). Body 3: bad roads (potholes, no signs, dead streetlights, eroded roads). Conclusion: accidents come from driver behaviour, vehicle condition and road quality, so stricter law enforcement, public education and investment in roads are needed.

units.activity: Write a 400-word expository essay on 'The roles and responsibilities of a good citizen' or 'The main causes and effects of the erosion of cultural values in your community'. Write a thesis for: 'The benefits of a digital literacy programme in secondary schools.'

units.title: Structure: Nouns and Noun Phrases
units.summary: Types of nouns, the parts of a noun phrase, the five functions of a noun phrase and the difference between a noun phrase and a noun clause.

p: Proper: names (Chinua, Abuja, Christmas). Common: general names (artist, city). Abstract: ideas and qualities (freedom, bravery, justice). Collective: groups (team, flock, fleet). Concrete: things the senses can perceive (rain, sand, perfume). Countable: have plurals (book, books; child, children). Uncountable: no plural (advice, furniture, information).

A noun phrase is a group of words built round a noun (the headword) which works as one unit. Structure: (determiner) + (pre-modifiers) + headword + (post-modifiers). Determiners: a, an, the, this, my, some, five. Pre-modifiers: adjectives or other nouns ('university student'). Post-modifiers: prepositional phrases, relative clauses, participle phrases.
Examples: 'a brilliant idea' (determiner, pre-modifier, headword); 'a brilliant idea for a new project' (adds a post-modifier); 'the tall, intelligent boy who won the prize'.

Subject (S): [The diligent student] passed the exam. Object (O): He bought [a new bicycle]. Subject complement (C): Mr Bello is [a dedicated teacher]. Object complement (C): They elected him [their chairman]. Object of a preposition (OP): She put the book on [the wooden table].

A noun phrase has no subject and verb of its own: 'I know [the correct answer to the question].' A noun clause has its own subject and verb and works as a noun. It is introduced by words such as that, what, why, how, whether, whoever: 'I know [what you did last summer].' '[Why he resigned] remains a mystery' (the clause is the subject). 'The truth is [that she never arrived]' (the clause is the subject complement).

units.activity: Identify the noun phrase and its function: 'He painted the old garden fence.' (the old garden fence: object.) 'Her greatest ambition is to become a surgeon.' (Her greatest ambition: subject; a surgeon: subject complement of the infinitive.) Is it a noun phrase or clause: 'I understand what you mean'? (noun clause.)

units.title: Oral English: Transcription and Stress Marking
units.summary: The International Phonetic Alphabet, pure vowels and diphthongs, and basic rules for marking word stress.

p: Transcription is writing speech sounds with the symbols of the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), so pronunciation can be recorded exactly, whatever the spelling. Word stress is extra force on one syllable, making it louder, longer and higher in pitch. Correct stress is often more important for being understood than perfect individual sounds.

Pure vowels (monophthongs): /iː/ see, beat; /ɪ/ sit, bin; /e/ bed, pen; /æ/ cat, bad; /ɑː/ car, father; /ɒ/ hot, clock; /ɔː/ saw, born; /ʊ/ put, book; /uː/ too, food; /ʌ/ cup, luck; /ɜː/ bird, fern; /ə/ about, sister (the schwa, the most common vowel sound).
Diphthongs (gliding vowels): /eɪ/ day, make; /aɪ/ my, time; /ɔɪ/ boy, coin; /aʊ/ now, house; /əʊ/ go, home; /ɪə/ here, beard; /eə/ hair, care; /ʊə/ pure, tour.

The stress mark (ˈ) is put before the stressed syllable. One-syllable words carry the stress (dog, run). Two-syllable nouns and adjectives usually take stress on the first syllable (PRESent, HAPpy); two-syllable verbs usually on the second (preSENT, deCIDE, beGIN). In longer words the suffix often decides: stress the syllable before -tion, -sion, -ic, -ity, -graphy (eduCAtion, ecoNOmic, aBILity, phoTOgraphy); stress falls on -ee and -eer (employEE, engiNEER).
photograph /ˈfəʊtəɡrɑːf/ (first syllable); photographer /fəˈtɒɡrəfə/ (second syllable, because of -grapher); photographic /ˌfəʊtəˈɡræfɪk/ (third syllable, before -ic).

units.title: Structure: Pronouns
units.summary: The eight kinds of pronoun (personal, possessive, demonstrative, interrogative, reflexive, relative, reciprocal and indefinite) and the rules for using them correctly.

p: A pronoun takes the place of a noun or noun phrase to avoid repetition. 'The student said the student would bring the student's book' becomes 'The student said she would bring her book.'
They change form (case) with their job in the sentence.

Subject form for the doer: 'She is here.' 'He and I went to the market.' Object form after verbs and prepositions: 'He saw me.' 'I gave the book to him.' 'This is between you and me.' The common error 'between you and I' is wrong because 'between' is a preposition and needs the object form.

Possessive adjective (before a noun) and possessive pronoun (stands alone): my / mine; your / yours; his / his; her / hers; its / its; our / ours; their / theirs. 'This is my book.' 'This book is mine.' Note: 'its' (belonging to it) has no apostrophe; 'it's' means 'it is' or 'it has'.

Demonstrative: this, that (singular); these, those (plural). Interrogative (ask questions): who (subject), whom (object, formal), whose (possession), which (choice), what (things). Reflexive (the object is the same as the subject): myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves; also used for emphasis ('I myself will do it'). Relative (introduce a clause about a noun): who, whom, whose, which, that. Reciprocal (mutual): each other (usually two) and one another (usually more than two). Indefinite: anybody, everyone, nothing, each, either, neither (singular); both, few, many, several (plural); all, any, more, most, none, some (either).
Rule: singular indefinite pronouns take a singular verb: 'Everyone is here', not 'Everyone are here'.

units.title: Summary Writing: Reading to Summarise
units.summary: The five steps for writing a good summary: interrogate the question, read for gist, read for extraction, paraphrase, and write and connect.

p: A good summary is the result of careful reading. The skill is not writing quickly but reading intelligently.
Step 1: question the question. Read the summary question first. Find the command: 'summarise the causes', 'list the effects', 'state the solutions'. This gives you a filter for reading.
Step 2: first reading for gist. Read once at a steady pace to see the topic, the main argument and the plan of the passage.

Step 3: second reading for extraction. Read slowly with a pen. Underline only the sentences that answer the question. Ignore examples, illustrations, statistics (unless central), rhetorical questions, repetition and personal stories. Make a numbered skeleton outline of the key ideas.

Step 4: paraphrase. Express each idea in your own words by using synonyms (important becomes crucial), changing sentence structure (active to passive: 'The storm damaged the crops' becomes 'The crops were damaged by the storm') or changing the word class (nominalisation: 'The company decided to invest' becomes 'The company's decision was to invest'). Example: 'The pervasive and unrelenting nature of unemployment among the youth has led to a disturbing level of restiveness' becomes 'Widespread youth unemployment is a major cause of social unrest.'

Step 5: write and connect. Turn the points into fluent prose with connectives: adding (furthermore, moreover), contrast (however, nevertheless), cause and effect (consequently, as a result, therefore), sequence (firstly, subsequently, finally). Obey the sentence or word limit strictly.

units.title: Oral English: Word Stress
units.summary: Rules of word stress for two-syllable words, longer words with suffixes and compounds, with the noun-verb stress shift and worked examples.

p: Word stress is the rhythm of English: one syllable in a longer word is louder, longer and higher. Wrong stress can make a word hard to recognise. Notice the family: PHOtograph (the picture), phoTOgrapher (the person), photoGRAphic (the adjective).

Most two-syllable nouns and adjectives are stressed on the first syllable: TAble, CLImate, HAPpy, CLEver. Many two-syllable verbs are stressed on the second: preSENT, deCIDE, reCEIVE, beGIN. Many words are both noun and verb, and the stress moves: CONduct (noun) / conDUCT (verb); REcord / reCORD; CONflict / conFLICT; REbel / reBEL; PROduce / proDUCE; IMport / imPORT.

Stress the syllable immediately BEFORE these endings: -tion, -sion (examiNAtion, deCIsion); -ic, -ical (ecoNOmic, hisTORical); -ity (aBILity, possiBILity); -graphy (phoTOgraphy, geOgraphy); -logy (biOlogy, psyCHOlogy).
Stress falls ON these endings: -ee (employEE, refuGEE); -eer (engiNEER, pioNEER); -ette (cigarETTE); -esque (picturESQUE).
Words ending in -ify (and -efy) are usually stressed on the third syllable from the end: PURify, SIGnify, CLASSify, JUStify. Your lesson plan marks pu-RI-fy and sig-NI-fy; that is not correct.

Compound nouns stress the first element: BLACKboard, FOOTball, SUNlight, HEADphones, BIRTHday. Compound adjectives and verbs stress the second: well-KNOWN, old-FASHioned, overFLOW, underSTAND. So the noun GREENhouse and the adjective green-FINgered follow different patterns.

POLitics, poLITical, politiCIan (before -ical and -ian). DEMocrat, deMOCracy, demoCRATic. Some words need a dictionary: analysis is aNAlysis; responsibility is responsiBILity; development is deVELopment; textbook is TEXTbook; overcome is overCOME.

units.title: Listening Skills
units.summary: The five stages of listening, three kinds of barrier to listening and a listening practice with answers.

p: Listening is the most used language skill, yet it is often neglected. Hearing is passive: sound reaches the ear. Listening is active: you receive, build meaning from and respond to spoken language.

1. Hearing: sound waves reach the ear and the brain. 2. Attending: you focus on the message and ignore other sounds. 3. Understanding: you give meaning to the sounds by decoding words and grammar and linking them to what you know. 4. Responding: you give feedback, in words (a question) or without words (nodding, eye contact). 5. Remembering: you store the information. This is where note-taking helps.

Physical barriers: noise, a poor phone line, a speaker who talks too fast or too softly. Psychological barriers: your bias, prejudice or feelings (anger, worry) twist the message. Mental barriers: inner distractions such as daydreaming, boredom, or planning your reply instead of listening (the 'rebuttal tendency').

Your teacher reads: 'The National Electricity Regulatory Commission has announced a new tariff that takes effect next month. The Chairman, at a press conference in Abuja, said the new system is designed to be fairer, with consumers who use more electricity paying a higher rate. He assured the public that lifeline tariffs would remain for low-income households. The increase, he argued, is needed to attract investment and improve the failing national grid, which has suffered decades of underfunding.'

Questions and answers: Who announced the tariff? The National Electricity Regulatory Commission. What is the main principle? Heavier users pay more. What assurance was given to low-income households? Lifeline tariffs remain. Why the increase? To attract investment and improve the grid.

units.title: Writing: the Argumentative Essay
units.summary: The structure of an argumentative essay with a clear contention, two supporting points, a counter-argument with rebuttal and a strong conclusion, with a worked outline on banning single-use plastics.

p: An argumentative essay researches a topic, weighs evidence and takes a firm position. Its aim is to persuade. Unlike an expository essay, which is neutral, it defends a stand with logic and evidence.

Introduction: a hook (a startling statistic, a provocative question or a quotation); background (the context of the debate); and the thesis or contention, a clear, debatable and forceful statement of your stand ('This essay will argue that...').

Body paragraph 1: your first point with a topic sentence and evidence (facts, statistics, examples, reasoning) and an explanation of how it supports your point. Body paragraph 2: a second and stronger point (use transitions: furthermore, moreover) with new evidence.

Body paragraph 3: the counter-argument and rebuttal, which is what marks out an argumentative essay. Counter-argument: state the opposite view fairly ('Opponents say that...'). Rebuttal: knock it down at once with stronger reasons ('However...').
Conclusion: restate the thesis in new, strong words; sum up your points and the rebuttal; end with a clincher (a warning, prediction or call to action).

Topic: 'Should single-use plastics be banned in Nigeria?' Thesis (for the ban): 'The damage to the environment caused by single-use plastics is so severe that a government ban is justified and necessary for our ecosystems and citizens.' Body 1: plastics are a main cause of pollution (clogged drains, litter, harm to animals). Body 2: pollution threatens health and costs money (flooding, mosquito breeding, clean-up costs). Body 3: critics say a ban means job losses and inconvenience; rebuttal: a phased ban allows adjustment and creates jobs in paper, glass and reusable cloth, and the short-term inconvenience is a small price. Conclusion: the costs of doing nothing are greater than the difficulties of a ban.

units.title: Structure: Plural Forms of Nouns
units.summary: Regular plurals, plurals of nouns in -o, -y, -f and -fe, irregular and foreign plurals, and plurals of compound nouns.

p: Add -s: boy, boys; car, cars. Add -es after -s, -ss, -x, -ch, -sh, -z: bus, buses; box, boxes; church, churches; wish, wishes; quiz, quizzes. Nouns in -o: some take -es (potato, tomato, hero) and some only -s (photo, piano, kilo). Nouns in -y: after a consonant change y to ies (baby, babies; city, cities); after a vowel add -s (boy, day, key). Nouns in -f or -fe usually change to -ves (leaf, leaves; wife, wives; knife, knives; shelf, shelves); exceptions: chief, chiefs; roof, roofs; belief, beliefs; proof, proofs.

Vowel change: man, men; woman, women; foot, feet; tooth, teeth; goose, geese; mouse, mice. -en plurals: child, children; ox, oxen. Zero plurals (no change): species, series, means, crossroads, sheep, deer, fish (fishes refers to several kinds).

From Latin and Greek, common in academic English: -us to -i (cactus, cacti; syllabus, syllabi; radius, radii); -a to -ae (formula, formulae; larva, larvae; vertebra, vertebrae); -um to -a (datum, data; medium, media; bacterium, bacteria; curriculum, curricula); -is to -es (crisis, crises; analysis, analyses; thesis, theses; oasis, oases); -on to -a (criterion, criteria; phenomenon, phenomena).

Usually pluralise the main word: mother-in-law, mothers-in-law; passer-by, passers-by; court-martial, courts-martial; attorney-general, attorneys-general; man-of-war, men-of-war. units.title: Comprehension: Reading to Find Main Points
units.summary: How to tell the main idea of a paragraph from its supporting details, with a worked example on fast food and practice.

p: Summary writing, critical reading and note-taking rest on one skill: separating the main idea (the core point of a paragraph) from the supporting details (facts, examples and explanations that support it). The main idea is often in the topic sentence, usually the first or last sentence.

Passage: 'The growth of fast-food outlets in cities has started a debate about public health. Supporters say they give cheap, convenient meals to busy workers and families and create jobs in local communities. Critics point to the health damage of a diet high in processed food: more obesity, heart disease and diabetes. The environmental impact of the packaging waste is also a growing concern.'

Question: what are the two main opposing viewpoints? The paragraph is about the debate on fast food. 'Cheap and convenient meals' and 'jobs' are details for the positive view. 'Obesity, heart disease' and 'packaging waste' are details for the negative view. Answer: (1) fast food is useful because it is cheap and gives jobs; (2) it is harmful because of its health risks and effect on the environment.

'Many students think that cramming the night before an exam works. But educational psychologists have shown that it is very inefficient. Information learned by cramming sits in short-term memory and is soon forgotten. Spaced repetition, studying over several sessions, moves knowledge into long-term memory.' Main idea: cramming is an inefficient way to study, and spaced repetition is better. One supporting detail: cramming information is stored in short-term memory and quickly forgotten.

units.title: Comprehension: Reading and Note-Taking
units.summary: Why note-taking is an active skill, and three methods: the outline method, the Cornell method, and abbreviations and symbols.

p: Note-taking joins passive reading to active understanding. It makes you look for the structure of a text and produce a short personal record for later. It improves understanding and memory.

A structured, layered format that follows the text's own order (I, A, 1, a). Example from a text on climate change: I. Causes of climate change. A. Greenhouse gas emissions: 1. burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas); 2. deforestation. B. Agricultural practices: 1. methane from livestock; 2. nitrogen fertilisers.

Divide the page into three parts: the main notes column on the right (about 70 per cent) for your notes in your own words; the cue column on the left (about 20 per cent), where, afterwards, you write key questions or keywords; and a summary area at the bottom (about 10 per cent), where you write a two- or three-sentence summary of the page. It is excellent for revision because you can cover the notes and answer the cues.

Example. Cue: 'What is nominalisation?' Notes: 'Turning verbs or adjectives into nouns; makes writing more formal; decide to decision.' Summary: 'Nominalisation forms nouns from other word classes and is vital for academic writing.'

Develop your own short forms: & or + (and); w/ (with); w/o (without); e.g. (for example); i.e. (that is); an arrow (leads to); ∴ (therefore); govt (government); dept (department); diff (difference); info (information).

This can lower the quality of face-to-face talk. Studies show that too much phone use in company can bring feelings of exclusion and less satisfaction in relationships.'

units.title: Oral English: Emphatic Stress
units.summary: How stressing a particular word in a sentence changes its meaning, with a worked example and practice.

p: Emphatic (contrastive or sentence) stress puts special force on one word in a sentence to show a contrast or correct a misunderstanding. The same sentence can mean different things depending on which word is stressed. It carries nuance and hidden meaning.
In a neutral statement the stress usually falls on the last content word (noun, verb, adjective, adverb): 'My brother bought a new CAR.'

Emphatic stress changes the meaning: 'MY brother bought a new car' (mine, not yours). 'My BROTHER bought a new car' (not my sister or father). 'My brother BOUGHT a new car' (he bought it, he did not steal or borrow it). 'My brother bought a NEW car' (new, not second-hand). 'My brother bought a new CAR' (a car, not a motorbike or a van).
Implied question: 'Did the tall student answer the easy question?' Reply: 'No, the tall student answered the DIFFICULT question.' The stress on 'difficult' contrasts with the unstated 'easy'.

units.title: Summary Writing: Summarising Arguments
units.summary: How to summarise an argumentative passage: find the contention, the supporting reasons and the rebuttal, then paraphrase in the given limit.

p: When you summarise an argumentative passage you do not list facts; you boil down the author's persuasive case. You must find the central claim and the plan of the reasoning.
1. Find the contention (thesis): the main claim, usually in the introduction and conclusion. Signal phrases: 'I argue that...', 'This essay will show...'.
2. Find the supporting reasons: the main pillars of the argument, usually one per paragraph (two or three). Signals: 'Firstly...', 'Furthermore...', 'Another reason...'.
3. Find the rebuttal: a strong writer states a counter-argument and refutes it. Include this in your summary. Signals: 'Some may argue that...', 'While it is true that...', 'However...'.
4. Combine and paraphrase in a short, connected summary in your own words, within the limit.

'Homework should be abolished in secondary schools. It puts needless pressure on students who already spend six or more hours in class. Furthermore, it worsens social inequality, since students from richer homes have more resources and help. While some say homework reinforces learning, this is mistaken: tired, frustrated work late at night leads to shallow learning and resentment of education.'

Contention: homework should be abolished. Reason: it overloads students (and worsens inequality). Counter-argument and rebuttal: some say it reinforces learning, but tired late-night work produces shallow learning. Summary: 'The author argues that homework should be abolished because it overloads students and widens inequality, and rejects the claim that it aids learning, saying tired work is shallow.'

units.title: Listening: Tone, Purpose and Figurative Expressions
units.summary: How to decode a speaker's tone and purpose and recognise idioms, similes, metaphors and hyperbole.

p: Advanced listening means understanding not only what is said but how it is said: the speaker's tone (attitude), purpose (goal) and figurative language.

Tone is the speaker's feeling towards the subject or audience: sarcastic, angry, joyful, sombre, nostalgic, condescending, urgent, wistful, ironic. Purpose is the main aim: to inform (a news report), to persuade (a political speech), to entertain (a comedian), to warn (a safety announcement) or to instruct (a teacher).

An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is not clear from its words ('It's raining cats and dogs' means it is raining heavily). A simile compares using like or as ('as quiet as a mouse'). A metaphor says one thing is another ('The news was a dagger to his heart'). Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration ('I've told you a million times').

A firefighter showing schoolchildren how to leave a building: calm, clear tone; purpose to instruct. A film critic calling a film 'a soulless, derivative cash-grab': scornful tone; purpose to criticise. 'The politician's speech was a lot of hot air' is an idiom meaning it was empty talk. 'Her smile was a ray of sunshine' is a metaphor.

units.title: Writing: the Scientific Report
units.summary: The seven-part structure of a scientific report, its formal passive style and a worked example about light and bean seedlings.

p: A scientific report describes the process and results of an investigation so that others can understand it and repeat it. It is formal and objective, usually in the past tense and passive voice to stress the action rather than the doer ('the beaker was heated', not 'I heated the beaker').

1. Title: clear and specific, such as 'An Experiment to Find the Effect of Light on the Growth of Bean Seedlings'. 2. Aim: one sentence stating what you set out to find ('To find whether bean seedlings grow taller in direct sunlight or in complete darkness'). 3. Apparatus or materials: a list of everything used. 4. Method: a numbered, step-by-step account in the past tense, detailed enough to be repeated. 5. Results: the data without interpretation (tables, graphs, observations). 6. Discussion: the most important part: what the results mean, why they came out so, and any odd results. 7. Conclusion: a short answer to the aim.

Method: 1. Two bean seedlings were planted in identical pots with the same soil. 2. Plant A was placed on a sunny windowsill. 3. Plant B was put in a dark cupboard. 4. Each plant was given 50 ml of water daily. 5. The height of each plant was measured every 48 hours for two weeks.

Discussion: 'Plant A grew tall and green. Plant B grew tall but was yellow and spindly. This suggests that light is needed for photosynthesis, which produces chlorophyll and supports healthy growth.' Conclusion: 'Bean seedlings will grow in darkness, but need sunlight for healthy growth and chlorophyll.'

units.activity: Put in order: Discussion, Aim, Title, Method, Conclusion, Results. (Title, Aim, Method, Results, Discussion, Conclusion; apparatus comes before method.) Why is 'I think we should heat the mixture' wrong in a method? (It is an opinion, in the present tense and the first person.) Write a 300 to 400-word report on a simple experiment.

units.title: Revision
units.summary: A summary of the term's grammar, oral English, writing, comprehension and vocabulary, with revision tasks.

p: Nominalisation: verbs and adjectives become nouns by suffix (decide, decision; pure, purity; strong, strength) or conversion (a run). Noun phrases: determiner, pre-modifiers, headword, post-modifiers; functions: subject, object, subject complement, object complement, object of a preposition; a noun clause has its own subject and verb. Pronouns: personal, possessive, demonstrative, interrogative, reflexive, relative, reciprocal and indefinite. Plurals: regular, irregular (men, children, sheep), foreign (cacti, data, crises, criteria) and compound (mothers-in-law). Adverbs and adverbial phrases: manner, place, time, frequency, degree.

Voiced consonants vibrate the vocal cords (b, d, g, v, z); voiceless do not (p, t, k, f, s). Clusters: initial (street) and final (desks, glimpsed); avoid epenthesis. Transcription uses the IPA. Stress: first syllable for two-syllable nouns and adjectives, second for many verbs; before -tion, -ic, -ity; on -ee and -eer; first element of compound nouns. Emphatic stress changes meaning.

Expository essay: hook, background, thesis; three body paragraphs; conclusion; objective tone. Argumentative essay: contention, two points, counter-argument and rebuttal, conclusion with a clincher. Scientific report: title, aim, apparatus, method (past tense, passive), results, discussion, conclusion.

Summary: read the question; read for gist; read again and underline; paraphrase; write and connect within the limit. Main idea and supporting details. Notes: outline and Cornell methods. Listening stages: hearing, attending, understanding, responding, remembering. Tone and purpose; idioms, similes and metaphors.

Nominalise five verbs and five adjectives. Find a complex sentence and list its noun phrases and their functions. Write the plurals of crisis, formula, brother-in-law, goose and radius. Transcribe and stress: development, political, engineer, overcome. Write an outline for an expository and an argumentative essay on a current issue. Summarise an editorial in three sentences. Make flashcards for 20 words of the week.

units.title: Oral English: Voiced and Voiceless Consonants (Revision)
units.summary: A fuller look at voicing, with minimal pairs, the always-voiced nasals, approximants and the voiceless /h/, and worked examples.

p: A consonant is a speech sound made by partly or completely blocking the air from the lungs. The main way of grouping them is by voicing: voiceless sounds have the vocal cords apart and sound like a puff, hiss or whisper; voiced sounds have the vocal cords together and vibrating. Test by touching your larynx (Adam's apple): 'ssss' (no buzz, voiceless /s/) and 'zzzz' (buzz, voiced /z/).
Study the table.
Nasals (all voiced): /m/ man, /n/ no, /ŋ/ sing; air flows through the nose. Approximants (all voiced): /l/ leg, /r/ run, /w/ wet, /j/ yes; less obstruction. The glottal /h/ (hat) is voiceless.
Odd one out by final sound: push, laugh, breathe, rich. push ends /ʃ/ (voiceless); laugh ends /f/ (voiceless); breathe ends /ð/ (voiced); rich ends /tʃ/ (voiceless). So 'breathe' is the odd one out.
Voiced consonants in 'ledge' /ledʒ/: /l/ and /dʒ/ (the vowel is always voiced but is not a consonant). The final sound of 'judge' is /dʒ/, voiced.

units.title: Structure: the Possessive Apostrophe
units.summary: The six rules for showing ownership with an apostrophe, the apostrophe in contractions and the 'its' versus 'it's' rule.

p: The apostrophe shows contraction (do not, don't) and possession (the car of my sister, my sister's car). This lesson is about possession first.
1. Singular nouns not ending in s: add 's: the cat's tail, the woman's car, a student's pen, Mr Bako's house.
2. Plural nouns ending in s: add only an apostrophe: the cats' tails, the students' pens, the Joneses' house.
3. Plural nouns not ending in s: add 's: the children's toys, the men's room, the sheep's field.
4. Singular nouns ending in s: modern British English prefers 's: James's book, the boss's office. (James' book is older and less common; be consistent.)
5. Compound nouns: add 's to the last word: my mother-in-law's car, the Attorney General's office.
6. Joint possession (one thing shared): 's on the last name only: John and Mary's house. Separate possession: 's on both: John's and Mary's houses.
The apostrophe replaces missing letters: it is, it's; you are, you're; they are, they're; who is, who's; do not, don't.

The golden rule: 'it's' is only ever 'it is' or 'it has' ('It's a hot day'). 'Its' with no apostrophe shows possession ('The company is famous for its service'). Similarly 'who's' means 'who is' and 'whose' shows possession.

units.title: Comprehension: Main Points and Topic Sentences
units.summary: How to find the main point and the topic sentence of a paragraph by testing candidate sentences, with a worked example on sleep.

sections.h: Main point, details and topic sentence
p: Understanding means getting the author's central message, not just single words. A well-built paragraph has one main point (the controlling idea), often stated in a topic sentence. Supporting details (facts, examples, reasons, statistics, stories) explain or prove it. The topic sentence is often first but may be in the middle or at the end.

1. Read the whole paragraph. 2. Ask: what single idea does the author most want me to understand? 3. Look for a sentence broad enough to cover the others but specific enough to mean something. 4. Test it: do all the other sentences explain, give examples of or develop it?

'A new study has revealed that sleep is far more important than previously thought. While the body rests, the brain is hard at work. It consolidates memories, processing the day's events and storing important information. Furthermore, during sleep the brain clears out toxic by-products that build up while we are awake. This cleaning is vital for long-term brain health. Without enough sleep, a person's ability to learn, focus and make decisions is badly harmed.'

Sentence 1 is a good, general introduction. Sentence 2 makes a clear claim. Sentences 3 to 6 give the evidence (memory, toxin clearing, results of too little sleep). So the best topic sentence is the second: 'While the body rests, the brain is hard at work.'

Finally, it releases endorphins which improve mood and reduce stress.' (The first sentence.) Take three paragraphs from a passage and write each topic sentence.

units.title: Structure: Question Mark, Exclamation Mark, Colon, Semi-colon and Hyphen
units.summary: How and when to use five punctuation marks correctly, with examples of common errors.

p: Punctuation tells the reader when to pause, stop or turn. Correct punctuation gives clarity, meaning and rhythm.

sections.h: The question mark and the exclamation mark
p: Question mark (?): at the end of a direct question ('What is your name?'). Do not use it after an indirect question: 'He asked me what my name was.' Exclamation mark (!): ends a sentence or phrase of strong feeling or a forceful command ('What a fantastic goal!' 'Stop!'). Use it sparingly in formal writing.

A colon follows a complete clause and introduces a list, an explanation or a quotation. Correct: 'You will need the following ingredients: flour, eggs, milk and sugar.' Incorrect: 'The ingredients you need are: flour...' (not a complete sentence before the colon). Explanation: 'He had one overriding passion: football.' Quotation: 'The head made an announcement: "All students must return their books by Friday."'

Use 1: join two closely related independent clauses with no conjunction: 'The rain fell relentlessly; the streets began to flood.' Use 2: separate items in a list when the items already contain commas: 'Delegates came from London, England; Paris, France; Tokyo, Japan; and Abuja, Nigeria.'

Join words that act as one adjective before a noun: 'a well-behaved student', 'a last-minute decision' (but 'the student is well behaved'). With prefixes ex-, self-, all-: ex-president, self-confidence. In fractions and numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine: two-thirds, forty-five.

units.title: Listening: Appreciating Poetry
units.summary: Tone, purpose and figurative devices in poetry (simile, metaphor, personification, alliteration, onomatopoeia), with a worked analysis of a short poem.

p: Poetry is language at its most musical and concentrated. When you listen to a poem you experience an art, so you attend to the speaker's tone, the poem's purpose and the figures that make its images.

Tone: the speaker's attitude (sad, joyful, angry, nostalgic, sarcastic, reflective). Purpose: why the poem was written: to tell a story (narrative), to describe a scene or feeling (lyric), to mourn (elegy), to praise (ode) or to criticise or mock (satire).

Figures of speech: simile (like or as: 'Her smile was as bright as the sun'); metaphor ('The world is a stage'); personification ('The wind whispered secrets'); alliteration ('The slippery snake slithered silently'); onomatopoeia (words that imitate sounds: buzz, bang, pop, sizzle).

Poem read aloud: 'The city breathes, a beast of steel and stone, / Its heart a steady, pulsing, electric groan. / Cars hiss and growl on wet, black streets, / While lonely people pass in silent beats. / The night is a black velvet cloak, worn and deep, / Under which the tired world falls asleep.'

Tone: sombre, a little threatening, tired. Purpose: to describe the city at night as a living but cold and wearying being. Devices: 'The city breathes' and 'Its heart...groan' are personification; 'hiss and growl' is onomatopoeia; 'lonely people' has alliteration of the l sound; 'The night is a black velvet cloak' is a metaphor.

units.title: Oral English: Intonation for Surprise and Disbelief
units.summary: The high-rising tone for surprise and the fall-rise tone for doubt, compared with plain statements and questions.

p: Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice, which adds emotion. Besides normal patterns for statements and questions we can change them to show surprise, shock or disbelief.

The high-rising tone (↗), the 'Really?!' pattern: the voice rises sharply at the end, turning a statement into a question of disbelief. Statement (falling): 'He passed his \exam.' Surprise: 'He passed his ↗exam?!' ('I can't believe it!'). Others: 'You're moving to ↗London?' 'She sold the ↗car?'

The fall-rise tone (V): the voice falls and then rises on the key word. It shows doubt, hesitation or scepticism more than shock: 'He Vpassed his exam' means 'That is what he says, but I am not sure I believe it.'

'The headmaster is \dancing' (neutral statement, informing). 'Is the headmaster /dancing?' (a yes/no question). 'The headmaster is ↗dancing?!' (shocked). The word 'Really?' as a plain question falls ('Rea\lly?'); to express shock it rises high ('↗Really?!').

units.title: Structure: Sentence Types by Function
units.summary: The four types of sentence by function (declarative, imperative, interrogative and exclamatory) with their punctuation and examples.

p: Sentences can be sorted by what they do: inform, command, ask or exclaim.

Declarative: makes a statement (fact or opinion); ends with a full stop. 'The sun rises in the east.' 'I enjoy reading historical fiction.' 'He asked me where I lived' is still declarative (a statement about a question).

Imperative: gives a command, request or instruction; the subject 'you' is understood; ends with a full stop or an exclamation mark. 'Close the door.' 'Please take a seat.' 'Stop talking!' 'First, mix the flour and eggs.'
Interrogative: asks a question; ends with a question mark. 'What is the time?' (wh-question) 'Are you feeling better?' (yes/no question) 'You've finished your homework, haven't you?' (tag question).
Exclamatory: expresses strong feeling; ends with an exclamation mark; often begins with 'What' or 'How' but is not a question. 'What a beautiful painting!' 'How incredible that is!'

units.title: Writing: the Formal Letter of Complaint
units.summary: The layout, tone and three-paragraph content of a formal letter of complaint, with example wording.

p: A formal letter is professional, respectful and follows a strict format. A letter of complaint expresses dissatisfaction about a product, service or situation and asks for a remedy such as a refund, replacement or apology.

1. Your address at the top right (do not put your name). 2. The date below it. 3. The recipient's address on the left, below the date (for example The Manager, Quality Goods Ltd., 15 Industrial Road, Ikeja, Lagos). 4. Salutation: 'Dear Sir', 'Dear Madam' or 'Dear Sir/Madam'. 5. A heading, underlined and in capitals: 'LETTER OF COMPLAINT: FAULTY HAIR DRYER (MODEL HD-500)'. 6. The body. 7. Closing: 'Yours faithfully' (the only correct ending when you begin 'Dear Sir/Madam'). 8. Your signature. 9. Your full name printed beneath.

Paragraph 1 (purpose): say at once why you are writing, with key details. 'I am writing to complain about a hair dryer I bought from your Ikeja branch on 1st March. The SuperDry HD-500 has proved faulty.'

Paragraph 2 (the problem): describe it factually and precisely, without emotional language. 'The dryer worked for two days, then gave off a burning smell and stopped completely. I have not misused it.'

Paragraph 3 (the remedy): say clearly and reasonably what you want. 'As it is under warranty, I would like it replaced. Otherwise I would accept a full refund of ₦25,000. I attach a copy of the receipt.'

units.title: Oral English: the Falling Tone
units.summary: The falling tone for statements, commands and wh-questions, with the nucleus and a comparison with rising and high-rising tones.

p: The falling tone, or 'glide-down', is the commonest pattern in British English. It shows certainty, finality and completeness. The voice starts fairly high and glides down to a lower pitch on the most important word of the sentence, the nucleus. We mark it with a backslash (\) before the nucleus. The nucleus is the word that carries the most meaning, the one you would stress even in a monotone.

Statements of fact (declaratives): 'My name is \John.' 'The sky is \blue.' 'I am going to the mar\ket.' Commands (imperatives), firm and direct: 'Sit \down.' 'Open your \books.' '\Stop!' Wh-questions (who, what, where, when, why, how), which expect specific information, not yes or no: 'What is your \name?' 'Where do you \live?' 'How did you \do that?'

units.title: Comprehension: Implied Meaning
units.summary: How to make inferences by combining the clues in a text with common sense, with worked examples including sarcasm.

p: Not everything is stated directly. Implied meaning (inference) is what is hinted at. The reader or listener acts as a detective, using clues from the text and personal knowledge to 'read between the lines'.
1. Find the stated facts (the clues). 2. Combine them with common sense and experience. 3. Draw a logical conclusion that makes sense of the clues.
Clue: 'As soon as he walked into the warm room, his glasses fogged up.' Inference: the room was much warmer than outside.
Clue: 'When the teacher asked for the homework, Chinedu avoided eye contact and began frantically searching through his empty bag.' Inference: he had not done it and was afraid of being caught.

Clue (tone): 'The "magnificent" new council building, which cost the taxpayers millions, already had cracks in its foundation and no running water.' Inference: the author is sarcastic; the building is badly built and a waste of money.

'The children ran inside, clothes soaked and hair dripping, laughing as they left puddles on the floor.' We can infer that it had been raining. 'Despite studying for ten hours straight, she still felt completely unprepared.' We can infer she was very anxious or that she had not studied effectively.

units.title: Writing: the Informal Letter
units.summary: The layout, warm tone and content of a letter to a friend or relative, with the features of an informal style.

p: An informal (friendly) letter goes to someone you know well: a friend, relative or close acquaintance. The tone is casual, conversational and warm.

1. Your address at the top right. 2. The date below it. 3. The salutation on the left, with a first name: 'Dear Sarah,', 'Hi Tom,', 'Dearest Mum,'. 4. The body: opening paragraph with greetings, a question about their health and your reason for writing ('I hope this letter finds you well. I'm writing to tell you all about...'); the main paragraphs with your news or story; a closing paragraph (regards to the family, a request to write back, future plans). 5. A friendly closing: 'Best wishes,', 'Yours sincerely,', 'Lots of love,', 'Your friend,'. 6. Your first name only.

Contractions (I'm, don't, it's, we'll); informal words, idioms and colloquial expressions ('It was raining cats and dogs!'); personal questions ('How is your new job?'); exclamation marks for excitement. Compared with a formal letter, you do not write the recipient's address and you do not end with 'Yours faithfully'.

units.title: Oral English: Rhyme Scheme
units.summary: How to label the pattern of end rhymes in a poem, the common patterns (couplet, alternate and enclosed) and a correction to the notes' example.

p: Rhyme gives a poem rhythm, music and structure. A rhyme scheme is the ordered pattern of rhymes at the ends of lines.

1. Read aloud and listen to the last word of each line. 2. Give the first line's end sound the letter A. 3. Give the same letter to any other line that rhymes with it. 4. When a new sound appears, use the next letter (B, then C). 5. Carry on stanza by stanza.

Couplet (AABB): pairs of rhyming lines. Alternate rhyme (ABAB): first and third lines rhyme, second and fourth rhyme. Enclosed rhyme (ABBA): the first and fourth lines rhyme, enclosing the second and third.
'Twinkle, twinkle, little star (A) / How I wonder what you are (A) / Up above the world so high (B) / Like a diamond in the sky (B)': AABB, a couplet pattern.
'The seed you sow (A) / Another reaps (B) / The wealth you find (C) / Another keeps (B)': ABCB.

'I wandered lonely as a cloud (A) / That floats on high o'er vales and hills (B) / When all at once I saw a crowd (A) / A host, of golden daffodils (B)': ABAB. 'The sun is clear and bright (A) / A welcome and a sight (A) / That makes the world feel new (B) / For me and also you (B)': AABB.

Your notes label Robert Frost's lines 'He gives his harness bells a shake / To ask if there is some mistake. / The only other sound's the sweep / Of easy wind and downy flake' as AABB. But 'sweep' and 'flake' do not rhyme: the scheme is AABA (shake, mistake, sweep, flake). In Frost's poem the unrhymed third line starts the next stanza's rhyme.

units.title: Structure: Personal and Relative Pronouns
units.summary: A deeper look at the case of personal pronouns, the 'between you and me' rule and the relative pronouns who, whom, whose, which and that, with the who/whom trick.

p: The case of a personal pronoun shows its job. Subject case (the doer): I, you, he, she, it, we, they: 'He and I went to the cinema' (not 'Him and me'). Object case (the receiver): me, you, him, her, it, us, them: 'The teacher gave the prize to him and me' (not 'he and I'). After 'between' always use the object case: 'This is a secret between you and me.'
A relative pronoun introduces a clause that describes a noun.

Who: people (subject) 'The woman who called you is my boss.' Whom: people (object) 'The woman whom you called is my boss.' Whose: possession 'The student whose book was lost is here.' Which: things and animals 'The book, which is on the table, is mine.' That: people, things and animals, less formal 'The book that you gave me is brilliant.'

sections.h: A trick for who and whom
p: Replace the pronoun with he or him. If 'he' fits, use 'who'. If 'him' fits, use 'whom'. 'He called you' gives 'Who called you?' 'You called him' gives 'Whom did you call?'

Correct: 'Him and me are best friends' (He and I are best friends); 'The invitation was for my sister and I' (my sister and me).

units.title: Comprehension: Note-Making from Spoken Information
units.summary: Techniques for making clear, short notes while listening: skeleton not flesh, abbreviations, outline format and signpost words.

p: Note-making is a key study and work skill. You actively process spoken information so as to capture its main ideas and structure in a clear short form for later review.

Be prepared: a notebook and pen, with the date and topic written at the top. Listen for the skeleton, not the flesh: write the main ideas (bones) and key details, not every word. Use abbreviations and symbols for speed: e.g. (for example), i.e. (that is), an arrow (leads to), ∴ (therefore), & (and), w/ (with), w/o (without), govt (government), devt (development). Use an outline: I. Main idea; A. detail; B. detail; II. Main idea. Listen for signpost words that show importance: 'The three main causes are...', 'On the other hand...', 'Most importantly...', 'In conclusion...'.

units.title: Oral English: the Rising Tone
units.summary: The rising tone for yes/no questions, politeness, uncertainty and lists, and how it contrasts with falling and high-rising tones.

p: The rising tone (glide-up) shows incompleteness, uncertainty and openness. It is the sound of questions, politeness and tentative suggestions. The voice starts at a normal pitch and glides up on the nucleus. We mark it with a forward slash (/) before the nucleus.
1. Yes/no questions (the main use): 'Are you /coming?' 'Is that your /book?' 'Have you /eaten?' It shows you await an answer.
2. Politeness and friendliness: 'Good /morning' sounds warmer than 'Good \morning'; 'Come /in'; 'Can I /help you?'
3. Tentativeness or uncertainty: 'I think it's /blue...' (not completely sure); 'Perhaps we should /go?' (a suggestion, not a command).
4. Listing: use the rising tone on every item but the last, which falls to show the list is complete: 'I bought /bread, /milk, /sugar and \eggs.'

units.title: Writing: Creative Writing and the Short Story
units.summary: The five elements of a short story (plot, character, setting, conflict and theme), the four types of conflict and the story-writing tasks.

p: Creative writing expresses ideas in an imaginative, often symbolic way. Its purpose is to entertain, move the reader and tell a story, not just to inform. The commonest form is the short story.

1. Plot: the series of events: exposition (we meet characters and setting), rising action (a conflict starts and tension builds), climax (the turning point of highest tension), falling action (events after the climax) and resolution (the conflict is settled for better or worse).
2. Character: the people (or animals or things) in the story. The main character is the protagonist; the character or force opposing him or her is the antagonist.
3. Setting: the time and place. A good setting uses sensory detail (sight, sound, smell, touch).

4. Conflict: the central problem. Types: character against character; character against nature (a storm, a wild animal); character against society (its rules or norms); character against self (fear, doubt, a moral dilemma).
5. Theme: the central idea or message about life ('the importance of family', 'the danger of greed'). It is not the plot but the meaning behind it.

units.title: Oral English: Consonant Contrasts in Minimal Pairs
units.summary: Drills with minimal pairs for /p/ and /b/, /t/ and /d/, and /s/ and /z/ to sharpen hearing and speaking.

p: A minimal pair is two words that differ in only one sound in the same position. Practising them trains your ear and mouth to hear and make the small differences that change meanings. Confusing these sounds can cause real misunderstanding.
/p/ (voiceless) and /b/ (voiced), the lip plosives made with both lips: pat / bat, pig / big, pack / back, rapid / rabid. Sentence: 'The pig slept in the big pen.'
/t/ and /d/, the alveolar plosives made with the tongue against the ridge behind the teeth: town / down, tie / die, write / ride, bet / bed. Sentence: 'I don't want to tie and dye this fabric.'
/s/ and /z/, the alveolar fricatives, a hiss against a buzz: sip / zip, sue / zoo, price / prize, bus / buzz. Sentence: 'The surprise prize was a trip to the zoo.'

units.title: Structure: Sequence of Tenses and Reported Speech
units.summary: How tenses, pronouns and time words change when speech is reported, the back-shift rule, the exceptions and worked examples.

p: When we report what someone said, we often change the tense. If the reporting verb (said, told, explained, asked) is in the past, the verb in the reported clause usually moves one step back into the past.

head: Direct speech
Reported speech
rows: Simple past: He said he worked here.
Past continuous: He said he was working.
Past perfect: He said he had finished.
Past perfect: He said he had finished it.

sections.h: Changes in time and place words
p: now becomes then; today becomes that day; tomorrow becomes the next day or the following day; yesterday becomes the day before or the previous day; this becomes that; these becomes those; here becomes there. Pronouns also change to fit the reporter's view.

If the reporting verb is in the present (says, explains), or if the reported fact is still true or is a general truth, the tense need not change. Direct: 'I am 16 years old.' Reported: 'He says he is 16.' or 'He said he is 16.' 'She said the Earth revolves around the sun.'

Direct: 'I cannot attend the meeting tomorrow because I have a doctor's appointment,' she said. Reported: She said that she could not attend the meeting the following day because she had a doctor's appointment.

units.title: Comprehension: Reading for Critical Evaluation
units.summary: The critical reader's questions: purpose, tone, bias, strength of argument (including two logical fallacies) and reliability of the source.

p: Critical evaluation goes beyond understanding to analysing and judging a text: examining the argument, spotting bias and weighing the evidence. It makes you a discerning reader.
1. Author's purpose: to inform (news, textbook), to persuade (opinion piece, advertisement, speech), to entertain (novel, comic strip) or to satirise (use humour to criticise).
2. Author's tone: objective and neutral (facts, little emotion), subjective and emotional (loaded language, exclamation marks), or sarcastic, angry, enthusiastic or dismissive.

3. Author's bias: a pre-formed opinion that affects fairness. Look for loaded language ('heroic freedom fighters' against 'ruthless terrorists'), one-sided argument, missing key facts or heavy emotional appeals.

4. Validity of the argument: is it based on facts, statistics and examples, or on personal stories and feelings? Watch for logical fallacies, such as ad hominem (attacking the person instead of the argument) and hasty generalisation (a big claim from a small sample).
5. Reliability of the source: is the author an expert? Is the publication reputable, or a personal blog? Is it checked by experts (peer-reviewed)?

units.summary: How to write a magazine or newspaper article with a headline, by-line, hooking opening, structured body and conclusion, and how it differs from a formal letter.

p: An article is a piece written for a newspaper, magazine or online platform. Unlike a formal letter, it speaks to a wide public audience. Its purpose may be to inform, persuade or entertain, and its tone can be set to match.

1. Headline: catchy and engaging, giving a clear idea of the content (for example 'The Silent Epidemic: Fighting Loneliness in a Hyper-Connected World'). 2. units.title: Structure: Active and Passive Voice
units.summary: The difference between active and passive voice, the rules for changing one to the other and a table of conversion for each tense.

p: Voice shows how the verb's action relates to the subject and object. Active voice: the subject performs the action ('The dog chased the cat'). Passive voice: the subject receives the action ('The cat was chased by the dog'); the focus is on the action or receiver, not the doer. The passive is common in formal and scientific writing.

1. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive. 2. The verb becomes a form of 'to be' + the past participle (am, is, are, was, were, be, being, been). 3. The old subject becomes the agent introduced by 'by', or is left out if unknown or unimportant ('Someone has stolen my bicycle' becomes 'My bicycle has been stolen').

units.title: Oral English: Recognising Stress Patterns
units.summary: Primary and secondary stress, common patterns in two- and three-syllable words and the effect of suffixes on stress.

p: A stressed syllable is louder, longer and often higher. Primary stress is the strongest, marked with a high vertical line (ˈ) before the syllable. Secondary stress is weaker, marked with a low vertical line (ˌ). Wrong stress can make a word hard to understand.
Two-syllable words: stress on the first syllable (often nouns and adjectives): TAble, MOTHer, HAPpy; stress on the second (often verbs): preSENT, reCORD, deCIDE.
Three-syllable words: first syllable: HOSpital, MANagement; second: toMORrow, conDItion; third: engiNEER, volunTEER.

Suffixes that shift stress: -tion, -sion, -ic, -ity: the stress falls on the syllable before the suffix: inforMAtion, deCIsion, ecoNOmic, aBILity. Suffixes that usually do not change the stress of the root: -ful, -less, -ness, -ly (BEAUtiful, HOPEless).

Your lesson notes say that 'MUSic' becomes 'muSIcal'. That is not right: the stress stays on the first syllable in 'MUsical'. Words like 'MEMory' and 'MEMorise' also keep the first-syllable stress. When in doubt, check the stress in a dictionary.

The pattern for 'computer' is x 'x x (comPUter).

units.title: Grammar: Revision of Tenses
units.summary: The twelve English tenses by time and aspect, their forms, main uses and examples, with the difference between the present perfect and simple past.

p: Tense shows time (past, present, future) and aspect (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). Together they give twelve tenses.

Simple present (base verb, add -s for he, she, it): habits ('She walks to school every day'), general truths ('Water boils at 100 degrees'), timetables ('The film starts at 9 PM'), stative verbs ('I believe you').

Present continuous (am, is, are + verb-ing): actions now ('I am studying'), temporary situations ('He is staying with his cousin'), definite plans ('We are travelling to Lagos tomorrow'), annoyance with 'always' ('You are always interrupting').

Present perfect (has, have + past participle): a past action with a present result ('I have lost my wallet'), life experience ('She has visited Ghana three times'), unfinished action ('He has lived in London for ten years'; 'She has worked here since 2020').
Present perfect continuous (has, have + been + verb-ing): stresses duration ('She has been painting the room all morning'); recent temporary action ('I have been running').
Simple past (verb + -ed, or irregular): a completed action at a definite time ('I finished my homework last night'); a series of actions ('I woke up, brushed my teeth and went to work').

Past continuous (was, were + verb-ing): an action in progress at a past moment ('At 8 PM yesterday I was watching a film'); an interrupted action ('I was sleeping when the phone rang'); two actions at once ('While I was cooking, he was cleaning').
Past perfect (had + past participle): the past before the past ('When we arrived, the film had already started').
Past perfect continuous (had been + verb-ing): duration before another past action ('He had been waiting for an hour before she arrived').
Simple future (will + base verb; shall with I and we in formal offers): predictions ('I think it will rain'), spontaneous decisions ('The phone is ringing. I will get it'), promises and offers.
Future continuous (will be + verb-ing): in progress at a future time ('This time next Friday I will be flying to Abuja'); polite questions ('Will you be using the car tonight?').
Future perfect (will have + past participle): completed before a future time ('By 2030 I will have graduated').

Two people look at an empty parking space. 'I sold it' (simple past: finished, and we may ask when). 'I have sold it' (present perfect: the result matters now, the car is gone). 'I was watching television when the lights went out' (interruption). 'She was late because she had missed her bus' (the missed bus came first).

units.title: Grammar: Conditional and Complex Sentences
units.summary: Types 0, 1, 2 and 3 of the conditional, the subjunctive 'were', and complex sentences with main and subordinate clauses.

p: A conditional sentence has an if-clause (the condition) and a main clause (the result).
Type 0 (general truths): if + simple present, simple present. 'If you heat ice, it melts.'
Type 1 (likely): if + simple present, will + base verb. 'If it rains tomorrow, the match will be cancelled.'

Type 2 (unlikely or imaginary, present or future): if + simple past, would + base verb. 'If I won the lottery, I would buy a private jet.' In careful English use 'were' for all subjects: 'If I were you, I would apologise.' (the subjunctive).
Type 3 (impossible, past; regret): if + past perfect, would have + past participle. 'If I had studied harder, I would have passed.' 'If she had taken the earlier train, she would not have been late.'

Type 1: 'If I have enough money, I will buy a car' (a real plan). Type 2: 'If I had enough money, I would buy a car' (a dream; I do not have it). Type 3: 'If I had had enough money, I would have bought a car' (a past regret). 'If he spoke French, he would get the job in Paris' is Type 2 (he does not speak French). 'If I see him, I will tell him' is a real possibility; 'If I saw him, I would tell him' is unlikely.

A complex sentence has one main (independent) clause and at least one subordinate (dependent) clause. A main clause can stand alone. A subordinate clause cannot; it often begins with if, when, because, although, who, which or that. 'The match will be cancelled [main] if it rains tomorrow [subordinate].' 'The student [who won the prize] was very happy.' 'Although it was raining [subordinate], we went for a walk [main].'

units.title: Writing: Speech Writing
units.summary: The features and structure of a speech (title, salutation, introduction, body with rhetorical devices and conclusion), how it differs from an article, and a prize-giving day outline.

p: A speech is a formal address to an audience. It is written to be heard, not read, and that shapes its structure and language. It may inspire, persuade, inform or entertain.

Title: clear and striking ('The Peril of Plastic: A Call to Action'). Salutation: a formal greeting that respects the audience's ranks ('The Honourable Minister of Education, the Principal, members of the Board of Governors, dedicated staff, proud parents and my fellow students'). Introduction: a hook (a quotation, statistic, question or short story); the occasion; the thesis or central message. Body: two to four organised paragraphs using rhetorical devices: rhetorical questions ('How many of you wish to see a cleaner environment?'), repetition or anaphora ('We must act. We must lead. We must change.'), the rule of three ('honour, duty and legacy'), personal stories and direct address ('we', 'you', 'our'). Conclusion: sum up, end with a memorable statement, a call to action or hope, and thank the audience.
Study the table.

sections.h: Outline for a prize-giving day speech
p: Title: 'Celebrating Excellence, Inspiring Futures'. Salutation to the chairman, principal, teachers, parents, guests and fellow students. Introduction: a greeting and honour of the occasion; thesis: we honour achievers and reflect on the qualities that lead to success. Body 1: congratulate the winners ('diligence bears sweet fruit'). Body 2: encourage those without prizes ('let this ceremony be a catalyst, not a conclusion'). Body 3: thank teachers and parents. Conclusion: today's excellence is the foundation of tomorrow's success; thanks; a closing line.

units.title: Grammar: Affixation (Prefixes)
units.summary: What a morpheme and a prefix are, and the main negative, time, number and other prefixes with examples.

p: Affixation adds a morpheme (the smallest unit of meaning) to a root word to make a new word. A prefix goes at the beginning (un- + happy = unhappy); a suffix goes at the end (hope + -ful = hopeful). A prefix usually changes meaning but not word class. The choice of prefix often depends on the first letter of the root.
Study the table.

Add a negative prefix: responsible becomes irresponsible (r); legal becomes illegal (l). 'Unappear' is not a word; 'disappear' means to vanish. The prefix un- often reverses an action: lock, unlock; do, undo; wrap, unwrap; plug, unplug.

units.title: Writing: Summarising a Talk or Lecture
units.summary: The three-step process (before, during and after the lecture), signpost language and shorthand.

p: You cannot re-read a speaker's words, so summarising a talk depends on active listening and efficient notes that separate main ideas from details at once.
Before: find out the topic if you can (background makes key terms easier), and have a notebook and pen; avoid distractions.

During: do not transcribe; capture ideas. Listen for signpost language: introducing the main idea ('My central argument is...', 'The key point is...'); listing ('There are three main reasons... First... Second... Finally...'); examples ('For instance...', 'To illustrate...'); emphasis ('It is crucial to remember...', 'Most importantly...'); concluding ('In conclusion...', 'To sum up...'). Use shorthand: & or + (and), w/ (with), w/o (without), an arrow (leads to), e.g., cf. (compare), govt, devt. Keep the skeleton (thesis and main supporting arguments); skip jokes, long stories and repetition.

After: review your notes at once while memory is fresh and fill gaps; find the core message (thesis); list two to four key points; write one paragraph in your own words combining them with no opinion; edit for brevity and clarity.

units.title: Grammar: Forming and Using the Passive Voice
units.summary: The four-step method for changing active to passive, a tense table, and four situations in which the passive is the better choice.

p: In the active voice the subject does the action ('The chef cooked the meal'): direct and strong. In the passive voice the subject receives the action ('The meal was cooked by the chef'): used when the doer is unknown, unimportant or when the action or receiver is to be stressed.

1. Find subject, verb and object: [The company] [built] [the house]. 2. Make the object the new subject: [The house]. 3. Change the verb to a form of 'to be' + the past participle, keeping the same tense: built becomes 'was built'. 4. Make the old subject the agent with 'by' (optional): 'The house was built by the company.'

units.title: Oral English: the Dictionary and Spelling
units.summary: How to read a dictionary entry (spelling, pronunciation, word class, definitions, examples, derived forms and origin) and three spelling rules.

p: A dictionary tells you much more than spelling. Take 'profound': pro•found /prəˈfaʊnd/ adj. 1 very great or intense (profound despair). 2 showing great knowledge or insight (a profound philosopher). Derived form: profoundly. Origin: from Latin profundus 'deep'.

Spelling and word division (pro•found); pronunciation in the IPA (the stress mark shows stress on the second syllable); word class (adj. = adjective); numbered definitions, from most to least common; example phrases that show use; derived forms; and origin (etymology), which helps you remember the meaning.
'i' before 'e' except after 'c' when the sound is /iː/: believe, field, piece; receive, deceive, ceiling. Exceptions: weird, seize, height, foreign.
Drop a final silent 'e' before a suffix that begins with a vowel: make, making; use, usable. Keep the 'e' to keep a soft 'c' or 'g': change, changeable.

Double the final consonant of a one-syllable word ending in a single vowel plus one consonant before a vowel suffix: run, running; big, bigger. This also applies to longer words stressed on the last syllable: begin, beginning.
