units.title: Writing: Article Writing
units.summary: The structure of a compelling article (catchy headline, by-line, hooking introduction, developed body, closing) with Nigerian topics and a comparison with a formal letter.

p: An article is written for a wide audience in a newspaper, magazine, journal or online. It informs, explains, describes or persuades. Unlike a speech it is written to be read, and unlike a letter it has no named addressee.

1. Headline: catchy (alliteration, a play on words or a question) and informative: 'The Plastic Plague: Choking Our Oceans'. 2. By-line: the author's name below the title. 3. Introduction (the hook): a startling statistic, an anecdote, a rhetorical question or a direct statement; it introduces the topic and your angle. 4. Body: one main idea per paragraph, each opening with a topic sentence, backed by facts, examples, quotations or statistics, linked with connectives (furthermore, on the other hand, as a result). 5. Conclusion: sum up, offer a solution, recommendation or prediction, and end with a strong final sentence.

An article has no addresses, no salutation, no 'Yours faithfully'; the author's name appears in the by-line under the title. A formal letter has both addresses, a salutation, a complimentary close and a signature. An article can be formal or informal but is always engaging; a letter is strictly formal.

units.title: Oral English: Stress in Two-Syllable Words
units.summary: The noun/verb stress rule for two-syllable words, with prepositions and a minimal-pairs drill.

p: We do not say every syllable with the same force. A stressed syllable is louder, longer and higher. Wrong stress makes a word sound odd or even changes its meaning, especially in two-syllable words, where stress separates nouns and adjectives from verbs.
Rule 1: most two-syllable nouns and adjectives are stressed on the FIRST syllable: REcord (a disc or account), PREsent (a gift), CONflict (a disagreement), HAPpy, CLEver.
Rule 2: most two-syllable verbs are stressed on the SECOND: reCORD (to write down), preSENT (to give), conFLICT (to clash), deCIDE, beGIN.
Rule 3: most two-syllable prepositions are stressed on the second: beTWEEN, aBOVE, aCROSS.
'The INcrease in prices will inCREASE our costs.' 'There was a REbel in the army. The soldiers decided to reBEL.' Pairs: CONduct / conDUCT; PROduce / proDUCE; OBject / obJECT; PERmit / perMIT.

units.title: Comprehension: Paraphrasing Poems and Dramatic Works
units.summary: How to turn dense or old-fashioned poetry and drama into plain modern prose, with a table of archaic words, a worked example from Julius Caesar and a stanza of Blake.

p: To paraphrase is to restate a text in your own words. Poems and older plays (such as Shakespeare's) use old words, tangled word order and dense figures. Paraphrasing turns them into clear modern prose.

Step 1: read the whole stanza or speech for the overall sense and mood. Step 2: work line by line: translate old words (thou, thee, thy, thine = you, your, yours; art = are; hast = have; dost = do; hath = has; wherefore = why: 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?' means 'Why are you Romeo?', not 'Where are you?'); untangle figures (metaphor 'All the world's a stage' = life is like a theatre performance; simile 'My love is like a red, red rose' = his love is beautiful and delicate; personification 'The wind whispered through the trees' = the wind blew softly with a whispering sound). Step 3: restate the literal meaning in simple sentences; ignore rhyme and rhythm.
Also identify theme (love, power, betrayal, time), mood (melancholic, joyful, tense), imagery (language that appeals to the senses) and dramatic features: dialogue, monologue and stage directions.

'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears; I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him. The evil that men do lives after them; the good is oft interred with their bones.' 'Lend me your ears' is an idiom for 'listen to me'. Paraphrase: 'My fellow citizens, please listen. I have come to bury Caesar, not to praise him. People are remembered for the bad they did, while the good is often forgotten when they die.' Theme: the fickleness of opinion and the nature of legacy.

William Blake's 'The Tyger' opens: 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night; / What immortal hand or eye, / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?' A paraphrase: 'Tiger, shining like fire in the dark forests, what divine being could have made you so awesome and so perfectly formed?' Imagery: 'burning bright'. A metaphor: the tiger as a burning fire.

units.title: Grammar: Concord (Subject-Verb Agreement)
units.summary: Eight rules of concord: basic agreement, compound subjects with 'and', 'or' and 'nor', indefinite pronouns, collective nouns, 'there is/are', intervening phrases, and titles and quantities.

p: A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. 'The boy runs.' 'The boys run.'
1. Compound subjects joined by 'and' are usually plural: 'Tola and Bola are here.' Exception: two nouns that name one thing: 'Rice and beans is my favourite meal.'
2. With 'or' or 'nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject (proximity rule): 'Neither the teacher nor the students are late.' 'Neither the students nor the teacher is late.'

3. These indefinite pronouns are singular: each, every, either, neither, one, no one, everyone, someone, anyone, nobody, everybody, somebody, anybody, nothing, everything, something, anything: 'Everyone has a pen.'

4. Collective nouns (team, committee, family, class, government, staff): singular when the group acts as one ('The team is winning'); plural when members act separately, more usual in British English ('The committee are arguing among themselves').
5. 'There is' or 'There are' agrees with the subject that follows: 'There is a book on the table.' 'There are many books on the table.'
6. Phrases such as as well as, along with, together with and in addition to do not change the number: 'The manager, as well as the assistants, is responsible.'
7. Titles of books, films and countries are singular: 'The Brothers Karamazov is a long novel.'
8. Amounts seen as one sum are singular: 'Ten thousand naira is a lot of money.' Subjects such as mathematics and news are singular: 'Mathematics is a challenging subject.'

units.title: Oral English: Vowel Contrasts
units.summary: Short and long vowels /ɪ/ and /iː/, /ʊ/ and /uː/, /æ/ and /ɑː/ with minimal pairs and sentences.

p: Vowels are made with an open vocal tract. The difference between short and long vowels is not only length but also the tongue position and mouth shape. Mispronouncing them causes misunderstanding because many words form minimal pairs.

/ɪ/ as in 'sit': short and relaxed, tongue in the centre-front: ship, slip, bin, hit, grin, sin. /iː/ as in 'seat': long and tense, tongue high and front, lips slightly spread: sheep, sleep, bean, heat, green, scene. 'Don't slip on the deck of the ship.' 'The sheep are sleeping.' 'I feel fit.' 'I have sore feet.'

/ʊ/ as in 'pull': short, tongue high and back but relaxed, lips slightly rounded: pull, full, could, wood, book, look. /uː/ as in 'pool': long and tense, lips tightly rounded: pool, fool, cool, shoe, blue, food. 'The pull of the current was strong.' 'Let's swim in the pool.' 'Look at that!' 'His name is Luke.'

/æ/ as in 'cat': short, jaw open, tongue low and front: man, cat, bat, hat, pack, sad. /ɑː/ as in 'cart': long, jaw open, tongue low and drawn back: mark, cart, barn, heart, park, calm. 'The cat sat on the mat.' 'We put the shopping in the cart.' 'He wore a hat.' 'She has a kind heart.'

units.title: Structure: Adjuncts, Conjuncts and Disjuncts
units.summary: Three kinds of adverbial: adjuncts that modify the verb, conjuncts that link ideas and disjuncts that comment on a whole sentence.

p: Adverbials add information. They fall into three types by function.

Part of the core of the clause; they modify the verb and tell us how, when, where, how often or why. Remove one and the sentence is still complete but loses detail. Manner: 'He ran quickly.' Place: 'She is sitting in the garden.' Time: 'We will leave tomorrow.' Frequency: 'He often visits his grandparents.' Reason: 'He left because he was tired.'

Not part of the core meaning; they connect sentences or clauses logically. They show addition (furthermore, moreover), contrast (however), result (therefore) or sequence (meanwhile, first, next). They are usually set off by a comma: 'He is rich; moreover, he is generous.' 'However, he did not agree.' 'Therefore, the project was cancelled.'

Stand outside the core and give the speaker's attitude or judgment about the whole statement. Honesty: frankly, honestly. Judgment: obviously, clearly. Evaluation: luckily, unfortunately, surprisingly. Style: briefly. Usually set off by a comma: 'Luckily, no one was hurt.' 'Surprisingly, he passed the exam.'

units.title: Comprehension: Simple, Compound and Complex Sentences
units.summary: How to recognise the three basic sentence structures and why mixing them improves flow and readability.

p: Advanced reading includes noticing how sentences are built. Seeing structure helps you follow how ideas are linked and improves your own writing.

Simple sentence: one independent clause (a subject and a verb giving a complete thought). It may have a compound subject or verb, but only one clause: 'The dog barked.' 'Tola and Bola studied for the exam and passed.'

Compound sentence: two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so: FANBOYS) or a semicolon; the ideas are equally important: 'The dog barked, and the cat ran away.' 'I wanted to go to the party, but I was too tired.' 'She is intelligent; she is also hardworking.'

Complex sentence: one independent clause and at least one dependent clause, which cannot stand alone; it often starts with because, since, although, when, if, after, before, which, that or who: 'The dog barked when the postman arrived.' 'Although it was raining, we went for a walk.' 'This is the book that I recommended.'

units.title: Writing: the Expository Essay
units.summary: A planned expository essay on how to improve family functioning, with brainstorming, a full outline and the task.

p: An expository essay explains or informs in a clear, logical and objective way. It does not argue a point or tell a story. It presents facts, statistics, examples and explanations in a balanced way, in a neutral tone.

sections.h: Brainstorm and outline: 'How to improve family functioning'
p: Brainstorm: communication, mutual respect, quality time, shared responsibilities, financial planning, conflict resolution, love and support. Choose the three strongest.

Title: 'The Pillars of a Functional Family'. Introduction: hook (the family is the basic unit of society); context (all families face challenges, but a well-functioning one overcomes them); thesis ('A family's strength can be greatly improved by open communication, mutual respect and quality time together').

Body 1, open communication: topic sentence ('The cornerstone of a healthy family is open and honest communication'); explanation (builds trust, prevents misunderstanding, solves problems); examples (family meetings, listening without judgement, a safe place to speak). Body 2, mutual respect: valuing opinions, privacy and differences; respecting boundaries, avoiding harsh criticism, celebrating achievements. Body 3, quality time: love is shown by shared experience; meals without distraction, outings, joint projects, traditions.
Conclusion: restate the thesis in new words; recap the three pillars; end with a hopeful sentence about a happy, supportive family.

units.title: Structure: Prepositional Phrases
units.summary: What a prepositional phrase is and how it works as an adjective (which? what kind?) or as an adverb (where? when? how? why?), with worked examples.

p: A preposition shows a relationship of time, space or logic. A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and ends with a noun or pronoun (its object). It works as one unit that modifies.

It modifies a noun by answering 'Which one?' or 'What kind?' and usually stands right after the noun. 'The house on the hill has a beautiful view.' (Which house?) 'I admire a person with a sense of humour.' (What kind?) 'The suggestion from the committee was accepted.'

It modifies a verb, adjective or adverb by answering where, when, how or why, and can stand at the start, middle or end. 'We will meet at the restaurant.' (where) 'The concert starts in the evening.' (when) 'She completed the task with incredible speed.' (how) 'He went to the market for some bread.' (why)

'The book on the shelf in the library is by my favourite author': 'on the shelf' (which book?), 'in the library' (which shelf?) and 'by my favourite author' (what kind of book?) are all adjectival. 'The dog slept under the table' (where? adverbial, modifies 'slept'). 'The dog under the table is sleeping' (which dog? adjectival, modifies 'dog').

units.title: Writing: Summarising Implied Meaning
units.summary: How to read between the lines in summary tasks: analyse tone, word choice (connotation), figurative language, and put facts together to see the hidden argument.

p: Advanced summary needs implied meaning: what the author suggests without stating. You infer it from tone, word choice and context. This is vital for critical thinking and for editorials and literature.
Tone: 'Another brilliant idea from the management,' he said as the clumsy new policy was announced. Implied: the idea is terrible.
Word choice (connotation): 'The politician stated his position' (neutral); 'admitted his position' (reluctance, or a negative position); 'boasted about his position' (arrogance).
Figurative language: 'The new tax law is a bitter pill for the middle class.' Implied: unpleasant and hard to accept.

Putting facts together: 'The company reported record profits. The CEO's bonus rose 200%. Meanwhile staff were told there will be a pay freeze.' Implied: executives are rewarded at the staff's expense.

'The government's new "affordable housing initiative" will build 500 luxury apartments, starting at 100 million naira each. The Minister declared it a "victory for every Nigerian family."' The quotation marks around 'affordable housing' show doubt. The contrast between 'affordable' and 'luxury apartments at 100 million naira' is ironic. The Minister's words are left to stand against the facts. Implied summary: the programme is wrongly named and out of touch with ordinary Nigerians.

units.title: Comprehension: Critical Evaluation and Fallacies
units.summary: How to spot logical fallacies (hasty generalisation, ad hominem, false cause, bandwagon), bias (loaded language, omission, opinion as fact) and weak evidence.

p: Critical reading judges the quality, validity and persuasiveness of a text. You question the author's arguments, evidence and motives, tell fact from opinion and detect bias.

Hasty generalisation: a conclusion from too little evidence ('I met two rude people from that city, so everyone from there is rude'). Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument ('We should not listen to his views on climate change because he failed science at school'). False cause (post hoc): thinking that because B followed A, A caused B ('The new mayor was elected and then crime rose, so the mayor caused the crime wave'). Bandwagon: saying something is true because it is popular ('Everyone is buying this phone, so it must be the best').

Loaded language: words with strong positive or negative feeling ('the government's reckless scheme' against 'bold new scheme'). Omission: leaving out facts that go against the writer. Opinion presented as fact. Test evidence: is it relevant, sufficient and from a credible source?

'The "Clean City" initiative is a complete waste of taxpayer money. The councillor who proposed it, Mr Jones, is a known liar who was once fined for littering himself! Furthermore, my neighbour said the new bins are already broken. It is obvious that this project is a failure and should be scrapped immediately.' Ad hominem: attacking Mr Jones's character. Weak evidence: a single neighbour's remark (a hasty generalisation). Tone: angry and scornful, which reduces the writer's credibility.

units.title: Revision: Algebraic Expressions
units.summary: Terms, like and unlike terms, simplifying, expanding brackets and factorising (common factor, difference of two squares and simple trinomials).

p: In 3x² + 5x − 7 the coefficient of x² is 3, the linear term is 5x and −7 is the constant term. Terms are separated by + or −. Like terms have the same letters with the same powers (3x and 5x; 2y² and −7y²) and can be combined. Unlike terms (3x and 5y; 2x² and 2x) cannot.
Simplify 7x + 3y − 2x + 5y: group the x terms (7x − 2x = 5x) and the y terms (3y + 5y = 8y). Answer: 5x + 8y.

Expanding multiplies every term inside the bracket: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12; −2(3x − 5) = −6x + 10 (negative times negative is positive). Two brackets: (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 3x + 2x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6. (2x − 1)(x + 4) = 2x² + 8x − x − 4 = 2x² + 7x − 4.

Common factor: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3); 4x² + 8x = 4x(x + 2). Difference of two squares: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), so x² − 9 = (x + 3)(x − 3); 4x² − 25 = (2x + 5)(2x − 5). Simple trinomials: find two numbers that multiply to the constant and add to the middle coefficient: x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3) because 2 × 3 = 6 and 2 + 3 = 5. Always check by expanding.

units.title: Revision: Fractions, Decimals, Percentages and Linear Equations
units.summary: Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages, adding, multiplying and dividing fractions, and solving linear equations.

p: Fraction to decimal: divide top by bottom (3/4 = 0.75). Decimal to percentage: multiply by 100 (0.75 = 75%). Percentage to fraction: put over 100 and simplify (75% = 75/100 = 3/4). Percentage to decimal: divide by 100.

Add: use a common denominator: 1/4 + 1/3 = 3/12 + 4/12 = 7/12. Multiply: top times top, bottom times bottom: 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15. Divide: keep the first, change to times, flip the second: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6.

An equation is like a balance: do the same to both sides. 3x + 5 = 14: subtract 5 to get 3x = 9; divide by 3 to get x = 3. 2x + 3 = 11 gives x = 4. With letters on both sides: 5x − 3 = 2x + 9; collect: 5x − 2x = 9 + 3; 3x = 12; x = 4. With brackets: 3(x + 2) = 18; expand 3x + 6 = 18; 3x = 12; x = 4.
Always check by substituting: for 5x − 7 = 13 with x = 4: 5(4) − 7 = 13 and 20 − 7 = 13, which is correct.

units.title: Revision: Angles and Geometry
units.summary: Types of angle, angle facts (straight line, point, vertically opposite), angles in parallel lines and in triangles and polygons.

p: Acute: between 0° and 90°. Right: 90°. Obtuse: between 90° and 180°. Straight: 180°. Reflex: between 180° and 360°. Complete turn: 360°.

Complementary angles add up to 90°; supplementary angles add up to 180°. Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles at a point add up to 360°. Vertically opposite angles (where two lines cross) are equal.
With parallel lines cut by a transversal: corresponding angles are equal; alternate angles are equal; co-interior (allied) angles add up to 180°.

The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. The interior angles of a polygon with n sides add up to (n − 2) × 180°: a quadrilateral has 360° and a pentagon 540°. The exterior angles of any convex polygon add up to 360°.

units.title: Numbers: Standard Form
units.summary: Writing very large and very small numbers as A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10, and multiplying and dividing numbers in standard form.

p: A number is in standard form when it is written as A × 10ⁿ, where A is at least 1 and less than 10, and n is a whole number (an integer). It makes huge and tiny numbers easy to read and compare.

Large number: 5 600 000 = 5.6 × 10⁶ (the decimal point moves 6 places to the left, so the power is positive). 345 000 = 3.45 × 10⁵. Small number: 0.00034 = 3.4 × 10⁻⁴ (the point moves 4 places to the right, so the power is negative). 0.000456 = 4.56 × 10⁻⁴; 0.00072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴. Check: 4.56 × 0.0001 = 0.000456.
Multiply: multiply the A parts and add the powers: (2 × 10³) × (3 × 10⁴) = 6 × 10⁷. If A comes out 10 or more, adjust: (6 × 10⁵) × (5 × 10⁴) = 30 × 10⁹ = 3 × 10¹⁰.
Divide: divide the A parts and subtract the powers: (4.5 × 10⁶) ÷ (1.5 × 10³) = 3 × 10³.
Add or subtract: first give both numbers the same power: 3.2 × 10³ + 4.5 × 10² = 3200 + 450 = 3650 = 3.65 × 10³.

units.title: Numbers: Significant Figures and Percentage Error
units.summary: Counting and rounding to significant figures and working out percentage error.

p: Rules: non-zero digits are always significant (234 has 3). Zeros between non-zero digits are significant (2003 has 4). Leading zeros are not (0.0025 has 2). Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant (2.500 has 4). A number such as 500 is ambiguous (1 or 3 significant figures) unless stated.

Find the required digits, look at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up; less than 5 rounds down. 0.035682 to 3 s.f.: digits 3, 5, 6; next is 8, so round up: 0.0357. 3.14159 to 4 s.f.: 3.141 and next is 5, so round up: 3.142. 0.0078234 to 3 s.f.: 7, 8, 2, next is 3, so 0.00782.

Percentage error = (|approximate − exact| ÷ exact) × 100%. A desk measured as 1.23 m but really 1.25 m: error 0.02; 0.02 ÷ 1.25 = 0.016; × 100 = 1.6%. A weight of 48.5 kg read when the true value is 50 kg: 1.5 ÷ 50 = 0.03 = 3%. Using π ≈ 3.14 when π = 3.14159: error 0.00159; 0.00159 ÷ 3.14159 × 100 ≈ 0.05%, a very good approximation.

units.title: Logarithms: Meaning and Laws
units.summary: What a logarithm is, common logarithms (base 10), and the product, quotient, power and root laws.

p: A logarithm is the power to which a base must be raised to give a number. If bˣ = y then log_b y = x. Examples: 10² = 100 so log₁₀ 100 = 2; 2³ = 8 so log₂ 8 = 3; 10⁰ = 1 so log 1 = 0. Logarithms to base 10 are called common logarithms and are written log x.

log 1 = 0, log 10 = 1, log 100 = 2, log 1000 = 3, log 10 000 = 4. Each time the number is multiplied by 10 the logarithm goes up by 1. A number between 1 and 10 has a logarithm between 0 and 1; between 10 and 100, between 1 and 2. So log 50 is between 1 and 2 (it is about 1.699).
Product: log(M × N) = log M + log N. Example: log(100 × 1000) = 2 + 3 = 5 (and 100 000 = 10⁵).
Quotient: log(M ÷ N) = log M − log N. Example: log(1000 ÷ 10) = 3 − 1 = 2.
Power: log(Mⁿ) = n log M. Example: log(10³) = 3.
Root: log(ⁿ√M) = (1/n) log M. Example: log(√100) = ½ × 2 = 1.

Special values: log 1 = 0; log 10 = 1; log 10ⁿ = n; log of a base to the same base is 1. In short: multiply means add logs; divide means subtract; power means multiply the log; root means divide the log.

units.title: Logarithms: Characteristic, Mantissa and Tables
units.summary: The two parts of a logarithm, finding logs and antilogs from four-figure tables and bar notation for numbers below 1.

p: log 456 = 2.6590. The whole-number part (2) is the characteristic; the decimal part (0.6590) is the mantissa, which is always positive and comes from the tables.

For a number of 1 or more, characteristic = (number of digits before the decimal point) − 1: 456 gives 2; 4.56 gives 0; 45 600 gives 4. For a number less than 1, characteristic = −(number of zeros after the point + 1), written with a bar: 0.456 gives 1̄; 0.0456 gives 2̄; 0.00456 gives 3̄.

Write the number in standard form. log 456: 456 = 4.56 × 10². Characteristic 2. In the tables, find row 45 and column 6: mantissa 0.6590. So log 456 = 2.6590. For a fourth digit, add the number from the mean difference column. Same digits give the same mantissa: 567, 56.7, 5.67, 0.567 and 0.0567 all have mantissa 0.7536, so their logs are 2.7536, 1.7536, 0.7536, 1̄.7536 and 2̄.7536.

The antilogarithm undoes the logarithm: if log x = y then x = antilog y. Find antilog 2.6590: mantissa 0.6590 gives 4.56 in the antilog table; characteristic 2 means × 10²; so the number is 456. For antilog 2̄.5340: mantissa 0.5340 gives 3.42; 2̄ means × 10⁻²; the number is 0.0342.

units.title: Sequences: Meaning and Types
units.summary: What a sequence is, terms and the nth term, and the main kinds of sequence: arithmetic, geometric and others.

p: A sequence is a list of numbers arranged by a rule. Each number is a term: T₁, T₂, T₃... and Tₙ is the nth term. A rule for Tₙ lets us find any term: if Tₙ = 2n + 1, then T₁ = 3, T₂ = 5, T₃ = 7, T₄ = 9.
Arithmetic progression (AP): each term is found by adding the same number (the common difference d): 2, 5, 8, 11 (d = 3); 20, 15, 10, 5 (d = −5).
Geometric progression (GP): each term is found by multiplying by the same number (the common ratio r): 2, 6, 18, 54 (r = 3).
Other sequences: square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16 (Tₙ = n²); Fibonacci numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 (each term is the sum of the two before).
For 3, 7, 11, 15, the differences are all 4, so it is an AP with a = 3 and d = 4. For 5, 10, 20, 40, the ratios are all 2, so it is a GP. The next term in 1, 4, 9, 16 is 25, since the terms are n².

units.title: Quadratic Equations: Roots and Forming Equations
units.summary: What a quadratic equation is, what its roots are, how the sum and product of the roots are linked to the coefficients, and how to build an equation from its roots.

p: A quadratic equation is an equation in which the highest power of the unknown is 2. Its standard form is ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b and c are numbers and a is not 0. For example, x² − 5x + 6 = 0 has a = 1, b = −5 and c = 6.
The values of x that make the equation true are called the roots (or solutions) of the equation. A quadratic equation has at most two roots.

To test whether a number is a root, put it in place of x. If the left side becomes 0, it is a root. Test x = 2 in x² − 5x + 6: 4 − 10 + 6 = 0. So x = 2 is a root. Test x = 4: 16 − 20 + 6 = 2, which is not 0, so x = 4 is not a root.

sections.h: Sum and product of the roots
p: Suppose the roots of a quadratic equation are α and β (alpha and beta). Then the equation can be written (x − α)(x − β) = 0. Expand it: x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0.
So, for x² + (b/a)x + c/a = 0, that is for ax² + bx + c = 0 with both sides divided by a:
Sum of the roots = α + β = −b/a. Product of the roots = αβ = c/a.
Example: for 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0, the sum of the roots is 7/2 and the product is 3/2. You can check: the roots are 3 and 1/2. Their sum is 3½ = 7/2 and their product is 3/2. Correct.

sections.h: Forming an equation from its roots
p: Use this rule: x² − (sum of roots)x + (product of roots) = 0.
Example 1. Roots 2 and 3. Sum = 5, product = 6. The equation is x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
Example 2. Roots −1 and 4. Sum = 3, product = −4. The equation is x² − 3x − 4 = 0.

Example 3. Roots 1/2 and −3. Sum = 1/2 − 3 = −5/2 and product = −3/2. The equation is x² + (5/2)x − 3/2 = 0. Multiply every term by 2 to remove the fractions: 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0. Check x = 1/2: 2 × 1/4 + 5/2 − 3 = 0.5 + 2.5 − 3 = 0. Correct.
One root of x² − 5x + k = 0 is 2. Find k. Put x = 2: 4 − 10 + k = 0, so k = 6. The equation is x² − 5x + 6 = 0 and the other root is 3 (because the sum of the roots is 5).

units.title: Solving Quadratic Equations by Factorisation
units.summary: Writing a quadratic equation in the form ax² + bx + c = 0 and factorising it, then using the rule that if two things multiply to give 0, one of them is 0.

p: If A × B = 0, then A = 0 or B = 0 (or both). This is called the zero product rule. So if we can write a quadratic as a product of two brackets equal to 0, each bracket gives one root.
Important: first move every term to one side so that the other side is 0. For example x² = 5x − 6 must first be written x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
Find two numbers whose product is c and whose sum is b.
Example: x² − 5x + 6 = 0. Two numbers with product 6 and sum −5 are −2 and −3. So (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. Therefore x = 2 or x = 3.
Example: x² + x − 12 = 0. Two numbers with product −12 and sum +1 are +4 and −3. So (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0. Therefore x = −4 or x = 3.

sections.h: Case 2: when a is not 1 (splitting the middle term)
p: Multiply a by c. Find two numbers with that product and with sum b. Use them to split the middle term, then factorise in pairs.
Example: 2x² + 7x + 3 = 0. a × c = 6. Two numbers with product 6 and sum 7 are 6 and 1. So 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 0. Group: 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = 0, so (2x + 1)(x + 3) = 0. Therefore x = −1/2 or x = −3.

Example: 6x² − x − 2 = 0. a × c = −12. Two numbers with product −12 and sum −1 are −4 and +3. So 6x² − 4x + 3x − 2 = 0. Group: 2x(3x − 2) + 1(3x − 2) = 0, so (3x − 2)(2x + 1) = 0. Therefore x = 2/3 or x = −1/2.
Difference of two squares: x² − 9 = 0 gives (x − 3)(x + 3) = 0, so x = 3 or x = −3.
No constant term: x² − 3x = 0 gives x(x − 3) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 3. Never divide both sides by x, because you will lose the root x = 0.
Put each root back in the original equation. For x = −4 in x² + x − 12: 16 − 4 − 12 = 0. Correct.

units.title: Solving Quadratic Equations by Completing the Square
units.summary: A method that works for every quadratic equation, even when the roots are not whole numbers: make one side a perfect square.

p: A perfect square looks like (x + p)² = x² + 2px + p². Notice that the number at the end, p², is the square of half the coefficient of x. So to turn x² + bx into a perfect square, add (b/2)².
Examples: x² + 10x needs 25 to become (x + 5)². x² − 6x needs 9 to become (x − 3)². x² + x needs 1/4 to become (x + 1/2)².
1. Make the coefficient of x² equal to 1 (divide every term by a if a is not 1).
2. Move the constant term to the right side.
3. Add (half the coefficient of x)² to both sides.
4. Write the left side as a square, then take the square root of both sides. Remember ±.
5. Solve for x.

units.summary: The quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a, with worked examples where the roots are whole numbers, fractions and surds.

This is the quadratic formula. It works for every quadratic equation, so it is the safest method when factorising is hard.
1. Write the equation as ax² + bx + c = 0 and list a, b, c with their signs.
2. Work out b² − 4ac first (this is called the discriminant).
3. Substitute into the formula, then work out the + answer and the − answer.

units.title: Nature of Roots: The Discriminant
units.summary: Using b² − 4ac to tell, without solving, whether a quadratic equation has two different real roots, two equal roots or no real roots.

p: In the quadratic formula the part under the square root, D = b² − 4ac, decides what kind of roots we get. It is called the discriminant because it discriminates (tells apart) the different cases.
See the table below. Remember that you cannot take the square root of a negative number in real numbers.

head: Value of D
Roots
Graph touches the x-axis
rows: Two equal real roots (one repeated root)

p: D = 16 − 16 = 0. So the roots are equal. Indeed (x − 2)² = 0, so x = 2 twice.
D = 4 − 20 = −16. D is negative, so there are no real roots.
D = 9 + 16 = 25. D is positive, so there are two different real roots. Also, 25 is a perfect square, so the roots are rational: x = (3 ± 5)/4, so x = 2 or x = −1/2.
Find k so that x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots. For equal roots, D = 0: k² − 4(1)(9) = 0, so k² = 36 and k = 6 or k = −6.
For which values of k does x² + 4x + k = 0 have real roots? We need D ≥ 0: 16 − 4k ≥ 0, so k ≤ 4.

units.title: Word Problems with Quadratic Equations
units.summary: Turning everyday and number problems into quadratic equations, solving them and rejecting answers that do not make sense.

p: 1. Read the problem and choose a letter for the unknown. Write down what it stands for.
2. Write the other quantities using that letter.
3. Form an equation from the facts given.
4. Rearrange to ax² + bx + c = 0 and solve.
5. Check each answer in the problem. Reject any answer that is impossible (for example a negative length).

The product of two consecutive positive integers is 56. Find them. Let the integers be n and n + 1. n(n + 1) = 56, so n² + n − 56 = 0. (n + 8)(n − 7) = 0. n = 7 or n = −8. They are positive, so n = 7 and the numbers are 7 and 8. (If negative numbers were allowed, −8 and −7 would also work.)

The length of a rectangle is 3 cm more than its width. Its area is 40 cm². Find its dimensions. Let the width be w. Then length = w + 3. w(w + 3) = 40, so w² + 3w − 40 = 0. (w + 8)(w − 5) = 0. w = 5 or w = −8. A width cannot be negative, so w = 5 cm and length = 8 cm. Check: 5 × 8 = 40. Correct.

The two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle are x cm and (x + 7) cm. The hypotenuse is 13 cm. Find x. By Pythagoras, x² + (x + 7)² = 13². x² + x² + 14x + 49 = 169. 2x² + 14x − 120 = 0. Divide by 2: x² + 7x − 60 = 0. (x + 12)(x − 5) = 0. x = 5 (reject −12). The sides are 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm. Check: 25 + 144 = 169. Correct.

sections.h: Problem 4: a number and its square
p: A number added to its square gives 30. x² + x − 30 = 0. (x + 6)(x − 5) = 0. The number is 5 or −6. Both work: 25 + 5 = 30 and 36 − 6 = 30.

units.title: Simultaneous Linear Equations
units.summary: Solving two linear equations in two unknowns by elimination and by substitution, and checking the answer.

p: Two equations with two unknowns, such as x + y = 10 and x − y = 2, have a pair of values of x and y that work in both equations at the same time. To find them we remove (eliminate) one unknown, or we replace one unknown with an expression (substitute).

Example 1: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2. The y terms are +y and −y, so add the equations: 3x = 9, so x = 3. Put x = 3 in x − y = 2: 3 − y = 2, so y = 1. Check in 2x + y: 6 + 1 = 7. Correct. Answer: x = 3, y = 1.
Example 2: 3x + 2y = 16 and x + y = 6. Multiply the second equation by 2: 2x + 2y = 12. Subtract this from the first: x = 4. Then y = 6 − 4 = 2. Check: 12 + 4 = 16. Correct.

Example 3 (multiply both): 2x + 3y = 13 and 3x − 2y = 0. Multiply the first by 2: 4x + 6y = 26. Multiply the second by 3: 9x − 6y = 0. Add: 13x = 26, so x = 2. Put in the first: 4 + 3y = 13, so y = 3. Check the second: 6 − 6 = 0. Correct.

sections.h: Rule for choosing add or subtract
p: Make the numbers in front of one letter the same size. If their signs are the same, subtract the equations. If their signs are different, add the equations.
Example: y = 2x − 1 and 3x + y = 9. Replace y in the second equation: 3x + 2x − 1 = 9, so 5x = 10 and x = 2. Then y = 2(2) − 1 = 3. Check: 6 + 3 = 9. Correct. Answer: x = 2, y = 3.

units.title: One Linear and One Quadratic Equation
units.summary: Solving simultaneous equations when one is linear and the other is quadratic, by substitution. There are usually two pairs of answers.

p: 1. Make one letter the subject of the linear equation.
2. Substitute it into the quadratic equation. You get a quadratic equation in one letter.
3. Solve it. You usually get two values.
4. Put each value into the linear equation to find the matching value of the other letter. Always use the linear equation for this, because it is easier and avoids false pairs.

sections.h: Example 1: a line and a circle
p: y = x + 1 and x² + y² = 25. Substitute: x² + (x + 1)² = 25. 2x² + 2x + 1 = 25, so 2x² + 2x − 24 = 0, so x² + x − 12 = 0. (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0. x = 3 gives y = 4. x = −4 gives y = −3. Solutions: (3, 4) and (−4, −3). Check (−4, −3): 16 + 9 = 25. Correct.

sections.h: Example 2: a line and a parabola
p: y = 2x − 3 and y = x² − 2x − 3. The two y values are equal, so x² − 2x − 3 = 2x − 3. x² − 4x = 0, so x(x − 4) = 0. x = 0 gives y = −3. x = 4 gives y = 5. Solutions: (0, −3) and (4, 5). You will see these on a graph in Unit 24.

x + y = 5 and xy = 6. From the first, y = 5 − x. So x(5 − x) = 6, which gives 5x − x² = 6, so x² − 5x + 6 = 0. (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. x = 2 gives y = 3 and x = 3 gives y = 2. Solutions: (2, 3) and (3, 2).

sections.h: Example 4: x − y = 1 and x² + y² = 13
p: x = y + 1. Substitute: (y + 1)² + y² = 13. 2y² + 2y + 1 = 13, so y² + y − 6 = 0. (y + 3)(y − 2) = 0. y = 2 gives x = 3. y = −3 gives x = −2. Solutions: (3, 2) and (−2, −3). Check: 4 + 9 = 13. Correct.

units.title: Word Problems with Simultaneous Equations
units.summary: Forming two equations from a story, solving them, and checking that the answers fit the story.

p: Choose two letters for the two unknowns. Write two equations, one from each fact in the story. Solve and check against both facts.

Three pens and two books cost ₦1 100. Two pens and three books cost ₦1 150. Find the price of each. Let a pen cost p naira and a book cost b naira. 3p + 2b = 1 100 and 2p + 3b = 1 150. Multiply the first by 3: 9p + 6b = 3 300. Multiply the second by 2: 4p + 6b = 2 300. Subtract: 5p = 1 000, so p = 200. Then 2b = 1 100 − 600 = 500, so b = 250. Check: 400 + 750 = 1 150. Correct. A pen costs ₦200 and a book costs ₦250.
Two numbers add up to 12 and their product is 35. Find them. x + y = 12 and xy = 35. y = 12 − x, so x(12 − x) = 35, which gives x² − 12x + 35 = 0. (x − 5)(x − 7) = 0. The numbers are 5 and 7.

The perimeter of a rectangle is 28 cm and its area is 48 cm². Find the sides. Half the perimeter is 14, so l + w = 14 and lw = 48. l = 14 − w, so w(14 − w) = 48, giving w² − 14w + 48 = 0. (w − 6)(w − 8) = 0. The sides are 6 cm and 8 cm.

Adult tickets cost ₦300 and child tickets cost ₦100. 20 tickets were sold for ₦4 000. Let a = adults and c = children. a + c = 20 and 300a + 100c = 4 000, which simplifies to 3a + c = 40. Subtract the first equation: 2a = 20, so a = 10 and c = 10. Check: 3 000 + 1 000 = 4 000. Correct.

units.title: Graphs of Linear Equations
units.summary: Drawing a straight line from a table of values, finding the gradient and intercepts, and writing an equation from two points.

sections.h: The equation of a straight line
p: Any equation that can be written y = mx + c has a straight-line graph. m is the gradient (the steepness) and c is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis).
Gradient = rise / run = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁).

sections.h: Drawing a line from a table
p: Draw y = 2x + 1. Choose some values of x and work out y.

img.alt: Graph of the straight line y = 2x + 1 showing the y-intercept at (0, 1), the x-intercept at (-0.5, 0) and a run of 1 and rise of 2
img.cap: The line y = 2x + 1. For every 1 step right it goes 2 steps up.

p: The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 1), so c = 1. It crosses the x-axis where y = 0: 2x + 1 = 0, so x = −1/2. The gradient is 2: for each 1 unit across, the line rises 2 units.
Tips for graphs: draw straight lines with a ruler and a sharp pencil, use a suitable scale, label both axes, and write the equation next to the line.

sections.h: Finding the gradient and equation from two points
p: The line passes through (1, 3) and (3, 7). Gradient m = (7 − 3)/(3 − 1) = 4/2 = 2. So y = 2x + c. Put in (1, 3): 3 = 2 + c, so c = 1. The equation is y = 2x + 1.

sections.h: Intercepts of a line in another form
p: For 2x + 3y = 6: when x = 0, y = 2, so the y-intercept is (0, 2). When y = 0, x = 3, so the x-intercept is (3, 0). Rearranged: 3y = −2x + 6, so y = −(2/3)x + 2. The gradient is −2/3 (the line slopes downward).
Lines with the same gradient are parallel. y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 5 never meet.

units.title: Graphs of Quadratic Equations
units.summary: Drawing the curve (parabola) y = ax² + bx + c from a table, and reading its roots, turning point, axis of symmetry and intercepts.

sections.h: The shape of a quadratic graph
p: The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a smooth curve called a parabola. If a is positive the curve is U-shaped and has a lowest point (a minimum). If a is negative it is shaped like an upside-down U and has a highest point (a maximum). This point is called the turning point or vertex.
The curve is symmetrical about a vertical line through the turning point, called the axis of symmetry. Its equation is x = −b/(2a).
Make a table of values and work out y for each x. For x = −2: 4 + 4 − 3 = 5. For x = 3: 9 − 6 − 3 = 0.

img.alt: Graph of the parabola y = x squared minus 2x minus 3 with roots at -1 and 3, minimum point (1, -4), y-intercept (0, -3) and axis of symmetry x = 1
img.cap: The parabola y = x² − 2x − 3.

p: Roots: where the curve crosses the x-axis, x = −1 and x = 3. These are the solutions of x² − 2x − 3 = 0. Check by factorising: (x + 1)(x − 3) = 0.
y-intercept: (0, −3). The number c is always the y-intercept.
Turning point: the lowest point is (1, −4). The axis of symmetry is x = 1, which is halfway between the roots: (−1 + 3)/2 = 1.
Notice that the table is symmetrical: the y values 5, 0, −3 on the left come back as −3, 0, 5 on the right.

sections.h: A graph with a maximum: y = 3 + 2x − x²
p: Here a = −1 (negative), so the curve is an upside-down U. Table: x = −1 gives 3 − 2 − 1 = 0. x = 0 gives 3. x = 1 gives 3 + 2 − 1 = 4. x = 2 gives 3 + 4 − 4 = 3. x = 3 gives 3 + 6 − 9 = 0. The maximum point is (1, 4) and the roots are −1 and 3.
Use at least seven points. Plot them carefully with small crosses. Join them with a smooth curve drawn freehand, not with a ruler. The bottom of the curve should be round, not pointed.

units.title: Solving Equations Graphically
units.summary: Using a drawn parabola to solve quadratic equations, and using a straight line drawn on the same axes to solve other equations and simultaneous equations.

p: The solution of an equation is where two graphs meet. If one graph is the curve and the other is a line, the x-coordinates of the crossing points are the solutions.
Take y = x² − 2x − 3 (drawn in the last unit). The equation says y = 0, so the roots are where the curve crosses the x-axis: x = −1 and x = 3.

Draw the line y = 2 on the same axes. It crosses the curve at two points. Read the x-values: x ≈ −1.45 and x ≈ 3.45. Check by algebra: x² − 2x − 5 = 0 gives x = 1 ± √6 = 1 ± 2.449, so x = −1.45 or x = 3.45. The graph answer agrees.

sections.h: Solving a different equation with the same curve
p: Solve x² − 3x − 4 = 0 using the graph of y = x² − 2x − 3. Rearrange so that x² − 2x − 3 appears: x² − 3x − 4 = (x² − 2x − 3) − (x + 1). So the equation becomes x² − 2x − 3 = x + 1. Draw the line y = x + 1 and read the crossing points: x = −1 and x = 4. Check: at x = 4 the line gives y = 5 and the curve gives 16 − 8 − 3 = 5. They meet.
Solve y = x² − 2x − 3 and y = 2x − 3 together. Draw both on the same axes. They cross at (0, −3) and (4, 5), which matches the algebra from Unit 20.

units.summary: The different forms of the equation of a straight line and how to find where the line crosses the x-axis and the y-axis.

sections.h: Forms of the equation of a line
p: The same straight line can be written in different ways. Choose the form that suits the information you are given.

head: Name
Form
What it tells you
rows: m is the gradient, c is the y-intercept
useful for rearranging and finding intercepts
the line has gradient m and passes through (x₁, y₁)
the line passes through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂)
a is the x-intercept and b is the y-intercept

p: The y-intercept is where the line crosses the y-axis. At that point x = 0, so put x = 0 and solve for y. The point is (0, y).
The x-intercept is where the line crosses the x-axis. At that point y = 0, so put y = 0 and solve for x. The point is (x, 0).
Example 1. y = −2x + 6. When x = 0, y = 6, so the y-intercept is (0, 6). When y = 0, −2x + 6 = 0, so x = 3 and the x-intercept is (3, 0). Two points are enough to draw the line.
Put y = 0: 4x = 20, so x = 5. The x-intercept is (5, 0). Put x = 0: −5y = 20, so y = −4. The y-intercept is (0, −4). Join these two points with a ruler to draw the line.

sections.h: Example 3: from standard form to y = mx + c
p: Find the gradient and y-intercept of 3x + 2y = 12. Make y the subject: 2y = −3x + 12, so y = −1.5x + 6. The gradient is −1.5 and the y-intercept is 6. For the x-intercept put y = 0: 3x = 12, so x = 4, giving (4, 0).
If a line crosses the x-axis at 4 and the y-axis at 6, then x/4 + y/6 = 1. Multiply every term by 12: 3x + 2y = 12. This is the same line as Example 3.
Find the line through (1, 4) and (5, 12). (y − 4)/(12 − 4) = (x − 1)/(5 − 1). So (y − 4)/8 = (x − 1)/4. Multiply by 8: y − 4 = 2(x − 1), so y = 2x + 2. Check (5, 12): 2 × 5 + 2 = 12. Correct.

units.title: Gradient, Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
units.summary: How steep a line is, how to calculate gradient from two points, and the rules for parallel and perpendicular lines.

p: The gradient (or slope) of a line measures its steepness. It is the change in y for each 1 unit change in x.

Gradient m = rise / run = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁), where (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) are any two points on the line. It does not matter which point you call the first one, as long as you use the same order on top and bottom.
Example 2. A(2, 3) and B(6, 8). Rise = 5, run = 4, so m = 5/4 = 1.25.

A positive gradient slopes upward from left to right. A negative gradient slopes downward. A horizontal line (y = a number) has gradient 0. A vertical line (x = a number) has no gradient: it is undefined because the run is 0 and we cannot divide by 0.

img.alt: Four small graphs showing a line sloping up (m greater than 0), a line sloping down (m less than 0), a horizontal line (m = 0) and a vertical line (undefined gradient)
img.cap: The four kinds of gradient.

p: Parallel lines never meet. They have equal gradients: m₁ = m₂. For example y = 2x + 3 and y = 2x − 1 are parallel because both have gradient 2.
Example. Find the line parallel to y = 2x − 3 through (5, 8). The gradient is 2, so y − 8 = 2(x − 5), which gives y = 2x − 2.
Two lines are perpendicular (meet at 90°) if the product of their gradients is −1: m₁ × m₂ = −1. In other words m₂ = −1/m₁. Turn the fraction upside down and change the sign.
Example 1. Gradient 2 is perpendicular to gradient −1/2, because 2 × (−1/2) = −1.

Example 2. Show that 2x + 3y = 15 and 3x − 2y = 10 are perpendicular. First line: 3y = −2x + 15, so m₁ = −2/3. Second line: −2y = −3x + 10, so y = 1.5x − 5 and m₂ = 3/2. m₁ × m₂ = (−2/3) × (3/2) = −1. They are perpendicular.
Example 3. Find the line through the origin perpendicular to 4x + 3y = 12. 3y = −4x + 12, so m₁ = −4/3. m₂ = 3/4. The line through the origin is y = (3/4)x.

units.title: Finding the Equation of a Line, Tangents and Applications
units.summary: Using the point-gradient form to find equations, testing whether points are on one line, drawing a tangent to a curve, and using lines in real life.

sections.h: Equation from a gradient and a point
p: Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
Example 1. Gradient 3 through (2, 7). y − 7 = 3(x − 2), so y = 3x − 6 + 7 = 3x + 1.
Example 2. A line passes through (3, 2) with gradient −1. y − 2 = −1(x − 3), so y = −x + 5. It crosses the y-axis at (0, 5).
Example 3. Gradient 4 through (1, 7). y − 7 = 4(x − 1), so y = 4x + 3. The y-intercept is (0, 3). For the x-intercept put y = 0: 4x = −3, so x = −3/4.
First find the gradient, then use one of the points.

sections.h: Do three points lie on one line?
p: Points that lie on one straight line are called collinear. Find the gradient between the first two points and between the next two. If they are equal, the points are collinear.
Example. A(2, 3), B(5, 9), C(8, 15). Gradient AB = 6/3 = 2. Gradient BC = 6/3 = 2. They are equal and B is shared, so A, B and C lie on one straight line.
A tangent is a straight line that touches a curve at one point without crossing it there. Its gradient tells us how steeply the curve rises at that point.

How to draw a tangent: plot the curve carefully, mark the point, place a ruler so that it just touches the curve there, and draw the line. Then choose two points far apart on the tangent and find the gradient.

Example. The curve y = x² at P(2, 4). The tangent passes through (1, 0) and (2, 4), so its gradient is (4 − 0)/(2 − 1) = 4. Its equation is y − 4 = 4(x − 2), so y = 4x − 4. (A drawn tangent is only an estimate, but here the exact answer is 4.)

img.alt: Graph of y = x squared with the tangent y = 4x - 4 touching the curve at the point (2, 4) and a triangle showing run 1 and rise 4
img.cap: The tangent to y = x² at P(2, 4) has gradient 4.

p: Straight line graphs are used in physics (speed and distance), economics (cost and revenue), business (break-even), geography (temperature) and engineering.

Break-even example. A trader's cost is C = 2 000 + 50n naira for n items. Revenue is R = 130n naira. The break-even point is where cost equals revenue: 2 000 + 50n = 130n, so 80n = 2 000 and n = 25 items. At that point both are ₦3 250. After 25 items the trader makes a profit.

units.title: Circle Geometry I: Parts of a Circle
units.summary: The names of the parts of a circle and the formulas for circumference, arc length and sector area.

p: A circle is the set of all points that are the same distance from a fixed point called the centre. See the picture and the list below.

img.alt: A circle with the centre, a radius, a diameter, a chord, an arc and a tangent labelled
img.cap: The parts of a circle.

p: Centre (O): the fixed point in the middle.
Radius: the distance from the centre to any point on the circle.
Diameter: a chord through the centre. Diameter = 2 × radius.
Circumference: the distance round the circle.
Chord: a straight line joining any two points on the circle. The diameter is the longest chord.
Arc: part of the circumference. The shorter one is the minor arc and the longer one is the major arc.
Sector: the region between two radii and an arc, like a slice of pizza.
Segment: the region between a chord and an arc.
Tangent: a line that touches the circle at exactly one point.
Secant: a line that cuts the circle at two points.
Circumference = 2πr. Area = πr². For an arc or sector with angle θ at the centre: arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr and sector area = (θ/360) × πr².

units.activity: Draw a circle of radius 5 cm with a pair of compasses. Mark a radius, a diameter, a chord, a minor arc and a sector, and label them. Find the circumference using π = 3.14 (31.4 cm).

units.title: Tangent Properties
units.summary: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and two tangents from the same outside point are equal.

p: A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact. The angle between them is 90°. This is why a wheel touches the ground at one point: the radius there is vertical and the ground (the tangent) is horizontal.

sections.h: Property 2: tangents from an outside point
p: Two tangents drawn from the same outside point P to a circle are equal in length: PA = PB. Also, the line OP from the centre to P bisects (cuts in half) the angle APB and bisects the angle AOB.

img.alt: Left: a tangent touching a circle with the radius to the point of contact at 90 degrees. Right: two tangents from point P to a circle with OP = 13 cm, PA = PB = 12 cm and radius 5 cm
img.cap: A tangent is at 90° to the radius. Tangents from P are equal.

p: Two tangents PA and PB are drawn from P to a circle with centre O. PA = 12 cm and OP = 13 cm. Find the radius. Since PA is a tangent, angle OAP = 90°. In the right-angled triangle OAP, by Pythagoras: OP² = OA² + PA². 13² = r² + 12². 169 = r² + 144. r² = 25, so r = 5 cm.
The centre is O, the radius is 8 cm and OP = 17 cm, where P is outside the circle. The length of the tangent from P is √(17² − 8²) = √(289 − 64) = √225 = 15 cm.

In the quadrilateral OAPB, angle OAP = 90° and angle OBP = 90°. The four angles add up to 360°, so angle AOB + angle APB = 360° − 180° = 180°. If angle AOB = 110°, then angle APB = 70°, and angle APO = 35° (half of 70°).

units.title: Angle in a Semicircle and the Alternate Segment Theorem
units.summary: Two important theorems: the angle in a semicircle is 90°, and the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.

p: Theorem: the angle subtended at the circumference by a diameter is a right angle (90°). If AC is a diameter and B is any point on the circle (not A or C), then angle ABC = 90°. This is true for every point on the circle.

img.alt: A circle with diameter AC and two points B and D on the circle joined to A and C, with right angle marks at B and D
img.cap: Angle ABC = angle ADC = 90°.

p: Join B to the centre O. OA = OB = OC (radii). So triangles OAB and OBC are isosceles. Let angle OAB = angle OBA = α and angle OCB = angle OBC = β. In triangle ABC the angles add up to 180°: α + β + (α + β) = 180°, so α + β = 90°. But angle ABC = α + β. So angle ABC = 90°.
AB is a diameter and C is on the circle. If angle CAB = 35°, find angle ACB and angle CBA. Angle ACB = 90° (angle in a semicircle). Angle CBA = 180° − 90° − 35° = 55°.
The angle between a tangent and a chord, drawn from the point of contact, is equal to the angle in the alternate (opposite) segment.
In the picture below, the tangent at T makes 60° with chord TA. The angle at B, in the alternate segment, is also 60°. The word alternate means on the other side of the chord.

img.alt: A circle with a tangent at point T, a chord TA and a point B in the opposite segment; the angle between the tangent and the chord and the angle at B are both marked 60 degrees
img.cap: The angle between the tangent and chord TA equals the angle at B.

p: A tangent PT touches a circle at T. A chord TA makes an angle of 40° with the tangent. Find the angle in the alternate segment. The angle is 40° (alternate segment theorem).

sections.h: Example 3: a triangle in a circle
p: A triangle ABC is drawn in a circle. The tangent at A makes an angle of 48° with AB and an angle of 62° with AC (on the other side). Angle ACB = 48° (alternate segment to AB) and angle ABC = 62° (alternate segment to AC). So angle BAC = 180° − 48° − 62° = 70°. Check along the tangent line: 48° + 70° + 62° = 180°. Correct.

units.title: Circle Geometry II: Chords
units.summary: The perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord, equal chords are the same distance from the centre, and chords that cross inside a circle.

p: 1. The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
2. Equal chords are the same distance from the centre (equidistant).
3. Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre.
4. The converse is also true: chords the same distance from the centre are equal in length.
A chord AB of length 16 cm is 6 cm from the centre O. Find the radius. M is the midpoint of AB, so AM = 8 cm. In the right-angled triangle OMA: r² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100, so r = 10 cm.

img.alt: A circle with a chord AB of 16 cm, a perpendicular OM of 6 cm from the centre to the chord, and radius OA
img.cap: Right-angled triangle OMA: r² = 6² + 8².

sections.h: Example 2: a chord 5 cm from the centre
p: A chord of length 24 cm is 5 cm from the centre. Half the chord = 12 cm. r² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169, so r = 13 cm.

The radius is 10 cm and the chord is 6 cm from the centre. Half the chord = √(10² − 6²) = √64 = 8 cm. The chord is 16 cm long. The angle at the centre: sin(½ angle) = 8/10 = 0.8, so ½ angle = 53.13° and the angle at the centre is 106.26°, about 106.3°.
Two equal chords of length 12 cm are 8 cm apart, on opposite sides of the centre. Each is 4 cm from the centre (equal chords are equidistant). Radius² = 4² + 6² = 16 + 36 = 52, so r = √52 ≈ 7.21 cm.
If two chords AB and CD cross at a point E inside a circle, then AE × EB = CE × ED. Example: AE = 3 cm, EB = 4 cm and CE = 2 cm. 3 × 4 = 2 × ED, so ED = 6 cm.

units.title: Angle at the Centre and Angle at the Circumference
units.summary: The angle subtended at the centre by an arc is twice the angle subtended at the circumference by the same arc.

p: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre of a circle is twice the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining part of the circumference.
In the figure the arc AB subtends 140° at the centre O and 70° at the point P on the circumference. We write: angle AOB = 2 × angle APB.

img.alt: A circle with centre O; lines from A and B to O show 140 degrees, and lines from A and B to point P on the circle show 70 degrees
img.cap: 140° at the centre and 70° at P.

p: An arc AB subtends an angle of 140° at the centre. Find the angle it subtends at a point P on the major arc. Angle at circumference = 140° ÷ 2 = 70°.
An arc subtends 120° at the centre. At the circumference it subtends 60°. An angle of 80° at the circumference means 160° at the centre.

The angle at the centre is 100°. Find the angles of triangle OAB. OA = OB (radii), so the triangle is isosceles. The base angles are (180° − 100°)/2 = 40° each. The angle at the circumference on the major arc is 50°.
If the arc is a semicircle, the angle at the centre is 180° (a straight line, the diameter). So the angle at the circumference is 90°. This is the angle in a semicircle theorem.

units.title: Cyclic Quadrilaterals
units.summary: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four corners on a circle. Its opposite angles add up to 180°.

p: A cyclic quadrilateral is a four-sided figure whose four vertices all lie on a circle.
1. Opposite angles are supplementary: they add up to 180°.
2. An exterior angle (made by extending one side) equals the interior opposite angle.

img.alt: A quadrilateral ABCD inside a circle with angles 100, 85, 80 and 95 degrees, and side BC extended to E with the exterior angle at C equal to 100 degrees
img.cap: A + C = 180° and B + D = 180°. The exterior angle at C equals angle A.

p: The angle at the centre standing on arc BCD is double the angle at A, and the angle at the centre standing on arc BAD is double the angle at C. The two angles at the centre together make 360°, so 2A + 2C = 360° and A + C = 180°.
PQRS is cyclic with angle P = 75° and angle Q = 85°. Then angle R = 180° − 75° = 105° (opposite to P) and angle S = 180° − 85° = 95° (opposite to Q).
ABCD is cyclic with angle BAD = 3x and angle BCD = 2x + 20°. These are opposite angles: 3x + 2x + 20 = 180, so 5x = 160 and x = 32°. Angle BAD = 96° and angle BCD = 84°.
In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = 2x + 15° and angle C = 3x − 10°. 5x + 5 = 180, so x = 35°. A = 85° and C = 95°. If angle B = 90°, then angle D = 90°.

Some textbooks ask: PQRS is cyclic, angle P = 110° and angle R = 70°; find Q and S. We cannot find them separately. P and R are opposite, so they always add to 180° and tell us nothing more. We can only say Q + S = 180°. Always check that the question gives enough information.

units.title: Circle Geometry III: Angles in the Same Segment
units.summary: Angles standing on the same chord and on the same side of it are equal; angles on opposite sides add up to 180°.

p: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal. This means that angles subtended by the same chord (or arc) at different points on the same side of the chord are equal.
In the figure the chord AB subtends the angles at P, Q and R, which are all on the same arc. Each angle is 40°.

img.alt: A circle with chord AB and three points P, Q and R on the upper arc, each joined to A and B, with each angle marked 40 degrees
img.cap: Angles APB, AQB and ARB are equal.

p: The angle at the centre standing on chord AB is 80°. Each angle at the circumference on the same arc is half of that angle, which is 40°. So they are all equal.

Angles in opposite segments (one on each side of the chord) add up to 180°. For example, if the angle in the major segment is 65°, the angle in the minor segment is 180° − 65° = 115°. This is the same as the cyclic quadrilateral rule.
The angle APB = 50°, where P is on the major arc. Then the angle AQB = 50° for any other point Q on the major arc. The angle at the centre AOB = 100°.
Chords AC and BD of a circle cross at X. Angle CAB = 35°. Angle CAB and angle CDB both stand on chord CB and are on the same side of it, so angle CDB = 35°.

ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Its diagonals AC and BD cross at X. Angle ABD = 42° and angle BAC = 70°. Angle ACD = 42° (angles ABD and ACD both stand on chord AD and are on the same side of it). In triangle ABX, angle AXB = 180° − 42° − 70° = 68°.

p: 1. Draw the diagram larger and write all the given angles on it.
2. Mark any radii, because they give isosceles triangles, and any diameters, because they give right angles.
3. Look for the theorem that matches what you see. Say the reason for each step in brackets.
4. Use the angle facts you know: angles on a straight line = 180°, angles in a triangle = 180°, angles at a point = 360°.
5. Check that your answer is sensible.

ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle ABC = 75° and angle BCD = 110°. (a) Angle ADC = 180° − 75° = 105° (opposite angles). (b) Angle DAB = 180° − 110° = 70° (opposite angles). (c) AB is extended to E. The exterior angle CBE = angle ADC = 105° (exterior angle equals interior opposite angle).

AB is a diameter of a circle and C is a point on the circle. Angle CAB = 28°. The tangent at C meets the line AB extended at T. Angle ACB = 90° (angle in a semicircle). Angle ABC = 180° − 90° − 28° = 62°. The angle between the tangent and chord CB is equal to the angle in the alternate segment: 28°. The angle between the tangent and chord CA is 62°. At C: 62° + 90° + 28° = 180° (angles on a straight line). Correct.

O is the centre and angle AOB = 100°. P is on the major arc and Q is on the minor arc. Angle APB = 50° (half of the angle at the centre). Angle AQB = 180° − 50° = 130° (opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral APBQ).

units.title: Trigonometry I: The Sine Rule
units.summary: How to label any triangle and use the sine rule to find a missing side or angle, including the ambiguous case.

p: In triangle ABC, the angles are written with capital letters A, B, C at the corners. The sides are written with small letters. Side a is opposite angle A, side b is opposite angle B and side c is opposite angle C.
The sine and cosine rules work for every triangle, not only for right-angled ones. Remember that the angles of a triangle always add up to 180°.

img.alt: A triangle with corners A, B and C and the sides a, b and c opposite them
img.cap: Side a is opposite angle A, and so on.

p: In any triangle, a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C. You can also turn it upside down: sin A / a = sin B / b = sin C / c. Use the upside-down form when you are finding an angle.
Use the sine rule when you know (1) two angles and one side, or (2) two sides and an angle opposite one of them.
In triangle ABC, A = 40°, B = 65° and a = 8 cm. Find b. a / sin A = b / sin B, so b = 8 × sin 65° / sin 40° = 8 × 0.9063 / 0.6428 = 11.28 cm.

In triangle XYZ, X = 35°, Y = 75° and z = 20 cm. Find Z, x and y. Z = 180° − 35° − 75° = 70°. x = 20 × sin 35° / sin 70° = 20 × 0.5736 / 0.9397 = 12.21 cm. y = 20 × sin 75° / sin 70° = 20 × 0.9659 / 0.9397 = 20.56 cm. (The largest side, 20.56, is opposite the largest angle, 75°.)

sections.h: Example 3: finding an angle and the ambiguous case
p: In triangle ABC, a = 10 cm, b = 14 cm and A = 38°. Find B. sin B / b = sin A / a, so sin B = 14 × sin 38° / 10 = 14 × 0.6157 / 10 = 0.8619. Your calculator gives B = 59.5°. But sin of an angle is also positive in the second quadrant, so B = 180° − 59.5° = 120.5° is also possible. Is it? 38° + 120.5° = 158.5°, which is less than 180°, so the triangle can exist.

Both answers are correct: there are two possible triangles. This is called the ambiguous case. (Some books say that B must be acute because b is larger than a. That is not correct: b > a only tells us that B is larger than A.) When the question does not give a diagram or other information, give both answers.

units.title: The Cosine Rule
units.summary: Using the cosine rule to find a side when two sides and the angle between them are known, or to find an angle when all three sides are known.

p: In any triangle ABC: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, b² = a² + c² − 2ac cos B and c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
To find an angle, rearrange it: cos A = (b² + c² − a²) / (2bc).
Use the cosine rule when you know (1) two sides and the angle between them (SAS) to find the third side, or (2) all three sides (SSS) to find an angle.
If the angle is 90°, then cos 90° = 0 and the rule becomes Pythagoras: a² = b² + c².
Two sides of a triangle are 8 cm and 11 cm and the angle between them is 64°. The third side: a² = 64 + 121 − 2 × 8 × 11 × cos 64° = 185 − 176 × 0.4384 = 185 − 77.15 = 107.85. a = 10.39 cm.

A triangle has sides 5 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm. The largest angle is opposite the longest side. cos B = (5² + 7² − 9²) / (2 × 5 × 7) = (25 + 49 − 81) / 70 = −7 / 70 = −0.1. The negative answer tells us that the angle is obtuse: B = 95.74°.
Be careful with the calculator: work out the product 2bc cos A first, then subtract it. Writing (b² + c² − 2bc) first and then multiplying by cos A is a common mistake.

Area = ½ × a × b × sin C, where C is the angle between sides a and b. The same applies to the other two pairs of sides.
Example. Two sides of 8 cm and 11 cm with 64° between them. Area = ½ × 8 × 11 × sin 64° = 44 × 0.8988 = 39.55 cm².

Sides 13, 14, 15. The largest angle is opposite 15: cos = (13² + 14² − 15²) / (2 × 13 × 14) = 140 / 364 = 0.3846, so the angle is 67.38°. The smallest angle is opposite 13: 53.13°. The third angle is 180° − 67.38° − 53.13° = 59.49°.

units.title: Trigonometry II: Pythagoras and the Trigonometric Ratios
units.summary: A review of Pythagoras' theorem and of sine, cosine and tangent in right-angled triangles, with values for 30°, 45° and 60°.

p: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides: c² = a² + b².

Example 1. Legs 3 and 4: c² = 9 + 16 = 25, c = 5. Example 2. Hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5: other leg² = 169 − 25 = 144, so the other leg = 12. These are Pythagorean triples: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17).
Name the sides from the point of view of the angle θ: the hypotenuse is the longest side, the opposite is the side facing θ, and the adjacent is the side next to θ (not the hypotenuse).
sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse. cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse. tan θ = opposite / adjacent. A way to remember: SOH CAH TOA.

img.alt: A right-angled triangle with the angle theta marked and the sides labelled adjacent, opposite and hypotenuse, with the formulas sin, cos and tan
img.cap: SOH CAH TOA.

p: These values come from the equilateral triangle and the square and are worth learning.
sin θ = cos (90° − θ). For example sin 30° = cos 60° = 0.5.
A right-angled triangle has an angle of 35° and the adjacent side is 7 cm. Opposite = 7 × tan 35° = 7 × 0.7002 = 4.90 cm. Hypotenuse = 7 / cos 35° = 7 / 0.8192 = 8.55 cm.

Opposite 5 and adjacent 12: tan θ = 5/12 = 0.4167, so θ = 22.62°. If cos θ = 0.6 then θ = 53.13°. With hypotenuse 10 cm and an angle of 30°: opposite = 10 × sin 30° = 5 cm and adjacent = 10 × cos 30° = 8.66 cm.

units.title: Angles of Elevation and Depression
units.summary: Using trigonometry to find heights and distances when we look up at an object (elevation) or look down at it (depression).

p: The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look UP at an object. The angle of depression is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look DOWN at an object.

Both angles are measured from the horizontal line, never from the vertical. The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point P on the ground is equal to the angle of depression of P from the top of the tower, because they are alternate angles between parallel lines (the ground and the horizontal from the top).

img.alt: An observer on the ground looking up at the top of a tower, showing the angle of elevation at the observer and the equal angle of depression at the top of the tower
img.cap: Angle of elevation = angle of depression.

p: 1. Draw a clear diagram with a horizontal line and a vertical line. 2. Mark the angle and the lengths. 3. Find the right-angled triangle. 4. Choose sine, cosine or tangent. 5. Solve and give the answer with units.
From a point 50 m from the foot of a flagpole, the angle of elevation of its top is 35°. Height = 50 × tan 35° = 50 × 0.7002 = 35.0 m.
A ladder 6 m long makes an angle of 65° with the ground. Height reached = 6 × sin 65° = 5.44 m. Distance of its foot from the wall = 6 × cos 65° = 2.54 m.
From the top of a cliff 40 m high, the angle of depression of a boat is 25°. The boat is a distance d from the foot of the cliff. tan 25° = 40 / d, so d = 40 / tan 25° = 40 / 0.4663 = 85.78 m.

From a point A the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is 30°. From a point B, 20 m nearer to the tower (in the same straight line), it is 45°. Let the tower be h m high and let B be d m from its foot. From B: h = d (since tan 45° = 1). From A: h = (d + 20) tan 30° = 0.5774 (d + 20). So d = 0.5774 d + 11.547, which gives 0.4226 d = 11.547 and d = 27.32 m. The tower is 27.3 m high.

units.title: Algebraic Fractions: Simplifying, Adding and Subtracting
units.summary: Simplifying fractions by factorising, and adding and subtracting algebraic fractions with a common denominator.

p: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. We find a common denominator (the LCM of 2 and 3 is 6), write each fraction with it, and add the tops. Algebraic fractions work in the same way.
To simplify, factorise the top and the bottom completely, then cancel common factors. You can only cancel factors that multiply the whole top and the whole bottom, never terms that are added.
Wrong: (x + 3)/3 does not simplify to x + 1. The 3 in the top is added, not multiplied.
Example 1. 1/x + 2/(x + 1). The common denominator is x(x + 1). 1/x = (x + 1) / (x(x + 1)) and 2/(x + 1) = 2x / (x(x + 1)). Sum = (x + 1 + 2x) / (x(x + 1)) = (3x + 1) / (x(x + 1)).
Example 2. x/3 + (x + 1)/4. The common denominator is 12. = 4x/12 + 3(x + 1)/12 = (4x + 3x + 3)/12 = (7x + 3)/12.

Example. 3/(x − 1) − 2/(x + 2). The common denominator is (x − 1)(x + 2). = (3(x + 2) − 2(x − 1)) / ((x − 1)(x + 2)) = (3x + 6 − 2x + 2) / ((x − 1)(x + 2)) = (x + 8) / ((x − 1)(x + 2)). Take care with the minus sign: it changes the sign of every term in the second bracket.
A denominator can never be 0. In (x − 3)/(x − 2), x cannot be 2.

units.title: Multiplying and Dividing Algebraic Fractions
units.summary: Multiply tops and bottoms after factorising and cancelling; to divide, turn the second fraction upside down and multiply.

p: Factorise everything first, cancel, then multiply the tops together and the bottoms together.
Example 1. (x + 2)/(x − 1) × (x − 1)/(x + 3). The (x − 1) cancels. Answer: (x + 2)/(x + 3).
To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal (turn it upside down). A ÷ (B/C) = A × C/B.
Do not turn over the first fraction. Do not cancel across a plus or minus sign. Do not forget to factorise before cancelling.

units.title: Equations with Fractions and Everyday Problems
units.summary: Solving equations that contain fractions by multiplying by the common denominator, and using fractions to solve work, money and tank problems.

p: Find the lowest common denominator of all fractions. Multiply every term on both sides by it to remove the fractions. Solve the resulting equation. Check your answer in the original equation (and that it does not make a denominator zero).
x/2 + x/3 = 10. Multiply by 6: 3x + 2x = 60, so 5x = 60 and x = 12. Check: 6 + 4 = 10. Correct.
(x + 1)/3 = (x − 1)/2. Cross-multiply: 2(x + 1) = 3(x − 1), so 2x + 2 = 3x − 3 and x = 5. Check: 6/3 = 2 and 4/2 = 2. Correct.
2/(x − 1) = 3/(x + 2). Cross-multiply: 2(x + 2) = 3(x − 1), so 2x + 4 = 3x − 3 and x = 7. Check: 2/6 = 1/3 and 3/9 = 1/3. Correct.
1/2 + 1/x = 3/4. Multiply every term by 4x: 2x + 4 = 3x, so x = 4. Check: 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4. Correct.
Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and pipe B fills it in 3 hours. Together they fill 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2 of the tank each hour. So the tank is full in 2 hours.
Ade can do a job in 10 days and Bola can do it in 15 days. In one day they do 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 of the job. Together they take 6 days.

A man spends 1/3 of his salary on rent and 1/4 on food. He has ₦25 000 left. Fraction left = 1 − 1/3 − 1/4 = 12/12 − 4/12 − 3/12 = 5/12. So 5/12 of the salary is ₦25 000 and the salary is 25 000 × 12 / 5 = ₦60 000. Check: rent ₦20 000, food ₦15 000, left ₦25 000. Total ₦60 000.

units.title: Further Trigonometry: Bearings
units.summary: What a bearing is, how to write bearings with three figures, how to change compass directions to bearings and how to find a back bearing.

p: A bearing is a direction. It is measured as an angle clockwise from North. A bearing is written with three figures, so 65° is written 065° and 5° is written 005°. Due North is 000°.
To find the bearing of B from A: stand at A, face North, and turn clockwise until you face B. The angle you turn through is the bearing. Draw a North line at A, not at B.

img.alt: A North arrow from point O with the angle 065 degrees to point A and 290 degrees to point B, both measured clockwise from North
img.cap: Bearings are measured clockwise from North.

p: Eight main directions have these bearings.
Sometimes a direction is written from North or South towards East or West, for example N30°E. Start at N (or S) and turn the given angle towards E (or W).
The back bearing is the bearing of the starting point seen from the finishing point. Because the two North lines are parallel, the back bearing differs by 180°.
If the bearing is less than 180°, add 180°. If it is 180° or more, subtract 180°.
Example 1. The bearing of B from A is 070°. The bearing of A from B is 070° + 180° = 250°.
Example 2. If the bearing is 125°, the back bearing is 305°. If it is 310°, the back bearing is 130°.

units.title: Navigation Problems
units.summary: Using bearings with Pythagoras, trigonometry and the sine and cosine rules to find distances between ships, planes and towns.

p: 1. Draw a North line at each place where the direction changes. 2. Mark the bearings and distances. 3. Find the angle inside the triangle by using the rules about parallel lines and angles on a straight line. 4. Use Pythagoras, trigonometry, or the sine or cosine rule. Distance = speed × time.

A ship sails 20 km North and then 15 km East. The distance from the start is √(20² + 15²) = √625 = 25 km. The bearing of the final point from the start: tan θ = 15/20 = 0.75, so θ = 36.87°. The bearing is 037° (to the nearest degree).

Two ships leave a port at the same time. One travels at 30 km/h on a bearing of 040° and the other at 25 km/h on a bearing of 130°. How far apart are they after 2 hours? First ship: 30 × 2 = 60 km. Second ship: 25 × 2 = 50 km. The angle between their paths is 130° − 40° = 90°, so by Pythagoras, d² = 60² + 50² = 3 600 + 2 500 = 6 100 and d = 78.10 km.

A boat sails 40 km on a bearing of 065° and then 30 km on a bearing of 140°. How far is it from its starting point? The angle inside the triangle at the turning point is 180° − (140° − 65°) = 180° − 75° = 105°. By the cosine rule, d² = 40² + 30² − 2 × 40 × 30 × cos 105° = 1 600 + 900 + 2 400 × 0.2588 = 2 500 + 621.2 = 3 121.2. d = 55.87 km.

sections.h: Example 4: finding a bearing back home
p: A plane flies 40 km on a bearing of 060° and then 30 km on a bearing of 150°. The turn is 90°, so the distance from start is √(40² + 30²) = 50 km. The angle at the start between the first leg and the line to the end is tan⁻¹(30/40) = 36.87°. The bearing of the end point from the start is 060° + 36.87° = 096.87°, about 097°. The bearing of the start from the end (the way home) is 097° + 180° = 277°.

units.title: Chords, Arcs, Distance and Direction
units.summary: Using trigonometry to find the length of a chord or an arc, and to split a journey into east and north parts.

p: A chord AB subtends an angle θ at the centre O of a circle of radius r. Draw OM perpendicular to AB. M is the midpoint, and the angle AOM is θ/2. So AM = r sin (θ/2), and chord AB = 2r sin (θ/2).
Example 1. r = 8 cm and θ = 60°. Chord = 2 × 8 × sin 30° = 8 cm. (The triangle OAB is equilateral, so the chord equals the radius.)
Example 2. r = 10 cm and θ = 80°. Chord = 2 × 10 × sin 40° = 20 × 0.6428 = 12.86 cm.
Example 3. r = 13 cm and the chord is 24 cm. sin (θ/2) = 12/13 = 0.9231, so θ/2 = 67.38° and θ = 134.76°, about 134.8°.

Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr. Example. r = 10 cm and θ = 80°. Arc = (80/360) × 2 × 3.1416 × 10 = 0.2222 × 62.83 = 13.96 cm. Notice that the arc (13.96 cm) is a little longer than the chord (12.86 cm), as it should be.

sections.h: Distance and direction: east and north parts
p: A journey on a bearing can be split into two parts. For a distance d on a bearing θ: the East part = d sin θ and the North part = d cos θ. (For bearings above 90° these may be negative: a negative North part means going South.)

Example. A town B is 30 km from A on a bearing of 050°. East part = 30 × sin 50° = 30 × 0.7660 = 22.98 km. North part = 30 × cos 50° = 30 × 0.6428 = 19.28 km. B is about 23.0 km east and 19.3 km north of A.
Reverse example. A man walks 5 km east and 12 km north. The distance is √(25 + 144) = 13 km. tan θ = 5/12, so θ = 22.62°. The bearing is 023°.

units.title: Linear Programming: Meaning and Terms
units.summary: What linear programming is, the words used in it, why it is called linear, and where it is used in real life.

p: Linear programming (LP) is a mathematical method for finding the best possible result, such as the greatest profit or the lowest cost, when we have limited resources like time, money, land or materials.
Example: a tailor has 60 hours a week and 90 metres of cloth. How many agbada and how many suits should be sewn to earn the most money? Linear programming answers this kind of question.

sections.h: The parts of a linear programming problem
p: 1. Decision variables: the quantities we can choose, usually called x and y. For example x = the number of agbada and y = the number of suits.
2. Objective function: the quantity we want to make as large (maximise) or as small (minimise) as possible, written for example P = 5x + 3y.
3. Constraints: the limits on what we can do, written as linear inequalities, for example x + 2y ≤ 100.
4. Non-negativity conditions: x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0, because we cannot make a negative number of things.
5. Feasible region: the set of all points (x, y) that satisfy all the constraints.
6. Feasible solution: any point in the feasible region. It may not be the best one.
7. Optimal solution: the feasible solution that gives the best (largest or smallest) value of the objective function.

All the relationships are linear: the variables appear only to the power 1 and are not multiplied together. So 3x + 2y ≤ 12 is linear, but x² + y ≤ 10 and xy ≥ 6 are not. On a graph, a linear constraint is a straight line.

Manufacturing: how many units of each product to make for the greatest profit. Agriculture: how much land to give to each crop. Diet planning: the cheapest food that gives enough nutrients. Transport: the cheapest way to send goods from warehouses to shops. Investment: how to share money to get the best return. Everyday Nigerian examples: a farmer choosing between rice and cassava on 10 hectares; a trader with ₦50 000 choosing which goods to buy; a filling station deciding how much petrol and diesel to stock; a school sharing its budget between science and art equipment.
