units.title: Formulating Linear Programming Problems
units.summary: The five steps for turning a word problem into a linear programming model, with worked examples from factories, farms, bakeries and tailors.

p: Step 1. Decide what to choose: define the decision variables, for example Let x = the number of dining chairs and y = the number of office chairs.
Step 2. Write the objective function: Maximise P = ... or Minimise C = ...
Step 3. Write each constraint as an inequality, using the same units on both sides.
Step 4. Add x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.
Step 5. Write the complete model neatly.

A factory makes dining chairs and office chairs. A dining chair needs 2 hours of labour and 3 kg of wood. An office chair needs 3 hours of labour and 2 kg of wood. There are 120 hours of labour and 150 kg of wood each week. The profit is ₦5 000 on a dining chair and ₦6 000 on an office chair.
Let x = number of dining chairs and y = number of office chairs. Maximise P = 5000x + 6000y subject to: 2x + 3y ≤ 120 (labour), 3x + 2y ≤ 150 (wood), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
A farmer has 100 hectares. Rice needs 2 workers per hectare and maize needs 1 worker per hectare. He has 150 workers. Profit is ₦80 000 per hectare of rice and ₦50 000 per hectare of maize.
Let x = hectares of rice and y = hectares of maize. Maximise P = 80000x + 50000y subject to: x + y ≤ 100 (land), 2x + y ≤ 150 (workers), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

A baker makes cakes and bread. A cake takes 2 hours in the oven and uses 3 kg of flour. A bread takes 1 hour and uses 2 kg of flour. The baker has 40 oven hours and 60 kg of flour. A cake sells for ₦2 000 and a bread for ₦800.
Let x = number of cakes and y = number of breads. Maximise R = 2000x + 800y subject to: 2x + y ≤ 40 (oven time), 3x + 2y ≤ 60 (flour), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
An agbada takes 4 hours and 6 metres of cloth. A suit takes 3 hours and 4 metres. The tailor has 60 hours and 90 metres each week. Profit is ₦15 000 per agbada and ₦12 000 per suit.
Let x = agbada and y = suits. Maximise P = 15000x + 12000y subject to: 4x + 3y ≤ 60, 6x + 4y ≤ 90, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
Make a small table of the data, with one row for each product and one column for each resource. Then each column gives one constraint.

Suppose x = trips by route A (each using 2 drivers, 1 mechanic) and y = trips by route B (each using 1 driver, 1 mechanic). Write the constraints (2x + y ≤ 15, x + y ≤ 8, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0).

units.title: Formulating Minimising Problems and What Is Not Linear Programming
units.summary: Problems where the aim is the lowest cost with minimum requirements (using ≥), and how to tell whether a problem is linear.

p: Sometimes we want the lowest cost while meeting minimum requirements. These constraints use ≥ (at least).

Example (a diet problem). A diet must have at least 300 calories and at least 50 g of protein. Food A gives 100 calories and 20 g of protein per serving and costs ₦200. Food B gives 150 calories and 10 g of protein per serving and costs ₦250.
Let x = servings of Food A and y = servings of Food B. Minimise C = 200x + 250y subject to: 100x + 150y ≥ 300 (calories), 20x + 10y ≥ 50 (protein), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
It is easier to graph if you divide to make the numbers small. 100x + 150y ≥ 300 becomes 2x + 3y ≥ 6 (divide by 50). 20x + 10y ≥ 50 becomes 2x + y ≥ 5 (divide by 10).

sections.h: Example: a baker with eggs and flour
p: A baker makes meat pies and sausage rolls. A pie needs 2 eggs and 100 g of flour. A roll needs 1 egg and 50 g of flour. There are 100 eggs and 5 000 g of flour each day. A pie makes ₦200 profit (₦500 − ₦300) and a roll makes ₦150 profit (₦300 − ₦150). Let x = pies and y = rolls. Maximise P = 200x + 150y subject to: 2x + y ≤ 100, 100x + 50y ≤ 5 000 (which is the same as 2x + y ≤ 100), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Notice that the two constraints are the same line!

sections.h: Which of these are linear programming problems?
p: (a) Maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x² + y ≤ 10. Not linear: it has x².
(b) Minimise C = 5x + 4y subject to 2x + 3y ≥ 12, x + y ≤ 8, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Linear: the objective function and every constraint are linear.
(c) Maximise P = xy subject to x + y ≤ 20. Not linear: the objective function has xy, a product of the two variables.

units.title: Graphing Linear Inequalities
units.summary: How to draw the graph of an inequality in two variables and shade the region that satisfies it, using a test point.

p: 1. Replace the inequality sign by = and draw the boundary line (find two points, usually the intercepts).
2. Use a solid line for ≤ or ≥ (points on the line are included). Use a dashed line for < or > (points on the line are not included).
3. Choose a test point not on the line, usually (0, 0), and substitute it into the inequality.
4. If the statement is true, shade the side with the test point. If it is false, shade the other side.
The line x + y = 6 passes through (0, 6) and (6, 0). Draw it solid. Test (0, 0): 0 + 0 ≤ 6 is true, so shade the side that contains the origin. Everything on and below the line is in the region.

img.alt: Graph of the line x + y = 6 with the region below and to the left of the line shaded to show x + y is less than or equal to 6
img.cap: The shaded region is x + y ≤ 6.

p: The line 2x + 3y = 12 passes through (6, 0) and (0, 4). Draw it solid. Test (0, 0): 0 ≥ 12 is false, so shade the side that does NOT contain the origin (above and to the right of the line).
The line y = 2x − 1 passes through (0, −1) and (1, 1). Draw it dashed because the sign is >. Test (0, 0): 0 > −1 is true, so shade the side with the origin (above the line).

x ≤ 4 means everything on and to the left of the vertical line x = 4. y ≥ 1 means everything on and above the horizontal line y = 1. x ≥ 0 means the right of the y-axis and y ≥ 0 means above the x-axis.

In this unit we shade the region that satisfies the inequality. Some books and examinations shade the unwanted region and leave the wanted region clear. Always read the question: it will say which to do.

units.title: The Feasible Region and Corner Points
units.summary: Finding the region that satisfies all constraints together and finding its corner points by reading axis intercepts and by solving pairs of equations.

p: The feasible region is the area where all the shaded regions overlap. It is the set of all points that satisfy every constraint at the same time. Its corners are called vertices or corner points.
Find the feasible region and the corner points for x + y ≤ 6, 2x + y ≤ 10, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
The line x + y = 6 passes through (0, 6) and (6, 0). The line 2x + y = 10 passes through (0, 10) and (5, 0). The region is below both lines and in the first quadrant.

Corner points: A (0, 0). B (0, 6): at x = 0 the lower of 6 and 10 is 6. D (5, 0): at y = 0 the lower of 6 and 5 is 5. C: where the two lines cross. Subtract: (2x + y) − (x + y) = 10 − 6 gives x = 4, then y = 6 − 4 = 2. So C = (4, 2). Check in both equations: 4 + 2 = 6 and 8 + 2 = 10. Both correct.
(Some printed notes first write C as (2, 4). That is wrong, because 2 + 4 = 6 but 2(2) + 4 = 8, not 10. Always check your intersection in both equations.)
Constraints: 2x + 3y ≤ 120 (labour), 3x + 2y ≤ 150 (wood), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

Labour line: intercepts (60, 0) and (0, 40). Wood line: intercepts (50, 0) and (0, 75). On the x-axis the wood line is nearer (50 < 60), so B = (50, 0). On the y-axis the labour line is nearer (40 < 75), so D = (0, 40).

The lines cross where 2x + 3y = 120 and 3x + 2y = 150. Multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2: 6x + 9y = 360 and 6x + 4y = 300. Subtract: 5y = 60, so y = 12. Then 2x = 120 − 36 = 84, so x = 42. C = (42, 12). Check: 3(42) + 2(12) = 126 + 24 = 150. Correct.

img.alt: A shaded four-sided region with corners at (0, 0), (50, 0), (42, 12) and (0, 40) formed by the labour line and the wood line, with the profit at each corner shown on the right
img.cap: The feasible region for the chair factory and the profit at each corner.

p: If a linear programming problem has an optimal solution, it occurs at a corner point of the feasible region. So we do not need to test every point: we only test the corners.

units.title: Solving Linear Programming Problems Graphically
units.summary: The six steps for solving a linear programming problem with a graph, with maximising and minimising examples and special cases.

p: 1. Graph all the constraints. 2. Shade the feasible region. 3. Find the corner points. 4. Work out the objective function at each corner. 5. Choose the largest (to maximise) or the smallest (to minimise) value. 6. State the answer in words.
Subject to x + y ≤ 6, 2x + y ≤ 10, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. The corners are (0, 0), (0, 6), (4, 2) and (5, 0).
Maximise P = 5000x + 6000y. The corners are (0, 0), (50, 0), (42, 12) and (0, 40).
At (0, 0): P = 0. At (50, 0): P = 250 000. At (42, 12): P = 210 000 + 72 000 = 282 000. At (0, 40): P = 240 000. The maximum is ₦282 000 when 42 dining chairs and 12 office chairs are made each week.
Subject to x + y ≥ 4, 2x + y ≥ 6, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Shade the region above both lines. The region has no upper limit (it is unbounded), but a minimum still exists because the costs are positive.
The corners are (0, 6) [where the line 2x + y = 6 meets the y-axis], (2, 2) [the lines cross: subtracting gives x = 2, y = 2] and (4, 0) [where x + y = 4 meets the x-axis].

At (0, 6): C = 18. At (2, 2): C = 4 + 6 = 10. At (4, 0): C = 8. The minimum is 8 at (4, 0). (Some printed notes give 10 at (2, 2). That misses the corner (4, 0), which satisfies both constraints: 4 ≥ 4 and 8 ≥ 6.)

Minimise C = 200x + 250y subject to 2x + 3y ≥ 6, 2x + y ≥ 5, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. The corners are (0, 5), (3, 0) and the crossing point: subtract 2x + y = 5 from 2x + 3y = 6 to get 2y = 1, so y = 0.5 and x = 2.25. At (0, 5): C = 1 250. At (3, 0): C = 600. At (2.25, 0.5): C = 450 + 125 = 575. The minimum cost is ₦575 for 2.25 servings of A and 0.5 serving of B.

Corn needs 3 hours per hectare and beans need 2 hours. There are 60 hours and 25 hectares. Profit is ₦50 000 per hectare of corn and ₦40 000 per hectare of beans. Let x = hectares of corn and y = hectares of beans. Constraints: 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x + y ≤ 25. The lines cross where 3x + 2y = 60 and x + y = 25: 3x + 2(25 − x) = 60, so x = 10 and y = 15. Corners: (0, 0), (20, 0), (10, 15), (0, 25). P at these: 0, 1 000 000, 500 000 + 600 000 = 1 100 000, 1 000 000. Plant 10 hectares of corn and 15 hectares of beans for a profit of ₦1 100 000.

Redundant constraint: maximise P = 2000x + 3000y subject to x + 2y ≤ 40 and 3x + 5y ≤ 120. Both lines pass through (40, 0), and the second line is above the first everywhere else, so it does not change the region: the region is the triangle (0, 0), (40, 0), (0, 20). P at (40, 0) is 80 000 and at (0, 20) is 60 000. Make 40 chairs and no tables.
Several optimal solutions: if the objective function line is parallel to a side of the region, two corners give the same best value and so do all the points between them.
No feasible solution: the constraints contradict each other, for example x + y ≤ 2 and x + y ≥ 5.

units.title: Bearings: Three-Figure, Compass and Back Bearings
units.summary: Revising how directions are described with bearings, how to change between the different ways of writing them, and how to find back bearings and angles between directions.

p: A bearing is the direction of one place from another. It is measured clockwise from North and written with three figures (000° to 360°). To find the bearing of B from A, draw a North line at A, then measure the clockwise angle from the North line to the line AB.

img.alt: A North arrow with the angle 065 degrees to point A and 290 degrees to point B, both measured clockwise from North
img.cap: Bearings are measured clockwise from North.

p: A direction such as N30°E means 30° from North towards East: 030°. S40°E means 40° from South towards East: 180° − 40° = 140°. S25°W = 180° + 25° = 205°. N50°W = 360° − 50° = 310°.
The North lines at two places are parallel. So the back bearing is the bearing plus or minus 180°. If the bearing is below 180°, add 180°. If it is 180° or above, subtract 180°.
Bearing of B from A is 050°, so the bearing of A from B is 230°. Bearing of B from A is 310°, so the bearing of A from B is 130°.

sections.h: Finding the angle between two directions
p: The bearing of B from A is 070°. The bearing of C from B is 140°. Find angle ABC. The bearing of A from B is 070° + 180° = 250°. Angle ABC is the angle between BA (250°) and BC (140°): 250° − 140° = 110°.

Check with parallel lines: the angle between AB and the North line at A is 70°. The angle between BA and the North line at B is 360° − 250° = 110°. These are co-interior angles between the parallel North lines, so 70° + 110° = 180°. Correct.

Always draw a North line at every point where you need a bearing. Write every bearing with three figures. Use the fact that angles on a straight line add up to 180° and that co-interior angles between parallel lines add up to 180°.

units.title: Bearings: Problems with Triangles
units.summary: Solving journey problems with bearings using Pythagoras, the cosine rule and the sine rule, and finding the final bearing.

p: 1. Draw a North line at each turning point. 2. Mark each bearing and distance. 3. Work out the angle inside the triangle at the turning point: interior angle = 180° − (second bearing − first bearing), when the second bearing is bigger and the turn is to the right. 4. Use Pythagoras, or the cosine rule, or the sine rule. 5. Use the angle at the start to get the final bearing.

A helicopter flies 50 km on a bearing of 040° from A to B, then 70 km on a bearing of 130° to C. The interior angle at B is 180° − (130° − 40°) = 90°. So AC = √(50² + 70²) = √(2 500 + 4 900) = √7 400 = 86.02 km. The angle BAC: tan (BAC) = 70/50 = 1.4, so BAC = 54.46°. The bearing of C from A is 040° + 54.46° = 094.46°, which is 094° to the nearest degree. The bearing of A from C is 094.46° + 180° = 274.46°, about 274°.
A ship sails 50 km on a bearing of 070° from A to B, then 40 km on a bearing of 150° from B to C. The interior angle at B = 180° − (150° − 70°) = 100°.

Use the sine rule to find angle A: sin A / 40 = sin 100° / 69.24, so sin A = 40 × 0.9848 / 69.24 = 0.5689 and A = 34.67°. The bearing of C from A is 070° + 34.67° = 104.67°, about 105°. The bearing of A from C is 285°.

Two ships leave a port. One travels 60 km on 040° and the other travels 50 km on 130°. The angle between the paths is 130° − 40° = 90°, so the distance between them is √(60² + 50²) = √6 100 = 78.10 km.

units.title: Angles of Elevation and Depression: Meaning and Scale Drawing
units.summary: The meaning of angles of elevation and depression, how to measure them, and how to find heights by making a scale drawing.

p: The angle of elevation is the angle above the horizontal when you look up at something. The angle of depression is the angle below the horizontal when you look down at something. Both are measured from the horizontal line.
The angle of elevation from P to the top T of a tower is equal to the angle of depression from T to P, because they are alternate angles.

img.alt: An observer on the ground looking up at the top of a tower, with the angle of elevation at the observer and the equal angle of depression at the top of the tower
img.cap: Angle of elevation = angle of depression.

p: A clinometer (a protractor with a straw and a hanging string) can be used. Look at the top of the tree through the straw and read the angle where the string crosses the protractor. Remember to add your eye height to the height you calculate.

sections.h: Finding a height by scale drawing
p: A tree is 60 m away on level ground and the angle of elevation of its top is 40°. Use a scale of 1 cm to 10 m. Draw a horizontal line AB 6 cm long (60 m). At A draw an angle of 40° with a protractor, and at B draw a line at 90° (upwards). Where the two lines meet, call the point C. Measure BC: it should be about 5.0 cm, which is about 50 m.
Check by calculation: height = 60 × tan 40° = 60 × 0.8391 = 50.3 m. Scale drawings give a good estimate but are less accurate than calculations.
A boy 1.5 m tall stands 20 m from a tree. The angle of elevation of its top is 40°. Height above his eyes = 20 × tan 40° = 20 × 0.8391 = 16.78 m. The tree is 16.78 + 1.5 = 18.28 m high, about 18.3 m.
A flagpole is 12 m high. The angle of elevation of the sun is 50°. The length of its shadow = 12 / tan 50° = 12 / 1.1918 = 10.07 m.

units.title: Elevation and Depression: Problems
units.summary: Harder problems with lighthouses, planes and cliffs, including problems with two observations.

sections.h: Problem 1: two boats and a lighthouse
p: From the top of a lighthouse 60 m high, the angles of depression of two boats in line with it are 30° and 45°, on the same side. The nearer boat (45°) is 60 / tan 45° = 60 m from the foot. The farther boat (30°) is 60 / tan 30° = 60 / 0.5774 = 103.92 m from the foot. The distance between the boats is 103.92 − 60 = 43.92 m.
If the boats are on opposite sides of the lighthouse, the distance between them is 103.92 + 60 = 163.92 m.

From an aeroplane flying at a height of 800 m, the angle of depression of the airport is 20°. The horizontal distance to the airport is 800 / tan 20° = 800 / 0.3640 = 2 198 m. The direct distance from the aeroplane to the airport (along the line of sight) is 800 / sin 20° = 800 / 0.3420 = 2 339 m.

From a point A on level ground the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is 30°. From a point B, 20 m nearer to the tower, it is 45°. Let B be d m from the foot. At B: h = d × tan 45° = d. At A: h = (d + 20) × tan 30°. So d = 0.5774(d + 20), 0.4226 d = 11.547 and d = 27.32 m. The tower is 27.3 m high.

sections.h: Problem 4: a ladder and a wall
p: A ladder 6 m long leans against a wall and makes 65° with the ground. It reaches 6 × sin 65° = 5.44 m up the wall. Its foot is 6 × cos 65° = 2.54 m from the wall.

units.title: Frequency Distribution: Meaning and Ungrouped Data
units.summary: What frequency means, the difference between discrete and continuous data, and how to make a frequency table from raw data using tally marks.

p: Statistics is the science of collecting, organising and understanding data. The frequency of a value is the number of times it occurs in the data. A frequency distribution (or frequency table) lists each value with its frequency.
Raw data is data just as it was collected, in no order. A frequency table makes it easy to see which values are common and which are rare.

Discrete data can be counted and takes separate values, for example the number of children in a family (0, 1, 2, 3...) or the number of goals in a match. Continuous data is measured and can take any value in a range, for example height, mass or time. The kind of data affects how we group it.

sections.h: Making a frequency table with tally marks
p: 1. List all the different values in order. 2. Go through the data once, putting one tally mark (|) beside the value each time it appears. Group the tallies in fives: four upright strokes and a fifth stroke across them. 3. Count the tallies to get each frequency. 4. Add the frequencies: the total must equal the number of observations. This check catches mistakes.
A football team scored these goals in 15 matches: 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 4, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 0.

The most common number of goals (the mode) is 2. The total number of goals is 0×3 + 1×4 + 2×5 + 3×2 + 4×1 = 0 + 4 + 10 + 6 + 4 = 24, so the mean number of goals per match is 24 ÷ 15 = 1.6. Arranged in order the data is 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, ... The middle (8th) value is 2, so the median is 2.

Total children = 0×2 + 1×4 + 2×7 + 3×4 + 4×2 + 5×1 = 0 + 4 + 14 + 12 + 8 + 5 = 43. The mean is 43 ÷ 20 = 2.15 children per family. The mode is 2. The 10th and 11th values are both 2, so the median is 2.

units.title: Grouped Frequency Tables
units.summary: How to group many values into class intervals, and the words class limits, class boundaries, class width and class midpoint.

p: When there are many different values (for example marks out of 100), a table with one row for every value would be long and not helpful. So we group the values into classes or class intervals such as 20 to 29, 30 to 39, and so on.
Class limits: the smallest and largest values written in a class. For the class 20–29 the lower limit is 20 and the upper limit is 29.
Class boundaries: the true edges of a class for whole-number data. Go halfway to the next class: 20–29 has boundaries 19.5 and 29.5.

Class width (class size): the length of the class = upper boundary − lower boundary. For 20–29 this is 29.5 − 19.5 = 10. You can also take the difference between two consecutive lower limits: 30 − 20 = 10. (Do not use 29 − 20 = 9: that is a common mistake.)
Class midpoint (class mark): the middle of the class = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2. For 20–29: (20 + 29) ÷ 2 = 24.5.
Frequency: the number of observations in the class.

sections.h: Steps to make a grouped frequency table
p: 1. Find the range = largest value − smallest value. 2. Choose the number of classes, usually 5 to 10. 3. Class width ≈ range ÷ number of classes, rounded up to a convenient number (like 5 or 10). 4. Write the class intervals, starting at or just below the smallest value, with no gaps and no overlaps. 5. Tally the data and count. 6. Check: total of the frequencies = number of observations.

Marks: 23, 45, 38, 52, 31, 47, 29, 60, 41, 35, 28, 49, 33, 56, 42, 37, 25, 44, 39, 51. The range is 60 − 23 = 37. With 5 classes the width is 37 ÷ 5 = 7.4, so we choose the convenient width 10, starting at 20.

units.title: Cumulative Frequency and Histograms
units.summary: Running totals of frequencies, and how to draw a histogram, the picture of a grouped frequency table.

p: Cumulative frequency is the running total of the frequencies. A 'less than' cumulative frequency tells us how many observations are below the upper boundary of each class.
Marks of 30 students: the table below will be used in the rest of this term.

3 students scored less than 19.5. 9 students scored less than 29.5. 18 students scored less than 39.5. The last cumulative frequency, 30, equals the total number of students. A 'more than' cumulative frequency works from the bottom: 30 students scored more than 9.5, 27 more than 19.5, 21 more than 29.5, 12 more than 39.5, 5 more than 49.5 and 1 more than 59.5.

A histogram is used for continuous data grouped into classes. It is like a bar chart, but: the bars touch (no gaps), because the classes are continuous; the bars are drawn between the class boundaries; and for equal class widths the height of a bar is the frequency.

img.alt: A histogram of the marks of 30 students with bars of heights 3, 6, 9, 7, 4 and 1 drawn between the class boundaries 9.5 to 69.5
img.cap: A histogram of the marks of 30 students.

p: 1. Choose a scale for the horizontal axis (class boundaries) and the vertical axis (frequency). 2. Draw a bar for each class between its boundaries, with height equal to its frequency. 3. Label both axes and give the graph a title.

A frequency polygon joins the tops of the bars at the class midpoints with straight lines. Here the points are (14.5, 3), (24.5, 6), (34.5, 9), (44.5, 7), (54.5, 4) and (64.5, 1). Add (4.5, 0) and (74.5, 0) at the ends so that the polygon touches the axis.
Use a bar chart for separate categories or discrete data (bars separated by gaps). Use a histogram for grouped continuous data (bars touching).

units.title: Drawing an Ogive
units.summary: How to draw a cumulative frequency curve (an ogive): plotting the upper class boundaries against the cumulative frequencies and joining the points smoothly.

p: An ogive (say 'OH-jive') is a graph of cumulative frequency. It has an S-shape and is used to estimate the median, quartiles and percentiles.
1. Make a cumulative frequency table with the upper class boundaries.
2. Draw axes: upper class boundaries on the x-axis and cumulative frequency on the y-axis. Choose scales that use most of the page.
3. Plot each point (upper boundary, cumulative frequency). Plot at the UPPER boundaries, not the midpoints.
4. Add the starting point: the lower boundary of the first class with cumulative frequency 0. Here this is (9.5, 0).
5. Join the points with a smooth curve, not with straight zig-zag lines.
6. Label the axes and give the graph a title.

The points are (9.5, 0), (19.5, 3), (29.5, 9), (39.5, 18), (49.5, 25), (59.5, 29) and (69.5, 30). The curve climbs slowly at first, steeply in the middle (where most students are) and flattens at the end.

img.cap: The ogive of the 30 marks, with the median and quartiles marked.

units.title: Reading Information from an Ogive
units.summary: Using an ogive to estimate the median, quartiles, interquartile range and percentiles, and to answer questions about numbers and percentages.

p: Let n be the total frequency (here n = 30). The median is the value at n/2 = 15. The lower quartile Q₁ is the value at n/4 = 7.5. The upper quartile Q₃ is the value at 3n/4 = 22.5. The interquartile range (IQR) is Q₃ − Q₁. A percentile P_k is the value below which k% of the data lies; it is at position (k/100) × n.
To read a value: find the position on the cumulative frequency axis, draw a line across to the curve, then draw a line down to the x-axis and read off the value.

Median: position 15, reading ≈ 36 marks. Q₁: position 7.5, reading ≈ 27 marks. Q₃: position 22.5, reading ≈ 46 marks. IQR ≈ 46 − 27 = 19 marks: the middle half of the students scored marks in a range of about 19.
How many students scored less than 45? Read the cumulative frequency at 45: about 22 students.
How many scored 40 or more? Read at 39.5: 18 scored less than that, so 30 − 18 = 12 students scored 40 or more. That is 12/30 × 100 = 40%.
What percentage scored less than 30? Read at 29.5: 9 students, so 9/30 × 100 = 30%.
What is the 80th percentile? Position 0.8 × 30 = 24. Reading ≈ 48 marks. So about 80% of the students scored below 48.
Top 10% of students: the 90th percentile is at position 27 and is about 54.5 marks, so the cut-off for the top 10% is about 54 to 55 marks.
A curve further to the right means higher values: a higher median. A steeper curve means the data is more bunched together (a smaller spread). Compare medians and interquartile ranges.

Setting pass marks and grade boundaries; finding the top 10% of students; studying incomes (how many people earn below a given amount); child growth charts; quality control (what percentage of products are below a standard).

units.title: The Mean from Grouped Data
units.summary: How to find the mean of grouped data using class midpoints and the formula mean = Σfx ÷ Σf, with several worked examples.

p: The mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values. For grouped data we do not know the exact values, so we use the class midpoint x to stand for every value in the class.
Mean = Σfx ÷ Σf, where f is the frequency, x is the class midpoint, Σfx is the sum of all the f × x, and Σf is the total frequency.
1. Find the midpoint x of each class. 2. Multiply each frequency by its midpoint to get fx. 3. Add up all the fx values. 4. Add up the frequencies. 5. Divide Σfx by Σf.
Use the table below.

The classes are 40–44, 45–49, 50–54, 55–59, 60–64 and 65–69 with frequencies 4, 9, 15, 12, 7 and 3. The midpoints are 42, 47, 52, 57, 62 and 67. The fx values are 168, 423, 780, 684, 434 and 201. Σfx = 2 690 and Σf = 50. Mean mass = 2 690 ÷ 50 = 53.8 kg.

The mean age of 40 students is 16 years. Ten new students with a mean age of 18 years join them. Total age of the 40 = 40 × 16 = 640 years. Total age of the 10 = 10 × 18 = 180 years. Mean of all 50 = (640 + 180) ÷ 50 = 820 ÷ 50 = 16.4 years.

The mean of 20 numbers is 35. When one number is removed, the mean of the remaining 19 numbers is 34. Find the number removed. Total of 20 numbers = 20 × 35 = 700. Total of the 19 numbers = 19 × 34 = 646. The number removed = 700 − 646 = 54.

units.title: The Median and Mode from Grouped Data
units.summary: The formulas for estimating the median and the mode of grouped data, with examples and the modal class.

p: The median class is the class that contains the middle position n/2. Then:
Median = L + ((n/2 − CF) ÷ f) × c
where L = lower boundary of the median class, CF = cumulative frequency before the median class, f = frequency of the median class and c = class width.

n/2 = 15. The cumulative frequencies are 3, 9, 18, ... so the 15th value lies in the class 30–39 (the cumulative frequency passes 15 there). L = 29.5, CF = 9, f = 9, c = 10. Median = 29.5 + ((15 − 9) ÷ 9) × 10 = 29.5 + 6.67 = 36.17 marks.
n/2 = 25. Cumulative frequencies: 4, 13, 28, ... so the median class is 50–54. L = 49.5, CF = 13, f = 15, c = 5. Median = 49.5 + ((25 − 13) ÷ 15) × 5 = 49.5 + 4 = 53.5 kg.
The modal class is the class with the highest frequency. A better estimate of the mode is:
Mode = L + (f₁ − f₀) ÷ ((f₁ − f₀) + (f₁ − f₂)) × c
where L = lower boundary of the modal class, f₁ = its frequency, f₀ = the frequency of the class before it, f₂ = the frequency of the class after it and c = class width.
These are only estimates, because we do not know the exact values inside each class.

units.activity: For the distribution with classes 0–9, 10–19, 20–29 and frequencies 4, 6, 10: n = 20, so n/2 = 10. The cumulative frequencies are 4, 10, 20. The median class is 10–19, because the cumulative frequency first reaches 10 there. Median = 9.5 + ((10 − 4) ÷ 6) × 10 = 19.5. The modal class is 20–29 (frequency 10). Now check these steps yourself on a different table.

units.title: Comparing the Mean, Median and Mode
units.summary: The strengths and weaknesses of each average, what skewness means, and how to choose the best average for a situation.

p: Mean: uses all the data and is good for further calculation, but it is affected by extreme (very large or very small) values.
Median: the middle value. It is not affected by extreme values and is good for skewed data, but it does not use all the data.

Mode: the most common value. It is the only average that can be used for categories (for example the favourite colour), and it is not affected by extremes. But it may not exist or there may be more than one.
Symmetrical data: mean = median = mode.
Positively skewed (a long tail to the right): mode < median < mean. A few very high values pull the mean up.
Negatively skewed (a long tail to the left): mean < median < mode. A few very low values pull the mean down.
Our marks data: mean 36.5, median 36.17, mode 35.5. Because mode < median < mean, it is slightly positively skewed. The masses: mean 53.8, median 53.5, mode 52.83, also slightly positively skewed.

A data set has mean 42, median 45 and mode 48. Since the mean < median < mode, the data is negatively skewed. There are some unusually low values pulling the mean down, and most values are towards the higher end.

For data that is only moderately skewed, Mode ≈ 3 × Median − 2 × Mean. Example: if the median is 42 and the mode is 45, then 45 = 3 × 42 − 2 × Mean, so 2 × Mean = 126 − 45 = 81 and Mean ≈ 40.5. (Some printed notes give the formula Mean ≈ (Mode + 2 × Median) ÷ 3. That formula is not correct; it would give 43.)

Incomes or house prices, where a few are extremely high: use the median. Test scores with no extreme values and when you need calculations: use the mean. Shoe sizes sold by a shop, or the most popular colour: use the mode. A symmetrical distribution: any of the three will do.

units.title: Probability: Meaning and Sample Space
units.summary: What probability measures, the probability scale from 0 to 1, how to find the probability of an event, and how to list the sample space for coins, dice and cards.

p: Probability is a number that tells us how likely an event is. It is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain). It can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.

img.alt: A line from 0 to 1 showing impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain with examples
img.cap: The probability scale.

p: For outcomes that are equally likely: P(E) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes = n(E) ÷ n(S). Here S is the sample space (the set of all possible outcomes) and E is the event.
Facts: 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. P(certain event) = 1. P(impossible event) = 0. The probabilities of all the outcomes add up to 1. P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
A coin: S = {H, T}. A die: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Two coins: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}. Three coins have 8 outcomes (2 × 2 × 2).
Two dice: there are 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes. The grid below shows the sum of the scores.

img.alt: A 6 by 6 grid showing the sum of two dice for each of the 36 outcomes with the six cells that give a sum of 7 highlighted
img.cap: The 36 outcomes for two dice.

p: A bag has 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls (10 in all). P(red) = 5/10 = 1/2. P(blue) = 3/10. P(not green) = 1 − 2/10 = 8/10 = 4/5.
P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. P(greater than 4) = P(5 or 6) = 2/6 = 1/3. P(7) = 0 (impossible). P(a number less than 7) = 6/6 = 1 (certain).

sections.h: Example 3: two coins and two dice
p: Two coins: P(two heads) = 1/4. P(at least one head) = 3/4 (HH, HT, TH). Two dice: P(sum is 7) = 6/36 = 1/6. P(sum greater than 9) = P(10, 11 or 12) = (3 + 2 + 1)/36 = 6/36 = 1/6. P(both dice the same) = 6/36 = 1/6.

Experimental probability = the number of times the event happened ÷ the number of trials. If you toss a coin 20 times and get 12 heads, the experimental probability of a head is 12/20 = 0.6. The theoretical probability is 0.5. With more trials, the experimental value gets closer to the theoretical value.

units.title: Types of Events and the Addition Rule
units.summary: Mutually exclusive and non-mutually exclusive events, complementary events, and the rules for finding the probability of 'A or B'.

p: A simple event has one outcome (rolling a 4). A compound event has more than one outcome (rolling an even number: 2, 4 or 6).
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time, for example rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 on one die.
Complementary events are opposites: A and 'not A'. P(A) + P(not A) = 1. For example rain or no rain.

sections.h: The addition rule for mutually exclusive events
p: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Example: if P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4 and A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A or B) = 0.7. Example: a die is rolled: P(2 or 5) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3.
If A and B can both happen, we must not count the overlap twice: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Example 1. A die is rolled. A = even number {2, 4, 6}, B = greater than 4 {5, 6}. 6 is in both. P(A or B) = 3/6 + 2/6 − 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3. Check by listing: {2, 4, 5, 6} has 4 outcomes: 4/6 = 2/3.
Example 2. A card is drawn from 52. P(King or Heart) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13 (the King of Hearts is in both).

In a class of 30 students, 18 study Mathematics, 15 study Physics and 10 study both. Start with the overlap: 10 study both. Then Maths only = 18 − 10 = 8 and Physics only = 15 − 10 = 5. Together 8 + 10 + 5 = 23 study at least one of the subjects, so 30 − 23 = 7 study neither.

p: P(Maths or Physics) = 23/30. P(neither) = 7/30. P(Maths only) = 8/30 = 4/15. P(both) = 10/30 = 1/3. By the rule: P(M or P) = 18/30 + 15/30 − 10/30 = 23/30. Correct.
A spinner has 8 equal sectors numbered 1 to 8. If P(even) = 0.5, the number of even sectors is 0.5 × 8 = 4.

units.title: The Multiplication Rule: With and Without Replacement
units.summary: Independent and dependent events, and how to find the probability that two or more things happen, including draws without replacement.

p: Two events are independent if one does not change the probability of the other. Tossing a coin twice is an example. For independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
Example 1. P(head then tail) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Example 2. Three tosses: P(exactly two heads) = 3/8, because the outcomes HHT, HTH and THH are 3 of the 8 equally likely outcomes.
Example 3. Two dice: P(the second die shows the same as the first) = 1/6, so P(both dice the same) = 6/36 = 1/6.
If an item is taken out and not put back, the second draw depends on the first, because the numbers have changed. Then P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B after A).
Example 4. A bag has 6 red and 4 blue marbles. Two are drawn one after the other without replacement.
Check: 1/3 + 2/15 + 8/15 = 5/15 + 2/15 + 8/15 = 1. All possibilities add up to 1.
If the first marble is put back, the draws are independent. Both red = 6/10 × 6/10 = 36/100 = 0.36.
It is often easier to use the complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none). Example: P(at least one head in three tosses) = 1 − P(three tails) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.
Two cards are drawn from a pack without replacement. P(two aces) = 4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2 652 = 1/221.

units.title: Vocabulary: Words About Ceremonies
units.summary: Words used for traditional titles, festivals, rituals, naming, initiation and marriage, with an example sentence for each.

p: A strong vocabulary helps you in comprehension, summary and essay writing. This week's words come from culture, institutions and ceremonies. They appear often in WAEC and NECO passages about African life and history.
A ceremony is a formal act or series of acts performed in a set order, usually to mark an important occasion.
Installation is the formal ceremony of placing someone in a new position of authority. Example: The installation of the new Obi was attended by guests from across the country.
Investiture is the formal act of giving someone the authority and symbols (such as a staff or medal) of an office. Example: The investiture included the handing over of the sacred staff.
Homage is a public show of respect or loyalty to a superior, such as a king. Example: The chiefs came to pay homage to their new monarch.

Coronation is the ceremony of crowning a king or queen. A sceptre is a decorated staff that a ruler carries as a symbol of power. Regalia are the special clothes, jewellery and ornaments worn or carried by a ruler on state occasions: the crown, beaded necklaces and embroidered robes of an Oba are his regalia.
A festival is a day or period of celebration, usually for religious or cultural reasons. Example: The Eyo Festival in Lagos is a colourful display of culture and history.

A ritual is a solemn ceremony made up of actions done in a set order. Libation is the pouring of a drink, such as palm wine or gin, on the ground as an offering to a god, spirit or ancestor. A masquerade is a performer or group of performers in masks and costumes, often representing ancestral spirits. A carnival is a public festival with processions, music, dancing and masquerades. A procession is a number of people or vehicles moving forward in an orderly way as part of a ceremony.
Initiation is a rite of passage that marks entrance into a group or society, often with special rituals. Example: The young men went through a hard initiation into the age-grade society.
A rite of passage is a ceremony that marks an important stage in life, such as birth, puberty, marriage or death.

Dowry and bride price: in some places dowry means what the bride brings to her husband, while bride price (common in West Africa) is money or property that the groom's family gives to the bride's family.

units.title: Vocabulary: Words About Institutions
units.summary: Words for the rules, customs and structure of a society: norms, customs, tradition, taboo, social class, caste, kinship, family types, polygamy and monogamy.

p: An institution is an established organisation or foundation (such as a school), or the established laws, practices and customs of a society.
Norms are the unwritten rules that tell us what behaviour is acceptable in a group. Example: In many parts of Nigeria it is a social norm for children to kneel or bow when greeting elders.
A custom is a traditional and widely accepted way of behaving that belongs to a particular society, place or time. Example: The custom of celebrating the New Yam festival is centuries old.

Tradition is the passing of customs or beliefs from one generation to the next. Morality is the set of principles about right and wrong. A taboo is a custom that forbids or restricts a practice, person, place or thing. Example: In that community it is a taboo to whistle at night.

A custom is something people are expected to do, such as greeting elders in a special way. A taboo is something people are forbidden to do, such as speaking a sacred name. Both are part of a society's culture.

Social class is a division of society based on social and economic status. A caste is a rigid class system that a person is born into and cannot leave. Example: The caste system, though officially abolished, still influences social life in some societies.
Kinship is a blood relationship, or a sharing of common origins.
A nuclear family is a couple and their dependent children. An extended family includes grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins and other relatives.
Polygamy is having more than one wife or husband at the same time. Monogamy is being married to one person at a time.

units.activity: Write sentences that show the difference between (a) a custom and a taboo, and (b) a nuclear family and an extended family. Give one example of a social norm in your community.

units.title: Vocabulary: African Arts and Culture
units.summary: Words for the arts of Africa: sculpture, griot, folklore, lyrics and age grades, with practice on using them in writing.

p: Sculpture is the art of making two- or three-dimensional forms by carving (wood, ivory) or casting (bronze). The Benin bronzes and Ife heads are famous African sculptures.
A griot is a West African historian, storyteller, praise singer, poet or musician who keeps oral tradition alive.
Folklore is the traditional beliefs, customs and stories of a community, passed on by word of mouth.
Lyrics are the words of a song.

An age group or age set is a social category of people of about the same age who share status, rights and duties and are initiated together. Example: The age group in charge of road maintenance this year is the Umu Chineke.

sections.h: Using new words in your own writing
p: To learn a word, use it. Write a sentence about something you really know. Weak: The griot is a griot. Better: At the wedding, the griot praised both families in song and recalled the deeds of their ancestors.
Remember to use the word in the correct form. For example, folklore is uncountable and takes a singular verb: Folklore is an important part of our culture.

Institutions: norms, customs, tradition, morality, taboo, social class, caste, kinship, nuclear and extended family, polygamy, monogamy. Arts: sculpture, griot, folklore, lyrics, age group.

units.title: Spoken English: The Falling Tone
units.summary: What intonation is, what the nucleus is, and when to use the falling tone: statements, commands and Wh- questions.

p: Intonation is the rise and fall of the pitch (the high or low note) of your voice when you speak. It is the music of the language. It carries meaning beyond the words: it shows whether you are giving a fact, asking a question or showing surprise. Wrong intonation can cause confusion even if your grammar is perfect.
In every utterance one word is stressed more than the others. This is the nucleus (or tonic syllable). The movement of the voice, called the glide, happens on the nucleus.
Symbol: a downward arrow before the nucleus. The voice falls from a higher to a lower note. The falling tone gives a sense of finality, certainty and completeness. It sounds definite and confident.

Use the falling tone for: (a) ordinary statements: My name is \Bola. She lives in \London. It's a beautiful \day. (b) commands: Shut the \door. Go to your \room. \Stop. (c) information questions (Wh- questions, which need a specific answer): What is your \name? Where are you \going? How did you \do it?

Say the sentence aloud and listen for your voice dropping on the nucleus. Try a deep breath, say the word before the nucleus on a middle note, then let the nucleus start high and slide down. Practise with a friend and record yourself if possible.

units.title: Spoken English: The Rising Tone and the Fall-Rise
units.summary: When to use the rising tone: yes/no questions, lists, surprise and polite requests; and the fall-rise tone for doubt.

p: Symbol: an upward arrow before the nucleus. The pitch rises from a lower to a higher note. The rising tone gives a sense of incompleteness, uncertainty, politeness or a request for confirmation.

Use it for: (a) Yes/No questions: Is your name /Bola? Are you going /home? Did you see the /film? (b) Lists: the tone rises on each item and falls on the last, to show the list is finished: I bought some /apples, some /oranges and some \bananas. (c) Surprise or disbelief, to turn a statement into a question: You're leaving al/ready? He won the /lottery? (d) Polite requests: Can you help me, /please?
(Some printed notes write the nucleus of 'He won the lottery?' with a falling arrow. A question of surprise or disbelief uses the rising tone, so the correct mark is lott/ery.)

The fall-rise tone (the voice falls and then rises) is common in British English. It often shows hesitation, doubt or a slight correction. Example: It's good... (but it could be better). I like him... (but I don't trust him).

sections.h: Changing the meaning by moving the nucleus
p: The nucleus changes the meaning. Take I didn't say he stole the money. Stress I: someone else said it. Stress say: I only hinted it. Stress he: I said someone else stole it. Stress stole: he did something else with it. Stress money: he stole something else.

units.title: Nouns: Types of Nouns
units.summary: Proper, common, collective, abstract, concrete, countable and uncountable nouns, with a common error and its correction.

p: Proper nouns are the specific names of people, places and organisations; they begin with a capital letter: Chinua, Lagos, Nigeria, United Nations, Christmas. City is a common noun, but Port Harcourt is a proper noun.
Common nouns are general names for a person, place, thing or idea: woman, country, river, happiness, month.
Collective nouns name a group as one unit: a choir of singers, a board of directors, a pride of lions, a school of fish, a flock of birds, a fleet of ships, a bunch of bananas, a set of tools.
In British English a collective noun can take a singular verb (the group as a unit: The team is playing well) or a plural verb (the members as individuals: The team are putting on their boots).

Abstract nouns name ideas, qualities, states or feelings that you cannot see, touch, smell, taste or hear: bravery, freedom, knowledge, poverty, beauty, childhood. Concrete nouns name things you can perceive with the senses: rain, sand, whisper, perfume, sugar.

Countable nouns can be counted and have a singular and a plural: one book, three books; a chair, several chairs. Uncountable (mass) nouns cannot be counted. They have no plural form and take a singular verb: furniture, advice, information, water, equipment.

Common error: I have many furnitures. Correct: I have a lot of furniture, or I have many pieces of furniture. Likewise: He gave me good advice (not advices). Use a piece of, an item of or a bit of with uncountable nouns.

units.title: Nouns: Forming Plurals
units.summary: Regular plural rules and irregular, zero and foreign plurals that are often used in academic English.

p: Add -s to most nouns: dog, dogs; table, tables.
Add -es to nouns that end in -s, -ss, -x, -z, -sh, -ch: bus, buses; box, boxes; church, churches.
If a noun ends in a consonant plus -y, change -y to -ies: baby, babies; country, countries. (If a vowel comes before -y, just add -s: boy, boys.)
Some nouns that end in -o add -es: potato, potatoes; tomato, tomatoes; hero, heroes. Others add -s: photo, photos; piano, pianos. There is no perfect rule, so learn them.
Many nouns that end in -f or -fe change to -ves: leaf, leaves; wife, wives; knife, knives. Exceptions: chief, chiefs; roof, roofs; belief, beliefs.
Vowel change: man, men; woman, women; foot, feet; tooth, teeth; mouse, mice.
Zero plurals (no change): sheep, deer, series, species, aircraft.
-en plurals: child, children; ox, oxen.

These come from Latin and Greek and are used often in academic English: datum, data; criterion, criteria; phenomenon, phenomena; analysis, analyses; crisis, crises; index, indices (or indexes); syllabus, syllabi (or syllabuses).
Note: criteria and phenomena are already plural. Say one criterion, two criteria.

units.title: Noun Phrases
units.summary: What a noun phrase is, its parts (determiner, pre-modifiers, headword, post-modifiers) and its grammatical functions in a sentence.

p: A noun phrase (NP) is a word or group of words that does the work of a single noun in a sentence. It always has a main noun, the headword. Structure: (determiner) + (pre-modifiers) + HEADWORD + (post-modifiers).

Determiners: a, an, the, this, that, my, your, numbers. Pre-modifiers: adjectives or other nouns before the headword. Post-modifiers: groups of words after it, such as prepositional phrases (of the king) or relative clauses (who lives next door).
Examples, getting longer: the car; the sleek, black car; the sleek, black car parked in the driveway; the sleek, black car which he bought last week. In all of them the headword is car.

A noun phrase can be: (a) Subject: [The diligent student] passed the exam. (b) Object of the verb: She admired [the diligent student]. (c) Complement: He became [a diligent student]. (d) Object of a preposition: She gave the award to [the diligent student].

In the sentence The three talented musicians from the village played a beautiful melody, the subject is the noun phrase the three talented musicians from the village. Its headword is musicians. The object is a beautiful melody, with headword melody.

units.title: Expository Essay: Features
units.summary: The purpose of an expository essay and its five hallmarks: clarity, objectivity, formal tone, logical organisation and evidence.

p: Continuous writing (essay writing) carries a large share of the marks in your English examination. An expository essay does not tell a story, paint a picture or win a debate. It explains, clarifies and informs. Think of yourself as a knowledgeable teacher or a careful reporter, presenting facts and examples in an organised way.
1. Clarity and conciseness: it is easily understood; use simple words where they will do.

2. Objectivity and impersonality: it is based on facts, not feelings. Avoid I believe, I think, in my opinion. Weak: I feel that corruption is bad for the country. Strong: Corruption has clearly harmful effects on national development.
3. Formal and academic tone: no contractions (write do not, not don't), no slang.
4. Logical organisation: a clear five-paragraph structure (the next unit).
5. Evidence-based support: every claim is supported with facts, examples, statistics or reasons.

Narrative essays tell a story. Descriptive essays paint a picture. Argumentative essays take a side and try to persuade. Expository essays explain. Read the topic: words like Explain, Discuss the causes of, Write on the importance of usually signal an expository essay.

units.title: Expository Essay: Structure
units.summary: The introduction (hook, background, thesis statement), body paragraphs (topic sentence, supporting details, link) and conclusion (restated thesis, summary, final thought).

p: The introduction is the foundation, the body paragraphs are the walls and the conclusion is the roof.

It has three parts. The hook is a general statement to catch the reader's interest: a striking fact, a rhetorical question or a short quotation. The background narrows down from the hook and gives context or a definition. The thesis statement is the most important sentence of the essay. It states clearly the main purpose and the points that the body will explain.
Example thesis: The scourge of drug abuse, driven mainly by peer pressure and economic hardship, damages the health and social standing of the individual and weakens the wider community.

Each paragraph develops one main idea that supports the thesis. It begins with a topic sentence (the main idea, linked to the thesis). Then come the supporting details: facts, examples and explanations that answer How? Why? Can I give an example? The paragraph ends with a concluding or linking sentence. Use transition words: furthermore, in addition, consequently, as a result, on the other hand.
It restates the thesis in different words (do not copy it), summarises the main points and ends with a final thought: a remark, warning, prediction or recommendation.

units.title: Planning an Expository Essay: Drug Abuse
units.summary: A complete model plan: brainstorming ideas, writing an outline and building the thesis, topic sentences and conclusion for an essay on drug abuse.

p: Write down all your ideas before you write the essay. For drug abuse: What is it? The harmful or addictive use of narcotic substances. Causes: peer pressure, unemployment, poverty, curiosity, mental health problems, poor parental guidance. Effects on the individual: addiction, mental illness, organ damage, dropping out of school, financial ruin, crime. Effects on society: more crime, broken families, a burden on hospitals, loss of workers. Solutions: public education, stricter law enforcement, job creation, rehabilitation centres.
Title: The Menace of Drug Abuse in Contemporary Society.

Introduction: hook (a statistic or a rhetorical question about young people and drugs); background (define drug abuse and say how common it is); thesis: Drug abuse, a complex problem fuelled by social and economic factors, leads to devastating health consequences for the individual and threatens the safety and unity of society.

Body 1, causes. Topic sentence: The descent into drug abuse is often triggered by peer influence and economic hardship. Details: how peer pressure works; how unemployment leads to idleness and despair.

Body 2, effects on the individual. Topic sentence: The consequences for the user are severe, affecting both physical health and social standing. Details: addiction as a disease of the brain; lung damage and overdose; stigma and isolation.

Body 3, effects on society. Topic sentence: The effects of drug abuse extend far beyond the individual, destabilising families and communities. Details: theft and robbery to fund the habit; the emotional cost to families; the cost of policing and health care.

Conclusion: restate the thesis (In summary, the cycle of drug abuse, started by social and economic pressure, causes personal tragedy and wide social harm); summarise; final thought (A combined approach of education, economic empowerment and accessible rehabilitation is not just advisable but necessary).

Many examinations give a word limit, for example 400 words. Plan about 60 to 80 words for the introduction, 80 to 90 for each of three body paragraphs and 50 to 60 for the conclusion. Keep a margin so you do not exceed the limit.

units.title: Comprehension: Silent Reading Strategies
units.summary: Skimming, scanning and intensive reading, and when to use each one in the examination.

p: Comprehension is understanding, interpreting and judging what you read. In your SSCE examination it is a silent, timed skill. Silent reading is faster, helps you concentrate and lets you think about ideas without the distraction of reading aloud.

Purpose: to get the main idea or gist quickly. How: read the title and any headings; read the first and last paragraphs (they often contain the thesis and conclusion); read the first sentence of each paragraph; let your eyes move quickly and notice words in bold or italic or words that are repeated. Use it before reading a passage in detail.

Purpose: to find one piece of information quickly, such as a name, date or number. How: know exactly what you are looking for; move your eyes quickly over the text without reading every word; use cues such as numbers, capital letters or key words. Use it to answer a factual question.

Purpose: to understand all the details, arguments and implications. How: after skimming, read slowly, paragraph by paragraph; underline key points and unknown words; stop at the end of each paragraph and say its main point to yourself; ask: What is the author's main argument? What evidence is used? What is the tone? Use it when you must answer detailed questions.

sections.h: A good order in the examination
p: First skim the passage. Then read the questions. Then read intensively, scanning for facts. Answer in complete sentences in your own words unless you are asked to quote. Keep to the time.

units.activity: Take a short article from a newspaper. Skim it for 30 seconds and write the main idea in one sentence. Then scan it for the first number or date. Finally read it intensively and write the main point of each paragraph.

units.title: Comprehension: Words in Context and Question Types
units.summary: Using synonym, antonym and example clues to find the meaning of words, and recognising the five kinds of comprehension questions.

p: An examination often asks the meaning of a word as used in the passage. The dictionary meaning may not fit, so use clues.

Synonym or restatement clue: the writer gives a meaning nearby. His obdurate nature, his stubborn refusal to change his mind, made negotiation impossible. (stubborn refusal to change his mind explains obdurate.)
Antonym or contrast clue: the writer gives an opposite. While the manager was often loquacious, his assistant was a man of very few words. (the contrast shows loquacious means talkative.)

Example clue: examples explain the word. The museum had various relics from the war, including torn uniforms, rusted weapons and old letters. (the examples show a relic is an old object from the past.)
1. Factual (direct): the answer is stated in the text. Key words: What is, Who, When, List. Scan for the information.
2. Inferential: the answer is implied, not stated. Key words: suggest, infer, imply, what conclusion can you draw. Combine the text with logical thinking.
3. Vocabulary in context: As used in the passage, what does X mean? Use the clues above.
4. Main idea or global: the central theme or purpose. Look at the title, the thesis in the first paragraph and the conclusion.

5. Reference or grammar: What does the word it refer to? What is the grammatical name and function of the expression? Look back to the nearest noun for a pronoun; name the construction (noun phrase, adverbial clause) and its job.

units.title: Comprehension Practice: Youth Restiveness
units.summary: A practice passage on youth restiveness with five questions of different types and model answers.

p: Read the passage silently first, then answer the questions.

Youth restiveness, a term that describes the agitated and often disruptive behaviour of a nation's young people, has become a gargantuan challenge in many developing countries. This phenomenon does not emerge from a vacuum. Its primary catalyst is the pervasive and debilitating spectre of unemployment. When a significant portion of the educated and able-bodied youth is left idle, their energies, which ought to be channelled towards productive ventures, are often diverted into social vices. Furthermore, the decay in societal values, where wealth is celebrated without questioning its source, makes the problem worse. Young people observe individuals with ostentatious lifestyles, often products of corruption, and are pressured to attain such wealth by any means necessary. This creates a fertile ground for political thuggery, cybercrime and armed robbery.

To curb this menace, a multi-pronged approach is essential. It is not enough to simply police the youth; we must create real economic opportunities. Revitalising the nation's industries, fostering entrepreneurship and a systematic re-orientation of values are the only long-term solutions to this endemic problem.
1. (Factual) What is the primary catalyst for youth restiveness? Answer: The primary catalyst is unemployment.
2. (Factual) Name two social vices. Answer: Political thuggery, cybercrime and armed robbery are mentioned. Any two are correct.
3. (Vocabulary) The meaning of ostentatious. Answer: Showy, meant to impress others, especially with wealth.

4. (Inferential) What does 'This phenomenon does not emerge from a vacuum' mean? Answer: Youth restiveness does not appear for no reason; it has definite causes, such as unemployment and the decay of values.
5. (Main idea) The author's purpose. Answer: To explain the causes of youth restiveness and to suggest ways of solving the problem.

(a) Three solutions in the last paragraph: reviving the nation's industries, encouraging entrepreneurship and a systematic re-orientation of values. (b) A multi-pronged approach means using several different methods at the same time. (c) The expression 'a pervasive and debilitating spectre of unemployment' is a noun phrase; here it is the complement of the verb (is) in 'Its primary catalyst is ...'. (d) Synonyms: gargantuan, huge; idle, unoccupied or jobless; endemic, widespread or constantly present.

Answer in complete sentences. Use your own words, but keep the meaning exactly. Do not copy long parts of the passage. Match your answer to the question word: list means give items, explain means give reasons.

units.title: Summary Writing: Steps for a Written Passage
units.summary: The five steps of summary writing: first reading, annotation, paraphrasing, connecting and editing, and the difference between lifting and paraphrasing.

p: A summary reduces a long text to its most important points, in your own words. It is not copying. It is processing, selecting and restating the key information briefly and clearly. This skill is needed in examinations, in research and in professional life.
1. First reading: read the whole passage once without stopping to see what it is about and what the writer wants to say.

2. Second reading: read again with a pen. In each paragraph underline the topic sentence (the sentence with the main idea). Mark key supporting details, but be ready to throw away examples, illustrations, repetitions and decorative language.
3. Drafting: write the main ideas in your own words (paraphrase).
4. Connecting: join the points with connectives such as furthermore, consequently, as a result, however, therefore and subsequently so that the summary reads smoothly and is not a list.

5. Editing: check the word limit (for example three sentences or not more than 60 words) and cut carefully. Remove remaining examples, adjectives and repeated phrases. Combine short sentences into longer ones to save words. Read the final summary aloud to check that it is clear.
Lifting is copying phrases or sentences straight from the passage. It is penalised in examinations. Paraphrasing shows that you understand.

Original: The relentless onslaught of deforestation is systematically eradicating the habitats of countless species. Lifting (bad): Deforestation is eradicating the habitats of species. This is still too close to the original. Paraphrase (good): The continuous clearing of forests is destroying the natural homes of many animals.

Write in complete sentences, in the present or past tense used by the passage, and in your own words. Do not add your own opinion. Count your words. Always answer the exact question: if you are asked for the effects, do not give the causes.

units.title: Summarising a Talk or Lecture
units.summary: Active listening, signposts, note-taking with abbreviations, and a worked example summarising a passage on corruption in three sentences.

p: You cannot re-listen to a live talk, so good note-taking becomes the key skill. Active listening means focused listening. Watch for signposts, the verbal cues that show the structure of the talk.

Introducing the main point: My central argument is..., The key thing to remember is... Listing points: Firstly..., Another important factor..., Finally... Giving examples: For instance..., To illustrate... Concluding: In conclusion..., To sum up..., Therefore...

Do not write word for word: you cannot write as fast as people speak. Use abbreviations and symbols: & or + (and), w/ (with), w/o (without), → (leads to), ∴ (therefore), e.g. (for example), govt (government), cf (compared with). Write key words: nouns, strong verbs and important numbers. Ignore filler words. Keep asking: What is the topic? What is the main point? What are the two to four key points?
After the talk, your notes become the source text for your summary, and you follow the five steps from the last unit.

Passage: Corruption, in simple terms, is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. This menace has eaten deep into many nations and slows development. Its most visible effect is the diversion of public funds. When money meant for schools, hospitals and roads is siphoned into private pockets, the public is denied these services. This contributes to poverty and widens the gap between rich and poor. Furthermore, corruption erodes public trust and weakens the government. When citizens believe their leaders are corrupt, they become cynical and less willing to take part in democracy or to obey the law. This creates a cycle of lawlessness. Finally, corruption frightens away foreign investment, because investors see the nation as unstable.
Question: In three sentences, summarise the effects of corruption.

Main points: (1) diversion of public funds leading to lack of services and poverty; (2) loss of public trust leading to cynicism and lawlessness; (3) loss of foreign investment because of apparent instability.

Rough draft: Corruption makes public money be stolen, so there is no money for schools and hospitals and people become poorer. It also makes people distrust the government, so they do not obey the law. It also makes foreign companies not want to invest.

Final answer: Firstly, corruption leads to the misappropriation of public funds, resulting in inadequate social amenities and worsening poverty. Secondly, it undermines public trust in government, encouraging cynicism and lawlessness. Finally, it deters foreign investment by creating an impression of national instability.

It has exactly three sentences, as required. Each sentence covers one main point. It uses connectives (firstly, secondly, finally). It contains no examples and no opinions. The wording is the writer's own, though some key words (public funds, foreign investment) cannot easily be changed.

units.title: Spoken English: Consonant Clusters (Two Consonants)
units.summary: What a consonant cluster is, why Nigerian speakers insert extra vowels (epenthesis), and how to pronounce two-consonant final clusters clearly.

p: A consonant cluster (or consonant blend) is a sequence of two or more consonant sounds together in one syllable, with no vowel between them. In strong, the beginning has the cluster /str/. In tests, the end has the cluster /sts/.

Many Nigerian languages have few consonant clusters. So speakers often insert a short vowel (usually /ɪ/ or /ʊ/) to break the cluster. This is epenthesis. For example task may be said as task-i and film as fi-lum. To speak more standard and internationally understood English, practise saying the cluster smoothly without any vowel in between.
Move smoothly from one consonant to the next, without a vowel break.
/sk/: ask, task, desk, mask, risk. Please complete the task.
/st/: first, last, lost, ghost, wrist. She was first in the race.
/sp/: wasp, grasp, lisp, crisp. It was a crisp morning.
/nd/: hand, land, send, found, behind. Please send a reply.
/ŋk/: bank, thank, link, drink, trunk. I thank you for your help. (/ŋ/ is the 'ng' sound.)
/ld/: gold, hold, mild, child, field. The child played in the field.
/lt/: belt, salt, melt, built. Fasten your seat belt.
/mp/: jump, camp, lamp, limp. The frog can jump.
/pt/: kept, wept, slept, adopt. He slept soundly.
Say the word slowly in two parts, then speed up: as-k, then ask. Do not add a vowel. Listen to a good radio newsreader and copy the clusters. Practise with the example sentences, five times each.

units.title: Spoken English: Three- and Four-Consonant Clusters
units.summary: Final clusters with three and four consonants, usually made by adding plural -s or past -ed, with practice words and sentences.

p: The last sound is often the plural -s or the past tense -ed. Pronounce all three sounds clearly.
/sts/: ghosts, tests, lists, wrists. The students finished their tests.
/sks/: tasks, desks, masks, risks. We have many tasks to complete.
/mps/: jumps, lamps, camps, limps. All the street lamps were on.
/nts/: wants, pants, tents, hints. He wants new pants.
/lts/: belts, salts, melts. The sun melts the ice.
/lpt/: gulped, helped. She helped her friend.
/kst/: next, text, fixed. Read the next text.
/lfθ/: twelfth. He was born on the twelfth.
These are the most difficult and are often simplified even by native speakers. Try to say them as clearly as you can.
/lfθs/: twelfths. /ŋkθs/: lengths, strengths. They measured the different lengths. /mpts/: prompts, attempts. The actor needed prompts. /ksts/: texts, contexts. She studied the historical texts.
The word glimpsed /glɪmpst/ ends in a four-consonant cluster: /m/, /p/, /s/ and /t/.

units.title: Vocabulary: Motor Vehicles — Body and Interior
units.summary: British English words for the outside parts of a car and for the controls and instruments inside it, with American equivalents.

p: A strong vocabulary covers practical things as well as ideas. Words for motor vehicles help you in descriptive writing, in technical passages and in real life, for example in maintaining a car or in a driving test. We use British English terms and note the American words.
Chassis (/ˈʃæsi/): the strong framework on which the body, engine and other parts are fixed, the skeleton of the vehicle. After the accident the chassis was bent beyond repair.
Bonnet (US hood): the hinged cover over the engine at the front. He lifted the bonnet to check the oil.
Boot (US trunk): the storage space at the back. We put our luggage in the boot.
Windscreen (US windshield): the large front window. The wipers cleared the heavy rain from the windscreen.
Wing (US fender): the part of the body that frames the wheel. He scraped the wing against the wall.

Bumper: a bar at the front and back that absorbs impact in a small collision. Number plate (US license plate): the plate that shows the registration number. Tyres (US tires): the rubber, air-filled coverings of the wheels. Silencer (US muffler): the part of the exhaust that reduces engine noise.

Dashboard (or facia): the panel in front of the driver with instruments and controls. Steering wheel: used to control the direction. Gear lever (US gear shift): changes gear. Handbrake (US parking brake): a hand-operated brake that holds the parked vehicle still. Clutch pedal: pressed to disconnect the engine from the gears before changing gear. Accelerator (US gas pedal): controls engine power and speed. Fuel gauge: shows how much fuel is in the tank. Speedometer: shows the speed. Rev counter (or tachometer): shows engine revolutions per minute.

units.title: Vocabulary: Motor Vehicles — Engine and Lights
units.summary: Words for the parts under the bonnet and for lights and electrical parts, with practice sentences.

p: Engine (or motor): the machine that gives power to move the vehicle, usually by burning fuel.
Radiator: part of the cooling system that removes heat from the engine coolant to prevent overheating. The car began to overheat because the radiator had a leak.
Alternator: charges the battery and powers the electrical system while the engine is running. A faulty alternator will drain the battery completely.

Carburettor: in older engines, mixes air and fuel in the correct proportions (modern cars use fuel injection). Battery: stores electrical energy to start the engine and to run electrical parts when the engine is off. Spark plug: delivers an electric spark in the cylinder to ignite the fuel and air.

Headlights: the strong lights at the front for night driving or poor visibility. Sidelights (US parking lights): dimmer lights at the front and rear that make the vehicle visible when parked or at dusk. Indicators (US turn signals): flashing lights to show that you will turn or change lane. Hazard lights: all four indicators flash together to warn other drivers of danger or a breakdown. Brake lights: bright red lights at the back that come on when the brake pedal is pressed. Rear lights (tail lights): red lights at the back that are on whenever the headlights or sidelights are on.

(a) Before a long journey, check the oil and water levels under the bonnet. (b) The driver used his indicator to show he was moving into the right-hand lane. (c) If the radiator fails, the engine will quickly overheat. (d) She stopped because the alternator warning light was on, showing a problem with the charging system. (e) After parking on a hill, he always applied the handbrake.

units.title: Pronouns: Personal and Possessive
units.summary: Subject and object pronouns, possessive determiners and possessive pronouns, and the common errors 'between you and I' and 'its' with 'it's'.

p: A pronoun is a word that takes the place of a noun or a noun phrase. It avoids repeating the same noun. Without pronouns: Chinua said Chinua would bring Chinua's book, but Chinua forgot the book. With pronouns: Chinua said he would bring his book, but he forgot it.
Personal pronouns refer to particular people or things and change their form (case) according to their job in the sentence.
Subject pronouns do the action: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. She is a brilliant lawyer. They are playing football.
Object pronouns receive the action or follow a preposition: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. The teacher praised him. Give the letter to me.

Common error: using a subject pronoun where an object pronoun is needed. Incorrect: This is between you and I. Correct: This is between you and me, because me is the object of the preposition between.
Possessive determiners (some books call them adjective pronouns) come before a noun: my, your, his, her, its, our, their. That is my car. Have you seen their new house?
Possessive pronouns stand alone and replace the whole noun phrase: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. That car is mine. Our results are similar to theirs.

Its and it's: its (no apostrophe) shows possession: The dog wagged its tail. It's is the short form of it is or it has: It's a beautiful day. No possessive pronoun has an apostrophe: yours, hers, ours, theirs.

units.activity: Correct these: The secret is safe between you and I (between you and me). The team celebrated it's victory (its victory). Write one sentence with a possessive pronoun that stands alone.

units.title: Pronouns: Reflexive and Relative
units.summary: Reflexive pronouns and their emphatic use, and relative pronouns (who, whom, whose, which, that) that introduce relative clauses.

p: Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject, so the subject does the action and also receives it: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves. She cut herself while cooking.
They are also used for emphasis. I myself saw the incident.
Common error: using a reflexive pronoun as a subject. Incorrect: My brother and myself will attend. Correct: My brother and I will attend.
A relative pronoun introduces a relative (adjective) clause that gives more information about a noun. The noun is called the antecedent. The relative pronouns are who, whom, whose, which and that.
The woman who called you is my aunt. (who refers to the woman and is the subject of called.)
The man whom you met is the director. (whom is the object of met.)
This is the house whose roof was damaged. (whose shows possession.)
The book, which is on the table, is mine. (which is for things and animals.)
I need a phone that has a good camera. (that may be used for people or things, usually in restrictive clauses, which are clauses that are necessary to identify the noun.)

Use who when the pronoun is the subject of the clause (who called). Use whom when it is the object (whom you met). In everyday speech, many people use who for both: The man who you met. In formal writing, use whom when the pronoun is the object.

units.title: Pronouns: Demonstrative and Indefinite, with Practice
units.summary: This, that, these and those; indefinite pronouns and their agreement with verbs; and corrections of five common pronoun errors.

p: Demonstrative pronouns point to things and show how near or far they are. This (singular, near): This is my favourite song. That (singular, far): That was a memorable day. These (plural, near): These are the documents you asked for. Those (plural, far): Look at those beautiful flowers!
Indefinite pronouns refer to non-specific people or things.
Singular (take a singular verb): someone, anybody, nobody, nothing, everything, everybody, each, either, neither. Everybody is welcome to attend. Each of the players has a unique skill.
Plural: both, few, many, several. Several of the students are absent.
Singular or plural, depending on meaning: all, some, any, none, most. Some of the cake is gone (a mass, singular). Some of the biscuits are gone (countable, plural).
(a) Incorrect: Myself and my family are going on holiday. Correct: My family and I are going on holiday.
(b) Incorrect: Each of the players have a unique skill. Correct: Each of the players has a unique skill (each is singular).
(c) Incorrect: That is the man who I saw at the cinema. In formal English: That is the man whom I saw at the cinema (who or that is common in speech).
(d) Incorrect: The team celebrated it's victory. Correct: The team celebrated its victory.
(e) Incorrect: She is more intelligent than him and I. Correct: She is more intelligent than he and I (are), or, in less formal English, than him and me.

units.title: Listening Comprehension: Barriers to Good Listening
units.summary: What listening comprehension is, and four common barriers to effective listening with strategies to overcome each.

p: Listening comprehension is active. It means paying attention to spoken language, understanding its meaning, judging the message and responding properly. In the examination it tests whether you can focus, filter information, find the speaker's main ideas and understand the purpose and tone.

sections.h: Four barriers and how to overcome them
p: 1. External distractions: noise, poor sound quality, things happening around you. Strategy: choose a quiet place for practice; in the examination, block out background noise.
2. Internal distractions: your own thoughts, worries, tiredness or lack of interest. Strategy: notice the distracting thought, then deliberately bring your attention back to the speaker.
3. Prejudice or bias: judging a speaker by accent, appearance or topic, and so ignoring the message. Strategy: listen to the content and keep your feelings about the speaker separate.

4. Rebuttal listening: forming your own answer or argument while the speaker is still talking, so you miss key points. Strategy: understand the speaker's whole point before you start to judge or reply.

Before a listening test, read the questions if you can. They tell you what to listen for. Sit upright, have a pencil ready and keep your eyes on your paper. Listen to the first sentences carefully, because they usually give the topic.

units.activity: Which of the four barriers is the biggest problem for you? Write two things you will do this week to improve. Practise by listening to a 5-minute radio talk without any other distraction.
