units.title: Listening Comprehension: Note-Taking, Purpose and Practice
units.summary: Strategic note-taking, signposts, main ideas versus details, purpose and tone, and a practice listening script on the digital divide with model answers.

p: You cannot remember everything you hear, so take notes. Use a personal shorthand: & or + (and), w/ (with), w/o (without), → (leads to), ← (comes from), ∴ (therefore), e.g. (for example), i.e. (that is), govt (government), info (information). Do not write sentences; write the key nouns, verbs and ideas.

Heard: One of the most significant consequences of deforestation is the loss of biodiversity, which ultimately disrupts entire ecosystems. Notes: deforestation → loss biodiversity → disrupts ecosystems.

sections.h: Signposts, main idea, purpose and tone
p: Listen for signposts: introducing the main idea (My primary argument is..., The key thing to remember is...); listing (Firstly..., Another important factor..., On the one hand... on the other hand...); examples (For instance..., To illustrate..., Consider the case of...); emphasis (Crucially..., Above all...); concluding (In conclusion..., Therefore...).

The main idea is the most important point. Details, examples and statistics support it. Purpose: does the speaker want to inform, persuade, instruct or entertain? Tone: the speaker's attitude, such as serious, urgent, sarcastic, enthusiastic, critical or neutral, shown by choice of words, pace and intonation.

sections.h: Practice script (to be read aloud twice)
p: Good morning, students. My name is Dr. Bako, and I am here to talk about a critical issue of our time: the digital divide. The digital divide is not merely a buzzword; it refers to the growing gap between those who have ready access to modern information and communication technology, like computers and the internet, and those who do not. This is not just about owning a smartphone; it is a profound social and economic issue.

In Nigeria this divide is particularly stark. A secondary school student in Victoria Island, Lagos, might have unlimited Wi-Fi to stream educational videos and do research, while a student of the same age in a remote village in Borno State may have never seen a working computer. This creates a massive and deeply unfair inequality in educational opportunity from a very young age.

Why does this matter so much? Digital literacy is no longer a luxury or an optional skill; it has become the fundamental currency for taking part in the twenty-first-century economy. Without access to technology and the skills to use it, millions of our young people are being left behind on the global stage before they have even started the race. Therefore, I argue that it is the urgent and non-negotiable responsibility of both government and the private sector to invest heavily in rural broadband infrastructure and public digital literacy programmes. Thank you.

1. Topic: the digital divide. 2. It refers to the growing gap between those who have easy access to modern information and communication technology and those who do not. 3. The contrast shows the unfair inequality in educational opportunity between well-connected urban students and rural students with no technology. 4. It means that digital skills are as necessary for taking part in the modern economy as money is for buying things. 5. The purpose is to persuade (and inform) the audience that government and the private sector must invest in rural broadband and digital literacy programmes.

units.title: Spoken English: The Schwa /ə/
units.summary: The most common vowel sound in English: what the schwa is, why it occurs only in unstressed syllables, and how it gives English its stress-timed rhythm.

p: The schwa, written /ə/, is the most common vowel sound in English. It is a short, weak, neutral vowel, like a soft 'uh'. It is the sound you make when your mouth, jaw and tongue are completely relaxed. It is the first and last sound in ago /əˈɡəʊ/.
Golden rule: the schwa occurs only in unstressed syllables. Any vowel letter (a, e, i, o, u) can be pronounced as a schwa when it is in a weak, unstressed syllable.

English is a stress-timed language: stressed syllables are strong and prominent and unstressed syllables are weakened, often to a schwa. Many Nigerian languages are syllable-timed, where every syllable has about the same weight. Mastering the schwa is a key step towards natural, fluent British English rhythm.
For example, in teacher /ˈtiːtʃə/, the first syllable is stressed and the second is a weak schwa. If every syllable is given a full vowel (tea-cher said as tea-cheh), the rhythm sounds unnatural.

In this term we concentrate on the schwa at the end of a word. It is very common in words that end in -er, -or, -ar, -our, -a and -re. It also occurs at the beginning and middle of words in unstressed syllables (about, along, again, amazing, supply, police).

units.title: Government Vocabulary: Systems and Concepts
units.summary: Words for how a country is governed: democracy, democratic, national policy, revenue, bureaucracy and agency.

p: A register is the special vocabulary used in a particular area of life, such as government and administration. These are the exact terms used in political talk, news reports, legal documents and civic life. Knowing them helps you with comprehension passages and with discussing political and social issues clearly. We group the words by theme.

Democracy: a system of government in which power belongs to the people, who use it directly or through elected representatives. Example: Nigeria's return to democracy in 1999 ended decades of military rule. Think of a general election in which citizens queue to vote.

Democratic: an adjective that describes anything connected with or supporting the principles of democracy: fairness, equality and popular participation. Example: The selection of the student council was highly democratic, with a secret ballot and open debates.

National policy: a plan or course of action begun, accepted and followed by a country's government. Example: The new national policy on agriculture aims at food security by encouraging local rice production.

Revenue: the total income of a government, from taxes, customs duties and the sale of natural resources. Example: A large part of the government's revenue comes from crude oil exports. Compare expenditure: the money a government spends.

Bureaucracy: the complex structure of government officials, departments and procedures. It is often criticised as slow and bound by too many rules, which is called red tape. Example: Getting a passport can be frustrating because of the layers of bureaucracy.

Agency: a specific government department or organisation responsible for one area of public service. Example: The National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) protects Nigeria's environment.
Democracy is a noun. Democratic is an adjective. Democratically is an adverb. Democratise is a verb. Bureaucracy (noun) gives bureaucratic (adjective) and bureaucrat (a person).

units.title: Government Vocabulary: Official Documents and Meetings
units.summary: White paper, gazette, circular, memorandum, agenda and minutes, and the difference between an agenda and minutes.

p: White paper: an official government report that states policy or gives the final response to the findings of a committee or commission of inquiry. It shows the government's official position and what it will do. Example: After the panel investigated the disaster, the state government issued a White Paper accepting all its recommendations.

Gazette: an official government publication used to announce public notices, new laws, appointments and orders. To publish something in it is to gazette it. Example: The new judges will start work only after their names have been gazetted.

Circular: a formal letter or notice sent to many people or departments at the same time so that all take the same action or receive the same information. Example: A circular from the Ministry of Education told all principals about the new school calendar.

Memorandum (memo): a short, informal written message for communication inside an organisation, to inform, remind or request. Example: The Head of Department sent a memo reminding all staff of the project deadline.

Agenda: a list of the items to be discussed at a formal meeting. It gives structure and makes sure that all topics are covered. Example: The first item on the agenda of the parents' meeting was the proposed increase in school fees.

Minutes: the official written record of what happened at a meeting: the discussions, decisions and actions agreed. They are usually approved at the next meeting. Example: The secretary was asked to take the minutes.
The difference: the agenda is written BEFORE the meeting and says what will be discussed. The minutes are written DURING or AFTER the meeting and say what was discussed and decided.

sections.h: Typical order of a formal meeting
p: Call to order and opening prayer; reading and approval of the minutes of the last meeting; matters arising; the main items; any other business; the date of the next meeting; closing.

units.title: Government Vocabulary: Personnel, Structure and Practice
units.summary: Permanent secretary, cadre and official rank, followed by practice exercises with all the words from Weeks 1 and 2.

p: Permanent Secretary: the most senior non-political civil servant, the administrative head of a government ministry. The Minister, who is a politician, decides the policy direction, and the Permanent Secretary is responsible for carrying it out and for the day-to-day running of the ministry. Example: The new Minister of Health met the Permanent Secretary to learn about the ministry's problems.

Cadre: a small group of people trained for a particular purpose or with a particular skill, especially in an organisation with ranks such as the civil service or the army. Example: After her promotion she joined the senior management cadre of the federal civil service.

Official rank: a person's formal position or grade in a structured hierarchy such as the army, police or civil service. It shows the level of authority and responsibility. Example: Despite his high official rank, he was known for his humble manner.

Fill in the gaps using: policy, agency, agenda, minutes, circular. The Permanent Secretary sent a (a) circular to all staff, informing them of a new government (b) policy on transportation. To discuss its implementation, a meeting was called. The first item on the (c) agenda was to read the (d) minutes of the last meeting. It was announced that the policy would be carried out by a new (e) agency created for that purpose.

Governing systems: democracy, democratic, national policy, revenue, bureaucracy, agency. Documents: white paper, gazette, circular, memorandum, agenda, minutes. Personnel: Permanent Secretary, cadre, official rank. Practise using each in a sentence about an event in the news.

units.title: Spoken English: Reading and Appreciating Poetry
units.summary: How to read a poem aloud: rhythm and metre, rhyme, tone and intonation, punctuation and enjambment.

p: Reading poetry aloud is interpretation, not just recitation. You must pay attention to its prosody, the patterns of rhythm and sound.

Rhythm is the heartbeat of a poem: the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. Finding the metre, such as iambic pentameter, helps you find the natural beat. An iamb is an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one; pentameter means five of them in a line.
Example: Shall I com-PARE thee TO a SUM-mer's DAY? The line has ten syllables: weak, strong, weak, strong, and so on. Tip: read aloud and tap on the desk at each stressed syllable.
Rhyme is the repetition of similar sounds, usually at the ends of lines. The rhyme scheme is the pattern of rhymes, marked with letters. A Shakespearean sonnet usually follows ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.
Your voice must show the mood or tone of the poem: sad, sarcastic, joyful or thoughtful. Use a rising tone for uncertainty or questions and a falling tone for statements and a sense of finality.

Do not stop at the end of every line. Pause only where there is punctuation (commas, full stops, semicolons). Enjambment is when a sentence runs from one line into the next without a pause. Example: Let me not to the marriage of true minds / Admit impediments. The thought continues across the line break. Reading with enjambment is like driving over small hills: you keep your speed and do not stop at the top of each one.

units.activity: Choose a poem from your literature text. Mark the stressed syllables in one stanza, find its rhyme scheme and note where there is enjambment. Then read it aloud, pausing only at punctuation.

units.title: Arguing Effectively and Following Arguments
units.summary: How to build a strong argument (contention, logos, ethos, pathos, rebuttal) and how to follow and judge someone else's argument, including logical fallacies.

p: A formal argument is a structured way of persuading. It is not a quarrel. It needs both the skill to build a case and the skill to take another case apart.

sections.h: Building an argument as a speaker
p: 1. A clear contention (thesis): one debatable statement. Example: This house believes that single-use plastics should be banned immediately.
2. Logical reasoning (logos): evidence, data and logical steps. Example: Only 9% of all the plastic ever produced has been recycled, so a ban is a logical necessity.
3. Ethical appeal (ethos): show that you are credible and that your position is moral. Example: As future custodians of this planet, we have an ethical duty to act.

4. Emotional appeal (pathos): connect with the audience's feelings, but use it sparingly to support logic, not replace it. Example: Imagine sea creatures choking on this plastic. This is the legacy we are creating.
5. Rebuttal: expect and answer the other side's main points. Example: They will say a ban is inconvenient, but is convenience worth the permanent destruction of our environment?

sections.h: Following an argument as a listener
p: Identify the core: what is the speaker's central claim? Map the structure: what are the main supporting points, the pillars? Evaluate the evidence: are the examples relevant and the statistics believable? Spot logical fallacies, which are errors of reasoning, such as a personal attack on the speaker instead of the idea (ad hominem) or an exaggerated chain of consequences (slippery slope).

Useful phrases: I strongly believe that..., The evidence clearly shows..., My opponent has argued that... but this overlooks..., In conclusion, we maintain... Speak slowly, face the audience and support every claim.

units.activity: Prepare a one-minute speech for or against: School uniforms should be abolished. Include a contention, one reason with evidence, one emotional appeal and one rebuttal. Identify which of your sentences are logos, pathos and rebuttal.

units.title: Writing for Different Audiences
units.summary: How purpose, tone and register change when you write to a teacher or principal and when you write to a newspaper, with model openings.

p: The same information must be written differently for different readers. This is a matter of register (the level of language) and tone (the attitude).

sections.h: Writing to your teacher or principal
p: Purpose: to request, explain or apologise formally. Tone: respectful and polite. Register: standard formal English, no contractions (write cannot, not can't), with correct titles and salutations.
Model opening: Dear Mr. Adekunle, I am writing to respectfully request a brief meeting to discuss my academic progress in your subject...

sections.h: Writing to a newspaper or magazine
p: Purpose: to inform, persuade or complain in a public place. Tone: formal, objective and confident, because you are speaking to a wide, unknown readership. Register: clear, direct and forceful. Get to the point quickly and do not assume that readers know you or the situation.
Model opening (letter to the editor): Sir, I wish to draw public attention to the deplorable and increasingly dangerous state of the Oron Road, which has been neglected for over a year...

Salutation: Dear Sir or Dear Madam or Dear Mr. Name to a person you know; Sir or Dear Editor for a newspaper letter. Tone: deferential to a principal; confident and objective to the public. Content: with the principal you can refer to personal details; for a newspaper, give the facts of a matter of public interest.

sections.h: A short model letter (to the principal)
p: Dear Sir, I am writing respectfully to ask for a testimonial in support of my application for the State Scholarship. I have been a student of this school for six years and have been a member of the Debating Society and the Science Club. I would be grateful if the testimonial could be ready by the end of the month, because the application closes on the fifteenth of next month. I thank you for your time and consideration. Yours faithfully, (name), SS3A.

units.title: Grammar: Adjuncts (Forms and Functions)
units.summary: What an adjunct is, and its five main functions: time, place, manner, reason and frequency.

p: An adjunct is a word, phrase or clause that gives extra (optional) information about the action in a sentence. It acts as an adverbial and gives context. A test: if you remove it, the sentence is still grammatically complete. (She wrote the letter quickly. Without quickly the sentence is still complete.) Be careful: some adverbials are required by the verb and cannot be removed, as in He put the book on the table. These are not true adjuncts.
An adjunct may be one word (tomorrow), a phrase (in the main hall) or a clause (because it rained).
1. Time: answers When? or How long? The meeting will begin tomorrow. She lived in Kano for five years.
2. Place: answers Where? They held the concert in the main hall. Please wait outside.
3. Manner: answers How? In what way? He completed the task with incredible efficiency. She spoke confidently.
4. Reason: answers Why? The match was postponed because of heavy rain. Because of the traffic, I was late.
5. Frequency: answers How often? I always review my notes after class. We have meetings twice a week.

In She worked diligently throughout the night: diligently is an adjunct of manner, and throughout the night is an adjunct of time (how long). Ask the questions when, where, how, why and how often of the verb to find the adjuncts.

units.activity: Write one sentence for each type of adjunct (time, place, manner, reason, frequency) and underline the adjunct. Identify the adjuncts in: They sometimes play football on the field after school.

units.title: Reading: Paraphrasing Drama
units.summary: How to paraphrase dramatic passages written in older English, with worked examples from Hamlet and Romeo and Juliet.

p: To paraphrase is to say a text again in your own words while keeping its meaning and feeling. In drama this is hard because of subtext (the unspoken meaning behind the words) and old-fashioned (archaic) language.

1. Read the passage carefully to understand its overall meaning and emotion. 2. Find the meaning of unfamiliar or old words: thou (you), thee (you), thy (your), hath (has), art (are), wherefore (why), 'tis (it is), wilt (will). 3. Rewrite the passage in modern standard English, keeping the character's intention, not just the literal words.

Original: To be, or not to be: that is the question: Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, or to take arms against a sea of troubles, and by opposing end them?

Paraphrase: The basic choice is between going on living and choosing death. Is it more honourable to patiently endure the endless pain and unfairness that life throws at you, or to fight back against all your troubles, even if the fight ends in your death?
Original: O Romeo, Romeo! wherefore art thou Romeo? Deny thy father and refuse thy name; Or, if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love, and I'll no longer be a Capulet.
Notice that wherefore means why, not where. Juliet is not asking where Romeo is. She is asking why he has to be a Montague, the family that is the enemy of hers.
Paraphrase: Romeo, why do you have to be Romeo, a Montague? Give up your father and your name, or if you will not, simply promise to love me and I will stop being a Capulet.

units.activity: Paraphrase the following from Romeo and Juliet into one clear modern sentence: What's in a name? That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. (A name is only a label; a thing is what it is whatever it is called.)

units.title: Listening: Paraphrasing a Poem You Hear
units.summary: The three-phase technique for understanding a poem from listening alone: first listen, second listen for key devices, then paraphrase from figurative to literal language.

p: Paraphrasing a poem that you only hear is harder than paraphrasing written drama, because the sound disappears as soon as it is spoken. You must catch the essence of the poem from its sound and performance.
Goal: understand the overall mood and subject. Do not get stuck on difficult words. Ask: What is the dominant feeling (tone)? What is the poem mainly about (love, loss, nature, injustice)?

Goal: notice the poet's tools. Listen for key images (the pictures the poet creates, such as a lone tree in a barren field or a noisy market), figurative language (metaphor, simile and personification) and repetition of words or phrases for emphasis. Jot down key images and phrases as you hear them.

Metaphor: one thing is said to be another (Hope is the thing with feathers). Simile: a comparison using like or as (My love is like a red, red rose). Personification: giving human qualities to a non-human thing (The wind whispered).
Turn the poet's artistic language into clear, plain prose that explains the meaning.
Heard: Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul. Paraphrase: Hope is a strong and lasting feeling that lives inside a person.
Heard: My love is like a red, red rose. Paraphrase: The speaker thinks his love is extremely beautiful and delicate.

units.activity: Ask a friend to read a short poem twice. Write the tone and subject after the first reading; list three images after the second; then write a paraphrase of two or three sentences.

units.title: Reading: Summarising by Outlining Main Points
units.summary: A step-by-step method: find the thesis, find each topic sentence, build a skeleton outline with Roman numerals and capital letters, and then write a flowing summary.

p: Outlining is a very effective way to make a precise and logical summary, because it makes you see the structure of the passage.
Step 1: find the thesis, the central argument or main message, usually in the introduction or conclusion. Ask: What is the one thing the author most wants me to understand?
Step 2: read each body paragraph and find its topic sentence (the main idea), often the first or last sentence.

Step 3: make a skeleton outline. Put the thesis at the top as a title. Use Roman numerals (I, II, III) for the main points (the topic sentences) and capital letters (A, B, C) for the key supporting details.
Step 4: write the summary. Turn the outline into flowing prose in your own words, joining the points with transitions.
Thesis: Corruption is a major obstacle to national development.
I. Diversion of public funds. A. Money for schools and hospitals is stolen. B. This increases poverty and inequality.
II. Loss of public trust in government. A. It leads to widespread cynicism. B. It encourages lawlessness.
III. Foreign investors stay away. A. The nation seems unstable and unpredictable.

Summary: Corruption severely hinders national development. Firstly, it leads to the diversion of public funds, depriving citizens of essential services and worsening poverty. Secondly, it erodes public trust in government, fostering cynicism and lawlessness. Finally, it deters foreign investment, because the nation is seen as unstable.

units.title: Vocabulary: Latin and Greek Roots
units.summary: Common Latin and Greek roots that help you decode unfamiliar words, with examples and practice.

p: A large part of advanced English comes from Latin and Greek roots, prefixes and suffixes. If you know the roots you can guess the meaning of unfamiliar words in the examination and improve your vocabulary quickly.

aqua- (water): aquarium, aquatic, aquifer. port- (carry): transport, portable, export, portfolio. scrib- or script- (write): scribe, describe, manuscript, prescription. terra- (earth): territory, terrain, terrestrial, subterranean. mal- (bad): malpractice, malignant, malice, malnourished. bene- (good): benefactor, benefit, benevolent, benign.

bio- (life): biology, biography, antibiotic, biosphere. tele- (far): telescope, telephone, television, telepathy. graph- or gram- (write, draw): autograph, biography, diagram, grammar. -logy (study of): biology, geology, psychology, anthropology. phon- (sound): telephone, symphony, microphone, phonics. chron- (time): chronological, chronic, synchronise, chronicle.

Chronograph: chron- (time) + -graph (write or record) = a device that records time precisely, such as a stopwatch. Aquaphobia: aqua- (water) + -phobia (fear) = an irrational fear of water. Malnutrition: mal- (bad) + nutrition = poor nourishment. Benefactor: bene- (good) + factor (one who does) = a person who does good, especially by giving money. Telegraph: tele- (far) + -graph (write) = writing over a long distance.
Break the word into parts. Find a part you know. Check the sentence for support. Example: The aquifer under the desert supplies water to the town. Aqua- tells you the aquifer has to do with water.

units.activity: Give the meaning of: biography (writing about a life), telescope (instrument to see far), malpractice (bad practice), subterranean (under the earth), benevolent (wishing good), geology (study of the earth).

units.title: Writing: Revising an Expository Essay
units.summary: A six-point checklist for improving a first draft: thesis, unity, evidence, coherence, tone and conclusion.

p: Revision is looking at your draft again with a critical eye. It turns a good essay into an excellent one by improving clarity, logic and impact. Leave your draft for a while, then read it as if someone else wrote it.
a. Thesis: is it specific, clearly stated in the introduction and a reliable map of the whole essay?
b. Paragraph unity: does each body paragraph begin with a strong topic sentence that supports the thesis? Is every sentence in the paragraph about that topic?

c. Evidence: have you moved beyond vague statements to concrete examples, facts and reasons? Instead of Drug abuse is bad, write Drug abuse leads to specific health problems such as liver cirrhosis and mental illness.
d. Coherence and transitions: do ideas flow from one to the next? Use transitions such as furthermore, consequently, in contrast and as a result.
e. Formal, objective tone: remove personal opinions (I think, I believe) and informal language (slang, contractions). Keep the tone academic.
f. Conclusion: does it restate the thesis in different words and summarise the main points without adding new information? Does it end with a strong final thought?
Spelling, punctuation, capital letters, verb tenses and subject-verb agreement. Read the essay aloud: your ear will catch mistakes that your eye misses. Check the word limit.

units.title: Grammar: Adjectival Clauses (Defining and Non-Defining)
units.summary: Relative clauses that describe nouns, the difference between defining and non-defining clauses, and how to punctuate them.

p: An adjectival (relative) clause is a dependent clause that tells us more about a noun or pronoun. It is introduced by who, whom, whose, which or that.

A defining clause gives information that is essential for identifying the noun: it tells us which one we mean. If you remove it, the meaning changes. No commas are used. Example: The student who top-scored in the exam received a scholarship. (Without the clause we do not know which student.) Tip: if you can put that in place of who or which, it is probably defining.

A non-defining clause gives extra, non-essential information about a noun that is already identified. It can be removed without changing the basic meaning. It must be separated by commas. Example: Mr. Bello, who is our Mathematics teacher, is travelling to a conference. (We already know who Mr. Bello is.) That cannot be used for a non-defining clause.

a. The man who lives next door is a doctor. (defining; no commas.) b. Mr. Adebayo, who is our maths teacher, is travelling today. (non-defining; commas.) c. The car that I bought last week has broken down. (defining; no commas.) d. Lagos, which is the economic hub of Nigeria, has a population of over 20 million. (non-defining; commas.)

The book that you lent me was excellent (no commas). Explain how the first sentence changes if you have several sisters (no commas: it identifies which sister).

units.title: Vocabulary: Law and Order (Part 1)
units.summary: Words about the police, courts and legal process: police, plaintiff, defendant, tribunal, justice, civil rights and societal norms.

p: After the midterm, we study the language of justice and social order. It is important for discussing crime, justice and civic responsibility accurately.
Police: the civil force of a state responsible for preventing and detecting crime and keeping public order.

Plaintiff: the party who begins a lawsuit in a civil court; the person who says he has been wronged and asks for a legal remedy such as compensation. Example: The plaintiff sued the company for damages after he slipped on a wet floor.
Defendant: the person, company or institution against whom a civil or criminal case is brought. Example: The defendant stood silently in the dock while the charges were read.

Tribunal: a body set up to settle certain kinds of dispute, often less formal than a full court but with legal authority, such as an Industrial Tribunal or an Election Petitions Tribunal. Example: The dispute between landlord and tenant was settled by a rent tribunal.

Justice: (1) the quality of being fair and reasonable, and the use of law to keep it (The families of the victims cried out for justice); (2) a judge of a superior court (The ruling was delivered by Justice Amina Augie).

Civil rights: the rights of citizens to political and social freedom and equality, protecting them from unfair treatment by the state or by other individuals. Example: The right to vote is a fundamental civil right.

Societal norms: the unwritten, shared rules about behaviour in a society. They are different from laws but powerfully guide conduct. Example: Queuing in an orderly way is a societal norm in many cultures.

units.title: Vocabulary: Law and Order (Part 2)
units.summary: Litigation, verdict, acquitted, convicted, barrister and solicitor, and listening practice with a new poem.

p: Litigation: the process of taking legal action, suing someone or defending a lawsuit. Example: The company faced years of litigation over the damage it caused to the environment.
Verdict: the formal decision of a jury or judge on the facts at the end of a trial. Example: After three days, the jury returned a guilty verdict.
Acquitted: formally declared not guilty of a criminal charge. Example: Because of lack of evidence, the accused was acquitted and set free.
Convicted: formally found guilty of a criminal offence. Example: He was convicted of fraud and sentenced to five years in prison.

Barrister and solicitor: in the British legal system, which has influenced Nigeria's, a solicitor usually gives legal advice and prepares documents, while a barrister is a specialist advocate who speaks for clients in the higher courts.

Acquitted means found not guilty; convicted means found guilty. A verdict is the decision of guilt or innocence; a sentence is the punishment. A judge is the person who presides in court; a jury is a group of citizens who give the verdict (in Nigeria, most trials are decided by a judge alone).

Use the three-phase technique from the last lesson on a new poem that your teacher reads: first listen for tone and subject; second listen for key images and figurative language; then paraphrase into plain prose.

units.title: Writing: A Letter to the Editor
units.summary: The complete format of a formal letter to a newspaper editor, with a model letter on a community problem.

p: A letter to the editor is a formal letter by a citizen giving an informed opinion on a matter of public interest. It is a powerful way to take part in civic life.
1. Your address and the date: top right-hand corner. Example: 15, Educational Lane, Sabo, Yaba, Lagos State. 20th May, 2025.
2. The editor's address: left-hand side, below your address. Example: The Editor, The Guardian Newspapers, Isolo, Lagos State.
3. Salutation: formal and general: Dear Sir, or Dear Madam, (if you do not know the editor's sex, Dear Sir or Madam is also correct).
4. Title or heading: a short, strong phrase in capital letters or bold that sums up your argument. Example: THE MENACE OF EROSION ON AJAO ROAD.

5. The body: Paragraph 1 states your purpose and main point at once. Paragraphs 2 and 3 give specific details, evidence and consequences, using facts and logic. Paragraph 4 gives a clear recommendation or call to action: what should be done, and by whom?
6. Sign-off: Yours faithfully, (with a comma), your signature and your full printed name. Your town is optional.

Paragraph 1: I am writing through your esteemed newspaper to bring to the urgent attention of the Lagos State Government and the relevant authorities the deplorable state of Ajao Road, which has been made worse by severe erosion.

Paragraphs 2 and 3: The deep gullies have become a danger to motorists and pedestrians. Just last week a commercial motorcyclist was injured. Furthermore, the erosion is moving close to the foundations of houses.
Paragraph 4: I therefore urge the State Ministry of Works to send a team at once to assess the situation and begin repairs before a major tragedy occurs.

units.title: Grammar: Simple, Compound and Complex Sentences
units.summary: The three sentence types, the three kinds of subordinate clause (adverbial, adjectival and noun) and how to identify them.

p: A simple sentence has one independent clause (a subject and a verb that make a complete thought): The lawyer presented her case.

A compound sentence has two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so: FANBOYS) or a semicolon: The lawyer presented her case, and the judge listened attentively.

A complex sentence has one independent (main) clause and at least one subordinate (dependent) clause. The subordinate clause cannot stand alone; it depends on the main clause: Although the evidence was strong, the defendant was acquitted. (Subordinate: Although the evidence was strong. Main: the defendant was acquitted.)
Adverbial clause: does the work of an adverb. The case was adjourned because a key witness was ill.
Adjectival clause: does the work of an adjective. The barrister who led the prosecution was very skilled.
Noun clause: does the work of a noun, as subject, object or complement. What the witness said shocked the courtroom. (subject)
The jury deliberated until they reached a verdict. The subordinate clause until they reached a verdict is adverbial (of time).
a. He left the courtroom after the verdict was announced. Subordinate clause: after the verdict was announced (adverbial, time).
b. The evidence that the prosecutor presented was irrefutable. Subordinate clause: that the prosecutor presented (adjectival).
c. I do not know why the judge dismissed the case. Subordinate clause: why the judge dismissed the case (noun clause, the object of know).

units.title: Report Writing: The Official (Incident) Report
units.summary: The features of a formal report (formal tone, past tense, passive voice) and the format of an incident report with a model.

p: A report is a formal, structured document that presents facts about an event, situation or investigation. Its main purpose is to inform, not to entertain or give personal opinion. Objectivity and clarity matter most.

Formal tone: use standard English, no contractions (do not, not don't) and no slang. Past tense: a report describes things that have already happened. Passive voice: often used to stress the action rather than the doer, which makes the report more objective. Active: The student broke the window. Passive: The window was broken.

Title: clear and descriptive, such as REPORT ON THE VANDALISM OF SCHOOL PROPERTY. To: the reader (The Principal). From: your name and position (John Bako, Senior Prefect). Date: the date of submission.
Introduction: the purpose, what happened, where and when. Example: This report describes the vandalism that took place in the SS3 Science Laboratory on the evening of Monday, 12th November, 2025.

Body (findings): a chronological, factual account in paragraphs. Example: At about 4:15 p.m. I was alerted by a noise from the laboratory. On investigation, I found that three glass beakers had been broken. The laboratory attendant, Mr. Musa, was called and the scene was secured.

Conclusion and recommendation: the outcome and next steps. Example: In conclusion, property worth about ₦25,000 was destroyed. It is recommended that the school management review security after hours and that the culprits, if identified, be made to replace the damaged items.
Sign-off: signature and full name.

Give times, places and names. Report only what you saw or what you were told, and say which is which. Do not add opinions. Use the passive voice where it helps, but do not use it so much that the report is hard to read.

units.title: Report of a Meeting: Minutes
units.summary: How to write the minutes of a meeting: title, attendance, apologies, agenda, matters arising, business, any other business and adjournment.

p: Minutes are the official report of a meeting. They record who attended, what was discussed, what was decided and who is to do what. They are written in the past tense, in a formal and objective tone.
Title: MINUTES OF THE MEETING OF THE LITERARY AND DEBATING SOCIETY HELD ON (date) AT (place).
Present: the list of people who attended. Absent with apology: those who told the secretary beforehand that they could not come.
Agenda: the list of topics.
1. Opening: the time and any formalities such as the opening prayer.
2. Matters arising: reading and approving the minutes of the last meeting, and follow-up on actions from it.
3. Business of the day: an account of each item on the agenda, with the discussion, the decisions and who is responsible for each action. An Action column may help.
4. Any other business (A.O.B.): topics not on the main agenda.
5. Adjournment: the time the meeting ended.
Signatures: the secretary and the chairman or president.

The body of an incident report is a chronological account of what happened. The business of the day in minutes is organised by agenda item, not by time, and records decisions and responsibilities. Both use formal language and the past tense.

The meeting was called to order at 2:00 p.m. by the President, Miss Amaka Obi, who led the opening prayer. The minutes of the last meeting were read, corrected and adopted. Under business of the day, the Secretary reported that the society's debate against Government College would hold on 3rd March. It was resolved that five members would represent the society. Mr. Eze was asked to prepare the team. There being no other business, the meeting was adjourned at 3:15 p.m.

units.title: Comprehension: Corruption
units.summary: A comprehension passage on corruption with five questions of different types and model answers.

p: Corruption is a cancer that has metastasized to every part of our nation's body politic. It is not just the politician who embezzles public funds; it is the clerk who demands a 'softener' to find your file, the student who pays to have exam questions leaked, and the citizen who offers a 'tip' to a police officer to avoid a penalty. This endemic culture of 'cutting corners' has dire consequences.

Firstly, it destroys meritocracy. When jobs and contracts are awarded because of nepotism or bribes rather than skill and qualification, the most competent people are pushed aside. This leads to profound inefficiency: bridges collapse because the contractor used substandard materials, and public services fail because the managers are incompetent. Secondly, it creates a deep public cynicism. Citizens begin to believe that success is impossible through hard work and honesty, leading to a breakdown of societal values and an increase in petty and grand corruption.

1. (Factual) Besides politicians, what two other examples of corrupt acts are given? Answer: A clerk who demands a softener (a bribe) to find a file, a student who pays to have exam questions leaked, and a citizen who gives a tip to a police officer to avoid a penalty. Any two.

2. (Vocabulary) What does 'metastasized' suggest about corruption? Answer: It suggests that corruption has spread from one place to every part of society, as a cancer spreads through the body, and is dangerous and hard to remove.
3. (Vocabulary) The meaning of 'nepotism'. Answer: Favouring relatives or friends, for example by giving them jobs, without regard to merit.

4. (Inferential) The first major consequence and its direct result. Answer: Corruption destroys meritocracy (the system of rewarding ability); the direct result is profound inefficiency because the most competent people are sidelined.

5. (Global) The author's main argument about citizens' attitudes. Answer: Corruption makes citizens cynical; they come to believe that hard work and honesty cannot bring success, so values break down and corruption increases.

Unqualified people get contracts and jobs. A contractor who got a contract through bribes uses poor materials, so bridges collapse. Managers who got their posts through nepotism are incompetent, so public services fail.

units.title: Vocabulary: Idioms and Idiomatic Expressions
units.summary: Six common idioms with meanings and examples, and how to use idioms in your own writing.

p: Idioms are fixed expressions whose meanings are not clear from the words themselves. They are an important part of fluent, natural English and are often tested in comprehension and essays.
Born with a silver spoon in one's mouth: to be born into a rich and privileged family. Example: He never worried about tuition fees; he was born with a silver spoon in his mouth.

The black sheep of the family: a person whom the family sees as a disgrace or failure, often because he is different or has done something shameful. Example: While all his brothers are doctors and lawyers, Ade is the black sheep of the family for becoming an artist.

Take the bull by the horns: to face a difficult or dangerous situation directly and bravely. Example: Instead of ignoring the debts, the manager took the bull by the horns and reorganised the company's finances.
Spill the beans: to reveal a secret, often by accident. Example: We were planning a surprise party, but her brother spilled the beans a day before.
Once in a blue moon: very rarely. Example: He visits his hometown once in a blue moon.

A chip on one's shoulder: an attitude of constant hostility or defensiveness because of a feeling of having been wronged or of being inferior. Example: He has had a chip on his shoulder ever since he was passed over for promotion.

Use an idiom only when it fits the meaning. Do not change the words: say take the bull by the horns, not take the cow by the horns. Do not use too many in one piece of writing. In formal essays use idioms sparingly. In the examination, if you are asked for the meaning of an idiom, give the figurative meaning, not the literal one.

units.title: Listening: Following Instructions Accurately
units.summary: Strategies for following spoken instructions: signal words, prepositions, visualising and checking, with a practice example.

p: Following instructions correctly is vital in school, at work and in daily life. It needs active, focused listening and careful processing.
a. Remove distractions and listen actively. Do not assume you know what comes next.
b. Notice signal words. Sequence: first, then, next, after that, finally. Condition: before you begin, once you have, if... then... Priority: the most important step is, make sure that, crucially.
c. Notice small prepositions that change meaning: in the box and on the box; through the door and towards the door.
d. Visualise the process: make a mental film of yourself doing the steps.
e. Confirm and clarify: repeat the instructions in your own words or ask a precise question, such as So, after I connect the red wire, should I turn the switch on or off?

Instruction: To assemble this bookshelf, first lay the side panels on the floor. Then, using the longer screws, attach the back panel to the side panels. Before you tighten them completely, slot in the middle shelves. Finally, tighten all the screws fully and turn the bookshelf upright.

Analysis: the sequence words (first, then, finally) and the condition (before you tighten them completely) are vital. If you tighten the screws before slotting in the shelves, the shelves will not fit.
Make a list: 1. Lay the side panels on the floor. 2. Attach the back panel with the longer screws. 3. Slot in the middle shelves. 4. Tighten all the screws. 5. Stand the bookshelf upright.

In the examination, the instructions on the paper are the first test of this skill. Read them carefully: 'in one sentence', 'list two', 'not more than 50 words' and 'answer any three questions' all change what you must do.

units.title: Reading: Summarising Argumentative Passages
units.summary: How to find the thesis, supporting reasons, counter-argument and rebuttal in an argumentative passage, and how to write a short summary from them.

p: Summarising an argument means finding not only what the author says but how the case is built.

a. Find the core argument (thesis): the one sentence that shows the author's stand, in the introduction or conclusion. Example: The government should introduce a sugar tax to combat rising obesity and diabetes.

b. Find the supporting reasons (pillars): usually one in each body paragraph. Pillar 1: A sugar tax would reduce the consumption of sugary drinks. Pillar 2: The money raised could pay for public health campaigns.

c. Find the counter-argument and rebuttal, if present. A strong argument admits the opposing view and then answers it. Counter-argument: Critics say a sugar tax is regressive and unfairly hits the poor. Rebuttal: However, the health benefits for poorer communities, who suffer most from these diseases, would far outweigh the small financial cost.
d. Write the summary: join these elements in a short paragraph.

The author argues for a sugar tax to improve public health, saying it would reduce consumption and pay for health programmes. Although he admits that the tax may be regressive, he maintains that the health benefits for vulnerable groups justify it.
argues, claims, maintains, contends, admits, acknowledges, concedes, rejects, refutes, concludes.

units.title: Grammar: Adverbial Clauses
units.summary: Adverbial clauses of cause, purpose, condition and contrast, with signal words, examples and practice.

p: An adverbial clause is a subordinate clause that works as an adverb. It modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb and gives information about time, reason, condition and so on. It cannot stand alone as a sentence.
Cause or reason (Why?): because, since, as. The match was cancelled because the pitch was waterlogged.
Purpose (For what aim?): so that, in order that. He saved his money so that he could buy a new laptop.
Condition (Under what condition?): if, unless, provided that, as long as. If it rains tomorrow, the outdoor concert will be moved indoors. You will not succeed unless you work hard.

Contrast or concession (In spite of what?): although, though, even though, while, whereas. Although he was the favourite, he lost the election. I prefer romantic comedies, while my brother prefers action films.
(Adverbial clauses of time use when, before, after, until, while. Clauses of place use where and wherever.)

Do not use two conjunctions together: Although he was very rich, he was not happy (not Although he was very rich but he was not happy). Use a comma after an adverbial clause that comes first. Unless means if not: do not write unless you do not work.

I will not speak to him again unless he apologises (condition). She left the house early so that she would not miss the bus (purpose). Although he was injured, he managed to finish the race (contrast). The students were excited because the trip had been confirmed (cause).
In 'She studied every day so that she would pass her exams', the adverbial clause is so that she would pass her exams: a clause of purpose.

units.title: Report Writing: The Investigative Report
units.summary: The template of a formal investigative report: terms of reference, procedure, findings, conclusion and recommendations, with a model on missing sports equipment.

p: An investigative report is a formal document that presents the findings of an inquiry. It must be objective and based on evidence, and it must lead the reader logically from the question to the conclusion.
Title: REPORT OF THE INVESTIGATION INTO THE THEFT OF SPORTS EQUIPMENT. To: The Principal. From: your name, Chairman, Students' Disciplinary Committee. Date.

1.0 Introduction (terms of reference): why the investigation was held and what it was to find out. Example: This report presents the findings of the investigation begun on 18th May, 2025, on the instruction of the Principal, into the disappearance of footballs and jerseys from the sports store.

2.0 Procedure: how the investigation was done. Example: The committee examined the store's inventory and sign-out log and interviewed the Sports Prefect, the storekeeper and three members of the football team.

3.0 Findings: a neutral presentation of the evidence, in numbered points. 3.1 The inventory check showed a shortage of five footballs and ten jerseys. 3.2 The sign-out log for the past month was incomplete. 3.3 The Sports Prefect stated that he had lent the equipment to a community youth team without permission. 3.4 The storekeeper confirmed this and said he had been pressed to release the items.

4.0 Conclusion: a short summary of the facts established. The committee concludes that the missing equipment was taken from the store by the Sports Prefect, who lent it to an unauthorised outside group against school policy.

5.0 Recommendations: practical suggestions based on the conclusion. The committee recommends that: (i) the Sports Prefect be relieved of his duties; (ii) the missing equipment be recovered at once; (iii) a stricter system for checking out sports equipment be introduced.
Sign-off: signature, name and position.
Findings are the facts and evidence discovered, set out neutrally in detail. The conclusion is a short statement of what those facts prove. Recommendations say what should be done about it.

units.title: Drama: Listening to Plays and the Architecture of a Play
units.summary: How to listen for meaning in a dramatic performance, and the terms act, scene, dialogue, monologue, soliloquy, aside, stage directions, plot, climax and theme.

p: When you listen to a radio play or a performance, you are an aural detective. There is no picture, so every sound is a clue.

Tone of voice and delivery: a character's true feelings are often shown by how something is said: trembling with fear, booming with authority, sneering, hesitant. Pace, pitch and volume carry subtext.
Sound effects: rain and thunder set a scene of trouble; a door slamming shows an argument; approaching footsteps build suspense.
Music and silence: music sets the mood (tense, romantic, tragic). Silence can be stronger than words, showing shock or deep thought.

Plot is the chain of events. Find the central conflict: man against man (two characters opposed), man against society (a character challenging traditions or laws) or man against himself (inner doubt). Theme is the central idea the play explores: the corrupting effect of power, the struggle between tradition and change, the strength of love.
Act: a major division of a play, like a chapter. Scene: a part of an act, usually a change of place or a jump in time.

Dialogue: conversation between characters, the main way of telling the story. Monologue: a long speech by one character to others who are on stage. Soliloquy: a speech by a character alone on stage, speaking his private thoughts aloud to the audience; Hamlet's To be, or not to be is a soliloquy. Aside: a short remark spoken to the audience that the other characters on stage, by convention, cannot hear.

Stage directions are the bracketed or italic words in a script that are not spoken. They describe the setting, movements, expressions, tones and sound effects. Example: [KOLA enters abruptly, slamming the door. He is breathing heavily and looks frantic.]
Climax: the highest point of tension, or the turning point of the plot, where the main conflict must be faced and resolved.

units.title: Revision of a Prescribed Text: The Blood of a Stranger
units.summary: The plot, characters and themes of Dele Charley's play The Blood of a Stranger, with corrections to common mistakes about the story.

p: The Blood of a Stranger is a play by the Sierra Leonean playwright Dele Charley. (Some printed notes give the author as D.K. Gbegba; the author is Dele Charley.) It is set in the traditional kingdom of Mandoland and is a symbolic story of colonial exploitation.
Check this text against your own copy of the play and your teacher's notes, because published summaries differ in small details.

Maligu, the king's literate chief adviser, persuades the priest Soko to invent a prophecy that a stranger is coming. King Santigi and the people accept it; only Kindo, the chief warrior and heir to the throne, doubts it. Mr. Whitehead, a white colonial agent, arrives and says that he wants to farm tobacco, but he really wants the land's diamonds. He refuses to pay homage to the king and gives the villagers liquor, and the community begins to break down. His Black assistant, Parker, does his dirty work.

Soko, afraid, wants to withdraw from the scheme, and Whitehead has him killed by Parker. Kindo then kills Parker. A false sacrifice is staged, in which Maligu plays the priest and Parker's blood is spilled instead of that of a maiden. Kindo exposes the plot, but Maligu and Whitehead have him banished and the king agrees. At the end, Whitehead dies at Kindo's spear and Kindo goes into exile.

Whitehead: a colonial agent, greedy and dishonest; his name is symbolic. Maligu: the greedy, literate adviser who betrays his people for money. Kindo: the brave and honest warrior, the only one who sees the truth. Soko: the priest who is forced to lie and pays with his life. Santigi: the weak and easily led king. Wara: Kindo's woman, treated as an outsider because of her mother's background; she resists Whitehead. Parker: Whitehead's assistant.

Colonial exploitation: Whitehead is a symbol of colonial powers that came to Africa under false pretences to take its wealth. Greed and betrayal: Maligu and Soko betray the community for personal gain. Tradition and its misuse: the priest's authority is used for selfish ends. Integrity: Kindo alone questions the lies. Outsiders: Wara is a stranger in her own community.
Types of conflict: man against man (Kindo against Whitehead and Maligu), man against society (Kindo against the king and a deceived people).

sections.h: A note on what the earlier notes got wrong
p: Some textbooks say that Kindo is killed, that Soko is exiled and that the villagers rise up under Wara to kill Whitehead. In the play, Kindo is banished, Soko is killed on Whitehead's order, and Whitehead dies at Kindo's spear. Always use the text itself in an examination.

units.title: Energy Conversion and the Conservation of Energy
units.summary: What energy conversion means, the principle of conservation of energy, and the main forms of energy with their conversions.

p: Energy is part of every physical process: the movement of objects, the working of machines and the functions of living things. One of the most important ideas about energy is that it can change from one form to another. This is called energy conversion. A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy. An electric iron converts electrical energy into thermal (heat) energy.

sections.h: The principle of conservation of energy
p: Energy cannot be created or destroyed in an isolated system. It can only be changed from one form into another, and the total amount of energy stays the same. So the total energy before a process and the total energy after it are equal, even though the energy may appear in different forms. Machines do not make energy. They only change it.

sections.h: Forms of energy and what they can become
p: Chemical energy: stored in the bonds of chemical substances. It becomes electrical energy in a battery, or thermal and mechanical energy when fuel burns.
Mechanical energy: kinetic energy (energy of motion) and potential energy (energy of position). It becomes electrical energy in a generator and thermal energy through friction.
Electrical energy: energy of moving charges. It becomes mechanical energy in a motor, thermal energy in a heater and light in a bulb.
Thermal energy: energy of the motion of particles. It is made in most conversions, for example by friction, and is often wasted.
Nuclear energy: stored in the nuclei of atoms. In a nuclear reactor it becomes heat and then electrical energy.
Radiant (light) energy: carried by electromagnetic waves. It becomes electrical energy in solar panels and chemical energy in photosynthesis.
Sound energy: energy of vibrating particles, usually made from mechanical energy, for example by a loudspeaker.

units.title: Efficiency and Energy Loss
units.summary: Why no machine is 100% efficient, the causes of energy loss, and how to calculate efficiency.

sections.h: Energy is always lost as waste
p: In real systems energy conversion is never 100% efficient. Some energy is always changed into forms we do not want, usually heat. The main causes: friction (mechanical energy turns into heat), resistance in electrical circuits (electrical energy turns into heat), vibration and sound (unwanted noise) and air drag (reduces the efficiency of vehicles and turbines). The wasted energy is not destroyed; it is spread out as heat in the surroundings.

Efficiency shows how much of the input energy becomes useful output energy: Efficiency = (useful energy output ÷ total energy input) × 100%. It can also be written with power: efficiency = (useful power output ÷ power input) × 100%.
An electric filament bulb may change only about 10% of its electrical energy into light. The other 90% is lost as heat. Its efficiency is about 10%.
4 000 J of energy is supplied to a system, and 2 800 J is useful output. Efficiency = (2 800 ÷ 4 000) × 100% = 70%. The wasted energy is 4 000 − 2 800 = 1 200 J.

img.alt: A bar showing 4000 joules of input split into 2800 joules of useful output and 1200 joules wasted, with the efficiency calculation of 70 percent

p: A machine receives 5 000 J and produces 3 500 J of useful work. Efficiency = (3 500 ÷ 5 000) × 100% = 70%.

sections.h: Why a car engine is not 100% efficient
p: Only part of the chemical energy of the fuel becomes the motion of the car. Much is lost as heat through the exhaust and the engine body, as friction between moving parts, as sound and as air drag. A petrol engine is typically about 25 to 30% efficient.

units.title: Power Transmission: Meaning and Methods
units.summary: What power transmission is, why it matters, and the mechanical, electrical and hydraulic ways of transmitting energy.

p: Power transmission is the transfer of energy from the place where it is produced (a power station or an engine) to the place where it is used to do work (homes, factories or machines). It makes energy available far from where it is generated.

Its importance: it allows industries, towns and villages to use electricity or mechanical power; energy can be generated in one central plant and used over a wide area; it is cheaper than many small generators, which are costly and hard to maintain; and the networks (grids) join regions and let states or countries share energy.

Energy is passed through physical parts. Belts are flexible loops joining pulleys on different shafts, used in lathes and conveyors. Gears are toothed wheels that interlock and pass motion and force between shafts, used in clocks and engines. Chains and sprockets are used on bicycles and motorcycles.
Advantages: simple and cheap to build. Limitations: parts wear out and the distance is short.

Electrical energy is carried by conductors such as copper or aluminium wires. Overhead cables carry high voltages (for example 132 kV and 330 kV) over long distances. Underground cables are used in towns to avoid ugly wires and hazards.
Advantages: long distances with small loss (especially high-voltage AC), and easy change of voltage with transformers. Limitations: expensive to build; open to weather, vandalism and sabotage.

A pressurised liquid, usually oil, carries the energy. It is used in construction machines, aircraft and presses. Advantages: large forces can be sent through small pipes; control is smooth and exact. Limitations: leaks can be dangerous; it works over short distances and moderate speeds.

units.title: Transformers
units.summary: How a transformer works, the difference between step-up and step-down transformers, the transformer equations and worked examples.

p: A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating current by electromagnetic induction. It has two coils of wire, the primary and the secondary, wound on a soft iron core. An alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field in the core. This field induces an alternating voltage in the secondary coil.

img.alt: A transformer with a primary coil of 400 turns, a secondary coil of 40 turns on an iron core, and the equation Vp over Vs equals Np over Ns equals Is over Ip
img.cap: A step-down transformer: 150 V in, 15 V out.

p: A step-up transformer has more turns in the secondary than in the primary (Ns > Np). It raises the voltage and lowers the current. It is used at power stations to prepare electricity for long-distance transmission. A step-down transformer has fewer turns in the secondary (Ns < Np). It lowers the voltage and raises the current. It is used near homes and factories.
In an ideal transformer, power in = power out, because energy is conserved: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. So if the voltage is stepped down, the current is stepped up in the same ratio.
Vp / Vs = Np / Ns = Is / Ip (ideal transformer, 100% efficient), where Vp and Vs are the primary and secondary voltages, Np and Ns the numbers of turns, and Ip and Is the currents.
Primary 400 turns, secondary 40 turns, input 150 V. Vp / Vs = Np / Ns: 150 / Vs = 400 / 40 = 10, so Vs = 15 V.
Primary 100 turns, secondary 200 turns, primary voltage 100 V. Np < Ns, so it is a step-up transformer. Vs = 100 × 200 / 100 = 200 V.

The 150 V to 15 V transformer in Example 1 takes 0.5 A from the supply. Power in = 150 × 0.5 = 75 W. In an ideal transformer the output current is Is = 75 / 15 = 5 A. The current is stepped up 10 times as the voltage is stepped down 10 times.
A transformer has 400 turns in the primary and 100 in the secondary and a primary voltage of 240 V. Vs = 240 × 100 / 400 = 60 V (step-down).

units.title: Why Power Is Transmitted at High Voltage
units.summary: Power loss in cables (P = I²R), why high voltage reduces loss, a worked example and problems of power transmission in Nigeria.

p: A cable has resistance R. When a current I flows, the power lost as heat is P(loss) = I²R. Because the loss depends on the square of the current, a small reduction in current gives a big reduction in loss.

Power sent = voltage × current (P = IV). For the same power, a higher voltage means a smaller current. So transmitting at high voltage reduces the loss. That is why step-up transformers are used at power stations.
A generator rated 12 kW, 2 kV sends power through a cable of resistance 20 Ω. Find the power loss. I = P / V = 12 000 / 2 000 = 6 A. Power loss = I²R = 6² × 20 = 36 × 20 = 720 W.

Now step the voltage up to 20 kV. I = 12 000 / 20 000 = 0.6 A. Power loss = 0.6² × 20 = 0.36 × 20 = 7.2 W. Raising the voltage 10 times made the current 10 times smaller and the loss 100 times smaller.
Transformers keep the voltage steady at different points in the grid: stepped up for the long-distance lines and stepped down at substations for homes and factories.

sections.h: Problems of power transmission in Nigeria
p: Vandalism of cables and towers, theft of conductors, bush fires and weather damage; long lines that pass through remote areas and give losses; poor maintenance and old equipment; and the high cost of building and protecting lines. These cause blackouts and reduce industrial output. Environmental problems include clearing forests for line routes and the danger of fallen lines and electrocution in rural villages.

units.title: Machines: Meaning, Functions and Classes
units.summary: What a machine is, what machines do, and the simple machines (lever, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle) and compound machines.

p: A machine is a device that makes work easier. It can multiply force, change the direction of a force, or increase speed or distance. A machine does not create energy; it only helps us use available energy more conveniently.

Simple machines are basic mechanical devices. The lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fulcrum. There are three classes: first class (fulcrum between load and effort: seesaw, crowbar), second class (load between fulcrum and effort: wheelbarrow, nutcracker) and third class (effort between fulcrum and load: forearm, fishing rod).

img.alt: Diagrams of the three classes of lever with the load, effort and fulcrum marked
img.cap: The three classes of lever.

p: A pulley is a grooved wheel with a rope. A fixed pulley changes the direction of the force. A movable pulley multiplies the force. A block and tackle is a combination of pulleys. An inclined plane (ramp) is a sloping surface used to raise heavy objects. A wedge tapers to a thin edge and is used for splitting (an axe). A screw is an inclined plane wound round a cylinder. A wheel and axle is a large wheel fixed to a small axle (a door handle, a car steering wheel).

A compound machine has two or more simple machines working together: a wheelbarrow (lever + wheel and axle), a crane (pulley + lever), scissors (two levers + a wedge) and a bicycle (wheel and axle + levers + gears). In real machines, efficiency is always less than 100% because of friction, heat and deformation.

units.title: Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency of Machines
units.summary: The formulas for mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency of a machine, with corrected worked examples.

p: Mechanical advantage (MA) = load ÷ effort. It tells how many times the machine multiplies the force.

Velocity ratio (VR) = distance moved by the effort ÷ distance moved by the load. For a block and tackle, VR equals the number of rope sections supporting the load. For an inclined plane, VR = length of slope ÷ vertical height. For a wheel and axle, VR = radius of the wheel ÷ radius of the axle.
Efficiency = (MA ÷ VR) × 100%. It is also (work output ÷ work input) × 100%. MA is never greater than VR.
A load of 100 N is lifted by an effort of 20 N. MA = 100 / 20 = 5.
A machine has VR = 4 and MA = 3. Efficiency = (3 / 4) × 100% = 75%.

sections.h: Example 3: a machine with the numbers corrected
p: A machine lifts a 500 N load through 2 m when the effort moves 6 m. VR = 6 / 2 = 3. (A printed exercise says the effort is 125 N, but then MA = 500 / 125 = 4, which is more than VR. This is impossible because it would give an efficiency of 133%.) With an effort of 200 N, MA = 500 / 200 = 2.5 and efficiency = (2.5 / 3) × 100% = 83.3%.
Check with work: work output = 500 × 2 = 1 000 J. Work input = 200 × 6 = 1 200 J. Efficiency = 1 000 / 1 200 = 83.3%.
A system of pulleys has 4 rope sections supporting the load, so VR = 4. An effort of 125 N lifts a load of 400 N. MA = 400 / 125 = 3.2. Efficiency = 3.2 / 4 × 100% = 80%.
A 5 m long ramp rises 1 m. VR = 5. A load of 500 N is pushed up with an effort of 125 N. MA = 4. Efficiency = 4 / 5 × 100% = 80%.

units.title: Uses of Machines and Their Role in Nigeria's Economy
units.summary: How machines are used in agriculture, construction, transport and the home, and how they help productivity and development in Nigeria.

p: A metre rule pivoted on a fulcrum, with the effort and load at different places, shows the three classes of lever. Pulley systems made from string and wheels can be used to lift weights and study MA and VR. An inclined plane can be used to compare the effort needed to lift a load along a slope with lifting it straight up.
Agriculture: ploughs, harvesters, tractors and hoes. Mechanisation reduces the time and labour needed and raises farm output.
Construction: cranes (pulleys and levers), bulldozers and forklifts move heavy materials with less human effort.
Transportation: bicycles, cars and aeroplanes combine levers, wheels and axles. They improve mobility and the speed of travel.
Domestic use: scissors, knives, blenders and sewing machines make everyday tasks more efficient.

sections.h: Machines and the economy of Nigeria
p: 1. Higher productivity: fewer workers produce more. 2. Time saving: tilling a farm that took days by hand can take hours with a tractor. 3. Less fatigue: hard and repetitive work becomes easier. 4. Industrial growth: factories mass-produce goods. 5. Jobs: machines reduce some manual work but create jobs in manufacturing, repair, maintenance and design. 6. National income: efficient industries increase exports and GDP.
Limits in Nigeria: unreliable electricity, poor roads and other infrastructure, too few technically trained people and the high cost of equipment.

units.title: Maintenance of Machines: Importance and Types
units.summary: Why machines need regular maintenance, and the three types: preventive, predictive and corrective.

p: Machines are used in homes, factories and transport. Because of continuous use they wear out. Without care their efficiency falls and they may break down or cause accidents. Learning how to maintain and repair machines is an important skill for work in technology and industry.

Benefits of regular maintenance: better performance (less wasted energy), longer life, prevention of big failures by finding small faults early, safety, less downtime (time when the machine is not working) and lower cost, because preventing a fault is cheaper than repairing it or buying a new machine.

Preventive maintenance is done regularly whether or not the machine has a fault: cleaning, lubrication, inspection and tightening of bolts. Its aim is to prevent failures. Example: changing the engine oil every 5 000 km.

Predictive maintenance is based on data, sensors or trends: vibration analysis or thermal imaging can predict a failure before it happens. It is cost-effective because servicing is done only when needed. Example: a thermal camera shows a hot bearing in a factory motor.
Corrective (reactive) maintenance is done after a fault has occurred: replacing parts, major repairs or an overhaul to restore function. Example: replacing a burnt-out motor.
Preventive maintenance is planned and prevents breakdowns; it is cheaper over time. Corrective maintenance is a reaction to a breakdown; it is often more expensive and causes downtime.

Switch off and unplug the machine before repair. Wear gloves, goggles and boots. Work in a dry, well-ventilated place. Use the right tool for each job. Follow the maker's manual.

Maintenance raises productivity, makes the workplace safer, saves money, helps to meet legal safety standards and protects the environment because well-kept machines are more efficient and pollute less.

units.title: Dams: Structure and Functions
units.summary: What a dam is, its main parts (reservoir, spillway, penstock, turbine, generator, powerhouse) and its many functions.

p: A dam is a large structure built across a river or stream to hold back water and form a reservoir or lake. It is a strong barrier, usually of concrete, earth or stone, made to control the natural flow of water.

Reservoir: the man-made lake behind the dam that stores water. Intake: the opening that lets water into the penstock. Spillway: a channel that safely releases extra water downstream to prevent overflow. Penstock: a large pipe that carries water from the reservoir to the turbine. Turbine: a wheel that is turned by the flowing water. Generator: changes the mechanical energy of the turbine into electrical energy. Powerhouse: the building that houses the turbines and generators.

img.cap: A hydroelectric dam in cross-section.

p: 1. Water storage: provides water through the year, especially in the dry season. 2. Irrigation: water for farmland. 3. Hydroelectric power generation. 4. Flood control: regulates the flow of the river. 5. Domestic and industrial water supply. 6. Recreation: fishing, boating and tourism.

units.title: Hydroelectric Power Generation and Its Efficiency
units.summary: How the energy of water becomes electricity, a power calculation, and the advantages of hydroelectric power over fossil fuels and other renewables.

p: 1. Water stored at height in the reservoir has gravitational potential energy. 2. When released, it flows down the penstock and gains kinetic energy. 3. The fast water strikes the turbine blades and makes the turbine spin (mechanical energy). 4. The turbine turns a generator, which changes the mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction. 5. Transformers step up the voltage for transmission.
The process is clean and renewable: it does not burn fossil fuels or release greenhouse gases.

Water of mass m falling through a height h loses potential energy mgh. If a mass of 1 000 kg of water falls through 100 m every second, and g = 10 m/s², the power of the falling water is mgh ÷ t = 1 000 × 10 × 100 ÷ 1 = 1 000 000 W = 1 MW. If the power station is 90% efficient, the electrical output is 0.9 MW = 900 kW.

Hydroelectric stations are 85% to 95% efficient, much higher than fossil fuel plants. They are reliable as long as there is enough water, renewable (the water cycle refills the reservoir), have low running costs once built, and give no air pollution.
Hydroelectric power is more steady than solar or wind power, which depend on the weather.

units.title: Major Dams in Nigeria and Environmental Issues
units.summary: Kainji, Jebba, Shiroro and Zungeru dams, and the environmental and social problems that dams cause.

p: Kainji Dam: on the River Niger, Nigeria's first big hydroelectric dam, with a capacity of about 760 MW. It supplies the national grid and supports agriculture and fishing.
Jebba Dam: downstream of Kainji on the River Niger, about 578 MW. It supplements Kainji and supports irrigation.
Shiroro Dam: on the River Kaduna in Niger State, about 600 MW. It is a major source of power for the north.
Zungeru Dam: on the River Kaduna, about 700 MW. (Older notes call it under development. It has since been completed and brought into service in stages.)
1. Displacement of people: large areas are flooded and whole communities have to move. Resettlement during the Kainji project is an example.
2. Ecological change: river life is disturbed, and water quality and the flow of silt downstream change.
3. High cost: very large capital and many years to build.
4. Risk of failure: a broken dam can cause catastrophic flooding and loss of life.
5. Siltation: mud and sand collect in the reservoir and reduce its storage over time.

Plan and pay for fair resettlement of affected communities; carry out environmental impact assessments before building; manage the catchment area by planting trees to reduce siltation; regularly inspect and maintain the dam; and release enough water downstream to protect aquatic life and farmers.

units.title: Rockets: How They Work
units.summary: How a rocket works (Newton's third law), the parts and stages of a multistage rocket, thrust, and escape velocity with calculations.

p: A rocket is a vehicle pushed forward by the high-speed ejection of gases produced by burning fuel under high pressure. It is used for space exploration, military uses and launching satellites. A rocket works in the atmosphere and in the vacuum of space because it carries its own oxidiser and does not need oxygen from the air.

sections.h: The working principle: Newton's third law
p: Newton's third law says that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The rocket pushes hot gas downwards at high speed (action). The gas pushes the rocket upwards (reaction). This force is called thrust. The burning fuel makes high-pressure gas in the combustion chamber, and the gas escapes through a narrow nozzle at the bottom.
Thrust = (mass of gas ejected per second) × (velocity of the gas) = (Δm/Δt) × v. Example: a rocket ejects 25 kg of gas per second at 4 000 m/s. Thrust = 25 × 4 000 = 100 000 N = 100 kN.

The main parts are the payload (the cargo, such as a satellite), the propellant system (fuel and oxidiser), the engine with nozzle, the control system (gyroscopes, computers and sensors for guidance) and the stage structure. A multistage rocket has two or more stages, each with its own engine and fuel. As each stage uses its fuel it drops away, so the rocket gets lighter and the next stage can work more efficiently. The first stage lifts the rocket off the ground, the second stage continues the climb and the final stage puts the payload into its orbit.

img.alt: A rocket with a payload, a second stage, a first stage and a nozzle with exhaust gas going down and thrust acting upwards
img.cap: A multistage rocket.

p: Escape velocity is the minimum speed that an object must have to leave the gravitational pull of a planet without further propulsion. For the Earth it is about 11.2 km/s, which is 11 200 m/s or about 40 300 km/h. (11.2 km/s × 3 600 = 40 320 km/h; some books give 40 270.)
It can be calculated from v = √(2gR) where g = 9.8 m/s² and the radius of the Earth R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m: v = √(2 × 9.8 × 6.4 × 10⁶) = √(1.2544 × 10⁸) = 11 200 m/s.
