units.title: Satellites and Orbits
units.summary: Natural and artificial satellites, types and uses of artificial satellites, orbits (LEO, MEO and GEO) and the risks of space operations.

p: A satellite is any object that orbits another object in space. A natural satellite, like the Moon, orbits a planet. An artificial satellite is a man-made object put into orbit for a purpose.

sections.h: Types and uses of artificial satellites
p: Communication satellites carry radio, television, telephone and internet signals. Navigation satellites give GPS services for position and tracking. Weather satellites observe clouds, storms and climate. Surveillance satellites are used for military watching and border control. Research satellites carry out scientific observations.

In everyday life: meteorology (forecasting storms and rainfall), agriculture (crop monitoring and land use), telecommunications (phones, internet, TV), disaster monitoring (floods, fires, drought) and the military (surveillance and navigation).

A satellite stays in orbit because gravity provides the force that keeps it moving round the Earth, while its sideways speed (orbital velocity, about 7.8 km/s near the Earth) stops it falling to the ground. Orbits are described by altitude, orbital velocity and inclination (the angle between the orbit and the equator).

img.alt: The Earth with three orbit rings: low Earth orbit, medium Earth orbit and geostationary orbit
img.cap: Low, medium and geostationary orbits (not to scale).

p: Low Earth orbit (LEO): 160 to 2 000 km; used for Earth observation. Medium Earth orbit (MEO): about 2 000 to 35 000 km; used for GPS. Geostationary orbit (GEO): about 35 786 km above the equator; the satellite takes 24 hours to go round, the same time as the Earth turns, so it stays above the same point on the Earth. This is ideal for communication satellites.

Space debris (dead satellites and rocket parts) can collide with working satellites. Technical failures during launch or in orbit can end a mission. The cost of building, launching and running satellites is high. Satellites can be used for spying, causing tension between countries. Cosmic rays and solar radiation can damage the electronics.

units.title: NigeriaSat-1: Nigeria's First Earth Observation Satellite
units.summary: The launch, aims, technical features and benefits of NigeriaSat-1, and the work of NASRDA.

p: NigeriaSat-1 was Nigeria's first Earth observation satellite. (Some course outlines write it as Niger-SAT 1; the correct name is NigeriaSat-1.) It was launched on 27 September 2003 from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in Russia on a Kosmos-3M rocket. It joined the Disaster Monitoring Constellation (DMC), a network of small Earth observation satellites owned by different countries which cooperate in monitoring the environment and disasters. It was built with the help of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd (SSTL) in the United Kingdom.

1. Environmental monitoring: changes in land cover, deforestation, desertification and water bodies. 2. Disaster management: quick pictures of floods, oil spills, droughts and fires. 3. Land use and urban planning: high-resolution images for maps and planning. 4. Agricultural planning: crop health, land use and seasonal changes for food security. 5. Population and resource mapping: help for censuses and for finding resources.

NigeriaSat-1 was a microsatellite of about 100 kg. Its multispectral imager had a ground resolution of 32 m and a swath width of about 600 km. It could revisit any point on the Earth every few days (the DMC as a whole gives daily coverage). It stored images and sent them to ground stations, and the images were analysed and distributed by the National Space Research and Development Agency (NASRDA).

Urban planning and infrastructure: monitoring the growth of cities and roads. Disaster preparedness: early warnings and damage assessment after disasters. Agriculture and food security: crop monitoring, drought prediction and mapping of farmland. Environment: watching erosion, oil spills and illegal logging. Education and research: images used by universities for research and training.

NASRDA is Nigeria's main space agency. It coordinates satellite launches and missions, manages ground stations, trains Nigerian engineers, works with other space agencies and the DMC, and plans future projects such as NigeriaSat-2, NigeriaSat-X and the communication satellite NigComSat-1R. NigeriaSat-2 and NigeriaSat-X (launched in 2011) are further Earth observation satellites, with NigeriaSat-2 giving much sharper pictures.

units.title: NigComSat-1: Nigeria's Communication Satellite
units.summary: The launch, failure and replacement of NigComSat-1, its transponders and frequency bands, and its impact and challenges.

p: NigComSat-1 (in some outlines written as NICOM-SAT 1) was Nigeria's first communication satellite. It was built to improve the country's ICT network and to reduce the digital divide in rural and underserved areas. It was built for Nigeria by the China Great Wall Industry Corporation (CGWIC) and launched by a Chinese rocket. It was designed to support telecommunications, satellite broadcasting, broadband internet, telemedicine and distance education.

Launched on 13 May 2007 from the Xichang Satellite Launch Centre in China by a Long March 3B rocket. Placed in geostationary orbit at longitude 42.5° East. In November 2008 a fault in its solar array caused a loss of power and the satellite was shut down early. Its replacement, NigComSat-1R, was launched by CGWIC from China on 19 December 2011 and continues to serve Nigeria and Africa.

1. Telecommunication: voice and data for mobile operators and private networks. 2. Broadcasting: satellite TV and radio for media houses. 3. Internet access: broadband for places with no fibre-optic cables. 4. Telemedicine: rural clinics linked to hospitals in cities for diagnosis and consultation. 5. Distance learning: online classes and learning materials for remote students.
NigComSat-1 had 28 active transponders in four frequency bands.

head: Band
Main use
rows: Wide coverage and little affected by weather; satellite TV and voice
Higher bandwidth: data broadcasting and broadband internet
High-speed internet and multimedia with great capacity

p: Impact: spreads services to remote areas (digital inclusion), improves broadband, supports e-government, helps the ICT industry to create jobs and supports smart education and health. Economically it earns revenue and reduces the cost of leasing foreign satellite capacity; in education and health it brings distance learning and telemedicine.

Challenges: technical failure (the 2008 solar array fault); the very high cost of launch and running; security threats such as hacking and jamming; too few trained Nigerian satellite engineers; and slow policies and weak infrastructure. To succeed, Nigeria must encourage STEM education, invest in local space research, partner with other space agencies and inspire young people to choose careers in space science.

units.title: Logarithms: Meaning and Laws
units.summary: Revision of what a logarithm is, the laws of logarithms and the change of base formula.

p: A logarithm is the inverse of an exponent. If aˣ = y, then log_a y = x. Here a is the base (a > 0 and a ≠ 1), x is the logarithm (the power), and y is the number (y > 0). Read log_a y = x as 'log to base a of y is x'.
Examples: 2³ = 8 means log₂ 8 = 3. 10² = 100 means log₁₀ 100 = 2. 5² = 25 means log₅ 25 = 2. 3⁴ = 81 means log₃ 81 = 4. 2⁻³ = 1/8 means log₂ (1/8) = −3.
1. Product law: log_a (mn) = log_a m + log_a n. Example: log₂ (8 × 4) = 3 + 2 = 5, and 2⁵ = 32 = 8 × 4.
2. Quotient law: log_a (m/n) = log_a m − log_a n. Example: log₂ (16/4) = 4 − 2 = 2.
3. Power law: log_a (mⁿ) = n log_a m. Example: log₂ (8³) = 3 × 3 = 9, and 8³ = 512 = 2⁹.
4. log_a 1 = 0 for any base, because a⁰ = 1.
5. log_a a = 1, because a¹ = a.
6. Change of base: log_a m = log_b m ÷ log_b a. Example: log₂ 8 = log₁₀ 8 ÷ log₁₀ 2 = 0.9031 ÷ 0.3010 = 3.
Evaluate log₅ 125 + log₅ 25 − log₅ 5 = 3 + 2 − 1 = 4.
Evaluate 3 log₂ 8 − 2 log₂ 4 + log₂ 16 = 9 − 4 + 4 = 9.
Evaluate 2 log₂ 4 + 3 log₂ 2 − log₂ 8 = 4 + 3 − 3 = 4.
Express as a single logarithm: 2 log₁₀ x + log₁₀ y − 3 log₁₀ z = log₁₀ (x²y / z³).
The common logarithm has base 10 (the log button on a calculator). The natural logarithm has base e ≈ 2.718 (the ln button). They are related by ln x = 2.3026 × log₁₀ x.

units.title: Logarithmic and Exponential Equations and Calculations
units.summary: Solving equations that contain logarithms or unknown powers, checking for invalid answers, and using logarithms for calculations.

p: Change to exponential form. log₂ x = 5 gives x = 2⁵ = 32. log₁₀ x = 3 gives x = 1000. log₅ x = −2 gives x = 5⁻² = 1/25 = 0.04. log₃ (2x − 1) = 2 gives 2x − 1 = 9, so x = 5.

Example 1. log₂ x + log₂ (x − 3) = 2. Combine: log₂ [x(x − 3)] = 2, so x² − 3x = 4 and x² − 3x − 4 = 0. (x − 4)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 4 or x = −1. A logarithm needs a positive number, so x = −1 is rejected. Check x = 4: log₂ 4 + log₂ 1 = 2 + 0 = 2. Correct.
Example 2. log₃ (x + 2) − log₃ (x − 1) = 1. (x + 2)/(x − 1) = 3, so x + 2 = 3x − 3 and x = 2.5.
Example 3. 2 log₅ x = log₅ 9. x² = 9, so x = 3 (x = −3 is rejected).
Example 4. log₃ x + log₃ (x + 6) = 3. x(x + 6) = 27, x² + 6x − 27 = 0, (x + 9)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 3.
Example 6. log₂ x + log₂ (x − 7) = 3. x(x − 7) = 8, x² − 7x − 8 = 0, (x − 8)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 8.
If the bases can be matched, compare the powers: 3^(2x + 1) = 27 = 3³, so 2x + 1 = 3 and x = 1. 3^(x + 2) = 81 = 3⁴, so x = 2.
If not, take logarithms of both sides: 2ˣ = 10. x log 2 = 1, so x = 1 ÷ 0.3010 = 3.32. 5ˣ = 20: x = log 20 ÷ log 5 = 1.3010 ÷ 0.6990 = 1.86.

A population grows by P = P₀ × 2^(t/10), where t is in years. How long does 50 000 take to reach 200 000? 200 000 = 50 000 × 2^(t/10), so 2^(t/10) = 4 = 2². t/10 = 2, so t = 20 years. (By logarithms: (t/10) log 2 = log 4 = 2 log 2, so t/10 = 2.)
Use log to turn multiplication into addition and division into subtraction. 45.6 × 78.2: log 45.6 = 1.6590 and log 78.2 = 1.8932. Sum = 3.5522. Antilog = 3 566. Check: 45.6 × 78.2 = 3 565.9.
Always check your answer with a calculator.
2 log₅ x − log₅ (x − 4) = log₅ 4 gives x²/(x − 4) = 4, so x² − 4x + 16 = 0. Its discriminant is 16 − 64 = −48, which is negative, so there is no real solution.

units.title: Logic: Statements and Connectives
units.summary: What a statement is, and the connectives not, and, or, with their truth tables.

p: Logic is the science of correct reasoning. A statement (proposition) is a sentence that is either true or false, but not both. 'Lagos is in Nigeria' is true. '5 + 3 = 7' is false. 'Go to school!' is a command and 'What is your name?' is a question: neither is a statement. 'x + 5 = 10' is not a statement until x is given a value.
A simple statement has one idea (p: It is raining). A compound statement joins simple statements with connectives (It is raining and I am hungry).
The negation of p is written ~p or ¬p. It is true when p is false and false when p is true. If p is 'It is raining', ~p is 'It is not raining'.
p ∧ q is true only when both p and q are true.
p ∨ q is true when at least one of p and q is true (the inclusive or).
For two statements there are 4 rows (2²). For three there are 8 rows (2³). Work in steps, one column for each part.
Example: (p ∨ q) ∧ ~p. For p = T, q = T: (T) ∧ F = F. For T, F: T ∧ F = F. For F, T: T ∧ T = T. For F, F: F ∧ T = F. So the statement is true only when p is false and q is true.

units.title: Logic: Conditional and Biconditional Statements
units.summary: The conditional p → q and biconditional p ↔ q, and the converse, inverse and contrapositive of a conditional.

p: p → q reads 'if p, then q'. p is the hypothesis and q is the conclusion. Example: If it rains (p), then the ground is wet (q). The conditional is false only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false. If the hypothesis is false the conditional is true (vacuous truth): a false hypothesis tells us nothing about the conclusion.
p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value. Example: A number is divisible by 2 if and only if it is even.

For p → q: the converse is q → p (If the ground is wet, then it rained). The inverse is ~p → ~q (If it does not rain, the ground is not wet). The contrapositive is ~q → ~p (If the ground is not wet, then it did not rain).

A conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent (they always have the same truth value). The converse and inverse are equivalent to each other, but not to the original. In the example, the ground can be wet from a burst pipe, so the converse can be false even when the original is true.

sections.h: Show that p → q is equivalent to ~q → ~p
p: Row T, T: p → q is T; ~q → ~p is F → F = T. Row T, F: p → q is F; ~q → ~p is T → F = F. Row F, T: p → q is T; ~q → ~p is F → T = T. Row F, F: p → q is T; ~q → ~p is T → T = T. The two columns are identical (T, F, T, T), so they are equivalent.
(p → q) ∧ (q → p) has the same truth table as p ↔ q. The statement (p ∧ q) → r is false only when p and q are true and r is false.

units.title: Logic: Equivalence, Tautology and Valid Arguments
units.summary: Logical equivalence and De Morgan's laws, tautologies and contradictions, and testing whether an argument is valid.

p: Two statements are logically equivalent (≡) if their truth tables are identical.
De Morgan's laws: ~(p ∧ q) ≡ ~p ∨ ~q and ~(p ∨ q) ≡ ~p ∧ ~q.
Check the first: for T, T: ~(T) = F and F ∨ F = F. For T, F: ~(F) = T and F ∨ T = T. For F, T: T and T ∨ F = T. For F, F: T and T ∨ T = T. The columns match.
Other equivalences: p ∧ T ≡ p, p ∨ F ≡ p, p ∧ p ≡ p, p ∨ p ≡ p.
A tautology is always true: p ∨ ~p. A contradiction is always false: p ∧ ~p. A contingency can be true or false: p ∧ q.
An argument has premises (statements assumed true) and a conclusion. It is valid if the conclusion must be true whenever all the premises are true.
Valid: p → q, p, therefore q (modus ponens). In the only row where both premises are true (p = T, q = T), q is also true.
Valid: p → q, ~q, therefore ~p (modus tollens).
Invalid: p → q, q, therefore p (affirming the consequent). Take p = F and q = T: both premises are true but the conclusion p is false.

Premise 1: If a student studies, he passes. Premise 2: John studied. Conclusion: John passed. This is valid. But Premise 2: John passed; conclusion: John studied is invalid, because he may have passed in some other way.

units.title: Surds: Simplifying and Rationalising
units.summary: Simplifying surds, adding and multiplying them, and rationalising denominators.

p: A surd is an irrational root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction, such as √2, √3 and √5. We keep them in surd form for exact answers.
Remove the surd from the bottom. 1/√3 = √3/3. 2/√5 = 2√5/5.

With a binomial denominator multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (change the sign between the terms). 1/(1 + √2) = (1 − √2) / ((1 + √2)(1 − √2)) = (1 − √2) / (1 − 2) = √2 − 1. 3/(√5 − √2) = 3(√5 + √2) / (5 − 2) = √5 + √2.

units.title: Exact Trigonometric Values for 30°, 45° and 60°
units.summary: The exact values of sine, cosine and tangent of 30°, 45° and 60°, the CAST rule and worked examples with surds.

p: Use a right-angled isosceles triangle (sides 1, 1, √2) for 45° and half of an equilateral triangle (sides 1, 2, √3) for 30° and 60°.

In the four quadrants (0° to 360°): All ratios are positive in the first quadrant (0° to 90°). Sine only is positive in the second (90° to 180°). Tangent only is positive in the third (180° to 270°). Cosine only is positive in the fourth (270° to 360°). 'All Students Take Calculus' helps you remember.
sin²45° + cos²45° = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1 (so sin²θ + cos²θ = 1).

If sin θ = √3/2 and θ is acute: cos²θ = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4, so cos θ = 1/2, and tan θ = √3. So θ = 60°. Solve 2 cos x = √3 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 90°: cos x = √3/2, so x = 30°. If tan θ = √3 (acute), θ = 60°, sin θ = √3/2 and cos θ = 1/2.
An exercise asks to prove (sin 60° − sin 30°) / (cos 30° − cos 60°) = √3. Numerator = √3/2 − 1/2 = (√3 − 1)/2. Denominator = √3/2 − 1/2 = (√3 − 1)/2. They are equal, so the value is 1, not √3.

units.title: Graphs of Sine and Cosine and Solving Trigonometric Equations
units.summary: The shapes and properties of y = sin x and y = cos x for 0° to 360°, and solving simple trigonometric equations from the graph and by calculation.

p: Both graphs are smooth waves. Period: 360° (the pattern repeats every 360°). Amplitude: 1 (the greatest height). Range: −1 ≤ y ≤ 1.

y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90°, falls to 0 at 180°, to −1 at 270° and returns to 0 at 360°. y = cos x starts at 1, falls to 0 at 90°, to −1 at 180°, rises to 0 at 270° and returns to 1 at 360°. The cosine graph is the sine graph shifted 90° to the left: cos x = sin (x + 90°).
The two graphs meet where sin x = cos x, at x = 45° and x = 225°.

units.title: Matrices: Meaning, Order and Types
units.summary: What a matrix is, how to state its order, and the common types of matrix.

p: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns, placed in brackets. Rows run across and columns run down. The number in row i and column j is written aᵢⱼ. In this book a matrix is written row by row, with a semicolon between rows: A = [1 2 3 ; 4 5 6] has two rows, (1 2 3) and (4 5 6).
In A, a₁₂ = 2 (row 1, column 2) and a₂₃ = 6 (row 2, column 3).
The order is m × n, where m is the number of rows and n the number of columns (rows first). A = [1 2 3 ; 4 5 6] is 2 × 3. [5 ; 3 ; 1] is 3 × 1. [5 3 −1 8] is 1 × 4.
Row matrix: only one row, for example [5 3 −1 8] (order 1 × 4). Column matrix: only one column, for example [5 ; 3 ; 1] (3 × 1).
Square matrix: rows = columns, for example [1 2 ; 3 4] (2 × 2).
Diagonal matrix: a square matrix with zeros everywhere except possibly on the main diagonal, for example [3 0 ; 0 7].
Identity (unit) matrix I: a diagonal matrix with 1s on the diagonal, for example [1 0 ; 0 1]. For any matrix A, AI = IA = A.
Zero (null) matrix: every element is 0.
Scalar matrix: a diagonal matrix with equal diagonal elements, for example [5 0 ; 0 5].
Upper triangular: a square matrix with zeros below the main diagonal, for example [1 2 ; 0 3]. Lower triangular: zeros above the main diagonal, for example [1 0 ; 2 3].
Two matrices are equal if they have the same order and equal corresponding elements. If [x + 1 3 ; 2 y − 2] = [4 3 ; 2 5], then x + 1 = 4 and y − 2 = 5, so x = 3 and y = 7.

units.title: Matrix Operations: Addition, Scalar Multiplication and Multiplication
units.summary: How to add and subtract matrices, multiply by a number, and multiply two matrices, with the rule for when it is possible.

p: Matrices can be added or subtracted only if they have the same order. Add or subtract the corresponding elements. Let A = [1 2 ; 3 4] and B = [3 1 ; 2 5]. A + B = [4 3 ; 5 9]. A − B = [−2 1 ; 1 −1]. A + B = B + A, and A + O = A.
Multiply every element by the number. 3A = [3 6 ; 9 12]. −2[1 5 ; 0 3] = [−2 −10 ; 0 −6].

A (order m × n) times B (order p × q) is possible only if n = p (the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B). The product has order m × q. Each element of AB is found by multiplying a row of A by a column of B and adding.
Properties: (AB)C = A(BC); A(B + C) = AB + AC; AI = IA = A.

units.title: Transpose and Determinants
units.summary: The transpose of a matrix, and how to find the determinant of a 2 × 2 and a 3 × 3 matrix.

p: The transpose Aᵀ is found by interchanging rows and columns. If A = [1 2 3 ; 4 5 6], then Aᵀ = [1 4 ; 2 5 ; 3 6]. A 2 × 3 matrix has a 3 × 2 transpose. Properties: (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A; (A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ; (kA)ᵀ = kAᵀ; (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ (the order is reversed). A matrix with A = Aᵀ is symmetric, for example [3 4 ; 4 6].

For A = [a b ; c d], |A| = ad − bc. Example: [3 2 ; 1 4] has determinant 3 × 4 − 2 × 1 = 10. [5 −2 ; 3 1] has determinant 5 × 1 − (−2)(3) = 11. [2 4 ; 1 2] has determinant 4 − 4 = 0: it is singular (it has no inverse).
For A = [a b c ; d e f ; g h i], expand along the first row: |A| = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh − eg). Notice the minus sign before b.
Example 2. [1 2 3 ; 4 5 6 ; 7 8 9]: |A| = 1(45 − 48) − 2(36 − 42) + 3(32 − 35) = −3 + 12 − 9 = 0. The rows are dependent, so the matrix is singular.
Another way is the rule of Sarrus: copy the first two columns to the right, add the three downward diagonals and subtract the three upward diagonals.

If a row or column is all zeros, |A| = 0. If two rows (or columns) are identical, |A| = 0. |AB| = |A||B|. Interchanging two rows changes the sign of the determinant. For an n × n matrix, |kA| = kⁿ|A|.

units.title: Inverse of a 2 × 2 Matrix and Simultaneous Equations
units.summary: How to find the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix and use it to solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations.

p: The inverse A⁻¹ of a square matrix A satisfies AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I. It exists only if |A| ≠ 0.
For A = [a b ; c d]: A⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc)) × [d −b ; −c a]. Steps: find the determinant; swap a and d; change the signs of b and c; divide by the determinant.
Write the equations as AX = B. Then X = A⁻¹B.

If the determinant is zero the equations either have no solution or have infinitely many. Example: 2x + 4y = 6 and x + 2y = 5 have the matrix [2 4 ; 1 2] with determinant 0, and the equations contradict each other (the second gives 2x + 4y = 10).

units.title: Simultaneous Linear and Quadratic Equations
units.summary: Solving a linear and a quadratic equation together by substitution, including cases with surd answers.

p: A linear equation is y = mx + c: a straight line. A quadratic equation is y = ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0): a parabola, which opens up if a > 0 and down if a < 0. To solve them together, substitute the linear equation into the quadratic one.

y = x + 2 and y = x² − 4. Substitute: x + 2 = x² − 4, so x² − x − 6 = 0, (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 3 or x = −2. Then y = 5 or y = 0. Solutions: (3, 5) and (−2, 0). Check (3, 5): 3 + 2 = 5 and 9 − 4 = 5.

y = 2x − 1 and y = x² + x − 5. 2x − 1 = x² + x − 5, so x² − x − 4 = 0. By the formula, x = (1 ± √17)/2, that is x ≈ 2.56 or x ≈ −1.56. Then y = 2x − 1 gives y ≈ 4.12 or y ≈ −4.12. Solutions: (2.56, 4.12) and (−1.56, −4.12).
x + y = 5 and x² + y² = 13. y = 5 − x, so x² + (5 − x)² = 13, 2x² − 10x + 25 = 13, x² − 5x + 6 = 0. x = 2 or 3. Solutions (2, 3) and (3, 2).

After substitution, the discriminant of the quadratic decides. If b² − 4ac > 0 the line cuts the curve at two points. If it is 0 the line is a tangent (one solution). If it is negative the line misses the curve (no real solution).

units.title: Graphical Solutions and Word Problems
units.summary: Solving a line and a curve together by graph, counting solutions, and word problems that lead to quadratic equations.

p: Draw both graphs on the same axes and read the coordinates of the points where they cross. Example: y = x + 1 and y = x² − 2x. Table for the curve: x = −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 gives y = 3, 0, −1, 0, 3, 8. The line crosses the curve near (−0.3, 0.7) and (3.3, 4.3). (By algebra: x² − 3x − 1 = 0, so x = (3 ± √13)/2 = 3.30 or −0.30.)

Number of solutions: two crossing points mean two solutions. A tangent touches at one point (a repeated root). A line that does not touch the curve means no real solution. Example: y = 2x − 1 and y = x² give x² − 2x + 1 = 0, so x = 1 twice: the line is a tangent at (1, 1). But y = 2x − 2 and y = x² give x² − 2x + 2 = 0, with discriminant −4: no solution.
The sum of two numbers is 10 and their product is 21. x + y = 10 and xy = 21. x(10 − x) = 21, x² − 10x + 21 = 0, (x − 3)(x − 7) = 0. The numbers are 3 and 7.

A rectangular field has length 5 m more than its width, and its area is 84 m². x(x + 5) = 84, x² + 5x − 84 = 0, (x + 12)(x − 7) = 0. The width is 7 m (reject −12) and the length is 12 m. Check: 7 × 12 = 84.

An investor buys (100 − x) shares at ₦x each and spends ₦2 400. x(100 − x) = 2 400, x² − 100x + 2 400 = 0, (x − 40)(x − 60) = 0. So the price is ₦40 and the number of shares is 60, or the price is ₦60 and the number of shares is 40. Both answers fit the information given.

units.title: Spheres and Hemispheres: Surface Area and Volume
units.summary: The formulas for the surface area and volume of a sphere and a hemisphere, with worked examples including the reverse problem of finding the radius.

p: A sphere is a perfectly round solid: every point on its surface is the same distance (the radius r) from the centre. Examples: a football, a globe, an orange and a marble. The diameter is d = 2r.
Surface area of a sphere = 4πr². (It is exactly 4 times the area of a circle with the same radius.) Volume of a sphere = (4/3)πr³.
1. Radius 7 cm. Surface area = 4 × (22/7) × 49 = 616 cm².
2. A balloon of radius 14 cm: surface area = 4 × (22/7) × 196 = 2 464 cm².
3. The surface area is 1 386 cm². Find the radius. 4 × (22/7) r² = 1 386, so r² = 1 386 × 7/88 = 110.25 and r = 10.5 cm.
6. A spherical tank of radius 1.5 m (π = 3.142): volume = (4/3)(3.142)(3.375) = 14.14 m³ = 14 140 litres (1 m³ = 1 000 litres).
Curved surface area = 2πr². Total surface area (with the flat circular face) = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr². Volume = (2/3)πr³.
Example. A hemispherical bowl of radius 7 cm: curved area = 2 × (22/7) × 49 = 308 cm²; total area = 462 cm²; volume = (2/3)(22/7)(343) = 718.67 cm³, about 0.72 litre.
Volume stays the same when a solid is melted and recast. A sphere of radius 6 cm is melted into small spheres of radius 2 cm. Number = (4/3)π(6)³ ÷ (4/3)π(2)³ = (6/2)³ = 27 small spheres.

units.title: Latitude and Longitude
units.summary: The geography of the globe: poles, equator, great and small circles, latitude and longitude, and the radius and length of a parallel of latitude.

p: The Earth is nearly a sphere. It spins about an axis through the North Pole and the South Pole. The equator is the circle halfway between the poles. A great circle is a circle on the sphere whose centre is the centre of the sphere (the equator and all meridians are great circles). A small circle is any other circle on the sphere, such as a parallel of latitude (other than the equator).

Latitude measures how far a place is north or south of the equator, as an angle at the centre of the Earth, from 0° at the equator to 90° at the poles (for example 6.5°N). Lines of latitude are called parallels. They are small circles, except the equator. Important latitudes: the equator 0°, the Tropic of Cancer 23.5°N, the Tropic of Capricorn 23.5°S.

Longitude measures how far a place is east or west of the prime meridian (the meridian through Greenwich, 0°), from 0° to 180°. Lines of longitude are called meridians and join the two poles. Each meridian is half of a great circle. The 180° meridian is roughly the International Date Line. A place is given as (latitude, longitude), for example Lagos is about (6.5°N, 3.4°E) and Abuja is about (9°N, 7.5°E).

sections.h: Radius of a parallel of latitude
p: The radius of the parallel of latitude θ is r = R cos θ, where R is the radius of the Earth (about 6 400 km in these notes). At the equator (θ = 0°) r = R. At the poles (θ = 90°) r = 0.

4. A parallel has radius 3 200 km. Then cos θ = 3 200/6 400 = 0.5, so θ = 60° (60°N or 60°S).

units.title: Distances on the Earth: Along Meridians and Parallels
units.summary: Finding angular distances and real distances between two places on the same meridian or the same parallel of latitude.

p: On the same meridian (same longitude), the angular distance is the difference of the latitudes if both places are on the same side of the equator, and the sum if they are on opposite sides. A(30°N, 15°E) and B(10°S, 15°E): 30° + 10° = 40°. C(50°N, 20°W) and D(20°N, 20°W): 50° − 20° = 30°.

On the same parallel (same latitude), the angular difference at the centre of the parallel is the difference of the longitudes if both are east or both west (subtract), and the sum if one is east and one west (add), as long as the sum is less than 180°. P(60°N, 30°E) and Q(60°N, 50°E): 20°.

Every meridian is part of a great circle, and the circumference is 2πR. Distance = (θ/360) × 2πR, where θ is the angular distance. With R = 6 400 km and π = 22/7, 2πR = 40 228.57 km, so 1° along a meridian is about 111.7 km. (With a circumference of 40 000 km, 1° is about 111 km.)
Example 1. Two places on the same meridian at 40°N and 10°N. θ = 30°. Distance = (30/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 6 400 = 3 352.38 km.

Example 2. Towns A (60°N) and B (30°S) on longitude 45°E. θ = 60° + 30° = 90°. Distance = (90/360) × 40 228.57 = 10 057.14 km. (Some printed notes give 10 228.57 km, which is not correct for these values.)
A parallel of latitude is a small circle of radius r = R cos (latitude). Distance = (θ/360) × 2πr, where θ is the difference in longitude.
Example 3. P and Q are on latitude 60°N, at longitudes 20°E and 80°E. θ = 60°. r = 6 400 × cos 60° = 3 200 km. Distance = (60/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 3 200 = 3 352.38 km.
Example 4. Ships on latitude 45°S at longitudes 30°W and 45°W. θ = 15°. r = 6 400 × cos 45° = 4 525.48 km. Distance = (15/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 4 525.48 = 1 185.25 km.
For the same angle, distance along a parallel = distance along a meridian × cos (latitude). If an angle gives 4 000 km along a meridian, it gives 4 000 × cos 60° = 2 000 km along the 60° parallel.

units.title: Nautical Miles, Time Differences and Speed on the Globe
units.summary: Nautical miles and knots, the relation between longitude and time, and journeys along great circles.

p: A nautical mile is the length of the arc of a great circle that makes an angle of one minute (1/60 of a degree) at the centre of the Earth. So the distance in nautical miles along a great circle equals the angle at the centre in minutes. One nautical mile is about 1.85 km. A speed of one nautical mile per hour is called one knot.
Example. A ship sails along a meridian from 30°N to 10°S: 40° × 60 = 2 400 nautical miles. At 20 knots it takes 2 400 ÷ 20 = 120 hours, which is 5 days.
The Earth turns through 360° in 24 hours, so it turns 15° in 1 hour. Places farther east have later local times than places farther west. Time difference = longitude difference ÷ 15.

Example 1. Longitudes 45°E and 30°W. Difference = 45° + 30° = 75° (one east, one west, so add). Time difference = 75 ÷ 15 = 5 hours. When it is 12 noon at 45°E, it is 7 a.m. at 30°W (the west is behind).
Example 2. Longitudes 15°E and 105°W: difference = 120°, so the time difference is 8 hours.
Example 3. Lagos (3.4°E) and a place at 41.6°E: difference 38.2°; time difference 38.2 ÷ 15 = 2 h 33 min about.

A plane flies from P(60°N, 20°E) to Q(60°N, 80°E) along the parallel at 800 km/h. Distance = 3 352.38 km (see the previous unit). Time = 3 352.38 ÷ 800 = 4.19 hours, about 4 hours 11 minutes. The time difference between P and Q is 60 ÷ 15 = 4 hours, so local time at Q is 4 hours ahead of P. If the plane leaves P at 8:00 a.m. local time, it lands at Q at about 8:00 + 4 h 11 min + 4 h = 4:11 p.m. local time at Q.
The shortest route between two places on the Earth is along the great circle through them. This is why aeroplanes on long journeys fly curved routes on a flat map.

units.title: Binary Operations: Meaning and Tables
units.summary: What a binary operation is, how to evaluate and solve with operations defined by a rule, and how to build an operation table.

p: A binary operation is a rule that combines two elements of a set to give one element. Addition, subtraction and multiplication are binary operations on numbers. We can also define new ones, using a symbol such as *, ⊕ or ∘.
Example: a * b = a + b + 1. Then 3 * 4 = 3 + 4 + 1 = 8, and 2 * (−5) = 2 − 5 + 1 = −2. Example: a ⊕ b = 2a + b. Then 3 ⊕ 4 = 10 and 4 ⊕ 3 = 11.
If a * b = a + b + 1, solve 3 * x = 8. 3 + x + 1 = 8, so x = 4. If a ∘ b = a² + b, solve x ∘ 3 = 28. x² + 3 = 28, x² = 25, so x = 5 or x = −5.
For a small set we can show the operation in a table. Addition modulo 4 on {0, 1, 2, 3} (add, then take the remainder on division by 4, like clock arithmetic).
On {1, 2, 3, 4}, multiply and take the remainder on division by 5. For example 3 × 4 = 12, and 12 = 2 × 5 + 2, so 3 × 4 ≡ 2 (mod 5).

The row element is the first element and the column element is the second. In the mod 5 table, 2 × 3 = 1 (row 2, column 3). Every entry is inside the set, so the operation is closed. The table is symmetrical about the main diagonal, which shows that the operation is commutative.

units.title: Properties of Binary Operations
units.summary: Closure, commutativity, associativity, identity element, inverse and distributivity, tested on several operations.

p: Let * be an operation on a set S.
Closure: for all a, b in S, a * b is also in S.
Commutative: a * b = b * a for all a, b.
Associative: (a * b) * c = a * (b * c) for all a, b, c.
Identity element e: a * e = e * a = a for every a in S.
Inverse of a: an element a′ such that a * a′ = a′ * a = e.
Distributive: * is distributive over ∘ if a * (b ∘ c) = (a * b) ∘ (a * c). For example, multiplication is distributive over addition.

sections.h: Example 1: a * b = a + b + 1 on the real numbers
p: Closed: a + b + 1 is a real number. Commutative: a + b + 1 = b + a + 1. Associative: (a * b) * c = a + b + 1 + c + 1 = a + b + c + 2, and a * (b * c) = a + b + c + 2. They agree.
Identity e: a * e = a gives a + e + 1 = a, so e = −1. Inverse: a * a′ = −1 gives a + a′ + 1 = −1, so a′ = −a − 2. Check: a * (−a − 2) = a − a − 2 + 1 = −1 ✓.

sections.h: Example 2: a * b = a + b − ab
p: Commutative: yes. Identity: a * e = a gives a + e − ae = a, so e(1 − a) = 0, so e = 0. Inverse: a + a′ − aa′ = 0, so a′(1 − a) = −a and a′ = a/(a − 1). The inverse does not exist for a = 1.
Not commutative: 1 ⊕ 2 = 4 but 2 ⊕ 1 = 5. Not associative: (1 ⊕ 2) ⊕ 3 = 4 ⊕ 3 = 11, but 1 ⊕ (2 ⊕ 3) = 1 ⊕ 7 = 9.
Closed, commutative and associative. Identity: 1. Inverses: 1 → 1, 2 → 3 (2 × 3 = 6 ≡ 1), 3 → 2, 4 → 4 (4 × 4 = 16 ≡ 1). Every element has an inverse.

units.title: Arithmetic of Finance: Interest and Depreciation
units.summary: Simple and compound interest, and depreciation by the straight-line and reducing-balance methods.

p: I = PRT/100, where P is the principal (the money invested), R the rate per cent per year and T the time in years. The amount is A = P + I. Example: ₦50 000 at 8% for 3 years: I = 50 000 × 8 × 3 / 100 = ₦12 000.
Interest is added each year and then earns interest itself. A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ, where n is the number of years. The compound interest is A − P.
Example 1. ₦50 000 at 8% for 3 years: A = 50 000 × 1.08³ = ₦62 985.60. The compound interest is ₦12 985.60 (compare ₦12 000 by simple interest).
Example 3. ₦75 500 at 9% for 6 years: A = 75 500 × 1.09⁶ = ₦126 621.06. Compound interest = ₦51 121.06.
Depreciation is the loss of value of an asset (a machine, vehicle or computer) over time.

Straight-line method: the same amount is lost each year. Annual depreciation = (cost − scrap value) ÷ life in years. A machine costs ₦600 000, has a scrap value of ₦100 000 and lasts 5 years: ₦(600 000 − 100 000) ÷ 5 = ₦100 000 a year.

Reducing-balance method: the value falls by a fixed percentage of the current value each year. Value after n years = C(1 − r/100)ⁿ. The same machine, depreciating by 20% a year: after 3 years its value is 600 000 × 0.8³ = ₦307 200, so it has lost ₦292 800. After 5 years it is worth 600 000 × 0.8⁵ = ₦196 608.
With the straight-line method, the yearly loss is constant. With the reducing-balance method, the yearly loss is largest at first and then gets smaller.

units.title: Shares, Bonds, Income Tax and VAT
units.summary: Ordinary and preference shares and dividends, bonds and debentures, simple income tax and value added tax calculations.

p: A company raises money by selling shares. A shareholder owns part of the company. Ordinary shares carry a share of the profit that varies from year to year. Preference shares carry a fixed dividend and are paid before ordinary shares. The nominal (face) value is the value printed on the share; the market price is what it is sold for.
A dividend is a share of the profit, usually quoted as a percentage of the nominal value.

Example 1. 800 shares are bought at ₦35 each. The company pays a 12% dividend on a nominal value of ₦40. Cost = 800 × 35 = ₦28 000. Dividend per share = 12% of ₦40 = ₦4.80. Total dividend = 800 × 4.80 = ₦3 840. Return on the investment = 3 840 / 28 000 × 100% = 13.7%.
Example 2. Shares of nominal value ₦25 pay a 16% dividend and are bought at ₦30. Dividend per share = ₦4. Return = 4/30 × 100% = 13.3%.
Example 3. 500 preference shares pay 8% on ₦50 nominal. Dividend per share = ₦4. Total = ₦2 000.

A bond or debenture is a loan to the government or a company. The holder is paid interest (the coupon) each year and gets the face value back at the end. Example: a bond with face value ₦80 000 pays 9%: ₦80 000 × 9% = ₦7 200 a year. A company issues debentures of ₦2 000 000 at 7% for 8 years. Annual interest = ₦140 000. Total interest = 140 000 × 8 = ₦1 120 000.
Current yield = annual interest ÷ market price × 100%. A ₦100 000 bond with a 10% coupon selling at ₦95 000: interest ₦10 000, yield = 10 000 / 95 000 × 100% = 10.5%.
Tax is calculated on taxable income, which is income minus allowances, in bands. (The bands below are for practice. Real tax rates are set by law and change.)

Example. A worker earns ₦1 800 000 a year. Tax-free allowance ₦300 000, so taxable income = ₦1 500 000. Suppose the tax is 10% on the first ₦500 000 and 15% on the rest. Tax = 50 000 + 15% × 1 000 000 = 50 000 + 150 000 = ₦200 000.
VAT is a tax on goods and services. At 7.5%: VAT on goods worth ₦150 000 = 0.075 × 150 000 = ₦11 250, so the price including VAT is ₦161 250.
Finding the price before VAT: an item costs ₦53 750 including 7.5% VAT. The price before VAT = 53 750 ÷ 1.075 = ₦50 000.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: An introduction to SS3 Mathematics Second Term and the list of all units: coordinate geometry, loci and constructions, differentiation, integration, and functions and mapping.

p: This term begins with coordinate geometry of the straight line and with loci and constructions. It then introduces calculus: differentiation (the gradient of a curve, rates of change, maximum and minimum values) and integration (the reverse of differentiation and the area under a curve). The term ends with functions and mapping and a general review of calculus.

Calculus is a new way of thinking, so go slowly. Work every example yourself first, and check each integral by differentiating. The check questions at the end of each unit do not count towards a mark.

units.title: Coordinate Geometry: Distance, Midpoint and Gradient
units.summary: The formulas for the distance between two points, the midpoint of a line segment and the gradient, and the point dividing a line in a ratio.

p: Every point has coordinates (x, y), where x is the distance across from the origin and y is the distance up. Let A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) be two points. We use A(1, 2) and B(7, 10) in the examples.
AB = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). This comes from Pythagoras' theorem. For A(1, 2) and B(7, 10): AB = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10.
The midpoint M has coordinates ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). For A and B: M = ((1 + 7)/2, (2 + 10)/2) = (4, 6).
m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). For A and B: m = 8/6 = 4/3. A vertical line has no gradient (undefined). A horizontal line has gradient 0.

sections.h: Point dividing a line in a ratio
p: The point P that divides AB in the ratio m : n (from A to B) is ((n x₁ + m x₂)/(m + n), (n y₁ + m y₂)/(m + n)). For A(1, 2), B(7, 10) and ratio 1 : 2, P = ((2 × 1 + 1 × 7)/3, (2 × 2 + 1 × 10)/3) = (3, 14/3). The midpoint is the special case m = n.
1. Show that the triangle P(0, 0), Q(3, 4), R(6, 0) is isosceles. PQ = 5, QR = √(9 + 16) = 5 and PR = 6. Two sides are equal, so it is isosceles.
2. The midpoint of AB is (2, 3) and A is (−1, 5). Find B. (−1 + x)/2 = 2 so x = 5; (5 + y)/2 = 3 so y = 1. B = (5, 1).
3. Are (2, 3), (5, 9) and (8, 15) on one line? The gradient from the first to the second is 6/3 = 2, and from the second to the third is 6/3 = 2. Yes: they are collinear.

units.title: The Equation of a Straight Line
units.summary: The four forms of a straight-line equation, and the conditions for lines to be parallel or perpendicular.

p: 1. Slope-intercept form: y = mx + c (m = gradient, c = y-intercept).
2. Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
3. Two-point form: (y − y₁)/(y₂ − y₁) = (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
4. General form: ax + by + c = 0.
2. Gradient 3 through (2, 7): y − 7 = 3(x − 2), so y = 3x + 1.
3. Find the gradient and intercepts of 3x + 2y = 12: y = −1.5x + 6. m = −1.5; y-intercept 6; x-intercept 4.
Parallel lines have the same gradient: m₁ = m₂. Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1: m₁ m₂ = −1.
Example 1. The line through (5, 8) parallel to y = 2x − 3: gradient 2, so y − 8 = 2(x − 5), giving y = 2x − 2.
Example 2. The line through the origin perpendicular to 4x + 3y = 12. The gradient of 4x + 3y = 12 is −4/3, so the perpendicular has gradient 3/4: y = (3/4)x.
Example 3. Are y = 3x + 2 and y = −x/3 + 5 perpendicular? 3 × (−1/3) = −1, so yes.
Example 4. Show that 2x + 3y = 15 and 3x − 2y = 10 are perpendicular. m₁ = −2/3 and m₂ = 3/2, and the product is −1.
A line with x-intercept a and y-intercept b has the equation x/a + y/b = 1. For intercepts 4 and 6, x/4 + y/6 = 1, which is 3x + 2y = 12.

units.title: Intersecting Lines, Perpendicular Bisectors and Area of a Triangle
units.summary: Finding where two lines meet, the perpendicular bisector of a segment, and the area of a triangle from its coordinates.

p: Solve the two equations together. 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2: add them to get 3x = 9, so x = 3 and y = 1. The lines meet at (3, 1).

The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint and is perpendicular to AB. For A(1, 2) and B(7, 10): midpoint (4, 6); gradient of AB = 4/3; gradient of the bisector = −3/4. Then y − 6 = −(3/4)(x − 4), so 4y − 24 = −3x + 12 and 3x + 4y = 36.
Check: the point (0, 9) is on this line, and it is √50 from A and from B.

Find the equation of the set of points P(x, y) that are equidistant from A(1, 2) and B(7, 10). PA² = PB²: (x − 1)² + (y − 2)² = (x − 7)² + (y − 10)². Expanding: −2x − 4y + 5 = −14x − 20y + 149, so 12x + 16y = 144 and 3x + 4y = 36. This is the perpendicular bisector again.
For vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃): area = ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.
Example. (1, 1), (5, 1) and (3, 5): ½ |1(1 − 5) + 5(5 − 1) + 3(1 − 1)| = ½ |−4 + 20 + 0| = 8. Check: base 4, height 4, area ½ × 4 × 4 = 8. If the area is 0, the three points are collinear.

units.title: Locus: The Basic Loci
units.summary: What a locus is, and the four basic loci: a circle, a perpendicular bisector, an angle bisector and a pair of parallel lines.

p: A locus (plural loci) is the set of all the points that satisfy a given condition or rule. For example, the locus of points that are 4 cm from a fixed point P is a circle of radius 4 cm with centre P.

img.alt: Three diagrams: a circle as the locus of points a fixed distance from a point, a perpendicular bisector as the locus of points equidistant from A and B, and an angle bisector as the locus of points equidistant from two lines
img.cap: Three basic loci.

sections.h: 1. Fixed distance from a point: a circle
p: Mark point P. Set a compass to the distance (say 4 cm). Put the point on P and draw a complete circle.

sections.h: 2. Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector
p: Draw AB = 6 cm. Open the compass to more than half of AB (say 4 cm). With centre A draw arcs above and below AB. With centre B and the same radius draw arcs that cross the first ones. Join the two crossing points P and Q. The line PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB: every point on it is the same distance from A and B.

sections.h: 3. Equidistant from two intersecting lines: the angle bisector
p: Draw angle ABC. With centre B draw an arc that cuts both arms at P and Q. With centres P and Q and the same radius, draw arcs that cross at R. Join B to R. The line BR bisects the angle: every point on it is the same distance from the two arms.

sections.h: 4. Fixed distance from a line: two parallel lines
p: The locus of points 3 cm from a line AB is a pair of parallel lines, one on each side of AB, each 3 cm from it (with semicircles at the ends if the line is a segment).

The locus of points 5 units from the origin is x² + y² = 25. The locus of points equidistant from (0, 0) and (4, 0) is the line x = 2. The locus of points equidistant from the x-axis and the y-axis is the pair of lines y = x and y = −x.

units.title: Intersection of Loci and Practical Problems
units.summary: Combining two or more loci to find a required point or region, with worked problems.

p: Often a point must satisfy two conditions at once. We draw both loci. The required points are where they cross. If a region is wanted, we shade the part that satisfies all the conditions.

Points are 5 cm from A and 3 cm from B, where AB = 6 cm. Draw a circle of radius 5 cm at A and a circle of radius 3 cm at B. They cut at two points, P and Q. By calculation with A(0, 0) and B(6, 0): x² + y² = 25 and (x − 6)² + y² = 9. Subtract: −12x + 36 = −16, so x = 4.33. Then y² = 25 − 18.78 = 6.22 and y = ±2.49. The points are (4.33, 2.49) and (4.33, −2.49).

Draw (1) a circle of radius 5 km at A and shade inside it; (2) a circle of radius 3 km at B and shade outside it; (3) the perpendicular bisector of AB and shade the side nearer to A. The region where all three shadings overlap is where the mast can be placed.

When the rope wraps round the corner 4 m away, 2 m of rope is left, giving a quarter circle of radius 2 m. When it wraps round the corner 3 m away, 3 m is left, giving a quarter circle of radius 3 m. units.title: Circumcircle, Incircle and Escribed Circle of a Triangle
units.summary: The three circles connected with a triangle, how to construct them, and the formulas for their radii.

p: The circumcircle is the circle that passes through all three vertices of a triangle. Its centre, the circumcentre O, is the point where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet. Construction: draw triangle ABC; construct the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC; they meet at O; with centre O and radius OA, draw the circle through A, B and C.
For a right-angled triangle, the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

The incircle touches all three sides from the inside. Its centre, the incentre I, is where the angle bisectors meet. Construction: bisect two of the angles; they meet at I; drop a perpendicular from I to one side to find the radius; draw the circle.

img.alt: A triangle with its circumcircle through the three vertices and the perpendicular bisectors meeting at O, and another triangle with its incircle and angle bisectors meeting at I
img.cap: The circumcircle and the incircle.

p: An escribed circle touches one side of the triangle and the extensions of the other two sides, from outside. Its centre is where the bisector of one interior angle meets the bisectors of the two exterior angles at the other vertices. A triangle has three escribed circles.
Let the sides be a, b, c, the semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c)/2 and the area K. Circumradius R = abc/(4K). Inradius r = K/s. Exradius opposite a: rₐ = K/(s − a).

Example 1. A 3, 4, 5 triangle: K = 6, s = 6. R = (3 × 4 × 5)/(4 × 6) = 2.5, which is half the hypotenuse. r = 6/6 = 1. Exradii: opposite 3: 6/(6 − 3) = 2; opposite 4: 6/(6 − 4) = 3; opposite 5: 6/(6 − 5) = 6.

units.title: Differentiation: Limits and the Idea of a Derivative
units.summary: The idea of a limit, the gradient of a curve at a point as a limit of gradients of chords, and the meaning of the derivative.

p: Calculus is the mathematics of change. It has two parts: differentiation, which finds how fast something changes (the gradient of a curve), and integration, which adds up many small quantities (such as areas).

lim (x → a) f(x) = L means that f(x) gets as near as we like to L when x gets near to a. Examples. lim (x → 5) (x² + 2x) = 25 + 10 = 35. lim (x → 4) (x² − 16)/(x − 4): we cannot put x = 4 (we would divide by zero), so first simplify: (x − 4)(x + 4)/(x − 4) = x + 4, and the limit is 8. lim (h → 0) [(3 + h)² − 9]/h = lim (6 + h) = 6. lim (x → 2) (x³ − 8)/(x − 2) = lim (x² + 2x + 4) = 12.

The gradient of a straight line is the same everywhere. The gradient of a curve changes from point to point. The gradient of the curve at a point is the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point.

To find it, take a second point near P on the curve and find the gradient of the chord joining them. As the second point moves closer to P, the chord gets closer to the tangent. The gradient of the tangent is the limit of the gradients of the chords.

img.cap: The gradient of the curve y = x² at (2, 4) is 4.

p: The derivative of y = f(x) is the function dy/dx (or f′(x)) that gives the gradient of the curve at any x. It also tells us the rate of change of y with respect to x: if s is distance and t is time, ds/dt is the speed.

units.title: Differentiation from First Principles and the Power Rule
units.summary: The definition of the derivative as a limit, worked from first principles, and the power rule for differentiating xⁿ.

p: dy/dx = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h. This is the gradient of the chord from x to x + h as h tends to 0.
1. f(x) = x². [(x + h)² − x²]/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h. As h → 0 this gives 2x. So d(x²)/dx = 2x.
2. f(x) = x³. [(x + h)³ − x³]/h = (3x²h + 3xh² + h³)/h = 3x² + 3xh + h². As h → 0: 3x².
3. f(x) = 3x + 2. [3(x + h) + 2 − 3x − 2]/h = 3h/h = 3. The derivative is 3 (the gradient of the line).
4. f(x) = x² + 4x. The derivative is 2x + 4.
If y = xⁿ, then dy/dx = n xⁿ⁻¹. The constant multiple rule: d/dx (c f(x)) = c f′(x). The sum and difference rules: d/dx (f ± g) = f′ ± g′. The derivative of a constant is 0.
Examples. y = x⁵ gives 5x⁴. y = 4x³ gives 12x². y = 3x² + 5x − 2 gives 6x + 5. y = 4x³ − 7x² + 2x − 9 gives 12x² − 14x + 2. y = 5x⁴ − 3x² + 7 gives 20x³ − 6x.

Negative and fractional powers: write the function as powers of x. y = 2/x = 2x⁻¹ gives −2x⁻² = −2/x². y = 3√x = 3x^(1/2) gives (3/2)x^(−1/2) = 3/(2√x). y = (2x² + 3)/x = 2x + 3x⁻¹ gives 2 − 3/x². y = 3√x + 2/x gives 3/(2√x) − 2/x².
Value at a point. f(x) = x⁵: f′(2) = 5 × 2⁴ = 80. y = x³ at x = 1: the gradient is 3 × 1² = 3.

units.title: Tangents, Normals and the Meaning of the Derivative
units.summary: Finding the equation of the tangent and the normal to a curve at a point, and interpreting the derivative as a rate of change.

p: Steps: 1. Find dy/dx. 2. Put x = x₁ to get the gradient m at the point. 3. Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
Example. Find the tangent to y = x² + 2x at (1, 3). dy/dx = 2x + 2 = 4 at x = 1. y − 3 = 4(x − 1), so y = 4x − 1.

The normal at a point is the line perpendicular to the tangent there. Its gradient is −1/m. For the same curve at (1, 3): m = 4, so the gradient of the normal is −1/4. y − 3 = −(1/4)(x − 1), so 4y − 12 = −x + 1 and x + 4y = 13.
The tangent to y = x² at P(2, 4). dy/dx = 2x = 4. y − 4 = 4(x − 2), so y = 4x − 4. (The tangent drawn in the earlier figure.)

sections.h: Finding where the gradient has a given value
p: Find the point on y = x² − 4x where the tangent is parallel to the x-axis. dy/dx = 2x − 4 = 0, so x = 2 and y = 4 − 8 = −4. The point is (2, −4).

If f(x) = ax² + bx + c with f′(1) = 8, f′(2) = 14 and f(0) = 5, find a, b and c. f′(x) = 2ax + b, so 2a + b = 8 and 4a + b = 14. Subtract: 2a = 6, so a = 3 and b = 2. f(0) = c = 5. So f(x) = 3x² + 2x + 5.

units.title: Differentiation II: The Product Rule
units.summary: How to differentiate a product of two functions, with examples and a check by expanding.

p: If y = uv, where u and v are functions of x, then dy/dx = u (dv/dx) + v (du/dx). In words: first times the derivative of the second plus second times the derivative of the first. Note that the derivative of a product is NOT the product of the derivatives.

y = (2x + 1)(x² − 3). Let u = 2x + 1 and v = x² − 3. Then u′ = 2 and v′ = 2x. dy/dx = u v′ + v u′ = (2x + 1)(2x) + (x² − 3)(2) = 4x² + 2x + 2x² − 6 = 6x² + 2x − 6. Check by expanding: y = 2x³ + x² − 6x − 3, so dy/dx = 6x² + 2x − 6. ✓
y = (x² + 1)(x³ − 2x). u = x² + 1, v = x³ − 2x, u′ = 2x, v′ = 3x² − 2. dy/dx = (x² + 1)(3x² − 2) + (x³ − 2x)(2x) = 3x⁴ + x² − 2 + 2x⁴ − 4x² = 5x⁴ − 3x² − 2.

y = x(2x + 1)³. u = x, v = (2x + 1)³. u′ = 1. For v′ we need the chain rule (next unit): v′ = 3(2x + 1)² × 2 = 6(2x + 1)². dy/dx = (2x + 1)³ + x × 6(2x + 1)² = (2x + 1)²[(2x + 1) + 6x] = (2x + 1)²(8x + 1).
Use the product rule when the expansion would be long. If a product is easy to expand, expanding first and then differentiating each term is also correct.

units.title: The Chain Rule
units.summary: How to differentiate a function of a function, with examples and combined use of the chain, product and quotient rules.

p: If y = f(u) and u = g(x), then dy/dx = (dy/du) × (du/dx). Think of an outer function and an inner function: differentiate the outside (leaving the inside alone) and multiply by the derivative of the inside.
1. y = (3x + 2)⁵. Let u = 3x + 2; then y = u⁵. dy/du = 5u⁴ and du/dx = 3. dy/dx = 15(3x + 2)⁴.
2. y = (x² + 1)³. Let u = x² + 1. dy/dx = 3u² × 2x = 6x(x² + 1)².
Product and chain: y = x(2x + 1)³. dy/dx = (2x + 1)³ + x × 6(2x + 1)² = (2x + 1)²(8x + 1).
Quotient and chain: y = (x² + 1)³/x. Write it with the quotient rule, using the chain rule for the top: dy/dx = [x × 6x(x² + 1)² − (x² + 1)³]/x² = (x² + 1)²(6x² − x² − 1)/x² = (x² + 1)²(5x² − 1)/x².

The chain rule links rates that depend on each other. If a circle's radius grows at 0.5 cm/s, how fast does the area grow when r = 10 cm? A = πr², so dA/dr = 2πr. dA/dt = dA/dr × dr/dt = 2π(10)(0.5) = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm²/s.

units.title: Maximum and Minimum Values and Optimisation
units.summary: Finding turning points where dy/dx = 0, deciding whether they are maxima or minima, and solving practical optimisation problems.

p: At a maximum or minimum of a smooth curve, the tangent is horizontal, so dy/dx = 0. Such a point is a stationary (turning) point. To decide which kind: use the second derivative. If d²y/dx² > 0 the point is a minimum. If d²y/dx² < 0 it is a maximum.
y = x² − 2x − 3. dy/dx = 2x − 2 = 0, so x = 1. d²y/dx² = 2 > 0, so a minimum. y = 1 − 2 − 3 = −4. The minimum point is (1, −4). This agrees with the graph drawn earlier.

y = −x² + 4x + 1. dy/dx = −2x + 4 = 0, so x = 2. d²y/dx² = −2 < 0: a maximum, y = −4 + 8 + 1 = 5.

units.title: Integration: The Reverse of Differentiation
units.summary: Integration as the reverse of differentiation, the power rule for integration, and the constant of integration.

p: Integration is the reverse of differentiation. If d/dx (x³) = 3x², then ∫ 3x² dx = x³ + C. The integral sign ∫ means 'integrate', dx shows the variable and C is the constant of integration. We need C because the derivative of any constant is 0, so many functions (x³, x³ + 5, x³ − 2) have the same derivative.
Power rule: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1. In words: add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power.
Constant multiple: ∫ k f(x) dx = k ∫ f(x) dx. Sum and difference: ∫ (f ± g) dx = ∫ f dx ± ∫ g dx. Constants: ∫ k dx = kx + C.
∫ 4x³ dx = x⁴ + C.
∫ (x² + 2x) dx = x³/3 + x² + C.
Check any integral by differentiating the answer: d/dx [(2/3)x³ − (5/2)x² + 3x] = 2x² − 5x + 3 ✓.
The power rule does not work for n = −1. ∫ (1/x) dx = ln |x| + C (natural logarithm), which you will meet in further study.

units.summary: Using definite integrals to find areas under curves and between curves, and the method of substitution for functions of a function.

p: The area between the curve y = f(x), the x-axis and the lines x = a and x = b is ∫ₐᵇ y dx, provided the curve is above the x-axis.
Example 1. The area under y = x² from x = 0 to x = 3 is ∫₀³ x² dx = [x³/3]₀³ = 9 square units.
Example 2. The area under y = 2x + 1 from x = 0 to x = 3 is [x² + x]₀³ = 12. (Check: a trapezium with parallel sides 1 and 7 and width 3 has area ½(1 + 7) × 3 = 12.)

p: Area = ∫ (upper curve − lower curve) dx. The curves y = x and y = x² meet where x = x², at x = 0 and x = 1. Between them, y = x is above. Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹ = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6.

units.title: Functions and Mapping
units.summary: The meaning of a function, domain, codomain and range, and mapping diagrams.

p: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. We write f(x) = 2x + 3, or f: x → 2x + 3. The set of allowed inputs is the domain. The set in which the outputs lie is the codomain. The set of actual outputs is the range, which is part of the codomain.

A mapping diagram shows the domain and codomain as two ovals, with arrows from each input to its output. In the left diagram below, f(x) = 2x maps {1, 2, 3} into {2, 4, 6, 8}. The range is {2, 4, 6}; the element 8 in the codomain is not an output. In the right diagram, g(x) = x² maps {−2, 2, 1} into {4, 1}: two different inputs, −2 and 2, give the same output 4.

img.alt: Two mapping diagrams: f of x equals 2x as a one-to-one mapping, and g of x equals x squared as a many-to-one mapping
img.cap: A one-to-one and a many-to-one mapping.

p: Some functions cannot accept every number. f(x) = 1/(x − 2) is not defined at x = 2 (division by zero), so the domain is all real numbers except 2. g(x) = √(x − 1) needs x − 1 ≥ 0, so the domain is x ≥ 1.
Think of f as a machine: put in x, apply the rule, and take out f(x). Example: f(x) = x² − 3x. f(5) = 25 − 15 = 10. If f(x) = 10, then x² − 3x − 10 = 0, (x − 5)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 5 or x = −2.

units.title: Types of Functions, Composite and Inverse Functions
units.summary: One-to-one, onto, many-to-one and bijective functions, composite functions and inverse functions.

p: One-to-one (injective): different inputs give different outputs. f(x) = 2x is one-to-one. Onto (surjective): every element of the codomain is an output, so the range equals the codomain. One-to-one and onto (bijective): a perfect pairing of inputs and outputs. Many-to-one: different inputs can give the same output. g(x) = x² is many-to-one because g(2) = g(−2) = 4.
The composite function fg means 'do g first, then f': fg(x) = f(g(x)).
Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x². fg(x) = f(x²) = 2x² + 3. gf(x) = g(2x + 3) = (2x + 3)² = 4x² + 12x + 9. Notice that fg ≠ gf in general. For x = 2: fg(2) = 11 and gf(2) = 49.
The inverse function f⁻¹ undoes f. Only a one-to-one function has an inverse. To find it: write y = f(x); make x the subject; then swap x and y.
Example 1. f(x) = 2x + 3. y = 2x + 3, so x = (y − 3)/2. f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2. Check: f(1) = 5 and f⁻¹(5) = 1.
The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.

units.title: Water Pollution: Causes, Effects and Control
units.summary: What environmental chemistry studies, how water becomes polluted, the harm it causes (including eutrophication and bioaccumulation) and how it can be controlled.

p: Environmental chemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies the chemical processes that happen in the environment and the effects of human activities on it. A major concern is pollution: the introduction of harmful substances into the environment, causing harm to people, animals, plants and ecosystems. Pollution affects health (breathing problems, skin diseases, water-borne diseases), agriculture (lower yields, damaged soil), climate (global warming, acid rain) and ecosystems (loss of living things, eutrophication). The two main kinds are water pollution and air pollution, and they are linked.

img.alt: A diagram of two overlapping circles showing air pollution from factories and vehicles, water pollution from heavy metals, acid rain and eutrophication
img.cap: Air pollution and water pollution overlap.

p: Water pollution is the contamination of rivers, lakes, seas and underground water by chemical, physical or biological agents that make the water harmful to living things and to people. Causes:
1. Industrial effluents: factories release heavy metals (lead, mercury, cadmium), acids, alkalis and dyes.
2. Domestic sewage: untreated waste with organic matter, detergents and disease-causing organisms.
3. Agriculture: run-off from farms carries fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides into water (nutrient pollution).
4. Oil spills: petroleum covers the surface and harms aquatic life (for example in the Niger Delta).
5. Mining: toxic minerals and chemicals enter rivers and lakes.
1. Health hazards: cholera, typhoid and dysentery; toxic metals can cause kidney failure, nerve disorders and cancer.

2. Eutrophication: nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers and detergents make algae grow very fast (an algal bloom). When the algae die, bacteria decay them and use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish and other water animals die.
3. Bioaccumulation: some poisons, such as mercury, are not broken down. They build up along the food chain, so animals at the top, including humans, hold the highest amounts.
4. Water that is unfit for fishing, recreation and irrigation causes economic loss.

Treat industrial and domestic waste water before releasing it. Use biodegradable detergents. Manage waste properly and recycle. Build ponds to hold run-off. Make and enforce laws against pollution. Use fertilisers and pesticides carefully.

Point and non-point sources: a point source is a single place that releases pollution, such as a pipe from a factory. A non-point source is spread over a wide area, such as fertiliser washing from many farms. Non-point sources are harder to control.

units.title: Air Pollution: Causes, Effects, Control and Links with Water Pollution
units.summary: Sources of air pollutants, acid rain, global warming and ozone depletion with equations, control measures and how air and water pollution are connected.

p: Air pollution is the introduction of harmful substances into the atmosphere. Causes: (1) industrial emissions of sulphur dioxide SO₂, nitrogen oxides NOₓ, carbon monoxide CO and particles; (2) vehicle exhaust, which gives CO, CO₂, NOₓ and unburnt hydrocarbons; (3) burning fossil fuels in power stations, refineries and homes; (4) agriculture: ammonia from fertilisers and smoke from burning crop waste; (5) natural sources such as volcanoes, forest fires and dust storms (harmattan dust).
Health: asthma, bronchitis, lung cancer, eye and skin irritation. Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin and stops it carrying oxygen.

Acid rain: SO₂ and NOₓ dissolve in rain water and form acids. S + O₂ → SO₂; 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ (sulphuric acid). 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4HNO₃ (nitric acid). Acid rain damages plants and soil, makes lakes acidic and corrodes buildings and metal roofs.
Global warming: carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour trap heat in the atmosphere (the greenhouse effect). More CO₂ from burning fuels raises the temperature of the Earth and changes the climate.
Ozone depletion: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) from old refrigerators and aerosols rise to the stratosphere and destroy ozone, so more harmful ultraviolet radiation reaches the Earth.
Economic effects: damage to buildings and vehicles by corrosion, and lower crop yields.

Use cleaner fuels (LPG, natural gas, solar energy). Fit filters and scrubbers to chimneys. Plant trees and green belts. Enforce vehicle emission standards and service engines. Use public transport. Stop gas flaring and the use of CFCs.

sections.h: How air and water pollution are linked
p: Pollutants in the air are washed into rivers and lakes by rain (acid rain). Smoke particles settle on water. Climate change affects the amount and quality of water. So controlling one kind of pollution helps to control the other.

Why study environmental chemistry? To understand the causes and effects of pollution, to protect health, to design clean chemical processes, to use resources in a sustainable way and to obey environmental laws.

units.title: Electrolysis: Electrolytes, Electrodes and Electrode Reactions
units.summary: What electrolysis is, the terms electrolyte, electrode, anode and cathode, and the reactions at the electrodes for molten sodium chloride, acidified water and copper sulphate.

p: Electrolysis is the decomposition of an ionic compound (an electrolyte), in the molten state or in solution, by passing a direct electric current through it. It uses the movement of ions. It is the basis of electroplating, extraction of metals, making chemicals and refining of metals.

Electrolyte: a substance, usually ionic, that conducts electricity when molten or dissolved and is decomposed by it: molten NaCl, aqueous H₂SO₄, aqueous CuSO₄. Non-electrolytes, such as sugar and ethanol, do not conduct.

Electrodes: the conductors (metal or graphite) through which current enters and leaves. The anode is the positive electrode and attracts anions (negative ions). The cathode is the negative electrode and attracts cations (positive ions).

Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons. At the cathode, cations gain electrons (reduction). At the anode, anions lose electrons (oxidation). Remember: C.R.A.O. (Cathode Reduction, Anode Oxidation).
The cell has a DC power source, the electrolyte and two electrodes connected to the source.
Ions: Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (sodium metal). Anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (chlorine gas). Overall: 2NaCl → 2Na + Cl₂.

img.alt: Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride with sodium ions moving to the cathode and chloride ions to the anode
img.cap: Electrolysis of molten NaCl.

p: The ions present are H⁺ and OH⁻ (from the acid and the water). Cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Anode: 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻. Overall: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Twice as much hydrogen as oxygen is collected by volume (2 : 1). The acid only makes the water conduct.

With copper electrodes: cathode Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (copper is deposited); anode Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (the anode dissolves). The solution stays the same blue colour. This is used in copper plating and refining.

With inert (graphite or platinum) electrodes: cathode Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; anode 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻ (oxygen is released). The blue colour fades and the solution becomes acidic because of the H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ left behind.

When several ions are present, the one lower in the electrochemical series is discharged at the cathode (Cu²⁺ before H⁺; H⁺ before Na⁺). At the anode, OH⁻ is usually discharged before SO₄²⁻ and NO₃⁻; in concentrated chloride solutions Cl⁻ is discharged. For brine (concentrated NaCl solution): cathode H₂ is formed, anode Cl₂ is formed, and NaOH is left in the solution.

units.title: Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis and Applications
units.summary: Faraday's first and second laws, the formula m = ZIt, calculations of mass deposited, charge and time, and the uses of electrolysis.

p: The mass of a substance liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed. m ∝ Q, so m = ZQ, where Z is the electrochemical equivalent (grams per coulomb). Since Q = It (current in amperes × time in seconds), m = ZIt.

When the same quantity of electricity passes through different electrolytes, the masses of substances liberated are proportional to their equivalent weights. Equivalent weight E = molar mass ÷ valency (the number of electrons per ion). One mole of electrons carries 96 500 C (the Faraday constant, F = 96 500 C/mol).
Mass deposited = (E × Q) ÷ F = (molar mass × I × t) ÷ (valency × 96 500).

A current of 2.5 A passes through CuSO₄ solution for 30 minutes. Find the mass of copper (Cu = 63.5, valency 2). t = 1 800 s. Q = 2.5 × 1 800 = 4 500 C. E = 63.5 ÷ 2 = 31.75. Mass = 31.75 × 4 500 ÷ 96 500 = 1.48 g.
5 A passes through AgNO₃ solution for 1 hour (Ag = 108, valency 1). Q = 5 × 3 600 = 18 000 C. Mass = 108 × 18 000 ÷ 96 500 = 20.1 g.

4 A passes through molten PbBr₂ for 30 minutes (Pb = 207, valency 2). (a) Q = 4 × 1 800 = 7 200 C. (b) Moles of electrons = 7 200 ÷ 96 500 = 0.0746 mol. (c) Mass of lead = 207 × 7 200 ÷ (2 × 96 500) = 7.72 g (0.0746 mol of electrons gives 0.0373 mol of Pb).
How long does 2 A take to deposit 3.175 g of copper? Q = 3.175 × 96 500 ÷ 31.75 = 9 650 C. t = Q ÷ I = 9 650 ÷ 2 = 4 825 s, which is about 80 minutes.
Two electrolytes in series (the second law): the same 9 650 C that deposits 3.175 g of Cu would deposit 10.8 g of Ag, because 31.75 : 108 is the ratio of their equivalent weights.
During the electrolysis of acidified water, 0.2 mol of O₂ is collected at the anode. 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, so H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1. Hydrogen = 0.4 mol.

Extraction of metals: aluminium is obtained by electrolysing aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite at about 950 °C (Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al at the carbon cathode). Electroplating: coating a metal with chromium, silver or nickel to prevent corrosion or improve appearance. Electrorefining: purifying copper, with impure copper as the anode and pure copper as the cathode. Making chemicals: NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂ from brine. Charging rechargeable batteries.

units.title: Electrochemical Cells: The Galvanic (Voltaic) Cell
units.summary: What an electrochemical cell is, how a galvanic cell such as the Daniell cell works, the salt bridge, cell notation and uses of galvanic cells.

p: An electrochemical cell is a device that changes chemical energy into electrical energy, or electrical energy into chemical energy, by chemical reactions. It has two electrodes and an electrolyte. There are two kinds: galvanic (voltaic) cells and electrolytic cells.

A galvanic cell is a cell in which a spontaneous chemical reaction produces electrical energy. Its features: the reaction happens by itself; chemical energy becomes electrical energy; the electrodes are usually metals in contact with solutions of their ions; and a salt bridge joins the two solutions.
It has a zinc electrode in zinc sulphate solution and a copper electrode in copper sulphate solution, joined by a wire (with a voltmeter) and by a salt bridge (for example KNO₃ solution).

Anode (negative): Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation). Cathode (positive): Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction). Overall: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Electrons flow in the wire from zinc to copper. The cell gives about 1.10 V.

img.alt: A Daniell cell with a zinc electrode in zinc sulphate solution, a copper electrode in copper sulphate solution, a salt bridge and a voltmeter
img.cap: The Daniell cell.

p: 1. Zinc loses electrons and zinc ions enter the solution. 2. The electrons flow through the wire to copper. 3. Copper ions gain electrons and copper is deposited on the copper electrode. 4. The flow of electrons is the electric current. 5. The salt bridge lets ions move so that each solution stays electrically neutral and the circuit is complete.
Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s). The anode is written on the left, the cathode on the right. A single bar | shows a boundary between phases and a double bar || shows the salt bridge.
Dry cells, lead-acid car batteries and lithium-ion batteries; torches and remote controls; and laboratory demonstrations of redox reactions.

units.title: Electrolytic Cells and the Comparison with Galvanic Cells
units.summary: How an electrolytic cell works, with the Downs cell for sodium, and a table comparing galvanic and electrolytic cells.

p: An electrolytic cell is a cell in which electrical energy is used to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction. It needs a power supply (a battery or generator). The electrodes may be inert (graphite or platinum) or active. The electrolyte is molten or dissolved ionic compound.

Example: electrolysis of molten NaCl with graphite electrodes. Cathode (negative): Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (reduction). Anode (positive): 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation). Sodium metal collects at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode.

Sodium is made industrially in the Downs cell. Molten sodium chloride (with calcium chloride added to lower the melting point) is electrolysed between a graphite anode and a steel cathode. Chlorine is collected at the anode, and molten sodium, which is less dense than the melt, rises and is collected at the top.

img.alt: A Downs cell with molten sodium chloride, a graphite anode, a cathode, a chlorine outlet and a liquid sodium outlet
img.cap: The Downs cell.

units.title: Acid-Base Titration: Apparatus, Indicators and Procedure
units.summary: What titration is, the apparatus and indicators, and the step-by-step method for a neutralisation titration with its precautions.

p: Acid-base titration is a method of finding the concentration of an acid or a base by reacting it with a solution of known concentration. It is a neutralisation reaction (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O) in the presence of an indicator that shows the end point. It is used in laboratories, the food and drink industry, medicine factories and environmental testing.
A measured volume of one solution (usually by pipette) goes into a conical flask. The other solution, the titrant, is added from a burette until neutralisation (the end point).

Arrhenius: acids give H⁺ ions in water and bases give OH⁻ ions. Brønsted-Lowry: an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Lewis: an acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a base is an electron-pair donor.

Burette: a graduated glass tube with a tap, for delivering exact volumes of titrant. Pipette: for measuring a fixed volume, for example 25.0 cm³. Conical flask: holds the solution being analysed. Measuring cylinder: approximate volumes. White tile: helps to see colour changes. Funnel: fills the burette without spilling. Wash bottle: distilled water for rinsing. Retort stand and clamp: hold the burette upright. Indicator: shows the end point.
Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in alkali (pH range 8.3 to 10.0). Used for strong acid with strong base and for weak acid with strong base.
Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in alkali, orange at the end point (pH range 3.1 to 4.4). Used for strong acid with strong base and for strong acid with weak base.
Litmus: red in acid and blue in alkali; not good for titrations because its change is not sharp.
1. Rinse the burette with the acid it will hold, the pipette with the alkali it will measure and the conical flask with distilled water only.
2. Fill the burette with the acid, clamp it upright, run a little out to remove air from the tip and record the initial reading at the bottom of the meniscus to 2 decimal places.
3. Use a pipette filler to put exactly 25.0 cm³ of the alkali (for example NaOH) into the flask.
4. Add 2 or 3 drops of indicator.
5. Stand the flask on a white tile. Run in the acid while swirling the flask. Near the end point add it drop by drop.
6. The end point is the first permanent colour change (for example colourless to faint pink).
7. Repeat until two or three titres are concordant (within 0.1 cm³) and take the average.

img.alt: A flow diagram of the titration procedure: fill the burette, pipette 25 cm3 of base, add indicator, titrate until the colour changes, record the titre, with the formula CaVa over CbVb equals na over nb
img.cap: The steps of an acid-base titration.

p: Rinse every piece of apparatus correctly. Read the burette at eye level to avoid parallax error. Add the titrant slowly near the end point. Repeat the titration for concordant values. Choose a suitable indicator. Work in good light with a white tile.
Finding the acidity of vinegar and soft drinks; quality control of medicines; alkalinity of water; adjusting acidity in food; and checking the purity of chemicals and fertilisers.

units.title: Titration Calculations
units.summary: The formula C_aV_a / C_bV_b = n_a / n_b, with worked examples for concentration in mol/dm³ and g/dm³, and how to use the average titre.

p: For a reaction a A + b B → products between an acid (A) and a base (B): (Cₐ × Vₐ) / (C_b × V_b) = nₐ / n_b. Here C is the concentration in mol/dm³, V is the volume (any unit, but the same for both), and n is the number of moles in the balanced equation.
Concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × molar mass. Moles = concentration × volume in dm³ (volume in cm³ ÷ 1 000).

25.0 cm³ of NaOH solution needs 24.8 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ HCl for neutralisation. Find the molarity of the NaOH. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, so nₐ = n_b = 1. 0.10 × 24.8 / (C_b × 25.0) = 1. C_b = 0.10 × 24.8 ÷ 25.0 = 0.0992 mol/dm³.

20.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄ is neutralised by 25.0 cm³ of NaOH. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, so nₐ : n_b = 1 : 2. 0.10 × 20.0 / (C_b × 25.0) = 1/2. C_b = 0.10 × 20.0 × 2 ÷ 25.0 = 0.16 mol/dm³. In grams per dm³ (NaOH = 40): 0.16 × 40 = 6.4 g/dm³.

Titres: 24.70, 24.75 and 24.80 cm³. They agree within 0.1 cm³, so the average titre = (24.70 + 24.75 + 24.80) ÷ 3 = 24.75 cm³. Use this value in the formula. (Do not include a titre that is far away from the others.)

2.00 g of impure NaOH is dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution. 25.0 cm³ of it needs 20.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ HCl. Moles of HCl = 0.20 × 0.0200 = 0.0040 mol, so moles of NaOH in 25.0 cm³ = 0.0040 mol. In 250 cm³: 0.040 mol. Mass = 0.040 × 40 = 1.60 g. Purity = 1.60 ÷ 2.00 × 100 = 80%.

units.title: Solubility and Factors Affecting It
units.summary: The meaning of solubility, saturated, unsaturated and supersaturated solutions, and the factors that affect solubility.

p: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature to give a saturated solution. It is usually expressed in g per 100 g of solvent, or in mol/dm³. The solute is the substance that dissolves (salt, sugar) and the solvent is the liquid that dissolves it (water, ethanol).

Saturated solution: holds the largest possible amount of solute at that temperature. Unsaturated solution: holds less than that. Supersaturated solution: holds more than the usual maximum; it is made by dissolving at a high temperature and cooling slowly, and it is unstable (a tiny crystal makes the extra solute crystallise).

img.alt: Four beakers showing an unsaturated solution, a saturated solution, a supersaturated solution and the precipitate that forms when a seed crystal is added
img.cap: Unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions.

p: 1. Nature of solute and solvent: 'like dissolves like'. Polar solutes (sugar, salt) dissolve in polar solvents (water). Non-polar solutes (iodine, oil) dissolve in non-polar solvents (carbon tetrachloride, hexane).

2. Temperature: the solubility of most solids increases when the temperature rises (KNO₃ dissolves much more in hot water). The solubility of gases decreases when the temperature rises, which is why fish struggle to breathe in warm water.
3. Pressure: it has little effect on solids and liquids. The solubility of a gas increases with pressure (Henry's law). Soft drinks are bottled under pressure to keep the CO₂ dissolved.
4. Particle size: smaller particles dissolve faster because they expose more surface area. This affects the rate of dissolving, not the maximum amount.
5. Stirring or shaking: it speeds up dissolving but does not change the solubility.

Solubility = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solvent) × 100. Example 1: 20 g of KNO₃ dissolves in 50 g of water at 40 °C: solubility = 20/50 × 100 = 40 g/100 g water. Example 2: 108 g of KCl dissolves in 200 g of water at 60 °C: 108/200 × 100 = 54 g/100 g water. Example 3: 30 g of salt dissolves in 75 g of water: 30/75 × 100 = 40 g/100 g water.
