units.title: Solubility Curves, Crystallisation and Uses
units.summary: How solubility curves are drawn and read, how much solute crystallises on cooling, and the applications of solubility.

p: A solubility curve is a graph of solubility (y-axis) against temperature (x-axis). To draw it: measure the solubility at different temperatures, plot the points and join them with a smooth curve.

img.alt: Solubility curves for potassium nitrate (steep rise) and sodium chloride (almost flat) from 0 to 100 degrees Celsius, with 136 g marked at 70 degrees and 64 g at 40 degrees
img.cap: Solubility curves for KNO₃ and NaCl.

p: A steep rising curve means the solubility rises a lot with temperature (KNO₃). A nearly flat curve means temperature has little effect (NaCl). A falling curve is typical of a gas (CO₂, O₂). Where two curves cross, the two substances have the same solubility at that temperature. A point on the curve is a saturated solution; below it is unsaturated; above it is supersaturated.

From the curve, KNO₃ dissolves 136 g in 100 g of water at 70 °C but only 64 g at 40 °C. If a saturated solution at 70 °C is cooled to 40 °C, the extra solute crystallises: 136 − 64 = 72 g per 100 g of water.

sections.h: Harder example: starting with 300 g of solution
p: 300 g of a saturated KNO₃ solution at 70 °C is cooled to 40 °C. How much KNO₃ crystallises? At 70 °C, 100 g of water holds 136 g, so 236 g of solution holds 136 g of KNO₃. In 300 g of solution: KNO₃ = 300 × 136/236 = 172.9 g and water = 300 − 172.9 = 127.1 g. At 40 °C this water can hold 64 × 127.1/100 = 81.4 g. Crystals = 172.9 − 81.4 = 91.5 g.

Purifying substances by crystallisation (impurities stay dissolved). Making medicines (drugs dissolve in body fluids). Making sugar and salt. Oxygen solubility decides whether fish survive in warm rivers; hot waste water from factories can kill fish. Scale in boilers. The carbonation of soft drinks (CO₂ under pressure). Sugar from sugarcane juice is obtained by evaporating the juice and crystallising the sugar.

units.title: Chemical Equilibrium: Reversible Reactions and Dynamic Equilibrium
units.summary: Reversible and irreversible reactions, how equilibrium is reached and why it is dynamic, and Le Chatelier's principle.

p: An irreversible reaction goes to completion and the products do not change back under the same conditions. Example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Once magnesium has burned, the oxide does not break down again.

A reversible reaction can go in both directions. We write it with a double arrow (⇌). Example: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). Nitrogen and hydrogen form ammonia, but ammonia also breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen.

At the start there are many reactant particles, so the forward reaction is fast. As reactants are used up and products build up, the reverse reaction speeds up. Eventually the forward and reverse rates become equal. From then on the concentrations of reactants and products do not change. This state is chemical equilibrium.

Equilibrium is dynamic, not static: the particles are still reacting in both directions, but at the same rate, so nothing seems to change. Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system (one from which nothing escapes).

img.alt: A balance showing the rate of the forward reaction equal to the rate of the reverse reaction at dynamic equilibrium
img.cap: At equilibrium the two rates are equal.

p: Irreversible: goes to completion; arrow →; cannot be reversed under the same conditions; example 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Reversible: does not go to completion; arrow ⇌; both reactants and products are present at equilibrium; example N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
If a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.

Concentration: adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right (forward); adding a product shifts it to the left. Pressure (gases): increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas. Temperature: raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction; lowering it favours the exothermic direction. Catalyst: speeds up both directions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner, but the position does not change.

Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. High pressure (about 200 atm) favours ammonia (4 moles of gas become 2). A low temperature would favour ammonia (exothermic), but it would be too slow, so about 450 °C is used with an iron catalyst. Contact process: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ with a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.
Haber process (ammonia for fertilisers); Contact process (sulphuric acid); carbonated drinks (CO₂ dissolved ⇌ CO₂ gas above the liquid); oxygen binding to haemoglobin in blood.

units.title: The Equilibrium Constant Kc and Calculations
units.summary: Writing the expression for Kc, what its size means, factors that do and do not change it, and worked calculations.

p: For a reversible reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD at equilibrium, Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / ([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ). The square brackets mean concentration in mol/dm³ at equilibrium. Products go on top and reactants at the bottom; the coefficients become powers. Solids and pure liquids are left out.
Examples. 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃: Kc = [SO₃]² / ([SO₂]²[O₂]). N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂: Kc = [NO₂]² / [N₂O₄].

sections.h: What the size of Kc tells us
p: Kc depends only on temperature. A large Kc (much greater than 1) means that the equilibrium mixture contains mostly products. A small Kc (much less than 1) means that it contains mostly reactants. If Kc is about 1, there are comparable amounts of both. Kc has no units when the number of moles of reactants equals that of products; otherwise it has units that you can work out from the expression.
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). At equilibrium [H₂] = 0.2, [I₂] = 0.2 and [HI] = 0.6 mol/dm³. Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]) = 0.6² / (0.2 × 0.2) = 0.36 / 0.04 = 9.0 (no units).
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). At equilibrium [N₂] = 0.1, [H₂] = 0.3, [NH₃] = 0.4 mol/dm³. Kc = 0.4² / (0.1 × 0.3³) = 0.16 / 0.0027 = 59.3 (units: mol⁻² dm⁶).
Another: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI at 500 K with [H₂] = 0.1, [I₂] = 0.1, [HI] = 0.8: Kc = 0.64 / 0.01 = 64.

1.0 mol of H₂ and 1.0 mol of I₂ are placed in a 1 dm³ flask and Kc = 9. Let x mol of each react. At equilibrium [H₂] = [I₂] = 1 − x and [HI] = 2x. Kc = 4x² / (1 − x)² = 9, so 2x / (1 − x) = 3, 2x = 3 − 3x and x = 0.6. Equilibrium: [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.4 mol/dm³ and [HI] = 1.2 mol/dm³. Check: 1.2² / (0.4 × 0.4) = 1.44 / 0.16 = 9 ✓.

sections.h: What changes Kc and what does not
p: Temperature changes Kc. For an exothermic reaction, a rise in temperature decreases Kc. For an endothermic reaction, a rise in temperature increases Kc. Changes in concentration or pressure shift the position of equilibrium but do not change Kc. A catalyst does not change Kc.

Note on the Haber process: at room temperature Kc for ammonia is very large, but the reaction is far too slow. At 450 °C Kc is much smaller, which is why high pressure is also used to raise the yield.

units.title: Chemical Kinetics: Rate of Reaction and Factors
units.summary: What kinetics is, how rate is measured, collision theory, and the factors that change the rate of a reaction.

p: Chemical kinetics is the study of how fast reactions happen and by what steps. Thermodynamics tells us whether a reaction can happen; kinetics tells us how quickly. The rusting of iron is possible but slow. The burning of petrol is possible and fast.

The rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. For a reactant the rate is written with a minus sign, because its concentration falls: rate = −Δ[reactant]/Δt. For a product it is +Δ[product]/Δt. Units: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

For 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂: rate = −(1/2) d[H₂O₂]/dt = d[O₂]/dt. The average rate is the change over a time interval; the instantaneous rate is the rate at one moment (the slope of the tangent to the concentration-time graph).
For a reaction to occur, particles must collide. Not every collision is effective. An effective collision needs (1) energy at least equal to the activation energy Eₐ and (2) the correct orientation.

1. Concentration: more particles in each volume means more frequent collisions, so the rate is higher. 2. Temperature: particles move faster and a larger fraction has energy of at least Eₐ. As a rough rule, the rate about doubles for every 10 °C rise. 3. Pressure (gases): more pressure means a higher concentration. 4. Surface area: powder reacts faster than lumps, because more particles are exposed. 5. Catalyst: provides another pathway with lower activation energy and is not used up (MnO₂ with H₂O₂). 6. Nature of reactants: ionic reactions such as neutralisation are very fast; reactions that break strong covalent bonds are slow.

units.title: Rate Laws and Order of Reaction
units.summary: The rate law, rate constant and order of reaction, how to find the order from experimental data, and first-order half-life calculations.

p: For A + B → products, the rate law is rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ. k is the rate constant (it depends on temperature and catalyst, not on concentration). m and n are the orders with respect to A and B. m + n is the overall order. The rate law must be found by experiment; it cannot be read from the balanced equation.
Example: if rate = k[NO]²[O₂] for 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, then the order with respect to NO is 2, with respect to O₂ is 1 and the overall order is 3.

Zero order: the rate does not depend on concentration; rate = k (decomposition of NH₃ on hot tungsten). First order: rate = k[A] (radioactive decay, decomposition of N₂O₅). Second order: rate = k[A]² or k[A][B]. Orders can also be fractions.

sections.h: Finding the order: the method of initial rates
p: Measure the initial rate for different starting concentrations. Suppose:
Experiment 1: [A] = 0.1, [B] = 0.1, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Experiment 2: [A] = 0.2, [B] = 0.1, rate = 4.0 × 10⁻³. Experiment 3: [A] = 0.2, [B] = 0.2, rate = 16 × 10⁻³.

From 1 to 2, [A] doubles and the rate doubles: first order in A. From 2 to 3, [B] doubles and the rate is four times as large: second order in B. So rate = k[A][B]². Then k = 2.0 × 10⁻³ / (0.1 × 0.1²) = 2.0 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹. The units of k depend on the overall order.
Zero order: concentration against time is a straight line. First order: ln[A] against time is a straight line. Second order: 1/[A] against time is a straight line.
The half-life t½ is the time for the concentration to fall to half. For a first-order reaction it is constant: t½ = 0.693 / k.
Example. A first-order reaction has t½ = 300 s and [A]₀ = 1.0 mol/dm³. k = 0.693 / 300 = 2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. After 600 s (two half-lives) the concentration is 1.0 → 0.5 → 0.25 mol/dm³.
It helps to find reaction mechanisms, to understand how medicines break down in the body and to control industrial processes such as the Haber process, the Contact process and catalytic cracking.

units.title: Heat of Reaction and Enthalpy Change
units.summary: Thermochemistry: heat of reaction, enthalpy change ΔH, exothermic and endothermic reactions, types of heat of reaction and a calorimetry calculation.

p: Chemical reactions give out or take in heat. Thermochemistry is the study of these heat changes. It helps to predict whether reactions will happen, to design industrial processes, to find the energy needed in factories and to understand energy changes in living things.

Enthalpy (H) is the heat content of a system at constant pressure. The enthalpy change is ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants), in kJ per mole. ΔH is a state function: it depends only on the starting and finishing states, not on the route.

Exothermic reaction: heat is given out, ΔH is negative, and the temperature of the surroundings rises (burning methane, neutralisation, respiration). Endothermic reaction: heat is taken in, ΔH is positive, and the surroundings get cooler (photosynthesis, thermal decomposition of CaCO₃, dissolving ammonium chloride).
Heat of formation: the heat change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements under standard conditions (25 °C, 1 atm). C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ/mol.
Heat of combustion: the heat change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ/mol.
Heat of neutralisation: the heat change when one mole of water is formed from an acid and a base. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, ΔH = −57 kJ/mol.
Heat of solution: the heat change when one mole of a substance dissolves in a large amount of solvent. Heat of atomisation: the heat needed to turn one mole of a substance into gaseous atoms.

50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ HCl is mixed with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ NaOH and the temperature rises by 6.8 °C. Find the heat of neutralisation. (Specific heat capacity of the solution = 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹; density = 1 g/cm³.) Heat produced q = m c ΔT = 100 × 4.2 × 6.8 = 2 856 J = 2.856 kJ. Moles of water formed = 0.050 × 1.0 = 0.050 mol. ΔH = −2.856 / 0.050 = −57.1 kJ/mol.

units.title: Hess's Law
units.summary: The statement of Hess's law, why it is true, and calculations with enthalpy cycles.

p: Hess's law of constant heat summation: the total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whatever route is taken, provided the starting and finishing conditions are the same. It is true because enthalpy is a state function.
It lets us calculate ΔH for reactions that cannot be measured directly (such as carbon burning to carbon monoxide only, with no carbon dioxide), and heats of formation, combustion and atomisation.
Direct route: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ/mol.
Indirect route: C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g), ΔH₁ = −110 kJ/mol; then CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH₂ = −284 kJ/mol. Total = −110 + (−284) = −394 kJ/mol. The two routes agree.

sections.h: Worked example: formation of nitrogen monoxide
p: Find ΔH for N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), given (1) N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), ΔH = +66 kJ and (2) 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), ΔH = −114 kJ.

Reverse equation (2): 2NO₂ → 2NO + O₂, ΔH = +114 kJ. Add it to (1): N₂ + 2O₂ + 2NO₂ → 2NO₂ + 2NO + O₂, which simplifies to N₂ + O₂ → 2NO. ΔH = +66 + 114 = +180 kJ. (Endothermic: this is why nitrogen oxides form in hot engines and in lightning.)

If you reverse an equation, change the sign of ΔH. If you multiply an equation by a number, multiply ΔH by the same number. Add the equations so that unwanted substances cancel, and add the ΔH values.

sections.h: Another example: using heats of combustion
p: Given the heats of combustion: C(s) −394 kJ/mol, H₂(g) −286 kJ/mol and CH₄(g) −890 kJ/mol, find the heat of formation of CH₄: C + 2H₂ → CH₄. ΔH = Σ(combustion of reactants) − Σ(combustion of products) = (−394) + 2(−286) − (−890) = −966 + 890 = −76 kJ/mol.

units.title: Energetics: Activation Energy and Energy Profile Diagrams
units.summary: Bond breaking and bond making, activation energy, energy profile diagrams for exothermic and endothermic reactions and the effect of a catalyst.

p: In every reaction, bonds in the reactants are broken and new bonds form in the products. Breaking bonds takes in energy (endothermic). Making bonds gives out energy (exothermic). The overall ΔH is the balance. If more energy is released than taken in, the reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative). If more is taken in than released, it is endothermic (ΔH positive).

Activation energy (Eₐ) is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have to start a reaction. Think of it as a hill that the reactants must climb. Even exothermic reactions need it: a match must be struck before it burns. High Eₐ means a slow reaction (rusting). Low Eₐ means a fast reaction (neutralisation). A catalyst lowers Eₐ.
An energy profile shows the energy of the system as the reaction proceeds.

Exothermic: the reactants start higher. The curve rises to a peak (the height above the reactants is Eₐ) and then falls to the products, which are lower. The difference in level between reactants and products is ΔH (negative).
Endothermic: the reactants start lower. The curve rises to a peak and ends at products that are higher than the reactants. ΔH is positive.
Catalyst: the catalysed pathway has a lower peak. Eₐ is smaller, but the levels of the reactants and products, and so ΔH, are the same.

img.alt: Three energy profile diagrams: an exothermic reaction with products lower than reactants, an endothermic reaction with products higher than reactants, and the effect of a catalyst which lowers the peak
img.cap: Energy profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions, and the effect of a catalyst.

p: Example 1. Eₐ = 150 kJ and ΔH = −75 kJ. ΔH is negative, so it is exothermic. The peak is 150 kJ above the reactants and the products are 75 kJ below the reactants. The activation energy of the reverse reaction is 150 + 75 = 225 kJ.
Example 2. ΔH = +120 kJ/mol and Eₐ = 200 kJ/mol. Endothermic. The peak is 200 kJ above the reactants; the products are 120 kJ above the reactants; the reverse Eₐ is 200 − 120 = 80 kJ/mol.
Example 3. H₂O₂ decomposes slowly because of a high activation energy. MnO₂ gives another pathway with lower Eₐ, so it decomposes quickly.

'Exothermic reactions need no activation energy': wrong; all reactions need some. 'A catalyst changes ΔH': wrong; it only lowers Eₐ. 'A faster reaction releases more heat': wrong; speed depends on Eₐ, heat released depends on ΔH. Rusting is slow although it is exothermic, because its activation energy is high.

Striking a match: friction supplies the activation energy. Respiration: enzymes lower the Eₐ of glucose oxidation. Cooking: heat supplies the activation energy. Industry: iron in the Haber process, vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process and nickel in the hydrogenation of oils.

units.title: Saponification: The Chemistry of Soap Making
units.summary: Fats and oils as triglycerides, saponification with an alkali, the laboratory preparation of soap and the types of soap.

p: People in ancient Babylon (about 2800 BC) boiled fats with ashes to make a crude soap. The ancient Egyptians used a similar mixture to wash linen and to treat skin diseases. In the 19th century soap making became a large industry as the chemistry of fats and alkalis was understood. Detergents were first made in 1916 in Germany, during the First World War, because of a shortage of natural fats and oils.

Fats and oils are triglycerides: esters formed when glycerol, C₃H₅(OH)₃, combines with three fatty acids. Fats are solid at room temperature and are rich in saturated fatty acids (tallow, butter). Oils are liquid at room temperature and are rich in unsaturated fatty acids (palm oil, groundnut oil).
Common fatty acids: stearic acid C₁₇H₃₅COOH, palmitic acid C₁₅H₃₁COOH and oleic acid C₁₇H₃₃COOH.
Saponification is the hydrolysis of a fat or oil by a strong alkali (NaOH or KOH) to give soap and glycerol.
C₃H₅(OOCR)₃ + 3NaOH → C₃H₅(OH)₃ + 3RCOONa
fat or oil + sodium hydroxide → glycerol + soap (the sodium salt of a fatty acid).
Materials: palm oil, NaOH pellets, distilled water, ethanol, concentrated sodium chloride solution.

1. Dissolve the NaOH pellets in water to make caustic soda solution (handle with care: it burns the skin). 2. Mix the palm oil with ethanol in a beaker (the ethanol helps the oil and alkali to mix). 3. Add the NaOH solution and heat gently for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring, without splashing. 4. A thick paste forms. 5. Add concentrated NaCl solution to make the soap separate (salting out). 6. Filter and wash the soap with a little distilled water. 7. Dry it and mould it.
Observation: the soap separates as a solid (it is less soluble in salt solution), while the glycerol stays in the liquid.

Hard soap: the sodium salt of a fatty acid, made with NaOH; solid; used for laundry. Soft soap: the potassium salt, made with KOH; soft or semi-liquid; used in shampoos and shaving creams. Medicated soap: contains an antiseptic such as triclosan or sulphur. Toilet soap: perfumed and mild on the skin. Transparent soap: made with extra glycerol and sugar.

units.title: Cleaning Action of Soap and Detergents
units.summary: Hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails, micelles, why soap fails in hard water, and how detergents are different and better in some ways.

p: A soap molecule has two parts. The hydrophobic tail (R–) is a long hydrocarbon chain that repels water and dissolves in oil and grease. The hydrophilic head (–COO⁻Na⁺) is polar and dissolves in water.

When soap meets greasy dirt on cloth, the tails go into the grease and the heads stay in the water. The soap molecules gather into balls called micelles with the grease trapped inside and the heads on the outside. The micelles stay suspended in the water (because the charged heads repel one another) and are washed away when we rinse.

img.alt: A soap micelle with a grease droplet in the middle, hydrophobic tails pointing inwards and hydrophilic heads pointing out towards water molecules
img.cap: A soap micelle traps grease.

p: Soap does not work well in hard water, which has Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ or Fe²⁺ ions. These ions form an insoluble scum: 2RCOO⁻Na⁺ + Ca²⁺ → (RCOO)₂Ca↓ + 2Na⁺. The scum wastes the soap and leaves a grey film on clothes. Soap also fails in acidic water, because H⁺ ions change the soap back to the fatty acid, which is insoluble: RCOO⁻ + H⁺ → RCOOH.

Detergents are synthetic cleaning agents made from petroleum products. They have a hydrocarbon tail like soap, but the head is a sulphonate (–SO₃⁻Na⁺) or sulphate (–OSO₃⁻Na⁺) group. Their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble, so they do not form scum.

Types: anionic (negative head, for example sodium alkylbenzene sulphonate in washing powders), cationic (positive head, for example quaternary ammonium salts in hair conditioners) and non-ionic (polar groups without charge, for example ethoxylated alcohols).
They work in both soft and hard water; they form no scum; they work in acidic and neutral solutions; and they can be designed for special jobs (dishwashing, shampoos, industrial cleaners).

Soaps are fully biodegradable. Early detergents had branched chains that bacteria could not break down. They caused thick foam on rivers and lakes, blocked the dissolving of oxygen and harmed aquatic life. Modern detergents have straight (linear) chains, which are biodegradable. Detergents that contain phosphates can also cause eutrophication.
Soap: bathing, laundry, textile industry, shaving creams. Detergents: washing powders, dishwashing liquids, shampoos, industrial degreasers, and emulsifiers in food and medicines.

units.title: Nuclear Chemistry: Radioactivity and Radioactive Emissions
units.summary: What nuclear chemistry studies, how nuclear and chemical reactions differ, and the nature of alpha, beta and gamma radiation with nuclear equations.

p: Nuclear chemistry studies the structure of the nucleus and the changes it undergoes. Ordinary chemistry deals with the outer electrons. Nuclear reactions involve the nucleus (protons and neutrons) and give enormous amounts of energy, about a million times more per atom than chemical reactions.

head: Feature
Chemical reaction
Nuclear reaction
rows: Affected by temperature, pressure and catalysts

p: 1896: Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in uranium salts. 1898: Marie and Pierre Curie isolated polonium and radium. Ernest Rutherford identified alpha and beta radiation. 1932: James Chadwick discovered the neutron.

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of particles (alpha, beta) or electromagnetic radiation (gamma) from the nucleus of an unstable atom, until it changes into a more stable form. Unstable atoms are called radioisotopes: uranium-238, thorium-232, carbon-14, radium-226, iodine-131.

An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons: a helium nucleus, ⁴₂He. Charge +2, relative mass 4. Slow (about a tenth of the speed of light). Penetrating power: very low (stopped by a sheet of paper or the skin). Ionising power: very high. Example: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He. Another: ²¹⁰₈₄Po → ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb + ⁴₂He. In alpha decay, the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.

A beta particle is a fast electron (β⁻, charge −1) or a positron (β⁺, charge +1). Its mass is negligible and its speed is close to the speed of light. Penetrating power: moderate (stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium). Ionising power: medium. Example: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e (β⁻). In beta decay, the mass number is unchanged and the atomic number increases by 1 (a neutron changes into a proton).

Gamma rays are high-frequency electromagnetic waves. No charge and no mass. They travel at the speed of light. Penetrating power: very high (they need thick lead or concrete to stop them). Ionising power: low. They usually come with alpha or beta emission and carry away extra energy; they do not change the atomic number or mass number.

p: It is spontaneous (heat, pressure and catalysts do not change it). It makes new nuclei (daughter nuclei). It gives out large amounts of energy. It follows a fixed rate measured by the half-life.

units.title: Half-Life, Applications and Dangers of Radioactivity
units.summary: The half-life of a radioisotope with calculations, the uses of radioactivity in medicine, farming, industry, archaeology and energy, and its dangers.

p: The half-life (T½) is the time taken for half of the nuclei in a sample to decay. It is constant for each radioisotope and does not depend on the amount, temperature or pressure.
Example 1. A sample of 80 g of a radioisotope has a half-life of 5 days. After 5 days: 40 g; after 10 days: 20 g; after 15 days: 10 g.

Example 2. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5 730 years. A fossil has one quarter of the carbon-14 of a living organism. One quarter is two half-lives (1 → ½ → ¼), so its age is about 2 × 5 730 = 11 460 years.
Medicine: cobalt-60 gamma rays destroy cancer cells (radiotherapy); technetium-99m is a tracer for imaging organs; iodine-131 treats an overactive thyroid and goitre.
Agriculture: radioisotopes trace how plants take up fertiliser; radiation sterilises pests and keeps food from spoiling (food irradiation).
Industry: beta radiation gauges the thickness of paper, plastic and metal sheets; tracers find leaks in pipes; gamma radiography finds cracks in metal parts.

Archaeology and geology: carbon-14 dating gives the age of fossils, bones and objects up to about 50 000 years old. Uranium-lead dating gives the age of rocks, which can be millions or billions of years old.
Energy: nuclear fission of uranium-235 and plutonium-239 in reactors heats water to make steam that drives turbines to produce electricity. A reactor uses far less fuel than a coal power station.

sections.h: Why is carbon-14 used for dating?
p: Carbon-14 is taken in by all living things. When an organism dies it stops taking in carbon, and the carbon-14 already in it decays with a known half-life (5 730 years). Measuring what is left gives the time since death.

Radiation can cause cancer, mutations (genetic damage) and burns, and radiation sickness at high doses. Nuclear waste stays dangerous for thousands of years and is difficult to store. Accidents such as Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011) show the risks. Nuclear weapons can cause mass destruction. Gamma rays are especially dangerous because they penetrate deep into the body, while alpha particles are most harmful if the source is swallowed or breathed in.

sections.h: Advantages and disadvantages of nuclear energy
p: Advantages: a very large amount of energy from a small mass of fuel and no carbon dioxide from the reactor. Disadvantages: dangerous waste, the risk of accidents, a very high building cost and the possible misuse of the technology for weapons.

units.title: The Halogens: Properties and Trends
units.summary: The Group 17 elements, their physical and chemical properties, displacement reactions, bleaching, and the trends down the group.

p: The halogens are the non-metals of Group 17 (Group VIIA): fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I) and astatine (At). The name means 'salt-former', because they combine easily with metals to form salts such as NaCl. They have seven electrons in the outer shell (ns²np⁵), so they readily gain one electron to form halide ions (X⁻) and are strong oxidising agents. They exist as diatomic molecules (F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) and are never found free in nature.

Fluorine is a pale yellow gas. Chlorine is a greenish-yellow gas. Bromine is a reddish-brown liquid. Iodine is a grey-black solid that sublimes to a purple vapour. The colour gets darker, and the melting point, boiling point and density increase down the group (stronger van der Waals forces between larger molecules). They are poor conductors. They are slightly soluble in water and more soluble in organic solvents such as hexane and CCl₄, in which they show clear colours.

img.alt: The halogens fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine with their colours and states and an arrow showing reactivity decreasing down the group
img.cap: Trends in Group 17.

p: 1. Reactivity decreases down the group: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. Reason: the atoms get larger and there is more shielding, so the atom attracts an extra electron less strongly (electronegativity falls).

2. Displacement: a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt. Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ (the solution turns red-brown). Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂ (brown or purple). Br₂ + 2KI → 2KBr + I₂. Iodine cannot displace chlorine or bromine.
3. With hydrogen: H₂ + X₂ → 2HX. Fluorine reacts explosively even in the dark; chlorine explosively in sunlight; bromine slowly on heating; iodine only partly (the HI formed breaks down easily).
4. With metals: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl (ionic halides).

5. With water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HOCl. Hypochlorous acid, HOCl, is the bleach and germ killer: HOCl → HCl + [O]. The released oxygen bleaches coloured substances. A damp litmus paper is bleached by chlorine.

Atomic radius increases; ionisation energy and electronegativity decrease; reactivity and oxidising power decrease; melting and boiling points increase. The reducing power of the halide ions increases: I⁻ is the strongest reducing agent.

units.title: Fluorine, Chlorine, Bromine and Iodine: Uses, Effects and Tests
units.summary: The occurrence, uses and health effects of each halogen, and simple laboratory tests.

p: A pale yellow, poisonous gas with a sharp smell; the most electronegative element. Occurs as fluorspar CaF₂, cryolite Na₃AlF₆ and fluorapatite. It reacts explosively with hydrogen even in the dark. Uses: making fluorocarbons such as Teflon (PTFE) for non-stick pans; making UF₆ for nuclear fuel; fluoride in toothpaste and water to prevent tooth decay. Too much fluoride causes fluorosis (brown teeth and weak bones).

A greenish-yellow gas with a choking smell, denser than air. Occurs mainly as sodium chloride. Uses: killing germs in drinking water and swimming pools; making hydrochloric acid, PVC, pesticides and antiseptics; bleaching cloth and paper; making chloroform and other chlorinated solvents. Chlorine is poisonous and was used as a weapon in the First World War. In water treatment the amount is very small and carefully controlled, so the water is safe to drink while the germs are killed.

A reddish-brown volatile liquid with suffocating fumes. Occurs in sea water as bromides. Uses: flame retardants, dyes, some medicines, silver bromide in photographic film, and water treatment. Its vapour irritates eyes and skin.

A grey-black shiny solid that sublimes to a purple vapour. Found in seaweed and iodised salts. The least reactive common halogen. Uses: tincture of iodine as an antiseptic; iodised salt to prevent goitre; making dyes and medicines; the starch test. Iodine is needed to make the thyroid hormone: lack of it causes goitre, and too much causes an overactive thyroid.

Displacement: chlorine water + potassium iodide solution gives a brown-purple colour of iodine; chlorine water + potassium bromide solution gives red-brown bromine. Starch test: iodine turns starch solution blue-black. Bleaching: damp litmus paper is bleached by chlorine gas.

Medicine (iodine antiseptic, halogenated drugs and anaesthetics); food (iodised salt, fluoride toothpaste); water treatment (chlorine); plastics (PVC and Teflon); photography (silver bromide and silver iodide); dyes and bleaches.

units.title: Alkali Metals (Group 1)
units.summary: Properties, trends, reactions and uses of lithium, sodium, potassium and the other Group 1 metals.

p: Lithium (Li), sodium (Na), potassium (K), rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs) and francium (Fr). They are called alkali metals because their hydroxides are strong alkalis. They are soft, silvery metals that react vigorously with water to give an alkaline hydroxide and hydrogen. Sodium and potassium are stored under oil because they react with air and water.

Electronic configuration ns¹: one outer electron, which is easily lost, so they form M⁺ ions. Metallic character and reactivity increase down the group (bigger atoms hold the outer electron less tightly). They are soft (they can be cut with a knife) and get softer down the group. Low melting and boiling points that decrease down the group. Low density: lithium, sodium and potassium float on water. Flame colours: lithium crimson-red, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, rubidium red-violet, caesium blue-violet.
1. With oxygen: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O (lithium gives the oxide; sodium also gives the peroxide Na₂O₂ in excess air).
2. With water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Sodium floats, melts into a ball, fizzes and moves about; potassium burns with a lilac flame. The solution turns red litmus blue.
3. With halogens: 2K + Cl₂ → 2KCl (ionic halides).
4. With acids: very violent (dangerous) reactions that give a salt and hydrogen.

Sodium vapour lamps for street lighting; lithium in rechargeable batteries; potassium compounds in fertilisers and soap making; liquid sodium as a coolant in some nuclear reactors; sodium hydroxide in making soap, paper and detergents; sodium chloride as food and a raw material in industry.

units.title: Alkaline Earth Metals (Group 2) and Flame Tests
units.summary: Properties, trends, reactions and uses of magnesium, calcium and the other Group 2 metals, and a comparison with Group 1.

p: Beryllium (Be), magnesium (Mg), calcium (Ca), strontium (Sr), barium (Ba) and radium (Ra). Their oxides and hydroxides are alkaline but less soluble than those of Group 1, and the metals are found in the Earth's crust (hence 'alkaline earth'). They are harder and denser than the alkali metals and less reactive.

Electronic configuration ns²: two outer electrons, so they form M²⁺ ions. Metallic character and reactivity increase down the group. Higher melting and boiling points than Group 1. Flame colours: calcium brick-red, strontium crimson, barium apple-green (magnesium gives no coloured flame).

img.alt: Flame test colours of lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium, strontium and barium
img.cap: Flame colours of alkali and alkaline earth metals.

p: 1. With oxygen: 2Ca + O₂ → 2CaO; magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame, 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

2. With water: reactivity increases down the group. Calcium reacts slowly with cold water: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but burns in steam: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂.
3. With acids: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.
4. With halogens: Sr + Cl₂ → SrCl₂.

Magnesium: light alloys for aircraft, fireworks and flares, and in medicine (antacids, milk of magnesia). Calcium: cement, plaster of Paris, building materials and lime for soil. Strontium: red colour in fireworks. Barium: the 'barium meal' used in X-ray pictures of the gut, paints and ceramics. Radium: once used in luminous paints; now used in cancer treatment.

Group 1 has ns¹, very high reactivity, soft metals, very low melting points, low ionisation energy and mostly soluble compounds. Group 2 has ns², moderate reactivity, harder metals, higher melting points, higher ionisation energy and less soluble compounds. Sodium and potassium are more reactive than magnesium and calcium because it is easier to lose one electron than two.

units.title: Transition Elements and Complex Compounds
units.summary: What a transition element is, electronic configurations, variable oxidation states, coloured compounds, catalytic action and complex ions.

p: Transition elements are the d-block elements, in the middle of the periodic table (Groups 3 to 12): titanium, vanadium, chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel, copper and others. A transition element is one that forms at least one stable ion with an incomplete d sub-shell. Zinc is not a typical transition element, because Zn²⁺ is [Ar]3d¹⁰ (a full d sub-shell). General configuration: (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻².

img.alt: A summary of the properties of transition elements: coloured ions, catalytic action, variable oxidation states and complex ions
img.cap: Properties of transition elements.

p: Iron: [Ar]3d⁶4s². Copper: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹. Chromium: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹. (Cr and Cu take an electron from 4s to give a half-full or full 3d sub-shell, which is more stable.) Zinc: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s².

Physical: high melting and boiling points (except Zn and Hg), hard and dense, good conductors, shiny, and some are magnetic (Fe, Co, Ni are ferromagnetic). Chemical: variable oxidation states, coloured ions and compounds, stable complex ions and catalytic activity.

The energy difference between the 3d and 4s electrons is small, so both can be lost. Iron: +2 (FeCl₂, green) and +3 (FeCl₃, yellow-brown). Manganese: +2 (pink), +4 (MnO₂, brown), +6, +7 (KMnO₄, purple). Chromium: +2 (blue), +3 (green), +6 (K₂Cr₂O₇, orange). Copper: +1 (CuCl, white) and +2 (CuSO₄, blue).

Colours come from d–d electron transitions. In a complex the d orbitals split into two levels. An electron absorbs light of the energy needed to jump between them, and we see the complementary colour. Examples: Fe²⁺(aq) pale green; Fe³⁺(aq) yellow-brown; Cu²⁺(aq) blue; Cr₂O₇²⁻ orange; MnO₄⁻ purple.

Fe in the Haber process; V₂O₅ in the Contact process; Ni in the hydrogenation of oils; MnO₂ in 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. They give another path with lower activation energy and can change their oxidation state easily.

A complex ion has a central metal ion surrounded by ligands, joined by coordinate (dative covalent) bonds. A ligand is a molecule or ion with a lone pair (H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻). The coordination number is the number of coordinate bonds. Examples: [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ deep blue; [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ yellow; [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ colourless (Tollens' reagent). Shapes: octahedral (6 ligands, [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺), tetrahedral (4, [CuCl₄]²⁻) and square planar (4, [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻).

Industry: catalysts, plating with nickel and chromium, pigments and dyes, and stainless steel (iron with chromium and nickel). Biology: haemoglobin (Fe²⁺) carries oxygen; vitamin B12 contains cobalt; cytochromes (Fe, Cu) carry electrons in respiration. Environment: Cr(VI), Cd and Hg are toxic pollutants.

units.title: The Reactivity Series of Metals
units.summary: The order of reactivity of metals, why it differs, how metals react with oxygen, water, acids and salt solutions, and what the series is used for.

p: Metals do not all react with the same vigour. Potassium and sodium are extremely reactive; gold and platinum are almost inert. Chemists list metals in order of reactivity in the reactivity series: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, (H), Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, Pt.

Top (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al): very reactive. Middle (Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb): moderately reactive, need heat or steam. Bottom (Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, Pt): least reactive, the noble metals, and are found uncombined in nature.

img.alt: A staircase diagram of the reactivity series of metals from potassium at the top to platinum at the bottom, with reactivity increasing upwards
img.cap: The reactivity series.

p: Reactivity depends on how easily a metal loses electrons to form positive ions. Metals with low ionisation energy (K, Na) lose electrons easily. Metals such as gold and platinum have high ionisation energy and do not form ions easily.

With oxygen: K and Na burn quickly in air; Mg burns with a dazzling white flame (2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO); Al forms a thin protective layer of Al₂O₃, which is why it does not corrode away; iron slowly forms rust (hydrated iron(III) oxide) in air and water; copper only tarnishes slowly; gold and platinum do not react.

With water: K and Na react violently with cold water (2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂); calcium reacts less violently (Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂); magnesium reacts slowly with hot water and burns in steam; zinc and iron react only with steam to give the oxide and hydrogen; copper, silver and gold do not react.
With dilute acids: metals above hydrogen displace hydrogen: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Metals below hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au) do not react.

Displacement from solutions: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from a salt solution. Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. An iron nail in copper(II) sulphate solution gets a brown coating of copper and the blue colour fades.

Order of Zn, Cu, Na, Fe from most to least reactive: Na, Zn, Fe, Cu. Zinc displaces copper from CuSO₄ because zinc is more reactive; copper cannot displace zinc from ZnSO₄ because it is less reactive. Calcium reacts more vigorously with water than magnesium, giving Ca(OH)₂ and H₂, while magnesium reacts only slowly. Aluminium is reactive but resists corrosion because of its protective oxide layer.

To predict which metals can extract others from their compounds; to explain corrosion resistance (gold for jewellery); to design sacrificial protection: zinc coating (galvanising) protects iron because zinc is more reactive and corrodes in its place; and in industry for choosing methods of extraction.

units.title: Refining of Metals
units.summary: Why metals must be refined and the methods used: electrolytic refining, liquation, distillation, zone refining and cupellation.

p: Metals obtained from their ores are not pure: they contain sand, clay or other metals. Refining improves strength, electrical conductivity and usefulness. Copper must be pure for electric wires, aluminium for aircraft, gold and silver for jewellery, and silicon and germanium must be ultra-pure for electronic chips.
The most common method, used for copper, silver, gold and others. The impure metal is the anode, a thin sheet of pure metal is the cathode, and the electrolyte is a solution of a salt of the metal.

Copper refining: electrolyte CuSO₄ with H₂SO₄. Anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (the impure copper dissolves). Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (pure copper is deposited). Metals less reactive than copper (silver, gold) do not dissolve and fall to the bottom as anode mud, which is valuable. More reactive impurities (such as zinc and iron) dissolve and stay in solution.
For metals with low melting points (tin, lead). The impure metal is heated on a sloping surface. The pure metal melts and flows down, and the impurities with high melting points stay behind.
For volatile metals such as zinc and mercury. The impure metal is heated until it vaporises; the vapour is condensed to pure metal.

For metals that must be extremely pure (silicon, germanium). A narrow molten zone is passed slowly along a rod by a moving heater. Impurities are more soluble in the molten zone, so they are carried to one end, leaving pure metal behind.

For silver and other noble metals. The impure metal is heated in a porous cup (a cupel) in air. Base metals such as lead and copper oxidise and are absorbed by the cupel, leaving the pure noble metal.
A 500 g sample of impure zinc contains 10% impurities. Mass of impurities = 10/100 × 500 = 50 g. Pure zinc = 500 − 50 = 450 g (if the refining removes all of the impurities).

units.title: Non-Metals: General Properties and Hydrogen
units.summary: General properties of non-metals, and the occurrence, preparation, properties and uses of hydrogen.

p: Non-metals are on the right of the periodic table (hydrogen is an exception). They usually gain electrons to form negative ions, or share electrons in covalent bonds. They are electronegative. They are not shiny, malleable or ductile. They may be solids (sulphur, phosphorus, carbon), a liquid (bromine) or gases (hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, chlorine).

They are poor conductors of electricity (except graphite); they have low melting and boiling points (except diamond and graphite); they form acidic oxides (CO₂, SO₂, P₂O₅); they form volatile covalent compounds with hydrogen (HCl, NH₃); and they have variable oxidation states.
Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe. On Earth it is found combined in water, hydrocarbons (CH₄), acids (HCl, H₂SO₄) and living matter (proteins, carbohydrates, fats).

Zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Use a flask, thistle funnel and delivery tube. Collect over water or by upward delivery (downward displacement of air), because hydrogen is much less dense than air. Dry it with calcium chloride or concentrated sulphuric acid.
Another way: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ (dangerous, only for demonstration). Test for hydrogen: it burns with a 'pop' when a lighted splint is put to it.
A colourless, odourless, tasteless gas. The lightest gas (density about 0.07 relative to air, which is 1). Slightly soluble in water. Neutral to litmus.

1. Burns in oxygen with a pale blue flame to form water: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 2. With chlorine in sunlight (explosive): H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. 3. As a reducing agent, it reduces metal oxides: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (black copper oxide turns pink-brown). 4. With nitrogen to make ammonia: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (iron catalyst, about 450 °C, 200 atm). 5. With unsaturated compounds in the presence of nickel (hydrogenation): C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆.

Making ammonia (Haber process) for fertilisers; hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make margarine; rocket fuel (liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen); oxy-hydrogen flames for welding; as a reducing agent in extracting metals; filling balloons (non-flammable helium is used instead, for safety).

units.title: Oxygen and Nitrogen
units.summary: Occurrence, preparation, properties and uses of oxygen and nitrogen, with a comparison table for hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen.

p: Oxygen makes up about 21% of air and is found in water, oxides and minerals. Laboratory preparations: (1) decomposition of hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide as catalyst: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂; (2) heating potassium chlorate with MnO₂: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. Collect over water. Dry with calcium chloride or concentrated H₂SO₄. Test: it relights a glowing splint. Industrially it is obtained by the fractional distillation of liquid air.

img.alt: A cycle diagram of hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen with their sources and uses
img.cap: Hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen and their uses.

p: Colourless, odourless, tasteless gas; slightly soluble in water; a little denser than air; neutral to litmus. It supports combustion (a candle burns brighter in it). With metals: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. With non-metals: C + O₂ → CO₂; S + O₂ → SO₂. Oxides may be basic (Na₂O, CaO), acidic (SO₂, CO₂) or amphoteric (ZnO, Al₂O₃).
Uses: respiration and combustion; oxygen for patients in hospitals; oxy-acetylene welding; steel making; and the oxidiser in rocket fuel.

Nitrogen makes up about 78% of air. It is found in nitrates (KNO₃, NaNO₃), proteins and fertilisers. Industrially it is obtained by the fractional distillation of liquid air (nitrogen boils at −196 °C, before oxygen at −183 °C). Removing oxygen from air with alkaline pyrogallol leaves nitrogen mixed with noble gases. Pure nitrogen in the laboratory: heat ammonium nitrite, NH₄NO₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O (usually made by warming ammonium chloride with sodium nitrite solution).

Colourless, odourless, tasteless gas, slightly soluble in water, a little lighter than air. It is very unreactive at room temperature because of the strong triple bond N≡N. At high temperature or in an electric spark: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (with Fe catalyst, 450 °C, 200 atm); N₂ + O₂ → 2NO; 3Mg + N₂ → Mg₃N₂ (magnesium nitride).

Uses: making ammonia and fertilisers; nitric acid (the Ostwald process); liquid nitrogen as a coolant; an inert atmosphere for packing food and in electric bulbs; and explosives (TNT, nitroglycerine).

units.title: Hardness of Water
units.summary: What makes water hard, temporary and permanent hardness, and methods of softening hard water with equations.

p: Hard water does not form a lather easily with soap but makes a white scum. It contains dissolved salts of calcium and magnesium. Soft water lathers easily. 2C₁₇H₃₅COONa + Ca²⁺ → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Ca↓ + 2Na⁺ (scum).

Caused by calcium hydrogencarbonate, Ca(HCO₃)₂, and magnesium hydrogencarbonate, Mg(HCO₃)₂. They form when rain water containing dissolved CO₂ flows over limestone or chalk: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂ (soluble).

Removal: (1) boiling: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + CO₂ + H₂O (the insoluble carbonate forms 'fur' or scale in kettles and boilers); (2) adding slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂ (Clark's method): Ca(HCO₃)₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2CaCO₃↓ + 2H₂O.
Caused by the sulphates and chlorides (and nitrates) of calcium and magnesium (CaSO₄, MgSO₄, CaCl₂, MgCl₂). They are soluble and cannot be removed by boiling.

Removal: (1) washing soda, Na₂CO₃: CaSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄ (also removes temporary hardness). (2) Ion exchange (zeolite or permutit): zeolite is a sodium aluminosilicate, Na₂Z. Na₂Z + Ca²⁺ → CaZ + 2Na⁺. When the zeolite is used up, it is regenerated by passing concentrated sodium chloride solution through it. (3) Calgon: sodium hexametaphosphate binds Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ in a soluble complex, so they cannot form scum.

sections.h: Advantages and disadvantages of hard water
p: Advantages: the calcium helps to build bones and teeth, and it gives a good taste. Disadvantages: it wastes soap, leaves scum, and forms scale in boilers, kettles and pipes, which wastes fuel and can block pipes.

Shake a sample with soap solution. Soft water gives a lather at once. Hard water gives scum, and more soap is needed before lather forms. After boiling, if the lather forms easily, the hardness was temporary.

units.title: Purification of Water and Water Quality Control
units.summary: The steps of municipal water treatment, distilled water, the parameters of water quality and why quality control is important.

p: Water purification removes unwanted chemical, biological and physical impurities to make water safe to drink and to use. Steps in a municipal water works:

img.alt: A flow diagram of water purification: screening, sedimentation, coagulation, filtration, chlorination and storage
img.cap: Steps in water treatment.

p: 1. Screening: wire screens remove leaves, sticks and plastics. 2. Sedimentation: the water stands in large tanks so that suspended particles settle. 3. Coagulation (flocculation): alum, KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O, is added. It hydrolyses to give jelly-like Al(OH)₃, which traps fine particles, bacteria and colloids in large lumps (flocs) that settle. 4. Filtration: through beds of sand, gravel and sometimes activated charcoal; the charcoal removes bad taste and smell. 5. Chlorination: a small amount of chlorine, or sodium hypochlorite, kills germs: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl, where hypochlorous acid is the germ killer. 6. Aeration: air is bubbled through to remove H₂S and CO₂ and to add oxygen, which improves the taste. 7. Softening where needed (lime-soda or ion exchange). 8. Distillation: for laboratories only; it gives pure water free from salts and germs.

Distilled water is pure water made by distillation, with no dissolved salts. It is used in laboratories, for preparing solutions and in car batteries, but it is not good for regular drinking because it lacks minerals. Potable water is safe to drink: it is free from harmful germs and poisons, though it contains useful dissolved minerals.
This means monitoring, testing and regulating water so that it meets safety standards.
Physical: colourless, tasteless, odourless and clear (low turbidity).
Chemical: pH 6.5 to 8.5; hardness below about 150 ppm; low chloride; no lead, cadmium, mercury or arsenic above safe limits.
Biological: free from harmful microbes; coliform bacteria show faecal contamination.

It prevents cholera, dysentery and typhoid; it protects public health; it prevents scale and corrosion in boilers and pipes; it ensures suitable water for medicines, drinks, textiles and electronics; and it meets standards set by WHO and NAFDAC. Governments can protect water quality by treating sewage, controlling industrial waste, testing supplies regularly, protecting water sources and educating the public.

units.title: Environmental Pollution: Types and Causes
units.summary: Pollution and pollutants, biodegradable and non-biodegradable pollutants, and the causes of air, water, soil, noise, thermal and radioactive pollution.

p: The environment is everything around us that affects living things: air, water, soil, plants and animals. Pollution is a harmful change in the physical, chemical or biological character of the environment. It may be natural (volcanic eruptions, dust storms) or man-made (industry, deforestation, burning of fuels). A pollutant is a substance that causes pollution.

Biodegradable pollutants are broken down by microbes (food waste, sewage, paper). Non-biodegradable pollutants stay in the environment and build up in food chains (plastics, heavy metals, DDT, radioactive isotopes).

Carbon monoxide: from incomplete burning of petrol; it combines with haemoglobin. Carbon dioxide: burning fuels and deforestation; global warming. Sulphur dioxide: coal burning, refineries, volcanoes; acid rain. Nitrogen oxides: vehicles and industry; smog and acid rain. Particulates (dust, smoke, soot, asbestos): factories and cement works; lung disease. CFCs: refrigerants and aerosols; they destroy the ozone layer. Smog in big cities reduces visibility and causes breathing problems.

Sewage and domestic waste (cholera, typhoid, dysentery). Industrial effluents with mercury, cadmium and lead (the Minamata disease in Japan was mercury poisoning from industrial waste). Agricultural run-off with nitrates and phosphates: eutrophication, from nutrients to algal bloom to oxygen loss to death of aquatic life. Oil spills coat the water surface and stop oxygen dissolving.
The damage of land by harmful chemicals, waste or bad land use: too much pesticide (for example DDT) and fertiliser; dumping of plastics, metals and glass; oil spills; acid rain; and mining waste.

Noise pollution: unwanted loud sound from traffic, generators, machines and loudspeakers; it causes stress and hearing loss. Thermal pollution: hot waste water from power stations and factories reduces the oxygen in rivers. Radioactive pollution: from nuclear accidents, nuclear tests and waste; the radiation lasts a very long time (Chernobyl 1986 and Fukushima 2011).

units.title: Effects and Control of Pollution
units.summary: How pollution harms health, plants, aquatic life, climate and ecosystems, and the control measures for each kind of pollution.

p: On health: breathing diseases (asthma, bronchitis, lung cancer) from air pollutants; brain and nerve damage from lead and mercury; stomach diseases from dirty water; stress and hearing loss from noise.
On plants and farming: acid rain destroys crops and washes out soil nutrients; heavy metals build up in plants and enter food chains; oil spills ruin farmland.
On water life: fish kills from oxygen loss after eutrophication; mercury and cadmium in fish are harmful when eaten; oil spills and acidification damage coral reefs.
On climate and ecosystems: global warming from CO₂ and CH₄; ozone layer damage that increases ultraviolet radiation (skin cancer and cataracts); loss of species and biodiversity.
SO₂ and NOₓ dissolve in rain to form H₂SO₄ and HNO₃. Effects: kills plants and fish in lakes, damages soil, corrodes buildings, statues and metal roofs, and harms health.

Use cleaner fuels (biofuel, LPG, solar); fit catalytic converters to vehicles (they change CO and NOₓ to CO₂ and N₂); fit scrubbers and filters to factory chimneys; plant trees (afforestation) to absorb CO₂.

Treat sewage before release; use biodegradable detergents; clean up oil spills quickly with dispersants and absorbents; control industrial effluent by law. Recycle and reuse materials; practise organic farming to reduce fertiliser and pesticide use; use controlled landfills and proper waste disposal.

Use silencers on engines and machines; separate residential and industrial areas by law; enforce noise rules. Cool hot waste water before releasing it, using cooling towers. Store nuclear waste securely underground, follow international treaties and use shielding and monitoring in nuclear plants.

It protects the health of people and animals; it protects living things and ecosystems; it helps to prevent climate change and disasters; it makes sure that resources can be used for a long time (sustainability); and it leaves a cleaner world for future generations.

units.title: Sulphur and Sulphur Dioxide
units.summary: Occurrence and allotropes of sulphur, and the preparation, properties, tests and uses of sulphur dioxide.

p: Sulphur (S) is a yellow, brittle non-metal, atomic number 16. It is found uncombined in volcanic regions (Sicily, USA) and combined in iron pyrites FeS₂, galena PbS, zinc blende ZnS, copper pyrites CuFeS₂ and gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O.

Allotropes (different forms of the same element): rhombic sulphur is stable at room temperature, with yellow crystals that melt at 114 °C (density 2.06 g/cm³); monoclinic sulphur is stable above 96 °C, with needle-shaped crystals that melt at 119 °C. Both are made of S₈ rings. Sulphur is insoluble in water but dissolves in carbon disulphide, and it burns with a blue flame to give sulphur dioxide.
Laboratory: Na₂SO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + SO₂, or Cu + 2H₂SO₄(conc.) → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O. It is collected by upward delivery (downward displacement of air), because it is denser than air.
Industry: burning sulphur, S + O₂ → SO₂, or roasting sulphide ores: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂ and 4FeS₂ + 11O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8SO₂.
A colourless gas with a sharp, choking smell, denser than air, very soluble in water. It dissolves to give sulphurous acid: SO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂SO₃.
1. An acidic oxide: it reacts with alkalis to give sulphites and hydrogensulphites. SO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₃ + H₂O; SO₂ + NaOH → NaHSO₃.

2. A reducing agent: it reduces iron(III) to iron(II): 2Fe³⁺ + SO₂ + 2H₂O → 2Fe²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ (yellow-brown to pale green). It reduces iodine: I₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O → 2HI + H₂SO₄. It changes acidified potassium dichromate from orange to green and decolourises purple potassium manganate(VII). These are tests for SO₂.
3. Bleaching: it bleaches wool, silk and paper by reducing the colouring matter. The bleaching is temporary because the colour returns in air as oxygen is taken up.
Uses: bleaching paper and textiles; preserving dried fruit and wine; making sulphuric acid (Contact process); fumigant and disinfectant.
Hazards: SO₂ is a major air pollutant. It irritates the lungs and causes acid rain: 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃, SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ (or overall SO₂ + H₂O + ½O₂ → H₂SO₄).

units.title: Sulphuric Acid: The Contact Process, Properties and Uses
units.summary: The manufacture of sulphuric acid by the Contact process, the physical and chemical properties of the acid, its uses and safety.

p: Raw materials: sulphur (or sulphide ores), air and water.

1. Burn sulphur: S + O₂ → SO₂. 2. Convert SO₂ to SO₃ over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH = −197 kJ (for 2 mol SO₂), at about 450 °C and 1 to 2 atm. 3. Absorb SO₃ in concentrated sulphuric acid to make oleum: SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇. 4. Dilute the oleum with water: H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄.

Why SO₃ is not dissolved straight into water: the reaction is violent and gives a fog of acid droplets that is hard to collect. Why these conditions: the reaction is exothermic and 3 mol of gas become 2, so low temperature and high pressure would give more SO₃; but a low temperature is too slow, so about 450 °C is used with a catalyst, and because the yield is already about 98% at 1 to 2 atm, high pressure is not worth its cost.

img.alt: A flow diagram of the Contact process from sulphur to sulphur dioxide, sulphur trioxide, oleum and sulphuric acid with the conditions
img.cap: The Contact process.

p: A colourless, thick, oily liquid. Density 1.84 g/cm³; boiling point 338 °C. It mixes with water and gives out a lot of heat, so always add the acid slowly to the water, never water to the acid. It is hygroscopic (takes in water) and corrosive to skin and metals.
1. A strong acid (dilute): it reacts with metals, bases and carbonates. Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂; H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.
2. A dehydrating agent (concentrated): it removes water from sugar, leaving black carbon: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O. It turns blue CuSO₄·5H₂O white. It dries gases (not NH₃).
3. An oxidising agent (hot, concentrated): Cu + 2H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O; C + 2H₂SO₄ → CO₂ + 2SO₂ + 2H₂O.
4. It forms sulphates with metals, bases and metal oxides.

Fertilisers (ammonium sulphate and superphosphate); detergents; petroleum refining; lead-acid battery electrolyte; paints, dyes, drugs and explosives; laboratory reagent for dehydration and oxidation.

Concentrated acid burns skin and eyes. Wear goggles and gloves. If it spills on skin, wash with plenty of water. Spills acidify soil and water. SO₂ from the plant must not be released into the air: it causes acid rain.

units.title: Carbon and the Oxides of Carbon
units.summary: Allotropes and special properties of carbon, and the preparation, properties, tests and uses of carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide.

p: Atomic number 6; electronic configuration 1s²2s²2p²; valency 4 (it forms four covalent bonds). Allotropes: crystalline (diamond, graphite) and amorphous (coal, charcoal, coke). Diamond is very hard, a poor conductor and clear; graphite is soft and slippery and conducts electricity. Special properties of carbon: tetravalency; catenation (joining to itself in long chains and rings); the ability to form single, double and triple bonds; and isomerism (same formula, different structure). These make carbon the basis of organic chemistry.

A colourless, odourless, very poisonous gas. Preparation: incomplete burning of carbon, 2C + O₂ → 2CO; or dehydration of methanoic acid with concentrated H₂SO₄, HCOOH → CO + H₂O. It burns with a blue flame: 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂. It is a strong reducing agent: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (used in the blast furnace). Uses: reducing agent in metallurgy; making methanol and synthetic fuels. Hazard: it combines with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen, and causes suffocation. (Never run a generator or a car engine in a closed room.)

A colourless, odourless gas, denser than air, slightly acidic. Preparation: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ (marble chips and dilute HCl), or heating a carbonate: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Collected by upward delivery or over water (it is only slightly soluble).

Properties: it does not burn and puts out fires; it dissolves slightly in water to give carbonic acid H₂CO₃ (a weak acid). Test: it turns limewater milky. Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O. With excess CO₂ the milkiness disappears: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂.
Uses: fire extinguishers; fizzy drinks; dry ice (solid CO₂) as a refrigerant; photosynthesis. As a greenhouse gas it contributes to global warming.

units.title: Carbonates and Introduction to Hydrocarbons
units.summary: Properties and uses of carbonates, and the three families of hydrocarbons: alkanes, alkenes and alkynes, with isomerism and laboratory preparation.

p: Carbonates are salts of carbonic acid: Na₂CO₃, CaCO₃, K₂CO₃. Sodium and potassium carbonates dissolve in water; most others do not. Heating: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (thermal decomposition; the carbonates of sodium and potassium are stable to heat). CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂ (green to black). Hydrogencarbonates: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. With acids: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
Uses: Na₂CO₃ in glass, soap and detergents (and as washing soda); CaCO₃ (limestone, marble, chalk) in cement and as a building material; K₂CO₃ in fertilisers and soft soap.
Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen.

Alkanes: saturated (single bonds only), general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆. Not very reactive; undergo substitution with halogens in UV light; burn with a clean flame: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
Alkenes: unsaturated (a double bond C=C), CₙH₂ₙ: ethene C₂H₄. Very reactive; undergo addition reactions (hydrogenation, halogenation); burn with a smoky flame; decolourise bromine water.
Alkynes: unsaturated (a triple bond C≡C), CₙH₂ₙ₋₂: ethyne C₂H₂. Very reactive; undergo addition; burn with a very sooty flame.

Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. C₄H₁₀ has two isomers: n-butane (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃) and isobutane or 2-methylpropane ((CH₃)₃CH). C₅H₁₂ has three (pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane).
Methane: heat sodium ethanoate with soda lime (NaOH and CaO): CH₃COONa + NaOH → CH₄ + Na₂CO₃. Ethyne: calcium carbide with water: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂.

Uses: fuels (LPG, petrol, kerosene, diesel); raw materials for plastics, alcohols, detergents, synthetic fibres and drugs. Effects: CO₂ from burning fuels causes global warming; CO is poisonous; burning fuels releases soot, CO, NO₂ and SO₂, which cause air pollution and acid rain.
Alkanes: saturated, substitution, CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. Alkenes: unsaturated, addition, C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂. Alkynes: triple bond, C₂H₂ + H₂ → C₂H₄ (and then C₂H₆).

units.title: Industrial Preparation of Hydrochloric Acid and Ammonia
units.summary: The industrial manufacture of hydrochloric acid and of ammonia by the Haber process, with the conditions, properties, uses and safety.

p: HCl, NH₃ and H₂SO₄ are basic industrial chemicals. They are raw materials for fertilisers, dyes, medicines, plastics, explosives and cleaning agents. The amounts made show how industrialised a country is.

img.alt: Three panels showing the manufacture of hydrochloric acid, ammonia by the Haber process and sulphuric acid by the Contact process
img.cap: Industrial preparation of HCl, NH₃ and H₂SO₄.

p: Raw materials: sodium chloride and concentrated sulphuric acid. NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl (about 150 °C); then at a higher temperature (about 400 °C) NaHSO₄ + NaCl → Na₂SO₄ + HCl. The HCl gas is absorbed in water in an absorption tower to give concentrated hydrochloric acid. (Today much HCl is also made by burning hydrogen in chlorine, and as a by-product of making chlorinated organic compounds.)

Properties: a colourless, choking gas, very soluble in water. Uses: removing rust from metals (pickling); making PVC and chlorides; adjusting pH in water treatment and food industries; regenerating ion-exchange resins; a laboratory reagent. Hazard: corrosive; the fumes are toxic, so work in a fume cupboard and wear protective clothing.
Raw materials: nitrogen (from air by fractional distillation) and hydrogen (from natural gas or water gas, or by electrolysis). N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol.

Conditions: temperature 400 to 500 °C (a compromise between rate and yield); pressure 200 to 250 atm (a high pressure favours ammonia because 4 mol of gas become 2); catalyst: iron with promoters such as potassium and aluminium oxides; unreacted gases are recycled. The mixture is cooled under pressure so that the ammonia liquefies and is separated.

Why recycling raises efficiency: only about 15% of the gases change to ammonia in one pass. The unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are passed back through the reactor, so almost all of them are finally used and little is wasted.

A colourless gas with a sharp smell; very soluble in water, giving a weakly alkaline solution: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ (often written as ammonium hydroxide, NH₄OH). Uses: nitrogenous fertilisers (urea, ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulphate); nitric acid by the Ostwald process; refrigerant; household cleaners; explosives and medicines. Hazard: toxic and irritating to eyes, lungs and skin; stored in strong pressurised tanks.

units.title: Industrial Chemicals Compared, with Environment and Safety
units.summary: A comparison of the manufacture and uses of HCl, NH₃ and H₂SO₄, why sulphuric acid is the 'king of chemicals', and safety and environmental precautions.

p: Study the table.

HCl: about 150 to 400 °C, atmospheric pressure, no catalyst. NH₃: 400 to 500 °C, 200 to 250 atm, iron catalyst. H₂SO₄ (SO₂ to SO₃ step): 450 °C, 1 to 2 atm, V₂O₅ catalyst. Both the Haber and Contact processes involve reversible, exothermic reactions, so a compromise temperature is chosen: low enough to give a good yield, high enough for a fast rate.

Sulphuric acid is called the king of chemicals because it is used in so many industries (fertilisers, detergents, dyes, plastics, paper, metals, batteries and petroleum refining), and the amount a country uses is a measure of its industry. Ammonia is the key chemical for farming, because it is the starting point for most fertilisers. Hydrochloric acid is used widely in metal treatment and in making other chemicals.

HCl: acid fumes pollute air and must be scrubbed (washed) before release. NH₃: toxic gas that can burn the eyes and lungs; pressure tanks need monitoring. H₂SO₄: spills acidify soil and water; it is a strong oxidiser and burns skin. Workers need goggles, gloves, aprons, ventilation, eye-wash stations and training. Waste gases (SO₂, NH₃, HCl) must be treated, and acids must be neutralised before disposal.

units.title: Organic Chemistry Revision: Classification, Homologous Series and Functional Groups
units.summary: What organic chemistry is, its sources and general characteristics, how organic compounds are classified, homologous series and functional groups.

p: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds (except the simple oxides of carbon, carbonates and carbides). Organic compounds are mostly covalent. Carbon is special because of tetravalency (four bonds), catenation (chains and rings) and the ability to form sp³ (single), sp² (double) and sp (triple) bonds. It is the basis of petrochemicals, plastics, medicines, cosmetics, farm chemicals, dyes and detergents, and of living matter.

Natural: petroleum (hydrocarbons), coal (aromatic compounds), natural gas (methane), and plants and animals (fats, oils, carbohydrates, proteins). Synthetic: made in laboratories and factories (plastics, drugs, fertilisers).

Low melting and boiling points (covalent molecules); poor conductors of electricity; usually insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents (benzene, ether); most are combustible; reactions are usually slower than those of inorganic compounds.

By structure: acyclic (open chain, aliphatic), cyclic (rings, non-aromatic) and aromatic (benzene and its derivatives). By saturation: saturated (single bonds only: alkanes) and unsaturated (double or triple bonds). By functional group.

A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same general formula, the same functional group, members that differ by CH₂, similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties.
A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives a compound its characteristic properties.

units.title: IUPAC Naming of Organic Compounds
units.summary: The rules for naming organic compounds step by step, with worked examples for alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and acids.

sections.h: Prefixes for the length of the chain
p: 1 carbon: meth-, 2: eth-, 3: prop-, 4: but-, 5: pent-, 6: hex-, 7: hept-, 8: oct-, 9: non-, 10: dec-.
1. Find the longest continuous carbon chain that includes the functional group. This is the parent chain.
2. Number the chain from the end that gives the lowest number to the principal functional group (then to double or triple bonds, then to substituents).
3. Name the substituents (side groups): methyl (CH₃–), ethyl (C₂H₅–), chloro, bromo.
4. Give each substituent and each double or triple bond a position number.
5. Join the parts: prefixes (substituents, in alphabetical order) + parent name + suffix of the functional group.
6. For identical groups use di-, tri-, tetra-: 2,2-dimethylpropane.
7. Functional groups have priority in numbering over double or triple bonds and substituents.

CH₃CH₂CH₃: propane (3-carbon alkane). CH₃CH₂OH: ethanol (–OH on carbon 1). CH₃CH₂CHO: propanal (aldehyde group at carbon 1). CH₃COCH₃: propanone (ketone at carbon 2). CH₃CH=CHCH₃: but-2-ene (double bond at carbon 2). CH≡C–CH₃: prop-1-yne. CH₃CH(OH)CH₃: propan-2-ol. CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃: 2-methylpropane. CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃: 2-methylbutane. CH₃COOH: ethanoic acid. CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl: 1-chloropropane. CH₃COOC₂H₅: ethyl ethanoate.

For an alcohol, remove the final –e of the alkane and add –ol (ethane → ethanol). For an aldehyde, the suffix is –al (the group is always at carbon 1). For a ketone it is –one, with the number of the carbonyl carbon if needed (pentan-2-one). For an acid, add –oic acid (butanoic acid).

units.title: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Alkynes and Their Reactions
units.summary: The three families of hydrocarbons compared, with combustion, substitution, addition and oxidation reactions and their equations.

p: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes have single bonds only (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) and are called saturated. Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) have one C=C. Alkynes (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂) have one C≡C. Alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated.

img.alt: A chart of hydrocarbons divided into alkanes, alkenes and alkynes with general formulae and examples
img.cap: The families of hydrocarbons.

p: Complete combustion (plenty of air) gives CO₂ and H₂O: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O; C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Incomplete combustion (limited air) gives carbon monoxide or carbon: 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O. Alkanes burn with a clean blue flame. Alkenes burn with a smoky flame and alkynes with a very sooty, luminous flame, because their molecules have a high percentage of carbon.
In UV light or heat, halogens replace hydrogen atoms: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl; CH₃Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl; and so on up to CHCl₃ and CCl₄. A mixture of products forms.

The double or triple bond opens and atoms add on. Hydrogenation (Ni catalyst): C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆. Halogenation: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ (bromine water is decolourised). Hydrogen halides: C₂H₄ + HBr → C₂H₅Br. Hydration (steam, H₃PO₄, about 300 °C, high pressure): C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH (industrial ethanol). Polymerisation: nCH₂=CH₂ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)ₙ.
Alkynes add twice because of the triple bond: C₂H₂ + 2Br₂ → C₂H₂Br₄; C₂H₂ + H₂ → C₂H₄, then C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆.

Mild oxidation of an alkene with cold dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII): C₂H₄ + [O] + H₂O → CH₂OH–CH₂OH (a diol); the purple colour disappears. Strong oxidation breaks the C=C bond to give carboxylic acids or ketones.

units.title: Laboratory Tests for Hydrocarbons, Uses and Environmental Effects
units.summary: Tests that distinguish alkanes, alkenes and alkynes, uses of hydrocarbons and their environmental effects.

p: 1. Bromine water test: add orange bromine water and shake. Alkanes: no change (without UV light). Alkenes and alkynes: the colour disappears (they are unsaturated).
2. Baeyer's test: add acidified purple KMnO₄. Alkanes: no change. Alkenes and alkynes: the purple colour disappears (and a brown MnO₂ may form).
3. Ignition test: burn in a Bunsen flame. Alkanes: clean blue flame. Alkenes: smoky. Alkynes: very sooty, luminous.

4. Ammoniacal silver nitrate: terminal alkynes (R–C≡CH, for example ethyne) give a white precipitate of silver acetylide: HC≡CH + 2AgNO₃ + 2NH₃ → AgC≡CAg↓ + 2NH₄NO₃. Alkenes and alkanes give none. (Dry silver acetylide can explode; the precipitate must be destroyed with dilute acid after the test.)

img.alt: A flow chart for identifying an unknown hydrocarbon using bromine water and ammoniacal silver nitrate
img.cap: A flow chart for identifying hydrocarbons.

p: Alkanes: cooking gas (propane and butane), petrol (octane), lubricants, wax. Alkenes: polyethene and PVC plastics, ethanol, synthetic rubber. Alkynes: oxy-acetylene welding, synthetic rubber, plastics and solvents.

Air pollution: incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide and soot. Greenhouse effect: CO₂ from burning fuels causes global warming. Oil spills: hydrocarbons float on water and harm aquatic life and birds. Smog: unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides react in sunlight to make photochemical smog, which causes breathing problems.

units.title: Alcohols: Classification, Preparation, Reactions and Uses
units.summary: The structure and classification of alcohols, their properties, preparation by fermentation and hydration, and their reactions and uses.

p: Alcohols are derivatives of alkanes in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by a hydroxyl group (–OH). General formula for simple alcohols: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH.
By the number of –OH groups: monohydric (one: ethanol CH₃CH₂OH); dihydric (two: ethane-1,2-diol, glycol); trihydric (three: propane-1,2,3-triol, glycerol); polyhydric (many: sugars such as glucose).

By the carbon carrying the –OH: primary (1°): attached to a carbon bonded to one other carbon (CH₃CH₂OH); secondary (2°): attached to a carbon bonded to two other carbons (CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, propan-2-ol); tertiary (3°): attached to a carbon bonded to three other carbons ((CH₃)₃COH, 2-methylpropan-2-ol).

Boiling points are higher than those of alkanes of similar size, because of hydrogen bonding between molecules. The lower alcohols (methanol, ethanol, propanol) dissolve in water because they can form hydrogen bonds with water; solubility falls as the molecules get larger. They have a characteristic smell and are poor conductors.

1. Fermentation of carbohydrates: glucose is changed by the enzyme zymase in yeast: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (at about 35 °C, without air). This is how palm wine, beer and industrial ethanol from molasses are made.
2. Hydration of ethene: C₂H₄ + H₂O ⇌ C₂H₅OH, with phosphoric acid on a support as catalyst, at about 300 °C and 60 to 70 atm.
3. Reduction of aldehydes and ketones: an aldehyde gives a primary alcohol and a ketone gives a secondary alcohol.
1. Combustion: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O (clean flame).
2. With sodium: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂ (sodium ethoxide; hydrogen is given off).

3. Oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (orange to green): a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde and then a carboxylic acid (CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO → CH₃COOH); a secondary alcohol gives a ketone (CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ → CH₃COCH₃); a tertiary alcohol is not oxidised easily.
4. Esterification: with a carboxylic acid and concentrated H₂SO₄: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.
5. Dehydration: with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 170 °C ethanol gives ethene: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O.

Ethanol: drinks, solvent, antiseptic, motor fuel (blended with petrol), making esters, perfumes and medicines. Methanol: making methanal (formaldehyde), solvent, antifreeze and fuel (methanol is very poisonous and can cause blindness). Glycerol: cosmetics, explosives (nitroglycerine) and food. Ethylene glycol: antifreeze and polyester.
