units.title: Ethers and Phenols, and Comparison with Alcohols
units.summary: The structure, preparation, reactions and uses of ethers and phenols, and a comparison of alcohols, ethers and phenols.

p: Ethers have two alkyl or aryl groups joined to the same oxygen atom: R–O–R′. Examples: diethyl ether C₂H₅–O–C₂H₅ (symmetrical) and methyl ethyl ether CH₃–O–C₂H₅ (unsymmetrical).

Physical properties: volatile and highly flammable; slightly soluble in water; boiling points much lower than alcohols of the same molar mass, because ether molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other. They are more volatile than the alcohols for this reason.

Preparation: (1) dehydration of an alcohol with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 140 °C: 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O. (2) Williamson synthesis: sodium alkoxide with an alkyl halide: C₂H₅ONa + CH₃I → CH₃OC₂H₅ + NaI.
Reactions: burn to give CO₂ and H₂O; react with hot concentrated HI: C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + HI → C₂H₅I + C₂H₅OH; and form explosive peroxides when kept in air.
Uses: diethyl ether as an anaesthetic (less used now because it is flammable), solvents in laboratories and industry, and starting materials for plastics, perfumes and drugs.
Phenols have an –OH group bonded directly to a benzene ring. The simplest is phenol, C₆H₅OH. It is a colourless solid with a characteristic smell, fairly soluble in water, and weakly acidic.

Preparation: (1) fusing sodium benzenesulphonate with NaOH: C₆H₅SO₃Na + 2NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + Na₂SO₃ + H₂O, then acidifying: C₆H₅ONa + HCl → C₆H₅OH + NaCl. (2) Hydrolysing chlorobenzene with NaOH at high temperature and pressure.

Reactions: with sodium (hydrogen is given off); with NaOH to give sodium phenoxide and water, C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O (ethanol does not react with NaOH); with bromine water to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr; with dilute nitric acid to give nitrophenols. Test: neutral iron(III) chloride gives a violet colour.
Uses: antiseptics and disinfectants; making aspirin and other drugs; making plastics (Bakelite), dyes and explosives.

sections.h: Why phenol is more acidic than ethanol
p: When phenol loses H⁺, the negative charge on the phenoxide ion is spread (delocalised) into the benzene ring, which makes the ion stable. In the ethoxide ion the charge stays on the oxygen and is less stable. So phenol gives up H⁺ more readily and reacts with NaOH, but ethanol does not.

units.title: Aldehydes and Ketones: Structure and Preparation
units.summary: The carbonyl group, general formulae and examples of aldehydes and ketones, and their preparation.

p: Aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl group, C=O. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the group is polar: the carbon is slightly positive and attracts nucleophiles. Aldehydes: R–CHO, with the carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one hydrogen (methanal HCHO, ethanal CH₃CHO, benzaldehyde C₆H₅CHO). Ketones: R–CO–R′, with the carbonyl carbon bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups (propanone CH₃COCH₃, butanone CH₃COC₂H₅).
1. Oxidation of a primary alcohol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distilling off the aldehyde as it forms (so that it is not oxidised further): CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O.

2. Methanal from methanol: air and a hot silver (or copper) catalyst: CH₃OH + ½O₂ → HCHO + H₂O. Methanal is also made by the oxidation of methane over molybdenum or copper catalysts: CH₄ + O₂ → HCHO + H₂O.
3. Hydroformylation (oxo process): alkene + CO + H₂ with a cobalt or rhodium catalyst: CH₂=CH₂ + CO + H₂ → CH₃CH₂CHO (propanal).
1. Oxidation of a secondary alcohol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O.
2. Friedel-Crafts acylation (aromatic ketones): C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl → C₆H₅COCH₃ + HCl, with AlCl₃ as catalyst.
3. Heating the calcium salt of a carboxylic acid: (CH₃COO)₂Ca → CH₃COCH₃ + CaCO₃.
4. Hydration of an alkyne (water, dilute H₂SO₄ and Hg²⁺): propyne gives propanone (Markovnikov's rule: the –OH goes to the carbon with fewer hydrogens). (Ethyne itself gives an aldehyde, ethanal.)
Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid (with strong oxidation). Secondary alcohol → ketone (which resists further oxidation). Tertiary alcohols are resistant.

units.title: Identification Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones
units.summary: The 2,4-DNP, Tollens', Fehling's, Benedict's and Schiff's tests, a comparison of aldehydes and ketones, and their uses.

sections.h: General test for the carbonyl group
p: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP): both aldehydes and ketones give a yellow-orange crystalline precipitate (a hydrazone). This shows a carbonyl group is present.
Tollens' test (ammoniacal silver nitrate), warmed: aldehydes give a silver mirror. RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O. Ketones give no reaction.

Fehling's test (Fehling's solution A and B, warmed): aldehydes reduce the deep blue Cu²⁺ complex to a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O. Ketones do not react. (Benzaldehyde, which is aromatic, does not give a positive Fehling's test.)
Benedict's test: like Fehling's: a red precipitate with aldehydes (aliphatic).
Schiff's test: aldehydes restore the pink or magenta colour of Schiff's reagent. Ketones do not.

img.alt: A decision tree for carbonyl compound tests using 2,4-DNP, Tollens' test and Fehling's test
img.cap: Testing carbonyl compounds.

sections.h: Why aldehydes are oxidised but ketones are not
p: An aldehyde has a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, so it can easily be oxidised to a carboxylic acid (this is what reduces the silver or copper ions). A ketone has no such hydrogen, so it is resistant to mild oxidation.

units.title: Carboxylic Acids: Structure, Properties and Reactions
units.summary: The carboxyl group, naming, physical properties, acidity and reactions of carboxylic acids, and their uses.

p: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group, –COOH (a C=O and an –OH on the same carbon). General formula RCOOH. Examples: methanoic acid HCOOH (formic acid, from ants), ethanoic acid CH₃COOH (acetic acid, in vinegar) and benzoic acid C₆H₅COOH. IUPAC name: change the –e of the alkane to –oic acid.

The lower members (methanoic and ethanoic acids) are colourless liquids with a sharp smell; higher members are solids. Boiling points are higher than those of alcohols of similar size, because acid molecules form pairs (dimers) joined by two hydrogen bonds. Small acids dissolve in water; solubility falls as the chain gets longer. They taste sour and are corrosive when concentrated.

Carboxylic acids are weak acids, partly ionised in water: RCOOH ⇌ RCOO⁻ + H⁺. They turn blue litmus red. They are stronger acids than alcohols, because the carboxylate ion is stabilised by resonance (the negative charge is shared by the two oxygen atoms).
1. With bases: CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O.
2. With carbonates: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂ (effervescence of CO₂ is a test for an acid).
3. With reactive metals: 2CH₃COOH + 2Na → 2CH₃COONa + H₂.
4. Esterification with an alcohol and concentrated H₂SO₄: CH₃COOH + CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O.
5. Reduction with LiAlH₄ gives a primary alcohol.
Oxidation of a primary alcohol: CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, heating under reflux). Oxidation of an aldehyde: CH₃CHO + [O] → CH₃COOH.

Ethanoic acid (vinegar): food and preserving, solvent, making esters. Methanoic acid: tanning leather, dyeing cloth and preserving silage. Benzoic acid: a preservative in soft drinks and juices. Dicarboxylic acids: raw materials for nylon and polyester.

units.title: Esters: Structure, Preparation, Hydrolysis and Uses
units.summary: The structure and naming of esters, esterification, acid and alkaline hydrolysis, and the uses of esters.

p: An ester is formed when the hydrogen of the –COOH group of a carboxylic acid is replaced by an alkyl group: R–COOR′. Naming: alkyl alkanoate, with the alkyl part from the alcohol and the alkanoate from the acid. CH₃COOCH₃ is methyl ethanoate; CH₃COOC₂H₅ is ethyl ethanoate; C₂H₅COOCH₃ is methyl propanoate.

A carboxylic acid and an alcohol, heated with a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid (a catalyst and also a dehydrating agent), form an ester and water: RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O. The reaction is reversible. In the mechanism, the acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen, the alcohol attacks the carbonyl carbon, a proton moves and water is lost. The acid supplies the –OH that is lost with the H of the alcohol.

img.alt: The reversible esterification reaction of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol with sulphuric acid as catalyst to give an ester and water
img.cap: Esterification is reversible.

p: Propanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl propanoate. Methanoic acid + propan-1-ol → propyl methanoate. Benzoic acid + methanol → methyl benzoate.

Esters have pleasant fruity smells. The smaller esters are liquids and the larger are waxy solids. They do not dissolve in water. Their boiling points are lower than those of acids of the same molar mass, because there are no hydrogen bonds between ester molecules.

Acid hydrolysis (reversible): CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH (dilute acid catalyst). Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification, not reversible): CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + C₂H₅OH. This is how soap is made from fats and oils (esters of glycerol). Esters burn with a clean flame to CO₂ and H₂O.

Perfumes and flavours (isoamyl ethanoate smells of bananas; ethyl butanoate of pineapple); solvents for paints and varnishes (ethyl ethanoate); making plastics and synthetic fibres (polyesters such as Terylene); soap making; plasticisers in PVC.

units.title: Polymers and Plastics: Types and Uses
units.summary: Monomers and polymers, natural and synthetic polymers, addition and condensation polymerisation, thermoplastics and thermosets, and the uses of common plastics.

p: Poly means many and meros means parts. A polymer is a very large molecule (a macromolecule) made of many repeating small units (monomers) joined by covalent bonds. The reaction is polymerisation. The number of repeating units in a chain is the degree of polymerisation. Molar masses can reach millions. Examples: ethene → polyethene; glucose → starch and cellulose; isoprene → natural rubber; amino acids → proteins.

img.alt: A chart classifying polymers into natural polymers (DNA, protein, rubber) and synthetic polymers (addition polymers like polyethene and condensation polymers like nylon)
img.cap: Classification of polymers.

p: Natural polymers: starch, cellulose and glycogen (from glucose); proteins (from amino acids); DNA and RNA (from nucleotides); natural rubber (polyisoprene). Synthetic polymers: polyethene, polystyrene, PVC, nylon, Terylene, Bakelite and silicone rubbers.

Unsaturated monomers (with C=C) join without losing any small molecule (heat, pressure and a catalyst are needed). nCH₂=CH₂ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)ₙ polyethene. PVC from chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl); polystyrene from styrene (C₆H₅CH=CH₂); Teflon (PTFE) from tetrafluoroethene (CF₂=CF₂): nCF₂=CF₂ → (–CF₂–CF₂–)ₙ.

Monomers with two functional groups join, and a small molecule such as water or HCl is lost each time. Nylon-6,6: hexane-1,6-diamine H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ + hexanedioic (adipic) acid HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH → –[NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO]ₙ– + H₂O (an amide, or peptide, link). Terylene (polyester): ethane-1,2-diol + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid) → –[O–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO]ₙ– + H₂O. Bakelite: phenol + methanal.

img.alt: The repeating units of polyethene, polypropene, PVC, polystyrene, Terylene and a polyurethane
img.cap: Repeating units of some polymers.

p: Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be re-moulded: they have long chains with no cross-links (polyethene, PVC, polystyrene). Thermosetting plastics harden permanently when heated and cannot be re-moulded: they have many cross-links between chains (Bakelite, melamine, epoxy resins). By mechanical properties: elastomers are stretchy (natural rubber, neoprene), fibres are strong threads (nylon, Terylene, silk) and plastics are rigid or flexible solids.

Polyethene: bags, films, bottles, buckets and pipes. PVC: wire insulation, water pipes, floor tiles and roofing. Polystyrene: disposable cups, packaging foam, insulation. Teflon: non-stick pans and gaskets. Nylon: clothes, ropes, nets, toothbrush bristles and parachutes. Terylene: clothes, curtains and conveyor belts. Bakelite: electric switches and plugs, handles of pans. Rubber: tyres, shoes and shock absorbers. PVC is good for cable insulation because it does not conduct and it is flexible and cheap; Bakelite is used for switches because it does not soften when heated.

units.title: Dangers of Plastics and How to Control Them
units.summary: The harm done by plastics to the environment and health, and recycling, biodegradable alternatives and other solutions.

p: 1. Non-biodegradable: plastics stay in soil and water for decades. They block drains and cause flooding and ugly rubbish heaps.
2. Poisonous when burnt: burning PVC releases hydrogen chloride; incomplete burning of plastics gives carbon monoxide and dioxins, which can cause cancer.
3. Marine pollution: fish, turtles and birds swallow plastic and die. Tiny pieces (microplastics) enter the food chain and reach humans.
4. Health hazards: plastic packaging can release additives such as phthalates and BPA into food and drinks, which can disturb hormones.
5. Resource use: most plastics are made from petroleum, which is running out.
6. Fire risk: many plastics burn easily and give off dense, poisonous smoke.

Recycling and reuse: collect, melt and re-mould plastics (sort them by type). Biodegradable plastics: made from starch or polylactic acid (PLA), which microbes can break down. Waste management: collect and dispose of waste properly, with laws against dumping. Replacement: use paper, cloth, glass, metal or clay containers. Education: teach people to reduce, reuse and recycle. Laws: ban or tax single-use plastics such as shopping bags and straws.

In many Nigerian cities, plastic sachets and bottles block gutters and make floods worse during the rainy season. Collecting bottles for recycling, using reusable bags and cups, and keeping drains clear are simple things that students can start with.

units.title: Nutrition and the Alimentary Canal: From Mouth to Stomach
units.summary: The five stages of nutrition, the parts of the alimentary canal, and how the mouth, oesophagus and stomach digest food.

p: Nutrition is the process by which an organism takes in and uses food to support life. It has five stages.

Ingestion: taking food into the body. Digestion: breaking large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble ones that can be absorbed. Absorption: the passage of digested food from the gut into the blood and lymph. Assimilation: the use of the absorbed nutrients by the body's cells for energy, growth and repair. Egestion: the removal of undigested food (such as cellulose fibre) as faeces. Egestion is not excretion, because the material was never part of the body's cells.
The alimentary canal is a continuous muscular tube about 9 m long, from the mouth to the anus. The associated organs (salivary glands, liver, gall bladder and pancreas) add secretions.

img.alt: A diagram of the human digestive system with the mouth, salivary glands, oesophagus, liver, gall bladder, stomach, pancreas, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus labelled
img.cap: The human digestive system.

p: Teeth chew food (mechanical digestion) into a soft bolus and increase its surface area for enzymes. The tongue moves food, mixes it with saliva and starts swallowing. There are three pairs of salivary glands (parotid, sublingual, submandibular). Saliva contains water (to moisten), mucin (to lubricate) and salivary amylase (ptyalin), which begins the digestion of starch into maltose.
A muscular tube from the pharynx to the stomach. Peristalsis, a wave of contraction of the smooth muscle that pushes the bolus along, works even if you swallow while upside down.

A J-shaped, stretchy muscular bag that stores food and mixes it. Gastric glands in its wall secrete gastric juice, which has: hydrochloric acid (pH about 1.5 to 2.0: it denatures proteins, kills most germs and activates pepsinogen to pepsin); pepsin, an enzyme that breaks proteins into shorter polypeptides; and rennin (in infants) that clots milk protein so that it stays longer. Three layers of muscle churn the food into a semi-liquid called chyme. The pyloric sphincter lets small amounts into the small intestine at a time.
The stomach shows both kinds of digestion: mechanical (churning) and chemical (pepsin and acid).

sections.h: What happens to a piece of bread
p: In the mouth the teeth crush it and saliva wets it; amylase starts changing starch to maltose. Peristalsis carries the bolus down the oesophagus. In the stomach, the acid stops the action of salivary amylase (which needs a neutral pH). The bread is churned into chyme; the small amount of protein in bread (gluten) starts to be digested by pepsin, but starch digestion has paused.

units.title: The Small and Large Intestine and the Liver and Pancreas
units.summary: The three parts of the small intestine, the large intestine, and the roles of the liver (bile) and pancreas (pancreatic juice) in digestion.

p: The main place for digestion and absorption. It has three parts. The duodenum (about 25 cm) is C-shaped: chyme mixes with bile and pancreatic juice here and most chemical digestion is completed. The jejunum (about 2.5 m) is the middle part, where some absorption begins. The ileum (about 3.5 m) is the longest part and is specialised for absorption of digested food.

Wider but shorter than the small intestine. It absorbs water and minerals from the undigested residue, making it solid as faeces. It contains friendly (symbiotic) bacteria that make vitamin K and some B vitamins. The rectum stores faeces until they leave through the anus.

The liver makes bile, a greenish-yellow alkaline fluid. Bile is not an enzyme. It has two jobs: (1) emulsification: bile salts break large fat droplets into tiny droplets, which increases the surface area many times so that the enzyme lipase can act quickly; (2) neutralisation: it neutralises the acid chyme from the stomach and gives the right pH (alkaline) for the pancreatic and intestinal enzymes. The gall bladder stores and concentrates bile and releases it through the bile duct into the duodenum when fat arrives.

The pancreas is both an exocrine and an endocrine gland. Its exocrine part makes pancreatic juice, which has sodium hydrogencarbonate (to neutralise acid), pancreatic amylase (digests starch), trypsin (digests proteins) and pancreatic lipase (digests fats). These enter the duodenum by the pancreatic duct. (Its endocrine part makes insulin and glucagon.)

sections.h: Why bile matters even though it has no enzyme
p: Fat does not mix with water, so lipase can only reach the surface of large fat globules. Bile breaks the globules into a fine emulsion, so the total surface area for lipase is much larger and digestion is fast.

units.title: Digestive Enzymes and Enzyme Specificity
units.summary: How digestive enzymes work (hydrolysis, lock and key), a table of the main enzymes, their pH and products, and an experiment on amylase.

p: Enzymes are biological catalysts, almost always proteins, that speed up reactions and are not used up. Digestive enzymes are hydrolases: they split large molecules by adding water (hydrolysis). Each enzyme is specific: its active site has a shape that fits only one kind of substrate, like a key in a lock. That is why starch, proteins and fats each need a different enzyme.

sections.h: Why are some enzymes made inactive?
p: Pepsinogen and trypsinogen are made as inactive forms so that they do not digest the cells that make them. They are activated (by acid, or by an intestinal enzyme) only inside the gut.

Aim: to show that amylase digests starch. Hypothesis: starch will disappear and sugar will appear when amylase is added. Method: mix starch solution with saliva (or amylase solution) at 37 °C. At intervals, take drops and test with iodine solution: blue-black means starch is present; brown means starch is gone. Test the mixture with Benedict's solution and heat: an orange-brown colour shows reducing sugar (maltose). Control: starch with boiled saliva or with water gives no change. Result: the iodine test becomes negative and the Benedict's test positive over time.

units.title: Absorption in the Ileum and Assimilation
units.summary: The adaptations of the ileum and the villus for absorption, how nutrients are absorbed, where they go, and the role of the liver in assimilation.

p: 1. Great length (over 3 m in the ileum alone). 2. Folds of Kerckring: circular folds of the wall. 3. Villi: millions of finger-like projections about 1 mm long. 4. Microvilli: the cells on each villus have a brush border of tiny projections, giving a huge extra surface. 5. A very good blood supply: every villus has a network of capillaries and a central lacteal (a lymph vessel). The epithelium is only one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is short.

img.alt: A diagram of the small intestine and an enlarged villus showing the blood capillaries, the lacteal and the epithelium
img.cap: The structure of a villus.

p: Simple diffusion: fatty acids, glycerol and some vitamins move down their concentration gradient. Facilitated diffusion: carrier proteins without energy (fructose). Active transport: uses ATP to move nutrients against a gradient (glucose, galactose, amino acids), so absorption is complete even when the gut has little of them.
Glucose, fructose, galactose and amino acids enter the blood capillaries of the villi. These join to form the hepatic portal vein, which takes them straight to the liver.

Fatty acids and glycerol diffuse into the epithelial cells, are rebuilt into triglycerides, and are packed with protein into tiny droplets called chylomicrons. These are too big for the capillaries and enter the lacteals instead. The lymph later empties into the bloodstream near the heart. If a lacteal is blocked, fat absorption is poor and fats (and fat-soluble vitamins) are lost in the faeces.

sections.h: Assimilation: the role of the liver
p: Glucose control: the liver turns excess glucose into glycogen (glycogenesis) for storage, and turns glycogen back to glucose (glycogenolysis) when blood sugar is low.

Amino acids: used to build body proteins. Excess amino acids cannot be stored, so the liver removes the amino group (–NH₂) (deamination) and turns it into urea, which the kidneys excrete. The rest (the carbon part) is used for energy or made into fat.
Fats: the liver changes and repackages fats, makes cholesterol and breaks down old red blood cells.
The liver is vital because everything absorbed from the gut (except most fat) passes through it first, so it can store, change or remove substances to keep the blood composition steady.

Meat protein → pepsin (stomach) → shorter peptides → trypsin (duodenum) → peptidases (ileum) → amino acids → absorbed by active transport into the capillaries → hepatic portal vein → liver → blood → muscle cell, where the amino acids are joined to make muscle protein.

units.title: Why Organisms Need Transport Systems: Surface Area to Volume Ratio and Diffusion
units.summary: The SA:V ratio and why large organisms need transport systems, and diffusion with the factors that affect its rate.

sections.h: The surface area to volume ratio
p: As an object gets bigger, its volume grows faster than its surface area, so the ratio of surface area to volume (SA:V) falls. Example: a cube with 1 mm sides has a surface area of 6 mm² and a volume of 1 mm³, so SA:V = 6 : 1. If the same volume is cut into 1 000 cubes of 0.1 mm, the total surface area is 60 mm² and SA:V = 60 : 1. A cube with 10 cm sides has SA:V = 600/1 000 = 0.6 : 1.

Unicellular organisms such as Amoeba are small and have a high SA:V. Oxygen, food and wastes cross the cell membrane quickly by diffusion, and streaming of the cytoplasm (cyclosis) spreads materials inside. They need no transport system.

Large multicellular organisms (humans, elephants, trees) have a low SA:V. Cells deep inside are too far from the outside for diffusion to supply them fast enough. So they have transport systems: the circulatory system in animals and xylem and phloem in plants. Flatworms are flat so that every cell is near the surface and they do not need a heart; an elephant is very big with a small SA:V and needs one.

Diffusion is the net movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration (down a concentration gradient). It is a passive process (no ATP) driven by the kinetic energy of the particles.

Factors affecting its rate: (1) concentration gradient (the steeper, the faster); (2) temperature (higher means faster); (3) surface area (larger means more particles cross); (4) distance (shorter means faster); (5) size of molecules (smaller diffuse faster).
Examples: gas exchange in alveoli; movement of neurotransmitters across a synapse; absorption of some digested food in the ileum; oxygen entering a leaf.

units.title: Osmosis and Active Transport
units.summary: Osmosis and water potential, the effects of osmosis on animal and plant cells, active transport, and a comparison of the three transport processes.

p: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential (a dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (a concentrated solution) through a selectively permeable membrane. Pure water has the highest water potential (Ψ = 0); adding solute lowers it (makes it more negative). Osmosis is passive.

sections.h: Osmosis in animal cells (red blood cells)
p: Isotonic solution (same water potential as the cell): the cell stays normal. Hypotonic solution (outside more dilute): water enters, the cell swells and may burst (lysis). Hypertonic solution (outside more concentrated): water leaves and the cell shrinks and becomes spiky (crenation).

img.alt: Three beakers showing a red blood cell in isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic solutions: normal, swollen and shrunken
img.cap: Red blood cells in isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic solutions.

p: In a hypotonic solution (such as pure water), water enters, the cytoplasm pushes on the strong cell wall and the cell becomes turgid. This supports non-woody plants. In a hypertonic solution, water leaves the vacuole, the cytoplasm shrinks away from the wall (plasmolysis) and the plant wilts.
Examples: a dried apricot swells in pure water because its cells take up water by osmosis. A fresh cucumber in concentrated salt water becomes limp because water leaves its cells by osmosis.

Active transport is the movement of substances from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration, against the gradient. It needs energy (ATP from respiration) and specific carrier proteins in the membrane, which act as pumps and change shape to carry the substance across.

Examples: the sodium-potassium pump (needed for nerve impulses); uptake of mineral ions by root hair cells (soil water is very dilute, so ions must be pumped in); reabsorption of glucose and amino acids in the kidney tubules; absorption of glucose in the ileum.

units.title: The Mammalian Circulatory System and the Heart
units.summary: Closed double circulation, the structure of the heart, valves and the cardiac cycle.

p: Mammals have a closed circulatory system: blood stays inside vessels (arteries, veins and capillaries), so blood pressure is high and flow can be controlled. It is a double circulation: the blood passes through the heart twice in each circuit of the body.

Pulmonary circulation: right side of the heart → lungs → left side of the heart (for gas exchange). Systemic circulation: left side of the heart → body tissues → right side of the heart (delivers oxygen and nutrients and removes wastes).
A four-chambered muscular organ in the chest, slightly to the left, protected by the ribs.

Atria (upper chambers, thin walls) receive blood. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins.

Ventricles (lower chambers, thick walls) pump blood out. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery. The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body through the aorta, and has the thickest wall because it must push blood through the long systemic circuit at high pressure.

Valves: atrioventricular valves (tricuspid on the right with 3 flaps, bicuspid or mitral on the left with 2 flaps) stop blood flowing back into the atria. Semilunar valves at the base of the pulmonary artery and aorta stop blood flowing back into the ventricles.

img.alt: A labelled diagram of the heart showing the vena cava, atria, ventricles, valves, pulmonary artery and veins, and aorta
img.cap: The structure of the heart and the flow of blood.

p: One heartbeat takes about 0.8 s. (a) Atrial systole: the atria contract and push blood into the ventricles. (b) Ventricular systole: the ventricles contract; the AV valves shut ('lub'); the semilunar valves open and blood is pushed into the arteries. (c) Diastole: all chambers relax; the semilunar valves shut ('dub'); the heart refills from the veins.
The coronary arteries, the first branches of the aorta, supply the heart muscle itself with blood. A blockage causes a heart attack (myocardial infarction).
Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid valve → left ventricle → aorta → body → vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle.

units.summary: Arteries, veins and capillaries compared, and plasma, red cells, white cells and platelets with blood clotting.

img.alt: Cross-sections of an artery and a vein showing the layers of the wall, the valve in the vein and the capillary network between them
img.cap: An artery, a vein and capillaries.

p: Blood is a connective tissue of cells in a liquid called plasma. Plasma (about 55%) is a straw-coloured liquid, 92% water. It carries blood cells, nutrients, hormones, urea, CO₂ and heat.

Red blood cells (erythrocytes) have no nucleus in mammals and are packed with haemoglobin. Their biconcave shape gives a large surface area for gas exchange and makes them flexible. Haemoglobin joins reversibly with oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin and releases it in the tissues.

White blood cells (leucocytes) are larger and have a nucleus. Phagocytes (neutrophils and macrophages) engulf and digest germs (phagocytosis): a non-specific defence. Lymphocytes give specific immunity: B cells make antibodies and T cells destroy infected body cells.

img.alt: A phagocyte engulfing a bacterium by phagocytosis
img.cap: Phagocytosis.

p: Platelets are small cell fragments that help blood to clot. When a vessel is cut: (1) the vessel narrows (vasoconstriction); (2) platelets stick to the damaged place and form a temporary plug; (3) coagulation: chemicals released by platelets and damaged tissue change the soluble protein fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads, which trap red cells and form a clot. The clot stops blood loss and keeps germs out until the wound heals.

units.title: The Respiratory System: Structure and Gas Exchange
units.summary: Breathing versus cellular respiration, the parts of the respiratory tract and how each is adapted, and the structure of the alveoli.

p: Breathing (ventilation) is the movement of air into and out of the lungs; it is a physical process. Cellular respiration is the chemical release of energy from glucose in cells. They are linked: breathing brings in the oxygen that cells need for respiration and removes the carbon dioxide that respiration produces.

1. Nostrils and nasal cavity: lined with hairs and ciliated mucous membrane. They filter (hairs and mucus trap dust and germs), warm (blood capillaries), moisten the air and contain the smell receptors.
2. Pharynx: a shared passage for air and food. The epiglottis, a flap of cartilage, closes over the glottis when we swallow so that food goes into the oesophagus and we do not choke.
3. Larynx (voice box): cartilage plates (the Adam's apple is the thyroid cartilage) and the vocal cords, which vibrate to make sound; pitch depends on their tension.

4. Trachea (windpipe): 10 to 12 cm long, held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage that stop it collapsing when pressure drops during breathing in. It is lined with ciliated cells and goblet cells. Goblet cells make mucus that traps dirt; the cilia beat upwards (the mucociliary escalator) to sweep it to the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed out.

5. Bronchi and bronchioles: the trachea divides into two bronchi (one to each lung) and then into smaller bronchioles. As they get smaller, there is less cartilage and more smooth muscle, which controls the flow of air.
6. Alveoli: the bronchioles end in clusters of tiny air sacs. There are about 300 to 500 million alveoli, giving a surface area of about 70 to 100 m².

1. A large surface area (millions of alveoli). 2. A thin diffusion path: the alveolus wall and the capillary wall are each one cell thick, and the respiratory membrane is only about 0.5 to 1 µm thick. 3. A moist surface so that gases can dissolve. 4. A rich blood supply of capillaries, which keeps a steep concentration gradient by bringing deoxygenated blood and carrying oxygenated blood away. 5. Surfactant, a detergent-like secretion that lowers the surface tension of the fluid so that the alveoli do not collapse when we breathe out. (That is about a quarter of the area of a tennis court, packed inside your chest.)

img.alt: Gas exchange between an alveolus and a pulmonary capillary with oxygen diffusing into the blood and carbon dioxide diffusing out
img.cap: Gas exchange in an alveolus.

units.title: The Mechanism of Breathing
units.summary: How the diaphragm, ribs and intercostal muscles change the pressure in the chest to move air in and out, and a simple lung model.

p: Air moves from a place of higher pressure to a place of lower pressure. Breathing works by changing the volume, and therefore the pressure, of the chest (thoracic) cavity. The lungs have no muscles of their own. They are pulled open and pushed shut by the diaphragm (a dome-shaped sheet of muscle under the lungs) and the intercostal muscles (between the ribs). Boyle's law says: when the volume of a gas increases, its pressure decreases (and the other way round).

img.alt: Diagrams of inhalation and exhalation showing the rib cage, diaphragm, and the movement of air into and out of the lungs
img.cap: Inhalation and exhalation.

p: 1. The external intercostal muscles contract and pull the rib cage up and out. 2. The diaphragm contracts and flattens, moving down. 3. The volume of the thoracic cavity increases. 4. The pressure inside the lungs falls below the pressure of the air outside. 5. Air rushes in until the two pressures are equal.

1. The external intercostal muscles relax and the rib cage moves down and in (its weight and the elastic pull of the lungs help). 2. The diaphragm relaxes and returns to its dome shape. 3. The volume of the thoracic cavity decreases. 4. The pressure in the lungs rises above the outside pressure. 5. Air is pushed out.
Forced exhalation, as in coughing, blowing out candles or hard exercise, is active: the internal intercostal muscles and the muscles of the abdomen contract and squeeze the air out.
Compare the two actions.

Take a plastic bottle and cut off the base. Push a Y-shaped tube into the neck with a balloon tied on each arm (the lungs). Seal the cut end with a rubber sheet (the diaphragm). Pull the rubber sheet down: the volume inside the bottle increases, the pressure drops and the balloons inflate (inhalation). Push the sheet up: the balloons deflate (exhalation).
Limit of the model: the model cannot show the ribs and intercostal muscles, and real lungs are not hollow bags but spongy tissue with millions of alveoli.

units.title: Cellular Respiration: ATP and Aerobic Respiration
units.summary: ATP as the cell's energy currency, the equation and the three stages of aerobic respiration, with a note on the exact ATP yield.

p: Cellular respiration is the controlled release of energy from food, mainly glucose, inside living cells using enzymes. The energy is stored in a molecule called ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the 'energy currency' of the cell. Think of glucose as a large banknote and ATP as small coins that the cell can spend on moving, making proteins, active transport, nerve impulses and keeping warm.

ATP/ADP cycle: ATP has three phosphate groups. When a cell needs energy, an enzyme removes the last phosphate: ATP → ADP + Pᵢ + energy. Respiration provides the energy to join the phosphate back on: ADP + Pᵢ + energy → ATP. The cell keeps recycling the same molecules.
Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP).
Balanced equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP (about 38 ATP in the school syllabus).
It is an oxidation reaction. The energy released was captured from sunlight in photosynthesis and stored in glucose.
1. Glycolysis (cytoplasm; no oxygen needed): one glucose (6 carbons) is split into two pyruvate molecules (3 carbons each). Net gain: 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
2. Krebs cycle (matrix of the mitochondrion; needs oxygen): pyruvate is completely broken down, giving off CO₂. It makes 2 ATP and loads many NADH and FADH₂ (electron carriers).

3. Electron transport chain (inner membrane of the mitochondrion): the electrons from NADH and FADH₂ pass along a chain of proteins and release energy that pumps hydrogen ions (H⁺) across the membrane. The ions flow back through the enzyme ATP synthase, which makes about 34 ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and joins with hydrogen to make water. This is why we must breathe in oxygen.

sections.h: A note on the ATP total
p: The figure 38 ATP is the traditional maximum used in Nigerian exams. Newer measurements show that, because of energy lost in moving molecules across the membranes, the real yield is closer to 30 to 32 ATP per glucose. For WAEC and NECO, write 38 (or 36 to 38); in higher studies use about 30 to 32. Either way, aerobic respiration gives about 15 times more ATP than anaerobic.

sections.h: Why mitochondria are called the powerhouse
p: Cells that need a lot of energy, such as muscle cells, sperm tails and the cells of the kidney tubule, have many mitochondria. The folded inner membrane (cristae) gives a large surface area for the electron transport chain.

units.title: Anaerobic Respiration, Oxygen Debt and Fermentation
units.summary: Respiration without oxygen in muscle and in yeast, oxygen debt, the uses of fermentation, and a comparison with aerobic respiration.

p: Anaerobic respiration is the partial breakdown of glucose without oxygen. It takes place in the cytoplasm only and yields just 2 ATP per glucose (from glycolysis), because most of the energy stays locked in the end product.

Equation: glucose → lactic acid + 2 ATP. During hard exercise, such as a sprint, the muscles use oxygen faster than the blood can bring it. Pyruvate is changed to lactic acid. This gives NAD⁺ back to the cell, so glycolysis can carry on making ATP quickly. The lactic acid builds up and causes tiredness, pain and cramp in the muscles.

Oxygen debt: after exercise we keep breathing hard and the heart beats fast. The extra oxygen is used to remove the lactic acid: the liver changes much of it back to glucose and some is oxidised completely to CO₂ and water. This extra oxygen is the oxygen debt that is being 'repaid'.

sections.h: In yeast and plants: alcoholic fermentation
p: Equation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + 2 ATP. Pyruvate first loses CO₂ to become ethanal (acetaldehyde), which is then changed to ethanol.

Uses: in baking, the CO₂ makes dough rise and the alcohol evaporates in the oven. In brewing, the ethanol makes palm wine, beer and other drinks (in Nigeria, burukutu and pito also use fermentation). In industry, yeast makes ethanol for biofuel from sugar cane or cassava starch.
Study the table.

sections.h: Is anaerobic respiration a waste of glucose?
p: It is a less efficient use of glucose, but it is very useful: it gives a quick burst of energy when oxygen is short (a sprint, escaping danger), it lets yeast and some bacteria live where there is no oxygen, and it is the basis of baking, brewing, yoghurt and bio-fuel production. So the statement is only partly true.

units.title: Excretion and the Organs That Excrete
units.summary: Excretion compared with egestion, and how the lungs, skin and liver remove wastes, including deamination and the breakdown of haemoglobin.

p: Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism (chemical reactions in cells) from the body. Examples: carbon dioxide from respiration, and urea from the breakdown of amino acids. Egestion (defecation) is the removal of undigested food, such as the fibre from yam peel, which was never part of the body's cells. Faeces are therefore egested, not excreted (a common exam trap).

img.alt: A diagram showing the excretory organs of the body: lungs, skin, liver and kidneys, with the waste each removes
img.cap: The excretory organs.

p: Carbon dioxide and water vapour from cell respiration diffuse from the blood into the alveoli and are breathed out.
Sweat glands release sweat: water, salts (NaCl), a little urea and lactic acid. Its main job is cooling by evaporation, but it also excretes a small amount of waste.

sections.h: The liver: the body's chemical factory
p: The liver does not expel wastes itself. It changes them so they can be excreted.

Deamination: excess amino acids cannot be stored. The liver removes the toxic amino group (–NH₂), which is changed into ammonia (NH₃) and quickly combined with CO₂ to make urea, a much less harmful substance. The remaining carbon part is used for energy or stored as fat. Urea goes into the blood to the kidneys.

Breakdown of haemoglobin: old red blood cells (they live about 120 days) are broken down in the liver and spleen. The iron is recycled to make new haemoglobin. The rest is turned into bile pigments (bilirubin), which leave in the bile into the intestine and give faeces its brown colour. In jaundice, bilirubin builds up and the skin and eyes turn yellow.
Detoxification: it changes alcohol, drugs and other poisons into harmless forms for the kidneys to excrete.
The main organs of excretion for nitrogenous waste (especially urea). They also control the water and salt content of the blood (osmoregulation), which is the next topic.

units.title: The Urinary System and the Nephron
units.summary: The organs of the urinary system, the structure of the nephron and the two stages of urine formation: ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption.

p: Kidneys (2): bean-shaped organs at the back of the abdomen. They filter the blood and make urine. Ureters (2): muscular tubes that carry urine to the bladder by peristalsis. Urinary bladder: a stretchy muscular bag that stores urine. Urethra: the tube that takes urine out of the body; it is longer in males than in females.
Blood reaches each kidney by the renal artery and leaves by the renal vein. A kidney has an outer cortex, an inner medulla and a space called the pelvis, which leads to the ureter.
Each kidney has about one million microscopic nephrons.

1. The Malpighian body (renal corpuscle) is the filter. It has the glomerulus (a knot of capillaries) and the Bowman's capsule, a cup around it that collects the filtrate. 2. The renal tubule is the modifier: the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), the loop of Henle (a U-shaped loop dipping into the medulla), the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) and the collecting duct, which takes urine to the pelvis.

img.alt: A labelled nephron showing the glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct and blood vessels
img.cap: The nephron and its blood supply.

p: The afferent arteriole bringing blood in is wider than the efferent arteriole taking blood out. This makes the blood pressure inside the glomerulus very high. The pressure forces water and small molecules (urea, glucose, amino acids, salts) through the capillary wall, the basement membrane and the podocytes into the Bowman's capsule. Blood cells and large proteins are too big to pass. The fluid is called the glomerular filtrate: it is like plasma without proteins.
More than 99% of the filtrate goes back into the blood in the capillaries around the tubule, so the body does not lose useful things.
PCT: all the glucose and amino acids, vitamins and most of the ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻) are taken back by active transport. Water then follows by osmosis (about 80%).
Loop of Henle: builds up a high salt concentration in the medulla, which is needed to save water.
DCT: fine-tunes the amount of salts and water, under the control of hormones.
Collecting duct: the last place where water is reabsorbed, under the control of ADH.

sections.h: What is in the filtrate, and what is in urine?
p: Compare these.
If glucose is in the urine, the tubule could not reabsorb all of it because the blood sugar was too high. This is one sign of diabetes mellitus, and a test strip dipped in urine can detect it.

units.title: Water Balance, ADH and Kidney Disorders
units.summary: How the hormone ADH controls the water content of the blood, and kidney stones, nephritis, kidney failure, dialysis and transplants.

p: The body must keep the water content of the blood steady. The hypothalamus in the brain detects the concentration of the blood. The pituitary gland releases the hormone ADH (antidiuretic hormone) into the blood, and ADH acts on the collecting ducts in the kidney.

img.alt: A diagram showing how ADH is released and acts on the kidney's collecting duct to control water reabsorption
img.cap: The action of ADH.

p: The blood becomes too concentrated (low water potential). The hypothalamus signals the pituitary to release more ADH. ADH makes the walls of the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water is drawn back into the blood by the salty medulla. The result: a small volume of dark, concentrated urine, and you also feel thirsty.

sections.h: When you have drunk a lot of water
p: The blood is too dilute. Less ADH is released. The collecting ducts are less permeable, so less water is reabsorbed. The result: a large volume of pale, dilute urine. So if a person drinks a large volume of water, urine output increases. This is a negative feedback loop: the body corrects any change to bring the water level back to normal.

If the body makes too little ADH (diabetes insipidus), a person passes very large volumes of dilute urine and is always thirsty. Alcohol blocks the release of ADH, which is why people urinate more and become dehydrated after drinking it.

Kidney stones (renal calculi): crystals of salts such as calcium oxalate form in the kidney. If they move into the ureter, they cause severe pain and may block urine flow. Prevention: drink plenty of water.
Nephritis: swelling of the kidney, usually from infection or from the body's own immune system, which damages the nephrons.

Kidney (renal) failure: the kidneys can no longer filter blood and urea builds up (uraemia). Treatment: dialysis, where a machine acts as an artificial kidney, filtering the blood through a membrane, or a kidney transplant, where a healthy kidney from a matching donor replaces the failed one. A person can live with one kidney, so a living relative can donate.
Ethical issues: there are too few donors, and selling organs is illegal in Nigeria and many countries. Always take medical advice.

units.title: Nutrient Cycling and the Water Cycle
units.summary: Why elements are recycled, and the processes of the water cycle: evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation and run-off.

p: The amount of matter on Earth is fixed. Nothing new arrives, so the elements that make life, such as carbon, nitrogen and water, must be used over and over again. These biogeochemical cycles show how elements move from the environment into living things and back. Without recycling, the soil would run out of nutrients and ecosystems would collapse.
Water moves continuously on, above and below the surface of the Earth, powered by the Sun's energy.

img.alt: The water cycle with evaporation from the sea, transpiration from plants, condensation into clouds, precipitation, run-off and infiltration
img.cap: The water cycle.

p: Evaporation: liquid water turns to vapour, mainly from oceans, lakes and rivers.
Transpiration: loss of water vapour from the leaves of plants through the stomata. Together with evaporation it is called evapotranspiration. A large tree may release hundreds of litres a day.
Condensation: rising vapour cools and condenses on dust particles to form clouds.
Precipitation: water falls as rain, snow, sleet or hail when droplets become too heavy.
Run-off: water flows over the land into streams and rivers and back to the sea.
Infiltration (percolation): water soaks into the soil and refills underground water (aquifers). We get well and borehole water from this store.
Water is the universal solvent for chemical reactions, the medium of transport in blood and in xylem, and it keeps plant cells turgid. It also gives a stable temperature to cells and lakes.

Human influence: cutting down forests reduces transpiration and rainfall, and paving over soil reduces infiltration and increases flooding, a serious problem in Nigerian cities during the rainy season.

units.title: The Carbon Cycle and Global Warming
units.summary: How carbon moves through photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion, and how people have upset the cycle.

p: Every organic molecule (sugar, fat, protein, DNA) is built on carbon. The carbon cycle also shows the flow of energy, because carbon in food carries the energy that organisms use.

img.alt: The carbon cycle showing carbon dioxide in the air, plants, animals, decomposers, fossil fuels and combustion
img.cap: The carbon cycle.

p: Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Green plants and algae take CO₂ from the air or water and build glucose. This is the main way carbon enters living things, and the main process that removes CO₂ from the air on a large scale (the oceans also dissolve some).
Respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP. All living things, including plants and decomposers, release CO₂ back to the air.
Feeding: carbon passes from plants to animals along food chains.

Decomposition: bacteria and fungi break down dead plants, animals and wastes, releasing CO₂ by respiration and returning nutrients to the soil. Where the dead remains are buried without oxygen over millions of years, they become coal, oil and natural gas (fossil fuels).
Combustion: burning wood or fossil fuels releases CO₂. Natural examples are bush fires; human examples are generators, vehicles, gas flaring and factories.

Burning of fossil fuels adds large amounts of 'old' carbon quickly, and deforestation reduces the number of plants that take in CO₂. The CO₂ level in the air has risen steadily. CO₂ is a greenhouse gas: it traps heat in the atmosphere, causing the enhanced greenhouse effect, global warming, melting ice, rising sea level and changes in rainfall.
Ways to help: plant trees, use solar and other clean energy, reduce gas flaring, use public transport, and recycle.

units.title: The Nitrogen Cycle
units.summary: The five processes of the nitrogen cycle, the bacteria that carry them out, and why leguminous crops improve the soil.

p: Nitrogen gas (N₂) is about 78% of the air, but it is so unreactive that plants and animals cannot use it directly. They need it in the form of nitrates to build proteins, DNA and chlorophyll. The nitrogen cycle, driven by microbes, changes it into useful forms and back.

img.cap: The nitrogen cycle.

p: Farmers use crop rotation or intercropping with legumes to put nitrogen back in the soil without buying fertiliser. Good drainage and ploughing keep soil aerated, so denitrification is low and nitrification is high. Too much nitrate fertiliser can be washed into rivers and lakes, causing eutrophication (a burst of algae growth that uses up the oxygen).
The Haber process fixes nitrogen industrially: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ makes fertiliser that feeds billions, but its misuse pollutes water. Both sides matter in the debate.

units.title: First Term Revision: Connecting the Systems
units.summary: The story of a glucose molecule and a protein molecule, a topic-by-topic revision guide and worked answers to the self-assessment questions.

p: The digestive, circulatory, respiratory and excretory systems work together. Cycles in nature connect the whole organism to the environment. Revise by following a molecule from the plate to the cell to the waste.

sections.h: The story of a glucose molecule (from bread)
p: Digestion: amylase in saliva and pancreatic juice and maltase in the ileum break starch to glucose. Absorption: glucose is actively transported into the villi of the ileum. Transport: the hepatic portal vein takes it to the liver, then the systemic circulation takes it to a muscle cell. Respiration: in the mitochondria, it is used in aerobic respiration to make ATP. Waste: CO₂ goes in the blood to the lungs and is breathed out; the water goes with the urine.

sections.h: The story of a protein molecule (from fish)
p: Digestion: pepsin (stomach), trypsin (duodenum) and peptidases (ileum) break it into amino acids. Absorption and transport: the amino acids go to the liver. Assimilation: used to build muscle and enzymes. Waste: excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver and make urea. Excretion: the urea is filtered by the kidneys and leaves in the urine.
Digestive system: the five stages of nutrition, enzyme table, villus, ileum adaptations, role of bile.
Transport: SA:V, diffusion, osmosis, active transport, heart, double circulation, vessels, blood and clotting.
Respiratory system: path of air, alveoli adaptations, breathing mechanism, aerobic and anaerobic respiration, oxygen debt.
Excretory system: excretion versus egestion, liver, nephron, ultrafiltration, reabsorption, ADH.
Nutrient cycles: water, carbon, nitrogen and the bacteria involved.

Diagrams to practise: alimentary canal; a villus; the heart; artery, vein and capillary; red cells in three solutions; respiratory tract; alveolus; breathing; urinary system; nephron; carbon and nitrogen cycles.

1. How do circulation and respiration supply a muscle cell? Air reaches the alveoli; oxygen diffuses into the blood and joins haemoglobin in the red cells; the heart pumps this blood through the aorta and arteries to the capillaries in the muscle; the oxygen is released and diffuses into the cell for respiration. CO₂ made by respiration diffuses into the blood, goes by the veins and vena cava to the heart, then through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it diffuses into the alveoli and is breathed out.

2. Fertiliser and fish deaths (eutrophication): nitrates wash into the lake after heavy rain. Algae grow rapidly (an algal bloom) and cover the surface. Light cannot reach plants below, which die. Bacteria decompose the dead algae and plants and use up the dissolved oxygen. The fish and other animals suffocate and die.
3. Celery in distilled water: the water has a higher water potential than the cells, so water enters the cells by osmosis. The cells become turgid and the celery stalk becomes firm and crisp.

units.title: Ecology: Levels of Organisation and Associations Between Organisms
units.summary: The meaning of ecology, biotic and abiotic factors, the levels from individual to biosphere, and the five kinds of association between living things.

p: Ecology is the scientific study of the relationships between living things and their surroundings. The word comes from the Greek oikos ('house') and logos ('study'): it is the study of the 'house' in which living things live.

Think of an ecosystem as a neighbourhood. Each organism has a job (its niche), deals with its neighbours (biotic factors, the living things such as plants, animals and microbes) and with the physical surroundings (abiotic factors, the non-living things such as rainfall, temperature, light, soil, pH and wind).
From the smallest to the largest:

Individual: one organism, for example one lion. Population: all the individuals of one species in one area, for example the pride of lions in Yankari Game Reserve. Community: all the populations of different species living and interacting in an area (lions, zebras, grasses, trees and bacteria). Ecosystem: the community together with its non-living environment (soil, rain, sunlight). Biome: a very large region with a similar climate and similar plants and animals, for example the tropical savanna or the tropical rainforest. Biosphere: all the parts of Earth where life exists, from the deepest ocean to the high mountains.
No organism lives completely alone. Species form close, long-term relationships, called associations or symbiosis. The signs + (benefits), – (harmed) and 0 (not affected) are used to show who gains.

head: Association
Effect
Example
rows: Bee and flower (nectar for the bee, pollination for the flower); Rhizobium in the root nodules of beans and groundnuts (the bacteria fix nitrogen, the plant gives sugar and a home)
+ / 0  one benefits, the other is not affected
Orchid growing on a tree branch (epiphyte); remora fish travelling on a shark and eating scraps
+ / –  the parasite benefits, the host is harmed
Ectoparasites on the surface: ticks, lice, fleas. Endoparasites inside: tapeworm, Plasmodium (malaria), Ascaris
Lion and zebra, hawk and chick, lizard and grasshopper
Lions and hyenas for the same prey; two crops for the same water and light

p: Strictly, scientists use 'symbiosis' for close living-together such as mutualism, commensalism and parasitism. Predation and competition are interactions but not always called symbiosis. Also, the lesson note says 'the tree is neither harmed nor helped' by the orchid; in a few cases a heavy load of epiphytes may harm a tree, but we treat the standard case as commensalism.
The Serengeti example in many books is in Tanzania. In Nigeria you can use Yankari, Gashaka-Gumti or Okomu National Park instead.

units.title: Tolerance and Adaptation
units.summary: Shelford's law of tolerance, the zones of the tolerance curve, and the structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations of organisms.

p: Tolerance is the ability of an organism to live and reproduce within a certain range of an environmental factor, such as temperature, pH or salt concentration. Shelford's law says that each organism has a minimum, an optimum and a maximum for each factor, and it cannot survive outside this range.

img.alt: A bell-shaped curve showing the zones of intolerance, physiological stress and optimum for an organism
img.cap: Shelford's law of tolerance.

p: Optimum range (the middle of the curve): the factor is at its best level, so the population is largest, healthiest and breeds well.
Zones of physiological stress (on both sides): the factor is too low or too high. The organism lives but is weak, grows slowly and cannot breed well.
Zones of intolerance (the far ends): the organism cannot live and soon dies.

Example: the fish tilapia has a temperature range. If the pond becomes too cold or too hot, the fish move into stress zones and die if they cannot escape. Different species have different ranges; a species with a wide range (such as the rat) is widespread, while one with a narrow range (such as some corals) is easily harmed by change.
An adaptation is an inherited feature that helps an organism to survive and reproduce in its environment. There are three kinds.

Structural adaptations are body features. Cactus (xerophyte): spines (leaves reduced to cut water loss), thick fleshy stem that stores water, deep or wide roots. Fish: streamlined body to reduce drag, gills to take oxygen from water, fins for steering. Camel: hump stores fat, long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep out sand, broad pads do not sink in sand.

Physiological adaptations are internal processes. Cactus (CAM photosynthesis): opens stomata at night to take in CO₂ and so loses less water in the hot day. Bears in cold lands hibernate (slow their body activity) to save energy. Salt-water fish pass out the extra salt through their gills and make little urine. Nigerian example: the lungfish aestivates in the mud during the dry season.

Behavioural adaptations are actions. Wildebeest migrate to areas with fresh grass and water. Desert animals are nocturnal (active at night) to avoid the heat. Birds make nests and weaver birds build hanging nests to avoid snakes.

units.title: Pollution: Air and Water
units.summary: The meaning of pollution, and the causes, effects and control of air pollution (including acid rain) and water pollution (including eutrophication).

p: Pollution is the introduction of harmful substances (pollutants) into the environment, causing harm to living things or to the environment itself. A pollutant is any substance in the wrong place, in the wrong amount, or at the wrong time.

Causes: factory fumes (sulphur dioxide SO₂ and oxides of nitrogen NOx); smoke and carbon monoxide from vehicles, generators and power plants; bush burning; dust from quarrying and cement factories; gas flaring in oil-producing areas; aerosol sprays (CFCs).

Effects: breathing diseases such as asthma, bronchitis and lung cancer; carbon monoxide (CO) joins with haemoglobin and prevents it from carrying oxygen (this is why using a generator in a closed room can kill); acid rain, in which SO₂ and NOx dissolve in rain to form acids that damage buildings (zinc roofs corrode), kill fish and harm crops and forests; global warming and climate change caused by greenhouse gases such as CO₂ and methane; and damage to the ozone layer by CFCs.

Control: use cleaner energy (solar, wind, hydro, natural gas); fit catalytic converters in vehicles and filters on factory chimneys; make and enforce laws about emissions; plant trees (afforestation); stop bush burning and gas flaring.

img.alt: A diagram showing how sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from factories and vehicles form acid rain that falls on forests, lakes and buildings
img.cap: How acid rain forms and what it harms.

p: Causes: untreated sewage and household waste; factory waste (effluent) containing metals and chemicals; run-off from farms carrying fertiliser and pesticides; oil spills from tankers and pipelines (a serious problem in the Niger Delta); dumping of refuse in drains and rivers.

Effects: eutrophication; water-borne diseases such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery; poisoning and death of fish and other water life; oil on the water surface cuts oxygen and light, and coats the feathers of water birds; heavy metals such as mercury build up in food chains and harm people who eat the fish.

Control: build and maintain sewage treatment plants; treat factory effluent before release; make laws against dumping and punish offenders; educate the public; use fertiliser in the right amounts; clean up oil spills with booms, skimmers and bacteria that eat oil.

1. Fertiliser or sewage, rich in nitrates and phosphates, enters a river or lake. 2. Algae grow very fast and cover the surface (an algal bloom). 3. The algae block the light, so the plants below die. 4. Bacteria decompose the dead algae and plants and use up the dissolved oxygen. 5. Fish and other animals suffocate and die. 6. The water becomes smelly and unfit to drink.

img.alt: A flow chart of eutrophication from fertiliser run-off to algal bloom, oxygen loss and death of fish
img.cap: The steps of eutrophication.

units.title: Pollution: Soil and Noise, and the Control of Pollution
units.summary: The causes, effects and control of land pollution and noise pollution, with a summary table of all four types.

p: Causes: dumping of domestic and industrial solid waste, especially non-biodegradable materials such as plastics, polythene bags and sachet-water bags; too much fertiliser and pesticide; mining and quarrying; oil spills and chemical waste; electronic waste (e-waste).

Effects: the soil loses fertility and crop yield falls; poisons seep through the soil into underground water (leaching); soil organisms such as earthworms and useful bacteria die; flooding, because refuse blocks drains; breeding places for flies, mosquitoes and rats which spread diseases.

Control: the 3 R's: Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again) and Recycle (turn waste into new things); use biodegradable products; bioremediation (using bacteria and fungi to clean polluted soil); organic farming; proper waste disposal and sanitary landfill; planting cover crops.
Noise is unwanted loud sound, measured in decibels (dB). Sound above about 85 dB over a long time can damage hearing.
Causes: traffic and horns, factories, generators, aircraft, loudspeakers at markets, churches, mosques and parties.
Effects: hearing loss; stress, headache and high blood pressure; poor sleep and poor concentration; it disturbs communication of animals and may drive them away.
Control: plant trees as sound barriers; use silencers on engines and generators; fit soundproof materials in buildings; keep factories away from homes; make and enforce laws about noise levels.
Study the table.

Do not litter, do not burn rubbish in the open, sort waste, use sachet-water bags only once and recycle them, service your generator, and write to local government about problems in your community. Good laws only work when people obey them.

units.title: Conservation of Natural Resources
units.summary: Conservation versus preservation, and the methods of conserving soil, water, forests and wildlife.

p: Conservation is the wise and sustainable use and management of natural resources so that they are not wasted, destroyed or made extinct, and are available for future generations.

Conservation is not the same as preservation. In conservation resources are used wisely (for example, selective felling, where only mature trees are cut). In preservation, nature is protected from any use at all (for example, a strict nature reserve where people cannot enter).

Importance: soil grows our food, filters water and supports many living things. Erosion by rain and wind removes the fertile top layer (a big problem in the south-east of Nigeria with gully erosion, and desert encroachment in the north).

Methods: contour ploughing (ploughing across the slope, not up and down, to slow run-off); terracing steep slopes; crop rotation (changing crops each season to keep nutrients); cover crops such as beans or sweet potato; mulching (covering the soil with dead leaves); planting trees and grass as windbreaks and shelter belts; adding manure; avoiding over-grazing.
Importance: water is needed for all life, for farming and for industry.

Methods: drip irrigation (water goes straight to the roots); rainwater harvesting; building dams and reservoirs; repairing leaking pipes; protecting river banks and wetlands; not wasting water; treating and reusing waste water.
Importance: forests give timber, firewood, food and medicine; they take in CO₂ and give out oxygen; they control climate and rainfall; they stop erosion and floods; and they shelter many species.

Methods: afforestation (planting trees where there were none) and reforestation (replanting where trees were cut); selective felling instead of clear-felling; forest reserves and national parks; laws against illegal logging; use of gas, kerosene or solar energy instead of firewood and charcoal; tree-planting campaigns.
Importance: keeps biodiversity and the balance of nature, gives food and medicine, supports tourism and has scientific and beauty value.

Methods: game reserves and national parks (for example Yankari, Kainji Lake, Cross River National Park and Okomu); laws against poaching (illegal hunting) and trade in animal products such as ivory and pangolin scales; captive breeding of endangered species (for example in zoos) to release later; education and community involvement; controlling hunting seasons.

units.title: Pests of Crops
units.summary: The kinds of crop pests (chewing, piercing and sucking, boring, nematodes, birds and rodents), the damage they do and the effects of pests on production.

p: A pest is any organism that harms crops, livestock or people or causes economic loss. Most crop pests are insects.

img.alt: A chart of common crop pests such as caterpillars, grasshoppers, aphids, weevils and rodents
img.cap: Some common crop pests.

p: Biting and chewing insects have strong jaws (mandibles) that cut leaves, stems and fruits. Examples: grasshoppers, locusts, beetles, caterpillars, fall armyworm. Damage: notched or eaten leaves (defoliation), holes in fruits.

Piercing and sucking insects have needle-like mouthparts (stylets) that pierce the plant and suck sap. Examples: aphids, mealybugs, whiteflies, leafhoppers, cotton stainers. Damage: yellow leaves (chlorosis), wilting, stunted growth, sticky honeydew on which sooty mould grows. They are dangerous as vectors: they carry viruses from sick plants to healthy ones as they feed (whiteflies spread cassava mosaic disease).

Boring insects have larvae (or adults) that bore into stems, fruits and seeds. Examples: stem borers in maize and sugar cane, maize weevils, bean weevils, cowpea beetles. Damage: hidden, because the harm is inside; plants wilt and die and stored grain is hollowed out.

img.alt: A stem borer larva inside a damaged maize stem
img.cap: A stem borer damaging maize.

p: Nematodes (eelworms) are tiny worms in the soil. Root-knot nematodes make swellings (galls) on roots, so the plant cannot take in water and minerals and becomes stunted and wilts.

Birds, such as quelea and weaver birds, eat ripening cereals (millet, sorghum, rice). Rodents (rats, squirrels, cane rats) gnaw stems and eat stored grain and tubers. Others: monkeys, snails and slugs.

Lower yield and lower quality, so the farmer earns less. Higher cost of production (chemicals and labour). Heavy losses in stores (post-harvest losses), leading to food shortage. Total crop failure in bad outbreaks (locust swarms, fall armyworm). Contamination of food with droppings and with poisons made by moulds. Fall armyworm, first found in Nigeria in 2016, has reduced the yields of maize across many states.

units.title: Diseases of Crops
units.summary: Fungal, bacterial and viral crop diseases, their symptoms, how they spread and the causal agent of each.

p: A disease is any change from the normal growth and working of a plant, caused by a pathogen (a germ) or by something in the environment (such as lack of a mineral). Most are caused by fungi, bacteria and viruses.

img.alt: A chart of crop diseases showing symptoms on cocoa pods, maize and cassava leaves
img.cap: Some crop diseases and their symptoms.

p: Fungi are the most common cause of plant disease. They spread by spores carried by wind, water splash, insects and soil.

Black pod of cocoa: black patches rot the pods and the beans. Maize smut: large black swellings (galls) full of powdery spores on the cobs, tassels or stalks. Rusts: orange, red or brown powdery spots on leaves (maize rust). Mildews: white, powdery or downy growth on leaf surfaces. Others: anthracnose and leaf spots on many crops.

Spread by splashes of rain, by tools, by insects and by infected planting material. Examples: Cassava bacterial blight (angular leaf spots, wilting and dying back of shoots); citrus canker (raised corky spots on fruits, leaves and stems); bacterial wilt of tomato and pepper.

Viruses are carried by vectors, mainly sap-sucking insects such as aphids and whiteflies, and by cuttings taken from sick plants. Examples: Cassava mosaic disease (yellow and green mosaic on leaves, small twisted leaves and a big loss of yield); Maize streak virus (yellow streaks along the veins, stunted plants; carried by leafhoppers); groundnut rosette (carried by aphids); cocoa swollen shoot (carried by mealybugs).
Viruses cannot be cured with sprays. We can only prevent them, by killing the vectors, removing sick plants and planting resistant varieties.
Maize smut: fungus. Citrus canker: bacterium. Cassava mosaic disease: virus. Black pod: fungus (Phytophthora, an oomycete often grouped with fungi). Cassava bacterial blight: bacterium.

Reduced yield and quality; money lost on chemicals; failure of whole crops in an epidemic; and mycotoxins (poisons made by some fungi, such as aflatoxin in groundnuts and maize) that can harm people and animals.

units.title: Control of Pests and Diseases
units.summary: Cultural, biological, chemical, physical, legal and genetic control, and the idea of integrated pest management.

p: There is no single best way. Farmers combine several, which is called integrated pest management (IPM).

img.alt: A diagram of integrated pest management with cultural, biological, chemical and physical control around a crop
img.cap: Integrated pest management.

p: Cultural control (changing the way we farm): crop rotation (pests of one crop starve when another is planted); field sanitation (removing and destroying crop remains and weeds that hide pests; burying or composting is better than burning, because open burning pollutes the air); using clean seeds and healthy planting materials; correct spacing for air flow, which lowers the humidity that fungi like; early or late planting to avoid the pest peak; clean weeding.

Biological control (using natural enemies): ladybirds eat aphids; the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) kills certain caterpillars but is harmless to people; parasitic wasps lay eggs in pests; encouraging insect-eating birds. It is safe and long-lasting, but slow and works only for some pests.

Chemical control (pesticides): insecticides for insects, fungicides for fungi, nematicides for nematodes, rodenticides for rodents, herbicides for weeds. It is fast and effective, but it is expensive, can pollute soil and water, can kill useful insects such as bees, and pests can become resistant. Always follow the label, wear protective clothing and keep chemicals away from children and food.
Physical or mechanical control: hand-picking caterpillars; traps (light, sticky and pheromone traps); nets and scarecrows against birds; drying and proper storage of grain; flooding or heating soil.
Legal (quarantine) control: laws and inspection at borders to stop foreign pests and diseases from being brought in on seeds and plants.
Genetic control (plant breeding): breeding resistant varieties, such as cassava resistant to mosaic disease (the TME varieties) and insect-resistant cowpea.

Biological: advantage, safe for the environment and long-lasting; disadvantage, slow and may not completely remove the pest. Chemical: advantage, fast and effective; disadvantage, harmful to the environment and non-target organisms, and pests may become resistant.

units.title: Reproduction in Vertebrates: Fertilisation and the Mammalian System
units.summary: Gonads, gametes, external and internal fertilisation, and the male and female reproductive organs of a mammal.

p: Reproduction produces new individuals. In vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals) it is mostly sexual: a male gamete (sperm) joins with a female gamete (egg or ovum) to make a zygote. The gonads are the main sex organs that make the gametes: testes in males and ovaries in females.

External fertilisation takes place outside the female's body, usually in water (most fish and amphibians). The female lays eggs and the male sheds sperm over them. Internal fertilisation takes place inside the female's body (reptiles, birds and mammals). Fewer eggs are needed because more of them are fertilised and protected.

sections.h: The male system of a mammal
p: Testes (2): make sperm and the hormone testosterone. They hang in the scrotum, where the temperature is about 2 to 3 °C lower than the body, which sperm need. Epididymis: a coiled tube where sperm mature and are stored. Vas deferens (sperm duct): carries sperm to the urethra. Glands (seminal vesicles, prostate gland): add fluids that feed and carry the sperm; sperm plus the fluid is semen. Urethra: carries both semen and urine (never at the same time). Penis: places sperm inside the female.

img.alt: Side by side diagrams of the male and female mammalian reproductive systems with the organs labelled
img.cap: The reproductive organs of a mammal.

sections.h: The female system of a mammal
p: Ovaries (2): make eggs and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone. Oviduct (Fallopian tube): has a funnel with cilia that catches the egg; fertilisation happens here; the egg is moved to the uterus. Uterus (womb): a muscular organ where the embryo implants and grows into a foetus. Cervix: the neck of the uterus; it opens wide in childbirth. Vagina: the birth canal and the place where sperm are deposited.
The lesson note says the urethra in males has a dual function (urine and semen); that is correct. In females the urethra only carries urine and opens separately from the vagina.

units.title: Comparing Reproduction in Fish, Amphibians, Reptiles, Birds and Mammals
units.summary: A comparison of fertilisation, development and parental care in the five vertebrate classes, the amniotic egg and the trends in evolution.

p: Study the table.
Oviparous means egg-laying with development outside the mother's body. Viviparous means giving birth to live young that developed inside the mother.

head: Class
Fertilisation
Development
Key features and parental care
rows: Very many small eggs; usually no parental care, so many young die
External, in water or damp places
Tadpole (larva) changes into adult by metamorphosis; little or no parental care
Amniotic egg with membranes (amnion, chorion, allantois, yolk sac); no larva; usually little care

p: The amniotic egg is a 'private pond' for the embryo. A shell protects it; the amnion holds a watery liquid that cushions it; the yolk sac is food; the allantois stores waste and helps with gas exchange; the chorion lets oxygen in. It lets reptiles and birds lay eggs on dry land, so they no longer need water to breed. This was a major step in evolution.

img.alt: A cutaway of a bird's egg showing the embryo, yolk, albumen, amnion, allantois, air space and shell
img.cap: The structure of a bird's egg.

p: 1. Fertilisation changes from external to internal (suits life on land). 2. The egg changes from a soft jelly egg to a shelled amniotic egg, and then to development inside the mother. 3. Fewer eggs or young are produced but each has a better chance of survival. 4. Parental care increases in length and complexity.

Notes and exceptions: some fish (sharks, guppies) have internal fertilisation and even give birth to live young; some snakes and lizards also give birth to live young; and the platypus and echidna are mammals that lay eggs (monotremes). These exceptions show that the table gives the general pattern.

Birds: internal fertilisation; the egg is laid with a hard shell and the chick develops outside, kept warm by the parent; parents feed it. Mammals: internal fertilisation and internal development; the placenta passes food and oxygen from mother to foetus and takes away waste; after birth, the young are fed on milk. Both show a lot of parental care.
